chunks.text: Q: Which of the following is another characteristic of fish? A: They breathe through gills. Fish absorb oxygen dissolved in water using their gills.
chunks.source: Fish absorb oxygen dissolved in water using their gills.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why does a fish die when removed from water? A: Its gills dry up and it cannot get oxygen. Out of water, a fish's gills collapse and dry, so it cannot absorb oxygen and suffocates.
chunks.source: Out of water, a fish's gills collapse and dry, so it cannot absorb oxygen and suffocates.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How is the foot of a climbing bird different from that of a perching bird? A: A climbing bird has two toes facing forward and two backward, while a perching bird has three forward and one backward. Climbing birds (like woodpeckers) grip tree trunks with two toes each way; perching birds grip branches with three toes forward and one back.
chunks.source: Climbing birds (like woodpeckers) grip tree trunks with two toes each way; perching birds grip branches with three toes forward and one back.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How does a skunk protect itself from enemies? A: By spraying a bad-smelling liquid. A skunk sprays a very bad-smelling liquid that drives enemies away.
chunks.source: A skunk sprays a very bad-smelling liquid that drives enemies away.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How does a wasp protect itself from enemies? A: By stinging them. A wasp defends itself by stinging attackers with its sharp sting.
chunks.source: A wasp defends itself by stinging attackers with its sharp sting.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How does a centipede protect itself from enemies? A: By biting with its poisonous claws. A centipede has poisonous front claws which it uses to bite attackers.
chunks.source: A centipede has poisonous front claws which it uses to bite attackers.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How does a porcupine protect itself from enemies? A: With its sharp quills (spines). A porcupine is covered with sharp quills that prick any enemy that touches it.
chunks.source: A porcupine is covered with sharp quills that prick any enemy that touches it.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What are mammals? A: Warm-blooded vertebrates that give birth to live young and suckle them. Mammals are warm-blooded vertebrates with hair; the mothers feed their babies on milk.
chunks.source: Mammals are warm-blooded vertebrates with hair; the mothers feed their babies on milk.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which of the following is a characteristic of mammals? A: They have hair on their bodies. All mammals have hair or fur on their bodies at some stage of life.
chunks.source: All mammals have hair or fur on their bodies at some stage of life.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which of the following is another characteristic of mammals? A: The mothers suckle their young on milk. Female mammals produce milk from mammary glands to feed their babies.
chunks.source: Female mammals produce milk from mammary glands to feed their babies.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which of the following is a group of mammals? A: Pouched mammals. Pouched mammals (marsupials), like the kangaroo, carry their babies in a pouch.
chunks.source: Pouched mammals (marsupials), like the kangaroo, carry their babies in a pouch.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give another group of mammals. A: Egg-laying mammals. Egg-laying mammals (monotremes), like the duckbilled platypus, lay eggs but still suckle their young.
chunks.source: Egg-laying mammals (monotremes), like the duckbilled platypus, lay eggs but still suckle their young.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: The table shows groups: A (Birds), B (Mammals), C (Amphibians). To which group does a bat belong? A: B (Mammals). A bat is a mammal because it gives birth to live young and suckles them, even though it flies.
chunks.source: A bat is a mammal because it gives birth to live young and suckles them, even though it flies.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: To which group does a frog belong? A: C (Amphibians). A frog lives part of its life in water and part on land, so it is an amphibian.
chunks.source: A frog lives part of its life in water and part on land, so it is an amphibian.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give any one way in which the reproduction of animals in B (mammals) is different from that of animals in C (amphibians). A: Mammals give birth to live young while amphibians lay eggs in water. Most mammals give birth to live babies, while amphibians lay soft eggs in water.
chunks.source: Most mammals give birth to live babies, while amphibians lay soft eggs in water.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: The table shows birds, mammals and amphibians. Give one other group of vertebrates missing from the table. A: Reptiles. Reptiles (like snakes and lizards) are vertebrates missing from the table; fish are also missing. Insects, worms and spiders are invertebrates.
chunks.source: Reptiles (like snakes and lizards) are vertebrates missing from the table; fish are also missing. Insects, worms and spiders are invertebrates.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How are bats different from hens in their way of reproduction? A: Bats give birth to live young while hens lay eggs. Bats are mammals that give birth to live young; hens are birds that lay eggs.
chunks.source: Bats are mammals that give birth to live young; hens are birds that lay eggs.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How is a layer of blubber (fats) important to sea mammals? A: It keeps them warm in cold water. Blubber is a thick layer of fat under the skin that insulates sea mammals like whales against the cold.
chunks.source: Blubber is a thick layer of fat under the skin that insulates sea mammals like whales against the cold.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give one example of a pouched mammal. A: Kangaroo. The kangaroo is a pouched mammal (marsupial) that carries its baby in a pouch.
chunks.source: The kangaroo is a pouched mammal (marsupial) that carries its baby in a pouch.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give one example of an egg-laying mammal. A: Duckbilled platypus. The duckbilled platypus lays eggs but suckles its young, so it is a mammal.
chunks.source: The duckbilled platypus lays eggs but suckles its young, so it is a mammal.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What are cold blooded animals? A: Animals whose body temperature changes with the surroundings. Cold-blooded animals cannot keep a constant body temperature; they warm up or cool down with their surroundings.
chunks.source: Cold-blooded animals cannot keep a constant body temperature; they warm up or cool down with their surroundings.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give one group of cold-blooded vertebrates. A: Fish. Fish are cold-blooded vertebrates; birds and mammals are warm blooded.
chunks.source: Fish are cold-blooded vertebrates; birds and mammals are warm blooded.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give another group of cold-blooded vertebrates. A: Reptiles. Reptiles like snakes and lizards are cold blooded - they bask in the sun to warm up.
chunks.source: Reptiles like snakes and lizards are cold blooded - they bask in the sun to warm up.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name the cold-blooded vertebrate with a shell. A: Tortoise. The tortoise is a cold-blooded reptile with a hard shell. (The snail also has a shell but it is an invertebrate.)
chunks.source: The tortoise is a cold-blooded reptile with a hard shell. (The snail also has a shell but it is an invertebrate.)

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: The diagram shows an animal. To which group of animals does it belong? A: Mammals. The animal is a rat, which is a mammal - it has hair and gives birth to live young.
chunks.source: The animal is a rat, which is a mammal - it has hair and gives birth to live young.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Apart from destroying people's property, how else is the rat dangerous in our houses? A: It spreads diseases and contaminates food. Rats spread diseases and spoil stored food with their droppings and urine.
chunks.source: Rats spread diseases and spoil stored food with their droppings and urine.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why is an ostrich unable to fly? A: It is too heavy and has small weak wings. An ostrich is a very large heavy bird with wings too small and weak to lift its body.
chunks.source: An ostrich is a very large heavy bird with wings too small and weak to lift its body.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Apart from an ostrich, name one other flightless bird. A: Penguin. The penguin is a flightless bird - its wings have become flippers for swimming.
chunks.source: The penguin is a flightless bird - its wings have become flippers for swimming.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name another flightless bird. A: Emu. The emu is a large flightless bird like the ostrich. The kiwi is another example.
chunks.source: The emu is a large flightless bird like the ostrich. The kiwi is another example.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name one scavenger in the environment. A: Vulture. A vulture is a scavenger - it feeds on dead animals it did not kill.
chunks.source: A vulture is a scavenger - it feeds on dead animals it did not kill.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name another scavenger in the environment. A: Hyena. Hyenas often scavenge on kills left by other animals. Crows and marabou storks are other scavengers.
chunks.source: Hyenas often scavenge on kills left by other animals. Crows and marabou storks are other scavengers.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: In which way are scavengers useful in the environment? A: They clean the environment by eating dead animals. Scavengers remove carcasses from the environment, keeping it clean and reducing disease.
chunks.source: Scavengers remove carcasses from the environment, keeping it clean and reducing disease.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give the difference between a predator and a scavenger. A: A predator hunts and kills its prey while a scavenger feeds on dead animals. Predators like lions kill their own food; scavengers like vultures eat animals that are already dead.
chunks.source: Predators like lions kill their own food; scavengers like vultures eat animals that are already dead.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How is the fertilization of eggs of amphibians different from those of reptiles? A: Amphibians have external fertilization in water while reptiles have internal fertilization. A female frog lays eggs in water and the male fertilizes them there; reptiles mate and fertilize eggs inside the female's body.
chunks.source: A female frog lays eggs in water and the male fertilizes them there; reptiles mate and fertilize eggs inside the female's body.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State one difference between birds and mammals. A: Birds lay eggs while mammals give birth to live young. Birds reproduce by laying hard-shelled eggs; most mammals give birth to live babies.
chunks.source: Birds reproduce by laying hard-shelled eggs; most mammals give birth to live babies.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State another difference between birds and mammals. A: Birds have feathers while mammals have hair. Feathers are unique to birds; hair or fur is unique to mammals.
chunks.source: Feathers are unique to birds; hair or fur is unique to mammals.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give one similarity between birds and mammals. A: Both are warm blooded. Birds and mammals both maintain a constant warm body temperature.
chunks.source: Birds and mammals both maintain a constant warm body temperature.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give another similarity between birds and mammals. A: Both breathe through lungs. Both birds and mammals are vertebrates that breathe air through lungs.
chunks.source: Both birds and mammals are vertebrates that breathe air through lungs.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: In which one way are fish similar to amphibians? A: Both are cold blooded. Fish and amphibians are both cold-blooded vertebrates.
chunks.source: Fish and amphibians are both cold-blooded vertebrates.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give another way in which fish are similar to amphibians. A: Both lay eggs. Fish and amphibians both reproduce by laying eggs (amphibians lay theirs in water).
chunks.source: Fish and amphibians both reproduce by laying eggs (amphibians lay theirs in water).

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give one difference between fish and amphibians. A: Fish live only in water while amphibians live both in water and on land. Fish spend their whole life in water; amphibians live in water when young and on land as adults.
chunks.source: Fish spend their whole life in water; amphibians live in water when young and on land as adults.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give another difference between fish and amphibians. A: Fish breathe through gills only while adult amphibians breathe through lungs and moist skin. Adult fish use gills all their lives; adult amphibians use lungs on land and moist skin as well.
chunks.source: Adult fish use gills all their lives; adult amphibians use lungs on land and moist skin as well.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How does a fish benefit from its slippery body? A: It moves easily through water and is hard for enemies to catch. Mucus makes the fish slippery, reducing friction in water and making it slide out of a predator's grip.
chunks.source: Mucus makes the fish slippery, reducing friction in water and making it slide out of a predator's grip.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give one example of a wading bird. A: Heron. Herons (and flamingos) wade in shallow water with their long legs to catch fish.
chunks.source: Herons (and flamingos) wade in shallow water with their long legs to catch fish.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give one example of a swimming bird. A: Duck. Ducks have webbed feet for swimming. Herons wade rather than swim.
chunks.source: Ducks have webbed feet for swimming. Herons wade rather than swim.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: The table lists P (Toad, Newt, Frog), Q (Chameleon, Snake, Lizard), R (Cow, Monkey, Rat). Which characteristic is common to all animals in the table? A: They are all vertebrates. Every animal listed has a backbone, so they are all vertebrates.
chunks.source: Every animal listed has a backbone, so they are all vertebrates.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How is the reproduction of animals in list P similar to those in list Q? A: Both lay eggs. Animals in P (amphibians) and Q (reptiles) both reproduce by laying eggs.
chunks.source: Animals in P (amphibians) and Q (reptiles) both reproduce by laying eggs.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which list has warm blooded animals? A: R. List R has the cow, monkey and rat - all mammals, which are warm blooded.
chunks.source: List R has the cow, monkey and rat - all mammals, which are warm blooded.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why do you place a tortoise in list Q? A: Because it is a reptile like the others in Q. A tortoise is a reptile - cold blooded, with scales and laying eggs on land - just like the chameleon, snake and lizard.
chunks.source: A tortoise is a reptile - cold blooded, with scales and laying eggs on land - just like the chameleon, snake and lizard.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Group the animals from the table (Toad, Newt, Frog, Chameleon, Snake, Lizard, Cow, Monkey, Rat) into cold-blooded and warm-blooded animals. A: Cold-blooded: Toad,Newt,Frog,Chameleon,Snake,Lizard; Warm-blooded: Cow,Monkey,Rat. Amphibians and reptiles are cold blooded; mammals (cow, monkey, rat) are warm blooded.
chunks.source: Amphibians and reptiles are cold blooded; mammals (cow, monkey, rat) are warm blooded.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why are eagles referred to as birds of prey? A: Because they hunt and feed on other animals. Eagles are birds of prey because they hunt live animals using their hooked beaks and sharp talons.
chunks.source: Eagles are birds of prey because they hunt live animals using their hooked beaks and sharp talons.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Use the list: monkey, parrot, crocodile, tilapia. In which class of vertebrates does a crocodile belong? A: Reptiles. A crocodile is a reptile - cold blooded, with dry scales, laying eggs on land.
chunks.source: A crocodile is a reptile - cold blooded, with dry scales, laying eggs on land.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name the class of vertebrates which is not represented in the list above. A: Amphibians. The list has a mammal (monkey), bird (parrot), reptile (crocodile) and fish (tilapia) - amphibians are missing.
chunks.source: The list has a mammal (monkey), bird (parrot), reptile (crocodile) and fish (tilapia) - amphibians are missing.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Identify any one animal from the list above which is cold blooded. A: Crocodile. The crocodile (and tilapia) are cold blooded; the monkey and parrot are warm blooded.
chunks.source: The crocodile (and tilapia) are cold blooded; the monkey and parrot are warm blooded.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How is the reproduction of tilapia different from that of a parrot? A: Tilapia lays eggs in water while a parrot lays eggs on land. Tilapia fertilize and hatch their eggs in water; parrots lay hard-shelled eggs in nests on land.
chunks.source: Tilapia fertilize and hatch their eggs in water; parrots lay hard-shelled eggs in nests on land.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: To which group of vertebrates do toads belong? A: Amphibians. Toads are amphibians - they lay eggs in water and live both in water and on land.
chunks.source: Toads are amphibians - they lay eggs in water and live both in water and on land.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State one way in which the jelly round the eggs of toads is important. A: It protects the eggs from enemies. The jelly coating protects the soft eggs from predators and damage.
chunks.source: The jelly coating protects the soft eggs from predators and damage.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State another way in which the jelly round the eggs of toads is important. A: It keeps the eggs moist. The jelly keeps the eggs moist and also sticks them together so they are not easily washed away.
chunks.source: The jelly keeps the eggs moist and also sticks them together so they are not easily washed away.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How is the reproduction of whales different from that of fish? A: Whales give birth to live young while fish lay eggs. Whales are mammals that give birth to live calves; fish reproduce by laying eggs.
chunks.source: Whales are mammals that give birth to live calves; fish reproduce by laying eggs.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: The table shows animals in A (Tilapia, Mosquito, Frog, Dog) and respiratory organs in B (Moist skin, Lungs, Gills, Spiracles). Write against each animal its correct respiratory organ. A: Tilapia: Gills; Mosquito: Spiracles; Frog: Moist skin; Dog: Lungs. Tilapia (fish) uses gills; mosquitoes (insects) use spiracles; frogs use moist skin; dogs use lungs.
chunks.source: Tilapia (fish) uses gills; mosquitoes (insects) use spiracles; frogs use moist skin; dogs use lungs.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: The table shows animals in A (Gecko, Newt, Bat, Kiwi) and groups in B (Mammals, Birds, Reptiles, Amphibians) in the wrong order. Write against each animal its correct class. A: Gecko: Reptiles; Newt: Amphibians; Bat: Mammals; Kiwi: Birds. Geckos are reptiles, newts are amphibians, bats are mammals and kiwis are flightless birds.
chunks.source: Geckos are reptiles, newts are amphibians, bats are mammals and kiwis are flightless birds.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give one reason why toads are classified as amphibians. A: They lay their eggs in water. Like all amphibians, toads lay soft eggs in water where the tadpoles hatch.
chunks.source: Like all amphibians, toads lay soft eggs in water where the tadpoles hatch.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give another reason why toads are classified as amphibians. A: They live both in water and on land. Toads spend part of their lives in water and part on land, the amphibian way of life.
chunks.source: Toads spend part of their lives in water and part on land, the amphibian way of life.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How important are the scales to a reptile? A: They protect the body and prevent water loss. A reptile's dry scales protect it from injury and stop water escaping from its body.
chunks.source: A reptile's dry scales protect it from injury and stop water escaping from its body.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give any one importance of a gecko in a residential house. A: It eats harmful insects like mosquitoes and cockroaches. Geckos feed on mosquitoes, cockroaches and other household insect pests.
chunks.source: Geckos feed on mosquitoes, cockroaches and other household insect pests.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How is a gecko able to move on a ceiling without falling down? A: It has adhesive pads on its feet that grip smooth surfaces. Tiny adhesive pads on a gecko's toes grip smooth surfaces, letting it walk upside down on ceilings.
chunks.source: Tiny adhesive pads on a gecko's toes grip smooth surfaces, letting it walk upside down on ceilings.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give any one reason why birds make nests. A: To lay their eggs and raise their young in safety. Birds build nests as safe places to lay eggs and care for their chicks until they can fly.
chunks.source: Birds build nests as safe places to lay eggs and care for their chicks until they can fly.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name a mammal that lives both on land and in water in Uganda. A: Hippopotamus. The hippopotamus spends days in water and nights grazing on land.
chunks.source: The hippopotamus spends days in water and nights grazing on land.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give one characteristic common to a frog and a crocodile, apart from being vertebrates. A: Both are cold blooded. Frogs (amphibians) and crocodiles (reptiles) are both cold-blooded vertebrates.
chunks.source: Frogs (amphibians) and crocodiles (reptiles) are both cold-blooded vertebrates.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give another characteristic common to a frog and a crocodile. A: Both lay eggs. Both frogs and crocodiles reproduce by laying eggs.
chunks.source: Both frogs and crocodiles reproduce by laying eggs.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How is fertilization of a frog different from that of a crocodile? A: A frog has external fertilization in water while a crocodile has internal fertilization. Frogs release eggs into water where males fertilize them; crocodiles mate and fertilize eggs inside the female.
chunks.source: Frogs release eggs into water where males fertilize them; crocodiles mate and fertilize eggs inside the female.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State the importance of the long and sticky tongue of the chameleon. A: To catch insects from a distance. The chameleon shoots out its long sticky tongue to snatch insects before they escape.
chunks.source: The chameleon shoots out its long sticky tongue to snatch insects before they escape.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give one characteristic of hoofed mammals. A: They have hooves on their feet. Hoofed mammals (ungulates) walk on hard hooves instead of claws.
chunks.source: Hoofed mammals (ungulates) walk on hard hooves instead of claws.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give another characteristic of hoofed mammals. A: They are herbivores (feed on plants). Most hoofed mammals like cows and goats feed on grass and other plants.
chunks.source: Most hoofed mammals like cows and goats feed on grass and other plants.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State any one example of a hoofed mammal. A: Cow. The cow is a hoofed mammal. Dogs, lions and monkeys have claws or nails, not hooves.
chunks.source: The cow is a hoofed mammal. Dogs, lions and monkeys have claws or nails, not hooves.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State one way you can distinguish between a venomous snake and a non-venomous snake. A: A venomous snake has hollow fangs while a non-venomous snake has no fangs. Venomous snakes inject poison through hollow fangs; non-venomous snakes lack fangs.
chunks.source: Venomous snakes inject poison through hollow fangs; non-venomous snakes lack fangs.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give any one example of a venomous snake. A: Puff adder. The puff adder (like cobras and mambas) is venomous; pythons and boas kill by constriction.
chunks.source: The puff adder (like cobras and mambas) is venomous; pythons and boas kill by constriction.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State the importance of a forked tongue to a snake. A: It helps the snake to smell its surroundings. A snake flicks its forked tongue to pick up scent particles and smell prey, enemies and mates.
chunks.source: A snake flicks its forked tongue to pick up scent particles and smell prey, enemies and mates.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State any one economic importance of reptiles to people. A: Their skins are used to make bags, shoes and belts. Crocodile and snake skins are valuable leather for making bags, shoes and belts.
chunks.source: Crocodile and snake skins are valuable leather for making bags, shoes and belts.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How does a gecko help in the control of food contamination in a house? A: It eats cockroaches and flies that contaminate food. By eating cockroaches, flies and other pests, geckos stop them from contaminating food.
chunks.source: By eating cockroaches, flies and other pests, geckos stop them from contaminating food.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Besides protection, how else is changing colour important to a chameleon? A: It helps to attract mates and control body temperature. Chameleons also change colour to attract mates and to absorb or reflect heat to control body temperature.
chunks.source: Chameleons also change colour to attract mates and to absorb or reflect heat to control body temperature.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name any one snake that produces living young ones. A: Puff adder. The puff adder gives birth to live young instead of laying eggs.
chunks.source: The puff adder gives birth to live young instead of laying eggs.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How does a crocodile protect itself from its enemies? A: With its tough scaly skin and powerful jaws and tail. A crocodile's armoured skin shields it, while its strong jaws and tail fight off attackers.
chunks.source: A crocodile's armoured skin shields it, while its strong jaws and tail fight off attackers.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What are omnivorous animals? A: Animals that feed on both plants and flesh. Omnivores, like people and pigs, eat both plant and animal food.
chunks.source: Omnivores, like people and pigs, eat both plant and animal food.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give one example of an omnivorous animal. A: Pig. Pigs eat both plants and animal matter. Cows and goats are herbivores; lions are carnivores.
chunks.source: Pigs eat both plants and animal matter. Cows and goats are herbivores; lions are carnivores.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give another example of an omnivorous animal. A: Man (human being). Human beings eat both plant foods and meat, so they are omnivores.
chunks.source: Human beings eat both plant foods and meat, so they are omnivores.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What does it mean for a rodent to gnaw? A: To bite or chew something persistently. Rodents gnaw - they keep biting and chewing hard things to wear down their ever-growing front teeth.
chunks.source: Rodents gnaw - they keep biting and chewing hard things to wear down their ever-growing front teeth.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give one example of a rodent. A: Rat. The rat is a rodent with sharp gnawing front teeth. (Rabbits are lagomorphs, bats are not rodents.)
chunks.source: The rat is a rodent with sharp gnawing front teeth. (Rabbits are lagomorphs, bats are not rodents.)

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give another example of a rodent. A: Squirrel. Squirrels are rodents. Mice and porcupines are other examples.
chunks.source: Squirrels are rodents. Mice and porcupines are other examples.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Insectivores and bats are nocturnal. What does this mean? A: They are active at night. Nocturnal animals are active at night and rest during the day.
chunks.source: Nocturnal animals are active at night and rest during the day.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What does it mean for a bird to wade? A: To walk in shallow water in search of food. Wading birds like herons walk through shallow water with their long legs looking for fish and frogs.
chunks.source: Wading birds like herons walk through shallow water with their long legs looking for fish and frogs.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How are reptile's hearts different from that of mammals? A: Reptiles have a three-chambered heart while mammals have a four-chambered heart. Most reptiles have three heart chambers (two atria, one partly divided ventricle); mammals have four fully separated chambers.
chunks.source: Most reptiles have three heart chambers (two atria, one partly divided ventricle); mammals have four fully separated chambers.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name the amphibian with a dry and rough skin. A: Toad. The toad is the amphibian with dry, rough, warty skin, unlike the smooth moist skin of frogs.
chunks.source: The toad is the amphibian with dry, rough, warty skin, unlike the smooth moist skin of frogs.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name the group of fish that use a swim bladder for balancing in water. A: Bony fish. Bony fish have a swim bladder filled with gas that helps them float and balance at different depths.
chunks.source: Bony fish have a swim bladder filled with gas that helps them float and balance at different depths.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why do fish have streamlined bodies? A: To reduce resistance so they can swim easily through water. A streamlined (smooth, torpedo) shape lets water flow past easily so the fish swims with little effort.
chunks.source: A streamlined (smooth, torpedo) shape lets water flow past easily so the fish swims with little effort.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: The table shows classes of vertebrates: Fish, Amphibians, Q, Birds, Mammals. Name the class of vertebrates represented by Q. A: Reptiles. The five classes of vertebrates are fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals - so Q is reptiles.
chunks.source: The five classes of vertebrates are fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals - so Q is reptiles.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Apart from having backbones, give one characteristic common to all fish, amphibians and vertebrates in class Q (reptiles). A: They are all cold blooded. Fish, amphibians and reptiles are all cold-blooded vertebrates.
chunks.source: Fish, amphibians and reptiles are all cold-blooded vertebrates.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give one characteristic common to birds and mammals. A: They are warm blooded. Birds and mammals are the two groups of warm-blooded vertebrates.
chunks.source: Birds and mammals are the two groups of warm-blooded vertebrates.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State the difference in reproduction between vertebrates in class Q (reptiles) and the amphibians. A: Reptiles lay eggs on land while amphibians lay eggs in water. Reptiles lay shelled eggs on land with internal fertilization; amphibians lay soft eggs in water with external fertilization.
chunks.source: Reptiles lay shelled eggs on land with internal fertilization; amphibians lay soft eggs in water with external fertilization.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which amphibians lay eggs in water covered with jelly, as shown in the diagrams? A: Frogs. Frogs (and toads) lay their eggs in water in jelly-coated masses or strings.
chunks.source: Frogs (and toads) lay their eggs in water in jelly-coated masses or strings.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How are rodents different from all other mammals? A: They have sharp front teeth for gnawing. Rodents are the only mammals with a pair of ever-growing sharp front teeth used for gnawing.
chunks.source: Rodents are the only mammals with a pair of ever-growing sharp front teeth used for gnawing.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name one mammal considered to be a predator. A: Lion. The lion is a predatory mammal that hunts other animals for food.
chunks.source: The lion is a predatory mammal that hunts other animals for food.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name another mammal considered to be a predator. A: Leopard. The leopard is a predatory mammal. Dogs and cats are other examples.
chunks.source: The leopard is a predatory mammal. Dogs and cats are other examples.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give any one difference between carnivores and herbivores. A: Carnivores feed on flesh while herbivores feed on plants. Carnivores are flesh eaters (like lions) while herbivores are plant eaters (like cows).
chunks.source: Carnivores are flesh eaters (like lions) while herbivores are plant eaters (like cows).

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What are invertebrates? A: Animals without a backbone. Invertebrates are animals that do not have a backbone, like insects and worms.
chunks.source: Invertebrates are animals that do not have a backbone, like insects and worms.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Mention one class of invertebrates. A: Insects. Insects are a class of invertebrates (arthropods) with six legs and no backbone.
chunks.source: Insects are a class of invertebrates (arthropods) with six legs and no backbone.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Mention another class of invertebrates. A: Arachnids. Arachnids (spiders, scorpions) are a class of invertebrates with eight legs.
chunks.source: Arachnids (spiders, scorpions) are a class of invertebrates with eight legs.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give any one characteristic of invertebrates. A: They have no backbone. The main characteristic of invertebrates is the absence of a backbone.
chunks.source: The main characteristic of invertebrates is the absence of a backbone.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What type of skeleton do worms have? A: Hydrostatic skeleton. Worms have a hydrostatic skeleton - fluid pressure in their bodies supports them.
chunks.source: Worms have a hydrostatic skeleton - fluid pressure in their bodies supports them.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give one example of an echinoderm. A: Starfish. The starfish is an echinoderm - a spiny-skinned sea animal without a backbone.
chunks.source: The starfish is an echinoderm - a spiny-skinned sea animal without a backbone.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give one example of a coelenterate. A: Jellyfish. The jellyfish (and hydra) is a coelenterate - a simple water animal with stinging tentacles.
chunks.source: The jellyfish (and hydra) is a coelenterate - a simple water animal with stinging tentacles.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How do earthworms carry out gaseous exchange? A: Through their moist skins. Earthworms absorb oxygen directly through their moist body surface.
chunks.source: Earthworms absorb oxygen directly through their moist body surface.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How do tapeworms reproduce? A: By producing eggs in their segments. A tapeworm's body segments produce eggs which pass out with the host's faeces.
chunks.source: A tapeworm's body segments produce eggs which pass out with the host's faeces.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give one example of a round worm. A: Ascaris. Ascaris is a round worm that lives in people's intestines. Hookworms are other round worms.
chunks.source: Ascaris is a round worm that lives in people's intestines. Hookworms are other round worms.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give another example of a round worm. A: Hookworm. Hookworms are round worms that enter through the skin of bare feet and live in the intestines.
chunks.source: Hookworms are round worms that enter through the skin of bare feet and live in the intestines.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Apart from earthworms, name any other example of a segmented worm. A: Leech. The leech is a segmented worm like the earthworm; it sucks blood.
chunks.source: The leech is a segmented worm like the earthworm; it sucks blood.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why do earthworms move out of the ground after it has rained? A: Because their burrows fill with water and they would drown. Rain fills the soil tunnels with water, so earthworms come to the surface to avoid drowning.
chunks.source: Rain fills the soil tunnels with water, so earthworms come to the surface to avoid drowning.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How do earthworms help in aeration of soil? A: By burrowing tunnels that let air into the soil. As earthworms burrow, they open tunnels through which air enters the soil.
chunks.source: As earthworms burrow, they open tunnels through which air enters the soil.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Apart from soil aeration, how else are earthworms important in the soil? A: Their droppings add fertility (manure) to the soil. Earthworm droppings (casts) enrich the soil, making it more fertile for plants.
chunks.source: Earthworm droppings (casts) enrich the soil, making it more fertile for plants.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give any one example of a flatworm. A: Tapeworm. The tapeworm is a flatworm with a flat ribbon-like body. The liver fluke is another example.
chunks.source: The tapeworm is a flatworm with a flat ribbon-like body. The liver fluke is another example.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How do tapeworms enter our bodies? A: By eating undercooked meat containing tapeworm cysts. Tapeworm cysts in raw or poorly cooked meat hatch into worms in the intestines.
chunks.source: Tapeworm cysts in raw or poorly cooked meat hatch into worms in the intestines.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How do hookworms enter our bodies? A: By penetrating the skin of bare feet. Hookworm larvae in contaminated soil bore through the skin, especially of people walking barefoot.
chunks.source: Hookworm larvae in contaminated soil bore through the skin, especially of people walking barefoot.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How do tapeworms obtain food from our bodies? A: By absorbing digested food through their body surface. Tapeworms have no mouth; they absorb the host's digested food through their skin in the intestines.
chunks.source: Tapeworms have no mouth; they absorb the host's digested food through their skin in the intestines.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How do hookworms obtain food from our bodies? A: By sucking blood from the walls of the intestines. Hookworms attach to the intestinal wall and suck the host's blood, causing anaemia.
chunks.source: Hookworms attach to the intestinal wall and suck the host's blood, causing anaemia.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What does the word mollusc mean? A: A soft-bodied animal, usually with a shell. Molluscs are soft-bodied invertebrates like snails, oysters and octopuses, many with shells.
chunks.source: Molluscs are soft-bodied invertebrates like snails, oysters and octopuses, many with shells.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give one characteristic of molluscs. A: They have soft bodies. Molluscs have soft unsegmented bodies, unlike arthropods with jointed legs.
chunks.source: Molluscs have soft unsegmented bodies, unlike arthropods with jointed legs.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give another characteristic of molluscs. A: Most of them have shells. Most molluscs, like snails and oysters, protect their soft bodies with hard shells.
chunks.source: Most molluscs, like snails and oysters, protect their soft bodies with hard shells.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How do molluscs reproduce? A: By laying eggs. Molluscs reproduce by laying eggs.
chunks.source: Molluscs reproduce by laying eggs.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How are molluscs different from all other invertebrates? A: They have soft unsegmented bodies, many covered with shells. Unlike worms (segmented) or arthropods (jointed legs), molluscs have soft unsegmented bodies, usually with shells.
chunks.source: Unlike worms (segmented) or arthropods (jointed legs), molluscs have soft unsegmented bodies, usually with shells.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Apart from a snail, mention one other example of a mollusc. A: Oyster. The oyster is a mollusc with a hard shell. Mussels, slugs, squids and octopuses are others.
chunks.source: The oyster is a mollusc with a hard shell. Mussels, slugs, squids and octopuses are others.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Mention another example of a mollusc. A: Mussel. Mussels are shellfish and molluscs like oysters and snails.
chunks.source: Mussels are shellfish and molluscs like oysters and snails.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How dangerous are fresh water snails to humans? A: They spread bilharzia (schistosomiasis). Fresh water snails carry the worms that cause bilharzia, which enter through the skin in infested water.
chunks.source: Fresh water snails carry the worms that cause bilharzia, which enter through the skin in infested water.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What are arthropods? A: Invertebrates with jointed legs and an exoskeleton. Arthropods are the largest group of invertebrates - insects, spiders and crabs - with jointed legs and hard outer skeletons.
chunks.source: Arthropods are the largest group of invertebrates - insects, spiders and crabs - with jointed legs and hard outer skeletons.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Mention one characteristic of arthropods. A: They have jointed legs. All arthropods have jointed legs, which is what their name means.
chunks.source: All arthropods have jointed legs, which is what their name means.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Mention another characteristic of arthropods. A: They have an exoskeleton. Arthropods have a hard outer covering (exoskeleton) that protects their bodies.
chunks.source: Arthropods have a hard outer covering (exoskeleton) that protects their bodies.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Mention one class of arthropods. A: Insects. Insects are the largest class of arthropods.
chunks.source: Insects are the largest class of arthropods.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Mention another class of arthropods. A: Crustaceans. Crustaceans (crabs, lobsters) are a class of arthropods. Arachnids and myriapods are others.
chunks.source: Crustaceans (crabs, lobsters) are a class of arthropods. Arachnids and myriapods are others.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What type of skeleton do arthropods have? A: Exoskeleton. Arthropods have an exoskeleton - a hard skeleton on the outside of the body.
chunks.source: Arthropods have an exoskeleton - a hard skeleton on the outside of the body.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How important is moulting in arthropods? A: It allows them to grow by shedding the rigid exoskeleton. Because the exoskeleton cannot stretch, arthropods must shed (moult) it to grow a bigger one.
chunks.source: Because the exoskeleton cannot stretch, arthropods must shed (moult) it to grow a bigger one.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give any one example of a myriapod. A: Millipede. Millipedes (and centipedes) are myriapods - arthropods with many legs.
chunks.source: Millipedes (and centipedes) are myriapods - arthropods with many legs.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How is the feeding of millipedes different from that of centipedes? A: Millipedes feed on decaying plants while centipedes feed on small animals. Millipedes are decomposers eating dead plant matter; centipedes are carnivores hunting small animals.
chunks.source: Millipedes are decomposers eating dead plant matter; centipedes are carnivores hunting small animals.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State one main difference between arachnids and insects. A: Arachnids have eight legs while insects have six legs. Spiders and other arachnids have 8 legs; insects have 6 legs.
chunks.source: Spiders and other arachnids have 8 legs; insects have 6 legs.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State another main difference between arachnids and insects. A: Arachnids have two body parts while insects have three body parts. An arachnid's body has two main parts; an insect's body has three (head, thorax, abdomen).
chunks.source: An arachnid's body has two main parts; an insect's body has three (head, thorax, abdomen).

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give one example of an arachnid. A: Spider. Spiders are arachnids with eight legs. Flies, bees and mosquitoes are insects.
chunks.source: Spiders are arachnids with eight legs. Flies, bees and mosquitoes are insects.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give another example of an arachnid. A: Scorpion. Scorpions (and ticks and mites) are arachnids.
chunks.source: Scorpions (and ticks and mites) are arachnids.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: The diagram is of an amoeba. What kind of organism is an amoeba? A: A single-celled (unicellular) organism. An amoeba is a tiny organism made of only one cell; it lives in water and soil.
chunks.source: An amoeba is a tiny organism made of only one cell; it lives in water and soil.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name the structure of the amoeba labelled O. A: Nucleus. Structure O is the nucleus, which controls all activities of the amoeba's cell.
chunks.source: Structure O is the nucleus, which controls all activities of the amoeba's cell.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name the structure of the amoeba labelled P. A: Pseudopod (false foot). Structure P is a pseudopod (false foot), a temporary projection of the cell.
chunks.source: Structure P is a pseudopod (false foot), a temporary projection of the cell.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How is an amoeba able to move from one place to another? A: By using pseudopods (false feet). The amoeba pushes out pseudopods and flows into them, dragging itself along.
chunks.source: The amoeba pushes out pseudopods and flows into them, dragging itself along.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How does a millipede protect itself from enemies? A: By curling into a tight ball. When attacked, a millipede curls into a hard ball so its soft underside is hidden (some also release a bad smell).
chunks.source: When attacked, a millipede curls into a hard ball so its soft underside is hidden (some also release a bad smell).

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State any one way in which spiders are different from insects. A: Spiders have eight legs while insects have six legs. Spiders are arachnids with 8 legs and 2 body parts; insects have 6 legs and 3 body parts.
chunks.source: Spiders are arachnids with 8 legs and 2 body parts; insects have 6 legs and 3 body parts.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give any one way in which a spider is similar to a cockroach. A: Both are arthropods with exoskeletons and jointed legs. Spiders and cockroaches are both arthropods - they have exoskeletons and jointed legs.
chunks.source: Spiders and cockroaches are both arthropods - they have exoskeletons and jointed legs.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: To which group of invertebrates does a snail belong? A: Molluscs. A snail is a mollusc - a soft-bodied animal with a shell.
chunks.source: A snail is a mollusc - a soft-bodied animal with a shell.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: To which group of invertebrates does a grasshopper belong? A: Insects (arthropods). A grasshopper is an insect - an arthropod with six legs.
chunks.source: A grasshopper is an insect - an arthropod with six legs.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: The diagrams show animals in the arthropod group: X (crab), Y (spider), Z (housefly). Name the group of arthropods to which each animal belongs. A: X (crab): Crustaceans; Y (spider): Arachnids; Z (housefly): Insects. Crabs are crustaceans, spiders are arachnids and houseflies are insects.
chunks.source: Crabs are crustaceans, spiders are arachnids and houseflies are insects.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give one reason why animal Y (spider) does not belong to the same group as animal Z (housefly). A: The spider has eight legs and two body parts while the housefly has six legs and three body parts. Spiders are arachnids (8 legs, 2 body parts) while houseflies are insects (6 legs, 3 body parts).
chunks.source: Spiders are arachnids (8 legs, 2 body parts) while houseflies are insects (6 legs, 3 body parts).

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How are animals X, Y and Z similar in the way they reproduce? A: They all lay eggs. Crabs, spiders and houseflies are all arthropods that reproduce by laying eggs.
chunks.source: Crabs, spiders and houseflies are all arthropods that reproduce by laying eggs.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give any one characteristic of crustaceans. A: They have a hard shell (exoskeleton). Crustaceans like crabs have a hard outer shell protecting their bodies.
chunks.source: Crustaceans like crabs have a hard outer shell protecting their bodies.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give one example of a crustacean. A: Crab. The crab is a crustacean. Prawns, lobsters and shrimps are other examples.
chunks.source: The crab is a crustacean. Prawns, lobsters and shrimps are other examples.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give another example of a crustacean. A: Lobster. Lobsters (and prawns and shrimps) are crustaceans.
chunks.source: Lobsters (and prawns and shrimps) are crustaceans.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name the breathing organs of crustaceans. A: Gills. Crustaceans live in water and breathe through gills like fish.
chunks.source: Crustaceans live in water and breathe through gills like fish.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give one characteristic of arachnids. A: They have eight legs. Arachnids like spiders and scorpions have eight legs.
chunks.source: Arachnids like spiders and scorpions have eight legs.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give another characteristic of arachnids. A: They have two main body parts. An arachnid's body is divided into two main parts (cephalothorax and abdomen).
chunks.source: An arachnid's body is divided into two main parts (cephalothorax and abdomen).

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How is the reproduction of scorpions different from that of other arthropods? A: Scorpions give birth to live young while most other arthropods lay eggs. Unlike most arthropods, scorpions give birth to live babies which ride on the mother's back.
chunks.source: Unlike most arthropods, scorpions give birth to live babies which ride on the mother's back.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: The diagram shows a tapeworm. Name the part marked A. A: Head (scolex). Part A is the head (scolex) of the tapeworm, which has hooks and suckers for gripping the intestines.
chunks.source: Part A is the head (scolex) of the tapeworm, which has hooks and suckers for gripping the intestines.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How is part B useful to a tapeworm? A: The suckers grip the intestinal wall so the worm is not swept away. Part B shows the suckers (and hooks) on the head that anchor the tapeworm to the host's intestines.
chunks.source: Part B shows the suckers (and hooks) on the head that anchor the tapeworm to the host's intestines.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: The diagram shows an insect. Name the part marked C. A: Abdomen. Part C is the abdomen, the rear part of the insect's body where the spiracles are found.
chunks.source: Part C is the abdomen, the rear part of the insect's body where the spiracles are found.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name the part marked D. A: Head. Part D is the head, which bears the eyes, antennae and mouthparts.
chunks.source: Part D is the head, which bears the eyes, antennae and mouthparts.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State the function of the part marked D (head). A: It bears the eyes, antennae and mouthparts for seeing, smelling and feeding. The head carries the sense organs and mouthparts the insect uses to find and eat food.
chunks.source: The head carries the sense organs and mouthparts the insect uses to find and eat food.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why would the insect die when the whole of the abdomen is dipped in oil? A: The oil blocks the spiracles, so the insect cannot breathe. Insects breathe through spiracles on the abdomen; oil seals them and the insect suffocates.
chunks.source: Insects breathe through spiracles on the abdomen; oil seals them and the insect suffocates.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: The table shows classification of plants. Name the group of plants shown by letter A. A: Flowering plants. Letter A represents flowering plants, which are divided into monocotyledonous and dicotyledonous plants.
chunks.source: Letter A represents flowering plants, which are divided into monocotyledonous and dicotyledonous plants.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name the group of plants shown by letter B. A: Non-flowering plants. Letter B represents non-flowering plants, which include spore-bearing plants and conifers.
chunks.source: Letter B represents non-flowering plants, which include spore-bearing plants and conifers.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name the group of plants shown by letter C. A: Spore-bearing plants. Letter C represents the spore-bearing non-flowering plants like mosses, ferns and liverworts.
chunks.source: Letter C represents the spore-bearing non-flowering plants like mosses, ferns and liverworts.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give any one example of a spore producing plant. A: Fern. Ferns (and mosses and liverworts) reproduce by spores, not seeds.
chunks.source: Ferns (and mosses and liverworts) reproduce by spores, not seeds.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which component of soil is used by plants to make their food? A: Mineral salts. Plants absorb mineral salts (dissolved in water) from the soil to help make food during photosynthesis.
chunks.source: Plants absorb mineral salts (dissolved in water) from the soil to help make food during photosynthesis.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How is the propagation of irish potatoes different from that of sweet potatoes? A: Irish potatoes are grown from tubers while sweet potatoes are grown from vine cuttings. Irish potatoes are planted as tubers; sweet potatoes are planted as vine (stem) cuttings.
chunks.source: Irish potatoes are planted as tubers; sweet potatoes are planted as vine (stem) cuttings.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Apart from lack of conditions necessary for germination, give one other factor that can make a seed fail to germinate. A: The seed is not viable (the embryo is dead). A seed with a dead embryo cannot germinate however good the conditions are.
chunks.source: A seed with a dead embryo cannot germinate however good the conditions are.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give another factor that can make a seed fail to germinate. A: The seed is dormant. Some seeds are dormant - they need a resting period or special treatment before they can germinate.
chunks.source: Some seeds are dormant - they need a resting period or special treatment before they can germinate.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: The diagram is of a maize grain. Name the part marked B. A: Embryo. Part B is the embryo - the young plant inside the grain that grows during germination.
chunks.source: Part B is the embryo - the young plant inside the grain that grows during germination.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How is the part marked C useful to the grain? A: The seed coat protects the inside of the grain. Part C is the seed coat (testa), which protects the embryo and stored food from damage.
chunks.source: Part C is the seed coat (testa), which protects the embryo and stored food from damage.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State the importance of the part marked A. A: The endosperm stores food used by the embryo during germination. Part A is the endosperm, the food store that feeds the growing embryo until it can make its own food.
chunks.source: Part A is the endosperm, the food store that feeds the growing embryo until it can make its own food.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which part of a grain is not important during germination? A: The seed coat (it is shed). The seed coat only protects the grain; once germination starts it splits and is discarded.
chunks.source: The seed coat only protects the grain; once germination starts it splits and is discarded.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Apart from mosses, give one other example of a spore bearing non-flowering plant. A: Fern. Ferns are spore-bearing non-flowering plants like mosses. (Pines are conifers with seeds.)
chunks.source: Ferns are spore-bearing non-flowering plants like mosses. (Pines are conifers with seeds.)

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why does a farmer cut off the leaves of a banana sucker before planting it? A: To reduce water loss through transpiration. Cutting the leaves reduces the surface for transpiration, so the sucker does not dry out before its roots develop.
chunks.source: Cutting the leaves reduces the surface for transpiration, so the sucker does not dry out before its roots develop.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: In the diagram, Q, R and S show stages of germination of a seed. Name the part marked X. A: Cotyledon. Part X is the cotyledon (seed leaf), which stores food for the young seedling.
chunks.source: Part X is the cotyledon (seed leaf), which stores food for the young seedling.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How is the part marked X useful to the seedling at stage R? A: It supplies stored food to the growing seedling. At stage R the cotyledon releases its stored food to feed the growing radicle and plumule.
chunks.source: At stage R the cotyledon releases its stored food to feed the growing radicle and plumule.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why is the part marked X useless at stage S? A: Because its stored food has all been used up. By stage S the seedling has leaves and makes its own food, and the cotyledon's store is finished.
chunks.source: By stage S the seedling has leaves and makes its own food, and the cotyledon's store is finished.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What type of germination is shown by the diagram? A: Epigeal germination. The cotyledons are carried above the ground, which is epigeal germination (as in beans).
chunks.source: The cotyledons are carried above the ground, which is epigeal germination (as in beans).

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: The diagrams Q, R and S show stages of germination. Arrange them in the order in which they occur. A: Q, R, S. Germination starts with the seed (Q), then the radicle and plumule emerge (R), then the seedling grows leaves (S).
chunks.source: Germination starts with the seed (Q), then the radicle and plumule emerge (R), then the seedling grows leaves (S).

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What name is given to a place where seedlings are grown before transplanting? A: Nursery bed. A nursery bed is a prepared place where young seedlings are raised before being transplanted.
chunks.source: A nursery bed is a prepared place where young seedlings are raised before being transplanted.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: A root system with many thin roots of about the same size growing from the base of the stem is called a ____ root system. A: fibrous. In a fibrous root system, many slender roots of similar size spread from the stem base, as in maize and grasses.
chunks.source: In a fibrous root system, many slender roots of similar size spread from the stem base, as in maize and grasses.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: The diagram shows a germinating seed. What type of germination is shown in the diagram? A: Hypogeal germination. The cotyledons remain below the soil surface, which is hypogeal germination (as in maize).
chunks.source: The cotyledons remain below the soil surface, which is hypogeal germination (as in maize).

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: To which group of flowering plants does the germinating seed belong? A: Monocotyledonous plants. The seed shows hypogeal germination with one cotyledon, typical of monocots like maize.
chunks.source: The seed shows hypogeal germination with one cotyledon, typical of monocots like maize.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name one type of pollination in flowering plants. A: Self-pollination. In self-pollination, pollen moves from the anther to the stigma of the same flower.
chunks.source: In self-pollination, pollen moves from the anther to the stigma of the same flower.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name another type of pollination in flowering plants. A: Cross-pollination. In cross-pollination, pollen moves from one flower to the stigma of another flower.
chunks.source: In cross-pollination, pollen moves from one flower to the stigma of another flower.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Write down one agent of pollination. A: Wind. Wind carries pollen from flower to flower, especially in grasses and maize.
chunks.source: Wind carries pollen from flower to flower, especially in grasses and maize.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Write down another agent of pollination. A: Insects. Insects like bees carry pollen as they visit flowers for nectar.
chunks.source: Insects like bees carry pollen as they visit flowers for nectar.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State any one characteristic of seeds which are dispersed by water. A: They are light and can float on water. Water-dispersed seeds, like the coconut, are light with fibrous husks so they float.
chunks.source: Water-dispersed seeds, like the coconut, are light with fibrous husks so they float.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How do conifers differ from other non-flowering plants? A: Conifers produce seeds in cones while other non-flowering plants reproduce by spores. Conifers (like pines) are non-flowering but make naked seeds in cones; ferns and mosses reproduce by spores.
chunks.source: Conifers (like pines) are non-flowering but make naked seeds in cones; ferns and mosses reproduce by spores.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is the importance of water during seed germination? A: It softens the seed coat and activates the embryo. Water soaks into the seed, softening the testa and starting the chemical processes of germination.
chunks.source: Water soaks into the seed, softening the testa and starting the chemical processes of germination.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is the importance of oxygen during seed germination? A: It is used to release energy from stored food. The germinating seed respires, using oxygen to release energy from stored food for growth.
chunks.source: The germinating seed respires, using oxygen to release energy from stored food for growth.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: The diagram is of a flower. Name the part marked A. A: Sepal. Part A is a sepal - the small leaf-like structure at the base that protects the flower bud.
chunks.source: Part A is a sepal - the small leaf-like structure at the base that protects the flower bud.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: On the diagram of the flower, the part that produces the male reproductive cells is the ____. (Mark it with letter P.) A: anther. The anther produces pollen grains, which are the male reproductive cells of the flower.
chunks.source: The anther produces pollen grains, which are the male reproductive cells of the flower.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: The diagram shows a germinating seed. State the type of germination shown. A: Epigeal germination. The cotyledons are pushed above the soil, which is epigeal germination (as in beans).
chunks.source: The cotyledons are pushed above the soil, which is epigeal germination (as in beans).

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Where does the seed above store food used during germination? A: In the cotyledons. The fleshy cotyledons store the food the seedling uses before it can photosynthesize.
chunks.source: The fleshy cotyledons store the food the seedling uses before it can photosynthesize.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give an example of a crop with the same type of germination. A: Beans. Beans show epigeal germination like the seed in the diagram; maize shows hypogeal.
chunks.source: Beans show epigeal germination like the seed in the diagram; maize shows hypogeal.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Apart from moisture, state any other condition necessary for seed germination. A: Warmth. Seeds also need warmth (suitable temperature) and oxygen to germinate.
chunks.source: Seeds also need warmth (suitable temperature) and oxygen to germinate.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name one type of seed dispersal. A: Dispersal by wind. Seeds can be dispersed by wind, water or animals.
chunks.source: Seeds can be dispersed by wind, water or animals.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State any one way in which seed dispersal is important in the environment. A: It reduces competition for light, water and nutrients among seedlings. Dispersal spreads seeds away from the parent plant so seedlings do not compete for the same resources.
chunks.source: Dispersal spreads seeds away from the parent plant so seedlings do not compete for the same resources.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give any one example of a plant with prop roots. A: Maize. Maize (and sugarcane) grows prop roots from the lower stem for extra support.
chunks.source: Maize (and sugarcane) grows prop roots from the lower stem for extra support.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Apart from absorption of water and mineral salts, state one other use of roots to a cassava plant. A: The roots store food (the cassava tuber). Cassava's swollen roots store starch, which is the tuber people eat.
chunks.source: Cassava's swollen roots store starch, which is the tuber people eat.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give the function of a micropyle to a germinating seed. A: It allows water and air to enter the seed. The micropyle is a tiny hole in the seed coat through which water and air enter during germination.
chunks.source: The micropyle is a tiny hole in the seed coat through which water and air enter during germination.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How is the reproduction in beans different from that in ferns? A: Beans reproduce by seeds while ferns reproduce by spores. Beans are flowering plants that make seeds; ferns are non-flowering and make spores.
chunks.source: Beans are flowering plants that make seeds; ferns are non-flowering and make spores.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: The diagram is of an irish potato tuber. What is the use of the part marked S? A: It is a bud (eye) that grows into a new plant. Part S is the eye (bud) of the tuber; each eye can sprout into a new potato plant.
chunks.source: Part S is the eye (bud) of the tuber; each eye can sprout into a new potato plant.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name the part of a flower that holds the anther head. A: Filament. The filament is the stalk that holds up the anther so it can release pollen.
chunks.source: The filament is the stalk that holds up the anther so it can release pollen.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: The diagram is of a sugarcane plant. Name the part marked M. A: Stem (stalk). Part M is the stem (stalk) of the sugarcane, where sugar is stored.
chunks.source: Part M is the stem (stalk) of the sugarcane, where sugar is stored.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name the part marked L. A: Leaf. Part L is a leaf of the sugarcane plant.
chunks.source: Part L is a leaf of the sugarcane plant.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What food value is got from eating sugarcane? A: Carbohydrates. Sugarcane is rich in sugar, which gives the body energy - a carbohydrate.
chunks.source: Sugarcane is rich in sugar, which gives the body energy - a carbohydrate.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How is sugarcane propagated? A: By planting stem cuttings (setts). Pieces of sugarcane stem with buds (setts) are planted and sprout into new plants.
chunks.source: Pieces of sugarcane stem with buds (setts) are planted and sprout into new plants.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why is a maize grain grouped under monocotyledonous seeds? A: Because it has one cotyledon. Mono means one - maize has a single cotyledon, so it is a monocotyledonous seed.
chunks.source: Mono means one - maize has a single cotyledon, so it is a monocotyledonous seed.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How are ferns, mosses and liverworts similar? A: They are all non-flowering plants that reproduce by spores. Ferns, mosses and liverworts do not flower and reproduce by means of spores.
chunks.source: Ferns, mosses and liverworts do not flower and reproduce by means of spores.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is leaf venation? A: The arrangement of veins in a leaf. Leaf venation describes how the veins are arranged in the leaf blade.
chunks.source: Leaf venation describes how the veins are arranged in the leaf blade.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: The diagram shows a leaf with veins running side by side from the base to the tip. Write down the type of venation shown. A: Parallel venation. When veins run parallel to each other, it is parallel venation, typical of monocots like maize.
chunks.source: When veins run parallel to each other, it is parallel venation, typical of monocots like maize.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why is photosynthesis important to plants? A: It enables plants to make their own food. Through photosynthesis plants make starch (food), which gives them energy to grow.
chunks.source: Through photosynthesis plants make starch (food), which gives them energy to grow.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: The diagram shows a seedling in a box. What colour will the leaves of the seedling be if left in this box with H covered for a week? A: Pale (yellowish-white). Without light entering, the seedling cannot make chlorophyll, so its leaves stay pale.
chunks.source: Without light entering, the seedling cannot make chlorophyll, so its leaves stay pale.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give a reason for your answer above. A: The leaves need light to make chlorophyll, which makes them green. Chlorophyll, the green pigment, is only made in the presence of light.
chunks.source: Chlorophyll, the green pigment, is only made in the presence of light.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give one thing likely to happen to the seedling if the part marked H is left open. A: The seedling will grow healthy and green. With light entering through H, the seedling makes chlorophyll and grows normally.
chunks.source: With light entering through H, the seedling makes chlorophyll and grows normally.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give another thing likely to happen if H is left open. A: The seedling will make food by photosynthesis. Light allows the leaves to photosynthesize and make food for growth.
chunks.source: Light allows the leaves to photosynthesize and make food for growth.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State any one reason why some plants climb others. A: To reach sunlight. Climbing plants grow up other plants to reach sunlight for photosynthesis.
chunks.source: Climbing plants grow up other plants to reach sunlight for photosynthesis.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give any one reason why plants are grouped among living things. A: Because they grow and reproduce. Plants are living because they grow, reproduce, feed, respire and respond to changes.
chunks.source: Plants are living because they grow, reproduce, feed, respire and respond to changes.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: The diagram shows an experiment about germination. Why did the seeds in A fail to germinate? A: They lacked moisture (water). Seeds in A were on dry cotton wool, so without water they could not germinate.
chunks.source: Seeds in A were on dry cotton wool, so without water they could not germinate.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is the purpose of the wet cotton wool in B? A: To provide moisture for germination. The wet cotton wool supplies the water seeds need to germinate.
chunks.source: The wet cotton wool supplies the water seeds need to germinate.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give any one example of a leguminous crop. A: Beans. Beans (and peas, groundnuts, soybeans) are leguminous crops with root nodules.
chunks.source: Beans (and peas, groundnuts, soybeans) are leguminous crops with root nodules.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Roots that grow from the stem above the ground to give the plant extra support are called ____ roots. A: prop. Prop roots grow out from the lower stem into the soil and prop the plant upright, as in maize.
chunks.source: Prop roots grow out from the lower stem into the soil and prop the plant upright, as in maize.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name any one crop with roots similar to prop roots. A: Sugarcane. Sugarcane, like maize, grows prop roots from its lower stem for support.
chunks.source: Sugarcane, like maize, grows prop roots from its lower stem for support.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give one plant that reproduces in the same way as a mushroom. A: Moss. Mushrooms reproduce by spores; mosses also reproduce by spores.
chunks.source: Mushrooms reproduce by spores; mosses also reproduce by spores.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give another plant that reproduces in the same way as a mushroom. A: Fern. Ferns reproduce by spores just like mushrooms do.
chunks.source: Ferns reproduce by spores just like mushrooms do.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What structures on a leaf of a plant help in the process of transpiration? A: Stomata. Stomata are tiny pores on leaves through which water vapour escapes during transpiration.
chunks.source: Stomata are tiny pores on leaves through which water vapour escapes during transpiration.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Use the diagram of the seed. How is the seed in the diagram dispersed? A: By wind. The seed has wings that let the wind carry it away from the parent plant.
chunks.source: The seed has wings that let the wind carry it away from the parent plant.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give a reason to support your answer that the seed is dispersed by wind. A: It is light and has wings that are easily carried by wind. Light seeds with wings or hairs are easily blown away by the wind.
chunks.source: Light seeds with wings or hairs are easily blown away by the wind.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: A compound trifoliate leaf is one that ____. A: has three leaflets. Tri means three - a compound trifoliate leaf (like a bean leaf) has three leaflets.
chunks.source: Tri means three - a compound trifoliate leaf (like a bean leaf) has three leaflets.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How are plants different from animals in the way they get food? A: Plants make their own food while animals feed on other organisms. Plants are producers that make food by photosynthesis; animals are consumers that eat plants or other animals.
chunks.source: Plants are producers that make food by photosynthesis; animals are consumers that eat plants or other animals.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: In which way is a seed important to a plant? A: It grows into a new plant. Seeds are the plant's way of reproducing - each seed can germinate into a new plant.
chunks.source: Seeds are the plant's way of reproducing - each seed can germinate into a new plant.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Apart from having bright colours, state any other characteristic of insect pollinated flowers. A: They produce scent (and nectar). Insect-pollinated flowers attract insects with sweet scent and nectar as well as bright colours.
chunks.source: Insect-pollinated flowers attract insects with sweet scent and nectar as well as bright colours.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: The diagram is of a flower. Name the part labelled X. A: Style. Part X is the style - the tube connecting the stigma to the ovary, through which the pollen tube grows.
chunks.source: Part X is the style - the tube connecting the stigma to the ovary, through which the pollen tube grows.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is the use of the part labelled Y to the flower? A: The petal attracts insects for pollination. Part Y is a petal; its bright colour attracts pollinators to the flower.
chunks.source: Part Y is a petal; its bright colour attracts pollinators to the flower.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What does the part labelled Z become after fertilization? A: The fruit. Part Z is the ovary; after fertilization it develops into the fruit.
chunks.source: Part Z is the ovary; after fertilization it develops into the fruit.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: The diagram shows an onion. Name the part labelled B. A: Fleshy scale leaf. Part B is a fleshy scale leaf, which stores food for the onion plant.
chunks.source: Part B is a fleshy scale leaf, which stores food for the onion plant.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is the function of the part labelled A? A: The green leaves make food for the plant by photosynthesis. Part A shows the green foliage leaves, which photosynthesize and make food.
chunks.source: Part A shows the green foliage leaves, which photosynthesize and make food.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What type of root system does the onion plant have? A: Fibrous root system. Onions have many thin adventitious roots of similar size - a fibrous root system.
chunks.source: Onions have many thin adventitious roots of similar size - a fibrous root system.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How is the onion plant propagated? A: By planting bulbs. Onions are propagated vegetatively by planting the bulbs.
chunks.source: Onions are propagated vegetatively by planting the bulbs.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is the importance of leaves to a plant? A: They make food for the plant. Leaves make food for the plant through photosynthesis.
chunks.source: Leaves make food for the plant through photosynthesis.

chunks.subject: Science
