chunks.text: Q: State any one agent responsible for dispersing mango seeds. A: Animals (including people). Animals eat mangoes and drop or pass the seeds far from the parent tree.
chunks.source: Animals eat mangoes and drop or pass the seeds far from the parent tree.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why is transpiration important in plants? A: It helps the plant to absorb water and mineral salts and cools the plant. As water evaporates from leaves, more water (with mineral salts) is pulled up from the roots; it also cools the plant.
chunks.source: As water evaporates from leaves, more water (with mineral salts) is pulled up from the roots; it also cools the plant.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: The diagram shows a bean seed. Name the part marked A. A: Testa (seed coat). Part A is the testa (seed coat), the outer covering that protects the seed.
chunks.source: Part A is the testa (seed coat), the outer covering that protects the seed.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name the part marked B. A: Cotyledon. Part B is the cotyledon, the fleshy seed leaf that stores food.
chunks.source: Part B is the cotyledon, the fleshy seed leaf that stores food.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State the function of part C. A: The embryo grows into a new plant. Part C is the embryo - the young plant that develops into roots and shoot during germination.
chunks.source: Part C is the embryo - the young plant that develops into roots and shoot during germination.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which food value is obtained from beans? A: Proteins. Beans are rich in proteins, which build the body.
chunks.source: Beans are rich in proteins, which build the body.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give any one way in which flowers are important to a plant. A: They are used for reproduction (they produce seeds and fruits). Flowers contain the reproductive parts; after pollination and fertilization they form fruits and seeds.
chunks.source: Flowers contain the reproductive parts; after pollination and fertilization they form fruits and seeds.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is the difference between seed dormancy and seed viability? A: A dormant seed is alive but resting, while viability is the ability of a seed to germinate. Dormancy is a resting state of a living seed; viability means the seed is alive and able to germinate.
chunks.source: Dormancy is a resting state of a living seed; viability means the seed is alive and able to germinate.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: A serrated leaf is one that ____. A: has toothed (jagged) edges. Serrated leaves have saw-like teeth along their edges, like a mango leaf.
chunks.source: Serrated leaves have saw-like teeth along their edges, like a mango leaf.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give any one example of a plant which grows from stem cuttings. A: Cassava. Cassava (and sweet potatoes, sugarcane) is planted using stem cuttings.
chunks.source: Cassava (and sweet potatoes, sugarcane) is planted using stem cuttings.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: The diagram shows an underground stem. State the type of underground stem shown in the diagram. A: Rhizome. The horizontal underground stem with buds and scale leaves is a rhizome, like ginger.
chunks.source: The horizontal underground stem with buds and scale leaves is a rhizome, like ginger.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name the part marked B. A: Terminal bud. Part B is the terminal bud, which grows into a new shoot.
chunks.source: Part B is the terminal bud, which grows into a new shoot.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State the function of part labelled A. A: The scale leaf protects the bud. Part A is a scale leaf that covers and protects the growing bud.
chunks.source: Part A is a scale leaf that covers and protects the growing bud.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State the function of part labelled C. A: The roots absorb water and mineral salts. Part C shows the adventitious roots, which absorb water and mineral salts from the soil.
chunks.source: Part C shows the adventitious roots, which absorb water and mineral salts from the soil.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: In which part of the plant does photosynthesis take place? A: In the leaves. Photosynthesis mainly takes place in the green leaves, which contain chlorophyll.
chunks.source: Photosynthesis mainly takes place in the green leaves, which contain chlorophyll.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name one raw material which enables photosynthesis to take place. A: Carbon dioxide. Plants take in carbon dioxide from the air as a raw material for photosynthesis.
chunks.source: Plants take in carbon dioxide from the air as a raw material for photosynthesis.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name another raw material which enables photosynthesis to take place. A: Water. Water absorbed by the roots is the other raw material for photosynthesis. (Sunlight provides energy and chlorophyll traps it.)
chunks.source: Water absorbed by the roots is the other raw material for photosynthesis. (Sunlight provides energy and chlorophyll traps it.)

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How do banana plants multiply? A: By suckers. Bananas are propagated vegetatively using suckers that grow from the base of the plant.
chunks.source: Bananas are propagated vegetatively using suckers that grow from the base of the plant.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What insect pest attacks bananas? A: Banana weevil. The banana weevil bores into banana stems and corms, damaging the plant.
chunks.source: The banana weevil bores into banana stems and corms, damaging the plant.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: The diagram shows a root system. Name the root system above. A: Taproot system. There is one main root growing deep with smaller side roots - a taproot system.
chunks.source: There is one main root growing deep with smaller side roots - a taproot system.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name the part marked C. A: Lateral (side) root. Part C is a lateral root branching from the main root.
chunks.source: Part C is a lateral root branching from the main root.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State the function of part B. A: The main root anchors the plant and absorbs water from deep in the soil. Part B is the primary (tap) root, which holds the plant firmly and reaches deep water.
chunks.source: Part B is the primary (tap) root, which holds the plant firmly and reaches deep water.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which group of plants have such roots? A: Dicotyledonous plants. Dicots like beans and mangoes have taproot systems; monocots have fibrous roots.
chunks.source: Dicots like beans and mangoes have taproot systems; monocots have fibrous roots.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give the difference between photosynthesis and transpiration. A: Photosynthesis makes food while transpiration loses water vapour. Photosynthesis builds food using sunlight; transpiration is the loss of water vapour from leaves.
chunks.source: Photosynthesis builds food using sunlight; transpiration is the loss of water vapour from leaves.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How can you tell, by looking at the roots, that a plant is a legume? A: It has nodules on its roots. Legumes have small swellings (nodules) on their roots where nitrogen-fixing bacteria live.
chunks.source: Legumes have small swellings (nodules) on their roots where nitrogen-fixing bacteria live.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give one example of a crop which is a legume. A: Beans. Beans are legumes with nitrogen-fixing root nodules.
chunks.source: Beans are legumes with nitrogen-fixing root nodules.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give another example of a crop which is a legume. A: Groundnuts. Groundnuts (and peas, soybeans) are leguminous crops.
chunks.source: Groundnuts (and peas, soybeans) are leguminous crops.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How do legumes increase the fertility of the soil? A: They fix nitrogen into the soil through their root nodules. Bacteria in legume root nodules change air nitrogen into forms plants can use, enriching the soil.
chunks.source: Bacteria in legume root nodules change air nitrogen into forms plants can use, enriching the soil.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Apart from use of seeds, what other part of a flowering plant can be used for propagation? A: The stem. Stems (as cuttings), and also roots, leaves and suckers, can grow into new plants.
chunks.source: Stems (as cuttings), and also roots, leaves and suckers, can grow into new plants.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Where does fertilization take place in a flowering plant? A: In the ovary (ovule). After pollination, the pollen tube grows to the ovule inside the ovary, where fertilization happens.
chunks.source: After pollination, the pollen tube grows to the ovule inside the ovary, where fertilization happens.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Apart from seeds, how else do plants reproduce? A: Vegetatively using stems, roots, leaves or suckers. Many plants reproduce vegetatively - new plants grow from stems, roots, leaves or suckers.
chunks.source: Many plants reproduce vegetatively - new plants grow from stems, roots, leaves or suckers.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What type of pollination is shown in the diagram? A: Self-pollination. Pollen is moving from the anther to the stigma of the same flower - self-pollination.
chunks.source: Pollen is moving from the anther to the stigma of the same flower - self-pollination.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give one characteristic of insect pollinated flowers. A: They are brightly coloured. Bright colours attract insects to the flower.
chunks.source: Bright colours attract insects to the flower.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give another characteristic of insect pollinated flowers. A: They produce scent and nectar. Scent and sweet nectar attract and reward insect visitors.
chunks.source: Scent and sweet nectar attract and reward insect visitors.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why is a moth able to pollinate plants at night? A: It is attracted by the scent of the flowers. Night-opening flowers give off strong scents that guide moths to them in the dark.
chunks.source: Night-opening flowers give off strong scents that guide moths to them in the dark.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State the difference between self-pollination and cross-pollination. A: Self-pollination happens within one flower while cross-pollination happens between different flowers. In self-pollination pollen goes to the stigma of the same flower; in cross-pollination it goes to another flower.
chunks.source: In self-pollination pollen goes to the stigma of the same flower; in cross-pollination it goes to another flower.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give one way in which mosses are similar to mushrooms in the way they reproduce. A: Both reproduce by spores. Mosses and mushrooms (fungi) both reproduce using tiny spores.
chunks.source: Mosses and mushrooms (fungi) both reproduce using tiny spores.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: The diagram shows a flowering plant. To which group of flowering plants does the above plant belong? A: Monocotyledonous plants. The plant is maize - a monocot with parallel-veined leaves and fibrous roots.
chunks.source: The plant is maize - a monocot with parallel-veined leaves and fibrous roots.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What type of root system does the plant have? A: Fibrous root system. Maize has many thin roots of similar size - a fibrous root system.
chunks.source: Maize has many thin roots of similar size - a fibrous root system.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State the importance of the type of root marked Y to the plant. A: The prop roots give extra support to the plant. Part Y shows prop roots growing from the lower stem into the soil, holding the tall plant upright.
chunks.source: Part Y shows prop roots growing from the lower stem into the soil, holding the tall plant upright.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: In which one way is part W different from X in their reproductive function? A: X (male flower) produces pollen while W (female flower) produces ovules. Maize has separate male (tassel, X) and female (cob, W) flowers on the same plant.
chunks.source: Maize has separate male (tassel, X) and female (cob, W) flowers on the same plant.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What kind of food is made by plants during photosynthesis? A: Starch (glucose). Photosynthesis produces glucose, which plants store as starch.
chunks.source: Photosynthesis produces glucose, which plants store as starch.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How is chlorophyll important during the process of photosynthesis? A: It traps (absorbs) sunlight energy. Chlorophyll, the green pigment, captures sunlight energy needed to make food.
chunks.source: Chlorophyll, the green pigment, captures sunlight energy needed to make food.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give a reason why photosynthesis doesn't take place at night. A: There is no sunlight at night. Photosynthesis needs sunlight energy, which is absent at night.
chunks.source: Photosynthesis needs sunlight energy, which is absent at night.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: The diagram shows a fruit crop. How is the above crop propagated? A: By suckers (crowns/slips). The crop is a pineapple, propagated by planting suckers, crowns or slips.
chunks.source: The crop is a pineapple, propagated by planting suckers, crowns or slips.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give one other crop which is propagated in the same way as the crop shown above. A: Banana. Bananas are also propagated by suckers like pineapples.
chunks.source: Bananas are also propagated by suckers like pineapples.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State any one characteristic of seeds dispersed by wind. A: They are light and have wings or hairs. Wind-dispersed seeds are light with wings, hairs or parachutes to catch the wind.
chunks.source: Wind-dispersed seeds are light with wings, hairs or parachutes to catch the wind.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: The diagram shows a plant. Name the type of leaf venation in the diagram. A: Parallel venation. The leaf veins run parallel to each other, which is parallel venation typical of monocots like maize.
chunks.source: The leaf veins run parallel to each other, which is parallel venation typical of monocots like maize.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Mention one crop with similar roots as the ones shown in the diagram. A: Millet. Millet (and sorghum, rice) is a monocot with fibrous roots like maize.
chunks.source: Millet (and sorghum, rice) is a monocot with fibrous roots like maize.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which part of a maize grain has a similar function as the cotyledon of a bean seed? A: The endosperm. In maize, the endosperm stores food for the embryo, just as the cotyledon does in beans.
chunks.source: In maize, the endosperm stores food for the embryo, just as the cotyledon does in beans.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: The diagram shows a method of plant propagation. Name the method of plant propagation shown in the diagram. A: Grafting. The diagram shows a scion joined onto a stock - this is grafting.
chunks.source: The diagram shows a scion joined onto a stock - this is grafting.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State any one advantage of the above method of propagation. A: It produces fruits faster and combines good qualities of two plants. Grafting joins a good fruiting shoot onto strong roots, so fruits come faster with desired qualities.
chunks.source: Grafting joins a good fruiting shoot onto strong roots, so fruits come faster with desired qualities.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is sound energy? A: Energy produced by vibrating objects. Sound energy is produced when objects vibrate, making the air vibrate too.
chunks.source: Sound energy is produced when objects vibrate, making the air vibrate too.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State one reason why animals make sound. A: To communicate with one another. Animals make sounds to pass messages, like warning of danger or calling their young.
chunks.source: Animals make sounds to pass messages, like warning of danger or calling their young.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State another reason why animals make sound. A: To attract mates. Many animals call to attract mates or to scare away enemies.
chunks.source: Many animals call to attract mates or to scare away enemies.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State any one use of sound to people. A: For communication. People use sound (speech, music, alarms) to communicate and pass information.
chunks.source: People use sound (speech, music, alarms) to communicate and pass information.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How is a reflected sound helpful to sailors? A: It helps them detect obstacles like icebergs in the water. Ships send sound into water and listen for the echo to find how deep the water is or what lies ahead (echo sounding).
chunks.source: Ships send sound into water and listen for the echo to find how deep the water is or what lies ahead (echo sounding).

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is the danger of having too much wax in the human ear? A: It blocks sound and can cause deafness. Too much wax blocks the ear canal so sound cannot reach the eardrum well.
chunks.source: Too much wax blocks the ear canal so sound cannot reach the eardrum well.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Apart from using solfa notation, mention one other way of storing sound. A: Recording on tape or disc. Sound can be stored by recording it on tapes, CDs or phones.
chunks.source: Sound can be stored by recording it on tapes, CDs or phones.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Mention another way of storing sound. A: Writing it down as notes (notation). Sound (music) can also be stored by writing it in solfa or staff notation.
chunks.source: Sound (music) can also be stored by writing it in solfa or staff notation.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name one instrument used to reproduce the sound stored by solfa notation. A: Piano. A piano plays back music written in solfa notation.
chunks.source: A piano plays back music written in solfa notation.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name another instrument used to reproduce the sound stored by solfa notation. A: Guitar. A guitar can also reproduce music stored in solfa notation.
chunks.source: A guitar can also reproduce music stored in solfa notation.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: The diagram shows a well-tuned musical instrument. The strings Q, R, S and T are of uniform thickness. Why does string T produce sound of the highest pitch? A: Because it is the shortest string, so it vibrates fastest. Shorter strings vibrate faster, producing a higher pitch - string T is the shortest.
chunks.source: Shorter strings vibrate faster, producing a higher pitch - string T is the shortest.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State one way in which echoes can be reduced in a hall. A: By fixing soft materials (like boards or curtains) on the walls. Soft materials absorb sound instead of reflecting it, which reduces echoes.
chunks.source: Soft materials absorb sound instead of reflecting it, which reduces echoes.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Study the diagram of the human ear. Name the part marked M. A: Eardrum (tympanic membrane). Part M is the eardrum, the thin skin that vibrates when sound waves hit it.
chunks.source: Part M is the eardrum, the thin skin that vibrates when sound waves hit it.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name the part marked N. A: Eustachian tube. Part N is the Eustachian tube, which connects the middle ear to the throat.
chunks.source: Part N is the Eustachian tube, which connects the middle ear to the throat.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give the function of the part marked P. A: The ear ossicles transmit and amplify vibrations to the inner ear. Part P shows the three tiny ear bones (ossicles) that pass vibrations from the eardrum to the cochlea.
chunks.source: Part P shows the three tiny ear bones (ossicles) that pass vibrations from the eardrum to the cochlea.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which part of the ear is responsible for balancing the body? (Mark it with letter B on the diagram.) A: Semicircular canals. The three semicircular canals in the inner ear detect head movement and keep the body balanced.
chunks.source: The three semicircular canals in the inner ear detect head movement and keep the body balanced.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which part of the ear equalizes pressure in and outside the ear? A: Eustachian tube. The Eustachian tube lets air in and out of the middle ear to balance pressure on both sides of the eardrum.
chunks.source: The Eustachian tube lets air in and out of the middle ear to balance pressure on both sides of the eardrum.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How can the pitch of a string instrument be changed? A: By changing the length, tightness or thickness of the strings. Shorter, tighter or thinner strings vibrate faster and give a higher pitch.
chunks.source: Shorter, tighter or thinner strings vibrate faster and give a higher pitch.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Mary shouted in a big house and she heard the same sound repeated. Name the repeated sound she heard. A: Echo. The repeated sound is an echo - her voice reflected off the walls.
chunks.source: The repeated sound is an echo - her voice reflected off the walls.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How was the echo named in the question above formed? A: By reflection of sound off a hard surface. An echo forms when sound waves hit a hard surface like a wall and bounce back.
chunks.source: An echo forms when sound waves hit a hard surface like a wall and bounce back.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name the sense organ for hearing. A: The ear. The ear is the sense organ that detects sound.
chunks.source: The ear is the sense organ that detects sound.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State one natural source of sound. A: Thunder. Thunder is a natural source of sound. Others include waterfalls, wind and animal calls.
chunks.source: Thunder is a natural source of sound. Others include waterfalls, wind and animal calls.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How does a guitar produce sound when its string is plucked? A: The string vibrates. Plucking makes the string vibrate rapidly, and the vibrations produce sound.
chunks.source: Plucking makes the string vibrate rapidly, and the vibrations produce sound.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How can the pitch of a guitar be changed? A: By pressing the strings to change their vibrating length (or tightening them). Shortening the vibrating part of a string (by pressing it) makes the pitch higher.
chunks.source: Shortening the vibrating part of a string (by pressing it) makes the pitch higher.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name any one way of storing sound. A: Recording it on a tape or disc. Sound can be stored by recording, or written down in solfa notation.
chunks.source: Sound can be stored by recording, or written down in solfa notation.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: The diagram is of a musical instrument. Name the group of musical instruments to which the instrument above belongs. A: Wind instruments. The instrument is a flute-like wind instrument played by blowing air through it.
chunks.source: The instrument is a flute-like wind instrument played by blowing air through it.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How can the pitch of the above instrument be varied? A: By opening and closing the holes to change the length of the air column. Covering and uncovering holes changes the vibrating air column length, changing the pitch.
chunks.source: Covering and uncovering holes changes the vibrating air column length, changing the pitch.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give a reason why sound cannot travel through a vacuum. A: There are no particles in a vacuum to vibrate. Sound needs particles (of air, water or solids) to carry its vibrations; a vacuum has none.
chunks.source: Sound needs particles (of air, water or solids) to carry its vibrations; a vacuum has none.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why is thunder heard after lightning has been seen during a rainy day? A: Because light travels faster than sound. Light from lightning reaches our eyes almost instantly, while the sound of thunder travels more slowly.
chunks.source: Light from lightning reaches our eyes almost instantly, while the sound of thunder travels more slowly.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Apart from hearing, give any other function of the human ear. A: Balancing the body. The semicircular canals in the inner ear keep the body balanced.
chunks.source: The semicircular canals in the inner ear keep the body balanced.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How do wind instruments produce sound? A: By vibrating a column of air inside them. Blowing into a wind instrument makes the air column inside vibrate and produce sound.
chunks.source: Blowing into a wind instrument makes the air column inside vibrate and produce sound.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give any one example of a wind instrument. A: Flute. Flutes (and trumpets, recorders) are wind instruments played by blowing.
chunks.source: Flutes (and trumpets, recorders) are wind instruments played by blowing.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How does sound travel from its source? A: In waves through a medium. Sound travels as vibrations (waves) through air, water or solids.
chunks.source: Sound travels as vibrations (waves) through air, water or solids.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How is sound produced by an object? A: By vibration of the object. All sound is produced when objects vibrate.
chunks.source: All sound is produced when objects vibrate.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How is sound produced by a human being? A: By vibrating the vocal cords. Air from the lungs makes the vocal cords in the throat vibrate, producing voice sounds.
chunks.source: Air from the lungs makes the vocal cords in the throat vibrate, producing voice sounds.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give one factor that affects the speed of sound. A: Temperature of the medium. Sound travels faster in warmer air because particles move more quickly.
chunks.source: Sound travels faster in warmer air because particles move more quickly.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give another factor that affects the speed of sound. A: The nature (density) of the medium. Sound travels fastest in solids, slower in liquids and slowest in gases.
chunks.source: Sound travels fastest in solids, slower in liquids and slowest in gases.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is an echo? A: A reflected sound. An echo is sound that has bounced off a hard surface back to the listener.
chunks.source: An echo is sound that has bounced off a hard surface back to the listener.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How is an echo similar to an image? A: Both are reflections. An echo is a reflection of sound just as an image in a mirror is a reflection of light.
chunks.source: An echo is a reflection of sound just as an image in a mirror is a reflection of light.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Apart from a bat, name any other echo locating animal. A: Dolphin. Dolphins (and whales) use echoes to find food and objects in water, like bats do in air.
chunks.source: Dolphins (and whales) use echoes to find food and objects in water, like bats do in air.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What enables a drum to produce sound when it is hit with a stick? A: The stretched skin vibrates. Hitting the drum makes its tight skin vibrate, producing sound.
chunks.source: Hitting the drum makes its tight skin vibrate, producing sound.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give a clear example that shows that light travels faster than sound. A: Lightning is seen before thunder is heard. We see the lightning flash first and hear the thunder later because light is much faster.
chunks.source: We see the lightning flash first and hear the thunder later because light is much faster.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name one way of reproducing stored sound. A: Playing it on a piano from solfa notation. Music stored in solfa notation can be reproduced by playing an instrument like the piano.
chunks.source: Music stored in solfa notation can be reproduced by playing an instrument like the piano.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name another way of reproducing stored sound. A: Playing back a recording. Recorded sound on tape, CD or phone can be played back to reproduce it.
chunks.source: Recorded sound on tape, CD or phone can be played back to reproduce it.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How does wind affect the speed of sound? A: Sound travels faster when moving with the wind. Wind carries sound waves along, so sound moves faster downwind and slower upwind.
chunks.source: Wind carries sound waves along, so sound moves faster downwind and slower upwind.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State any one difference between volume and pitch of sound. A: Volume is the loudness or softness while pitch is the highness or lowness. Volume tells how loud a sound is; pitch tells how high or low it is.
chunks.source: Volume tells how loud a sound is; pitch tells how high or low it is.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give one factor that affects the pitch of sound produced by a musical instrument. A: The length of the vibrating part. Shorter vibrating parts (strings, air columns) give higher pitch.
chunks.source: Shorter vibrating parts (strings, air columns) give higher pitch.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give another factor that affects the pitch of sound. A: The tightness (tension) of the vibrating part. Tighter strings vibrate faster and produce a higher pitch.
chunks.source: Tighter strings vibrate faster and produce a higher pitch.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is frequency of sound? A: The number of vibrations per second. Frequency measures how many vibrations happen each second; it determines pitch.
chunks.source: Frequency measures how many vibrations happen each second; it determines pitch.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give any one use of echoes to a bat. A: To find food and avoid obstacles in the dark. Bats send out sounds and listen to the echoes to locate insects and avoid hitting objects (echolocation).
chunks.source: Bats send out sounds and listen to the echoes to locate insects and avoid hitting objects (echolocation).

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give one way of caring for the human ear. A: Clean it gently and never push sharp objects inside. Sharp objects can pierce the eardrum; clean only the outer ear gently.
chunks.source: Sharp objects can pierce the eardrum; clean only the outer ear gently.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give another way of caring for the human ear. A: Avoid very loud noise. Very loud sounds can damage hearing, so protect ears from loud noise.
chunks.source: Very loud sounds can damage hearing, so protect ears from loud noise.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State the function of the cochlea of the human ear. A: It changes sound vibrations into nerve signals sent to the brain. The coiled cochlea converts vibrations into electrical messages that the brain understands as sound.
chunks.source: The coiled cochlea converts vibrations into electrical messages that the brain understands as sound.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why does sound travel slowest in gases? A: Because the particles in gases are far apart. In gases, particles are spread out, so vibrations pass slowly from one particle to the next.
chunks.source: In gases, particles are spread out, so vibrations pass slowly from one particle to the next.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: The diagram shows a musical instrument. How can the pitch of sound of the above instrument be changed? A: By changing the length or tightness of the string. Pressing the string to shorten it, or tightening it, raises the pitch.
chunks.source: Pressing the string to shorten it, or tightening it, raises the pitch.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: When a drum is hit, you hear sound. How does the ear drum help you to hear the sound? A: It vibrates when sound waves reach it. Sound waves from the drum hit the eardrum and make it vibrate, starting the hearing process.
chunks.source: Sound waves from the drum hit the eardrum and make it vibrate, starting the hearing process.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is the function of the wax in the ears? A: It traps dust and germs. Ear wax catches dust and germs, protecting the delicate inner ear.
chunks.source: Ear wax catches dust and germs, protecting the delicate inner ear.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What part of the ear is most likely to be damaged if you clean the ear with a sharp object? A: The eardrum. A sharp object can pierce the thin eardrum, causing pain and hearing loss.
chunks.source: A sharp object can pierce the thin eardrum, causing pain and hearing loss.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: The diagram shows three metallic rings Q, P and T. Which ring will produce sound of a low pitch? A: T (the largest ring). The largest ring T vibrates most slowly, producing the lowest pitch.
chunks.source: The largest ring T vibrates most slowly, producing the lowest pitch.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which ring will produce sound of a high pitch? A: Q (the smallest ring). The smallest ring Q vibrates fastest, producing the highest pitch.
chunks.source: The smallest ring Q vibrates fastest, producing the highest pitch.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name one device that can be used to store sound. A: Tape recorder. A tape recorder stores sound on magnetic tape.
chunks.source: A tape recorder stores sound on magnetic tape.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name another device that can be used to store sound. A: Compact disc (CD). CDs (and phones, flash drives) store sound digitally.
chunks.source: CDs (and phones, flash drives) store sound digitally.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: The diagram shows glass bottles A, B and C with water at different levels. If each bottle is blown separately, which one will produce the highest pitch of sound? A: B (the bottle with the most water). Bottle B has the shortest air column (most water), so the air vibrates fastest, giving the highest pitch.
chunks.source: Bottle B has the shortest air column (most water), so the air vibrates fastest, giving the highest pitch.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which bottle will produce the lowest pitch of sound? A: C (the bottle with the least water). Bottle C has the longest air column, so the air vibrates most slowly, giving the lowest pitch.
chunks.source: Bottle C has the longest air column, so the air vibrates most slowly, giving the lowest pitch.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What will happen to the sound produced by bottle C if water is increased to the level of bottle B? A: Its pitch will become higher (the same as B's). More water shortens the air column, so the air vibrates faster and the pitch rises to match B.
chunks.source: More water shortens the air column, so the air vibrates faster and the pitch rises to match B.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What will happen to the sound produced by each of the bottles if water was replaced by the same amount of milk? A: There will be no change in the sound. The pitch depends on the length of the vibrating air column, not on the type of liquid below it.
chunks.source: The pitch depends on the length of the vibrating air column, not on the type of liquid below it.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What would you do to a guitar string to make it produce a high-pitched sound? A: Tighten it or shorten its vibrating length. Tighter and shorter strings vibrate faster, giving a higher pitch.
chunks.source: Tighter and shorter strings vibrate faster, giving a higher pitch.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How is the eardrum useful in the process of hearing? A: It vibrates and passes the vibrations to the ear ossicles. The eardrum vibrates when sound waves hit it and passes the movement to the three small ear bones.
chunks.source: The eardrum vibrates when sound waves hit it and passes the movement to the three small ear bones.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Use the meanings in part B of the table to match each term: Volume, Pitch, Frequency, Echo. A: Volume: Loudness or softness of sound; Pitch: Highness or lowness of sound; Frequency: Number of vibrations per second; Echo: Reflected sound. Volume means how loud or soft; pitch means how high or low; frequency counts vibrations per second; an echo is reflected sound.
chunks.source: Volume means how loud or soft; pitch means how high or low; frequency counts vibrations per second; an echo is reflected sound.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name one disease of the ears. A: Otitis (ear infection). Otitis is an infection of the ear that causes pain and can affect hearing.
chunks.source: Otitis is an infection of the ear that causes pain and can affect hearing.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How are ear ossicles important to the ears? A: They amplify and transmit vibrations to the cochlea. The three tiny ossicles make the vibrations stronger as they pass them from the eardrum to the inner ear.
chunks.source: The three tiny ossicles make the vibrations stronger as they pass them from the eardrum to the inner ear.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How do insects like bees produce sound? A: By vibrating their wings rapidly. Bees beat their wings very fast, and the rapid movement produces the buzzing sound.
chunks.source: Bees beat their wings very fast, and the rapid movement produces the buzzing sound.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How do percussion instruments produce sound? A: By hitting or shaking a surface. Percussion instruments like drums make sound when their surface is struck or shaken.
chunks.source: Percussion instruments like drums make sound when their surface is struck or shaken.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give one example of a percussion musical instrument. A: Drum. Drums are percussion instruments played by hitting.
chunks.source: Drums are percussion instruments played by hitting.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give another example of a percussion musical instrument. A: Xylophone. The xylophone is a percussion instrument with bars that are struck to make sound.
chunks.source: The xylophone is a percussion instrument with bars that are struck to make sound.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How do string musical instruments produce sound? A: By vibrating their strings. String instruments like guitars make sound when their strings vibrate.
chunks.source: String instruments like guitars make sound when their strings vibrate.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State any one danger of echoes in the environment. A: They make speech unclear and cause confusion. Repeated reflected sounds overlap with new sounds, making it hard to understand speech or signals.
chunks.source: Repeated reflected sounds overlap with new sounds, making it hard to understand speech or signals.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How do soft boards help to reduce echoes in a cinema? A: They absorb sound instead of reflecting it. Soft boards soak up sound waves, so little sound bounces back as echoes.
chunks.source: Soft boards soak up sound waves, so little sound bounces back as echoes.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name any one disorder of the ears. A: Deafness. Deafness is a disorder where a person cannot hear well or at all.
chunks.source: Deafness is a disorder where a person cannot hear well or at all.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: The diagrams show three drums V, W and X. Which drum produces sound of the lowest pitch? A: V (the largest drum). The largest drum V has the biggest vibrating surface, which vibrates most slowly and gives the lowest pitch.
chunks.source: The largest drum V has the biggest vibrating surface, which vibrates most slowly and gives the lowest pitch.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give a reason to support your answer above. A: The largest drum vibrates most slowly. Bigger vibrating surfaces move more slowly, producing fewer vibrations per second - a lower pitch.
chunks.source: Bigger vibrating surfaces move more slowly, producing fewer vibrations per second - a lower pitch.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: In which group of instruments does a drum belong? A: Percussion instruments. Drums are percussion instruments because they are played by hitting.
chunks.source: Drums are percussion instruments because they are played by hitting.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is heat energy? A: Energy that makes things warm or hot. Heat energy is the form of energy that raises the temperature of things and makes them feel warm or hot.
chunks.source: Heat energy is the form of energy that raises the temperature of things and makes them feel warm or hot.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give one source of heat in the environment. A: The sun. The sun is the main natural source of heat on earth.
chunks.source: The sun is the main natural source of heat on earth.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give another source of heat in the environment. A: Fire. Burning firewood, charcoal or gas produces heat. Electricity is another source.
chunks.source: Burning firewood, charcoal or gas produces heat. Electricity is another source.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State one use of heat in the environment. A: Cooking food. Heat is used to cook food so it is safe and soft to eat.
chunks.source: Heat is used to cook food so it is safe and soft to eat.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State another use of heat in the environment. A: Drying harvested crops. Farmers use heat from the sun to dry crops like maize and beans for storage.
chunks.source: Farmers use heat from the sun to dry crops like maize and beans for storage.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give one method of heat transfer. A: Conduction. Conduction is the transfer of heat through solids, from one particle to the next.
chunks.source: Conduction is the transfer of heat through solids, from one particle to the next.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give another method of heat transfer. A: Convection. Convection transfers heat through liquids and gases by moving warm particles. (Radiation is the third method.)
chunks.source: Convection transfers heat through liquids and gases by moving warm particles. (Radiation is the third method.)

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State any one difference between a solute and a solvent. A: A solute is dissolved while a solvent dissolves the solute. In a salt solution, salt is the solute (it dissolves) and water is the solvent (it dissolves the salt).
chunks.source: In a salt solution, salt is the solute (it dissolves) and water is the solvent (it dissolves the salt).

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What do you understand by a mixture? A: A combination of substances that can be separated physically. A mixture, like sand and salt, combines substances without a chemical change, so they can be separated.
chunks.source: A mixture, like sand and salt, combines substances without a chemical change, so they can be separated.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What do you understand by a solution? A: A uniform mixture of a solute dissolved in a solvent. A solution, like salt water, is a uniform mixture where the solute has fully dissolved in the solvent.
chunks.source: A solution, like salt water, is a uniform mixture where the solute has fully dissolved in the solvent.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What do you understand by radiation? A: Transfer of heat through empty space by waves. Radiation carries heat as waves that need no medium - that is how the sun's heat reaches us.
chunks.source: Radiation carries heat as waves that need no medium - that is how the sun's heat reaches us.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How is conduction different from convection? A: Conduction transfers heat through solids while convection transfers heat through fluids. In conduction, heat passes from particle to particle in solids; in convection, warm fluids themselves move.
chunks.source: In conduction, heat passes from particle to particle in solids; in convection, warm fluids themselves move.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: The diagram shows electric wires under a certain weather condition. In which kind of weather condition do the electric wires appear as shown above? A: Hot weather. The wires sag loosely, which happens in hot weather when metals expand.
chunks.source: The wires sag loosely, which happens in hot weather when metals expand.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why do the electric wires appear as shown above? A: Because metals expand when heated. Heat makes the metal wires expand and become longer, so they sag between the poles.
chunks.source: Heat makes the metal wires expand and become longer, so they sag between the poles.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Apart from raising the temperature of a substance, give one other effect of heat on matter. A: Expansion. Heat makes the particles of matter move apart, so most substances expand when heated.
chunks.source: Heat makes the particles of matter move apart, so most substances expand when heated.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give another effect of heat on matter. A: Change of state (e.g. melting or evaporation). Enough heat can change matter from solid to liquid or liquid to gas.
chunks.source: Enough heat can change matter from solid to liquid or liquid to gas.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State one way in which heat transfer by conduction is important to people. A: It cooks food (heat passes through saucepans). Conduction carries heat through the metal base of saucepans to cook food.
chunks.source: Conduction carries heat through the metal base of saucepans to cook food.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State another way in which heat transfer by conduction is important to people. A: It irons clothes (heat passes through the flat iron). Heat conducts through the metal flat iron to smooth clothes.
chunks.source: Heat conducts through the metal flat iron to smooth clothes.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name the change of state which takes place when vapour changes to liquid. A: Condensation. When water vapour cools and becomes liquid, it is condensation.
chunks.source: When water vapour cools and becomes liquid, it is condensation.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name the change of state when a solid changes directly to gas. A: Sublimation. Some solids, like mothballs, change straight into gas without melting - this is sublimation.
chunks.source: Some solids, like mothballs, change straight into gas without melting - this is sublimation.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name any one scale in which temperature is measured. A: Celsius (centigrade). Temperature is measured in degrees Celsius (or Fahrenheit) using a thermometer.
chunks.source: Temperature is measured in degrees Celsius (or Fahrenheit) using a thermometer.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give a reason why heat travels fastest in gases. A: Because convection currents move fastest in gases. Particles in gases move freely and quickly, so convection currents carry heat fastest through gases.
chunks.source: Particles in gases move freely and quickly, so convection currents carry heat fastest through gases.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: The diagram shows a metallic rod made of two metals X and Y bound together as shown in A. When heated, the rod bends as shown in B. Which of the metals expands faster, X or Y? A: Y. The rod bends towards X, which means Y on the outside expanded more than X.
chunks.source: The rod bends towards X, which means Y on the outside expanded more than X.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give a reason for your answer above. A: The rod bent towards X, showing that Y expanded more. When heated, the faster-expanding metal (Y) becomes longer and forces the rod to bend towards the slower metal (X).
chunks.source: When heated, the faster-expanding metal (Y) becomes longer and forces the rod to bend towards the slower metal (X).

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: The diagram shows a piece of metal dipped in a jug containing hot water. How does part A become hot yet it is not in the hot water? A: By conduction - heat travels through the metal from particle to particle. Heat conducts up through the solid metal, so even the part above the water gets hot.
chunks.source: Heat conducts up through the solid metal, so even the part above the water gets hot.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State any one property of matter. A: Matter has mass and occupies space. Everything made of matter has mass and takes up space.
chunks.source: Everything made of matter has mass and takes up space.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State one effect of heat gain on matter. A: It expands. When matter gains heat, its particles move faster and spread apart, so it expands.
chunks.source: When matter gains heat, its particles move faster and spread apart, so it expands.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State another effect of heat gain on matter. A: Its temperature rises. Gaining heat makes the particles move faster, raising the temperature.
chunks.source: Gaining heat makes the particles move faster, raising the temperature.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give one way in which a blacksmith uses heat. A: To soften metal for shaping. A blacksmith heats metal until it is red hot and soft, then hammers it into shape.
chunks.source: A blacksmith heats metal until it is red hot and soft, then hammers it into shape.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give another way in which a blacksmith uses heat. A: To join (weld) pieces of metal together. Strong heat can melt and join metal pieces together.
chunks.source: Strong heat can melt and join metal pieces together.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: The diagram is of a thermos flask. Name the part labelled Y. A: Double glass walls. Part Y points to the double glass walls of the flask, which enclose the vacuum.
chunks.source: Part Y points to the double glass walls of the flask, which enclose the vacuum.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name the part labelled Z. A: Spring (support holding the flask). Part Z is the spring at the base that holds the glass flask safely in place.
chunks.source: Part Z is the spring at the base that holds the glass flask safely in place.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give any one material that can be used for making part W. A: Cork. Part W is the stopper, which can be made of cork, rubber or plastic - all poor conductors.
chunks.source: Part W is the stopper, which can be made of cork, rubber or plastic - all poor conductors.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why is part X able to prevent heat loss by conduction and convection? A: Because X is a vacuum with no air particles to carry heat. Part X is the vacuum between the walls; with no air, heat cannot travel by conduction or convection.
chunks.source: Part X is the vacuum between the walls; with no air, heat cannot travel by conduction or convection.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which method of heat transfer helps farmers to dry their harvested crops? A: Radiation. Heat from the sun reaches the crops by radiation and dries them.
chunks.source: Heat from the sun reaches the crops by radiation and dries them.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: The diagram shows a charcoal flat iron. Why is the handle of the iron box made of wood? A: Because wood is a poor conductor of heat and will not burn the hand. Wood is an insulator, so the handle stays cool while the iron box is hot.
chunks.source: Wood is an insulator, so the handle stays cool while the iron box is hot.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State one use of the holes labelled on the iron box. A: To let in air so the charcoal keeps burning. The holes allow oxygen in, which the burning charcoal needs.
chunks.source: The holes allow oxygen in, which the burning charcoal needs.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State another use of the holes on the iron box. A: To let out smoke and excess heat. The holes also let smoke escape so it does not dirty the clothes being ironed.
chunks.source: The holes also let smoke escape so it does not dirty the clothes being ironed.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How does heat from the iron box reach the user's body? A: By radiation. Heat radiates from the hot iron through the air to the person ironing.
chunks.source: Heat radiates from the hot iron through the air to the person ironing.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How do silvery walls of a vacuum flask reduce heat loss? A: They reflect heat back, reducing loss by radiation. The shiny silvery coating reflects heat rays back, so little heat escapes by radiation.
chunks.source: The shiny silvery coating reflects heat rays back, so little heat escapes by radiation.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which form of energy changes ice to water? A: Heat energy. Heat melts ice, changing it from solid to liquid.
chunks.source: Heat melts ice, changing it from solid to liquid.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How does heat travel through water? A: By convection. Water is a fluid, so heat moves through it by convection currents.
chunks.source: Water is a fluid, so heat moves through it by convection currents.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How does heat travel through a vacuum? A: By radiation. Only radiation needs no medium, so heat crosses a vacuum by radiation.
chunks.source: Only radiation needs no medium, so heat crosses a vacuum by radiation.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Explain how the sun heats the air around us. A: The sun heats the ground by radiation, and the ground warms the air above it. The sun's rays (radiation) warm the earth's surface, which then warms the air touching it; convection spreads the warmth.
chunks.source: The sun's rays (radiation) warm the earth's surface, which then warms the air touching it; convection spreads the warmth.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Equal volumes of hot water are poured into two glass containers A and B as shown. Why would the water in container B cool faster than in container A? A: Because B has a larger surface area exposed to the air. Container B is wide and shallow, so more water surface touches the air and heat escapes faster.
chunks.source: Container B is wide and shallow, so more water surface touches the air and heat escapes faster.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: By what process does smoke move out of the chimney of a kitchen? A: Convection. Hot smoke is lighter and rises through the chimney - a convection current.
chunks.source: Hot smoke is lighter and rises through the chimney - a convection current.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: The diagram shows an instrument. Name the liquid marked A. A: Mercury. Part A is mercury, the silvery liquid inside a clinical thermometer.
chunks.source: Part A is mercury, the silvery liquid inside a clinical thermometer.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is the importance of the part marked X? A: The constriction stops mercury flowing back so the temperature can be read. Part X is a narrow kink (constriction) that traps the mercury thread so the reading stays until shaken down.
chunks.source: Part X is a narrow kink (constriction) that traps the mercury thread so the reading stays until shaken down.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give any one reason why the liquid marked A is used in that instrument. A: It expands uniformly and is easily seen (does not stick to glass). Mercury expands evenly with temperature, is shiny and visible, and does not wet the glass.
chunks.source: Mercury expands evenly with temperature, is shiny and visible, and does not wet the glass.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is the use of the above instrument to a health worker? A: To measure the body temperature of patients. A clinical thermometer tells the health worker whether a patient has a fever.
chunks.source: A clinical thermometer tells the health worker whether a patient has a fever.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What types of energy does a ball have before it is kicked? A: Potential energy. A still ball has stored (potential) energy because of its position.
chunks.source: A still ball has stored (potential) energy because of its position.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What energy change takes place immediately a ball is kicked? A: Potential energy changes to kinetic energy. The stored energy becomes movement energy as the ball flies.
chunks.source: The stored energy becomes movement energy as the ball flies.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give one form of energy produced by the ball as the goalkeeper catches it. A: Sound energy. When the keeper stops the ball, some movement energy becomes the sound of the catch.
chunks.source: When the keeper stops the ball, some movement energy becomes the sound of the catch.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give another form of energy produced as the goalkeeper catches the ball. A: Heat energy. Friction between the ball and the keeper's hands produces heat.
chunks.source: Friction between the ball and the keeper's hands produces heat.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: In an experiment, salt is mixed with water and stirred until it dissolves. What does the salt act as in the experiment? A: Solute. Salt is the substance being dissolved, so it is the solute.
chunks.source: Salt is the substance being dissolved, so it is the solute.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What does the water act as in the experiment? A: Solvent. Water dissolves the salt, so it is the solvent.
chunks.source: Water dissolves the salt, so it is the solvent.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name any other substance that could be used instead of salt. A: Sugar. Sugar also dissolves in water to form a solution.
chunks.source: Sugar also dissolves in water to form a solution.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How can salt be recovered from the solution? A: By evaporation. Heating the solution evaporates the water, leaving the salt behind.
chunks.source: Heating the solution evaporates the water, leaving the salt behind.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What state of matter is smoke? A: Gas. Smoke is made of tiny particles carried in hot gases that rise into the air.
chunks.source: Smoke is made of tiny particles carried in hot gases that rise into the air.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How is convection different from radiation? A: Convection needs a medium (fluids) while radiation needs no medium. Convection carries heat through moving fluids; radiation sends heat as waves through empty space.
chunks.source: Convection carries heat through moving fluids; radiation sends heat as waves through empty space.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: The diagram shows two nails under three different conditions. In which case did the nail rust? A: wrapped in clean wet cloth. B: wrapped in clean dry cloth. C: smeared with oil and wrapped in clean wet cloth. A: A. Only nail A had both air and water, the two conditions needed for rusting.
chunks.source: Only nail A had both air and water, the two conditions needed for rusting.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is the importance of smearing with oil? A: It keeps air and water away from the nail so it does not rust. Oil coats the nail and blocks air and water from reaching the metal.
chunks.source: Oil coats the nail and blocks air and water from reaching the metal.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name one condition necessary for rusting. A: Air (oxygen). Iron needs oxygen from the air to form rust.
chunks.source: Iron needs oxygen from the air to form rust.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name another condition necessary for rusting. A: Water (moisture). Iron also needs water to rust - that is why the wet nail A rusted.
chunks.source: Iron also needs water to rust - that is why the wet nail A rusted.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: The diagram shows a setup of an experiment and its results. Why does the balloon swell out as shown in B? A: Because the air inside the bottle expands when heated. Hot water heats the air in the bottle; the air expands and blows up the balloon.
chunks.source: Hot water heats the air in the bottle; the air expands and blows up the balloon.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Suggest what you think the experiment above is intended to show. A: That gases expand when heated. The swelling balloon proves that the heated air (a gas) expanded.
chunks.source: The swelling balloon proves that the heated air (a gas) expanded.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Water and cooking oil were poured into a glass container and settled as shown. Which liquid is represented by Q (the top layer)? A: Cooking oil. Oil is less dense than water, so it floats on top as layer Q.
chunks.source: Oil is less dense than water, so it floats on top as layer Q.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which liquid is represented by R (the bottom layer)? A: Water. Water is denser than oil, so it settles at the bottom as layer R.
chunks.source: Water is denser than oil, so it settles at the bottom as layer R.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State any one method that can be used to separate the two liquids. A: Decanting (carefully pouring off the top layer). Because the liquids do not mix, the top oil layer can be gently poured off (decanted).
chunks.source: Because the liquids do not mix, the top oil layer can be gently poured off (decanted).

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why has liquid Q settled on top of liquid R? A: Because Q (oil) is less dense than R (water). Less dense liquids float on denser ones.
chunks.source: Less dense liquids float on denser ones.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give the difference between evaporation and condensation. A: Evaporation changes liquid to gas while condensation changes gas to liquid. Evaporation: liquid becomes vapour. Condensation: vapour becomes liquid.
chunks.source: Evaporation: liquid becomes vapour. Condensation: vapour becomes liquid.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Two containers A and B with water were heated as shown. In which container did water boil first? A: A. Container A holds less water, so it heats up and boils faster.
chunks.source: Container A holds less water, so it heats up and boils faster.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Explain your answer above. A: Container A has less water, so it gains heat faster and boils first. A smaller volume of water needs less heat energy to reach boiling point.
chunks.source: A smaller volume of water needs less heat energy to reach boiling point.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: The diagram shows a saucepan with some water on fire. How will heat from the fire travel to reach the water at the bottom of the saucepan? A: By conduction through the metal base. Heat conducts through the solid metal base of the saucepan to the water touching it.
chunks.source: Heat conducts through the solid metal base of the saucepan to the water touching it.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which method will enable the heat to reach all the water in the saucepan? A: Convection. Convection currents carry the warmed water up and bring cool water down, spreading heat through all the water.
chunks.source: Convection currents carry the warmed water up and bring cool water down, spreading heat through all the water.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: The circular movement of water in the heated saucepan (shown with arrows) is called a ____. A: convection current. Heated water rises and cooler water sinks, forming a convection current that spreads heat.
chunks.source: Heated water rises and cooler water sinks, forming a convection current that spreads heat.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What will happen to the water in the saucepan to show that it is boiling? A: Bubbles will form and steam will rise. Boiling water forms bubbles of steam that rise and burst at the surface.
chunks.source: Boiling water forms bubbles of steam that rise and burst at the surface.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: The diagram shows a type of thermometer. Why is part Q made of a metal? A: Because metal is a good conductor and quickly passes heat to the mercury. Part Q is the bulb; its thin metal wall conducts body heat quickly to the mercury inside.
chunks.source: Part Q is the bulb; its thin metal wall conducts body heat quickly to the mercury inside.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is the importance of shaking the thermometer after use? A: To bring the mercury back below the constriction (reset it). Shaking forces the mercury thread back past the kink into the bulb, ready for the next measurement.
chunks.source: Shaking forces the mercury thread back past the kink into the bulb, ready for the next measurement.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What name is given to the muscles of the heart? A: Cardiac muscles. The heart is made of cardiac muscles, which never get tired.
chunks.source: The heart is made of cardiac muscles, which never get tired.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which mineral helps in the formation of red blood cells in the human body? A: Iron. Iron is needed to make haemoglobin in red blood cells.
chunks.source: Iron is needed to make haemoglobin in red blood cells.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name the organ that destroys excess red blood cells in the body. A: Liver. The liver (together with the spleen) breaks down old and excess red blood cells.
chunks.source: The liver (together with the spleen) breaks down old and excess red blood cells.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State the importance of blood capillaries in the body. A: They link arteries to veins and allow exchange of materials with body cells. Capillaries are tiny vessels where food, oxygen and wastes pass between blood and body cells.
chunks.source: Capillaries are tiny vessels where food, oxygen and wastes pass between blood and body cells.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How do arteries withstand the pressure of blood pumped by the heart? A: They have thick elastic walls. Arteries have thick muscular elastic walls that stretch and survive the heart's pumping pressure.
chunks.source: Arteries have thick muscular elastic walls that stretch and survive the heart's pumping pressure.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Mention any one way of increasing the volume of blood in circulation. A: Drinking plenty of fluids. Drinking fluids (or receiving a blood transfusion) increases the amount of blood in the body.
chunks.source: Drinking fluids (or receiving a blood transfusion) increases the amount of blood in the body.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Apart from blood cells, name any other component of blood. A: Plasma. Blood is made of blood cells floating in plasma, the liquid part.
chunks.source: Blood is made of blood cells floating in plasma, the liquid part.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: The diagram shows a human heart. Name the blood vessel marked with letter B. A: Aorta. Vessel B is the aorta, the largest artery carrying oxygenated blood from the heart to the body.
chunks.source: Vessel B is the aorta, the largest artery carrying oxygenated blood from the heart to the body.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Mention any one disease that affects the heart. A: Heart attack. Heart attack (and high blood pressure) are diseases that affect the heart.
chunks.source: Heart attack (and high blood pressure) are diseases that affect the heart.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Blood vessel D (pulmonary vein) carries blood ____ the heart. A: into. The pulmonary vein brings oxygenated blood from the lungs into the left side of the heart.
chunks.source: The pulmonary vein brings oxygenated blood from the lungs into the left side of the heart.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State any one difference between the pulmonary artery and a pulmonary vein. A: The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood to the lungs while the pulmonary vein carries oxygenated blood from the lungs. The pulmonary artery is the only artery carrying deoxygenated blood (to the lungs); the pulmonary vein returns oxygenated blood.
chunks.source: The pulmonary artery is the only artery carrying deoxygenated blood (to the lungs); the pulmonary vein returns oxygenated blood.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How is the pulmonary vein similar to the pulmonary artery? A: Both carry blood between the heart and the lungs. Both vessels connect the heart to the lungs, one taking blood there and the other bringing it back.
chunks.source: Both vessels connect the heart to the lungs, one taking blood there and the other bringing it back.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name the liquid part of blood. A: Plasma. Plasma is the pale yellow liquid in which blood cells float.
chunks.source: Plasma is the pale yellow liquid in which blood cells float.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name one component of the liquid part of blood. A: Water. Plasma is mostly water, with dissolved proteins, salts, food and wastes.
chunks.source: Plasma is mostly water, with dissolved proteins, salts, food and wastes.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give one use of the liquid part of blood. A: It transports materials like food, hormones and wastes. Plasma carries digested food, hormones, waste products and proteins around the body.
chunks.source: Plasma carries digested food, hormones, waste products and proteins around the body.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give another use of the liquid part of blood. A: It distributes heat around the body. Plasma spreads heat from active parts to the whole body, keeping temperature even.
chunks.source: Plasma spreads heat from active parts to the whole body, keeping temperature even.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Mention any one type of blood cell. A: Red blood cell. Red blood cells (and white blood cells and platelets) are the cells found in blood.
chunks.source: Red blood cells (and white blood cells and platelets) are the cells found in blood.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State the function of blood platelets in the body. A: They help blood to clot. When skin is cut, platelets gather and form a clot that stops bleeding.
chunks.source: When skin is cut, platelets gather and form a clot that stops bleeding.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name one disease that affects blood platelets. A: Haemophilia. Haemophilia is a bleeding disorder where blood does not clot properly.
chunks.source: Haemophilia is a bleeding disorder where blood does not clot properly.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Where in the body are red blood cells produced? A: In the bone marrow. Red blood cells are made in the soft bone marrow inside bones.
chunks.source: Red blood cells are made in the soft bone marrow inside bones.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Mention any one non-communicable disease of blood. A: Anaemia. Anaemia (shortage of red blood cells or iron) cannot spread from person to person.
chunks.source: Anaemia (shortage of red blood cells or iron) cannot spread from person to person.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: The diagram shows two blood cells. Name the blood cell G. A: White blood cell. Cell G is irregular with a nucleus - a white blood cell.
chunks.source: Cell G is irregular with a nucleus - a white blood cell.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State the function of the blood cell F in the body. A: It carries oxygen around the body. Cell F is a red blood cell, which transports oxygen using haemoglobin.
chunks.source: Cell F is a red blood cell, which transports oxygen using haemoglobin.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Mention any one disease that affects blood cell G (white blood cells). A: Leukaemia. Leukaemia is a cancer of the white blood cells.
chunks.source: Leukaemia is a cancer of the white blood cells.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State any one functional difference between arteries and veins. A: Arteries carry blood away from the heart while veins carry blood towards the heart. Arteries take blood out from the heart; veins return blood to the heart.
chunks.source: Arteries take blood out from the heart; veins return blood to the heart.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: The diagram shows circulation of blood in the human body. Name the organ marked with letter X. A: Lungs. Organ X is the lungs, where blood picks up oxygen and drops carbon dioxide.
chunks.source: Organ X is the lungs, where blood picks up oxygen and drops carbon dioxide.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which blood vessel is marked with letter W? A: Pulmonary vein. Vessel W carries blood from the lungs back to the heart - the pulmonary vein.
chunks.source: Vessel W carries blood from the lungs back to the heart - the pulmonary vein.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State the similarity between blood vessel Y and blood vessel Z. A: Both carry blood away from the heart. Vessel Y (pulmonary artery) and vessel Z (aorta) both take blood away from the heart.
chunks.source: Vessel Y (pulmonary artery) and vessel Z (aorta) both take blood away from the heart.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why does blood vessel W bring blood back to the heart? A: To deliver oxygenated blood from the lungs so the heart can pump it to the body. The pulmonary vein (W) returns oxygen-rich blood from the lungs to be pumped round the body.
chunks.source: The pulmonary vein (W) returns oxygen-rich blood from the lungs to be pumped round the body.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Apart from respiratory gases and body wastes, name one other material carried in blood. A: Digested food. Blood carries digested food from the intestines to all body cells.
chunks.source: Blood carries digested food from the intestines to all body cells.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name another material carried in blood. A: Hormones. Blood also carries hormones - chemical messages from glands to body parts.
chunks.source: Blood also carries hormones - chemical messages from glands to body parts.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name the component of blood which transports oxygen in the human body. A: Red blood cells. Red blood cells contain haemoglobin, which picks up and carries oxygen.
chunks.source: Red blood cells contain haemoglobin, which picks up and carries oxygen.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which disease-causing germ attacks the white blood cells in humans? A: HIV (the virus that causes AIDS). HIV attacks white blood cells, weakening the body's defence against diseases.
chunks.source: HIV attacks white blood cells, weakening the body's defence against diseases.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name the human organ where filtration of blood takes place. A: Kidneys. The kidneys filter waste products out of the blood to make urine.
chunks.source: The kidneys filter waste products out of the blood to make urine.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name the human organ where blood gets oxygen while carbon dioxide is removed. A: Lungs. In the lungs, blood picks up oxygen and releases carbon dioxide.
chunks.source: In the lungs, blood picks up oxygen and releases carbon dioxide.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give the use of white blood cells in the body. A: They defend the body against germs. White blood cells are the body's soldiers that destroy germs causing diseases.
chunks.source: White blood cells are the body's soldiers that destroy germs causing diseases.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give the use of blood platelets in the body. A: They help blood to clot. Platelets seal cuts by forming clots that stop bleeding.
chunks.source: Platelets seal cuts by forming clots that stop bleeding.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which type of blood vessels return blood to the heart? A: Veins. Veins carry blood back towards the heart.
chunks.source: Veins carry blood back towards the heart.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is the function of valves in the blood vessels during blood circulation? A: To prevent backflow of blood. Valves act like one-way doors, stopping blood from flowing backwards, especially in veins.
chunks.source: Valves act like one-way doors, stopping blood from flowing backwards, especially in veins.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What type of blood is carried by most vessels with valves? A: Deoxygenated blood. Most veins (which have valves) carry deoxygenated blood back to the heart.
chunks.source: Most veins (which have valves) carry deoxygenated blood back to the heart.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give any one waste material carried by blood. A: Carbon dioxide. Blood carries carbon dioxide (and urea) as waste to be removed by the lungs and kidneys.
chunks.source: Blood carries carbon dioxide (and urea) as waste to be removed by the lungs and kidneys.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Match the items in list A with their functions in list B. List A: Red blood cells, Arteries, Valves, Platelets. List B: Stop bleeding when the skin is cut; Carry oxygen around the body; Carry blood away from the heart; Prevent back flow of blood in the veins. A: Red blood cells: Carry oxygen around the body; Arteries: Carry blood away from the heart; Valves: Prevent back flow of blood in the veins; Platelets: Stop bleeding when the skin is cut. Red blood cells carry oxygen; arteries take blood from the heart; valves stop backflow; platelets stop bleeding.
chunks.source: Red blood cells carry oxygen; arteries take blood from the heart; valves stop backflow; platelets stop bleeding.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: The diagram shows a human heart. What is the function of the part marked with letter Y? A: To carry oxygenated blood from the heart to the body. Part Y is the aorta, the main artery that distributes oxygenated blood to the whole body.
chunks.source: Part Y is the aorta, the main artery that distributes oxygenated blood to the whole body.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give the difference between the blood in the regions marked with letters T and M. A: T has deoxygenated blood while M has oxygenated blood. Region T is the right side with deoxygenated blood from the body; region M is the left side with oxygenated blood from the lungs.
