chunks.text: Q: What is the importance of a black lining inside a solar drier? A: The black colour absorbs heat from the sun. Black surfaces absorb the sun's heat, making the inside of the solar drier hot enough to dry food.
chunks.source: Black surfaces absorb the sun's heat, making the inside of the solar drier hot enough to dry food.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State any one use of a solar drier at home. A: It is used for drying foodstuffs. A solar drier uses sun heat to dry crops and food for storage.
chunks.source: A solar drier uses sun heat to dry crops and food for storage.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How is nitrogen gas important to plants? A: Plants use it to make proteins for growth. Nitrogen is a building block of proteins, which plants need to grow.
chunks.source: Nitrogen is a building block of proteins, which plants need to grow.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give any two importance of wind in the environment. (Select two) A: It helps in pollination of plants, It helps in winnowing. Wind carries pollen between flowers and blows chaff away in winnowing. Destroying houses, erosion and disease are harms.
chunks.source: Wind carries pollen between flowers and blows chaff away in winnowing. Destroying houses, erosion and disease are harms.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give any one example of a rare gas. A: Argon. Argon is a rare (noble) gas found in very small amounts in air. Oxygen, nitrogen and carbon dioxide are common gases.
chunks.source: Argon is a rare (noble) gas found in very small amounts in air. Oxygen, nitrogen and carbon dioxide are common gases.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What are fossil fuels? A: Fuels formed from the remains of dead organisms long ago. Coal, petrol and natural gas formed from dead plants and animals buried millions of years ago.
chunks.source: Coal, petrol and natural gas formed from dead plants and animals buried millions of years ago.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Apart from coal, give two other examples of fossil fuels. (Select two) A: Petrol, Natural gas. Petrol and natural gas are fossil fuels like coal. Wood, biogas and solar are not fossil fuels.
chunks.source: Petrol and natural gas are fossil fuels like coal. Wood, biogas and solar are not fossil fuels.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How is the use of fossil fuels dangerous to the environment? A: Burning fossil fuels pollutes the air. Burning coal, petrol and gas releases smoke and harmful gases that pollute the air.
chunks.source: Burning coal, petrol and gas releases smoke and harmful gases that pollute the air.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How is the use of solar energy friendly to the environment? A: It does not produce smoke or pollution. Solar energy is clean: it gives heat and electricity without smoke or harmful gases.
chunks.source: Solar energy is clean: it gives heat and electricity without smoke or harmful gases.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give any one way of harvesting solar energy. A: By using solar panels. Solar panels trap the sun's energy and change it into electricity or heat.
chunks.source: Solar panels trap the sun's energy and change it into electricity or heat.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Study the pie chart showing the proportion of air. Which letter represents the part that supports breathing and burning? A: D. Oxygen supports breathing and burning, and it is the part labelled D in the pie chart.
chunks.source: Oxygen supports breathing and burning, and it is the part labelled D in the pie chart.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Study the pie chart showing the proportion of air. What is the use of the gas labelled C? A: It is used for putting out fire. Gas C is carbon dioxide, which does not support burning and is used in fire extinguishers.
chunks.source: Gas C is carbon dioxide, which does not support burning and is used in fire extinguishers.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Study the pie chart showing the proportion of air. Name the gas labelled D. A: Oxygen. D is the second largest part of air, which is oxygen (about 21%).
chunks.source: D is the second largest part of air, which is oxygen (about 21%).

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Study the pie chart showing the proportion of air. Name the gas labelled A. A: Nitrogen. A is the largest part of air, which is nitrogen (about 78%).
chunks.source: A is the largest part of air, which is nitrogen (about 78%).

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give any one way in which you can re-use plastic objects at home. A: Using old plastic bottles for storing water. Re-using means using an item again, like storing water in old plastic bottles instead of throwing them away.
chunks.source: Re-using means using an item again, like storing water in old plastic bottles instead of throwing them away.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How does re-using of plastics help to protect the environment? A: It reduces the amount of plastic waste in the environment. Re-used plastics do not end up as rubbish, so the environment stays cleaner.
chunks.source: Re-used plastics do not end up as rubbish, so the environment stays cleaner.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give any two uses of water at home. (Select two) A: Cooking, Washing clothes. Water is used for cooking and washing at home. It cannot be burnt as fuel or used to drive cars.
chunks.source: Water is used for cooking and washing at home. It cannot be burnt as fuel or used to drive cars.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How is the resource plants replaced in the environment? A: Plants are replaced by planting seeds. New plants grow from seeds, so planting replaces the plants that are used.
chunks.source: New plants grow from seeds, so planting replaces the plants that are used.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How is the resource animals replaced in the environment? A: Animals are replaced through reproduction. Animals give birth to young ones, which replace those that die or are used.
chunks.source: Animals give birth to young ones, which replace those that die or are used.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What are biological changes? A: Changes that take place in living things. Biological changes, like growth and germination, happen in living organisms.
chunks.source: Biological changes, like growth and germination, happen in living organisms.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State any one characteristic of biological changes. A: They are irreversible. Biological changes like growth cannot be reversed: a grown plant cannot become a seed again.
chunks.source: Biological changes like growth cannot be reversed: a grown plant cannot become a seed again.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State any two examples of biological changes in plants. (Select two) A: Germination, Growth. Germination and growth are biological changes in plants. Melting, freezing and evaporation are physical changes.
chunks.source: Germination and growth are biological changes in plants. Melting, freezing and evaporation are physical changes.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why is transpiration called a biological change? A: Because it occurs in living plants. Transpiration is the loss of water from living plant leaves, so it is a biological change.
chunks.source: Transpiration is the loss of water from living plant leaves, so it is a biological change.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How is transpiration similar to sweating? A: Both involve the loss of water from a living body. In transpiration plants lose water and in sweating animals lose water: both are water loss from living bodies.
chunks.source: In transpiration plants lose water and in sweating animals lose water: both are water loss from living bodies.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Study the diagrams of the candle under a jar. What would happen to the flame in diagram 2 if the cover was removed after a short time? A: The flame would keep burning. Removing the cover lets fresh air reach the flame, so it keeps burning.
chunks.source: Removing the cover lets fresh air reach the flame, so it keeps burning.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Study the diagrams of the candle under a jar. Give a reason for your answer in the question above. A: Fresh air containing oxygen can reach the flame. Fire needs oxygen to burn. Removing the cover brings in fresh oxygen-rich air.
chunks.source: Fire needs oxygen to burn. Removing the cover brings in fresh oxygen-rich air.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Study the diagrams of the candle under a jar. If the cover had been left on the jar in diagram 2 for a long time, what would have happened to the flame? A: The flame would go out. The burning candle uses up the oxygen trapped in the covered jar, so the flame dies.
chunks.source: The burning candle uses up the oxygen trapped in the covered jar, so the flame dies.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Study the diagrams of the candle under a jar. Give a reason for your answer in the question above. A: The oxygen inside the jar would be used up. Burning uses oxygen. With the cover on, no fresh oxygen enters, so the flame goes out when the oxygen is finished.
chunks.source: Burning uses oxygen. With the cover on, no fresh oxygen enters, so the flame goes out when the oxygen is finished.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State any two differences between transpiration and sweating. (Select two) A: Transpiration occurs in plants while sweating occurs in animals, Transpiration gives off water vapour while sweating gives off liquid sweat. Transpiration is water loss from plant leaves as vapour; sweating is water loss from animal skin as liquid.
chunks.source: Transpiration is water loss from plant leaves as vapour; sweating is water loss from animal skin as liquid.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How is transpiration important to plants? A: It cools the plant. As water evaporates from leaves, it carries heat away and cools the plant.
chunks.source: As water evaporates from leaves, it carries heat away and cools the plant.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State any one way of managing biological changes in humans. A: By feeding on a balanced diet. Good feeding helps the body grow well and handle biological changes like growth and ageing.
chunks.source: Good feeding helps the body grow well and handle biological changes like growth and ageing.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What are chemical changes? A: Changes in which new substances are formed. In a chemical change, the original substance changes into a completely new substance, like wood changing to ash.
chunks.source: In a chemical change, the original substance changes into a completely new substance, like wood changing to ash.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give any two characteristics of chemical changes. (Select two) A: New substances are formed, They are irreversible. Chemical changes make new substances and cannot be reversed. The other choices describe physical changes.
chunks.source: Chemical changes make new substances and cannot be reversed. The other choices describe physical changes.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give any two examples of chemical changes. (Select two) A: Burning, Rusting. Burning and rusting form new substances. Melting, freezing and dissolving are physical changes.
chunks.source: Burning and rusting form new substances. Melting, freezing and dissolving are physical changes.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How is burning similar to germination? A: Both use oxygen. Burning uses oxygen to make fire, and germinating seeds use oxygen to grow.
chunks.source: Burning uses oxygen to make fire, and germinating seeds use oxygen to grow.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Study the diagram of the candle experiment. Why did the candle flame go off in B? A: The oxygen inside the jar was used up. The inverted jar trapped a little air. The flame used up its oxygen and went out.
chunks.source: The inverted jar trapped a little air. The flame used up its oxygen and went out.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Study the diagram of the candle experiment. Why did the level of water rise thereafter? A: The used-up oxygen left space which the water filled. When the oxygen was used up, air pressure inside fell and outside air pushed water up into the jar.
chunks.source: When the oxygen was used up, air pressure inside fell and outside air pushed water up into the jar.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Study the diagram of the candle experiment. Name the gas inside the jar when the candle flame is off. A: Carbon dioxide. Burning produces carbon dioxide, so the jar is left full of carbon dioxide when the flame goes out.
chunks.source: Burning produces carbon dioxide, so the jar is left full of carbon dioxide when the flame goes out.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give any one way in which rusting is different from burning. A: Rusting is slow while burning is fast. Rusting takes days or weeks, while burning happens in seconds.
chunks.source: Rusting takes days or weeks, while burning happens in seconds.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why is fermentation called a chemical change? A: Because a new substance is formed. Fermentation changes sugar into alcohol, a new substance, so it is a chemical change.
chunks.source: Fermentation changes sugar into alcohol, a new substance, so it is a chemical change.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What new substance is formed after fermentation? A: Alcohol. Fermentation turns sugars into alcohol (and carbon dioxide).
chunks.source: Fermentation turns sugars into alcohol (and carbon dioxide).

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What are physical changes? A: Changes in which no new substances are formed. In a physical change, like melting ice, the substance stays the same and the change can be reversed.
chunks.source: In a physical change, like melting ice, the substance stays the same and the change can be reversed.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give any two characteristics of physical changes. (Select two) A: No new substances are formed, They are reversible. Physical changes form no new substances and can be reversed, like freezing and melting.
chunks.source: Physical changes form no new substances and can be reversed, like freezing and melting.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Apart from changes in states of matter, give any two other examples of physical changes. (Select two) A: Breaking glass, Cutting paper. Breaking and cutting only change shape, not the substance. Burning, rusting and cooking form new substances.
chunks.source: Breaking and cutting only change shape, not the substance. Burning, rusting and cooking form new substances.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Mention one physical process that helps in rain formation: (i) A: Evaporation. Evaporation lifts water vapour into the air, the first step in forming rain.
chunks.source: Evaporation lifts water vapour into the air, the first step in forming rain.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Mention one physical process that helps in rain formation: (ii) A: Condensation. Condensation turns vapour into tiny water drops that gather into clouds and fall as rain.
chunks.source: Condensation turns vapour into tiny water drops that gather into clouds and fall as rain.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What type of change takes place when an egg is boiled? A: Chemical change. Boiling changes the egg into a new substance that cannot change back, so it is a chemical change.
chunks.source: Boiling changes the egg into a new substance that cannot change back, so it is a chemical change.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What type of change takes place when sugar is dissolved in water? A: Physical change. Dissolved sugar can be recovered by evaporation, so no new substance is formed: it is physical.
chunks.source: Dissolved sugar can be recovered by evaporation, so no new substance is formed: it is physical.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is environmental degradation? A: The spoiling of the environment. Environmental degradation is the damage of nature by harmful human activities.
chunks.source: Environmental degradation is the damage of nature by harmful human activities.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State any two natural causes of environmental degradation. (Select two) A: Drought, Earthquakes. Drought and earthquakes are natural events that damage the environment. Deforestation, overgrazing and pollution are human causes.
chunks.source: Drought and earthquakes are natural events that damage the environment. Deforestation, overgrazing and pollution are human causes.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How does drought affect food production in a community? A: It causes crops to dry up, reducing food. Without rain, crops wither and die, so less food is harvested.
chunks.source: Without rain, crops wither and die, so less food is harvested.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Mention any two human activities that degrade the environment. (Select two) A: Deforestation, Swamp drainage. Cutting forests and draining swamps destroy nature. Afforestation, recycling and terracing protect it.
chunks.source: Cutting forests and draining swamps destroy nature. Afforestation, recycling and terracing protect it.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State any one cause of loss of species diversity. A: Destruction of natural habitats. When habitats are destroyed, animals and plants lose their homes and some species disappear.
chunks.source: When habitats are destroyed, animals and plants lose their homes and some species disappear.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State any one importance of chemical changes in the environment. A: They produce useful substances like heat and light. Chemical changes like burning give us heat and light, and decomposition returns nutrients to soil.
chunks.source: Chemical changes like burning give us heat and light, and decomposition returns nutrients to soil.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is evaporation? A: The process by which water changes into vapour. Evaporation is when liquid water gains heat and changes into invisible vapour.
chunks.source: Evaporation is when liquid water gains heat and changes into invisible vapour.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State any two factors that affect the rate of evaporation. (Select two) A: Temperature, Wind. Heat speeds evaporation and wind carries vapour away. Colour, smell and taste do not affect it.
chunks.source: Heat speeds evaporation and wind carries vapour away. Colour, smell and taste do not affect it.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State any one way evaporation is important to people. A: It helps in drying clothes. Wet clothes dry because water evaporates from them into the air.
chunks.source: Wet clothes dry because water evaporates from them into the air.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is condensation? A: The process by which vapour changes into liquid. Condensation is when water vapour cools and changes back into liquid drops.
chunks.source: Condensation is when water vapour cools and changes back into liquid drops.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State any one importance of condensation. A: It helps in the formation of rain. Condensation forms the tiny drops that gather into clouds and fall as rain.
chunks.source: Condensation forms the tiny drops that gather into clouds and fall as rain.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give any one way rusting is different from germination. A: Rusting takes place in iron while germination takes place in seeds. Rusting is a chemical change in iron; germination is a biological change in seeds.
chunks.source: Rusting is a chemical change in iron; germination is a biological change in seeds.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What type of change takes place when an iron tool rusts? A: Chemical change. Rusting forms rust, a new substance that cannot change back to iron, so it is chemical.
chunks.source: Rusting forms rust, a new substance that cannot change back to iron, so it is chemical.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give two conditions necessary for rusting to take place on an iron tool. (Select two) A: Presence of oxygen (air), Presence of water (moisture). Iron rusts only when both air and water reach it. Oil, absence of air and paint prevent rusting.
chunks.source: Iron rusts only when both air and water reach it. Oil, absence of air and paint prevent rusting.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which new product is formed during rusting? A: Rust (iron oxide). Iron joins with oxygen and water to form rust, a reddish-brown new substance.
chunks.source: Iron joins with oxygen and water to form rust, a reddish-brown new substance.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State any one effect of rusting on metals. A: It makes metals weak. Rust eats into metal, making tools and structures weak and likely to break.
chunks.source: Rust eats into metal, making tools and structures weak and likely to break.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which chemical change in plants helps them to make starch? A: Photosynthesis. In photosynthesis, plants make glucose which is stored as starch.
chunks.source: In photosynthesis, plants make glucose which is stored as starch.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How do polythene bags lead to soil exhaustion? A: They block water and air from reaching the soil. Buried polythene does not rot. It seals the soil so water and air cannot enter, and the soil becomes exhausted.
chunks.source: Buried polythene does not rot. It seals the soil so water and air cannot enter, and the soil becomes exhausted.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Apart from being chemical changes, how else is germination similar to rusting? A: Both require water and oxygen to take place. Seeds need water and oxygen to germinate, and iron needs water and oxygen to rust.
chunks.source: Seeds need water and oxygen to germinate, and iron needs water and oxygen to rust.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name any one example of a people-made change in the environment. A: Building roads. Roads are built by people. Rainfall, earthquakes and floods are natural.
chunks.source: Roads are built by people. Rainfall, earthquakes and floods are natural.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State any one consequence of people-made changes to the environment. A: They lead to environmental degradation. People-made changes like deforestation and road building often damage the environment.
chunks.source: People-made changes like deforestation and road building often damage the environment.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Study the diagram of the experiment about rusting. In which of the containers will the iron rust after some days? A: Container B. Only container B has both air and water reaching the nail, so only its nail rusts.
chunks.source: Only container B has both air and water reaching the nail, so only its nail rusts.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Study the diagram of the experiment about rusting. Why would the iron nails in the container you have identified rust? A: Because both air and water reach the nail. Rusting needs both oxygen from air and moisture. Container B provides both.
chunks.source: Rusting needs both oxygen from air and moisture. Container B provides both.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Study the diagram of the experiment about rusting. Give one reason why oil was poured in container A. A: To prevent air from reaching the nail. The oil layer seals the water surface so air cannot reach the nail in container A.
chunks.source: The oil layer seals the water surface so air cannot reach the nail in container A.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Study the diagram of the experiment about rusting. What would happen to the nails if they were painted before being put in the containers? A: They would not rust because paint keeps out air and water. Paint coats the nail and stops air and water from touching the iron, so rusting cannot start.
chunks.source: Paint coats the nail and stops air and water from touching the iron, so rusting cannot start.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Apart from killing people, state any one way landslides affect people in hilly areas. A: They destroy houses and crops. Sliding soil buries houses, roads and gardens in hilly areas.
chunks.source: Sliding soil buries houses, roads and gardens in hilly areas.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Study the diagram of the kerosene lamp. Name the part marked with letter Z. A: Chimney. Z labels the glass chimney at the top of the lamp, which carries smoke away from the flame.
chunks.source: Z labels the glass chimney at the top of the lamp, which carries smoke away from the flame.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Study the diagram of the kerosene lamp. Why is the part marked R made of glass? A: So that light can pass through it. Glass is transparent, so the lamp's light shines through while the glass protects the flame from wind.
chunks.source: Glass is transparent, so the lamp's light shines through while the glass protects the flame from wind.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Study the diagram of the kerosene lamp. Give the importance of the part marked X when the lamp is in use. A: It produces light. X is the flame, which burns and gives out light.
chunks.source: X is the flame, which burns and gives out light.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Study the diagram of the kerosene lamp. Give the importance of the part marked Y when the lamp is in use. A: It draws up paraffin to burn. Y is the wick, which soaks up paraffin from the tank to feed the flame.
chunks.source: Y is the wick, which soaks up paraffin from the tank to feed the flame.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is weather? A: The condition of the atmosphere at a given time and place. Weather describes the atmosphere, like sunshine or rain, at a particular time and place.
chunks.source: Weather describes the atmosphere, like sunshine or rain, at a particular time and place.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name the type of weather when people commonly put on light clothes. A: Sunny (hot) weather. People wear light clothes when the weather is hot and sunny.
chunks.source: People wear light clothes when the weather is hot and sunny.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: In which basic units is rainfall measured? A: Millimetres. Rain gauges measure the depth of collected rain in millimetres.
chunks.source: Rain gauges measure the depth of collected rain in millimetres.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name the condition of weather shown in the diagram. A: Cloudy. The diagram shows a cloud covering the sky, which is cloudy weather.
chunks.source: The diagram shows a cloud covering the sky, which is cloudy weather.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What type of rainfall is received around mountain hills? A: Relief rainfall. When moist wind is forced up over hills, it cools and drops rain called relief rainfall.
chunks.source: When moist wind is forced up over hills, it cools and drops rain called relief rainfall.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Besides rainfall, give any other use of clouds to the environment. A: Clouds give shade. Clouds block sunshine and give shade, which cools the environment.
chunks.source: Clouds block sunshine and give shade, which cools the environment.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which type of clouds appear highest in the sky? A: Cirrus clouds. Cirrus are thin, feathery clouds found highest in the sky.
chunks.source: Cirrus are thin, feathery clouds found highest in the sky.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Who are meteorologists? A: Scientists who study weather. Meteorologists study the atmosphere and predict weather.
chunks.source: Meteorologists study the atmosphere and predict weather.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is the source of heat in the water cycle? A: The sun. The sun heats water bodies and causes evaporation in the water cycle.
chunks.source: The sun heats water bodies and causes evaporation in the water cycle.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is temperature? A: The degree of hotness or coldness. Temperature tells how hot or cold something is.
chunks.source: Temperature tells how hot or cold something is.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: In which units is temperature measured? A: Degrees Celsius. Thermometers measure temperature in degrees Celsius.
chunks.source: Thermometers measure temperature in degrees Celsius.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give one danger of clouds in the environment. A: They can bring hailstorms that destroy crops. Dark clouds can bring hailstorms whose ice stones destroy crops.
chunks.source: Dark clouds can bring hailstorms whose ice stones destroy crops.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How is sunshine helpful during photosynthesis? A: It gives plants energy to make food. Plants capture sunshine energy and use it to make food from water and carbon dioxide.
chunks.source: Plants capture sunshine energy and use it to make food from water and carbon dioxide.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why is the Stevenson screen painted with white colours? A: White reflects heat, keeping the instruments cool. White paint reflects the sun's heat so the thermometers inside read the true air temperature.
chunks.source: White paint reflects the sun's heat so the thermometers inside read the true air temperature.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: List down any two delicate weather instruments that can be kept in a Stevenson screen. (Select two) A: Thermometer, Hygrometer. Thermometers and hygrometers are delicate and kept in the Stevenson screen. Rain gauges, wind vanes and anemometers stay outside.
chunks.source: Thermometers and hygrometers are delicate and kept in the Stevenson screen. Rain gauges, wind vanes and anemometers stay outside.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is the role of the sun during the rainfall formation? A: It heats water to cause evaporation. The sun's heat evaporates water from water bodies, starting rainfall formation.
chunks.source: The sun's heat evaporates water from water bodies, starting rainfall formation.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State one way of harvesting rain water. A: Collecting it from roofs using gutters into tanks. Gutters channel roof rain water into tanks for later use.
chunks.source: Gutters channel roof rain water into tanks for later use.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is the main natural source of water? A: Rain. Rain feeds all other water sources like rivers, wells and boreholes.
chunks.source: Rain feeds all other water sources like rivers, wells and boreholes.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give one way in which water can be contaminated. A: By dumping rubbish in water sources. Rubbish dumped in water introduces germs and poisons the water.
chunks.source: Rubbish dumped in water introduces germs and poisons the water.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give two importance of keeping daily records of weather. (Select two) A: They help farmers to plan planting, They help to predict future weather. Weather records help farmers choose planting times and help predict coming weather.
chunks.source: Weather records help farmers choose planting times and help predict coming weather.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Apart from rainfall, give one other element of weather necessary for plant growth. A: Sunshine. Plants need sunshine for photosynthesis to make food and grow.
chunks.source: Plants need sunshine for photosynthesis to make food and grow.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: In which two ways is rainfall important for plant growth? (Select two) A: It provides water for plants, It helps dissolve nutrients in the soil. Rain gives plants water and dissolves nutrients for roots to absorb. Breaking stems, floods and washed seeds are harms.
chunks.source: Rain gives plants water and dissolves nutrients for roots to absorb. Breaking stems, floods and washed seeds are harms.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State any one disadvantage of too much rainfall to plants. A: It causes floods that destroy crops. Too much rain floods gardens, drowns roots and washes crops away.
chunks.source: Too much rain floods gardens, drowns roots and washes crops away.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Study the diagram of the weather instrument. What is the use of this instrument at a weather station? A: To show the direction of wind. The diagram shows a windsock, which points in the direction the wind is blowing.
chunks.source: The diagram shows a windsock, which points in the direction the wind is blowing.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Study the diagram of the water cycle. Name the type of clouds represented by letter A. A: Nimbus (rain) clouds. Cloud A is dropping rain, and rain-bearing clouds are called nimbus clouds.
chunks.source: Cloud A is dropping rain, and rain-bearing clouds are called nimbus clouds.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Study the diagram of the water cycle. State the process taking place at B. A: Evaporation. At B, vapour rises from the water body into the air, which is evaporation.
chunks.source: At B, vapour rises from the water body into the air, which is evaporation.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Study the diagram of the water cycle. State the process taking place at C. A: Transpiration. At C, vapour rises from the trees, which is transpiration: water loss from plants.
chunks.source: At C, vapour rises from the trees, which is transpiration: water loss from plants.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Study the diagram of the water cycle. What is the importance of the sun in the above diagram? A: It provides heat that causes evaporation. The sun heats the water body, causing the evaporation that drives the water cycle.
chunks.source: The sun heats the water body, causing the evaporation that drives the water cycle.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Study the diagram of the weather instrument. What is the use of the instrument in a weather station? A: To measure the amount of rainfall. The diagram shows a rain gauge, which collects and measures the amount of rainfall.
chunks.source: The diagram shows a rain gauge, which collects and measures the amount of rainfall.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give any one use of wearing sun glasses. A: To protect the eyes from bright sunlight. Sunglasses shield the eyes from harsh bright sunlight.
chunks.source: Sunglasses shield the eyes from harsh bright sunlight.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: The table below shows weather instruments and what they measure. Match the items in List A with those in List B. A: Wind vane: Direction of wind; Barometer: Amount of air pressure; Rain gauge: Amount of rain; Anemometer: Speed of wind. A wind vane points where wind blows from, a barometer measures air pressure, a rain gauge measures rainfall, and an anemometer measures wind speed.
chunks.source: A wind vane points where wind blows from, a barometer measures air pressure, a rain gauge measures rainfall, and an anemometer measures wind speed.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Study the diagram of the weather instrument. Name the weather instrument shown in the diagram. A: Rain gauge. The diagram shows a rain gauge: a funnel collecting rain into a measuring bottle, set 30cm above the ground.
chunks.source: The diagram shows a rain gauge: a funnel collecting rain into a measuring bottle, set 30cm above the ground.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Study the diagram of the weather instrument. What is the use of the instrument above at a weather station? A: To measure the amount of rainfall. A rain gauge measures how much rain has fallen.
chunks.source: A rain gauge measures how much rain has fallen.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Study the diagram of the weather instrument. Give a reason why people are advised to put the instrument in an open ground when using it. A: So that buildings and trees do not block the rain. In an open place, no building or tree blocks rain from falling into the funnel, so the reading is correct.
chunks.source: In an open place, no building or tree blocks rain from falling into the funnel, so the reading is correct.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Study the diagram of the weather instrument. Give a reason why people are advised to raise the instrument 30cm above the ground when using it. A: To prevent splashing water from entering the gauge. Raising the funnel 30cm stops muddy splashes from the ground bouncing into the gauge and spoiling the reading.
chunks.source: Raising the funnel 30cm stops muddy splashes from the ground bouncing into the gauge and spoiling the reading.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Study the diagrams of the weather instruments. Name instrument A. A: Anemometer. Instrument A has spinning cups that turn in the wind: it is an anemometer.
chunks.source: Instrument A has spinning cups that turn in the wind: it is an anemometer.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Study the diagrams of the weather instruments. Mention the element of weather recorded by instrument C. A: Sunshine. Instrument C is a sunshine recorder, which records the amount of sunshine.
chunks.source: Instrument C is a sunshine recorder, which records the amount of sunshine.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Study the diagrams of the weather instruments. How is the function of instrument B similar to that of D? A: Both show the direction of wind. B and D are both wind vanes: they turn to show the direction from which wind blows.
chunks.source: B and D are both wind vanes: they turn to show the direction from which wind blows.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Study the diagrams of the weather instruments. Which weather instrument shows the strength of wind? A: Anemometer. The anemometer's spinning cups turn faster in strong wind, so it shows wind strength (speed).
chunks.source: The anemometer's spinning cups turn faster in strong wind, so it shows wind strength (speed).

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name one liquid that floats on water. A: Paraffin. Paraffin is less dense than water, so it floats on top of water.
chunks.source: Paraffin is less dense than water, so it floats on top of water.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is volume as applied in measurements? A: The amount of space an object occupies. Volume tells how much space a solid, liquid or gas takes up.
chunks.source: Volume tells how much space a solid, liquid or gas takes up.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What are the standard units for measuring mass? A: Kilograms. Mass is measured in grams and kilograms. Litres measure volume, metres measure length, newtons measure weight.
chunks.source: Mass is measured in grams and kilograms. Litres measure volume, metres measure length, newtons measure weight.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State one characteristic of an object that floats on water. A: It is less dense than water. Objects less dense than water stay on top; denser objects sink.
chunks.source: Objects less dense than water stay on top; denser objects sink.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Calculate the mass of an object whose volume is 15cm3 and density is 30g/cm3. A: 450g. Mass = density x volume = 30 x 15 = 450g.
chunks.source: Mass = density x volume = 30 x 15 = 450g.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is weight as applied in measurements? A: The force of gravity acting on an object. Weight is the pull of gravity on an object's mass, measured in newtons.
chunks.source: Weight is the pull of gravity on an object's mass, measured in newtons.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What determines the weight of an object? A: Its mass. Weight = mass x gravity. A bigger mass means a bigger weight.
chunks.source: Weight = mass x gravity. A bigger mass means a bigger weight.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name the standard units for measuring volume. A: Cubic centimetres. Volume is measured in cubic units like cubic centimetres (cm3).
chunks.source: Volume is measured in cubic units like cubic centimetres (cm3).

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Study the diagram of the method of measuring an irregular object. Calculate the volume of the stone. A: 4cm3. Volume = water level after - water level before = 12cc - 8cc = 4cm3.
chunks.source: Volume = water level after - water level before = 12cc - 8cc = 4cm3.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Study the diagram of the method of measuring an irregular object. Name the method used to find the volume. A: Displacement method. Lowering the stone displaces water, and the rise in water level gives the stone's volume.
chunks.source: Lowering the stone displaces water, and the rise in water level gives the stone's volume.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State the difference in units used to measure mass and weight. A: Mass is measured in kilograms while weight is measured in newtons. Mass (amount of matter) uses kilograms; weight (force of gravity) uses newtons.
chunks.source: Mass (amount of matter) uses kilograms; weight (force of gravity) uses newtons.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Find the density of an object whose mass is 10g and volume is 5cm3. A: 2g/cm3. Density = mass / volume = 10 / 5 = 2g/cm3.
chunks.source: Density = mass / volume = 10 / 5 = 2g/cm3.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Study the diagram of the block and overflow can. What is the volume of the block? A: 84cm3. Volume = length x width x height = 3cm x 4cm x 7cm = 84cm3.
chunks.source: Volume = length x width x height = 3cm x 4cm x 7cm = 84cm3.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Study the diagram of the block and overflow can. If the block is lowered into the overflow can, what volume of water will be displaced? A: 84cm3. A sunk object displaces its own volume of water, so 84cm3 of water is pushed out.
chunks.source: A sunk object displaces its own volume of water, so 84cm3 of water is pushed out.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Study the diagram of the block and overflow can. How would you confirm your answer about the displaced water? A: By measuring the displaced water collected in the small container. The displaced water collects in the small container, where a measuring cylinder can measure it.
chunks.source: The displaced water collects in the small container, where a measuring cylinder can measure it.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: A piece of stone weighs 240g in air. It was placed in a measuring cylinder containing water and the level rose from point A to point B as shown in the diagram. What is the volume of the stone? A: 10cm3. Volume = level B - level A = 25cc - 15cc = 10cm3.
chunks.source: Volume = level B - level A = 25cc - 15cc = 10cm3.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: A piece of stone weighs 240g in air. It was placed in a measuring cylinder containing water and the level rose from point A to point B as shown in the diagram. Calculate the density of the stone. A: 24g/cm3. Density = mass / volume = 240g / 10cm3 = 24g/cm3.
chunks.source: Density = mass / volume = 240g / 10cm3 = 24g/cm3.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What happens to the volume when water vapour condenses? (i) A: It decreases. Vapour takes up more space than liquid, so condensing shrinks the volume.
chunks.source: Vapour takes up more space than liquid, so condensing shrinks the volume.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What happens to the mass when water vapour condenses? (ii) A: It remains the same. Condensing only changes the state; no water is added or lost, so mass stays the same.
chunks.source: Condensing only changes the state; no water is added or lost, so mass stays the same.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which method would you use to find the volume of an irregular object? A: Displacement method. Irregular objects cannot be measured with a ruler, so the water they displace gives their volume.
chunks.source: Irregular objects cannot be measured with a ruler, so the water they displace gives their volume.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State one difference between capacity and volume. A: Capacity is the amount a container can hold while volume is the space an object occupies. Capacity describes containers (how much they hold); volume describes objects (how much space they take).
chunks.source: Capacity describes containers (how much they hold); volume describes objects (how much space they take).

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How can a mixture of water and paraffin be separated? A: Using a separating funnel. Water and paraffin do not mix, so a separating funnel can run off the lower water layer.
chunks.source: Water and paraffin do not mix, so a separating funnel can run off the lower water layer.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why does a feather float when placed in water? A: It is less dense than water. A feather's density is lower than water's, so water holds it up.
chunks.source: A feather's density is lower than water's, so water holds it up.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give a reason why a stone thrown up falls back on the ground. A: Due to the force of gravity. Gravity pulls the stone back down to the earth.
chunks.source: Gravity pulls the stone back down to the earth.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Study the diagram of the experiment done by a P.7 class. When is such a method of finding volume used? A: When the object is too big to fit in a measuring cylinder. The overflow can method is used when an irregular object cannot fit into a measuring cylinder.
chunks.source: The overflow can method is used when an irregular object cannot fit into a measuring cylinder.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Study the diagram of the experiment done by a P.7 class. If the object above has a density of 2g/cm3, find its mass. A: 30g. The displaced water is 15cc, so volume = 15cm3. Mass = density x volume = 2 x 15 = 30g.
chunks.source: The displaced water is 15cc, so volume = 15cm3. Mass = density x volume = 2 x 15 = 30g.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why does 1kg of iron have less volume than 1kg of cotton wool? A: Iron is denser than cotton wool. Denser material packs more mass into less space, so 1kg of iron is much smaller than 1kg of cotton wool.
chunks.source: Denser material packs more mass into less space, so 1kg of iron is much smaller than 1kg of cotton wool.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why does an object weigh less when placed in water than in air? A: Water pushes it up (upthrust). Water exerts an upward force called upthrust, which reduces the object's weight in water.
chunks.source: Water exerts an upward force called upthrust, which reduces the object's weight in water.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name the force that enables rain to fall on the ground. A: Gravity. Gravity pulls rain drops down from the clouds to the ground.
chunks.source: Gravity pulls rain drops down from the clouds to the ground.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why does paraffin settle on top when mixed with water? A: It is less dense than water. Less dense liquids float on denser ones, so paraffin rests on top of water.
chunks.source: Less dense liquids float on denser ones, so paraffin rests on top of water.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why does a stone sink when it is placed in a bucket full of water? A: It is denser than water. A stone's density is greater than water's, so it sinks.
chunks.source: A stone's density is greater than water's, so it sinks.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Calculate the mass of an object whose volume is 15cm3 and density is 30g/cm3. A: 450g. Mass = density x volume = 30 x 15 = 450g.
chunks.source: Mass = density x volume = 30 x 15 = 450g.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Study the diagram of the two cylinders. What is the volume of the stone? A: 20cm3. Volume = level with stone - level without = 45cc - 25cc = 20cm3.
chunks.source: Volume = level with stone - level without = 45cc - 25cc = 20cm3.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Study the diagram of the two cylinders. Calculate the density of the stone if it has a mass of 450g. A: 22.5g/cm3. Density = mass / volume = 450g / 20cm3 = 22.5g/cm3.
chunks.source: Density = mass / volume = 450g / 20cm3 = 22.5g/cm3.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What happens to the volume when water freezes? (i) A: It increases. Water expands when it freezes, so ice takes up more space than the water it came from.
chunks.source: Water expands when it freezes, so ice takes up more space than the water it came from.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What happens to the mass when water freezes? (ii) A: It remains the same. Freezing only changes the state; no water is added or lost, so mass stays the same.
chunks.source: Freezing only changes the state; no water is added or lost, so mass stays the same.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Ayeko wants to find the volume of a stone of about 300cm3. He has 200cm3 of water, a measuring cylinder and an overflow can, but the cylinder method will not work. Give one way it can be made to work. A: Use the overflow can to collect the displaced water. The stone is too big for the measuring cylinder, but the overflow can handles large objects and its displaced water can be measured.
chunks.source: The stone is too big for the measuring cylinder, but the overflow can handles large objects and its displaced water can be measured.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Study the diagram of the box of chalk. Find its volume. A: 24cm3. Volume = length x width x height = 4cm x 3cm x 2cm = 24cm3.
chunks.source: Volume = length x width x height = 4cm x 3cm x 2cm = 24cm3.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How does an object less dense than water behave in water? A: It floats on water. Less dense objects are held up by water, so they float.
chunks.source: Less dense objects are held up by water, so they float.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give one liquid that sinks in water. A: Mercury. Mercury is denser than water, so it sinks. Paraffin, oil and alcohol float.
chunks.source: Mercury is denser than water, so it sinks. Paraffin, oil and alcohol float.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Study the diagram of the method of separating mixtures. What kind of mixture is separated by the above method? A: A mixture of two liquids that do not mix. The separating funnel separates immiscible liquids, like water and oil, which settle in layers.
chunks.source: The separating funnel separates immiscible liquids, like water and oil, which settle in layers.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Study the diagram of the method of separating mixtures. Name the liquid marked B. A: Water. The denser liquid settles at the bottom. Water is denser than oil-like liquids, so B is water.
chunks.source: The denser liquid settles at the bottom. Water is denser than oil-like liquids, so B is water.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Study the diagram of the method of separating mixtures. Name the container marked X. A: Separating funnel. X is the funnel-shaped container with a tap used to run off one liquid layer at a time.
chunks.source: X is the funnel-shaped container with a tap used to run off one liquid layer at a time.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Study the diagram of the irregular object lowered into container A. Name container A. A: Overflow can (displacement can). Container A is filled to the brim so the object pushes water out through the spout: an overflow can.
chunks.source: Container A is filled to the brim so the object pushes water out through the spout: an overflow can.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Study the diagram of the irregular object lowered into container A. Name container B. A: Measuring cylinder. Container B collects the displaced water and its scale measures the volume.
chunks.source: Container B collects the displaced water and its scale measures the volume.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Study the diagram of the irregular object lowered into container A. What is the volume of the irregular object? A: 10cm3. The displaced water in container B reaches 10cc, so the object's volume is 10cm3.
chunks.source: The displaced water in container B reaches 10cc, so the object's volume is 10cm3.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Study the diagram of the irregular object lowered into container A. Calculate the density of the irregular object if its mass is 60g. A: 6g/cm3. Density = mass / volume = 60g / 10cm3 = 6g/cm3.
chunks.source: Density = mass / volume = 60g / 10cm3 = 6g/cm3.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name the instrument used to measure mass. A: Beam balance. A beam balance compares an object with known masses to measure mass.
chunks.source: A beam balance compares an object with known masses to measure mass.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What happens when petrol is poured in a container with water? A: Petrol floats on top of the water. Petrol is less dense than water and does not mix with it, so it floats on top.
chunks.source: Petrol is less dense than water and does not mix with it, so it floats on top.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Study the diagram of the stone put into measuring cylinder A, with the water rising to the level in cylinder B. Work out the volume of the stone. A: 20cm3. Volume = level B - level A = 45cc - 25cc = 20cm3.
chunks.source: Volume = level B - level A = 45cc - 25cc = 20cm3.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Study the diagram of the stone put into measuring cylinder A, with the water rising to the level in cylinder B. If the mass of the stone is 60g, calculate its density. A: 3g/cm3. Density = mass / volume = 60g / 20cm3 = 3g/cm3.
chunks.source: Density = mass / volume = 60g / 20cm3 = 3g/cm3.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: When a piece of stone and a rubber are dropped from the same height, which one reaches the ground first? A: The stone. The heavier stone is pulled down more strongly and overcomes air resistance better, so it lands first.
chunks.source: The heavier stone is pulled down more strongly and overcomes air resistance better, so it lands first.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: When a piece of stone and a rubber are dropped from the same height, give a reason why the stone reaches the ground first. A: The stone is heavier than the rubber. Gravity pulls harder on the heavier stone, so it falls faster through the air.
chunks.source: Gravity pulls harder on the heavier stone, so it falls faster through the air.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: The density of sand is 3 grams per cubic centimeter. Its mass is 270 grams. Find its volume. A: 90cm3. Volume = mass / density = 270 / 3 = 90cm3.
chunks.source: Volume = mass / density = 270 / 3 = 90cm3.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is mass? A: The amount of matter in an object. Mass is how much matter an object contains, measured in grams or kilograms.
chunks.source: Mass is how much matter an object contains, measured in grams or kilograms.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is immunity? A: The ability of the body to resist diseases. Immunity is the body's power to fight germs so that we do not fall sick.
chunks.source: Immunity is the body's power to fight germs so that we do not fall sick.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Mention two types of immunity. (Select two) A: Natural immunity, Artificial immunity. Immunity is either natural (from the body itself) or artificial (from vaccines).
chunks.source: Immunity is either natural (from the body itself) or artificial (from vaccines).

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give any two ways babies can acquire immunity. (Select two) A: Through breastfeeding, Through immunisation. Breast milk passes natural immunity and vaccines give artificial immunity to babies.
chunks.source: Breast milk passes natural immunity and vaccines give artificial immunity to babies.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State any one importance of immunity to the body. A: It protects the body against diseases. Immunity fights germs, so the body stays healthy.
chunks.source: Immunity fights germs, so the body stays healthy.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What do we call the cells that defend the body against germs? A: White blood cells. White blood cells are the soldiers of the body that attack and destroy germs.
chunks.source: White blood cells are the soldiers of the body that attack and destroy germs.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Apart from the white blood cells, name any other part that makes up the immune system. A: Antibodies. Antibodies are body chemicals that mark germs for destruction by white blood cells.
chunks.source: Antibodies are body chemicals that mark germs for destruction by white blood cells.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Mention any two diseases that affect the immune system. (Select two) A: HIV/AIDS, Leukaemia. HIV/AIDS and leukaemia attack the immune system itself. Malaria, colds and tooth decay do not.
chunks.source: HIV/AIDS and leukaemia attack the immune system itself. Malaria, colds and tooth decay do not.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How does feeding on a balanced diet help to strengthen one's immunity? A: It gives the body nutrients needed to fight diseases. A balanced diet supplies vitamins and proteins that keep the immune system strong.
chunks.source: A balanced diet supplies vitamins and proteins that keep the immune system strong.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Mention any one disease that affects a person due to a weakened immunity. A: Tuberculosis. When immunity is weak, germs like those causing tuberculosis easily make a person sick.
chunks.source: When immunity is weak, germs like those causing tuberculosis easily make a person sick.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give any one way a baby can acquire natural immunity. A: Through breast milk. Breast milk carries the mother's antibodies, giving the baby natural immunity.
chunks.source: Breast milk carries the mother's antibodies, giving the baby natural immunity.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How do people acquire artificial immunity? A: Through immunisation (vaccination). Vaccines introduce weak or dead germs so the body learns to fight them: artificial immunity.
chunks.source: Vaccines introduce weak or dead germs so the body learns to fight them: artificial immunity.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State any one advantage of natural immunity over artificial immunity. A: Natural immunity lasts longer. Natural immunity, once developed, often protects for a very long time.
chunks.source: Natural immunity, once developed, often protects for a very long time.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State any one advantage of artificial immunity. A: It gives quick protection. Vaccines protect quickly, even before the body has met the real germs.
chunks.source: Vaccines protect quickly, even before the body has met the real germs.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is immunisation? A: The introduction of vaccines into the body. Immunisation puts vaccines (weak or dead germs) into the body to build immunity.
chunks.source: Immunisation puts vaccines (weak or dead germs) into the body to build immunity.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give any two advantages of immunisation in children. (Select two) A: It protects children against diseases, It reduces child deaths. Immunised children resist killer diseases, so fewer children die.
chunks.source: Immunised children resist killer diseases, so fewer children die.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why does the government of Uganda carry out mass immunisation of children? A: To prevent the spread of immunisable diseases. Mass immunisation protects whole communities by stopping diseases from spreading.
chunks.source: Mass immunisation protects whole communities by stopping diseases from spreading.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give a reason why immunisation of babies is free of charge in Uganda. A: To encourage all parents to immunise their babies. Free immunisation removes cost barriers so every baby gets protected.
chunks.source: Free immunisation removes cost barriers so every baby gets protected.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What are immunisable diseases? A: Diseases that can be prevented by immunisation. Immunisable diseases, like polio and measles, are stopped by vaccines.
chunks.source: Immunisable diseases, like polio and measles, are stopped by vaccines.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Mention any two examples of immunisable diseases caused by virus. (Select two) A: Measles, Polio. Measles and polio are caused by viruses. Tuberculosis, tetanus and whooping cough are caused by bacteria.
chunks.source: Measles and polio are caused by viruses. Tuberculosis, tetanus and whooping cough are caused by bacteria.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name the immunisable disease that affects the liver. A: Hepatitis B. Hepatitis B is a viral disease that attacks the liver, prevented by the hepatitis B vaccine.
chunks.source: Hepatitis B is a viral disease that attacks the liver, prevented by the hepatitis B vaccine.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name the immunisable disease that affects the lungs. A: Tuberculosis. Tuberculosis mainly attacks the lungs and is prevented by the BCG vaccine.
chunks.source: Tuberculosis mainly attacks the lungs and is prevented by the BCG vaccine.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name the immunisable disease that affects the bones and muscles. A: Tetanus. Tetanus causes stiffness of muscles and affects movement of bones and muscles.
chunks.source: Tetanus causes stiffness of muscles and affects movement of bones and muscles.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name the immunisable disease that affects the brain. A: Meningitis. Meningitis is an infection of the coverings of the brain, prevented by the Hib vaccine given to babies.
chunks.source: Meningitis is an infection of the coverings of the brain, prevented by the Hib vaccine given to babies.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name the immunisable disease whose germs enter the body through open wounds. A: Tetanus. Tetanus germs live in soil and enter through cuts and open wounds.
chunks.source: Tetanus germs live in soil and enter through cuts and open wounds.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name any one immunisable disease caused by bacteria. A: Tuberculosis. Tuberculosis is caused by bacteria. Measles, polio and mumps are caused by viruses.
chunks.source: Tuberculosis is caused by bacteria. Measles, polio and mumps are caused by viruses.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which immunisable disease causes paralysis of limbs? A: Polio. Polio attacks the nerves and can paralyse the limbs.
chunks.source: Polio attacks the nerves and can paralyse the limbs.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which immunisable disease causes stiffness of muscles? A: Tetanus. Tetanus causes painful stiffness and spasms of muscles.
chunks.source: Tetanus causes painful stiffness and spasms of muscles.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which immunisable disease causes swelling in the neck? A: Mumps. Mumps causes swelling of the glands in the neck and cheeks.
chunks.source: Mumps causes swelling of the glands in the neck and cheeks.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which immunisable disease causes swelling in the arm pit? A: Tuberculosis. Tuberculosis can cause swelling of lymph glands, including those in the arm pit.
chunks.source: Tuberculosis can cause swelling of lymph glands, including those in the arm pit.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What are vaccines? A: Weak or dead germs introduced into the body to build immunity. Vaccines contain harmless forms of germs that teach the body to fight the real disease.
chunks.source: Vaccines contain harmless forms of germs that teach the body to fight the real disease.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Mention two ways vaccines are introduced in the body. (Select two) A: Through injection, Through the mouth (oral drops). Vaccines are given by injection (like BCG) or by mouth (like polio drops).
chunks.source: Vaccines are given by injection (like BCG) or by mouth (like polio drops).

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Mention any one example of a vaccine. A: BCG. BCG is the vaccine against tuberculosis. Aspirin, paracetamol and chloroquine are medicines, not vaccines.
chunks.source: BCG is the vaccine against tuberculosis. Aspirin, paracetamol and chloroquine are medicines, not vaccines.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give any one way vaccines are important in the body. A: They help the body to develop immunity. Vaccines train the body to fight germs, building immunity.
chunks.source: Vaccines train the body to fight germs, building immunity.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which vaccine is administered against tuberculosis? A: BCG. BCG protects babies against tuberculosis and is given at birth.
chunks.source: BCG protects babies against tuberculosis and is given at birth.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which vaccine is administered against pertussis (whooping cough)? A: DPT. The P in DPT stands for pertussis (whooping cough).
chunks.source: The P in DPT stands for pertussis (whooping cough).

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which vaccine is administered against measles? A: Measles vaccine. The measles vaccine is given to babies at 9 months.
chunks.source: The measles vaccine is given to babies at 9 months.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why is BCG vaccine given to babies at birth? A: To protect the baby against tuberculosis from birth. Giving BCG at birth protects the newborn against tuberculosis from the very start of life.
chunks.source: Giving BCG at birth protects the newborn against tuberculosis from the very start of life.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why is measles vaccine administered to babies at 9 months? A: Because the natural immunity from the mother ends at about 9 months. The mother's protection passed to the baby fades by 9 months, so the vaccine takes over then.
chunks.source: The mother's protection passed to the baby fades by 9 months, so the vaccine takes over then.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name any two vaccines administered to babies at 6 weeks. (Select two) A: DPT, Polio vaccine. At 6 weeks babies receive DPT and polio vaccine. BCG is given at birth and measles vaccine at 9 months.
chunks.source: At 6 weeks babies receive DPT and polio vaccine. BCG is given at birth and measles vaccine at 9 months.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How can a health worker tell that a child was immunized against tuberculosis without looking at the child health card? A: By checking for the BCG scar on the child's upper arm. BCG leaves a small scar on the upper arm where it was injected.
chunks.source: BCG leaves a small scar on the upper arm where it was injected.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why is DPT vaccine called a triple vaccine? A: Because it protects against three diseases. DPT is triple because it fights diphtheria, pertussis (whooping cough) and tetanus: three diseases in one vaccine.
chunks.source: DPT is triple because it fights diphtheria, pertussis (whooping cough) and tetanus: three diseases in one vaccine.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Mention any two diseases vaccinated against using the DPT vaccine. (Select two) A: Diphtheria, Tetanus. DPT covers diphtheria, pertussis and tetanus. Measles, polio and tuberculosis have their own vaccines.
chunks.source: DPT covers diphtheria, pertussis and tetanus. Measles, polio and tuberculosis have their own vaccines.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give any two importance of the child health card to parents. (Select two) A: It records the child's immunisation, It shows the child's growth. The card tracks vaccines given and the child's growth. It is not money, food or treatment.
chunks.source: The card tracks vaccines given and the child's growth. It is not money, food or treatment.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why is it recommended for a parent taking a baby for immunisation to go with the child health card? A: For the health worker to record the immunisation given. The health worker writes each vaccine on the card so the baby's full record is kept.
chunks.source: The health worker writes each vaccine on the card so the baby's full record is kept.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name the enzyme that digests fats in the alimentary canal. A: Lipase. Lipase is the enzyme that breaks down fats into fatty acids and glycerol.
chunks.source: Lipase is the enzyme that breaks down fats into fatty acids and glycerol.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why are canine teeth suitable for tearing? A: They are pointed and sharp. Canine teeth are pointed and sharp, which makes them good for tearing food.
chunks.source: Canine teeth are pointed and sharp, which makes them good for tearing food.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why is it necessary to brush teeth after every meal? A: To remove food remains that cause tooth decay. Food remains left on teeth rot and cause tooth decay, so brushing removes them.
chunks.source: Food remains left on teeth rot and cause tooth decay, so brushing removes them.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give the function of the teeth in the process of digestion. A: To cut food into small pieces for easy swallowing. Teeth carry out mechanical digestion by cutting and crushing food into small pieces.
chunks.source: Teeth carry out mechanical digestion by cutting and crushing food into small pieces.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give any one sign of a dehydrated person. A: Dry mouth and thirst. A dehydrated person has lost a lot of water, so the mouth becomes dry and they feel thirsty.
chunks.source: A dehydrated person has lost a lot of water, so the mouth becomes dry and they feel thirsty.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What structures enable the absorption of food to take place in the small intestines? A: Villi. Villi are tiny finger-like structures in the ileum that absorb digested food into the blood.
chunks.source: Villi are tiny finger-like structures in the ileum that absorb digested food into the blood.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: The diagram shows the alimentary canal of a human being. Name the part marked D. A: Liver. Part D is the liver, the large organ next to the stomach that makes bile.
chunks.source: Part D is the liver, the large organ next to the stomach that makes bile.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: The diagram shows the alimentary canal of a human being. Name the part marked X. A: Pancreas. Part X is the pancreas, which lies below the stomach and produces digestive enzymes.
chunks.source: Part X is the pancreas, which lies below the stomach and produces digestive enzymes.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: The diagram shows the alimentary canal of a human being. State any one process that takes place in the part labelled Y. A: Absorption of digested food. Part Y is the ileum (small intestine), where digested food is absorbed into the blood.
chunks.source: Part Y is the ileum (small intestine), where digested food is absorbed into the blood.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: The diagram shows the alimentary canal of a human being. Give one function of the organ labelled X. A: It produces digestive enzymes. The pancreas (X) produces pancreatic juice containing enzymes that digest food.
chunks.source: The pancreas (X) produces pancreatic juice containing enzymes that digest food.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How is the absence of iodine harmful to our health? A: It causes goitre. Without iodine the thyroid gland swells, causing goitre.
chunks.source: Without iodine the thyroid gland swells, causing goitre.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give one use of saliva in the digestive system. A: It softens food for easy swallowing. Saliva moistens and softens food so it can be swallowed easily, and it starts digesting starch.
chunks.source: Saliva moistens and softens food so it can be swallowed easily, and it starts digesting starch.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give any one way of maintaining the proper working of the digestive system. A: Eating a balanced diet. A balanced diet with enough roughage keeps the digestive system working properly.
chunks.source: A balanced diet with enough roughage keeps the digestive system working properly.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which blood vessel transports digested food from the ileum to the liver? A: Hepatic portal vein. The hepatic portal vein carries digested food from the ileum to the liver.
chunks.source: The hepatic portal vein carries digested food from the ileum to the liver.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is an enzyme? A: A substance that speeds up digestion. An enzyme is a substance made in the body that speeds up the digestion of food.
chunks.source: An enzyme is a substance made in the body that speeds up the digestion of food.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which digestive disease makes a person pass out watery stool with blood? A: Dysentery. Dysentery is marked by passing watery stool mixed with blood.
chunks.source: Dysentery is marked by passing watery stool mixed with blood.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: The diagram shows two types of teeth in humans. Name the type of tooth marked A. A: Canine tooth. Tooth A is pointed and sharp, so it is a canine tooth used for tearing.
chunks.source: Tooth A is pointed and sharp, so it is a canine tooth used for tearing.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: The diagram shows two types of teeth in humans. Name the type of tooth marked B. A: Molar tooth. Tooth B has a broad flat top with cusps, so it is a molar tooth used for grinding.
chunks.source: Tooth B has a broad flat top with cusps, so it is a molar tooth used for grinding.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: In the diagram of the two teeth, give the use of tooth A. A: Tearing food. The pointed canine tooth A is used for tearing food.
chunks.source: The pointed canine tooth A is used for tearing food.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: In the diagram of the two teeth, give the use of tooth B. A: Grinding food. The broad molar tooth B is used for grinding and crushing food.
chunks.source: The broad molar tooth B is used for grinding and crushing food.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: The diagram shows part of the digestive system. Name the class of food which is digested in the part marked X. A: Proteins. Part X is the stomach, where the enzyme pepsin begins the digestion of proteins.
chunks.source: Part X is the stomach, where the enzyme pepsin begins the digestion of proteins.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Apart from tasting food, state any other function of the tongue during digestion of food. A: It rolls food into a bolus for swallowing. The tongue rolls chewed food into a round ball (bolus) and pushes it down for swallowing.
chunks.source: The tongue rolls chewed food into a round ball (bolus) and pushes it down for swallowing.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which enzyme is found in saliva? A: Salivary amylase. Saliva contains salivary amylase, which starts the digestion of starch in the mouth.
chunks.source: Saliva contains salivary amylase, which starts the digestion of starch in the mouth.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Arrange the following in the order they happen to food in the mouth. A: Teeth chew food into small pieces, Food mixes with saliva and is softened, Salivary amylase starts digesting starch. In the mouth, teeth first chew food, saliva then softens it, and salivary amylase begins digesting starch.
chunks.source: In the mouth, teeth first chew food, saliva then softens it, and salivary amylase begins digesting starch.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What class of food is digested in the duodenum? A: Fats. In the duodenum, bile emulsifies fats and lipase digests them.
chunks.source: In the duodenum, bile emulsifies fats and lipase digests them.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State the role of enzymes during the digestion of food. A: They speed up the digestion of food. Enzymes speed up the breakdown of food into tiny soluble particles.
chunks.source: Enzymes speed up the breakdown of food into tiny soluble particles.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why does absorption of food take place in the ileum? A: It has villi which absorb digested food. The ileum is lined with villi that absorb digested food into the blood.
chunks.source: The ileum is lined with villi that absorb digested food into the blood.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: The diagram shows a section of a human tooth. Name the part marked M. A: Enamel. Part M is the enamel, the hard outer covering of the tooth.
chunks.source: Part M is the enamel, the hard outer covering of the tooth.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: The diagram shows a section of a human tooth. Name the part marked K. A: Gum. Part K is the gum, the soft flesh that holds the tooth firmly in the jaw.
chunks.source: Part K is the gum, the soft flesh that holds the tooth firmly in the jaw.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which mineral salt helps to form part M of the tooth? A: Calcium. Calcium helps to form the enamel (M), making teeth strong and hard.
chunks.source: Calcium helps to form the enamel (M), making teeth strong and hard.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: The diagram shows a section of a human tooth. Give the function of the part labelled N. A: It carries blood and nerves to the tooth. The pulp cavity (N) contains blood vessels and nerves that nourish the tooth and feel pain.
chunks.source: The pulp cavity (N) contains blood vessels and nerves that nourish the tooth and feel pain.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How do enzymes speed up the digestion of food? A: By breaking food into tiny soluble particles quickly. Enzymes break large food molecules into tiny soluble ones very fast.
chunks.source: Enzymes break large food molecules into tiny soluble ones very fast.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: By what process does food move through the alimentary canal? A: Peristalsis. Peristalsis is the wave-like squeezing of the gut walls that pushes food along the alimentary canal.
chunks.source: Peristalsis is the wave-like squeezing of the gut walls that pushes food along the alimentary canal.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What causes constipation? A: Lack of roughages in the diet. Without enough roughage, undigested food moves too slowly and too much water is absorbed, causing constipation.
chunks.source: Without enough roughage, undigested food moves too slowly and too much water is absorbed, causing constipation.

chunks.subject: Science
