chunks.source: Dancing and storytelling are events.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words what **tradition** means. A: Tradition is a practice passed down from older people to younger people.
chunks.source: Tradition is a practice passed down from older people to younger people.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: What **rites** did the elders share? A: The elders shared rites that honor ancestors.
chunks.source: The elders shared rites that honor ancestors.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Boys and Girls Together. I can explain how boys and girls are equal and show respect in work and play. Boys and girls are **equal** and should **respect** each other in **work** and **play**. Keywords: gender: being a boy or a girl; equal: having the same rights and chances; respect: treating others kindly; boys: male children; girls: female children; work: tasks that need effort; play: games and fun activities
chunks.source: Boys and girls are **equal** and should **respect** each other in **work** and **play**.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: What does **gender** mean? A: Gender means being a boy or a girl.
chunks.source: Gender means being a boy or a girl.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: How are **boys** and **girls** **equal** in the story? A: They both work in the garden and play together.
chunks.source: They both work in the garden and play together.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Give an example of **respect** from the lesson. A: The children help each other carry water.
chunks.source: The children help each other carry water.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: What **work** do the children share? A: They share garden tools and carry water.
chunks.source: They share garden tools and carry water.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words what **equal** means. A: Equal means everyone gets the same chance.
chunks.source: Equal means everyone gets the same chance.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Why is **play** important for both **boys** and **girls**? A: Play helps them learn together and have fun.
chunks.source: Play helps them learn together and have fun.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Keeping Our Culture Alive. I can describe how preservation, promotion, and tolerance keep traditions alive. Preservation, promotion, and tolerance keep our traditions, stories, and practices alive. Keywords: preservation: keeping something safe for the future; promotion: sharing something with more people; tolerance: accepting different practices; practices: usual ways of doing things; tradition: a practice passed down from older people; stories: tales told to teach history
chunks.source: Preservation, promotion, and tolerance keep our traditions, stories, and practices alive.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: What is **preservation**? A: Preservation is keeping traditions safe for the future.
chunks.source: Preservation is keeping traditions safe for the future.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: How does **promotion** help culture? A: Promotion shares culture with more people.
chunks.source: Promotion shares culture with more people.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Give an example of **tolerance** from the story. A: Accepting different practices of other groups.
chunks.source: Accepting different practices of other groups.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: What **practices** did the elders show? A: They showed building a hut and cooking matooke.
chunks.source: They showed building a hut and cooking matooke.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words why **stories** are important. A: Stories carry history and teach values.
chunks.source: Stories carry history and teach values.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: What **tradition** was shared in the lesson? A: Cooking matooke and building a hut are traditions.
chunks.source: Cooking matooke and building a hut are traditions.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Keeping Our Bodies Healthy. I can describe a healthy daily routine. A daily routine of washing, clean eating, exercise, and sleep keeps our bodies healthy and strong. Keywords: routine: a fixed order of doing things; eating: putting food in the mouth; wash: clean with water and soap; clean: free from dirt; exercise: move the body to stay fit; sleep: rest with eyes closed
chunks.source: A daily routine of washing, clean eating, exercise, and sleep keeps our bodies healthy and strong.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: What is a **routine**? A: A fixed order of doing things each day.
chunks.source: A fixed order of doing things each day.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Why do we **wash** hands before **eating**? A: To remove dirt and germs so we stay healthy.
chunks.source: To remove dirt and germs so we stay healthy.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Name two kinds of **exercise** Amina does. A: Running and jumping.
chunks.source: Running and jumping.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: How does **sleep** help Amina? A: Sleep helps her brain grow and body rest.
chunks.source: Sleep helps her brain grow and body rest.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words why a healthy **routine** is important. A: A healthy routine with washing, eating well, exercise, and sleep keeps our bodies strong and free from sickness.
chunks.source: A healthy routine with washing, eating well, exercise, and sleep keeps our bodies strong and free from sickness.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: What does **clean** water do for us? A: Clean water washes away germs and keeps us healthy.
chunks.source: Clean water washes away germs and keeps us healthy.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Diseases and Prevention. I can explain how prevention stops diseases spread by vectors. Prevention stops diseases like malaria, HIV, and AIDS by controlling vectors and practicing safe habits. Keywords: diseases: sicknesses that spread; prevention: stopping something before it happens; vectors: animals that carry disease; malaria: fever disease from mosquitoes; hiv: virus that weakens the body; aids: sickness caused by HIV
chunks.source: Prevention stops diseases like malaria, HIV, and AIDS by controlling vectors and practicing safe habits.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: What are **vectors**? A: Small animals like mosquitoes that carry diseases.
chunks.source: Small animals like mosquitoes that carry diseases.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: How does **prevention** stop **malaria**? A: Sleeping under treated nets stops mosquito vectors from biting.
chunks.source: Sleeping under treated nets stops mosquito vectors from biting.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: What is the difference between **HIV** and **AIDS**? A: HIV is the virus; AIDS is the sickness it causes.
chunks.source: HIV is the virus; AIDS is the sickness it causes.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Name two ways to prevent **HIV**. A: Use clean needles and safe blood; do not share sharp tools.
chunks.source: Use clean needles and safe blood; do not share sharp tools.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words why knowing **vectors** helps **prevention**. A: If we know mosquitoes are vectors, we can use nets to stop them spreading malaria.
chunks.source: If we know mosquitoes are vectors, we can use nets to stop them spreading malaria.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: What **diseases** did Teacher Nankya teach about? A: Malaria, HIV, and AIDS.
chunks.source: Malaria, HIV, and AIDS.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Keeping Clean Every Day. I can describe the steps of daily ablutions using water, soap, and a brush. Daily ablutions with water, soap, brushing, and heeding warnings keep us clean and healthy. Keywords: ablutions: daily cleaning acts; bathe: wash the whole body; brush: clean teeth with a brush; soap: substance for cleaning; water: liquid for washing; warnings: safety notices on products
chunks.source: Daily ablutions with water, soap, brushing, and heeding warnings keep us clean and healthy.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: What are **ablutions**? A: Daily cleaning acts like bathing and brushing teeth.
chunks.source: Daily cleaning acts like bathing and brushing teeth.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Why do we use **soap** with **water**? A: Soap removes dirt and germs better than water alone.
chunks.source: Soap removes dirt and germs better than water alone.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: When should you **brush** your teeth? A: Brush teeth after bathing in the morning and before sleep at night.
chunks.source: Brush teeth after bathing in the morning and before sleep at night.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: What do **warnings** on soap tell us? A: Warnings tell us to keep soap out of eyes and not to drink it.
chunks.source: Warnings tell us to keep soap out of eyes and not to drink it.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words why **ablutions** are important every day. A: Ablutions keep our bodies clean, remove germs, and stop diseases so we stay healthy.
chunks.source: Ablutions keep our bodies clean, remove germs, and stop diseases so we stay healthy.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: What happens if you **bathe** without **soap**? A: Dirt and germs may stay on skin; soap helps wash them away.
chunks.source: Dirt and germs may stay on skin; soap helps wash them away.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Things Made by People. I can name things made by people and say if they are natural or artificial. People use **technology** to make things from **materials**. Some **materials** are **natural** like wood. Some are **artificial** like plastic. Each has a different **texture**. Keywords: technology: tools and ways people make things; made: created by people; materials: what things are made from; natural: from nature, not made by people; artificial: made by people, not from nature; texture: how something feels when touched
chunks.source: People use **technology** to make things from **materials**. Some **materials** are **natural** like wood. Some are **artificial** like plastic. Each has a different **texture**.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: What is **technology**? A: Tools and ways people make things, like a bicycle.
chunks.source: Tools and ways people make things, like a bicycle.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Give an example of something **made** by people. A: A house, a bucket, a mat.
chunks.source: A house, a bucket, a mat.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Name two **materials** that are **natural**. A: Wood and clay.
chunks.source: Wood and clay.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Name two **materials** that are **artificial**. A: Plastic and metal.
chunks.source: Plastic and metal.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: What does **texture** mean? Explain in your own words. A: Texture is how something feels when you touch it, like rough or smooth.
chunks.source: Texture is how something feels when you touch it, like rough or smooth.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Why is a clay pot **natural** but a plastic bucket **artificial**? A: Clay comes from the earth. Plastic is made by people in factories.
chunks.source: Clay comes from the earth. Plastic is made by people in factories.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Materials Around Us. I can identify common solids and say what they are made of. **Solids** keep their shape. Common **materials** are **wood**, **clay**, **metal**, and **plastic**. **Wood** and **clay** are **natural**. **Metal** and **plastic** are often **artificial**. Keywords: materials: what things are made from; solids: hard things that keep their shape; wood: material from trees; clay: soft earth used for pots; metal: strong, shiny material from rocks; plastic: light, artificial material
chunks.source: **Solids** keep their shape. Common **materials** are **wood**, **clay**, **metal**, and **plastic**. **Wood** and **clay** are **natural**. **Metal** and **plastic** are often **artificial**.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: What are **solids**? A: Hard things that keep their shape, like wood or stone.
chunks.source: Hard things that keep their shape, like wood or stone.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Name three **materials** that are **natural**. A: Wood, clay, stone.
chunks.source: Wood, clay, stone.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Name two **materials** that are **artificial**. A: Plastic and metal.
chunks.source: Plastic and metal.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Why is **metal** good for a hoe? A: It is strong and does not break easily.
chunks.source: It is strong and does not break easily.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Describe the **texture** of **plastic**. A: Smooth and light.
chunks.source: Smooth and light.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words the difference between **wood** and **plastic**. A: Wood comes from trees, it is natural. Plastic is made in factories, it is artificial.
chunks.source: Wood comes from trees, it is natural. Plastic is made in factories, it is artificial.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Following Instructions. I can follow and give simple instructions to make something. **Instructions** are **steps** to **make** or **build** something. Read all **steps** first. Get your **tools**. **Describe** what you will **make**. Follow each **step** in order. Keywords: instructions: steps that tell you how to do something; describe: say what something is like; build: put parts together to make something; tools: things that help you work; steps: the order of actions; make: create something new
chunks.source: **Instructions** are **steps** to **make** or **build** something. Read all **steps** first. Get your **tools**. **Describe** what you will **make**. Follow each **step** in order.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: What are **instructions**? A: Steps that tell you how to do something.
chunks.source: Steps that tell you how to do something.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Why should you read all **steps** before you **build**? A: So you know what **tools** and **materials** you need.
chunks.source: So you know what **tools** and **materials** you need.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Name two **tools** you need to **build** a wooden box. A: Saw and hammer.
chunks.source: Saw and hammer.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: What does **describe** mean? A: Say what something is like, its shape, size, or parts.
chunks.source: Say what something is like, its shape, size, or parts.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Give **instructions** to **make** a paper boat in three **steps**. A: Step 1: Get a paper. Step 2: Fold corners. Step 3: Open the bottom.
chunks.source: Step 1: Get a paper. Step 2: Fold corners. Step 3: Open the bottom.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words why following **steps** in order is important. A: If you skip a step, the thing you make might not work or fall apart.
chunks.source: If you skip a step, the thing you make might not work or fall apart.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Energy Around Us. I can name different forms of energy and say how we use them. **Energy** makes things happen. The **sun** gives **light** and **heat**. Fire gives **heat**. Fuel and **electricity** give **power**. We **use** **energy** every day. Keywords: energy: the power to do work; light: brightness that helps us see; power: strength or force to make things work; heat: warmth from fire or the sun; sun: the big star that gives light and heat; use: to do something with a tool or thing
chunks.source: **Energy** makes things happen. The **sun** gives **light** and **heat**. Fire gives **heat**. Fuel and **electricity** give **power**. We **use** **energy** every day.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Name two things that give us **light**. A: The **sun** and a **lamp**.
chunks.source: The **sun** and a **lamp**.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: What **energy** cooks our food? A: **Heat** from fire or a stove.
chunks.source: **Heat** from fire or a stove.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Complete: The **sun** gives us ____ and ____. A: **Light** and **heat**.
chunks.source: **Light** and **heat**.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: What does **power** do? A: **Power** makes things work or move.
chunks.source: **Power** makes things work or move.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: In your own words, what is **energy**? (Model: **Energy** is the power to do work, like move, heat, or light.) A: **Energy** is the power to do work.
chunks.source: **Energy** is the power to do work.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Solar Power. I can explain how solar power works and name its parts. **Solar power** is **electricity** from the **sun**. A **panel** catches **sunlight** and makes **electricity**. A battery stores it. The **lamp** uses it at night. The **sun** is free and always there. Keywords: solar: from the sun; solar power: energy from the sun changed into electricity; electricity: power that runs lights, phones, radios; panel: a flat board that catches sunlight; lamp: a small light that uses electricity; sun: the star that gives light and heat
chunks.source: **Solar power** is **electricity** from the **sun**. A **panel** catches **sunlight** and makes **electricity**. A battery stores it. The **lamp** uses it at night. The **sun** is free and always there.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: What does a **solar panel** do? A: It changes **sunlight** into **electricity**.
chunks.source: It changes **sunlight** into **electricity**.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: What stores **solar power** for night? A: A battery.
chunks.source: A battery.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Name one thing **solar power** can run. A: A **lamp**, a phone, or a radio.
chunks.source: A **lamp**, a phone, or a radio.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Why is **solar power** helpful in the village? A: It works when **electricity** lines fail.
chunks.source: It works when **electricity** lines fail.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: In your own words, how does **solar power** reach the **lamp**? (Model: The **panel** catches **sunlight**, makes **electricity**, wire carries it to battery, battery runs the **lamp**.) A: The **panel** catches **sunlight** and makes **electricity**. A wire takes it to a battery. The battery runs the **lamp**.
chunks.source: The **panel** catches **sunlight** and makes **electricity**. A wire takes it to a battery. The battery runs the **lamp**.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Saving Energy and Staying Safe. I can list ways to save energy and stay safe with electricity and fire. **Saving** **energy** means not **waste**ing **power**. **Switch off** lights and radios. **Fire** and **electricity** have **dangers**. Be **careful**: keep water near **fire**, never touch wires, tell an adult about problems. Keywords: saving: keeping something for later, not wasting; waste: to use more than you need; dangers: things that can hurt you; switch off: to turn off a light or machine; careful: watching out for danger; fire: hot flames that burn
chunks.source: **Saving** **energy** means not **waste**ing **power**. **Switch off** lights and radios. **Fire** and **electricity** have **dangers**. Be **careful**: keep water near **fire**, never touch wires, tell an adult about problems.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: What does **switch off** mean? A: To turn off a light or machine.
chunks.source: To turn off a light or machine.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Name one **danger** of **fire**. A: It can burn you or the house.
chunks.source: It can burn you or the house.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: How do we **waste** **energy**? A: Leaving lights on when not needed.
chunks.source: Leaving lights on when not needed.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: What should you do if you see a bare wire? A: Tell an adult. Do not touch it.
chunks.source: Tell an adult. Do not touch it.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: In your own words, tell two ways to be **careful** with **electricity**. (Model: **Switch off** when done. Do not touch wires. Keep water away from sockets.) A: **Switch off** appliances. Do not touch bare wires. Keep water away from sockets.
chunks.source: **Switch off** appliances. Do not touch bare wires. Keep water away from sockets.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Place Value to 10,000. I can identify the place value of digits in numbers up to 10,000. Each digit in a number up to 10,000 has a place value: thousands, hundreds, tens, or ones. Keywords: thousands: groups of one thousand; hundreds: groups of one hundred; tens: groups of ten; ones: single units; place value: the value of a digit by its position
chunks.source: Each digit in a number up to 10,000 has a place value: thousands, hundreds, tens, or ones.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: What is the place value of 7 in 7,214? A: Thousands
chunks.source: Thousands

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Write the value of the digit 6 in 6,305. A: Six thousands
chunks.source: Six thousands

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Which digit is in the hundreds place in 4,582? A: 5

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words what place value means. A: Place value shows how much a digit is worth based on its position.
chunks.source: Place value shows how much a digit is worth based on its position.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: What number has 2 thousands, 3 hundreds, 4 tens, and 5 ones? A: 2,345

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: If you add one thousand to 3,999, what is the new number? A: 4,999

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Adding Big Numbers. I can add four-digit numbers with regrouping. Adding four‑digit numbers uses columns, carry, and regroup to find the sum. Keywords: add: put numbers together; sum: the result of adding; carry: move extra value to next column; regroup: rearrange groups when adding; total: the final amount after adding
chunks.source: Adding four‑digit numbers uses columns, carry, and regroup to find the sum.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: What is the sum of 4,006 + 3,994? A: 8,000

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: When adding 7,889 + 1,111, what do you carry from the ones column? A: Carry 1 to the tens column
chunks.source: Carry 1 to the tens column

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words what it means to regroup when adding. A: Regroup means moving a group of ten to the next column when a column exceeds nine.
chunks.source: Regroup means moving a group of ten to the next column when a column exceeds nine.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: If you add 9,999 + 1, what is the result? A: 10,000

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Subtracting Big Numbers. I can subtract four-digit numbers with regrouping. Subtracting four‑digit numbers uses borrow and regroup to find the difference. Keywords: subtract: take one number away from another; difference: the result of subtracting; borrow: take one group from the next column; regroup: rearrange groups when subtracting; remain: what is left after subtracting
chunks.source: Subtracting four‑digit numbers uses borrow and regroup to find the difference.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Find the difference between 7,500 and 3,278. A: 4,222

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: When subtracting 6,004 - 2,789, what do you borrow from the hundreds column? A: Borrow 1 hundred to make 10 tens.
chunks.source: Borrow 1 hundred to make 10 tens.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words what it means to regroup when subtracting. A: Regroup means breaking a higher place value into ten of the next lower place to subtract.
chunks.source: Regroup means breaking a higher place value into ten of the next lower place to subtract.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: What remains after 9,999 - 5,555? A: 4,444

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: If you have 8,000 shillings and spend 3,456, how much remains? A: 4,544

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Ordering Big Numbers. I can compare and order numbers up to 10,000. To order numbers up to 10,000, compare each place value starting with thousands, then hundreds, tens, and ones. Keywords: order: put things in a line from smallest to biggest; greatest: the biggest number; smallest: the little number; compare: look at two numbers to see which is bigger; number line: a line that shows numbers in order
chunks.source: To order numbers up to 10,000, compare each place value starting with thousands, then hundreds, tens, and ones.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Order these numbers from smallest to greatest: 5,200; 4,800; 5,100; 4,950. A: 4,800; 4,950; 5,100; 5,200

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Which is the greatest: 7,345 or 7,354? A: 7,354

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Place 3,210 on a number line between 3,000 and 4,000. Where does it go? A: Closer to 3,000 because the hundreds digit is 2.
chunks.source: Closer to 3,000 because the hundreds digit is 2.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words how to order numbers up to 10,000. A: Write the numbers, compare thousands, then hundreds, then tens, then ones, and write them from smallest to greatest.
chunks.source: Write the numbers, compare thousands, then hundreds, then tens, then ones, and write them from smallest to greatest.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: If you have 6,789 and 6,798, which is smaller? A: 6,789

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Write the steps for ordering big numbers. A: Step 1: Write numbers. Step 2: Compare thousands. Step 3: Compare hundreds. Step 4: Compare tens. Step 5: Compare ones. Step 6: Write in order.
chunks.source: Step 1: Write numbers. Step 2: Compare thousands. Step 3: Compare hundreds. Step 4: Compare tens. Step 5: Compare ones. Step 6: Write in order.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Rounding Off Numbers. I can round numbers to the nearest 10 and 100 and use rounding to estimate. To round off, look at the digit right of the place you want. If it is 5 or more, round up; otherwise round down. Keywords: round off: change a number to a nearby easier number; nearest ten: the closest multiple of ten; nearest hundred: the closest multiple of one hundred; estimate: make a good guess using rounding; about: close to a number but not exact
chunks.source: To round off, look at the digit right of the place you want. If it is 5 or more, round up; otherwise round down.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Round 3,241 to the nearest ten. A: 3,240

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Round 3,241 to the nearest hundred. A: 3,200

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Estimate the sum of 4,567 + 2,389 by rounding each to the nearest hundred. A: 4,600 + 2,400 = 7,000

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words how to round a number to the nearest ten. A: Look at the ones digit. If it is 5 or more, increase the tens digit by one. Then change the ones to zero.
chunks.source: Look at the ones digit. If it is 5 or more, increase the tens digit by one. Then change the ones to zero.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: A boda fare is 1,876 shillings. Round it to the nearest hundred. A: 1,900

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Round 9,995 to the nearest ten. A: 10,000

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Number Patterns and Multiples. I can find multiples, describe patterns, and state the rule for a sequence. A multiple comes from skip counting. The rule tells you the step. The pattern shows the sequence. Keywords: multiple: a number you get by skip counting; pattern: a repeated design in numbers; sequence: an ordered list of numbers; skip count: count forward by a fixed number; rule: the instruction that tells how the pattern grows
chunks.source: A multiple comes from skip counting. The rule tells you the step. The pattern shows the sequence.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Write the first five multiples of 7. A: 7, 14, 21, 28, 35

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: What is the rule for the pattern 2, 4, 6, 8, 10? A: Add 2 each time.
chunks.source: Add 2 each time.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Continue the sequence: 9, 18, 27, __, __. A: 36, 45

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words what a multiple is. A: A multiple is a number you get when you skip count by another number.
chunks.source: A multiple is a number you get when you skip count by another number.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Which of these is not a multiple of 3: 12, 15, 22, 27? A: 22

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Skip count by 8 up to 40. A: 8, 16, 24, 32, 40

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Money: Notes to 10,000. I can name Ugandan notes and coins up to 10,000 shillings and say their value. Ugandan notes come in 1,000, 2,000, 5,000 and 10,000 shillings; each note shows its value and the bank prints them. Keywords: note: a paper piece of money; shilling: the unit of Ugandan money; money: coins and notes used to buy things; value: how much something is worth; bank: a place that keeps money safe
chunks.source: Ugandan notes come in 1,000, 2,000, 5,000 and 10,000 shillings; each note shows its value and the bank prints them.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: What is the value of a 2,000 shilling note? A: 2,000 shillings
chunks.source: 2,000 shillings

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Which note is worth 10,000 shillings? A: The 10,000 shilling note
chunks.source: The 10,000 shilling note

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: How many shillings are in a 5,000 note? A: 5,000 shillings
chunks.source: 5,000 shillings

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Where does the bank keep the money safe? A: In the bank vault
chunks.source: In the bank vault

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words what 'value' means for money. A: Value means how many shillings a note is worth.
chunks.source: Value means how many shillings a note is worth.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: If you have a 1,000 note and a 2,000 note, what is the total value? A: 3,000 shillings
chunks.source: 3,000 shillings

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Adding and Subtracting Money. I can add and subtract money amounts and find change. To find change, subtract the cost from the amount paid; add to find totals. Keywords: add: put numbers together; subtract: take one number away from another; change: money given back after paying; cost: the price you pay for something; total: the whole amount altogether
chunks.source: To find change, subtract the cost from the amount paid; add to find totals.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: If you pay 5,000 shillings for an item that costs 3,200 shillings, how much change do you get? A: 1,800 shillings
chunks.source: 1,800 shillings

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Add 2,500 shillings and 1,300 shillings. What is the total? A: 3,800 shillings
chunks.source: 3,800 shillings

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Subtract 1,200 shillings from 4,000 shillings. What is the result? A: 2,800 shillings
chunks.source: 2,800 shillings

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: A book costs 2,700 shillings. You give a 5,000 note. How much change? A: 2,300 shillings
chunks.source: 2,300 shillings

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words how you find change when you pay with a larger note. A: You subtract the cost from the amount you gave.
chunks.source: You subtract the cost from the amount you gave.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: What is the total cost of two items priced 1,500 and 2,200 shillings? A: 3,700 shillings
chunks.source: 3,700 shillings

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Market Word Problems. I can solve market word problems using addition and subtraction. Market problems use price, buy, sell and altogether; add to find totals, subtract to find change. Keywords: problem: a question that needs an answer; buy: to get something by paying money; sell: to give something for money; price: the amount of money for one item; altogether: the total amount combined
chunks.source: Market problems use price, buy, sell and altogether; add to find totals, subtract to find change.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: A pineapple costs 2,000 shillings. If you buy 3, what is the altogether price? A: 6,000 shillings
chunks.source: 6,000 shillings

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: You sell 4 tomatoes at 500 shillings each. How much money do you get altogether? A: 2,000 shillings
chunks.source: 2,000 shillings

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: If the price of a bunch of bananas is 1,500 shillings and you buy 2, what is the total cost? A: 3,000 shillings
chunks.source: 3,000 shillings

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: A customer buys a 3,000 shilling item and pays with a 5,000 note. How much change? A: 2,000 shillings
chunks.source: 2,000 shillings

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words what 'altogether' means in a market problem. A: Altogether means the total cost of all items combined.
chunks.source: Altogether means the total cost of all items combined.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Write a short market problem using the words buy, sell, price, and altogether. A: Example: I sell apples at 1,000 price each. A friend buys 3. Altogether he pays 3,000.
chunks.source: Example: I sell apples at 1,000 price each. A friend buys 3. Altogether he pays 3,000.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Measuring Length. I can measure length using metres and centimetres. We measure length using metre, centimetre, and kilometre. One metre equals 100 centimetres, and one kilometre equals 1000 metres. Keywords: metre: a unit of length; centimetre: a small unit of length; kilometre: a large unit of length; measure: to find the size of something; length: how long something is
chunks.source: We measure length using metre, centimetre, and kilometre. One metre equals 100 centimetres, and one kilometre equals 1000 metres.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: How many centimetres in one metre? A: 100 centimetres.
chunks.source: 100 centimetres.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Convert 3 metres to centimetres. A: 300 centimetres.
chunks.source: 300 centimetres.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: What unit would you use to measure the distance from home to school? A: kilometre.
chunks.source: kilometre.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: If a rope is 250 centimetres, how many metres is that? A: 2 metres and 50 centimetres.
chunks.source: 2 metres and 50 centimetres.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words how to change metres to centimetres. A: Multiply the number of metres by 100 to get centimetres.
chunks.source: Multiply the number of metres by 100 to get centimetres.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Which is longer: 1 kilometre or 900 metres? A: 1 kilometre (1000 metres) is longer.
chunks.source: 1 kilometre (1000 metres) is longer.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Mass: Kilograms and Grams. I can measure mass using kilograms and grams. We measure mass using kilogram and gram. One kilogram equals 1000 grams. Keywords: kilogram: a unit of mass; gram: a small unit of mass; mass: the amount of matter in an object; weigh: to find how heavy something is; scale: a tool for measuring mass
chunks.source: We measure mass using kilogram and gram. One kilogram equals 1000 grams.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: How many grams in one kilogram? A: 1000 grams.
chunks.source: 1000 grams.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Convert 4 kilograms to grams. A: 4000 grams.
chunks.source: 4000 grams.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: What unit would you use to measure the mass of a letter? A: gram.
chunks.source: gram.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: If a bag of rice is 3500 grams, how many kilograms is that? A: 3 kilograms and 500 grams.
chunks.source: 3 kilograms and 500 grams.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words how to change kilograms to grams. A: Multiply the number of kilograms by 1000 to get grams.
chunks.source: Multiply the number of kilograms by 1000 to get grams.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Which is heavier: 2 kilograms or 1500 grams? A: 2 kilograms (2000 grams) is heavier.
chunks.source: 2 kilograms (2000 grams) is heavier.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Capacity: Litres and Millilitres. I can measure capacity using litres and millilitres. We measure capacity using litre and millilitre. One litre equals 1000 millilitres. Keywords: litre: a unit of capacity; millilitre: a small unit of capacity; capacity: the amount a container can hold; measure: to find the size or amount; jug: a container for liquids
chunks.source: We measure capacity using litre and millilitre. One litre equals 1000 millilitres.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: How many millilitres in one litre? A: 1000 millilitres.
chunks.source: 1000 millilitres.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Convert 5 litres to millilitres. A: 5000 millilitres.
chunks.source: 5000 millilitres.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: What unit would you use to measure the capacity of a tea cup? A: millilitre.
chunks.source: millilitre.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: If a tank holds 2500 millilitres, how many litres is that? A: 2 litres and 500 millilitres.
chunks.source: 2 litres and 500 millilitres.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words how to change litres to millilitres. A: Multiply the number of litres by 1000 to get millilitres.
chunks.source: Multiply the number of litres by 1000 to get millilitres.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Which holds more: 1 litre or 900 millilitres? A: 1 litre (1000 millilitres) holds more.
chunks.source: 1 litre (1000 millilitres) holds more.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Collecting Weather Data. I can collect weather data using tally marks and tables. We collect **weather data** by making **tally** marks in a **table**. Then we **count** and **record** totals to see which weather is **most**. Keywords: data: information collected; tally: marks to count; record: write down; count: find how many; table: chart with rows and columns
chunks.source: We collect **weather data** by making **tally** marks in a **table**. Then we **count** and **record** totals to see which weather is **most**.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: What is **data**? A: Information we collect, like weather types.
chunks.source: Information we collect, like weather types.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: How do you show five with **tally** marks? A: Four lines and a cross: ||||
chunks.source: Four lines and a cross: ||||

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Why do we **record** totals in a **table**? A: To keep the **data** neat and easy to read.
chunks.source: To keep the **data** neat and easy to read.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: If you **count** three cloudy days, what **tally** do you draw? A: Three lines: |||
chunks.source: Three lines: |||

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words how to make a weather **table**. A: Draw columns for each weather type. Add **tally** marks each day. **Count** and write totals at the end.
chunks.source: Draw columns for each weather type. Add **tally** marks each day. **Count** and write totals at the end.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: What does the **table** tell you about the week's weather? A: It shows which weather happened **most** and **fewest**.
chunks.source: It shows which weather happened **most** and **fewest**.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Drawing Bar Graphs. I can draw and read a bar graph to show data. We draw a **bar graph** using **data** from a **table**. The **axis** lines hold categories and numbers. Bars show which is **most** and **fewest**. Keywords: bar graph: chart with bars; data: information collected; axis: lines with numbers or labels; most: largest amount; fewest: smallest amount
chunks.source: We draw a **bar graph** using **data** from a **table**. The **axis** lines hold categories and numbers. Bars show which is **most** and **fewest**.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: What is a **bar graph**? A: A chart with bars that show **data** amounts.
chunks.source: A chart with bars that show **data** amounts.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: What does the vertical **axis** show? A: Numbers that measure the **data**.
chunks.source: Numbers that measure the **data**.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: If Sunny has 5 and Rainy has 2, which is **most**? A: Sunny is **most**.
chunks.source: Sunny is **most**.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Which weather is **fewest** if Cloudy=1, Rainy=3? A: Cloudy is **fewest**.
chunks.source: Cloudy is **fewest**.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words how to draw a **bar graph** from a **table**. A: Draw **axis** lines. Label horizontal with categories. Label vertical with numbers. Draw bars to match **data**.
chunks.source: Draw **axis** lines. Label horizontal with categories. Label vertical with numbers. Draw bars to match **data**.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Why use a **bar graph** instead of a **table**? A: It lets you see **most** and **fewest** quickly.
chunks.source: It lets you see **most** and **fewest** quickly.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Reading Picture Graphs. I can read a picture graph and answer questions about the data. A **picture graph** uses **symbol**s to show **data**. Read the key, **count** **symbol**s, **compare** totals, and **answer** questions. Keywords: picture graph: graph with pictures; symbol: picture that stands for a number; data: information collected; compare: look at two things to see difference; answer: give a response to a question
chunks.source: A **picture graph** uses **symbol**s to show **data**. Read the key, **count** **symbol**s, **compare** totals, and **answer** questions.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: What is a **picture graph**? A: A graph that uses **symbol**s to show **data**.
chunks.source: A graph that uses **symbol**s to show **data**.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: If 1 **symbol** = 3 books, what do 2 **symbol**s mean? A: 6 books.
chunks.source: 6 books.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: How do you **compare** two rows on a **picture graph**? A: **Count** **symbol**s in each row, use the key, then see which is more.
chunks.source: **Count** **symbol**s in each row, use the key, then see which is more.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: What does the key on a **picture graph** tell you? A: How many items each **symbol** stands for.
chunks.source: How many items each **symbol** stands for.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words how to **answer** 'which is most?' using a **picture graph**. A: **Count** **symbol**s for each row. Use the key to find totals. The row with the biggest total is **most**.
chunks.source: **Count** **symbol**s for each row. Use the key to find totals. The row with the biggest total is **most**.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Why must you read the key before you **compare** **data**? A: The key tells you the value of each **symbol**. Without it, your **answer** will be wrong.
chunks.source: The key tells you the value of each **symbol**. Without it, your **answer** will be wrong.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Times Tables: 2, 3, 4 and 5. I can use the times table for 2, 3, 4 and 5 to multiply and find the product. Amina uses the times table for 2, 3, 4, and 5 to multiply quickly and find the product. Keywords: times table: a chart that shows multiplication facts; multiply: to add equal groups together; groups: sets of the same number; product: the answer when you multiply; twos: the number two repeated
chunks.source: Amina uses the times table for 2, 3, 4, and 5 to multiply quickly and find the product.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: What is 2 × 6? A: 12

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: What is 3 × 5? A: 15

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: What is 4 × 4? A: 16

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: What is 5 × 3? A: 15

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Explain how you find 4 × 5 using groups. A: Make 4 groups of 5, then count all to get 20.
chunks.source: Make 4 groups of 5, then count all to get 20.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Write the product of 5 × 4. A: 20

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Times Tables: 6 to 10. I can use the times table for 6, 7, 8, 9 and 10 to multiply and find the product. Peter uses the times table for 6 to 10 to multiply distances and find the product quickly. Keywords: times table: a chart that shows multiplication facts; multiply: to add equal groups together; product: the answer when you multiply; groups: sets of the same number; tens: the digit in the ten place
chunks.source: Peter uses the times table for 6 to 10 to multiply distances and find the product quickly.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: What is 6 × 4? A: 24

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: What is 7 × 5? A: 35

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: What is 8 × 3? A: 24

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: What is 9 × 2? A: 18

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Explain how you find 8 × 6 using groups. A: Make 8 groups of 6, count all to get 48.
chunks.source: Make 8 groups of 6, count all to get 48.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Write the product of 10 × 4. A: 40

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Multiplying Two-Digit Numbers. I can multiply a two-digit number by a one-digit number using tens and ones. Kato multiplies two-digit numbers by separating tens and ones, then adds the parts to get the product. Keywords: multiply: to add equal groups together; two-digit: a number with two digits like 23; product: the answer when you multiply; tens: the digit in the ten place; ones: the digit in the one place
chunks.source: Kato multiplies two-digit numbers by separating tens and ones, then adds the parts to get the product.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: What is 12 × 3? A: 36

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: What is 24 × 2? A: 48

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: What is 15 × 4? A: 60

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: What is 31 × 3? A: 93

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Explain how you multiply 26 × 3 using tens and ones. A: Multiply ones 6×3=18, multiply tens 20×3=60, add 60+18=78.
chunks.source: Multiply ones 6×3=18, multiply tens 20×3=60, add 60+18=78.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Write the product of 42 × 2. A: 84

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Division as Sharing and Grouping. I can divide numbers by sharing and grouping and find the quotient. Division means to **divide** a number into **equal** parts by **sharing** or **grouping**. The answer is the **quotient**. Keywords: divide: to split into parts; share: to give each person a part; group: to put things in equal sets; equal: the same in size or number; quotient: the answer in division
chunks.source: Division means to **divide** a number into **equal** parts by **sharing** or **grouping**. The answer is the **quotient**.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: What is 15 ÷ 3? A: 5

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: If you **share** 20 sweets among 4 children, how many does each get? A: 5

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Make **groups** of 4 from 16 stones. How many **groups**? A: 4

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words what the **quotient** is. A: The quotient is the answer when you divide. For example, in 12 ÷ 3 = 4, the quotient is 4.
chunks.source: The quotient is the answer when you divide. For example, in 12 ÷ 3 = 4, the quotient is 4.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Write a division sentence for: 18 pens **shared** equally among 6 pupils. A: 18 ÷ 6 = 3

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: True or false: When you **divide**, the parts must be **equal**. A: True
chunks.source: True

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Division with Remainders. I can divide numbers and find the remainder when things are left over. When we **divide** and cannot make **equal groups**, the amount **left over** is the **remainder**. The **remainder** is always smaller than the divisor. Keywords: divide: to split into parts; remainder: the amount left over after dividing; left over: not used up in equal groups; share: to give each person a part; group: to put things in equal sets
chunks.source: When we **divide** and cannot make **equal groups**, the amount **left over** is the **remainder**. The **remainder** is always smaller than the divisor.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: What is the **remainder** in 14 ÷ 4? A: 2

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: **Divide** 19 by 6. How many **groups** and what is the **remainder**? A: 3 groups, remainder 1
chunks.source: 3 groups, remainder 1

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: If you **share** 23 sweets among 5 children, how many sweets are **left over**? A: 3

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words what **remainder** means. A: The remainder is what is left over after making equal groups. It is smaller than the number you divide by.
chunks.source: The remainder is what is left over after making equal groups. It is smaller than the number you divide by.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Write the division with remainder: 22 ÷ 7. A: 22 ÷ 7 = 3 remainder 1
chunks.source: 22 ÷ 7 = 3 remainder 1

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: True or false: The **remainder** can be bigger than the number you **divide** by. A: False
chunks.source: False

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Fractions of Shapes. I can identify halves, quarters and thirds of shapes and name the fraction. A **fraction** shows a part of a whole cut into **equal parts**. **Half** = 2 parts, **quarter** = 4 parts, **third** = 3 parts. Keywords: fraction: a part of a whole; half: one of two equal parts; quarter: one of four equal parts; third: one of three equal parts; equal parts: pieces that are the same size
chunks.source: A **fraction** shows a part of a whole cut into **equal parts**. **Half** = 2 parts, **quarter** = 4 parts, **third** = 3 parts.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: What **fraction** is one of two **equal parts**? A: half
chunks.source: half

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: How many **quarters** make one whole? A: 4

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Shade one **third** of a rectangle divided into 3 **equal parts**. A: Shade 1 part out of 3.
chunks.source: Shade 1 part out of 3.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words what **equal parts** means. A: Equal parts means each piece is the same size. No piece is bigger or smaller.
chunks.source: Equal parts means each piece is the same size. No piece is bigger or smaller.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Which is smaller: ½ or ¼? A: ¼
chunks.source: ¼

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Write the **fraction** for one of four **equal parts**. A: ¼
chunks.source: ¼

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Fractions of Quantities. I can find a fraction of a quantity. A fraction of a whole tells a part; multiply the whole by the fraction to find the share. Keywords: fraction: a part of a whole; of: shows the link between fraction and whole; share: to divide equally; part: a piece of the whole; whole: the complete amount
chunks.source: A fraction of a whole tells a part; multiply the whole by the fraction to find the share.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: What is 1/2 **of** 10? A: 5

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: If you **share** 15 mangoes into 3 equal **parts**, how many in each **part**? A: 5

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words how to find a **fraction** **of** a **whole**. A: Count the whole, multiply by the fraction, the result is the part.
chunks.source: Count the whole, multiply by the fraction, the result is the part.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: A basket has 18 **oranges**. What is 2/3 **of** them? A: 12

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Write a **fraction** that shows one **part** of a **whole** divided into 5. A: 1/5

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Comparing Fractions. I can compare and order simple fractions. To compare fractions, make denominators equal then compare numerators; the smaller denominator means a bigger fraction. Keywords: compare: to see which is larger or smaller; bigger: larger in size; smaller: less in size; order: arrange from smallest to biggest; fraction: a part of a whole
chunks.source: To compare fractions, make denominators equal then compare numerators; the smaller denominator means a bigger fraction.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Which is **bigger**: 1/5 or 1/3? A: 1/3

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: **Compare** 2/5 and 3/5. Which is **smaller**? A: 2/5

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: **Order** these **fraction**s from **smallest** to **biggest**: 1/6, 1/2, 1/3. A: 1/6, 1/3, 1/2

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words how to **compare** two **fraction**s. A: Make denominators same, then compare numerators.
chunks.source: Make denominators same, then compare numerators.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: If you have 1/4 of a cake and your friend has 1/3, who has the **bigger** share? A: Friend
chunks.source: Friend

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Write a **fraction** that is **smaller** than 1/2. A: 1/3

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Time: Hours and Minutes. I can tell time to five minutes. The short hand tells the hour, the long hand tells the minute; half past is 30 minutes, quarter is 15 minutes. Keywords: hour: the number the short hand points to; minute: the number the long hand points to; clock: a device that shows time; half past: thirty minutes after the hour; quarter: fifteen minutes past or to the hour
chunks.source: The short hand tells the hour, the long hand tells the minute; half past is 30 minutes, quarter is 15 minutes.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: What time is **half past** 7? A: 7:30

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Write the time for **quarter** past 9. A: 9:15

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: If the **minute** hand points at 12 and the **hour** hand at 5, what is the time? A: 5 o'clock
chunks.source: 5 o'clock

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words how to read **half past** on a **clock**. A: The long hand at 6 means 30 minutes, so it is half past the hour.
chunks.source: The long hand at 6 means 30 minutes, so it is half past the hour.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: The **clock** shows 3:45. How do you say it using **quarter**? A: Quarter to four
chunks.source: Quarter to four

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Draw a **clock** showing **quarter** to 6. A: Long hand at 9, short hand near 6.
chunks.source: Long hand at 9, short hand near 6.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Adding and Subtracting Fractions. I can add and subtract fractions with the same denominator. To add or subtract fractions with the same denominator, keep the denominator and add or subtract the numerators. Keywords: add: put together; subtract: take away; denominator: bottom number; fraction: part of a whole; same: alike
chunks.source: To add or subtract fractions with the same denominator, keep the denominator and add or subtract the numerators.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Write the steps to add 2/6 + 3/6. A: Step 1: Check denominator same (6). Step 2: Add numerators 2+3=5. Step 3: Keep denominator 6. Answer: 5/6.
chunks.source: Step 1: Check denominator same (6). Step 2: Add numerators 2+3=5. Step 3: Keep denominator 6. Answer: 5/6.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Kato has 7/12 of a jackfruit. He gives 3/12 to Peter. How much left? A: 4/12

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words why the denominator stays the same when adding fractions. A: The denominator shows the size of the parts. Adding does not change the part size, only how many parts we have.
chunks.source: The denominator shows the size of the parts. Adding does not change the part size, only how many parts we have.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Equivalent Fractions. I can recognise fractions that are equal in value. Equivalent fractions have different numbers but show the same amount. Multiply or divide top and bottom by the same number to find them. Keywords: equivalent: equal in value; equal: the same amount; fraction: part of a whole; half: one of two equal parts; quarter: one of four equal parts
chunks.source: Equivalent fractions have different numbers but show the same amount. Multiply or divide top and bottom by the same number to find them.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Which fraction is equivalent to 1/3? A: 2/6

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Complete: 3/4 = ?/8 A: 6/8

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Are 2/3 and 4/6 equivalent? Yes or No. A: Yes
chunks.source: Yes

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Write two fractions equivalent to 1/2. A: 2/4, 3/6 (or 4/8, 5/10, etc.)

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words how to check if two fractions are equivalent. A: Multiply or divide the numerator and denominator of one fraction by the same number to see if you get the other fraction.
chunks.source: Multiply or divide the numerator and denominator of one fraction by the same number to see if you get the other fraction.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Mixed Word Problems. I can choose the right operation to solve word problems. Read the problem, find key words, choose the operation, solve step by step, and check your answer. Keywords: problem: a question to solve; operation: add, subtract, multiply or divide; altogether: in total; difference: how much more or less; answer: the result
chunks.source: Read the problem, find key words, choose the operation, solve step by step, and check your answer.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: One pen costs 500 shillings. Amina buys 4 pens. She pays 3,000 shillings. How much change? A: 500 × 4 = 2,000. 3,000 - 2,000 = 1,000 shillings.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Kato has 12 mangoes. He gives 3 to Peter and 4 to Musa. How many left? A: 3 + 4 = 7 given away. 12 - 7 = 5 mangoes.
chunks.source: 3 + 4 = 7 given away. 12 - 7 = 5 mangoes.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: A **matatu** carries 14 passengers. Each pays 800 shillings. How much money **altogether**? A: 14 × 800 = 11,200 shillings.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Nalongo reads 15 pages on Monday, 12 on Tuesday, 18 on Wednesday. How many pages **altogether**? A: 15 + 12 + 18 = 45 pages.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words how you decide which operation to use in a word problem. A: I look for key words: altogether or total means add; difference or left means subtract; groups of same size means multiply; sharing equally means divide.
chunks.source: I look for key words: altogether or total means add; difference or left means subtract; groups of same size means multiply; sharing equally means divide.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Shapes and Right Angles. I can find right angles in shapes around me. A right angle looks like the corner of a book. A square has four equal sides and four right angles. A rectangle also has four right angles but two sides are longer. You can test any corner with a paper corner. Keywords: angle: the space between two lines that meet; right angle: an angle that looks like the corner of a book; corner: the point where two sides meet; shape: the form of an object; square: a shape with four equal sides and four right angles
chunks.source: A right angle looks like the corner of a book. A square has four equal sides and four right angles. A rectangle also has four right angles but two sides are longer. You can test any corner with a paper corner.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: What is a right angle? A: An angle that looks like the corner of a book or exercise book.
chunks.source: An angle that looks like the corner of a book or exercise book.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: How many right angles does a square have? A: Four.
chunks.source: Four.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Name two things at home that have right angles. A: Table, window, book, door, tile (any two).
chunks.source: Table, window, book, door, tile (any two).

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: If a shape has four corners and all are right angles, what could it be? A: A square or a rectangle.
chunks.source: A square or a rectangle.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words how to check if a corner is a right angle. A: Use the corner of an exercise book or a folded paper. Place it in the corner. If it fits exactly, it is a right angle.
chunks.source: Use the corner of an exercise book or a folded paper. Place it in the corner. If it fits exactly, it is a right angle.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Draw a shape with four right angles. What is its name? A: A square or a rectangle.
chunks.source: A square or a rectangle.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Perimeter of Shapes. I can find the perimeter of squares and rectangles. Perimeter is the distance around a shape. For a rectangle, add the two long sides and two short sides. For a square, add all four equal sides or multiply one side by 4. Always measure each side first, then add. Keywords: perimeter: the distance all around a shape; side: one edge of a shape; around: going all the way round; add: put numbers together to find the total; distance: how far it is from one point to another
chunks.source: Perimeter is the distance around a shape. For a rectangle, add the two long sides and two short sides. For a square, add all four equal sides or multiply one side by 4. Always measure each side first, then add.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: What does perimeter mean? A: The distance all around a shape.
chunks.source: The distance all around a shape.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: A rectangle has sides 6 m and 4 m. What is its perimeter? A: 6 + 4 + 6 + 4 = 20 m.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: A square has side 5 m. Find the perimeter. A: 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 = 20 m or 5 × 4 = 20 m.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: If you walk around a square field of side 10 m, what distance do you cover? A: 40 m.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words how to find the perimeter of a rectangle. A: Measure the length and the width. Add them together twice: length + width + length + width. Or multiply (length + width) by 2.
chunks.source: Measure the length and the width. Add them together twice: length + width + length + width. Or multiply (length + width) by 2.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: A rectangular room is 4 m by 3 m. How many metres of skirting board are needed for the perimeter? A: 14 m.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Symmetry. I can find lines of symmetry in shapes and patterns. Symmetry means both halves are the same. The mirror line is where you fold. A square has four mirror lines, a rectangle has two, a circle has many. Fold shapes to check for symmetry in mats, leaves, and patterns. Keywords: symmetry: when one half matches the other half; mirror line: the line where you can fold to make both halves match; half: one of two equal parts; same: exactly alike; fold: bend one part over another
chunks.source: Symmetry means both halves are the same. The mirror line is where you fold. A square has four mirror lines, a rectangle has two, a circle has many. Fold shapes to check for symmetry in mats, leaves, and patterns.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: What is symmetry? A: When one half of a shape matches the other half exactly.
chunks.source: When one half of a shape matches the other half exactly.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: What is a mirror line? A: The line where you fold a shape so both halves match.
chunks.source: The line where you fold a shape so both halves match.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: How many mirror lines does a square have? A: Four.
chunks.source: Four.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: How many mirror lines does a rectangle have? A: Two.
chunks.source: Two.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words how to check if a shape has symmetry. A: Fold the shape in half. If the two halves lie exactly on top of each other, the shape has symmetry. The fold line is the mirror line.
chunks.source: Fold the shape in half. If the two halves lie exactly on top of each other, the shape has symmetry. The fold line is the mirror line.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Draw a shape with only one mirror line. Name it. A: A heart, an isosceles triangle, or an arrow shape.
chunks.source: A heart, an isosceles triangle, or an arrow shape.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Measuring at the Clinic. I can measure medicine in millilitres and weigh in kilograms using a scale. We learned to **measure** medicine in **millilitre** using a **scale**, and to weigh babies in **kilogram** on a **scale**. The correct **dose** keeps us healthy. Keywords: measure: to find how much or how many; millilitre: a small unit for liquid; kilogram: a unit for weight; scale: a tool that shows numbers for weight or volume; dose: the amount of medicine to take at one time
chunks.source: We learned to **measure** medicine in **millilitre** using a **scale**, and to weigh babies in **kilogram** on a **scale**. The correct **dose** keeps us healthy.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: What unit do we use to measure liquid medicine? A: We use **millilitre**.
chunks.source: We use **millilitre**.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: What does the **scale** on a syringe show? A: It shows the number of **millilitre**.
chunks.source: It shows the number of **millilitre**.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: If a baby weighs 4 **kilogram**, what unit is used? A: **kilogram**.
chunks.source: **kilogram**.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: What is a **dose**? A: A **dose** is the amount of medicine to take at one time.
chunks.source: A **dose** is the amount of medicine to take at one time.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words how to measure a 5 **millilitre** dose using a syringe. A: First read the **scale** on the syringe, then pull the plunger until the liquid reaches the 5 **millilitre** mark, then give the medicine.
chunks.source: First read the **scale** on the syringe, then pull the plunger until the liquid reaches the 5 **millilitre** mark, then give the medicine.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Why is it important to **measure** the correct **dose**? A: Too much or too little medicine can be harmful.
chunks.source: Too much or too little medicine can be harmful.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Telling Time to the Minute. I can tell the time to the minute using past and to. We learned to read the **hour** and **minute** hands on a **clock** and say the time using **past** and **to**. Keywords: minute: a unit of time, 60 seconds; hour: a unit of time, 60 minutes; past: used when minutes are before half past; to: used when minutes are after half past; clock: a device that shows time
chunks.source: We learned to read the **hour** and **minute** hands on a **clock** and say the time using **past** and **to**.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: What does the short hand on a **clock** show? A: The **hour**.
chunks.source: The **hour**.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: What does the long hand show? A: The **minute**.
chunks.source: The **minute**.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: When the minute hand is on 10, we say ____. A: 10 **past** the **hour**.
chunks.source: 10 **past** the **hour**.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: When the minute hand is on 55, we say ____. A: 5 **to** the next **hour**.
chunks.source: 5 **to** the next **hour**.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words how to tell 4:30 using **past** or **to**. A: The minute hand is on 6, so it is 30 minutes **past** 4.
chunks.source: The minute hand is on 6, so it is 30 minutes **past** 4.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Why is it useful to tell time to the **minute**? A: To catch the boda boda or reach school on time.
chunks.source: To catch the boda boda or reach school on time.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Clinic Records and Graphs. I can read a clinic table and graph to find the most common illness. We learned to keep a **record**, organise **data** in a **table**, show it on a **graph**, and find the **most** common illness. Keywords: data: information collected as numbers; table: a grid with rows and columns for data; graph: a picture that shows data with bars or lines; record: a written note of each patient's illness; most: the greatest amount or number
chunks.source: We learned to keep a **record**, organise **data** in a **table**, show it on a **graph**, and find the **most** common illness.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: What is a **record** in a clinic? A: A **record** is a written note of each patient's illness.
chunks.source: A **record** is a written note of each patient's illness.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Where do we write the **data** so we can compare easily? A: In a **table**.
chunks.source: In a **table**.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: What does a **graph** show? A: A **graph** shows the **data** with bars or lines.
chunks.source: A **graph** shows the **data** with bars or lines.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: How do we find the **most** common illness from a **graph**? A: Look for the tallest bar.
chunks.source: Look for the tallest bar.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words how to make a **table** from a **record**. A: Write headings like Day, Illness, Number. Then fill each row with the **record** information.
chunks.source: Write headings like Day, Illness, Number. Then fill each row with the **record** information.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Why is it helpful to have both a **table** and a **graph**? A: A **table** gives exact numbers, a **graph** lets us see the **most** quickly.
chunks.source: A **table** gives exact numbers, a **graph** lets us see the **most** quickly.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Solid Shapes. I can identify faces, edges and corners of solid shapes. Solid shapes like cubes and cylinders have faces, edges, and corners that we can count. Keywords: solid: a 3D shape; cube: a box shape with 6 square faces; cylinder: a shape with two circular faces; face: a flat side of a solid; edge: where two faces meet; corner: where edges meet
chunks.source: Solid shapes like cubes and cylinders have faces, edges, and corners that we can count.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: How many faces does a cube have? A: 6

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: How many edges does a cylinder have? A: 2

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: How many corners does a cube have? A: 8

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Name a solid shape you see at home. A: A box is a cube.
chunks.source: A box is a cube.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words what an edge is. A: An edge is where two faces meet.
chunks.source: An edge is where two faces meet.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: If you have 2 cubes, how many faces altogether? A: 12 (2 × 6 = 12)

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Measuring and Estimating Length. I can estimate and measure length in metres. Estimating gives a close guess; measuring gives the exact length in metres. Keywords: estimate: guess a close number; measure: find exact size; metre: unit of length; length: how long something is; about: close to
chunks.source: Estimating gives a close guess; measuring gives the exact length in metres.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: What does it mean to estimate? A: To guess a number close to the real length.
chunks.source: To guess a number close to the real length.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Which tool measures metres? A: A tape measure.
chunks.source: A tape measure.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: If a rope is about 3 metres and a stick is 2 metres, what is the total length? A: 5 metres.
chunks.source: 5 metres.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Write a sentence using the word 'about'. A: The tree is about 4 metres tall.
chunks.source: The tree is about 4 metres tall.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words the difference between estimate and measure. A: Estimate is a guess; measure is exact.
chunks.source: Estimate is a guess; measure is exact.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Find the length of your desk in metres. A: Measure with a tape and write the number of metres.
chunks.source: Measure with a tape and write the number of metres.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Multiplication Word Problems. I can solve multiplication word problems using groups. Multiplication problems use groups and multiply to find the product, which tells how many altogether. Keywords: multiply: add equal groups; groups: sets of same number; problem: a question to solve; product: answer of multiplication; altogether: total number
chunks.source: Multiplication problems use groups and multiply to find the product, which tells how many altogether.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: What is the product of 4 and 5? A: 20

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: If there are 6 groups of 3, how many altogether? A: 18

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Write a multiplication problem about buying eggs. A: There are 2 groups of 10 eggs. How many altogether?
chunks.source: There are 2 groups of 10 eggs. How many altogether?

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words what 'groups' means in multiplication. A: Groups are the number of sets.
chunks.source: Groups are the number of sets.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Solve: 7 groups of 2 = ? A: 14

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: A boda boda carries 3 passengers per trip. After 4 trips, how many passengers altogether? A: 12 (3 × 4 = 12)

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Saving Money and Budgets. I can make a simple budget and save money for my needs. A **budget** is a **plan** for your **money**. It helps you **spend** wisely and **save** for later. Write down what you have, what things cost, add the costs, check if you have enough, then **save** the rest. Keywords: save: keep money for later; budget: a plan for using money; spend: use money to buy things; money: coins and notes we use to buy; plan: think ahead what to do
chunks.source: A **budget** is a **plan** for your **money**. It helps you **spend** wisely and **save** for later. Write down what you have, what things cost, add the costs, check if you have enough, then **save** the rest.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: What is a **budget**? A: A **budget** is a plan for using **money**.
chunks.source: A **budget** is a plan for using **money**.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Amina has 5000 shillings. She **spend** 2000 shillings. How much does she **save**? A: 3000 shillings. 5000 - 2000 = 3000.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Kato wants to buy 3 exercise books at 1000 each. He has 2500. Does he have enough? A: No. 3 × 1000 = 3000. He needs 3000 but has 2500.
chunks.source: No. 3 × 1000 = 3000. He needs 3000 but has 2500.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Write the 5 steps to make a **budget**. A: 1. Write your **money**. 2. Write item costs. 3. Add costs. 4. Check if enough. 5. **Save** the rest.
chunks.source: 1. Write your **money**. 2. Write item costs. 3. Add costs. 4. Check if enough. 5. **Save** the rest.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: In your own words, why is it good to **save** **money**? (Model: Saving keeps money for future needs like school fees or emergencies.) A: Saving keeps **money** for future needs like school fees, new uniform, or emergencies.
chunks.source: Saving keeps **money** for future needs like school fees, new uniform, or emergencies.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: You have 4000 shillings. You need a bag (2500) and pencils (800). Make a **budget**. Do you have enough? How much to **save**? A: Total cost: 2500 + 800 = 3300. Yes, enough. **Save**: 4000 - 3300 = 700 shillings.
chunks.source: Total cost: 2500 + 800 = 3300. Yes, enough. **Save**: 4000 - 3300 = 700 shillings.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: All Operations Word Problems. I can solve word problems using add, subtract, multiply, and divide. To solve a word **problem**: read, find numbers, choose operation (**add**, **subtract**, **multiply**, **divide**), calculate, check. **Add** joins, **subtract** takes away, **multiply** makes equal groups, **divide** shares equally. Keywords: add: put numbers together; subtract: take one number from another; multiply: repeated addition of equal groups; divide: share equally into groups; problem: a question to solve using maths
chunks.source: To solve a word **problem**: read, find numbers, choose operation (**add**, **subtract**, **multiply**, **divide**), calculate, check. **Add** joins, **subtract** takes away, **multiply** makes equal groups, **divide** shares equally.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: A boda fare is 600 shillings. You have 3000 shillings. How many rides can you buy? A: 3000 ÷ 600 = 5 rides.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Musa buys 3 exercise books at 1000 each. He pays with 5000. How much change? A: 3 × 1000 = 3000. 5000 - 3000 = 2000 change.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Amina has 2000. Kato has 1500. They **add** their **money**. Then they **divide** by 5 to share equally. How much each? A: 2000 + 1500 = 3500. 3500 ÷ 5 = 700 each.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Write a **problem** using **multiply** about buying matooke bunches. A: Model: One bunch costs 3000. Buy 4 bunches. 4 × 3000 = 12000.
chunks.source: Model: One bunch costs 3000. Buy 4 bunches. 4 × 3000 = 12000.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: In your own words, how do you choose which operation to use in a **problem**? (Model: Read the story. If joining groups, **add**. If taking away, **subtract**. If equal groups, **multiply**. If sharing equally, **divide**.) A: Read the **problem**. Joining groups: **add**. Taking away: **subtract**. Equal groups: **multiply**. Sharing equally: **divide**.
chunks.source: Read the **problem**. Joining groups: **add**. Taking away: **subtract**. Equal groups: **multiply**. Sharing equally: **divide**.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Peter has 6000. He **spend** 2500 on posho and 1200 on beans. How much remains? A: 2500 + 1200 = 3700 spent. 6000 - 3700 = 2300 remains.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Counting in Hundreds and Thousands. I can skip count in hundreds and thousands and see patterns in large numbers. **Skip count** by **hundreds** adds 100: numbers end with two zeros. **Skip count** by **thousands** adds 1000: numbers end with three zeros. The **pattern** in **large numbers** shows the place value digit growing by 1 each step. Keywords: hundreds: groups of one hundred; thousands: groups of one thousand; skip count: count by jumping a fixed amount; pattern: a regular way numbers change; large numbers: numbers with many digits
chunks.source: **Skip count** by **hundreds** adds 100: numbers end with two zeros. **Skip count** by **thousands** adds 1000: numbers end with three zeros. The **pattern** in **large numbers** shows the place value digit growing by 1 each step.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: **Skip count** by **hundreds** from 200 to 800. Write the numbers. A: 200, 300, 400, 500, 600, 700, 800.

chunks.subject: Math
