chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Fill the gap: "He is ___ even when no one watches." A: He is **honest** even when no one watches.
chunks.source: He is **honest** even when no one watches.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words: What does **kind** mean? A: **Kind** means caring and doing good for others.
chunks.source: **Kind** means caring and doing good for others.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words: Give an example of **help** at home. A: I **help** my mother wash the dishes after supper.
chunks.source: I **help** my mother wash the dishes after supper.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Bad Behaviour. I can name and report bad behaviour using present continuous (He is fighting) and 'That is ...' (That is rude). Name bad behaviour to stop it: **He is fighting**, **they are quarrelling**, **she is stealing**, **he is cheating**, **she is lying**. Report: **That is rude**, **that is unkind**. Good behaviour grows when bad behaviour is named. Keywords: fight: to use fists or force; quarrel: to argue loudly; steal: to take what is not yours; cheat: to break rules to win; lie: to say what is not true; rude: not polite; unkind: not caring
chunks.source: Name bad behaviour to stop it: **He is fighting**, **they are quarrelling**, **she is stealing**, **he is cheating**, **she is lying**. Report: **That is rude**, **that is unkind**. Good behaviour grows when bad behaviour is named.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Complete: "Look! He ___ the teacher's chalk." A: Look! He **is stealing** the teacher's chalk.
chunks.source: Look! He **is stealing** the teacher's chalk.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Complete: "They ___ about who won the game." A: They **are quarrelling** about who won the game.
chunks.source: They **are quarrelling** about who won the game.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Complete: "She ___ in the spelling test." A: She **is cheating** in the spelling test.
chunks.source: She **is cheating** in the spelling test.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Complete: "He ___ about finishing his porridge." A: He **is lying** about finishing his porridge.
chunks.source: He **is lying** about finishing his porridge.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Choose the correct report: A) That is kind. B) **That is rude**. (for pushing in line) A: **That is rude**.
chunks.source: **That is rude**.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words: What does **cheat** mean? A: **Cheat** means breaking rules to win or get better marks.
chunks.source: **Cheat** means breaking rules to win or get better marks.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words: Give an example of **unkind** behaviour. A: **Unkind** is laughing when someone falls down.
chunks.source: **Unkind** is laughing when someone falls down.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: In the Shop. I can use present simple to talk about items, prices and what a shop sells. In a shop, each item has a price. We use present simple: The shop sells items. An item costs money. Cheap means low price. Expensive means high price. Keywords: item: a thing you can buy; price: the money you pay for something; cost: to need a certain amount of money; cheap: costing little money; expensive: costing a lot of money; shop: a place where things are sold; sell: to give something for money
chunks.source: In a shop, each item has a price. We use present simple: The shop sells items. An item costs money. Cheap means low price. Expensive means high price.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Complete: The shop ______ maize flour. A: sells
chunks.source: sells

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Complete: This item ______ two thousand shillings. A: costs
chunks.source: costs

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Choose: A bar of soap at 1,000 shillings is ______. (cheap / expensive) A: cheap
chunks.source: cheap

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Choose: A phone at 500,000 shillings is ______. (cheap / expensive) A: expensive
chunks.source: expensive

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Make a sentence: Use 'sells' and 'item'. A: The shop sells this item.
chunks.source: The shop sells this item.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Make a sentence: Use 'costs' and 'price'. A: The item costs a low price.
chunks.source: The item costs a low price.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words: What does 'cost' mean in shopping? A: Cost means the money you must pay to buy something.
chunks.source: Cost means the money you must pay to buy something.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: How Much Is It?. I can ask and answer about prices using 'How much is...?' and 'How much are...?' To ask the price of one thing, say 'How much is...?' For more than one, say 'How much are...?' The answer uses 'costs' or 'cost': It costs 500 shillings. They cost 2,000 shillings. Keywords: price: the money you pay for something; money: coins and notes used to buy things; shillings: Ugandan money units; cost: to need a certain amount of money; buy: to get something by paying money; sell: to give something for money; pay: to give money for something
chunks.source: To ask the price of one thing, say 'How much is...?' For more than one, say 'How much are...?' The answer uses 'costs' or 'cost': It costs 500 shillings. They cost 2,000 shillings.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Complete: ______ this banana? (How much is / How much are) A: How much is
chunks.source: How much is

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Complete: ______ these oranges? (How much is / How much are) A: How much are
chunks.source: How much are

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Answer: It costs 1,000 shillings. What was the question? A: How much is it?
chunks.source: How much is it?

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Answer: They cost 5,000 shillings. What was the question? A: How much are they?
chunks.source: How much are they?

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Choose: I ______ the bread. (buy / sell) A: buy
chunks.source: buy

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Choose: The trader ______ the bread. (buy / sell) A: sells
chunks.source: sells

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words: When do you use 'How much are'? A: We use 'How much are' when we ask about the price of more than one thing.
chunks.source: We use 'How much are' when we ask about the price of more than one thing.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Make a question: You want to know the price of two pineapples. A: How much are these pineapples?
chunks.source: How much are these pineapples?

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Units We Buy By. I can name and use common units for buying things in Uganda. We buy by different units: kilogramme for weight (flour, beans), litre for liquids (milk, oil), metre for length (cloth), packet for small bags (salt), bar for solid blocks (soap), bottle for drinks, tin for canned food. Keywords: kilogramme: unit for weight (1000 grams); litre: unit for liquid volume; metre: unit for length; packet: a small sealed bag or box; bar: a solid block shape; bottle: a container with a narrow neck; tin: a metal container for food
chunks.source: We buy by different units: kilogramme for weight (flour, beans), litre for liquids (milk, oil), metre for length (cloth), packet for small bags (salt), bar for solid blocks (soap), bottle for drinks, tin for canned food.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Complete: We buy maize flour by the ______. A: kilogramme
chunks.source: kilogramme

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Complete: Milk is sold by the ______. A: litre
chunks.source: litre

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Complete: Cloth is measured in ______. A: metres
chunks.source: metres

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Choose: A ______ of soap. (bar / bottle) A: bar
chunks.source: bar

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Choose: A ______ of soda. (bar / bottle) A: bottle
chunks.source: bottle

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Choose: A ______ of salt. (packet / tin) A: packet
chunks.source: packet

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Choose: A ______ of tomatoes. (packet / tin) A: tin
chunks.source: tin

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words: Why do we use different units for different things? A: Because things are different: solids by weight, liquids by volume, cloth by length, small items by packet.
chunks.source: Because things are different: solids by weight, liquids by volume, cloth by length, small items by packet.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Some, Any, Much and Many. I can use some, any, much, many, and a few correctly when shopping. Use some in positive sentences (I need some sugar). Use any in questions and negatives (Do you have any salt?). Use much for uncountable (How much flour?). Use many for countable (How many mangoes?). Use a few for a small number of countable things. Keywords: some: an amount of something (positive); any: an amount in questions or negatives; much: large amount for uncountable things; many: large number for countable things; a few: a small number of countable things; sugar: sweet white grains for tea; salt: white powder for flavour
chunks.source: Use some in positive sentences (I need some sugar). Use any in questions and negatives (Do you have any salt?). Use much for uncountable (How much flour?). Use many for countable (How many mangoes?). Use a few for a small number of countable things.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Complete: I need ______ flour. (some / any) A: some
chunks.source: some

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Complete: Do you have ______ milk? (some / any) A: any
chunks.source: any

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Complete: How ______ rice do you want? (much / many) A: much
chunks.source: much

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Complete: How ______ apples did you buy? (much / many) A: many
chunks.source: many

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Complete: I will take ______ oranges. (a few / a little) A: a few
chunks.source: a few

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Choose: Salt is uncountable. We say: How ______ salt? (much / many) A: much
chunks.source: much

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Choose: Eggs are countable. We say: I need ______ eggs. (some / any) A: some
chunks.source: some

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words: What is the difference between 'much' and 'many'? A: Much is for uncountable things like sugar. Many is for countable things like eggs.
chunks.source: Much is for uncountable things like sugar. Many is for countable things like eggs.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Parts of the Day. I can name and use words for parts of the day. The day has **morning**, **midday**, **afternoon**, **evening**, **night**, plus school **break time** and **lunch time**. Keywords: morning: the early part of the day; midday: the middle of the day when the sun is high; afternoon: the time after midday until evening; evening: the time when the sun goes down; night: the dark time after evening; break time: a short rest during school; lunch time: the time we eat the midday meal
chunks.source: The day has **morning**, **midday**, **afternoon**, **evening**, **night**, plus school **break time** and **lunch time**.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: What part of the day is early and cool? A: morning
chunks.source: morning

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: When do we eat the midday meal? A: lunch time
chunks.source: lunch time

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Which word means the dark time for sleeping? A: night
chunks.source: night

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words what **break time** means. A: A short rest during school to drink water or stretch.
chunks.source: A short rest during school to drink water or stretch.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Put these in order: morning, afternoon, evening, night. A: morning, afternoon, evening, night
chunks.source: morning, afternoon, evening, night

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: What Did You Do Yesterday?. I can talk about yesterday using past simple and before/after. **Yesterday** we use past simple. **Before** and **after** show order. **Early**, **late**, **spent**, **went** help give details. Keywords: yesterday: the day before today; before: earlier than something; after: later than something; early: near the start of a period; late: near the end of a period; spent: used time doing something; went: past of go
chunks.source: **Yesterday** we use past simple. **Before** and **after** show order. **Early**, **late**, **spent**, **went** help give details.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: What is the past of go? A: went
chunks.source: went

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Fill the gap: I ____ my teeth **before** bed. A: brushed
chunks.source: brushed

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Choose: She arrived ____ for class. A: late
chunks.source: late

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words what **spent** means. A: Used time doing something.
chunks.source: Used time doing something.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Write a short sentence using **yesterday**, **before**, and **after**. A: I **went** to the market **yesterday** **before** lunch **after** breakfast.
chunks.source: I **went** to the market **yesterday** **before** lunch **after** breakfast.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: While I Was Reading. I can use past continuous with while for actions in progress. Past continuous uses **was**/**were** + **‑ing**. **While** joins two actions happening together. Keywords: while: during the time that; was: past of am/is for singular; were: past of are for plural; playing: doing a game; reading: looking at a book; cooking: preparing food; raining: falling rain
chunks.source: Past continuous uses **was**/**were** + **‑ing**. **While** joins two actions happening together.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Fill the gap: She ____ **reading** when I called. A: was
chunks.source: was

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Choose: We ____ **playing** football. A: were
chunks.source: were

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Complete: It ____ **raining** all morning. A: was
chunks.source: was

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words what **while** means. A: During the time that something else happens.
chunks.source: During the time that something else happens.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Write a sentence with **while**, **was**, and **cooking**. A: Mother **was cooking** **while** father **was reading**.
chunks.source: Mother **was cooking** **while** father **was reading**.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Tomorrow and Next Week. I can talk about future times using shall and will. We use **shall** with I and we, and **will** with you, he, she, they to talk about tomorrow, next week, next month, and next year. Keywords: tomorrow: the day after today; next week: the week after this one; next month: the month after this one; next year: the year after this one; will: future verb for you, he, she, they; shall: future verb for I and we; arrive: to reach a place
chunks.source: We use **shall** with I and we, and **will** with you, he, she, they to talk about tomorrow, next week, next month, and next year.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Write a sentence using **shall** for **I**. A: I shall go to the market tomorrow.
chunks.source: I shall go to the market tomorrow.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Write a sentence using **will** for **he**. A: He will arrive next month.
chunks.source: He will arrive next month.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Choose the correct word: **I** ____ go to school next year. (shall/will) A: shall
chunks.source: shall

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Choose the correct word: **They** ____ visit the garden next week. (shall/will) A: will
chunks.source: will

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words when to use **shall**. A: We use shall with I and we for future plans.
chunks.source: We use shall with I and we for future plans.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words when to use **will**. A: We use will with you, he, she, they for future actions.
chunks.source: We use will with you, he, she, they for future actions.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Will You Come Tomorrow?. I can ask and answer about future actions using Will, Shall we, and negatives. Ask about the future with **Will** and **Shall we**; say no with **will not** or **shall not**. Keywords: will not: negative future for you, he, she, they; shall not: negative future for I and we; meeting: a planned gathering; visit: to go see someone or a place; tomorrow: the day after today; come: to move toward the speaker; play: to take part in a game
chunks.source: Ask about the future with **Will** and **Shall we**; say no with **will not** or **shall not**.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Write a question using **Will** for **you**. A: Will you come tomorrow?
chunks.source: Will you come tomorrow?

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Write a suggestion using **Shall we**. A: Shall we visit the garden tomorrow?
chunks.source: Shall we visit the garden tomorrow?

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Choose the correct negative for **I**: I ____ go to the meeting. (shall not / will not) A: shall not
chunks.source: shall not

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Choose the correct negative for **they**: They ____ play tomorrow. (shall not / will not) A: will not
chunks.source: will not

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words when to use **Shall we**. A: We use Shall we to suggest doing something together.
chunks.source: We use Shall we to suggest doing something together.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words the difference between **will not** and **shall not**. A: Will not is for you, he, she, they; shall not is for I and we.
chunks.source: Will not is for you, he, she, they; shall not is for I and we.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Keeping a Diary. I can write future plans in a diary with correct dates. A diary holds notes with day, month, year; write plans as **will** + verb + **on** + date. Keywords: diary: a book for daily notes; date: the number of the day; day: a 24‑hour period; month: one of twelve parts of a year; year: twelve months together; calendar: shows days, weeks, months; note: a short written reminder
chunks.source: A diary holds notes with day, month, year; write plans as **will** + verb + **on** + date.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Write a diary entry for **tomorrow** using **will**. A: I will read a book on 26th August.
chunks.source: I will read a book on 26th August.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Fill in the blank: I ____ go to the market on 5th September. A: will
chunks.source: will

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Choose the correct order: (a) I will visit on 12th July (b) On 12th July I will visit A: a
chunks.source: a

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words why we write the **date** in a diary. A: To know when the plan happens.
chunks.source: To know when the plan happens.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words the pattern for future plans. A: Subject + will + verb + on + date.
chunks.source: Subject + will + verb + on + date.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Write a note for **next month** in your diary. A: I will help at home on 10th October.
chunks.source: I will help at home on 10th October.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: My Study Time. I can describe study habits using usually and sometimes. Use **usually** for regular habits, **sometimes** for occasional ones; **borrow** from the **library**, **lend** your **notebook**, and **revise** often. Keywords: borrow: to take something for a short time; lend: to give something for a short time; library: place with many books; revise: to study again; notebook: book for writing notes; usually: most of the time; sometimes: occasionally
chunks.source: Use **usually** for regular habits, **sometimes** for occasional ones; **borrow** from the **library**, **lend** your **notebook**, and **revise** often.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Write a sentence with **usually** about your study. A: I usually revise my notes after school.
chunks.source: I usually revise my notes after school.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Write a sentence with **sometimes** about borrowing. A: I sometimes borrow books from the library.
chunks.source: I sometimes borrow books from the library.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Choose the correct word: Kato ____ his notebook to Musa. (borrow / lend) A: lend
chunks.source: lend

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Choose the correct word: Kato ____ a book from the library. (borrow / lend) A: borrow
chunks.source: borrow

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words the difference between **usually** and **sometimes**. A: Usually means most of the time; sometimes means occasionally.
chunks.source: Usually means most of the time; sometimes means occasionally.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words when to use **borrow** and **lend**. A: Borrow is to take; lend is to give.
chunks.source: Borrow is to take; lend is to give.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Games and Sports. I can describe games with adjectives and ask questions about players and results. We describe games with adjectives like fast, quick, high. We ask "What will ... do?" for future actions and "Who was the first ...?" for past events. Every player, coach, and referee has a role. Keywords: football: a game played with a round ball kicked by feet; netball: a game where players throw a ball through a high ring; volleyball: a game where two teams hit a ball over a net; player: a person who takes part in a game; coach: a person who trains and guides the team; referee: an official who makes sure rules are followed; win: to be the best in a game or contest; lose: to not win a game or contest
chunks.source: We describe games with adjectives like fast, quick, high. We ask "What will ... do?" for future actions and "Who was the first ...?" for past events. Every player, coach, and referee has a role.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Write a sentence describing **football** using two adjectives. A: Football is a fast and exciting game.
chunks.source: Football is a fast and exciting game.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Ask a question using "What will ... do?" about a **coach**. A: What will the coach do at half time?
chunks.source: What will the coach do at half time?

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Ask a question using "Who was the first ...?" about a **player**. A: Who was the first player to score?
chunks.source: Who was the first player to score?

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Use **win** and **lose** in one sentence about a match. A: Our team wants to win, but it is okay to lose if we try.
chunks.source: Our team wants to win, but it is okay to lose if we try.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words what a **referee** does during a game. A: A referee makes sure players follow the rules and decides on goals or faults.
chunks.source: A referee makes sure players follow the rules and decides on goals or faults.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Describe **netball** with two adjectives and name one **player** role. A: Netball is a quick and neat game. A shooter is a player role.
chunks.source: Netball is a quick and neat game. A shooter is a player role.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Make a question with "Which ... will ...?" about **volleyball**. A: Which team will win the volleyball match?
chunks.source: Which team will win the volleyball match?

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Music, Dance and Drama. I can use superlatives to compare performances and ask which person will do something. We use superlatives like **best** to compare three or more things. We ask "Which ... will ...?" to find out about future choices. Choirs sing, actors act in costumes, and festivals showcase many talents. Keywords: sing: to make musical sounds with the voice; recite: to say a poem or speech from memory; choir: a group of people who sing together; concert: a public performance of music or drama; actor: a person who performs in a play; costume: special clothes worn for a performance; festival: a special event with many performances; best: better than all others; superlative of good
chunks.source: We use superlatives like **best** to compare three or more things. We ask "Which ... will ...?" to find out about future choices. Choirs sing, actors act in costumes, and festivals showcase many talents.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Write a sentence using **best** to describe a **concert** item. A: The choir's song was the best item at the concert.
chunks.source: The choir's song was the best item at the concert.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Ask a question using "Which ... will ...?" about a **choir**. A: Which song will the choir sing next?
chunks.source: Which song will the choir sing next?

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Use **sing** and **recite** in one sentence about the **festival**. A: At the festival, the choir will sing and Amina will recite a poem.
chunks.source: At the festival, the choir will sing and Amina will recite a poem.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Describe an **actor**'s **costume** with two adjectives. A: The actor wore a bright and colourful costume.
chunks.source: The actor wore a bright and colourful costume.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words what a **choir** does at a **concert**. A: A choir sings songs together as a group for the audience.
chunks.source: A choir sings songs together as a group for the audience.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Make a superlative sentence about the **festival** using **best**. A: The dance was the best performance at the festival.
chunks.source: The dance was the best performance at the festival.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Write a question with "Which ... was the **best** ...?" about **actors**. A: Which actor was the best in the play?
chunks.source: Which actor was the best in the play?

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: School Elections. I can use relative pronouns who and whom to describe people in an election. We use **who** for the subject (the doer) and **whom** for the object (the receiver). In elections, **candidates** **campaign**, **voters** **vote** on a **ballot paper**, and the school **elects** a **prefect**. Keywords: prefect: a student leader chosen to help maintain order; vote: to make a choice in an election; voter: a person who has the right to vote; ballot paper: a paper used to record a vote; elect: to choose someone by voting; candidate: a person who stands for election; election: the process of voting to choose leaders; campaign: to work to get votes before an election
chunks.source: We use **who** for the subject (the doer) and **whom** for the object (the receiver). In elections, **candidates** **campaign**, **voters** **vote** on a **ballot paper**, and the school **elects** a **prefect**.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Write a sentence using **who** to describe a **candidate**. A: Amina is the candidate who promised more books.
chunks.source: Amina is the candidate who promised more books.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Write a sentence using **whom** to describe a **voter**'s choice. A: Peter is the boy whom the voters elected as prefect.
chunks.source: Peter is the boy whom the voters elected as prefect.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Use **elect** and **campaign** in one sentence about the **election**. A: The candidate will campaign before we elect the prefect.
chunks.source: The candidate will campaign before we elect the prefect.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words what a **ballot paper** is used for. A: A ballot paper is used to mark your vote secretly in an election.
chunks.source: A ballot paper is used to mark your vote secretly in an election.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Make a question with **whom** about the **prefect** election. A: Whom did the pupils elect as prefect?
chunks.source: Whom did the pupils elect as prefect?

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Describe a **candidate** using **who** and one promise. A: Musa is the candidate who wants new sports equipment.
chunks.source: Musa is the candidate who wants new sports equipment.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Write a sentence showing the difference between **vote** and **elect**. A: Each voter will vote, and together they will elect the prefect.
chunks.source: Each voter will vote, and together they will elect the prefect.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Standing for a Post. I can ask and answer election questions using whom and stand for a post. We ask "Whom are we electing as...?" and "Is ... standing for the post of...?" to learn about candidates. Pupils **stand** for a **post**, **campaign** with promises, and **voters** choose the best **leader** for each role. Keywords: head girl: the senior girl student leader; head boy: the senior boy student leader; monitor: a student chosen to help the teacher in class; captain: a leader of a sports team or house; leader: a person who guides or directs others; post: a position or job in a school or organisation; stand: to offer yourself as a candidate in an election; campaign: to work to get votes before an election
chunks.source: We ask "Whom are we electing as...?" and "Is ... standing for the post of...?" to learn about candidates. Pupils **stand** for a **post**, **campaign** with promises, and **voters** choose the best **leader** for each role.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Write a question using "Whom are we electing as ...?" for **head boy**. A: Whom are we electing as head boy?
chunks.source: Whom are we electing as head boy?

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Write a question using "Is ... standing for the post of ...?" for **monitor**. A: Is Peter standing for the post of monitor?
chunks.source: Is Peter standing for the post of monitor?

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Use **stand** and **campaign** in one sentence about a **candidate**. A: Amina will stand for head girl and campaign by talking to pupils.
chunks.source: Amina will stand for head girl and campaign by talking to pupils.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words the difference between **head girl** and **monitor**. A: Head girl leads the whole school; monitor helps the teacher in one class.
chunks.source: Head girl leads the whole school; monitor helps the teacher in one class.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Make a sentence with **leader** describing a **captain**. A: The captain is a leader who guides the sports team.
chunks.source: The captain is a leader who guides the sports team.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Write a campaign promise for the **post** of **captain**. A: I will organise more friendly matches for our house.
chunks.source: I will organise more friendly matches for our house.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Use **post** and **leader** in a sentence about school elections. A: Every post needs a good leader who serves the pupils.
chunks.source: Every post needs a good leader who serves the pupils.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Naming and Forming Sets. I can identify and form sets of objects from daily life. A **set** is a collection with a clear rule. Its **members** (or **elements**) follow the rule. We **group** them and write a **list**. Keywords: set: a collection of objects grouped together; member: one object that belongs to a set; group: objects put together because they are alike; list: names of members written down; element: another word for member of a set
chunks.source: A **set** is a collection with a clear rule. Its **members** (or **elements**) follow the rule. We **group** them and write a **list**.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: What is a **set**? A: A collection of objects grouped by a common rule.
chunks.source: A collection of objects grouped by a common rule.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: What do we call each object in a **set**? A: A **member** or **element**.
chunks.source: A **member** or **element**.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Write a **list** of 3 **members** of a set of cooking pots. A: Example: Big pot, Medium pot, Small pot.
chunks.source: Example: Big pot, Medium pot, Small pot.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: If you group all your exercise books, what is the **set**? A: Set of exercise books.
chunks.source: Set of exercise books.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words how to form a **set**. A: Choose a rule, pick objects that match, put them together, write a **list**.
chunks.source: Choose a rule, pick objects that match, put them together, write a **list**.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: True or false: A **set** can have zero **members**. A: True — this is called an empty set.
chunks.source: True — this is called an empty set.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Members of a Set. I can name members and find the number of members in a set. A **member** belongs to a **set** if it matches the rule. The **number of members** is found by **count**ing each **member** once. Keywords: member: one object that belongs to a set; number of members: how many objects are in a set; belong: to be part of a set; set: a collection of objects grouped together; count: to find how many members
chunks.source: A **member** belongs to a **set** if it matches the rule. The **number of members** is found by **count**ing each **member** once.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: What is a **member** of a **set**? A: One object that belongs to the set.
chunks.source: One object that belongs to the set.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: How do you find the **number of members**? A: Count each member that belongs to the set.
chunks.source: Count each member that belongs to the set.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: If a **set** has 7 stones and you add 3, what is the new **number of members**? A: 10

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: List the **members** of a **set** of 3 Ugandan coins. A: Example: 100 shilling, 200 shilling, 500 shilling coins.
chunks.source: Example: 100 shilling, 200 shilling, 500 shilling coins.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words what **belong** means for a **set**. A: An object belongs if it matches the rule of the set.
chunks.source: An object belongs if it matches the rule of the set.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: True or false: The **number of members** stays the same if you remove a **member**. A: False — it decreases by one.
chunks.source: False — it decreases by one.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: A **set** of mangoes has 12 **members**. 4 are rotten and thrown away. How many **members** remain? A: 8

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Empty and Equivalent Sets. I can identify empty sets, equal sets, and equivalent sets. An **empty set** has 0 **members**. **Equal sets** have identical **members**. **Equivalent sets** have the **same number** of **members**. Keywords: empty set: a set with no members; equivalent sets: sets with the same number of members; equal sets: sets with exactly the same members; member: one object that belongs to a set; same number: equal in count
chunks.source: An **empty set** has 0 **members**. **Equal sets** have identical **members**. **Equivalent sets** have the **same number** of **members**.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: What is an **empty set**? A: A set with no members.
chunks.source: A set with no members.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Define **equivalent sets**. A: Sets with the same number of members.
chunks.source: Sets with the same number of members.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Define **equal sets**. A: Sets with exactly the same members.
chunks.source: Sets with exactly the same members.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Set A = { }. Set B = { }. Are they equal, equivalent, or both? A: Both — they are empty sets, so equal and equivalent.
chunks.source: Both — they are empty sets, so equal and equivalent.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words the difference between equal and equivalent sets. A: Equal sets have identical members. Equivalent sets only have the same count.
chunks.source: Equal sets have identical members. Equivalent sets only have the same count.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Set M = {3 stones}. Set N = {3 sticks}. Are they equivalent? A: Yes, both have 3 members.
chunks.source: Yes, both have 3 members.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: If two sets are equal, are they always equivalent? A: Yes, because identical members means same number of members.
chunks.source: Yes, because identical members means same number of members.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Common Members. I can find common members of two sets. **Common members** are **members** that **belong** to **both** **sets**. The **sets** **share** these **members**. List each **set**, then find matches. Keywords: common members: members that belong to both sets; both: the two sets together; share: to have in common; set: a collection of objects grouped together; member: one object that belongs to a set
chunks.source: **Common members** are **members** that **belong** to **both** **sets**. The **sets** **share** these **members**. List each **set**, then find matches.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: What are **common members**? A: Members that belong to both sets.
chunks.source: Members that belong to both sets.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Set X = {cup, plate, spoon}. Set Y = {plate, bowl, spoon}. List the **common members**. A: Plate and spoon.
chunks.source: Plate and spoon.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: If two sets have no **common members**, what do we call that? A: They are disjoint (no shared members).
chunks.source: They are disjoint (no shared members).

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Set P has 5 **members**. Set Q has 4 **members**. They **share** 2. How many **common members**? A: 2

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words how to find **common members** of two sets. A: List both sets, then pick members that appear in both lists.
chunks.source: List both sets, then pick members that appear in both lists.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: True or false: A **member** can be a **common member** if it is in only one **set**. A: False — it must be in both sets.
chunks.source: False — it must be in both sets.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Draw two sets that **share** exactly one **common member**. Label it. A: Example: Set A = {cat, dog}, Set B = {dog, bird}. Common member = dog.
chunks.source: Example: Set A = {cat, dog}, Set B = {dog, bird}. Common member = dog.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Reading and Writing Big Numbers. I can read and write numbers up to 99,999 in figures and words We can write any whole number up to 99,999 in figures using digits and in words using place value names like thousands and hundreds. Keywords: whole number: a number without fractions; digits: the symbols 0 to 9 used to write numbers; figures: numbers written with digits; words: numbers written out in letters; thousands: the place value group of three digits
chunks.source: We can write any whole number up to 99,999 in figures using digits and in words using place value names like thousands and hundreds.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Write 34,560 in words. A: thirty four thousand five hundred sixty
chunks.source: thirty four thousand five hundred sixty

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Write 70,009 in words. A: seventy thousand and nine
chunks.source: seventy thousand and nine

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Write the number for: ninety two thousand three hundred four. A: 92,304

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words how you write a 5-digit number in words. A: Start with the ten thousands and thousands, then hundreds, then tens and units, using 'and' before the last part if there are no hundreds.
chunks.source: Start with the ten thousands and thousands, then hundreds, then tens and units, using 'and' before the last part if there are no hundreds.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: What is the **whole number** shown by the digits 5,0,0,0,0? A: 50,000

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Write 12,345 in **figures**. A: 12,345

chunks.id: L-P4-Math-Place Value and Value of Digits
chunks.subject: Math
chunks.unit: Place Value and Value of Digits
chunks.text: Place Value and Value of Digits. I can identify the place value and value of each digit up to 5 digits Each digit has a place value name and a value found by multiplying the digit by its place. Keywords: place value: the position name of a digit in a number; value: the digit multiplied by its place value; ten thousands: the place for the fifth digit from the right; thousands: the place for the fourth digit from the right; hundreds: the place for the third digit from the right
chunks.source: Each digit has a place value name and a value found by multiplying the digit by its place.

chunks.id: LQ-P4-Math-Place Value and Value of Digits
chunks.subject: Math
chunks.unit: Place Value and Value of Digits
chunks.text: Q: What is the **value** of the digit 9 in 29,401? A: 9,000

chunks.id: LQ-P4-Math-Place Value and Value of Digits
chunks.subject: Math
chunks.unit: Place Value and Value of Digits
chunks.text: Q: What is the **place value** of the digit 4 in 84,567? A: hundreds
chunks.source: hundreds

chunks.id: LQ-P4-Math-Place Value and Value of Digits
chunks.subject: Math
chunks.unit: Place Value and Value of Digits
chunks.text: Q: Write the **value** of each digit in 50,003. A: 5=50,000; 0=0; 0=0; 0=0; 3=3

chunks.id: LQ-P4-Math-Place Value and Value of Digits
chunks.subject: Math
chunks.unit: Place Value and Value of Digits
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words the difference between **place value** and **value**. A: Place value is the position name like thousands; value is the digit multiplied by that position.
chunks.source: Place value is the position name like thousands; value is the digit multiplied by that position.

chunks.id: LQ-P4-Math-Place Value and Value of Digits
chunks.subject: Math
chunks.unit: Place Value and Value of Digits
chunks.text: Q: If the digit 6 is in the **ten thousands** place, what is its **value**? A: 60,000

chunks.id: LQ-P4-Math-Place Value and Value of Digits
chunks.subject: Math
chunks.unit: Place Value and Value of Digits
chunks.text: Q: In 13,200, which digit is in the **thousands** place? A: 3

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Expanding Numbers. I can expand 5-digit numbers and write them in short form Expanding a number shows each digit's value; adding the parts gives the short form. Keywords: expand: write a number as a sum of each digit times its place value; place value: the value of the position of a digit; sum: the result of adding numbers together; digits: the symbols 0 to 9 used to write numbers; form: the way a number is written, either expanded or short
chunks.source: Expanding a number shows each digit's value; adding the parts gives the short form.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Write the short form of 60,000 + 4,000 + 200 + 50 + 8. A: 64,258

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words why we leave out zero parts when expanding. A: Zero parts add nothing to the sum, so we skip them.
chunks.source: Zero parts add nothing to the sum, so we skip them.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: What is the **sum** of the expanded parts of 45,600? A: 45,600

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Write 89,000 in expanded form. A: 80,000 + 9,000

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Rounding Off and Roman Numerals. I can round off to the nearest 10, 100, 1000 and write Roman numerals up to 20 Rounding makes numbers simpler for estimating; Roman numerals use letters to show values up to 20. Keywords: round off: change a number to the nearest ten, hundred, or thousand; nearest ten: the closest multiple of ten; nearest thousand: the closest multiple of one thousand; roman numerals: numbers written with letters I, V, X, L; estimate: find an approximate answer by rounding
chunks.source: Rounding makes numbers simpler for estimating; Roman numerals use letters to show values up to 20.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Round 5,678 to the nearest ten. A: 5,680

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Round 23,450 to the nearest hundred. A: 23,500

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Round 67,890 to the nearest thousand. A: 68,000

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Write 18 in Roman numerals. A: XVIII
chunks.source: XVIII

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words how you decide to round up or down. A: If the next digit is 5 or more, round up; if less than 5, round down.
chunks.source: If the next digit is 5 or more, round up; if less than 5, round down.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Estimate the sum of 12,345 + 8,765 by rounding each to the nearest thousand. A: 12,000 + 9,000 = 21,000

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Addition of Whole Numbers. I can add numbers up to 5 digits with and without regrouping. To **add** large numbers, write them in columns, start from the ones, and **carry** when a column **sum** is 10 or more. The final answer is the **total**. Keywords: add: to put numbers together; sum: the answer when we add; regroup: to change 10 ones into 1 ten, or 10 tens into 1 hundred; carry: to move a ten or hundred to the next column; total: the whole amount after adding
chunks.source: To **add** large numbers, write them in columns, start from the ones, and **carry** when a column **sum** is 10 or more. The final answer is the **total**.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Add 4,321 + 2,456. Show your working. A: 6,777

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Find the **sum** of 12,500 and 8,750. A: 21,250

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: A trader sells posho for 3,200 and beans for 2,800. What is the **total**? A: 6,000

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Add 9,999 + 1. Explain why you **carry** four times. A: 10,000. Each column adds to 10, so we **carry** 1 to the next column each time.
chunks.source: 10,000. Each column adds to 10, so we **carry** 1 to the next column each time.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Write a story problem where you **add** two 4-digit numbers. A: Any correct story with two 4-digit numbers and the correct **sum**.
chunks.source: Any correct story with two 4-digit numbers and the correct **sum**.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Subtraction of Whole Numbers. I can subtract numbers up to 5 digits with and without regrouping. To **subtract**, put the larger number on top. Start from ones. If the top digit is too small, **borrow** and **regroup** from the next column. The answer is the **difference** or what **remain**. Keywords: subtract: to take one number away from another; difference: the answer when we subtract; borrow: to take 1 ten from the next column and make it 10 ones; regroup: to change 1 ten into 10 ones, or 1 hundred into 10 tens; remain: what is left after subtracting
chunks.source: To **subtract**, put the larger number on top. Start from ones. If the top digit is too small, **borrow** and **regroup** from the next column. The answer is the **difference** or what **remain**.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Subtract 5,432 - 2,101. Show working. A: 3,331

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Find the **difference** between 10,000 and 4,567. A: 5,433

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: A boda fare is 2,500. You pay with 5,000. How much **remain**? A: 2,500

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Subtract 7,000 - 3,456. Explain the **borrow** steps. A: 3,544. Borrow across zeros: 7 becomes 6, then 10 hundreds, borrow to tens, borrow to ones.
chunks.source: 3,544. Borrow across zeros: 7 becomes 6, then 10 hundreds, borrow to tens, borrow to ones.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Write a story where you **subtract** two 4-digit numbers. A: Any correct story with larger minus smaller and correct **difference**.
chunks.source: Any correct story with larger minus smaller and correct **difference**.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Multiplication of Whole Numbers. I can multiply up to 3-digit numbers by 0, 10, 100 and 1-digit numbers. To **multiply** by a 1-digit number, multiply each digit from right to left and **carry** tens. **By 10** shifts digits left one place; **by 100** shifts two places. **Times** 0 always gives 0. Keywords: multiply: to add a number to itself a certain number of times; product: the answer when we multiply; times: another word for multiply; by 10: multiply by ten; digits shift one place left, add a zero; by 100: multiply by one hundred; digits shift two places left, add two zeros
chunks.source: To **multiply** by a 1-digit number, multiply each digit from right to left and **carry** tens. **By 10** shifts digits left one place; **by 100** shifts two places. **Times** 0 always gives 0.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Multiply 42 by 3. Show steps. A: 126

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Find the **product** of 125 and 4. A: 500

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: What is 56 **by 10**? What is 56 **by 100**? A: 560 and 5,600

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Multiply 307 by 0. Explain why the answer is 0. A: 0. Any number **times** 0 equals 0 because there are zero groups.
chunks.source: 0. Any number **times** 0 equals 0 because there are zero groups.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: A box holds 12 mangoes. How many mangoes in 8 boxes? Write the multiplication sentence. A: 12 **times** 8 = 96

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Division of Whole Numbers. I can divide up to 4-digit numbers by 1-digit numbers and solve word problems. To **divide**, use long division steps: **divide**, multiply, subtract, bring down. The answer is the **quotient**. Check by multiplying. **Word problem**s use **share** or **group** to know when to divide. Keywords: divide: to split a number into equal parts; quotient: the answer when we divide; share: to give each person the same amount; group: to put items into sets of the same size; word problem: a story question that needs maths to solve
chunks.source: To **divide**, use long division steps: **divide**, multiply, subtract, bring down. The answer is the **quotient**. Check by multiplying. **Word problem**s use **share** or **group** to know when to divide.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Divide 96 by 3 using long division. Show steps. A: 32

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Find the **quotient** of 4,800 ÷ 100. A: 48

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: A **word problem**: 450 pens are **shared** among 9 classes. How many per class? A: 50

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: **Group** 1,235 into sets of 5. What is the **quotient** and remainder? A: 247 r 0

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Explain how to check a division answer using multiplication. A: Multiply the **quotient** by the divisor. Add any remainder. The result should equal the original number.
chunks.source: Multiply the **quotient** by the divisor. Add any remainder. The result should equal the original number.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Even and Odd Numbers. I can identify even and odd numbers and explain the difference. **Even** **numbers** split into equal **pairs** with none left; **odd** **numbers** always leave one. Check the last digit: 0,2,4,6,8 are **even**; 1,3,5,7,9 are **odd**. Keywords: even: a number that can be shared into two equal groups; odd: a number that cannot be shared into two equal groups; pair: two things that go together; number: a symbol used for counting; sequence: a list of numbers that follow a rule
chunks.source: **Even** **numbers** split into equal **pairs** with none left; **odd** **numbers** always leave one. Check the last digit: 0,2,4,6,8 are **even**; 1,3,5,7,9 are **odd**.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Is 36 an **even** or **odd** **number**? Explain. A: 36 is **even** because it ends in 6 and makes 18 **pairs** with none left.
chunks.source: 36 is **even** because it ends in 6 and makes 18 **pairs** with none left.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Is 45 an **even** or **odd** **number**? Explain. A: 45 is **odd** because it ends in 5 and makes 22 **pairs** with one left.
chunks.source: 45 is **odd** because it ends in 5 and makes 22 **pairs** with one left.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Write the next two **numbers** in this **sequence**: 20, 22, 24, __, __. A: 26, 28 — the rule is add 2 to get the next **even** **number**.
chunks.source: 26, 28 — the rule is add 2 to get the next **even** **number**.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Write the next two **numbers** in this **sequence**: 11, 13, 15, __, __. A: 17, 19 — the rule is add 2 to get the next **odd** **number**.
chunks.source: 17, 19 — the rule is add 2 to get the next **odd** **number**.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Musa has 30 eggs. He packs them in **pairs**. How many **pairs**? Any left? A: 15 **pairs**, none left. 30 is **even**.
chunks.source: 15 **pairs**, none left. 30 is **even**.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Nalongo has 29 beads. She makes **pairs**. How many **pairs**? Any left? A: 14 **pairs**, one left. 29 is **odd**.
chunks.source: 14 **pairs**, one left. 29 is **odd**.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: In your own words, how do you know a **number** is **even**? A: A **number** is **even** if it can be grouped into **pairs** with nothing left over, or if it ends in 0, 2, 4, 6, or 8.
chunks.source: A **number** is **even** if it can be grouped into **pairs** with nothing left over, or if it ends in 0, 2, 4, 6, or 8.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Recognising Patterns. I can recognise patterns and sequences and find the rule. A **pattern** repeats by a **rule**. A **sequence** follows a **rule**. To find the **next term**, find the **rule** first — check differences for numbers, check order for **shapes**. Keywords: pattern: a repeated design or ordered set; sequence: a list of numbers or shapes that follow a rule; next term: the item that comes after the last one shown; rule: the instruction that tells how the pattern grows; shape: the form of an object like a circle or square
chunks.source: A **pattern** repeats by a **rule**. A **sequence** follows a **rule**. To find the **next term**, find the **rule** first — check differences for numbers, check order for **shapes**.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: What is the **next term** in this **sequence**: 3, 6, 9, 12, __? A: 15 — the **rule** is add 3.
chunks.source: 15 — the **rule** is add 3.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: What is the **next term** in this **shape** **pattern**: ★, ♥, ★, ♥, __? A: ★ — the **rule** is alternate star and heart.
chunks.source: ★ — the **rule** is alternate star and heart.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Find the **rule** for this **sequence**: 100, 200, 300, 400. A: Add 100 each time.
chunks.source: Add 100 each time.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Complete the **pattern**: □, △, △, □, △, △, __, __. A: □, △ — the **rule** is one square, two triangles, repeat.
chunks.source: □, △ — the **rule** is one square, two triangles, repeat.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: The **sequence** 7, 14, 21, 28 follows what **rule**? A: Add 7 each time.
chunks.source: Add 7 each time.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: In your own words, how do you find the **rule** of a number **sequence**? A: Subtract each term from the next term. If the difference is the same, that difference is the **rule** (add that number).
chunks.source: Subtract each term from the next term. If the difference is the same, that difference is the **rule** (add that number).

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Write the next three terms for this **sequence**: 25, 30, 35, __, __, __. A: 40, 45, 50 — the **rule** is add 5.
chunks.source: 40, 45, 50 — the **rule** is add 5.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Forming Patterns. I can form and continue patterns and sequences using multiples. To **form** a **sequence**, list **multiples** (number × 1, 2, 3...). To **continue**, add the same number each time. For shape **patterns**, repeat the **rule**. Keywords: form: to make or create something; pattern: a repeated design or ordered set; sequence: a list of numbers or shapes that follow a rule; multiples: numbers you get by multiplying a number by 1, 2, 3...; continue: to keep going the same way
chunks.source: To **form** a **sequence**, list **multiples** (number × 1, 2, 3...). To **continue**, add the same number each time. For shape **patterns**, repeat the **rule**.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: **Form** a **sequence** using the first five **multiples** of 9. A: 9, 18, 27, 36, 45

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: **Continue** this **sequence** for three more terms: 12, 24, 36, __, __, __. A: 48, 60, 72 — the **rule** is add 12 (multiples of 12).
chunks.source: 48, 60, 72 — the **rule** is add 12 (multiples of 12).

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: **Form** a **pattern** with **shapes** using the **rule**: triangle, square, square. Draw the first 6 **shapes**. A: Triangle, square, square, triangle, square, square.
chunks.source: Triangle, square, square, triangle, square, square.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Write the **multiples** of 6 up to 6 × 6. A: 6, 12, 18, 24, 30, 36

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Nalongo saves 500 shillings each week. **Form** a **sequence** showing her total after 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 weeks. A: 500, 1000, 1500, 2000, 2500 — **multiples** of 500.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: In your own words, how do you **continue** a **sequence** of **multiples**? A: Find the **rule** (the number you multiply by). Then keep adding that number to the last term to get the next terms.
chunks.source: Find the **rule** (the number you multiply by). Then keep adding that number to the last term to get the next terms.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: **Form** a **pattern** using two colours. State the **rule** and **continue** for 4 more items. A: Example: Red, green, green, red, green, green. Rule: one red, two green. Continue: red, green, green, red.
chunks.source: Example: Red, green, green, red, green, green. Rule: one red, two green. Continue: red, green, green, red.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Naming Fractions. I can name proper fractions, improper fractions and mixed numbers. A fraction has a numerator and denominator; proper fractions are less than one, improper fractions are more than one, and mixed numbers show a whole plus a fraction. Keywords: fraction: a part of a whole; numerator: the top number; denominator: the bottom number; proper: numerator smaller than denominator; improper: numerator bigger than denominator; mixed number: a whole number and a fraction
chunks.source: A fraction has a numerator and denominator; proper fractions are less than one, improper fractions are more than one, and mixed numbers show a whole plus a fraction.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: What is the numerator in 3/5? A: 3

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: What is the denominator in 7/8? A: 8

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Is 4/4 a proper fraction? A: No, it is an improper fraction.
chunks.source: No, it is an improper fraction.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Write 1 2/3 as an improper fraction. A: 5/3

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words what a mixed number is. A: A mixed number has a whole number and a proper fraction together.
chunks.source: A mixed number has a whole number and a proper fraction together.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Which of these is a proper fraction: 5/3, 2/5, 7/7? A: 2/5

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Equivalent Fractions. I can find equivalent fractions. Equivalent fractions have the same value; multiply or divide numerator and denominator by the same number to find them, then simplify. Keywords: equivalent: equal in value; equal: the same amount; multiply: to increase by a factor; divide: to split into equal parts; simplify: make a fraction smaller
chunks.source: Equivalent fractions have the same value; multiply or divide numerator and denominator by the same number to find them, then simplify.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Find an equivalent fraction for 2/3 with denominator 9. A: 6/9

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Simplify 6/9. A: 2/3

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Are 3/5 and 6/10 equivalent? A: Yes
chunks.source: Yes

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: What do you multiply to get equivalent fractions? A: Multiply numerator and denominator by the same number.
chunks.source: Multiply numerator and denominator by the same number.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words how to simplify a fraction. A: Divide the numerator and denominator by their greatest common factor.
chunks.source: Divide the numerator and denominator by their greatest common factor.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Which operation keeps fractions equal: multiply both parts by 2, or add 2 to both? A: Multiply both parts by 2.
chunks.source: Multiply both parts by 2.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Comparing and Ordering Fractions. I can compare and order fractions. To compare fractions, make denominators the same, then the larger numerator shows the greater fraction; order them from smallest to greatest. Keywords: compare: look at two things to see which is bigger; order: arrange from smallest to biggest; greater: bigger in size; smaller: less in size; denominator: the bottom number of a fraction
chunks.source: To compare fractions, make denominators the same, then the larger numerator shows the greater fraction; order them from smallest to greatest.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Which is greater: 2/5 or 3/5? A: 3/5

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Order 1/4, 3/4, 1/2 from smallest to greatest. A: 1/4, 1/2, 3/4

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: What is the first step to compare 2/3 and 3/5? A: Find a common denominator.
chunks.source: Find a common denominator.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: If two fractions have the same denominator, how do you compare them? A: Compare the numerators.
chunks.source: Compare the numerators.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words what 'greater' means for fractions. A: A fraction is greater if it represents a larger part of the whole.
chunks.source: A fraction is greater if it represents a larger part of the whole.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Which fraction is smaller: 5/8 or 3/8? A: 3/8

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Adding and Subtracting Fractions. I can add and subtract fractions with the same denominator. When fractions share the same denominator, add or subtract the numerators only; the denominator stays unchanged. Keywords: add: put together; subtract: take away; same denominator: bottom numbers are equal; fraction: a part of a whole; sum: the result of adding
chunks.source: When fractions share the same denominator, add or subtract the numerators only; the denominator stays unchanged.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Add 3/9 and 2/9. A: 5/9

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Subtract 4/10 from 9/10. A: 5/10

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: What is the sum of 1/6 and 2/6? A: 3/6

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: When adding fractions with the same denominator, what stays the same? A: The denominator stays the same.
chunks.source: The denominator stays the same.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words how to subtract fractions with the same denominator. A: Subtract the numerators and keep the denominator.
chunks.source: Subtract the numerators and keep the denominator.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: If you have 7/12 and eat 3/12, what fraction remains? A: 4/12

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Naming 2D Shapes. I can name common 2D shapes and count their sides and corners. A triangle has 3 sides and 3 corners. A square has 4 equal sides and 4 corners. A rectangle has 4 sides (2 long, 2 short) and 4 corners. A circle has no straight sides and no corners. Grown-up ask: Which shape did you see most today? Keywords: triangle: A shape with three sides and three corners.; square: A shape with four equal sides and four right angles.; rectangle: A shape with four sides, opposite sides equal, and four right angles.; circle: A round shape with no straight sides or corners.; side: A straight line that forms part of the edge of a shape.
chunks.source: A triangle has 3 sides and 3 corners. A square has 4 equal sides and 4 corners. A rectangle has 4 sides (2 long, 2 short) and 4 corners. A circle has no straight sides and no corners. Grown-up ask: Which shape did you see most today?

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Name the shape with three sides and three corners. A: Triangle
chunks.source: Triangle

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: How many sides does a rectangle have? A: Four sides
chunks.source: Four sides

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Which shape has four equal sides and four corners? A: Square
chunks.source: Square

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: How many corners does a circle have? A: Zero corners
chunks.source: Zero corners

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words the difference between a square and a rectangle. A: A square has four equal sides. A rectangle has two long sides and two short sides.
chunks.source: A square has four equal sides. A rectangle has two long sides and two short sides.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Draw a triangle and count its sides. A: A triangle has three sides.
chunks.source: A triangle has three sides.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Lines and Line Segments. I can tell the difference between a line and a line segment, and measure line segments in centimetres. A line goes on forever. A line segment has two end points and a fixed length. Use a ruler to draw and measure line segments in centimetres. Grown-up ask: Why do we start measuring at 0 cm? Keywords: line: A straight path that goes on forever in both directions.; line segment: A part of a line with two end points. It has a fixed length.; draw: To make a line or shape using a pencil and ruler.; measure: To find the length of something using a ruler or tape measure.; centimetre: A unit of length. 1 centimetre is about the width of your fingernail.
chunks.source: A line goes on forever. A line segment has two end points and a fixed length. Use a ruler to draw and measure line segments in centimetres. Grown-up ask: Why do we start measuring at 0 cm?

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: What is a line segment? A: A part of a line with two end points and a fixed length.
chunks.source: A part of a line with two end points and a fixed length.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: How many end points does a line have? A: A line has no end points.
chunks.source: A line has no end points.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: What tool do you use to draw a straight line segment? A: A ruler and pencil.
chunks.source: A ruler and pencil.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: If a line segment starts at 0 cm and ends at 10 cm, what is its length? A: 10 centimetres
chunks.source: 10 centimetres

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words the difference between a line and a line segment. A: A line goes on forever in both directions. A line segment has two ends and a fixed length.
chunks.source: A line goes on forever in both directions. A line segment has two ends and a fixed length.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Draw a line segment 4 cm long. Measure it to check. A: The line segment should be 4 cm long.
chunks.source: The line segment should be 4 cm long.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Angles in Shapes. I can find angles and right angles in 2D shapes and describe them as turns. An angle is the turn between two lines at a corner. A right angle is a quarter turn. Squares and rectangles have four right angles. Triangles have three angles. Circles have none. Grown-up ask: Can you find a right angle in the room right now? Keywords: angle: The amount of turn between two straight lines that meet at a corner.; right angle: A special angle that looks like the corner of a square. It is a quarter turn.; corner: The point where two sides of a shape meet.; turn: A rotation. A quarter turn makes a right angle.; shape: A flat figure like a triangle, square, rectangle, or circle.
chunks.source: An angle is the turn between two lines at a corner. A right angle is a quarter turn. Squares and rectangles have four right angles. Triangles have three angles. Circles have none. Grown-up ask: Can you find a right angle in the room right now?

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: What is an angle? A: The amount of turn between two straight lines that meet at a corner.
chunks.source: The amount of turn between two straight lines that meet at a corner.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: How many right angles does a rectangle have? A: Four right angles
chunks.source: Four right angles

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Which shape has no angles? A: Circle
chunks.source: Circle

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: How many right angles make a half turn? A: Two right angles
chunks.source: Two right angles

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words what a right angle is. A: A right angle is a quarter turn, like the corner of a square or a book.
chunks.source: A right angle is a quarter turn, like the corner of a square or a book.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Draw a shape with three angles. Name it. A: A triangle has three angles.
chunks.source: A triangle has three angles.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Perimeter of Squares and Rectangles. I can calculate the perimeter of squares and rectangles by adding the lengths of all sides. Perimeter is the distance around a shape. For a rectangle: add length and width, then multiply by 2. For a square: multiply one side by 4. Grown-up ask: If you walk around your bedroom, what are you measuring? Keywords: perimeter: The distance all the way around a shape.; length: The longer side of a rectangle.; width: The shorter side of a rectangle.; around: Going all the way along the outside edge.; add: To put numbers together to find the total.
chunks.source: Perimeter is the distance around a shape. For a rectangle: add length and width, then multiply by 2. For a square: multiply one side by 4. Grown-up ask: If you walk around your bedroom, what are you measuring?

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: What is the perimeter of a rectangle with length 8 cm and width 3 cm? A: 22 cm (2 × (8 + 3) = 22)

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: A square has side 6 m. What is its perimeter? A: 24 m (4 × 6 = 24)

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: What does perimeter mean? A: The distance all the way around a shape.
chunks.source: The distance all the way around a shape.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: If a rectangle has length 10 cm and width 5 cm, what is the perimeter? A: 30 cm (2 × (10 + 5) = 30)

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words how to find the perimeter of a square. A: Multiply the length of one side by 4 because all four sides are equal.
chunks.source: Multiply the length of one side by 4 because all four sides are equal.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Nalongo's garden is 12 m long and 8 m wide. How much fencing does she need? A: 40 m (2 × (12 + 8) = 40)

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Naming Solid Shapes. I can name five common 3D shapes using Ugandan objects. We learned to name five solids: cube, cuboid, cylinder, cone, and sphere using everyday Ugandan objects. Keywords: cube: a solid with six equal square faces; cuboid: a solid with six rectangular faces; cylinder: a solid with two circular faces and a curved surface; cone: a solid with a circular base and a pointed top; sphere: a perfectly round solid
chunks.source: We learned to name five solids: cube, cuboid, cylinder, cone, and sphere using everyday Ugandan objects.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Name the solid with six equal square faces. A: cube
chunks.source: cube

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Which solid has two circular faces and a curved surface? A: cylinder
chunks.source: cylinder

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: A matchbox is an example of which solid? A: cuboid
chunks.source: cuboid

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words what a cone looks like. A: A cone has a circular base and a pointed top.
chunks.source: A cone has a circular base and a pointed top.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: How many faces does a cube have? A: 6 faces
chunks.source: 6 faces

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Draw a sphere and label it. A: A round ball shape labelled sphere.
chunks.source: A round ball shape labelled sphere.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Faces, Edges and Vertices. I can count faces, edges and vertices of common solids. We counted faces, edges, and vertices of solids like cubes, cuboids, cones, and cylinders. Keywords: face: a flat surface of a solid; edge: a line where two faces meet; vertex: a corner where edges meet; vertices: more than one vertex; solid: a three‑dimensional object
chunks.source: We counted faces, edges, and vertices of solids like cubes, cuboids, cones, and cylinders.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: How many faces does a cube have? A: 6 faces
chunks.source: 6 faces

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: What is an edge? A: An edge is where two faces meet.
chunks.source: An edge is where two faces meet.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: A cuboid has how many vertices? A: 8 vertices
chunks.source: 8 vertices

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words what a vertex is. A: A vertex is a corner where edges meet.
chunks.source: A vertex is a corner where edges meet.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Which solid has only one vertex? A: cone
chunks.source: cone

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Count the edges of a cylinder. A: 2 edges (the circles)
chunks.source: 2 edges (the circles)

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Nets of Solids. I can match nets to the solids they form. We learned that a net is a flat pattern which we fold to make solids like cubes and cuboids. Keywords: net: a flat pattern that can be folded into a solid; fold: to bend a flat net along edges to make a solid; cube: a solid with six equal square faces; cuboid: a solid with six rectangular faces; open: showing all faces flat, not folded
chunks.source: We learned that a net is a flat pattern which we fold to make solids like cubes and cuboids.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: What is a net? A: A flat pattern that can be folded into a solid.
chunks.source: A flat pattern that can be folded into a solid.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: How many squares make a cube net? A: 6 squares
chunks.source: 6 squares

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Name the solid made from a net of six rectangles. A: cuboid
chunks.source: cuboid

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words what it means to fold a net. A: To fold a net means to bend the flat shapes along the edges to form a 3D solid.
chunks.source: To fold a net means to bend the flat shapes along the edges to form a 3D solid.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Draw a net for a cube. A: Six squares arranged in a cross shape.
chunks.source: Six squares arranged in a cross shape.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: What does an open net show? A: All faces of the solid laid out flat.
chunks.source: All faces of the solid laid out flat.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Collecting Data with Tallies. I can collect and organise data using tally marks We collect data, use tally marks to count, record the totals, and put them in a table. Keywords: data: information we collect; tally: marks used to count; count: find how many; record: write down the numbers; table: organised list of data
chunks.source: We collect data, use tally marks to count, record the totals, and put them in a table.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: What is a tally? A: Marks used to count items.
chunks.source: Marks used to count items.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: How do you show five in tally marks? A: Four vertical lines with a diagonal line across.
chunks.source: Four vertical lines with a diagonal line across.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: If you have 7 apples, how many tally marks do you draw? A: 7 marks (one group of five and two more).
chunks.source: 7 marks (one group of five and two more).

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words why we use a table. A: A table organises data so we can read it easily.
chunks.source: A table organises data so we can read it easily.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: What does it mean to record data? A: To write down the numbers you counted.
chunks.source: To write down the numbers you counted.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Give an example of data you could collect at home. A: Number of cups of tea each family member drinks.
chunks.source: Number of cups of tea each family member drinks.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Pictographs. I can draw and read a pictograph A pictograph uses symbols and a key to show data; the item with the most symbols is the most. Keywords: pictograph: chart using pictures; symbol: picture that stands for a number; key: explains what each symbol means; data: information we collect; most: the greatest amount
chunks.source: A pictograph uses symbols and a key to show data; the item with the most symbols is the most.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: What is a pictograph? A: A chart that uses pictures to show data.
chunks.source: A chart that uses pictures to show data.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: What does the key tell you? A: It explains what each symbol stands for.
chunks.source: It explains what each symbol stands for.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: If one symbol = 3 books, how many symbols for 12 books? A: 4 symbols.
chunks.source: 4 symbols.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words how to find the most in a pictograph. A: Count the symbols for each item; the one with the highest number of symbols is the most.
chunks.source: Count the symbols for each item; the one with the highest number of symbols is the most.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Why do we use a symbol instead of drawing each item? A: Symbols make the chart small and easy to read.
chunks.source: Symbols make the chart small and easy to read.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Create a key for a pictograph showing 8 oranges, 6 mangoes, 10 bananas using one fruit picture = 2 fruits. A: Key: 1 fruit picture = 2 fruits.
chunks.source: Key: 1 fruit picture = 2 fruits.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Bar Graphs. I can draw and read a bar graph A bar graph uses axes and a scale to show data; comparing bar heights lets us see which values are larger or smaller.
