Keywords: bar graph: chart with bars of different lengths; axis: the two lines that hold the graph; scale: the numbers marked on the axis; data: information we collect; compare: look at differences between bars
chunks.source: A bar graph uses axes and a scale to show data; comparing bar heights lets us see which values are larger or smaller.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: What is a bar graph? A: A chart with bars of different lengths to show data.
chunks.source: A chart with bars of different lengths to show data.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: What are the two axes called? A: Vertical axis and horizontal axis.
chunks.source: Vertical axis and horizontal axis.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: If the scale counts by 2s, what numbers appear on the vertical axis? A: 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words how to compare two days using a bar graph. A: Look at the height of the two bars; the taller bar means more rides.
chunks.source: Look at the height of the two bars; the taller bar means more rides.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Why is a scale important? A: It tells us the value of each bar height.
chunks.source: It tells us the value of each bar height.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Draw a bar graph for these data: Mon 5, Tue 9, Wed 7, Thu 10, Fri 6. Use a scale of 1. A: Bars at heights 5, 9, 7, 10, 6.
chunks.source: Bars at heights 5, 9, 7, 10, 6.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Ugandan Coins and Notes. I can recognise Ugandan coins and notes and say their values. Ugandan **money** comes as metal **coins** and paper **notes**. Each shows its **value** in **shillings**. Coins go up to 1,000 shillings. Notes go up to 50,000 shillings. Keywords: coin: a round metal piece of money; note: a paper piece of money; shilling: the unit of Ugandan money; value: how much money is worth; money: coins and notes used to buy things
chunks.source: Ugandan **money** comes as metal **coins** and paper **notes**. Each shows its **value** in **shillings**. Coins go up to 1,000 shillings. Notes go up to 50,000 shillings.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Name the **value** of a silver **coin** with '500' written on it. A: Five hundred shillings
chunks.source: Five hundred shillings

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Which **note** is brown and worth twenty thousand **shillings**? A: The 20,000 shilling note
chunks.source: The 20,000 shilling note

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Write the **value** in words: 2,000 shillings. A: Two thousand shillings
chunks.source: Two thousand shillings

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words the difference between a **coin** and a **note**. A: A coin is made of metal and is round. A note is made of paper or polymer and is rectangular.
chunks.source: A coin is made of metal and is round. A note is made of paper or polymer and is rectangular.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: If you have one 1,000 shilling **coin** and one 1,000 shilling **note**, do they have the same **value**? A: Yes, both are worth one thousand shillings.
chunks.source: Yes, both are worth one thousand shillings.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Arrange these from smallest to largest **value**: 50 shillings, 5,000 shillings, 500 shillings. A: 50 shillings, 500 shillings, 5,000 shillings
chunks.source: 50 shillings, 500 shillings, 5,000 shillings

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Adding and Subtracting Money. I can add and subtract amounts of money in shillings. To **add** money, line up digits and **add** each column to get the **total**. To **subtract**, line up digits, borrow if needed, and **subtract** to find **change** or what is **left**. Always write 'shillings'. Keywords: add: put amounts together to find the total; subtract: take one amount away from another; shillings: the unit we use for Ugandan money; total: the amount after adding; change: money given back after paying
chunks.source: To **add** money, line up digits and **add** each column to get the **total**. To **subtract**, line up digits, borrow if needed, and **subtract** to find **change** or what is **left**. Always write 'shillings'.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: **Add** 4,500 **shillings** + 2,300 **shillings**. Show your working. A: 4,500 + 2,300 = 6,800 shillings

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: **Subtract** 8,000 **shillings** - 3,500 **shillings**. Show your working. A: 8,000 - 3,500 = 4,500 shillings

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Find the **total** of 1,200, 800, and 3,000 **shillings**. A: 5,000 shillings
chunks.source: 5,000 shillings

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words when you would **add** money and when you would **subtract** money. A: We add money to find the total cost of several items. We subtract money to find change or how much is left after spending.
chunks.source: We add money to find the total cost of several items. We subtract money to find change or how much is left after spending.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: A book costs 2,500 **shillings**. A pen costs 500 **shillings**. What is the **total**? A: 3,000 shillings
chunks.source: 3,000 shillings

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Peter had 5,000 **shillings**. He spent 1,200 **shillings**. How much is **left**? A: 3,800 shillings
chunks.source: 3,800 shillings

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: **Add** 12,000 **shillings** + 8,000 **shillings**. A: 20,000 shillings
chunks.source: 20,000 shillings

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Buying, Selling and Change. I can solve shopping problems: find totals, give change, and understand buying and selling. To **buy**, the **customer** pays the **price**. To **sell**, the shopkeeper receives money. **Add** **prices** for the **total**. **Subtract** **total** from money given to find **change**. Check: money given = **total** + **change**. Keywords: buy: pay money to get something; sell: give something and receive money; price: the amount of money needed to buy; change: money returned after paying more than the price; customer: a person who buys something
chunks.source: To **buy**, the **customer** pays the **price**. To **sell**, the shopkeeper receives money. **Add** **prices** for the **total**. **Subtract** **total** from money given to find **change**. Check: money given = **total** + **change**.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: A **customer** **buys** soap at 1,500 **shillings** and salt at 500 **shillings**. **Total** = ? A: 2,000 shillings
chunks.source: 2,000 shillings

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: **Price** = 3,200 **shillings**. Money given = 5,000 **shillings**. **Change** = ? A: 1,800 shillings
chunks.source: 1,800 shillings

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Nalongo **sells** 2 kilos of sugar at 2,500 **shillings** per kilo. **Total** = ? A: 5,000 shillings
chunks.source: 5,000 shillings

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words what a shopkeeper does when a **customer** gives a large **note** but the **price** is small. A: The shopkeeper subtracts the price from the note to find the change, then gives the change using smaller notes and coins.
chunks.source: The shopkeeper subtracts the price from the note to find the change, then gives the change using smaller notes and coins.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: **Price** = 4,500 **shillings**. **Customer** gives 10,000 **shillings**. Show working for **change**. A: 10,000 - 4,500 = 5,500 shillings

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: A **customer** **buys** three pens at 300 **shillings** each. **Total** = ? A: 900 shillings
chunks.source: 900 shillings

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: If **change** is 1,500 **shillings** and **total** is 3,500 **shillings**, how much money did the **customer** give? A: 5,000 shillings
chunks.source: 5,000 shillings

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Money Word Problems. I can solve word problems about money using addition and subtraction. To solve a money **problem**: read twice, find numbers and key words. **Add** for **altogether** or **total**. **Subtract** for **spend**, **left**, or **change**. Write the answer in a full sentence with **shillings**. Keywords: problem: a question that needs a solution; spend: use money to pay for things; save: keep money for later use; altogether: the total after adding; left: what remains after spending
chunks.source: To solve a money **problem**: read twice, find numbers and key words. **Add** for **altogether** or **total**. **Subtract** for **spend**, **left**, or **change**. Write the answer in a full sentence with **shillings**.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Musa has 5,000 **shillings**. He **spends** 1,200 **shillings**. How much is **left**? A: 3,800 shillings
chunks.source: 3,800 shillings

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Amina **saves** 1,500 **shillings** each week for 3 weeks. How much **altogether**? A: 4,500 shillings
chunks.source: 4,500 shillings

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: A **problem**: Peter **buys** a ball for 3,500 **shillings** and a book for 2,500 **shillings**. He gives 10,000 **shillings**. Find the **change**. A: 4,000 shillings
chunks.source: 4,000 shillings

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words how you decide whether to **add** or **subtract** in a money **problem**. A: I look for key words. 'Altogether', 'total', 'in all' mean add. 'Spent', 'left', 'change', 'save' (finding remainder) mean subtract.
chunks.source: I look for key words. 'Altogether', 'total', 'in all' mean add. 'Spent', 'left', 'change', 'save' (finding remainder) mean subtract.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Nalongo has 7,000 **shillings**. She **spends** 2,000 **shillings** on matooke and 1,500 **shillings** on beans. How much **left**? A: 3,500 shillings
chunks.source: 3,500 shillings

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Kato and Musa put **money** **altogether**. Kato has 4,000 **shillings**. Musa has 3,500 **shillings**. **Total** = ? A: 7,500 shillings
chunks.source: 7,500 shillings

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: A **problem**: Teacher Nankya has 20,000 **shillings**. She **buys** 5 pens at 1,000 **shillings** each. How much **left**? A: 15,000 shillings
chunks.source: 15,000 shillings

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Write your own money **problem** using the words **spend** and **left**. Solve it. A: Example: I have 5,000 shillings. I spend 1,500 shillings. 5,000 - 1,500 = 3,500 shillings left.
chunks.source: Example: I have 5,000 shillings. I spend 1,500 shillings. 5,000 - 1,500 = 3,500 shillings left.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Telling the Time. I can tell time to five minutes on a clock face. You can tell time to five minutes using the hour and minute hands on a clock. Keywords: hour: the number the short hand points to; minute: the number the long hand points to times five; half past: 30 minutes after the hour; quarter past: 15 minutes after the hour; clock: a device that shows the time
chunks.source: You can tell time to five minutes using the hour and minute hands on a clock.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: What time is it when the minute hand points to 6 and the hour hand is between 2 and 3? A: 2:30 (half past two)
chunks.source: 2:30 (half past two)

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Write the time shown when the minute hand points to 3 and the hour hand is just after 5. A: 5:15 (quarter past five)
chunks.source: 5:15 (quarter past five)

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: How many minutes past the hour does the minute hand show when it points to 8? A: 40 minutes
chunks.source: 40 minutes

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words how to read 11:25 on a clock. A: The hour hand is near 11, the minute hand points to 5 (25 minutes).
chunks.source: The hour hand is near 11, the minute hand points to 5 (25 minutes).

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: If the clock shows 4:40, where does the minute hand point? A: At 8 (40 minutes).
chunks.source: At 8 (40 minutes).

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Draw a clock face showing 6:50. A: Hour hand near 7, minute hand at 10.
chunks.source: Hour hand near 7, minute hand at 10.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Converting Time. I can convert between hours, minutes, days and weeks. You can convert between hours, minutes, days and weeks using multiplication or division. Keywords: hours: units of 60 minutes each; minutes: units of 60 seconds each; days: 24 hours make one day; weeks: 7 days make one week; convert: change from one time unit to another
chunks.source: You can convert between hours, minutes, days and weeks using multiplication or division.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Convert 4 hours to minutes. A: 240 minutes (4 × 60).
chunks.source: 240 minutes (4 × 60).

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: How many hours in 2 days? A: 48 hours (2 × 24).

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Convert 3 weeks to days. A: 21 days (3 × 7).

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words how to change 150 minutes into hours. A: Divide 150 by 60 to get 2 hours and 30 minutes.
chunks.source: Divide 150 by 60 to get 2 hours and 30 minutes.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: If a journey takes 360 minutes, how many hours is that? A: 6 hours (360 ÷ 60).

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: A farmer works 5 days a week. How many hours does he work in a week if each day is 8 hours? A: 40 hours (5 × 8).

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: The Calendar. I can read a calendar to find days, weeks, months and dates. A calendar helps you see days, weeks, months and years so you can plan ahead. Keywords: calendar: a chart showing days, weeks and months; day: one 24‑hour period; week: seven days together; month: about 30 days, one of 12 in a year; year: 12 months or 365 days
chunks.source: A calendar helps you see days, weeks, months and years so you can plan ahead.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: What day comes after Friday? A: Saturday.
chunks.source: Saturday.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: How many weeks are in a year? A: About 52 weeks.
chunks.source: About 52 weeks.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: If today is 10th March and it is a Tuesday, what date is the next Tuesday? A: 17th March.
chunks.source: 17th March.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words how to find the number of days in July. A: July is the 7th month and has 31 days.
chunks.source: July is the 7th month and has 31 days.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: A school term starts on 1st September (Monday). What date is the third Monday of the term? A: 15th September.
chunks.source: 15th September.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: How many months have 30 days? A: Four months: April, June, September, November.
chunks.source: Four months: April, June, September, November.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Measuring Length. I can measure length in metres and centimetres and convert between them. We **measure** **length** using **metre** (m) and **centimetre** (cm). 1 m = 100 cm. To **convert** m to cm, multiply by 100. To **convert** cm to m, divide by 100. Keywords: metre: A unit for measuring longer lengths.; centimetre: A small unit for measuring short lengths.; measure: To find the size of something using a tool.; length: How long something is from end to end.; convert: To change a measurement to another unit.
chunks.source: We **measure** **length** using **metre** (m) and **centimetre** (cm). 1 m = 100 cm. To **convert** m to cm, multiply by 100. To **convert** cm to m, divide by 100.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Convert 5 metres to centimetres. A: 500 cm
chunks.source: 500 cm

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Convert 800 centimetres to metres. A: 8 m
chunks.source: 8 m

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: A rope is 3 m 75 cm. Write in metres. A: 3.75 m

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: A book is 25 cm long. Write in metres. A: 0.25 m

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words how to change metres to centimetres. A: Multiply the number of metres by 100 to get centimetres.
chunks.source: Multiply the number of metres by 100 to get centimetres.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words how to change centimetres to metres. A: Divide the number of centimetres by 100 to get metres.
chunks.source: Divide the number of centimetres by 100 to get metres.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Distance and Perimeter. I can measure distance in kilometres and find the perimeter of shapes. **Distance** between places uses **kilometre** (km). 1 km = 1000 m. **Perimeter** is the total length **around** a shape. For a rectangle: 2 × (length + width). For a square: 4 × side. Keywords: kilometre: A unit for measuring long distances.; distance: How far it is from one place to another.; perimeter: The total length around a shape.; around: Going all the way along the edges.; far: A long way from here.
chunks.source: **Distance** between places uses **kilometre** (km). 1 km = 1000 m. **Perimeter** is the total length **around** a shape. For a rectangle: 2 × (length + width). For a square: 4 × side.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Convert 7 kilometres to metres. A: 7000 m

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Convert 5000 metres to kilometres. A: 5 km
chunks.source: 5 km

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: A rectangle is 12 m by 8 m. Find its perimeter. A: 40 m

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: A square has side 15 cm. Find its perimeter. A: 60 cm
chunks.source: 60 cm

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: The perimeter of a square is 36 m. Find the side length. A: 9 m
chunks.source: 9 m

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words what perimeter means. A: Perimeter is the total distance around the outside of a shape.
chunks.source: Perimeter is the total distance around the outside of a shape.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words when we use kilometres instead of metres. A: We use kilometres for long distances like between towns or on roads.
chunks.source: We use kilometres for long distances like between towns or on roads.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Mass: Kilograms and Grams. I can measure mass in kilograms and grams and convert between them. **Mass** is measured in **kilogram** (kg) and **gram** (g). 1 kg = 1000 g. **Weigh** objects on a **balance** or scale. To **convert** kg to g, multiply by 1000. To **convert** g to kg, divide by 1000. Keywords: kilogram: A unit for measuring heavier mass.; gram: A small unit for measuring light mass.; mass: The amount of matter in an object.; weigh: To find the mass using a scale.; balance: A tool that compares mass.
chunks.source: **Mass** is measured in **kilogram** (kg) and **gram** (g). 1 kg = 1000 g. **Weigh** objects on a **balance** or scale. To **convert** kg to g, multiply by 1000. To **convert** g to kg, divide by 1000.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Convert 4 kilograms to grams. A: 4000 g

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Convert 3000 grams to kilograms. A: 3 kg
chunks.source: 3 kg

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: A bag of rice is 2.5 kg. Write in grams. A: 2500 g

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: A packet of biscuits is 200 g. Write in kilograms. A: 0.2 kg
chunks.source: 0.2 kg

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Two sacks of charcoal are 25 kg and 30 kg. Total mass? A: 55 kg
chunks.source: 55 kg

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words the difference between mass and weight. A: Mass is the amount of matter; weight is the force of gravity on that mass. On Earth they are similar but not the same.
chunks.source: Mass is the amount of matter; weight is the force of gravity on that mass. On Earth they are similar but not the same.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words how to change kilograms to grams. A: Multiply the number of kilograms by 1000 to get grams.
chunks.source: Multiply the number of kilograms by 1000 to get grams.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Capacity: Litres and Millilitres. I can measure capacity in litres and millilitres and convert between them. **Capacity** is what a container can hold. **Volume** is the liquid inside. Units: **litre** (L) and **millilitre** (ml). 1 L = 1000 ml. **Convert** L to ml × 1000; ml to L ÷ 1000. Use a **jug** or marked bottle to measure. Keywords: litre: A unit for measuring larger liquid amounts.; millilitre: A small unit for measuring tiny liquid amounts.; capacity: How much a container can hold.; volume: The amount of liquid inside a container.; jug: A container with a handle for pouring.
chunks.source: **Capacity** is what a container can hold. **Volume** is the liquid inside. Units: **litre** (L) and **millilitre** (ml). 1 L = 1000 ml. **Convert** L to ml × 1000; ml to L ÷ 1000. Use a **jug** or marked bottle to measure.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Convert 3 litres to millilitres. A: 3000 ml

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Convert 5000 millilitres to litres. A: 5 L
chunks.source: 5 L

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: A jug holds 2.5 L of juice. Write in millilitres. A: 2500 ml

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: A medicine bottle is 100 ml. Write in litres. A: 0.1 L

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Two jerrycans of 20 L each are filled. Total volume? A: 40 L

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words the difference between capacity and volume. A: Capacity is the maximum a container can hold; volume is the actual amount of liquid inside at a given time.
chunks.source: Capacity is the maximum a container can hold; volume is the actual amount of liquid inside at a given time.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words how to change litres to millilitres. A: Multiply the number of litres by 1000 to get millilitres.
chunks.source: Multiply the number of litres by 1000 to get millilitres.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Finding the Missing Number. I can find the missing number in a number sentence. A box stands for a missing number. Use the opposite operation to find its value in the equation. Keywords: missing number: the number we do not know yet; box: a square that stands for the unknown number; equation: a number sentence with an equal sign; find: to work out the answer; value: the amount the box stands for
chunks.source: A box stands for a missing number. Use the opposite operation to find its value in the equation.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: What is the missing number in 9 + □ = 20? A: 11

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Solve □ - 6 = 8. A: 14

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Find the value of the box: 5 × □ = 35. A: 7

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words how you find a missing number in an addition equation. A: Subtract the known addend from the total.
chunks.source: Subtract the known addend from the total.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Write an equation with a box for the unknown: 12 minus something equals 5. A: 12 - □ = 5

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Forming Simple Equations. I can form a simple equation from a word problem. Turn a word sentence into an equation by finding the unknown and choosing the right operation with the given numbers. Keywords: form: to make or create something; equation: a number sentence with an equal sign; sentence: a group of words that gives a complete idea; unknown: the number we do not know yet; number: a counting value like 1, 2, 3
chunks.source: Turn a word sentence into an equation by finding the unknown and choosing the right operation with the given numbers.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Write an equation for: "A packet of biscuits costs 1,200 shillings. John buys 4 packets." A: 4 × 1,200 = □

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Form an equation: "There are 6 rows of chairs. Each row has 8 chairs." A: 6 × 8 = □

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Create an equation for: "A jerrycan holds 20 litres. How many litres in 3 jerrycans?" A: 3 × 20 = □

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words how you decide which operation to use when forming an equation. A: Look for groups of the same size; multiply. If sharing equally, divide.
chunks.source: Look for groups of the same size; multiply. If sharing equally, divide.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Write a word sentence for the equation 7 × 300 = □. A: Seven groups of three hundred shillings each.
chunks.source: Seven groups of three hundred shillings each.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Solving Simple Equations. I can solve a simple equation without letters. Solving an equation means keeping both sides balanced. Do the opposite operation to isolate the unknown and find the answer. Keywords: solve: to work out the answer; equation: a number sentence with an equal sign; balance: to keep both sides equal; unknown: the number we do not know yet; answer: the final value we find
chunks.source: Solving an equation means keeping both sides balanced. Do the opposite operation to isolate the unknown and find the answer.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Find the unknown: 25 - □ = 9. A: 16

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Solve □ × 7 = 56. A: 8

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Work out □ ÷ 3 = 12. A: 36

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words why we must do the same thing to both sides of an equation. A: To keep the equation balanced so both sides stay equal.
chunks.source: To keep the equation balanced so both sides stay equal.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Solve 72 ÷ □ = 9. A: 8

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Parts of a Flowering Plant. I can name the six parts of a flowering plant and say what each part does. A flowering plant has six main parts: **root**, **stem**, **leaf**, **flower**, **fruit**, and **shoot**. Each part does a special job to help the plant live and make new plants. Keywords: root: the part under soil that holds the plant and takes water; stem: the main stalk that holds leaves and carries water; leaf: the green part that makes food for the plant; flower: the colourful part that makes seeds and fruit; fruit: the part that holds seeds, often good to eat; shoot: the young stem with leaves growing up from the ground
chunks.source: A flowering plant has six main parts: **root**, **stem**, **leaf**, **flower**, **fruit**, and **shoot**. Each part does a special job to help the plant live and make new plants.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What does the root do? A: The root holds the plant in the soil and takes up water.
chunks.source: The root holds the plant in the soil and takes up water.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What does the stem do? A: The stem holds the leaves up and carries water from the root.
chunks.source: The stem holds the leaves up and carries water from the root.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What does the leaf do? A: The leaf makes food for the plant using sunlight.
chunks.source: The leaf makes food for the plant using sunlight.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What grows from the flower after pollination? A: The fruit grows from the flower and holds seeds.
chunks.source: The fruit grows from the flower and holds seeds.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is a shoot? A: A shoot is a young stem with leaves growing up from the ground.
chunks.source: A shoot is a young stem with leaves growing up from the ground.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words why a plant needs all six parts. A: Each part has a job: root holds and drinks, stem carries and holds, leaf makes food, flower makes seeds, fruit protects seeds, shoot is the young plant.
chunks.source: Each part has a job: root holds and drinks, stem carries and holds, leaf makes food, flower makes seeds, fruit protects seeds, shoot is the young plant.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words how the stem and leaf work together. A: The stem lifts the leaf to the sunlight and brings water to it. The leaf uses the water and sunlight to make food.
chunks.source: The stem lifts the leaf to the sunlight and brings water to it. The leaf uses the water and sunlight to make food.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: How Plants Feed. I can explain how plants make food through photosynthesis. Plants make their own food through **photosynthesis** in the **leaf**. They need **sunlight**, **chlorophyll**, **carbon dioxide** from air, and water from the **root**. Keywords: photosynthesis: the process by which green plants make their own food; sunlight: light energy from the sun that plants use to make food; chlorophyll: the green pigment in leaves that traps sunlight; stomata: tiny holes on the leaf surface that let gases in and out; carbon dioxide: a gas from the air that plants use to make food; leaf: the flat green part of a plant where food is made
chunks.source: Plants make their own food through **photosynthesis** in the **leaf**. They need **sunlight**, **chlorophyll**, **carbon dioxide** from air, and water from the **root**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is photosynthesis? A: The process where green plants make food using sunlight, chlorophyll, carbon dioxide, and water.
chunks.source: The process where green plants make food using sunlight, chlorophyll, carbon dioxide, and water.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What does chlorophyll do? A: Chlorophyll is the green pigment that traps sunlight in the leaf.
chunks.source: Chlorophyll is the green pigment that traps sunlight in the leaf.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What are stomata? A: Tiny holes on the leaf that let carbon dioxide in and oxygen out.
chunks.source: Tiny holes on the leaf that let carbon dioxide in and oxygen out.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Where does the leaf get carbon dioxide? A: From the air through the stomata.
chunks.source: From the air through the stomata.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What gas do plants give out during photosynthesis? A: Oxygen.
chunks.source: Oxygen.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words why leaves are green. A: Leaves are green because chlorophyll traps sunlight. The green colour shows chlorophyll is there working.
chunks.source: Leaves are green because chlorophyll traps sunlight. The green colour shows chlorophyll is there working.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words what happens to the water the root takes up. A: The stem carries water to the leaf. The leaf uses water with carbon dioxide and sunlight to make food.
chunks.source: The stem carries water to the leaf. The leaf uses water with carbon dioxide and sunlight to make food.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Pollination and Fertilisation. I can describe how pollination and fertilisation make seeds and fruit. Pollination moves **pollen** to the **stigma** by **agents** like **wind** or **insect**s. **Fertilisation** joins male and female cells in the **ovary**, which becomes a **fruit** with seeds. Keywords: pollen: fine powder from the male part of a flower; stigma: the sticky top of the female part that catches pollen; ovary: the swollen base of the female part where seeds form; agent: something that moves pollen from one flower to another; wind: moving air that can carry light pollen between flowers; insect: a small animal like a bee that carries pollen between flowers
chunks.source: Pollination moves **pollen** to the **stigma** by **agents** like **wind** or **insect**s. **Fertilisation** joins male and female cells in the **ovary**, which becomes a **fruit** with seeds.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is pollen? A: Fine powder from the male part of a flower that carries male cells.
chunks.source: Fine powder from the male part of a flower that carries male cells.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is the stigma? A: The sticky top of the female part that catches pollen.
chunks.source: The sticky top of the female part that catches pollen.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What happens in fertilisation? A: The male cell from pollen joins the female cell in the ovary.
chunks.source: The male cell from pollen joins the female cell in the ovary.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name an insect agent. A: A bee or butterfly.
chunks.source: A bee or butterfly.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name a wind agent plant. A: Maize or grass.
chunks.source: Maize or grass.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words why maize does not need insects for pollination. A: Maize pollen is light and dry so wind can carry it. The flowers are dull and have no nectar for insects.
chunks.source: Maize pollen is light and dry so wind can carry it. The flowers are dull and have no nectar for insects.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words what the ovary becomes after fertilisation. A: The ovary swells and becomes a fruit that holds the seeds.
chunks.source: The ovary swells and becomes a fruit that holds the seeds.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Seed Dispersal and Germination. I can explain how seeds disperse and what they need to germinate. **Dispersal** spreads seeds by **agents** like **wind**, water, or animals. **Germination** needs **water**, **air**, and **warmth**. The **radicle** becomes the **root**; the **plumule** becomes the **shoot** and **leaf** of the **seedling**. Keywords: dispersal: the spreading of seeds away from the parent plant; agent: something that helps move seeds to new places; germination: the process of a seed starting to grow into a new plant; seedling: a young plant that has just grown from a seed; plumule: the part of the seed that grows into the shoot and leaves; radicle: the part of the seed that grows into the root
chunks.source: **Dispersal** spreads seeds by **agents** like **wind**, water, or animals. **Germination** needs **water**, **air**, and **warmth**. The **radicle** becomes the **root**; the **plumule** becomes the **shoot** and **leaf** of the **seedling**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is dispersal? A: The spreading of seeds away from the parent plant.
chunks.source: The spreading of seeds away from the parent plant.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name three agents of dispersal. A: Wind, water, and animals.
chunks.source: Wind, water, and animals.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What three things are needed for germination? A: Water, air, and warmth.
chunks.source: Water, air, and warmth.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is a seedling? A: A young plant that has just grown from a seed.
chunks.source: A young plant that has just grown from a seed.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What does the radicle become? A: The radicle grows down to become the root.
chunks.source: The radicle grows down to become the root.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What does the plumule become? A: The plumule grows up to become the shoot and leaves.
chunks.source: The plumule grows up to become the shoot and leaves.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words why seeds need to disperse. A: If seeds fall only under the parent, they compete for light, water, and space. Dispersal gives them a better chance.
chunks.source: If seeds fall only under the parent, they compete for light, water, and space. Dispersal gives them a better chance.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words what happens in the jar experiment if you turn it upside down. A: The radicle bends down toward gravity and the plumule bends up away from gravity.
chunks.source: The radicle bends down toward gravity and the plumule bends up away from gravity.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Preparing the Land. I can explain how to prepare land for planting crops. Preparing land means clearing, digging, harrowing, making a seedbed, raising a nursery, and transplanting seedlings. Keywords: clearing: removing bushes and grass; digging: turning soil with a hoe; harrowing: breaking soil clods to make it fine; seedbed: prepared ground for sowing seeds; nursery: place where young seedlings grow; transplant: moving seedlings to the main field
chunks.source: Preparing land means clearing, digging, harrowing, making a seedbed, raising a nursery, and transplanting seedlings.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is the first step in land preparation? A: Clearing the land.
chunks.source: Clearing the land.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which tool is used to make a fine seedbed? A: A harrow.
chunks.source: A harrow.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words why we harrow the field. A: Harrowing breaks soil clods to make a smooth seedbed.
chunks.source: Harrowing breaks soil clods to make a smooth seedbed.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is a nursery? A: A place where young seedlings grow before transplanting.
chunks.source: A place where young seedlings grow before transplanting.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: When should seedlings be transplanted? A: When they have 2-3 true leaves.
chunks.source: When they have 2-3 true leaves.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words the purpose of a seedbed. A: A seedbed is a prepared area where seeds are sown.
chunks.source: A seedbed is a prepared area where seeds are sown.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Caring for Crops. I can describe how to care for growing crops. Caring for crops includes weeding, mulching, pruning, staking, thinning, and watering to help plants grow strong. Keywords: weeding: removing unwanted plants; mulching: covering soil with dry grass or leaves; pruning: cutting extra branches; staking: supporting plants with sticks; thinning: removing extra seedlings to give space; watering: giving water to plants
chunks.source: Caring for crops includes weeding, mulching, pruning, staking, thinning, and watering to help plants grow strong.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is the first action when weeds grow? A: Weeding.
chunks.source: Weeding.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which practice helps keep soil moist? A: Mulching.
chunks.source: Mulching.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words why we prune plants. A: Pruning removes extra branches to improve air flow and fruit quality.
chunks.source: Pruning removes extra branches to improve air flow and fruit quality.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What does staking do for a plant? A: It supports the stem so the plant stands upright.
chunks.source: It supports the stem so the plant stands upright.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: When should we thin seedlings? A: When they are too close together.
chunks.source: When they are too close together.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words the importance of watering. A: Watering gives plants the moisture they need for growth.
chunks.source: Watering gives plants the moisture they need for growth.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Harvesting and Storing Crops. I can explain how to harvest and store crops safely. Harvest at the right time, dry well, winnow to clean, and store in a granary to keep pests away. Keywords: harvest: cutting and gathering ripe crops; dry: removing moisture from crops; store: keeping crops safely for later; granary: a building for storing grain; pests: insects or animals that damage crops; winnow: separating grain from chaff by wind
chunks.source: Harvest at the right time, dry well, winnow to clean, and store in a granary to keep pests away.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: When should maize be harvested? A: When kernels are hard.
chunks.source: When kernels are hard.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What does winnowing do? A: It separates grain from chaff using wind.
chunks.source: It separates grain from chaff using wind.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words why we dry crops before storage. A: Drying reduces moisture so mould and pests cannot grow.
chunks.source: Drying reduces moisture so mould and pests cannot grow.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is a granary? A: A storage building for dried grain.
chunks.source: A storage building for dried grain.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How can we protect stored grain from pests? A: Keep it in a clean, sealed granary.
chunks.source: Keep it in a clean, sealed granary.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words the steps after harvesting. A: Dry the crop, winnow to clean, then store in a granary.
chunks.source: Dry the crop, winnow to clean, then store in a granary.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Elements and Instruments of Weather. I can name weather elements and the instruments used to measure them. Weather elements like sunshine and rainfall are measured with tools such as a thermometer, rain gauge, wind vane, and anemometer. Keywords: thermometer: instrument that shows temperature; rain gauge: instrument that collects rain to measure rainfall; wind vane: instrument that points to wind direction; anemometer: instrument that measures wind speed; sunshine: bright light from the sun; rainfall: amount of rain that falls
chunks.source: Weather elements like sunshine and rainfall are measured with tools such as a thermometer, rain gauge, wind vane, and anemometer.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What does a thermometer measure? A: A thermometer measures temperature.
chunks.source: A thermometer measures temperature.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which instrument measures rainfall? A: A rain gauge measures rainfall.
chunks.source: A rain gauge measures rainfall.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What does a wind vane show? A: A wind vane shows wind direction.
chunks.source: A wind vane shows wind direction.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How does an anemometer work? A: An anemometer counts wind speed by spinning cups.
chunks.source: An anemometer counts wind speed by spinning cups.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words what sunshine is. A: Sunshine is the bright light and heat from the sun.
chunks.source: Sunshine is the bright light and heat from the sun.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words what rainfall means. A: Rainfall is the amount of rain that falls in a place.
chunks.source: Rainfall is the amount of rain that falls in a place.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Types of Clouds and Rain. I can identify common cloud types and explain how rain forms. Clouds come in different shapes: cumulus, stratus, cirrus, and nimbus. Nimbus clouds bring rain. Keywords: nimbus: cloud that brings rain; cumulus: fluffy white cloud with flat base; stratus: low grey cloud covering the sky; cirrus: high thin wispy cloud; rain: water falling from clouds; cloud: mass of water droplets in the sky
chunks.source: Clouds come in different shapes: cumulus, stratus, cirrus, and nimbus. Nimbus clouds bring rain.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What type of cloud brings rain? A: Nimbus clouds bring rain.
chunks.source: Nimbus clouds bring rain.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Describe cumulus clouds. A: Cumulus clouds are fluffy and white with flat bases.
chunks.source: Cumulus clouds are fluffy and white with flat bases.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Where do cirrus clouds form? A: Cirrus clouds form high in the sky.
chunks.source: Cirrus clouds form high in the sky.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words how rain forms. A: Rain forms when water droplets in a cloud join together and fall.
chunks.source: Rain forms when water droplets in a cloud join together and fall.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words the difference between stratus and cirrus clouds. A: Stratus clouds are low and grey; cirrus clouds are high and thin.
chunks.source: Stratus clouds are low and grey; cirrus clouds are high and thin.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which cloud type is a sign of fair weather? A: Cumulus clouds often mean fair weather.
chunks.source: Cumulus clouds often mean fair weather.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Managing Weather Changes. I can describe effects of extreme weather and ways to manage them. Extreme weather like flood and drought can be managed by using forecasts, mulching, irrigation, and good seasonal planning. Keywords: flood: overflow of water onto land; drought: long period without rain; mulching: covering soil with dry grass to keep moisture; irrigation: watering crops using pipes or canals; forecast: prediction of weather for coming days; season: time of year with typical weather
chunks.source: Extreme weather like flood and drought can be managed by using forecasts, mulching, irrigation, and good seasonal planning.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is a flood? A: A flood is an overflow of water onto land.
chunks.source: A flood is an overflow of water onto land.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What does mulching do? A: Mulching covers soil to keep moisture.
chunks.source: Mulching covers soil to keep moisture.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How does irrigation help during drought? A: Irrigation supplies water to crops when there is no rain.
chunks.source: Irrigation supplies water to crops when there is no rain.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words why a forecast is useful. A: A forecast tells you what weather to expect so you can prepare.
chunks.source: A forecast tells you what weather to expect so you can prepare.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words the difference between flood and drought. A: A flood is too much water; a drought is too little water for a long time.
chunks.source: A flood is too much water; a drought is too little water for a long time.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What should a farmer do at the start of the rainy season? A: A farmer should store water, repair roofs, and plant early.
chunks.source: A farmer should store water, repair roofs, and plant early.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Classes of Food. I can name the three classes of food and give examples from Uganda. **Carbohydrates** give **energy**. **Proteins** do **body-building**. **Vitamins** are **protective**. A good **meal** has all three. Keywords: carbohydrates: foods that give us energy; proteins: foods that build our body; vitamins: foods that protect us from sickness; energy: power to work and play; body-building: making muscles and bones strong; protective: keeping the body safe from disease
chunks.source: **Carbohydrates** give **energy**. **Proteins** do **body-building**. **Vitamins** are **protective**. A good **meal** has all three.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name one **carbohydrate** you eat at home. A: Posho, cassava, matooke, sweet potato, or rice.
chunks.source: Posho, cassava, matooke, sweet potato, or rice.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What job do **proteins** do in the body? A: They help **body-building** — muscles and bones.
chunks.source: They help **body-building** — muscles and bones.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which class of food is **protective**? A: **Vitamins** are **protective** foods.
chunks.source: **Vitamins** are **protective** foods.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give two examples of **vitamins** from the market. A: Mangoes, oranges, pawpaw, dodo, nakati.
chunks.source: Mangoes, oranges, pawpaw, dodo, nakati.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words why we need **energy** foods. A: We need **energy** to work, play, walk, and dig.
chunks.source: We need **energy** to work, play, walk, and dig.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: A Balanced Diet. I can explain a balanced diet and name two deficiency diseases. A **balanced diet** has **carbohydrates**, **proteins**, and **vitamins** at every **meal**. It prevents **kwashiorkor**, **marasmus**, and **malnutrition**. Keywords: balanced diet: a meal with all food classes; deficiency: lack of something the body needs; malnutrition: poor health from wrong food; kwashiorkor: disease from not enough protein; marasmus: disease from not enough food at all; meal: food eaten at one time
chunks.source: A **balanced diet** has **carbohydrates**, **proteins**, and **vitamins** at every **meal**. It prevents **kwashiorkor**, **marasmus**, and **malnutrition**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is a **balanced diet**? A: A **meal** with **carbohydrates**, **proteins**, and **vitamins**.
chunks.source: A **meal** with **carbohydrates**, **proteins**, and **vitamins**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name one disease caused by **protein** **deficiency**. A: **Kwashiorkor**.
chunks.source: **Kwashiorkor**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How is **marasmus** different from **kwashiorkor**? A: **Marasmus** is lack of all food. **Kwashiorkor** is lack of **protein** only.
chunks.source: **Marasmus** is lack of all food. **Kwashiorkor** is lack of **protein** only.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why is **malnutrition** dangerous for children? A: It stops growth, weakens the body, and causes sickness.
chunks.source: It stops growth, weakens the body, and causes sickness.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words how to prevent **kwashiorkor**. A: Eat **protein** foods like beans, fish, or eggs at every **meal**.
chunks.source: Eat **protein** foods like beans, fish, or eggs at every **meal**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Vitamins and Their Sources. I can match vitamins to local foods and name the sickness they prevent. **Vitamin C** from **fruit** and **vegetable** stops **scurvy**. **Vitamin D** from sun and fish stops **rickets**. **Vitamin A** from yellow **fruit** and dark **vegetable** stops **night blindness**. Keywords: vitamin: a nutrient that protects the body; scurvy: disease from lack of vitamin C; rickets: disease from lack of vitamin D; night blindness: cannot see well in dim light; fruit: sweet food from a plant, often with seeds; vegetable: plant eaten as food, often leaves or roots
chunks.source: **Vitamin C** from **fruit** and **vegetable** stops **scurvy**. **Vitamin D** from sun and fish stops **rickets**. **Vitamin A** from yellow **fruit** and dark **vegetable** stops **night blindness**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which **vitamin** prevents **scurvy**? A: **Vitamin C**.
chunks.source: **Vitamin C**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name two local sources of **vitamin A**. A: Mango, pawpaw, dodo, nakati, carrots.
chunks.source: Mango, pawpaw, dodo, nakati, carrots.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What sickness comes from lack of **vitamin D**? A: **Rickets**.
chunks.source: **Rickets**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How can a child get **vitamin D** without eating fish? A: Sunlight on the skin makes **vitamin D**.
chunks.source: Sunlight on the skin makes **vitamin D**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words why **fruit** and **vegetable** are important. A: They give **vitamins** that stop **scurvy**, **rickets**, and **night blindness**.
chunks.source: They give **vitamins** that stop **scurvy**, **rickets**, and **night blindness**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Keeping Food Safe. I can explain how food gets contaminated and name two ways to preserve it. **Contamination** by **bacteria** spoils food. **Cover** food, wash hands, use clean mats. **Drying** and **smoking** are good **preservation** methods. Keywords: contamination: dirt or germs getting into food; bacteria: tiny germs that spoil food; cover: put a lid or cloth over food; preservation: keeping food good for a long time; drying: removing water from food in the sun; smoking: using smoke to preserve fish or meat
chunks.source: **Contamination** by **bacteria** spoils food. **Cover** food, wash hands, use clean mats. **Drying** and **smoking** are good **preservation** methods.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is **contamination**? A: Dirt or germs getting into food.
chunks.source: Dirt or germs getting into food.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why do **bacteria** spoil food? A: They grow in warm, wet food and make it rot.
chunks.source: They grow in warm, wet food and make it rot.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name one way to **cover** food at home. A: Use a lid, clean cloth, or plate.
chunks.source: Use a lid, clean cloth, or plate.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How does **drying** preserve food? A: It removes water so **bacteria** cannot grow.
chunks.source: It removes water so **bacteria** cannot grow.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words why **smoking** keeps fish safe. A: Smoke dries the fish and kills **bacteria**.
chunks.source: Smoke dries the fish and kills **bacteria**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: The Brain and the Heart. I can name the position and function of the brain and heart. The brain in the skull controls the body. The heart behind the ribs pumps blood. Both need protection and healthy habits. Keywords: brain: organ in the head that controls the body; heart: organ in the chest that pumps blood; skull: bony box that protects the brain; ribs: bones around the chest that protect the heart; pump: to push liquid through a system; blood: red liquid that carries oxygen in the body
chunks.source: The brain in the skull controls the body. The heart behind the ribs pumps blood. Both need protection and healthy habits.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Where is the brain located? A: Inside the skull in the head.
chunks.source: Inside the skull in the head.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What does the heart do? A: It pumps blood around the body.
chunks.source: It pumps blood around the body.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which bones protect the heart? A: The ribs protect the heart.
chunks.source: The ribs protect the heart.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name one way to keep the heart healthy. A: Eat a balanced diet and exercise.
chunks.source: Eat a balanced diet and exercise.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words why the brain needs a steady flow of blood. A: The brain needs oxygen and nutrients from blood to think, move, and control the body.
chunks.source: The brain needs oxygen and nutrients from blood to think, move, and control the body.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: The Lungs and Breathing. I can describe the lungs, trachea, and the breathing process. The trachea carries air to the lungs in the chest. Lungs swap oxygen into blood and carbon dioxide out. Clean air and exercise keep lungs healthy. Keywords: lungs: two spongy organs in the chest for breathing; trachea: windpipe that carries air to the lungs; oxygen: gas in air that the body needs for energy; carbon dioxide: waste gas that the body breathes out; breathe: to take air in and out of the lungs; chest: front part of the body between neck and stomach
chunks.source: The trachea carries air to the lungs in the chest. Lungs swap oxygen into blood and carbon dioxide out. Clean air and exercise keep lungs healthy.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is the trachea? A: The windpipe that carries air to the lungs.
chunks.source: The windpipe that carries air to the lungs.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which gas do we breathe in? A: Oxygen.
chunks.source: Oxygen.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which gas do we breathe out? A: Carbon dioxide.
chunks.source: Carbon dioxide.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What happens to the chest when you breathe in? A: The chest expands as the lungs fill with air.
chunks.source: The chest expands as the lungs fill with air.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words why we breathe faster when we run. A: Muscles need more oxygen for energy, so lungs and heart work faster to supply it.
chunks.source: Muscles need more oxygen for energy, so lungs and heart work faster to supply it.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: The Kidneys, Liver and Skin. I can explain how kidneys, liver, and skin remove waste and protect the body. Kidneys filter blood into urine. Liver cleans blood and digests fats. Skin protects and cools with sweat. Water keeps all three working well. Keywords: kidney: organ that filters blood and makes urine; liver: large organ that cleans blood and helps digestion; skin: outer covering of the body that protects and sweats; urine: liquid waste made by kidneys; sweat: salty water that comes out through skin pores; filter: to remove unwanted substances from a liquid
chunks.source: Kidneys filter blood into urine. Liver cleans blood and digests fats. Skin protects and cools with sweat. Water keeps all three working well.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What do kidneys make from filtered blood? A: Urine.
chunks.source: Urine.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name one job of the liver. A: Cleans blood and helps digestion.
chunks.source: Cleans blood and helps digestion.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How does sweat help the body? A: It cools the body when it evaporates.
chunks.source: It cools the body when it evaporates.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why is drinking water important for these organs? A: Water helps kidneys filter, liver clean blood, and replace sweat.
chunks.source: Water helps kidneys filter, liver clean blood, and replace sweat.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words how the skin protects you. A: Skin is a barrier that stops germs entering and cools the body with sweat.
chunks.source: Skin is a barrier that stops germs entering and cools the body with sweat.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Keeping Body Organs Healthy. I can list habits that protect organs and explain dangers of alcohol and smoking. Exercise, rest, hygiene, and a balanced diet keep organs healthy. Alcohol damages liver and brain. Smoking harms lungs and heart. Choose healthy habits every day. Keywords: exercise: physical activity that makes the body stronger; alcohol: drink like waragi that harms organs; smoking: breathing in smoke from cigarettes; rest: sleep or quiet time to let the body recover; hygiene: clean habits that prevent disease; diet: the food and drink you eat regularly
chunks.source: Exercise, rest, hygiene, and a balanced diet keep organs healthy. Alcohol damages liver and brain. Smoking harms lungs and heart. Choose healthy habits every day.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name two benefits of exercise for organs. A: Strengthens heart and lungs; improves blood flow.
chunks.source: Strengthens heart and lungs; improves blood flow.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How does alcohol harm the liver? A: It damages liver cells and can cause liver disease.
chunks.source: It damages liver cells and can cause liver disease.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What does smoking do to the lungs? A: It deposits tar and poisons, making breathing difficult and causing disease.
chunks.source: It deposits tar and poisons, making breathing difficult and causing disease.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why do children need 9-10 hours of rest? A: Brain processes memories; liver and body repair during sleep.
chunks.source: Brain processes memories; liver and body repair during sleep.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words how a balanced diet protects your organs. A: It gives the right nutrients for each organ to work, repair, and fight disease.
chunks.source: It gives the right nutrients for each organ to work, repair, and fight disease.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Types of Teeth. I can name the four types of teeth and say what each one does. We have four types of teeth: incisors cut, canines tear, premolars crush, molars grind. Each shape matches its job. Keywords: incisors: front teeth for cutting; canines: pointed teeth for tearing; premolars: flat teeth behind canines; molars: big back teeth for grinding; cutting: slicing food into small pieces; tearing: pulling food apart with force
chunks.source: We have four types of teeth: incisors cut, canines tear, premolars crush, molars grind. Each shape matches its job.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name the teeth used for cutting. A: Incisors
chunks.source: Incisors

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name the teeth used for tearing. A: Canines
chunks.source: Canines

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which teeth crush food like posho? A: Premolars
chunks.source: Premolars

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which teeth grind food into a paste? A: Molars
chunks.source: Molars

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words why we need different types of teeth. A: Different teeth do different jobs: cutting, tearing, crushing, grinding. This helps us eat all kinds of food.
chunks.source: Different teeth do different jobs: cutting, tearing, crushing, grinding. This helps us eat all kinds of food.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Structure of a Tooth. I can name the parts of a tooth and say what each part does. A tooth has enamel (hard cover), dentine (support), pulp with nerve (living centre), root (anchor), and gum (cover). Each part has a job. Keywords: enamel: hard white outer layer; dentine: hard layer under enamel; pulp: soft centre with blood vessels; gum: pink flesh holding the tooth; root: part of tooth in the jawbone; nerve: tiny thread that feels pain
chunks.source: A tooth has enamel (hard cover), dentine (support), pulp with nerve (living centre), root (anchor), and gum (cover). Each part has a job.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name the hardest substance in the body. A: Enamel
chunks.source: Enamel

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which part has blood vessels and nerve? A: Pulp
chunks.source: Pulp

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What covers the root and protects it? A: Gum
chunks.source: Gum

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which part anchors the tooth in the jawbone? A: Root
chunks.source: Root

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words why enamel is important. A: Enamel is the hard outer layer that protects the tooth from damage when chewing and from decay.
chunks.source: Enamel is the hard outer layer that protects the tooth from damage when chewing and from decay.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Dental Care and Diseases. I can explain how to care for teeth and name common dental problems. Plaque causes decay. Brush twice daily with fluoride toothpaste. Visit the dentist every six months. Less sugar, more water. Healthy teeth last a lifetime. Keywords: decay: rotting of tooth by germs; plaque: sticky germ layer on teeth; fluoride: mineral that strengthens enamel; brush: clean teeth with a toothbrush; dentist: doctor for teeth; cavity: hole in tooth from decay
chunks.source: Plaque causes decay. Brush twice daily with fluoride toothpaste. Visit the dentist every six months. Less sugar, more water. Healthy teeth last a lifetime.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is the sticky layer of germs on teeth called? A: Plaque
chunks.source: Plaque

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What mineral in toothpaste strengthens enamel? A: Fluoride
chunks.source: Fluoride

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How many times a day should you brush? A: Twice
chunks.source: Twice

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is a hole in the tooth called? A: Cavity
chunks.source: Cavity

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Who treats cavities and checks teeth? A: Dentist
chunks.source: Dentist

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words how decay starts and how to prevent it. A: Germs in plaque make acid from sugar. Acid causes decay. Brush twice daily with fluoride toothpaste, eat less sugar, visit dentist regularly.
chunks.source: Germs in plaque make acid from sugar. Acid causes decay. Brush twice daily with fluoride toothpaste, eat less sugar, visit dentist regularly.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Keeping Our Surroundings Clean. I can explain sanitation and keep my compound clean. Good sanitation means a clean compound, covered dustbin, clear drainage, and a clean latrine. These stop flies and germs that cause disease. Keywords: sanitation: keeping our surroundings clean to stop disease; latrine: a toilet for safe waste disposal; dustbin: a container for collecting rubbish; rubbish: waste like peelings, paper, plastic; compound: the area around a home or school; drainage: channels that carry rain water away
chunks.source: Good sanitation means a clean compound, covered dustbin, clear drainage, and a clean latrine. These stop flies and germs that cause disease.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What does sanitation mean? A: Sanitation means keeping our surroundings clean to stop disease.
chunks.source: Sanitation means keeping our surroundings clean to stop disease.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why do we use a dustbin with a cover? A: To keep flies and smell away from rubbish.
chunks.source: To keep flies and smell away from rubbish.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What happens if rubbish blocks drainage? A: Water cannot flow, causing stagnant water and mosquitoes.
chunks.source: Water cannot flow, causing stagnant water and mosquitoes.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words how to clean your compound. A: Sweep rubbish, put it in a covered dustbin, empty the dustbin at a rubbish pit.
chunks.source: Sweep rubbish, put it in a covered dustbin, empty the dustbin at a rubbish pit.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words why we must wash hands after using the latrine. A: To remove germs and stop diseases like cholera.
chunks.source: To remove germs and stop diseases like cholera.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name two things that make a compound clean. A: No loose rubbish, covered dustbin, clear drainage, clean latrine.
chunks.source: No loose rubbish, covered dustbin, clear drainage, clean latrine.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What should you do with a full dustbin? A: Empty it at the rubbish pit, wash it, and return it.
chunks.source: Empty it at the rubbish pit, wash it, and return it.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Proper Use of Latrines. I can use and care for a latrine correctly. Use a latrine with a cover. Close the cover after use. Wash hands with soap. This stops flies, smell, and diseases. Keywords: pit latrine: a simple toilet with a hole in the ground; VIP latrine: a ventilated improved pit latrine with a pipe; cover: a lid that closes the latrine hole; flies: insects that carry germs from waste; smell: bad odour from waste; wash hands: clean hands with soap and water
chunks.source: Use a latrine with a cover. Close the cover after use. Wash hands with soap. This stops flies, smell, and diseases.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name two types of latrines. A: Pit latrine and VIP latrine.
chunks.source: Pit latrine and VIP latrine.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What does a VIP latrine have that a pit latrine does not? A: A vent pipe to remove smell and flies.
chunks.source: A vent pipe to remove smell and flies.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why must the cover be on the latrine hole? A: To keep flies out and stop smell.
chunks.source: To keep flies out and stop smell.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words how to use a latrine properly. A: Open cover, use latrine, close cover, wash hands with soap.
chunks.source: Open cover, use latrine, close cover, wash hands with soap.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words why washing hands after the latrine is important. A: It removes germs that cause diseases like cholera.
chunks.source: It removes germs that cause diseases like cholera.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What happens if flies enter the latrine? A: They carry germs to food and cause disease.
chunks.source: They carry germs to food and cause disease.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How do you clean a latrine floor? A: Sweep, scrub with water and ash or soap, rinse, ensure cover fits.
chunks.source: Sweep, scrub with water and ash or soap, rinse, ensure cover fits.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Effects of Poor Sanitation. I can explain how poor sanitation causes disease. Poor sanitation lets flies spread germs, causing contamination of food and water. This leads to cholera, dysentery, and other diseases. Cover latrines, use dustbins, boil water, and wash hands. Keywords: cholera: a severe diarrhoea disease from dirty water; dysentery: diarrhoea with blood from germs; germs: tiny living things that cause illness; contamination: when dirt or germs get into water or food; disease: an illness that makes the body unwell; flies: insects that carry germs from waste to food
chunks.source: Poor sanitation lets flies spread germs, causing contamination of food and water. This leads to cholera, dysentery, and other diseases. Cover latrines, use dustbins, boil water, and wash hands.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name two diseases caused by poor sanitation. A: Cholera and dysentery.
chunks.source: Cholera and dysentery.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How do flies spread germs? A: Flies land on faeces then on food, carrying germs.
chunks.source: Flies land on faeces then on food, carrying germs.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is contamination? A: When germs or dirt get into water or food.
chunks.source: When germs or dirt get into water or food.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words how cholera spreads. A: Cholera spreads when germs from faeces contaminate drinking water.
chunks.source: Cholera spreads when germs from faeces contaminate drinking water.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words why covering food stops disease. A: Covering food stops flies from landing on it and leaving germs.
chunks.source: Covering food stops flies from landing on it and leaving germs.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What should you do if someone has severe diarrhoea? A: Give ORS, go to health centre, clean area with bleach, wash hands.
chunks.source: Give ORS, go to health centre, clean area with bleach, wash hands.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: List three community actions to stop disease. A: Build latrines with covers, dig rubbish pits, clear drainage, teach handwashing.
chunks.source: Build latrines with covers, dig rubbish pits, clear drainage, teach handwashing.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: What Are Vectors?. I can define a vector and name six common vectors found in Uganda. A vector carries germs that cause disease. Common Ugandan vectors are mosquito, housefly, tsetse fly, cockroach, and lice. Each spreads different illnesses. Keywords: vector: an animal that carries germs from one person to another; mosquito: a small flying insect that bites and sucks blood; housefly: a common fly that lands on food and waste; tsetse fly: a fly that bites and causes sleeping sickness; cockroach: a flat, brown insect that runs fast in dirty places; lice: tiny insects that live in hair and suck blood
chunks.source: A vector carries germs that cause disease. Common Ugandan vectors are mosquito, housefly, tsetse fly, cockroach, and lice. Each spreads different illnesses.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Define vector in your own words. A: A vector is an animal that carries germs from a sick person or animal to a healthy one.
chunks.source: A vector is an animal that carries germs from a sick person or animal to a healthy one.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name three vectors that fly. A: Mosquito, housefly, tsetse fly.
chunks.source: Mosquito, housefly, tsetse fly.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which vector causes sleeping sickness? A: The tsetse fly.
chunks.source: The tsetse fly.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How do houseflies spread germs? A: They land on faeces and garbage, then on food, carrying germs on their legs and mouth.
chunks.source: They land on faeces and garbage, then on food, carrying germs on their legs and mouth.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What do lice feed on? A: Human blood from the scalp.
chunks.source: Human blood from the scalp.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Explain why cockroaches are vectors. A: They crawl in dirty places like latrines and drains, then run over food and utensils, leaving germs.
chunks.source: They crawl in dirty places like latrines and drains, then run over food and utensils, leaving germs.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: If your friend has lice, what should they do? A: Tell an adult and get special shampoo or medicine to kill the lice.
chunks.source: Tell an adult and get special shampoo or medicine to kill the lice.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: The Mosquito and Malaria. I can explain the mosquito life cycle, how malaria spreads, and how to prevent it. Female anopheles mosquitoes spread malaria by biting. They breed in stagnant water. Sleeping under a treated net and removing breeding sites stops the cycle. Keywords: anopheles: the type of mosquito that carries malaria; malaria: a disease caused by a germ carried by mosquitoes; net: a treated mosquito net hung over a bed; stagnant water: still water that does not flow, where mosquitoes lay eggs; plasmodium: the tiny germ that causes malaria; bite: the act of a mosquito piercing skin to suck blood
chunks.source: Female anopheles mosquitoes spread malaria by biting. They breed in stagnant water. Sleeping under a treated net and removing breeding sites stops the cycle.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name the four stages of the anopheles life cycle. A: Egg, larva, pupa, adult.
chunks.source: Egg, larva, pupa, adult.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Where does the female anopheles lay eggs? A: In stagnant water.
chunks.source: In stagnant water.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What germ causes malaria? A: Plasmodium.
chunks.source: Plasmodium.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How does plasmodium enter a person's body? A: Through the bite of an infected female anopheles mosquito.
chunks.source: Through the bite of an infected female anopheles mosquito.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words how a treated net prevents malaria. A: The net has insecticide that kills or repels mosquitoes. It stops them from biting you while you sleep.
chunks.source: The net has insecticide that kills or repels mosquitoes. It stops them from biting you while you sleep.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: List three places where stagnant water collects near homes. A: Old tins, tyre tracks, blocked drains, uncovered tanks, puddles.
chunks.source: Old tins, tyre tracks, blocked drains, uncovered tanks, puddles.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why do only female anopheles mosquitoes bite? A: They need blood to develop their eggs.
chunks.source: They need blood to develop their eggs.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: If you have fever and chills, what should you do? A: Go to the health centre for a malaria test and treatment.
chunks.source: Go to the health centre for a malaria test and treatment.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Controlling Vectors. I can describe six methods to control vectors in my home and community. Six ways to control vectors: drainage removes breeding water, spraying kills adults, nets prevent bites, covers stop contamination, clearing bush removes hiding places, and hygiene keeps the environment clean. Keywords: drainage: a system to remove waste water so it does not stand still; spraying: using chemicals to kill adult vectors; net: a treated mosquito net used over a bed; cover: to put a lid on food, water, or latrines; bush: thick grass and shrubs where vectors hide; hygiene: clean habits that stop vectors from spreading germs
chunks.source: Six ways to control vectors: drainage removes breeding water, spraying kills adults, nets prevent bites, covers stop contamination, clearing bush removes hiding places, and hygiene keeps the environment clean.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: List the six vector control methods from the lesson. A: Drainage, spraying, net, cover, clear bush, hygiene.
chunks.source: Drainage, spraying, net, cover, clear bush, hygiene.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How does drainage control mosquitoes? A: It removes stagnant water where mosquitoes lay eggs.
chunks.source: It removes stagnant water where mosquitoes lay eggs.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What does indoor residual spraying kill? A: Adult mosquitoes, houseflies, and cockroaches that rest on walls.
chunks.source: Adult mosquitoes, houseflies, and cockroaches that rest on walls.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Explain in your own words why covering food stops disease. A: It prevents houseflies and cockroaches from landing on food and leaving germs.
chunks.source: It prevents houseflies and cockroaches from landing on food and leaving germs.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why should you clear bush around your house? A: Tall grass and shrubs are resting and hiding places for mosquitoes, tsetse flies, and cockroaches.
chunks.source: Tall grass and shrubs are resting and hiding places for mosquitoes, tsetse flies, and cockroaches.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name three hygiene habits that control vectors. A: Wash hands with soap, bathe regularly, keep compound clean, use rubbish pit.
chunks.source: Wash hands with soap, bathe regularly, keep compound clean, use rubbish pit.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: If your net has a hole, what should you do? A: Sew it or patch it immediately so mosquitoes cannot enter.
chunks.source: Sew it or patch it immediately so mosquitoes cannot enter.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which method would you use first in a compound with many puddles? A: Drainage — fill puddles and clear drains to stop mosquito breeding.
chunks.source: Drainage — fill puddles and clear drains to stop mosquito breeding.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Types and Breeds of Rabbits. I can identify common rabbit breeds kept in Uganda. Common rabbit breeds in Uganda are **angora** for **fur**, **new zealand** and **californian** for meat. Each **breed** has different **ear** and **fur** traits. Keywords: breed: a group of animals with same traits; angora: a rabbit breed with long fur; new zealand: a white rabbit breed for meat; californian: a rabbit breed with coloured ears; ear: the part of the head for hearing; fur: the soft hair covering a rabbit
chunks.source: Common rabbit breeds in Uganda are **angora** for **fur**, **new zealand** and **californian** for meat. Each **breed** has different **ear** and **fur** traits.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is a rabbit **breed**? A: A group of rabbits with the same traits.
chunks.source: A group of rabbits with the same traits.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name three rabbit breeds kept in Uganda. A: **Angora**, **new zealand**, **californian**.
chunks.source: **Angora**, **new zealand**, **californian**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which breed has long fur for wool? A: The **angora** rabbit.
chunks.source: The **angora** rabbit.
