chunks.text: Simplifying Expressions. I can simplify an expression by collecting like terms. Simplifying means collecting like terms and adding or subtracting them to make the expression shorter. Keywords: simplify: to make an expression shorter by combining parts; like terms: terms that have the same letter and power; collect: to gather like terms together; expression: a group of numbers and letters showing a value; add: to put numbers or terms together
chunks.source: Simplifying means collecting like terms and adding or subtracting them to make the expression shorter.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Simplify 2x + 5x. A: 7x
chunks.source: 7x

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Simplify 4y + 3 - y + 2. A: 3y + 5

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Simplify 6a + 2b + 3a - b. A: 9a + b
chunks.source: 9a + b

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Simplify 7m + 4 - 2m + 6. A: 5m + 10

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Simplify 5k + 3k + 2k. A: 10k

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Simplify 9p + 1 - 4p - 3. A: 5p - 2

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Simplify 3c + 2d + c + 4d. A: 4c + 6d
chunks.source: 4c + 6d

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Solving Simple Equations. I can solve a one-step equation by keeping the balance. Solving an equation means keeping the balance while isolating the unknown to find its value. Keywords: solve: to find the value of the unknown; equation: a statement that two expressions are equal; unknown: the letter we need to find; balance: doing the same thing to both sides of an equation; value: the number that makes the equation true
chunks.source: Solving an equation means keeping the balance while isolating the unknown to find its value.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Solve x + 5 = 12. A: x = 7

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Solve y - 3 = 10. A: y = 13

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Solve 4z = 28. A: z = 7

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Solve w + 9 = 20. A: w = 11

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Solve 6k = 42. A: k = 7

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Solve m - 8 = 5. A: m = 13

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Solve 2n = 18. A: n = 9

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Substitution. I can substitute a number for a letter in an expression. Substitution means replacing the letter with a number and then calculating the expression to find its value. Keywords: substitute: to replace a letter with a number; value: the number that takes the place of the letter; replace: to put something in the place of another; expression: a group of numbers and letters showing a value; equals: shows that two things have the same value
chunks.source: Substitution means replacing the letter with a number and then calculating the expression to find its value.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Evaluate 3x + 4 when x = 2. A: 10

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Evaluate 5y - 3 when y = 4. A: 17

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Evaluate 2z + 6 when z = 5. A: 16

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Evaluate 7a - 2 when a = 3. A: 19

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Evaluate 4b ÷ 2 + 5 when b = 8. A: 21

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Evaluate 9c + 1 when c = 0. A: 1

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Evaluate 6d - 4 when d = 2. A: 8

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Crop Growing. I can explain how crop growing is an occupation that provides food and income. A farmer grows crops as an occupation. The harvest is sold at the market to earn income for the family. Keywords: farmer: a person who grows crops or keeps animals; crop: a plant grown for food or sale; harvest: to gather ripe crops from the field; market: a place where people buy and sell goods; income: money earned from work; occupation: a job or type of work people do
chunks.source: A farmer grows crops as an occupation. The harvest is sold at the market to earn income for the family.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What do we call a person who grows crops for a living? A: A farmer
chunks.source: A farmer

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is the name for plants grown for food or sale? A: A crop
chunks.source: A crop

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What does harvest mean? A: To gather ripe crops from the field
chunks.source: To gather ripe crops from the field

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Where does a farmer sell the harvest? A: At the market
chunks.source: At the market

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is income? A: Money earned from work
chunks.source: Money earned from work

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is an occupation? A: A job or type of work people do
chunks.source: A job or type of work people do

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why does a farmer dry maize before selling? A: To get a better price at the market
chunks.source: To get a better price at the market

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name two crops grown in Uganda. A: Maize and beans (or matooke, cassava, etc.)
chunks.source: Maize and beans (or matooke, cassava, etc.)

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Other Occupations. I can name occupations in my community and explain how they use science. Many occupations in our community use science. Teachers, nurses, carpenters, tailors, drivers, and traders all apply scientific knowledge daily. Keywords: teacher: a person who helps others learn; nurse: a person who cares for sick people; carpenter: a person who makes things from wood; tailor: a person who sews clothes; driver: a person who drives a vehicle; trader: a person who buys and sells goods
chunks.source: Many occupations in our community use science. Teachers, nurses, carpenters, tailors, drivers, and traders all apply scientific knowledge daily.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Who teaches children in school? A: A teacher
chunks.source: A teacher

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Who cares for sick people at the health centre? A: A nurse
chunks.source: A nurse

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Who makes furniture from wood? A: A carpenter
chunks.source: A carpenter

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Who sews clothes using a machine? A: A tailor
chunks.source: A tailor

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Who drives a matatu or boda boda? A: A driver
chunks.source: A driver

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Who buys and sells goods at the market? A: A trader
chunks.source: A trader

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How does a nurse use science? A: Uses biology and medicine to treat patients
chunks.source: Uses biology and medicine to treat patients

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How does a carpenter use science? A: Knows wood properties, measures, uses friction and glue
chunks.source: Knows wood properties, measures, uses friction and glue

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Tools Used in Occupations. I can match tools to occupations and explain how machines make work easier. Every occupation uses specific tools and machines. Tools are simple objects; machines have moving parts. Both make work easier and faster. Keywords: hoe: a tool for digging and weeding; saw: a tool for cutting wood; stethoscope: a tool for listening to heart and lungs; needle: a thin tool for sewing; tool: any object used to do work; machine: a device with moving parts that makes work easier
chunks.source: Every occupation uses specific tools and machines. Tools are simple objects; machines have moving parts. Both make work easier and faster.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What tool does a farmer use to dig? A: A hoe
chunks.source: A hoe

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What tool cuts wood for a carpenter? A: A saw
chunks.source: A saw

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What does a nurse use to hear the heart? A: A stethoscope
chunks.source: A stethoscope

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What thin tool does a tailor use for sewing? A: A needle
chunks.source: A needle

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is a tool? A: Any object used to do work
chunks.source: Any object used to do work

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is a machine? A: A device with moving parts that makes work easier
chunks.source: A device with moving parts that makes work easier

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why is a sharp hoe better than a blunt one? A: It cuts weeds easily and uses less energy
chunks.source: It cuts weeds easily and uses less energy

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How does a sewing machine help a tailor? A: It makes sewing faster and neater
chunks.source: It makes sewing faster and neater

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Keeping Poultry. I can name types of poultry and explain how to care for them. Poultry include **hen**, **cock**, and **chick**. The **hen** will **lay** **eggs**. All birds need daily **feed** and clean water to stay healthy. Keywords: hen: a female chicken; cock: a male chicken; chick: a baby chicken; lay: to produce eggs; eggs: oval objects laid by birds, used for food; feed: to give food to animals
chunks.source: Poultry include **hen**, **cock**, and **chick**. The **hen** will **lay** **eggs**. All birds need daily **feed** and clean water to stay healthy.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is a female chicken called? A: A **hen**.
chunks.source: A **hen**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is a male chicken called? A: A **cock**.
chunks.source: A **cock**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is a baby chicken called? A: A **chick**.
chunks.source: A **chick**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What does a **hen** do in the nest? A: She **lay** **eggs**.
chunks.source: She **lay** **eggs**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name two things we **feed** chickens. A: Maize bran and greens.
chunks.source: Maize bran and greens.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why do we collect **eggs** every morning? A: To keep them clean and fresh for eating or selling.
chunks.source: To keep them clean and fresh for eating or selling.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How does good **feed** help a **chick**? A: It helps the **chick** grow strong and healthy.
chunks.source: It helps the **chick** grow strong and healthy.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What sound does a **cock** make? A: It crows early in the morning.
chunks.source: It crows early in the morning.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Poultry Housing and Diseases. I can describe a good poultry house and name two common diseases. A good **coop** has wire mesh, a roof, **perch** bars, and dry **litter**. **Coccidiosis** comes from wet **litter**. **Newcastle** is prevented by **vaccinate** on schedule. Keywords: coop: a house for poultry; perch: a raised bar for birds to sleep on; litter: dry material on the floor like straw or wood shavings; coccidiosis: a disease causing bloody diarrhoea in poultry; newcastle: a deadly viral disease of poultry; vaccinate: to give a vaccine to prevent disease
chunks.source: A good **coop** has wire mesh, a roof, **perch** bars, and dry **litter**. **Coccidiosis** comes from wet **litter**. **Newcastle** is prevented by **vaccinate** on schedule.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is a **coop**? A: A house for poultry.
chunks.source: A house for poultry.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why do birds need a **perch**? A: To sleep off the damp floor.
chunks.source: To sleep off the damp floor.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is **litter**? A: Dry material like straw on the **coop** floor.
chunks.source: Dry material like straw on the **coop** floor.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which disease comes from wet dirty **litter**? A: **Coccidiosis**.
chunks.source: **Coccidiosis**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which disease spreads fast through air and droppings? A: **Newcastle**.
chunks.source: **Newcastle**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How do we prevent **newcastle**? A: **Vaccinate** chicks on schedule.
chunks.source: **Vaccinate** chicks on schedule.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name two signs of **coccidiosis**. A: Bloody diarrhoea and weak birds.
chunks.source: Bloody diarrhoea and weak birds.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What should you do if **litter** is wet? A: Remove it and put fresh dry **litter**.
chunks.source: Remove it and put fresh dry **litter**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Keeping Bees. I can name parts of a bee colony and explain how bees make honey. A **hive** holds a **colony** with one **queen**, many **worker** bees, and a few **drone** bees. **Worker** bees make **honey** from nectar. We harvest extra **honey** but leave enough for the **colony**. Keywords: hive: a box or structure where bees live; colony: a family of bees living together; queen: the mother bee who lays all the eggs; worker: a female bee that does all the work; drone: a male bee that mates with the queen; honey: sweet food made by bees from nectar
chunks.source: A **hive** holds a **colony** with one **queen**, many **worker** bees, and a few **drone** bees. **Worker** bees make **honey** from nectar. We harvest extra **honey** but leave enough for the **colony**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is a **hive**? A: A box or structure where bees live.
chunks.source: A box or structure where bees live.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is a **colony**? A: A family of bees living together.
chunks.source: A family of bees living together.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Who lays eggs in the **colony**? A: The **queen**.
chunks.source: The **queen**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What does a **worker** bee do? A: Collects nectar, makes **honey**, feeds the **queen**, cleans the **hive**.
chunks.source: Collects nectar, makes **honey**, feeds the **queen**, cleans the **hive**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is a **drone**? A: A male bee that mates with the **queen**.
chunks.source: A male bee that mates with the **queen**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How is **honey** made? A: **Worker** bees turn nectar into **honey** inside the **hive**.
chunks.source: **Worker** bees turn nectar into **honey** inside the **hive**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why do we leave some **honey** for the bees? A: So the **colony** has food during rainy season.
chunks.source: So the **colony** has food during rainy season.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why does Mr Okello use smoke? A: To calm the bees before opening the **hive**.
chunks.source: To calm the bees before opening the **hive**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Breeds and Housing of Rabbits. I can identify rabbit breeds and describe a good hutch. A good rabbit hutch is raised, has a wire floor, a solid roof, and a nesting box. Keep it dry. Bucks and does live apart. Common meat breeds are New Zealand White and California. Keywords: breed: a type of animal with special traits; hutch: a house for rabbits made of wood and wire; buck: a male rabbit; doe: a female rabbit; kindling: when a doe gives birth to baby rabbits; dry: not wet; free from moisture
chunks.source: A good rabbit hutch is raised, has a wire floor, a solid roof, and a nesting box. Keep it dry. Bucks and does live apart. Common meat breeds are New Zealand White and California.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name two rabbit breeds good for meat in Uganda. A: New Zealand White and California
chunks.source: New Zealand White and California

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is a male rabbit called? A: A buck
chunks.source: A buck

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is a female rabbit called? A: A doe
chunks.source: A doe

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What does kindling mean? A: When a doe gives birth to baby rabbits
chunks.source: When a doe gives birth to baby rabbits

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why must a hutch floor be wire mesh? A: To let droppings fall through and keep the floor dry
chunks.source: To let droppings fall through and keep the floor dry

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What should you do if the hutch gets wet? A: Add dry grass and fix the roof
chunks.source: Add dry grass and fix the roof

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why keep the buck and doe separate? A: They only meet for mating to avoid fighting
chunks.source: They only meet for mating to avoid fighting

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: List three features of a good hutch. A: Raised on legs, wire floor, solid roof, nesting box
chunks.source: Raised on legs, wire floor, solid roof, nesting box

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Feeding and Breeding Rabbits. I can explain what rabbits eat and how breeding is managed. Rabbits need pellets and forage twice daily plus clean water. Does gestate for 31 days. Kits are weaned at 6 to 8 weeks. Keep records of mating, litter size, and weaning to manage the project well. Keywords: pellets: compressed rabbit feed bought from a shop; forage: fresh green plants like grasses and leaves collected for rabbits; weaning: when baby rabbits stop drinking milk and eat solid food; gestation: the time a doe carries babies before birth; litter: the group of baby rabbits born at one time; record: a written note of important facts like dates and numbers
chunks.source: Rabbits need pellets and forage twice daily plus clean water. Does gestate for 31 days. Kits are weaned at 6 to 8 weeks. Keep records of mating, litter size, and weaning to manage the project well.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What two main foods do rabbits need daily? A: Pellets and fresh forage
chunks.source: Pellets and fresh forage

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How much pellets does an adult rabbit get per day? A: 100 grams morning and evening (200 grams total)
chunks.source: 100 grams morning and evening (200 grams total)

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name three examples of forage for rabbits. A: Elephant grass, sweet potato vines, cabbage leaves
chunks.source: Elephant grass, sweet potato vines, cabbage leaves

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How long is the gestation period for a rabbit? A: About 31 days
chunks.source: About 31 days

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is a litter? A: The group of baby rabbits born at one time
chunks.source: The group of baby rabbits born at one time

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: At what age are kits weaned? A: 6 to 8 weeks old
chunks.source: 6 to 8 weeks old

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why keep a record book for rabbits? A: To track mating dates, gestation, litter size, and weaning for good management
chunks.source: To track mating dates, gestation, litter size, and weaning for good management

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: When can a doe be mated for the first time? A: At about 5 months of age
chunks.source: At about 5 months of age

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Rabbit Diseases. I can identify common rabbit diseases and explain how to prevent them. Common rabbit diseases are coccidiosis, snuffles, and ear canker. Diarrhoea is a key sign of coccidiosis. Keep hutches clean and dry, isolate sick rabbits, and call the vet early. Prevention is better than cure. Keywords: coccidiosis: a gut disease caused by tiny parasites, causing diarrhoea and weight loss; snuffles: a breathing disease with sneezing and nasal discharge; ear canker: mites inside the ear causing scratching and brown crusts; diarrhoea: watery droppings that can kill a rabbit quickly; vet: an animal doctor who treats sick livestock; prevent: to stop something bad from happening before it starts
chunks.source: Common rabbit diseases are coccidiosis, snuffles, and ear canker. Diarrhoea is a key sign of coccidiosis. Keep hutches clean and dry, isolate sick rabbits, and call the vet early. Prevention is better than cure.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name three common rabbit diseases. A: Coccidiosis, snuffles, ear canker
chunks.source: Coccidiosis, snuffles, ear canker

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What causes coccidiosis? A: Tiny parasites in dirty, wet hutches
chunks.source: Tiny parasites in dirty, wet hutches

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What are the signs of snuffles? A: Sneezing and nasal discharge
chunks.source: Sneezing and nasal discharge

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How do you know a rabbit has ear canker? A: Head shaking and brown crusts inside the ears
chunks.source: Head shaking and brown crusts inside the ears

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why is diarrhoea dangerous for young rabbits? A: It can kill quickly and is often coccidiosis
chunks.source: It can kill quickly and is often coccidiosis

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What should you do first when a rabbit is sick? A: Isolate it and call the vet
chunks.source: Isolate it and call the vet

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How can you prevent rabbit diseases? A: Keep hutches clean and dry, avoid overcrowding, give clean water
chunks.source: Keep hutches clean and dry, avoid overcrowding, give clean water

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why keep a record of diseases? A: To track outbreaks and improve prevention
chunks.source: To track outbreaks and improve prevention

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Breeds of Goats. I can name and describe the main goat breeds kept in Uganda. Uganda keeps three main goat breeds: mubende (black, central), boer (white with brown head, fast growth), and small east african (small, hardy, everywhere). A kid is a young goat, a nanny is the mother, and a billy is the father. Keywords: mubende: A local goat breed from central Uganda, good for meat.; small east african: A common local breed, small and hardy.; boer: A big meat breed from South Africa, white with a brown head.; kid: A young goat, male or female, under one year old.; billy: An adult male goat used for breeding.; nanny: An adult female goat that gives milk and kids.
chunks.source: Uganda keeps three main goat breeds: mubende (black, central), boer (white with brown head, fast growth), and small east african (small, hardy, everywhere). A kid is a young goat, a nanny is the mother, and a billy is the father.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name the three main goat breeds kept in Uganda. A: mubende, boer, small east african
chunks.source: mubende, boer, small east african

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is a young goat under one year called? A: kid
chunks.source: kid

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What do we call an adult male goat? A: billy
chunks.source: billy

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What do we call an adult female goat? A: nanny
chunks.source: nanny

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which breed comes from South Africa and has a white body with a brown head? A: boer
chunks.source: boer

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which local breed has a shiny black coat and comes from central Uganda? A: mubende
chunks.source: mubende

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why do farmers keep a billy goat? A: To mate with nannies and produce kids
chunks.source: To mate with nannies and produce kids

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which breed is the most common and hardy in all parts of Uganda? A: small east african
chunks.source: small east african

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Goat Housing and Feeding. I can explain how to house and feed goats properly for good health and growth. Good goat housing has a strong fence, raised slatted stalls for sleeping, clean water daily, a salt lick for minerals, and a paddock with grass and browse trees like calliandra. Rotate paddocks to control worms. Keywords: paddock: A fenced area where goats graze and move freely.; browse: Leaves, twigs, and shrubs that goats eat from bushes and trees.; stall: A covered shelter inside the goat house where each goat sleeps.; salt lick: A block of mineral salt that goats lick for nutrients.; water: Clean drinking water that must be available all the time.; fence: A strong barrier around the paddock to keep goats in and predators out.
chunks.source: Good goat housing has a strong fence, raised slatted stalls for sleeping, clean water daily, a salt lick for minerals, and a paddock with grass and browse trees like calliandra. Rotate paddocks to control worms.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is a paddock? A: A fenced area where goats graze and move freely
chunks.source: A fenced area where goats graze and move freely

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What does browse mean? A: Leaves, twigs, and shrubs that goats eat from bushes and trees
chunks.source: Leaves, twigs, and shrubs that goats eat from bushes and trees

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why is the stall floor raised and slatted? A: To let droppings and urine fall through, keeping the stall dry and clean
chunks.source: To let droppings and urine fall through, keeping the stall dry and clean

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is a salt lick and why do goats need it? A: A block of mineral salt that gives calcium, phosphorus, and trace elements for strong bones and milk
chunks.source: A block of mineral salt that gives calcium, phosphorus, and trace elements for strong bones and milk

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How often should water be changed? A: Every day, fresh and clean
chunks.source: Every day, fresh and clean

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why rotate the paddock? A: To break worm cycles and let grass grow back
chunks.source: To break worm cycles and let grass grow back

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name two trees planted for browse in Uganda. A: Calliandra and leucaena
chunks.source: Calliandra and leucaena

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What happens if goats drink dirty water? A: They get worms and diarrhoea
chunks.source: They get worms and diarrhoea

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Goat Diseases and Care. I can identify common goat diseases and explain how to prevent and treat them. Common goat problems: worms (pale eyelids, weight loss), overgrown hooves (lameness), ticks (spread heartwater), and deadly diseases PPR and CCPP. Prevent by: deworm every 3 months, trim hoof every 2 months, spray ticks weekly in rains, vaccinate yearly. A healthy goat has a shiny coat, bright eyes, and eats well. Keywords: worms: Internal parasites that live in the stomach and intestines, causing weight loss and diarrhoea.; deworm: To give medicine that kills worms inside the goat.; hoof: The hard foot of a goat that needs regular trimming to prevent rot.; vaccinate: To give an injection that protects against specific diseases like PPR and CCPP.; tick: A small blood-sucking parasite that attaches to the goat's skin.; healthy: Strong, well-fed, free from disease, with shiny coat and bright eyes.
chunks.source: Common goat problems: worms (pale eyelids, weight loss), overgrown hooves (lameness), ticks (spread heartwater), and deadly diseases PPR and CCPP. Prevent by: deworm every 3 months, trim hoof every 2 months, spray ticks weekly in rains, vaccinate yearly. A healthy goat has a shiny coat, bright eyes, and eats well.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name two signs that a goat has worms. A: Pale eyelids (anaemia) and sharp back bones (weight loss)
chunks.source: Pale eyelids (anaemia) and sharp back bones (weight loss)

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How often should you deworm a goat? A: Every three months
chunks.source: Every three months

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why trim the hoof every two months? A: To prevent hoof rot and lameness, so the goat can walk and eat well
chunks.source: To prevent hoof rot and lameness, so the goat can walk and eat well

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Where do ticks usually hide on a goat? A: Ears, under the tail, around the hoof
chunks.source: Ears, under the tail, around the hoof

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which two diseases are prevented by vaccination in Uganda? A: PPR and CCPP
chunks.source: PPR and CCPP

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How often should you vaccinate against PPR and CCPP? A: Once a year
chunks.source: Once a year

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What does a healthy goat look like? A: Shiny coat, bright eyes, plays and eats well, good body condition
chunks.source: Shiny coat, bright eyes, plays and eats well, good body condition

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why keep a goat health calendar? A: To remember deworming, hoof trimming, vaccination, and tick spraying dates
chunks.source: To remember deworming, hoof trimming, vaccination, and tick spraying dates

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Measuring Length and Area. I can measure length and area using a tape measure and calculate area in square metres. We measure length and width with a tape measure, use metres and centimetres, and find area by multiplying length by width. Keywords: metre: a unit of length equal to 100 centimetres; centimetre: a small unit of length, 100 make a metre; length: the longest side of an object; width: the shorter side of an object; area: the space inside a flat shape, measured in square metres; tape measure: a flexible ruler used to measure length
chunks.source: We measure length and width with a tape measure, use metres and centimetres, and find area by multiplying length by width.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What unit is used to measure the length of a garden? A: metre
chunks.source: metre

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How many centimetres are in one metre? A: 100

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What tool do you use to measure length? A: tape measure
chunks.source: tape measure

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: If a rectangle has length 7 metres and width 3 metres, what is its area? A: 21 square metres
chunks.source: 21 square metres

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which formula gives the area of a rectangle? A: length × width
chunks.source: length × width

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Convert 250 centimetres to metres. A: 2.5 metres
chunks.source: 2.5 metres

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is the width of a door that is 80 centimetres wide? A: 80 centimetres
chunks.source: 80 centimetres

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why do we use metres instead of centimetres for a garden? A: Metres are larger and easier for big distances.
chunks.source: Metres are larger and easier for big distances.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Measuring Mass and Capacity. I can measure mass with a beam balance and capacity with a measuring cylinder using kilograms, grams, litres and millilitres. Mass is measured in kilograms and grams with a beam balance; capacity is measured in litres and millilitres with a measuring cylinder. Keywords: kilogram: a unit of mass equal to 1000 grams; gram: a small unit of mass, 1000 make a kilogram; beam balance: a scale with two pans for comparing mass; litre: a unit of capacity equal to 1000 millilitres; millilitre: a small unit of capacity, 1000 make a litre; measuring cylinder: a tall container marked for measuring liquid volume
chunks.source: Mass is measured in kilograms and grams with a beam balance; capacity is measured in litres and millilitres with a measuring cylinder.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What tool measures mass in the market? A: beam balance
chunks.source: beam balance

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How many grams are in one kilogram? A: 1000

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which unit measures liquid capacity? A: litre
chunks.source: litre

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Convert 2.5 litres to millilitres. A: 2500 millilitres
chunks.source: 2500 millilitres

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: If a sack weighs 3 kilograms, how many grams is that? A: 3000 grams
chunks.source: 3000 grams

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What do you use to measure 500 millilitres of milk? A: measuring cylinder
chunks.source: measuring cylinder

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why is a beam balance better than guessing? A: It gives an exact mass.
chunks.source: It gives an exact mass.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How many millilitres are in half a litre? A: 500 millilitres
chunks.source: 500 millilitres

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Measuring Time and Temperature. I can read a clock for seconds, minutes, hours and use a thermometer to measure temperature in degrees Celsius. Time is measured in seconds, minutes and hours with a clock; temperature is measured in degrees celsius with a thermometer. Keywords: second: the basic unit of time, 60 make a minute; minute: 60 seconds, 60 make an hour; hour: 60 minutes, 24 make a day; thermometer: an instrument that shows temperature; degrees celsius: the unit for temperature in Uganda; clock: a device that shows hours, minutes and seconds
chunks.source: Time is measured in seconds, minutes and hours with a clock; temperature is measured in degrees celsius with a thermometer.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How many seconds are in one minute? A: 60

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How many minutes are in one hour? A: 60

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What device shows hours, minutes and seconds? A: clock
chunks.source: clock

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What instrument measures temperature? A: thermometer
chunks.source: thermometer

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is the unit for temperature in Uganda? A: degrees celsius
chunks.source: degrees celsius

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: If a class starts at 8 hour and ends at 9 hour 30 minute, how long is it in minutes? A: 90

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Convert 2 hours to seconds. A: 7200 seconds
chunks.source: 7200 seconds

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why do we use a thermometer instead of guessing? A: It gives an exact temperature in degrees celsius.
chunks.source: It gives an exact temperature in degrees celsius.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Sources of Heat. I can name different sources of heat energy and give examples from daily life. Heat comes from different sources: the sun, fire, friction, and electricity. Fuel burns to make fire. Each source is useful in daily life. Keywords: sun: the star that gives light and heat; fire: burning flames that give heat; friction: heat made by rubbing two things together; electricity: power that can make heat in wires; fuel: material that burns to give heat; source: where something comes from
chunks.source: Heat comes from different sources: the sun, fire, friction, and electricity. Fuel burns to make fire. Each source is useful in daily life.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name three sources of heat energy. A: Sun, fire, friction, electricity (any three)
chunks.source: Sun, fire, friction, electricity (any three)

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What fuel does Nalongo use for the sigiri stove? A: Charcoal or wood
chunks.source: Charcoal or wood

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How does friction make heat? A: Rubbing two things together creates friction which produces heat
chunks.source: Rubbing two things together creates friction which produces heat

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which source of heat does an electric kettle use? A: Electricity
chunks.source: Electricity

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why is the sun a source of heat? A: The sun sends heat energy to earth
chunks.source: The sun sends heat energy to earth

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give one example of friction from daily life. A: Rubbing hands together, rubbing sticks, braking a bicycle
chunks.source: Rubbing hands together, rubbing sticks, braking a bicycle

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is a source? A: Where something comes from
chunks.source: Where something comes from

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: If you have no matches, how can you start a fire? A: Use friction by rubbing dry sticks together
chunks.source: Use friction by rubbing dry sticks together

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: How Heat Travels. I can explain the three ways heat moves and name materials that allow or stop heat flow. Heat travels three ways: conduction through solids, convection in liquids and gases, and radiation through space. Conductors like metal let heat pass. Insulators like wood stop heat. Keywords: conduction: heat moving through a solid by touching; convection: heat moving in liquids and gases as they rise; radiation: heat moving through air without touching; conductor: material that lets heat pass easily; insulator: material that stops heat from passing; metal: a shiny solid that conducts heat well
chunks.source: Heat travels three ways: conduction through solids, convection in liquids and gases, and radiation through space. Conductors like metal let heat pass. Insulators like wood stop heat.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name the three ways heat travels. A: Conduction, convection, radiation
chunks.source: Conduction, convection, radiation

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which way does heat move through a solid metal rod? A: Conduction
chunks.source: Conduction

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How does heat move in boiling water? A: Convection
chunks.source: Convection

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How does heat from the sun reach us? A: Radiation
chunks.source: Radiation

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Is a metal spoon a conductor or insulator? A: Conductor
chunks.source: Conductor

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Is a wooden spoon handle a conductor or insulator? A: Insulator
chunks.source: Insulator

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why do cooking pots have wooden or plastic handles? A: Wood and plastic are insulators; they stop conduction of heat to the hand
chunks.source: Wood and plastic are insulators; they stop conduction of heat to the hand

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give one example of convection in the kitchen. A: Hot air rising in an oven, water circulating in a boiling pot
chunks.source: Hot air rising in an oven, water circulating in a boiling pot

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Expansion and Uses of Heat. I can describe how heat makes things expand and contract, and give uses of heat in daily life. Heat makes things expand; cold makes them contract. Thermometers use this to measure temperature. We use heat for cooking, ironing, and sterilising to keep healthy. Keywords: expand: to become larger when heated; contract: to become smaller when cooled; thermometer: tool that uses expansion to show temperature; cooking: preparing food using heat; iron: using a hot tool to press clothes; sterilise: using heat to kill germs
chunks.source: Heat makes things expand; cold makes them contract. Thermometers use this to measure temperature. We use heat for cooking, ironing, and sterilising to keep healthy.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What happens to metal when heated? A: It expands
chunks.source: It expands

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What happens to metal when cooled? A: It contracts
chunks.source: It contracts

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How does a thermometer show temperature? A: Liquid inside expands when hot and rises; contracts when cold and falls
chunks.source: Liquid inside expands when hot and rises; contracts when cold and falls

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name three uses of heat at home. A: Cooking, ironing, sterilising (also warming, drying, baking)
chunks.source: Cooking, ironing, sterilising (also warming, drying, baking)

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why do railway rails have gaps? A: To allow for expansion on hot days
chunks.source: To allow for expansion on hot days

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What does sterilise mean? A: Using heat to kill germs
chunks.source: Using heat to kill germs

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why does a hot water bottle warm the bed? A: Heat transfers by conduction and radiation from the bottle
chunks.source: Heat transfers by conduction and radiation from the bottle

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: If a metal lid is stuck, why does hot water help? A: The metal lid expands more than the glass jar, loosening the fit
chunks.source: The metal lid expands more than the glass jar, loosening the fit

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: What Are Bacteria?. I can explain what bacteria are, where they live, and how they help or harm us. Bacteria are tiny living things seen only with a microscope. Some cause disease, but many help us — making yoghurt, decaying waste into soil, and protecting our gut. Good hygiene keeps harmful germs away. Keywords: bacteria: tiny living things seen only with a microscope; germ: a microbe that can make us sick; microscope: a tool that makes tiny things look big; disease: an illness caused by germs; yoghurt: a healthy food made with good bacteria; decay: rotting caused by microbes breaking things down
chunks.source: Bacteria are tiny living things seen only with a microscope. Some cause disease, but many help us — making yoghurt, decaying waste into soil, and protecting our gut. Good hygiene keeps harmful germs away.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What tool lets us see bacteria? A: A microscope.
chunks.source: A microscope.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name one disease caused by bacteria. A: Typhoid or cholera.
chunks.source: Typhoid or cholera.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How do bacteria help make yoghurt? A: They ferment milk, making it thick and sour.
chunks.source: They ferment milk, making it thick and sour.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is decay? A: Rotting where bacteria break down dead things into soil.
chunks.source: Rotting where bacteria break down dead things into soil.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why should we not eat mouldy bread? A: Bacteria roots spread inside; toxins can cause disease.
chunks.source: Bacteria roots spread inside; toxins can cause disease.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Where do helpful bacteria live in our body? A: In our gut, helping digestion.
chunks.source: In our gut, helping digestion.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What happens to bacteria when we boil water? A: Heat kills most bacteria, making water safe.
chunks.source: Heat kills most bacteria, making water safe.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give one way to stop bad germs spreading. A: Wash hands with soap and clean water.
chunks.source: Wash hands with soap and clean water.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: What Are Fungi?. I can describe fungi, name common types, and explain their roles in nature and food. Fungi include yeast, mould, and mushrooms. They are not plants — they absorb food from organic matter. Yeast makes bread rise; mould decays food and spreads by spores; mushrooms fruit from underground networks. Some fungi feed us, others spoil food or cause infection. Always identify wild mushrooms with an elder. Keywords: fungi: a group of living things including mould, yeast, and mushrooms; mushroom: the fruiting body of some fungi, often edible; mould: fuzzy fungi growing on damp food or walls; yeast: tiny fungi used to make bread rise and brew drinks; spores: tiny reproductive units that spread fungi like seeds; bread: a staple food made with yeast to rise
chunks.source: Fungi include yeast, mould, and mushrooms. They are not plants — they absorb food from organic matter. Yeast makes bread rise; mould decays food and spreads by spores; mushrooms fruit from underground networks. Some fungi feed us, others spoil food or cause infection. Always identify wild mushrooms with an elder.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What group do mushroom, mould, and yeast belong to? A: Fungi.
chunks.source: Fungi.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How do fungi get their food? A: They absorb nutrients from dead or living organic matter.
chunks.source: They absorb nutrients from dead or living organic matter.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What makes bread rise? A: Yeast fungi produce gas bubbles in dough.
chunks.source: Yeast fungi produce gas bubbles in dough.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What are spores? A: Tiny reproductive units that spread fungi like seeds.
chunks.source: Tiny reproductive units that spread fungi like seeds.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why is mould on food dangerous? A: It produces toxins that can cause illness.
chunks.source: It produces toxins that can cause illness.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How do mushrooms help the soil? A: They break down dead material, returning nutrients.
chunks.source: They break down dead material, returning nutrients.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What should you do before eating a wild mushroom? A: Ask an expert or elder to identify it.
chunks.source: Ask an expert or elder to identify it.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name one useful product from fungi. A: Bread (yeast), antibiotics, or edible mushrooms.
chunks.source: Bread (yeast), antibiotics, or edible mushrooms.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Controlling Harmful Microbes. I can explain methods to control harmful bacteria and fungi in daily life. Control harmful microbes by boiling water, pasteurising milk, sterilising baby items, practising hygiene (handwashing, antiseptic on cuts), and preserving food (salting, drying, airtight storage). These steps prevent disease and keep families healthy. Keywords: sterilise: kill all microbes on an object using heat or chemicals; boil: heat liquid to 100°C to kill most germs; pasteurise: heat food to a set temperature to kill pathogens without boiling; hygiene: practices that keep us clean and prevent disease; preserve: treat food to stop microbes spoiling it; antiseptic: a substance that kills germs on skin or wounds
chunks.source: Control harmful microbes by boiling water, pasteurising milk, sterilising baby items, practising hygiene (handwashing, antiseptic on cuts), and preserving food (salting, drying, airtight storage). These steps prevent disease and keep families healthy.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How long should you boil drinking water? A: At least five minutes at rolling boil.
chunks.source: At least five minutes at rolling boil.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What temperature is used to pasteurise milk? A: 72°C for 15 seconds.
chunks.source: 72°C for 15 seconds.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What does sterilise mean? A: Kill all microbes, including spores, usually by boiling 10 minutes.
chunks.source: Kill all microbes, including spores, usually by boiling 10 minutes.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name two hygiene practices that stop germs. A: Wash hands with soap; cover food; clean surfaces with antiseptic.
chunks.source: Wash hands with soap; cover food; clean surfaces with antiseptic.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why do we put antiseptic on a cut? A: To kill bacteria on the skin and prevent infection.
chunks.source: To kill bacteria on the skin and prevent infection.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How does salting fish preserve it? A: Salt draws out water; bacteria and fungi need water to grow.
chunks.source: Salt draws out water; bacteria and fungi need water to grow.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What should you do with cooked food left overnight? A: Reheat until steaming hot before eating.
chunks.source: Reheat until steaming hot before eating.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give one way to preserve grains at home. A: Store in airtight containers or dry in sun well.
chunks.source: Store in airtight containers or dry in sun well.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Formation and Components of Soil. I can explain how soil forms and name its main components. Soil forms by weathering of rocks over many years. It has five main components: mineral grains, humus, air, water and living organisms. All parts work together so plants can grow. Keywords: weathering: breaking down of rocks into small pieces; humus: dark part of soil from dead plants and animals; air: gas that fills spaces between soil particles; water: liquid held in soil pores for plants to use; mineral: tiny rock pieces that give soil nutrients; living organisms: small creatures like worms and bacteria in soil
chunks.source: Soil forms by weathering of rocks over many years. It has five main components: mineral grains, humus, air, water and living organisms. All parts work together so plants can grow.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is the slow breaking down of rocks into small pieces called? A: weathering
chunks.source: weathering

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name the dark part of soil made from dead plants and animals. A: humus
chunks.source: humus

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What do plant roots need from the soil to breathe? A: air
chunks.source: air

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What liquid do plants take up from soil pores? A: water
chunks.source: water

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What are the tiny rock pieces in soil that give nutrients called? A: mineral
chunks.source: mineral

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give two examples of living organisms found in soil. A: earthworms and bacteria
chunks.source: earthworms and bacteria

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How does humus help the soil? A: Humus holds water and air and feeds living organisms.
chunks.source: Humus holds water and air and feeds living organisms.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why is air important in soil? A: Roots need air to breathe and grow.
chunks.source: Roots need air to breathe and grow.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Types of Soil. I can identify sandy, clay and loam soil by their texture and drainage. Three main soil types: sandy (gritty, fast drainage, low fertility), clay (sticky, slow drainage, hard when dry), loam (crumbly, good drainage, high fertility). Loam is best for growing crops because it balances water, air and nutrients. Keywords: sandy: soil with large rough grains that feels gritty; clay: soil with very fine sticky grains that holds water; loam: soil with a mix of sand, silt and clay, good for crops; drainage: how fast water moves through soil; fertile: rich in nutrients so plants grow well; texture: how soil feels when rubbed between fingers
chunks.source: Three main soil types: sandy (gritty, fast drainage, low fertility), clay (sticky, slow drainage, hard when dry), loam (crumbly, good drainage, high fertility). Loam is best for growing crops because it balances water, air and nutrients.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which soil has large rough grains and feels gritty? A: sandy soil
chunks.source: sandy soil

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which soil has very fine grains that feel sticky when wet? A: clay soil
chunks.source: clay soil

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which soil is a mix of sand, silt and clay and is best for crops? A: loam soil
chunks.source: loam soil

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What does drainage mean? A: how fast water moves through soil
chunks.source: how fast water moves through soil

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why is loam soil called fertile? A: It holds water and air and has humus and minerals.
chunks.source: It holds water and air and has humus and minerals.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is the texture of sandy soil? A: rough and gritty
chunks.source: rough and gritty

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What happens to clay soil when it dries? A: It becomes hard and cracks.
chunks.source: It becomes hard and cracks.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How can you improve sandy soil for farming? A: Add compost or humus to hold water and nutrients.
chunks.source: Add compost or humus to hold water and nutrients.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Soil Erosion and Conservation. I can explain causes of soil erosion and name ways to conserve soil. Erosion removes topsoil by run-off and wind. Bare slopes erode fastest. Terracing, mulching and cover crops are three ways to conserve soil. They slow water, cover the ground and hold soil with roots. Keywords: erosion: wearing away of topsoil by water or wind; run-off: rain water that flows over the ground instead of soaking in; mulching: covering soil with dry grass or leaves to protect it; terracing: making flat steps on a slope to slow water flow; cover crops: plants grown to cover bare soil between main crops; wind: moving air that can blow away dry loose soil
chunks.source: Erosion removes topsoil by run-off and wind. Bare slopes erode fastest. Terracing, mulching and cover crops are three ways to conserve soil. They slow water, cover the ground and hold soil with roots.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is erosion? A: wearing away of topsoil by water or wind
chunks.source: wearing away of topsoil by water or wind

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is run-off? A: rain water that flows over the ground instead of soaking in
chunks.source: rain water that flows over the ground instead of soaking in

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name three methods to conserve soil on a slope. A: terracing, mulching, cover crops
chunks.source: terracing, mulching, cover crops

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How does mulching stop erosion? A: Dry grass covers soil so rain drops do not hit it directly and run-off slows.
chunks.source: Dry grass covers soil so rain drops do not hit it directly and run-off slows.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What do cover crops do? A: Protect soil from rain and wind, roots hold soil, add humus when cut.
chunks.source: Protect soil from rain and wind, roots hold soil, add humus when cut.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why is terracing useful on hills? A: It makes flat steps that slow run-off so water soaks in.
chunks.source: It makes flat steps that slow run-off so water soaks in.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What happens to bare soil when wind blows hard? A: Wind blows away dry loose soil causing erosion.
chunks.source: Wind blows away dry loose soil causing erosion.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: If your garden is on a slope, what will you do to stop soil washing away? A: Make terraces, add mulch, plant cover crops.
chunks.source: Make terraces, add mulch, plant cover crops.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Biological Changes. I can explain biological changes in living things and give examples from Uganda. **Biological** changes like **growth**, **metamorphosis**, **puberty**, and **germination** happen only in living things and are **permanent**. Keywords: growth: getting bigger and stronger; metamorphosis: complete change of form in insects; puberty: body changes from child to adult; germination: seed sprouting into a young plant; biological: relating to living things; permanent: lasting forever, not temporary
chunks.source: **Biological** changes like **growth**, **metamorphosis**, **puberty**, and **germination** happen only in living things and are **permanent**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name two **biological** changes in animals. A: **Metamorphosis** and **puberty** (or **growth**).
chunks.source: **Metamorphosis** and **puberty** (or **growth**).

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is **germination**? A: A seed sprouting into a young plant.
chunks.source: A seed sprouting into a young plant.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Is **puberty** **reversible**? Why? A: No, **puberty** is **permanent**; you cannot become a child again.
chunks.source: No, **puberty** is **permanent**; you cannot become a child again.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give one example of **growth** in plants. A: Maize growing taller after rain.
chunks.source: Maize growing taller after rain.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why is **metamorphosis** called a **biological** change? A: It happens in a living thing (insect).
chunks.source: It happens in a living thing (insect).

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What three things does a seed need for **germination**? A: Water, air, and warmth.
chunks.source: Water, air, and warmth.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Peter's voice is getting deeper. Which **biological** change is this? A: **Puberty**.
chunks.source: **Puberty**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Can a butterfly turn back into a caterpillar? A: No, **metamorphosis** is **permanent**.
chunks.source: No, **metamorphosis** is **permanent**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Physical and Chemical Changes. I can distinguish physical and chemical changes and identify examples in daily life. **Physical** changes (**melting**, **dissolving**) are **reversible** and make no new substance. **Chemical** changes (**rusting**, **burning**) make new substances and are not easily **reversible**. Keywords: melting: solid turning to liquid when heated; dissolving: solid mixing into liquid and disappearing; rusting: iron reacting with air and water to form rust; burning: material reacting with fire to make ash and smoke; reversible: can be changed back to original; chemical: change that makes new substances
chunks.source: **Physical** changes (**melting**, **dissolving**) are **reversible** and make no new substance. **Chemical** changes (**rusting**, **burning**) make new substances and are not easily **reversible**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Is **melting** ice a **physical** or **chemical** change? A: **Physical** change.
chunks.source: **Physical** change.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why is **dissolving** sugar **reversible**? A: You can evaporate the water to get sugar back; no new substance forms.
chunks.source: You can evaporate the water to get sugar back; no new substance forms.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name one **chemical** change you see at home. A: **Rusting** tools or **burning** firewood/charcoal.
chunks.source: **Rusting** tools or **burning** firewood/charcoal.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What new substance forms when iron **rusts**? A: Iron oxide (rust).
chunks.source: Iron oxide (rust).

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Can you reverse **burning** paper? A: No, **burning** is a **chemical** change; ash and smoke are new substances.
chunks.source: No, **burning** is a **chemical** change; ash and smoke are new substances.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give an example of a **reversible** change. A: **Melting** ice or **dissolving** salt in water.
chunks.source: **Melting** ice or **dissolving** salt in water.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why do we oil hoes and pangas? A: To prevent **rusting** (a **chemical** change).
chunks.source: To prevent **rusting** (a **chemical** change).

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Classify: **Melting** wax — **physical** or **chemical**? A: **Physical** change.
chunks.source: **Physical** change.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Changes in the Environment. I can describe environmental changes like weathering, erosion, flooding, and drought and their effects on Ugandan communities. **Weathering**, **erosion**, **flooding**, and **drought** are changes in the **environment**. Human actions like cutting trees can make **erosion** and **flooding** worse; planting trees helps protect the **environment**. Keywords: weathering: rocks breaking down by rain, wind, heat; erosion: soil or rock being carried away by water or wind; flooding: water covering land that is usually dry; season: time of year with typical weather; drought: long period with little or no rain; environment: the natural world around us
chunks.source: **Weathering**, **erosion**, **flooding**, and **drought** are changes in the **environment**. Human actions like cutting trees can make **erosion** and **flooding** worse; planting trees helps protect the **environment**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is **weathering**? A: Rocks breaking down by rain, wind, and heat over time.
chunks.source: Rocks breaking down by rain, wind, and heat over time.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How does **erosion** differ from **weathering**? A: **Weathering** breaks rocks in place; **erosion** moves the broken pieces away.
chunks.source: **Weathering** breaks rocks in place; **erosion** moves the broken pieces away.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name one cause of **flooding** in Uganda. A: Heavy rain during the rainy **season**.
chunks.source: Heavy rain during the rainy **season**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is a **drought**? A: A long period with little or no rain.
chunks.source: A long period with little or no rain.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give one way to reduce **erosion** on a slope. A: Plant grass or trees with deep roots.
chunks.source: Plant grass or trees with deep roots.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why is **drought** dangerous for farmers? A: Crops wither, animals die, food becomes scarce.
chunks.source: Crops wither, animals die, food becomes scarce.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which **season** in Uganda has the highest risk of **flooding**? A: The rainy **season** (March–May and September–November).
chunks.source: The rainy **season** (March–May and September–November).

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How does cutting trees affect the **environment**? A: It increases **erosion** and **flooding** because soil is exposed to rain.
chunks.source: It increases **erosion** and **flooding** because soil is exposed to rain.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: What Is Primary Health Care?. I can explain what Primary Health Care means and name its main elements. **PHC** (Primary Health Care) brings essential health services to every **community**. It has multiple **element**s like **immunisation**, **safe water**, and health education that work together to **prevent** illness. The **health centre** is the main place delivering these services near people's homes. Keywords: PHC: Primary Health Care; community: group of people living together; prevent: stop something bad before it happens; health centre: place where nurses and doctors treat patients; immunisation: giving vaccines to protect against diseases; element: one part of a whole thing
chunks.source: **PHC** (Primary Health Care) brings essential health services to every **community**. It has multiple **element**s like **immunisation**, **safe water**, and health education that work together to **prevent** illness. The **health centre** is the main place delivering these services near people's homes.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What does **PHC** stand for? A: Primary Health Care
chunks.source: Primary Health Care

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name three **element**s of **PHC**. A: Any three: health education, safe water, nutrition, immunisation, maternal care, disease control
chunks.source: Any three: health education, safe water, nutrition, immunisation, maternal care, disease control

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why is the **health centre** important in **PHC**? A: It brings essential health services close to the community.
chunks.source: It brings essential health services close to the community.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How does **immunisation** help the **community**? A: It protects people from specific diseases before they get sick.
chunks.source: It protects people from specific diseases before they get sick.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What does it mean to **prevent** illness? A: To stop sickness before it happens.
chunks.source: To stop sickness before it happens.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give one example of how your **community** can work together for **PHC**. A: Answers vary: cleaning the village, protecting water sources, encouraging clinic visits.
chunks.source: Answers vary: cleaning the village, protecting water sources, encouraging clinic visits.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: If a village has **immunisation** but no **safe water**, is **PHC** complete? A: No, all elements must work together for effective PHC.
chunks.source: No, all elements must work together for effective PHC.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Who is responsible for **PHC**? A: Everyone — health workers, community members, families, and leaders.
chunks.source: Everyone — health workers, community members, families, and leaders.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Personal and Community Hygiene. I can explain how personal and community hygiene keep us healthy. **Hygiene** and **sanitation** are vital **element**s of **PHC**. **Hand washing** with soap, using a clean **latrine**, protecting **safe water**, and keeping surroundings **clean** **prevent** diseases like diarrhoea and cholera. Every person in the **community** has a role. Keywords: hygiene: practices that keep us clean and healthy; latrine: a toilet for safe disposal of human waste; hand washing: cleaning hands with soap and water; safe water: water that is clean and free from germs; sanitation: systems for keeping the environment clean; clean: free from dirt and germs
chunks.source: **Hygiene** and **sanitation** are vital **element**s of **PHC**. **Hand washing** with soap, using a clean **latrine**, protecting **safe water**, and keeping surroundings **clean** **prevent** diseases like diarrhoea and cholera. Every person in the **community** has a role.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Define **hygiene**. A: Practices that keep us clean and healthy to prevent disease.
chunks.source: Practices that keep us clean and healthy to prevent disease.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: List three critical times for **hand washing**. A: After latrine, before eating/cooking, after cleaning baby, after touching animals.
chunks.source: After latrine, before eating/cooking, after cleaning baby, after touching animals.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why must a **latrine** have a cover? A: To stop flies from spreading germs from waste to food and water.
chunks.source: To stop flies from spreading germs from waste to food and water.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is **safe water**? A: Water that is clean and free from germs, safe for drinking and cooking.
chunks.source: Water that is clean and free from germs, safe for drinking and cooking.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How does **sanitation** protect **safe water**? A: Proper waste disposal keeps germs out of water sources.
chunks.source: Proper waste disposal keeps germs out of water sources.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name two ways to keep the compound **clean**. A: Sweep daily, dispose of rubbish in a pit, clear bushes, drain stagnant water.
chunks.source: Sweep daily, dispose of rubbish in a pit, clear bushes, drain stagnant water.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: If a family has no **latrine**, what health risks do they face? A: Diarrhoea, cholera, typhoid, worm infections, contamination of water sources.
chunks.source: Diarrhoea, cholera, typhoid, worm infections, contamination of water sources.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How can children promote **hygiene** in their **community**? A: Practice good habits, teach younger siblings, report problems, join school health clubs.
chunks.source: Practice good habits, teach younger siblings, report problems, join school health clubs.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Health Services Near Us. I can identify health services in my community and explain how they work together. Health services near us include **clinic**s, **outreach** teams, and **health worker**s at every level. They provide **medicine**, **vaccine**s, and basic care. **Referral** links them to hospitals for complex cases. This network delivers **PHC** to the whole **community**. Keywords: health worker: person trained to give health care; clinic: small health facility for basic treatment; outreach: health services taken to the community; referral: sending a patient to a higher level facility; medicine: drugs used to treat or prevent illness; vaccine: substance that gives immunity to a disease
chunks.source: Health services near us include **clinic**s, **outreach** teams, and **health worker**s at every level. They provide **medicine**, **vaccine**s, and basic care. **Referral** links them to hospitals for complex cases. This network delivers **PHC** to the whole **community**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Who is a **health worker**? A: A person trained to give health care, like a nurse, midwife, or clinical officer.
chunks.source: A person trained to give health care, like a nurse, midwife, or clinical officer.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What services does a **clinic** provide? A: Basic treatment, malaria testing, **immunisation**, antenatal care, **medicine** dispensing.
chunks.source: Basic treatment, malaria testing, **immunisation**, antenatal care, **medicine** dispensing.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is **outreach**? A: Health services taken to the **community**, especially hard-to-reach areas.
chunks.source: Health services taken to the **community**, especially hard-to-reach areas.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Explain **referral** in your own words. A: Sending a patient from a lower facility to a higher one for specialised care.
chunks.source: Sending a patient from a lower facility to a higher one for specialised care.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why are **vaccine**s given during **outreach**? A: To reach children who cannot easily travel to the **clinic** for **immunisation**.
chunks.source: To reach children who cannot easily travel to the **clinic** for **immunisation**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What should you do if the **health worker** gives you **medicine**? A: Take the full course as instructed, even if you feel better.
chunks.source: Take the full course as instructed, even if you feel better.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How does the **referral** system help patients? A: Ensures they get the right level of care; shares medical information; avoids delays.
chunks.source: Ensures they get the right level of care; shares medical information; avoids delays.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name the three levels of the health system from lowest to highest. A: Community/outreach → health centre/clinic → district hospital.
chunks.source: Community/outreach → health centre/clinic → district hospital.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Food Classes Revisited. I can name the six food classes and say what each does for my body. The six food classes are carbohydrates, proteins, vitamins, minerals, water, and roughage. Each has a special job in your body. Keywords: carbohydrates: energy giving food; proteins: body building food; vitamins: protect the body; minerals: strengthen bones and teeth; water: keeps body hydrated; roughage: helps digestion
chunks.source: The six food classes are carbohydrates, proteins, vitamins, minerals, water, and roughage. Each has a special job in your body.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What nutrient gives quick energy? A: **Carbohydrates** give quick energy.
chunks.source: **Carbohydrates** give quick energy.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which nutrient builds muscles? A: **Proteins** build muscles.
chunks.source: **Proteins** build muscles.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name a vitamin found in mangoes. A: Mangoes have **vitamins** like vitamin A.
chunks.source: Mangoes have **vitamins** like vitamin A.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What mineral helps make strong bones? A: **Minerals** such as calcium make strong bones.
chunks.source: **Minerals** such as calcium make strong bones.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why is **water** important? A: **Water** carries nutrients and keeps you hydrated.
chunks.source: **Water** carries nutrients and keeps you hydrated.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What does **roughage** do? A: **Roughage** helps food move through the gut.
chunks.source: **Roughage** helps food move through the gut.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give one local food for each nutrient. A: Posho for **carbohydrates**, beans for **proteins**, mango for **vitamins**, spinach for **minerals**, a glass of **water**, cassava leaves for **roughage**.
chunks.source: Posho for **carbohydrates**, beans for **proteins**, mango for **vitamins**, spinach for **minerals**, a glass of **water**, cassava leaves for **roughage**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: If you eat only posho, which nutrients are missing? A: You miss **proteins**, **vitamins**, **minerals**, **water**, and **roughage**.
chunks.source: You miss **proteins**, **vitamins**, **minerals**, **water**, and **roughage**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Deficiency Diseases. I can name common deficiency diseases and the nutrients they lack. Kwashiorkor, marasmus, scurvy, rickets, and anaemia are all caused by a deficiency of specific nutrients. Eating varied foods keeps you healthy. Keywords: kwashiorkor: protein deficiency disease; marasmus: severe energy and protein shortage; scurvy: vitamin C deficiency; rickets: vitamin D or calcium deficiency; anaemia: iron deficiency; deficiency: lack of a needed nutrient
chunks.source: Kwashiorkor, marasmus, scurvy, rickets, and anaemia are all caused by a deficiency of specific nutrients. Eating varied foods keeps you healthy.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which disease is caused by lack of protein? A: **Kwashiorkor** is caused by lack of protein.
chunks.source: **Kwashiorkor** is caused by lack of protein.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What does a child with **marasmus** look like? A: A child with **marasmus** is very thin and wasted.
chunks.source: A child with **marasmus** is very thin and wasted.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name the vitamin missing in **scurvy**. A: **Vitamin C** is missing in **scurvy**.
chunks.source: **Vitamin C** is missing in **scurvy**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which nutrient deficiency causes **rickets**? A: Lack of **vitamin D** or calcium causes **rickets**.
chunks.source: Lack of **vitamin D** or calcium causes **rickets**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What nutrient is low in **anaemia**? A: **Iron** is low in **anaemia**.
chunks.source: **Iron** is low in **anaemia**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give one food that prevents **anaemia**. A: Liver, beans, or dark green leaves give **iron**.
chunks.source: Liver, beans, or dark green leaves give **iron**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: If a child has swollen belly and hair changes, what disease might it be? A: It might be **kwashiorkor**.
chunks.source: It might be **kwashiorkor**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How can you prevent **deficiency** diseases? A: Eat a variety of foods every day.
chunks.source: Eat a variety of foods every day.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Breastfeeding and Weaning. I can explain why breast milk is best for infants and how to start weaning safely. Breast milk and colostrum give antibodies and all nutrients. Weaning starts at six months with soft porridge and other local foods. Keywords: breast milk: milk from mother; colostrum: first thick yellow milk; weaning: adding other foods to baby diet; porridge: soft cooked cereal; infant: baby under one year; antibodies: germ fighting proteins
chunks.source: Breast milk and colostrum give antibodies and all nutrients. Weaning starts at six months with soft porridge and other local foods.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is the first milk after birth called? A: **Colostrum** is the first milk after birth.
chunks.source: **Colostrum** is the first milk after birth.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What does **colostrum** contain that protects the baby? A: **Antibodies** protect the baby from germs.
chunks.source: **Antibodies** protect the baby from germs.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: At what age should **weaning** start? A: **Weaning** starts at six months.
chunks.source: **Weaning** starts at six months.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name a good first **weaning** food. A: **Porridge** made from millet or maize is a good first food.
chunks.source: **Porridge** made from millet or maize is a good first food.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why is **breast milk** best for an **infant**? A: **Breast milk** has all nutrients and **antibodies**.
chunks.source: **Breast milk** has all nutrients and **antibodies**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What happens if you stop breastfeeding at two months? A: The **infant** misses **antibodies** and may get sick.
chunks.source: The **infant** misses **antibodies** and may get sick.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give two local foods to add during **weaning**. A: Mashed beans and mashed matooke are good **weaning** foods.
chunks.source: Mashed beans and mashed matooke are good **weaning** foods.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How do **antibodies** help the **infant**? A: **Antibodies** fight germs and keep the **infant** healthy.
chunks.source: **Antibodies** fight germs and keep the **infant** healthy.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Accidents at Home. I can name common home accidents and say how to prevent them. Home accidents include burn, scald, poison, fall, cut, and electric shock. Prevent them by turning pot handles in, locking poisons, drying floors, using tools safely, and fixing bare wires. Check every room often. Keywords: burn: hurt by fire or hot things; scald: hurt by hot liquid or steam; poison: harmful substance if swallowed or breathed; fall: drop down by accident; cut: wound from a sharp thing; electric shock: hurt from electricity
chunks.source: Home accidents include burn, scald, poison, fall, cut, and electric shock. Prevent them by turning pot handles in, locking poisons, drying floors, using tools safely, and fixing bare wires. Check every room often.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name two causes of a burn at home. A: Hot sufuria, fire, hot iron, hot charcoal stove.
chunks.source: Hot sufuria, fire, hot iron, hot charcoal stove.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is the difference between a burn and a scald? A: Burn from fire or hot solid. Scald from hot liquid or steam.
chunks.source: Burn from fire or hot solid. Scald from hot liquid or steam.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why must poison never be put in a soda bottle? A: Children think it is a drink and may swallow it.
chunks.source: Children think it is a drink and may swallow it.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: List two ways to prevent a fall at home. A: Wipe wet floors, fix loose boards, keep paths clear, use non-slip mats.
chunks.source: Wipe wet floors, fix loose boards, keep paths clear, use non-slip mats.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What should you do before using a panga to avoid a cut? A: Check the blade, hold handle firmly, cut away from body, wear shoes.
chunks.source: Check the blade, hold handle firmly, cut away from body, wear shoes.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why is an electric shock dangerous? A: It can stop the heart, cause burns, or cause death.
chunks.source: It can stop the heart, cause burns, or cause death.

chunks.subject: Science
