chunks.text: Q: If you see a bare wire on an extension cable, what do you do? A: Do not touch. Tell an adult. Replace the cable.
chunks.source: Do not touch. Tell an adult. Replace the cable.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Walk through your home. Name one danger in each room. A: Kitchen: burn/scald. Store: poison. Veranda: fall. Garden: cut. Living room: electric shock. Bedroom: check for hazards.
chunks.source: Kitchen: burn/scald. Store: poison. Veranda: fall. Garden: cut. Living room: electric shock. Bedroom: check for hazards.

chunks.id: L-P5-Science-First Aid for Burns and Cuts
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: First Aid for Burns and Cuts
chunks.text: First Aid for Burns and Cuts. I can give first aid for burns, scalds and cuts. First aid for burns and scalds: cool water for ten minutes, then loose clean cloth. First aid for cuts: press clean cloth to stop bleeding, wash wound, apply clean bandage. Use clean water and clean cloth always. Seek hospital for serious injuries. Keywords: first aid: first help given before a doctor; cool water: water that is not hot or cold; bandage: cloth to cover a wound; bleeding: blood coming out of a wound; wound: an injury where skin is broken; clean: free from dirt or germs
chunks.source: First aid for burns and scalds: cool water for ten minutes, then loose clean cloth. First aid for cuts: press clean cloth to stop bleeding, wash wound, apply clean bandage. Use clean water and clean cloth always. Seek hospital for serious injuries.

chunks.id: LQ-P5-Science-First Aid for Burns and Cuts
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: First Aid for Burns and Cuts
chunks.text: Q: What is the first step for a burn or scald? A: Run cool water on it for at least ten minutes.
chunks.source: Run cool water on it for at least ten minutes.

chunks.id: LQ-P5-Science-First Aid for Burns and Cuts
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: First Aid for Burns and Cuts
chunks.text: Q: Why should you not put butter on a burn? A: Butter traps heat and adds germs, making the burn worse.
chunks.source: Butter traps heat and adds germs, making the burn worse.

chunks.id: LQ-P5-Science-First Aid for Burns and Cuts
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: First Aid for Burns and Cuts
chunks.text: Q: How long should you press a clean cloth on a cut to stop bleeding? A: At least five minutes without peeking.
chunks.source: At least five minutes without peeking.

chunks.id: LQ-P5-Science-First Aid for Burns and Cuts
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: First Aid for Burns and Cuts
chunks.text: Q: What should you do after bleeding stops on a cut? A: Wash the wound gently with clean water and soap, pat dry, apply a clean bandage.
chunks.source: Wash the wound gently with clean water and soap, pat dry, apply a clean bandage.

chunks.id: LQ-P5-Science-First Aid for Burns and Cuts
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: First Aid for Burns and Cuts
chunks.text: Q: When should you go to hospital for a burn? A: If the burn is big, on the face, on a joint, or has blisters.
chunks.source: If the burn is big, on the face, on a joint, or has blisters.

chunks.id: LQ-P5-Science-First Aid for Burns and Cuts
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: First Aid for Burns and Cuts
chunks.text: Q: Why must the cloth and water be clean for first aid? A: Dirty cloth or water can cause infection in the wound.
chunks.source: Dirty cloth or water can cause infection in the wound.

chunks.id: LQ-P5-Science-First Aid for Burns and Cuts
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: First Aid for Burns and Cuts
chunks.text: Q: What does a bandage do for a cut? A: It keeps the wound clean and protects it while it heals.
chunks.source: It keeps the wound clean and protects it while it heals.

chunks.id: LQ-P5-Science-First Aid for Burns and Cuts
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: First Aid for Burns and Cuts
chunks.text: Q: If bleeding soaks through the first cloth, what do you do? A: Add another clean cloth on top and keep pressing. Do not remove the first cloth.
chunks.source: Add another clean cloth on top and keep pressing. Do not remove the first cloth.

chunks.id: L-P5-Science-First Aid for Bites, Stings and Poisoning
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: First Aid for Bites, Stings and Poisoning
chunks.text: First Aid for Bites, Stings and Poisoning. I can give first aid for snake bites, stings and poisoning. For snake bite: keep still, no tourniquet, go to hospital. For sting: scrape out, wash, cold cloth. For swallowed poison: do not vomit, rinse mouth, take container to hospital. Stay calm. Act fast. Get help. Keywords: snake bite: bite from a snake; sting: sharp pain from insect or plant; poison: harmful substance swallowed or breathed; vomit: bring up food from stomach; hospital: place for medical treatment; tourniquet: tight band to stop blood flow
chunks.source: For snake bite: keep still, no tourniquet, go to hospital. For sting: scrape out, wash, cold cloth. For swallowed poison: do not vomit, rinse mouth, take container to hospital. Stay calm. Act fast. Get help.

chunks.id: LQ-P5-Science-First Aid for Bites, Stings and Poisoning
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: First Aid for Bites, Stings and Poisoning
chunks.text: Q: List three things you must NOT do for a snake bite. A: Do not use a tourniquet, do not cut the bite, do not suck the venom, do not let the person walk.
chunks.source: Do not use a tourniquet, do not cut the bite, do not suck the venom, do not let the person walk.

chunks.id: LQ-P5-Science-First Aid for Bites, Stings and Poisoning
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: First Aid for Bites, Stings and Poisoning
chunks.text: Q: How do you remove a bee sting safely? A: Scrape it out sideways with a card or fingernail. Do not squeeze.
chunks.source: Scrape it out sideways with a card or fingernail. Do not squeeze.

chunks.id: LQ-P5-Science-First Aid for Bites, Stings and Poisoning
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: First Aid for Bites, Stings and Poisoning
chunks.text: Q: Why should you not make a person vomit after swallowing kerosene? A: Vomit can burn the throat again and enter the lungs.
chunks.source: Vomit can burn the throat again and enter the lungs.

chunks.id: LQ-P5-Science-First Aid for Bites, Stings and Poisoning
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: First Aid for Bites, Stings and Poisoning
chunks.text: Q: What should you take to hospital for a poisoning case? A: The container or bottle of the poison.
chunks.source: The container or bottle of the poison.

chunks.id: LQ-P5-Science-First Aid for Bites, Stings and Poisoning
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: First Aid for Bites, Stings and Poisoning
chunks.text: Q: If a person is stung in the mouth and has trouble breathing, what do you do? A: Go to hospital immediately. This is an emergency.
chunks.source: Go to hospital immediately. This is an emergency.

chunks.id: LQ-P5-Science-First Aid for Bites, Stings and Poisoning
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: First Aid for Bites, Stings and Poisoning
chunks.text: Q: Why is a tourniquet dangerous for a snake bite? A: It cuts off blood flow, causing tissue death and does not stop venom spread.
chunks.source: It cuts off blood flow, causing tissue death and does not stop venom spread.

chunks.id: LQ-P5-Science-First Aid for Bites, Stings and Poisoning
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: First Aid for Bites, Stings and Poisoning
chunks.text: Q: What is the first action for any snake bite? A: Keep the person completely still and calm.
chunks.source: Keep the person completely still and calm.

chunks.id: LQ-P5-Science-First Aid for Bites, Stings and Poisoning
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: First Aid for Bites, Stings and Poisoning
chunks.text: Q: If you are not sure what poison was swallowed, what do you do? A: Rinse mouth with water. Do not guess. Go to hospital with any containers found.
chunks.source: Rinse mouth with water. Do not guess. Go to hospital with any containers found.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Vectors Around Us. I can name common disease vectors and the diseases they spread. A **vector** carries germs. Common **vectors** in Uganda are **mosquito**, **housefly**, **tsetse fly**, **black fly**, and **bed bug**. Each spreads specific diseases. Knowing them helps us protect our families. Keywords: vector: an animal that carries germs from one person to another; mosquito: a small flying insect that bites and spreads malaria; housefly: a common fly that lands on dirt and food; tsetse fly: a fly that bites and spreads sleeping sickness; black fly: a small black fly that bites and spreads river blindness; bed bug: a tiny bug that hides in beds and bites at night
chunks.source: A **vector** carries germs. Common **vectors** in Uganda are **mosquito**, **housefly**, **tsetse fly**, **black fly**, and **bed bug**. Each spreads specific diseases. Knowing them helps us protect our families.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is a **vector**? A: An animal that carries germs from one person to another.
chunks.source: An animal that carries germs from one person to another.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which **vector** spreads **malaria**? A: The **mosquito**.
chunks.source: The **mosquito**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name two diseases spread by the **housefly**. A: **Cholera** and **typhoid** (or **dysentery**).
chunks.source: **Cholera** and **typhoid** (or **dysentery**).

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Where do **black flies** breed? A: In fast-flowing rivers.
chunks.source: In fast-flowing rivers.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which **vector** hides in beds and bites at night? A: The **bed bug**.
chunks.source: The **bed bug**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What disease does the **tsetse fly** spread? A: **Sleeping sickness**.
chunks.source: **Sleeping sickness**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why should we cover food? A: To stop **houseflies** from landing on it and spreading germs.
chunks.source: To stop **houseflies** from landing on it and spreading germs.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name one place **mosquitoes** breed. A: Stagnant water.
chunks.source: Stagnant water.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: The Housefly and Diarrhoeal Diseases. I can explain how houseflies spread cholera, dysentery, and typhoid and how to stop them. The **housefly** carries germs from the **latrine** to food, causing **cholera**, **dysentery**, and **typhoid**. Stop it by covering food, covering the **latrine**, and keeping the compound clean. Keywords: housefly: a common fly that lands on dirt and food; cholera: a severe diarrhoea disease from dirty water or food; dysentery: diarrhoea with blood and mucus caused by germs; typhoid: a fever disease from germs in food or water; latrine: a toilet pit for human waste; cover food: put a lid or cloth over food to keep flies away
chunks.source: The **housefly** carries germs from the **latrine** to food, causing **cholera**, **dysentery**, and **typhoid**. Stop it by covering food, covering the **latrine**, and keeping the compound clean.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How does a **housefly** spread **cholera**? A: It lands on faeces in the **latrine**, picks up germs, then lands on uncovered food.
chunks.source: It lands on faeces in the **latrine**, picks up germs, then lands on uncovered food.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name three diseases spread by **houseflies**. A: **Cholera**, **dysentery**, **typhoid**.
chunks.source: **Cholera**, **dysentery**, **typhoid**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why must we **cover food**? A: To stop **houseflies** from landing on it and leaving germs.
chunks.source: To stop **houseflies** from landing on it and leaving germs.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What should you do with the **latrine** cover? A: Keep it closed after use.
chunks.source: Keep it closed after use.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: If a child has **typhoid**, what two things should the family do? A: Go to the health centre and **cover food** to stop **houseflies** spreading germs.
chunks.source: Go to the health centre and **cover food** to stop **houseflies** spreading germs.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Where do **houseflies** breed? A: In rubbish heaps, animal dung, and open **latrines**.
chunks.source: In rubbish heaps, animal dung, and open **latrines**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What happens when a **housefly** vomits on food? A: It leaves germs from the **latrine** that cause **cholera**, **dysentery**, or **typhoid**.
chunks.source: It leaves germs from the **latrine** that cause **cholera**, **dysentery**, or **typhoid**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why is **dysentery** dangerous? A: It causes diarrhoea with blood and can lead to severe dehydration.
chunks.source: It causes diarrhoea with blood and can lead to severe dehydration.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Controlling Vectors. I can describe integrated vector control methods used in Uganda. **Integrated vector control** uses **nets**, **insecticide**, **drainage**, **fumigation**, **bush clearing**, and **hygiene** together. Each method targets different **vectors**. Combined, they protect our community from **malaria**, **cholera**, **sleeping sickness**, and more. Keywords: insecticide: a chemical that kills insects; net: a treated mesh hung over a bed to stop mosquito bites; drainage: removing stagnant water so vectors cannot breed; fumigation: using smoke or gas to kill insects in an area; bush clearing: cutting grass and bushes around homes; hygiene: clean habits that stop germs and vectors
chunks.source: **Integrated vector control** uses **nets**, **insecticide**, **drainage**, **fumigation**, **bush clearing**, and **hygiene** together. Each method targets different **vectors**. Combined, they protect our community from **malaria**, **cholera**, **sleeping sickness**, and more.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is **integrated vector control**? A: Using many methods together like **nets**, **insecticide**, **drainage**, **fumigation**, **bush clearing**, and **hygiene**.
chunks.source: Using many methods together like **nets**, **insecticide**, **drainage**, **fumigation**, **bush clearing**, and **hygiene**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How does a treated **net** help? A: It stops **mosquitoes** from biting you while you sleep.
chunks.source: It stops **mosquitoes** from biting you while you sleep.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why is **drainage** important? A: It removes stagnant water where **mosquitoes** breed.
chunks.source: It removes stagnant water where **mosquitoes** breed.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What does **fumigation** do? A: Kills adult flying **vectors** like **mosquitoes** and **houseflies** quickly.
chunks.source: Kills adult flying **vectors** like **mosquitoes** and **houseflies** quickly.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How does **bush clearing** stop **tsetse flies**? A: It removes the shady bushes where **tsetse flies** rest.
chunks.source: It removes the shady bushes where **tsetse flies** rest.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give two examples of **hygiene** that stop **houseflies**. A: **Cover food** and keep the **latrine** covered.
chunks.source: **Cover food** and keep the **latrine** covered.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which method kills **mosquitoes** resting on walls? A: Spraying **insecticide** on walls.
chunks.source: Spraying **insecticide** on walls.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: If you only use a **net** but have stagnant water, what happens? A: **Mosquitoes** still breed and bite others; you need **drainage** too.
chunks.source: **Mosquitoes** still breed and bite others; you need **drainage** too.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: What Is Immunisation?. I can explain how a vaccine gives the body immunity against disease. A **vaccine** trains the body to make **antibodies**. Each **dose** on the **schedule** builds **immunity** to **prevent** disease. Keywords: vaccine: a medicine that trains the body to fight a germ; immunity: the body's power to stop a sickness; antibodies: tiny soldiers in the blood that attack germs; dose: one amount of medicine given at one time; schedule: a plan that shows when to get each injection; prevent: to stop something bad before it starts
chunks.source: A **vaccine** trains the body to make **antibodies**. Each **dose** on the **schedule** builds **immunity** to **prevent** disease.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is a **vaccine**? A: A medicine that trains the body to fight a germ.
chunks.source: A medicine that trains the body to fight a germ.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What do **antibodies** do? A: They attack germs in the blood.
chunks.source: They attack germs in the blood.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What does **immunity** mean? A: The body's power to stop a sickness.
chunks.source: The body's power to stop a sickness.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why follow the **schedule**? A: To get each **dose** at the right time for strong **immunity**.
chunks.source: To get each **dose** at the right time for strong **immunity**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How does a **vaccine** **prevent** disease? A: It makes **antibodies** ready before the real germ comes.
chunks.source: It makes **antibodies** ready before the real germ comes.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: If a child misses a **dose**, what should they do? A: Go to the health centre to catch up on the **schedule**.
chunks.source: Go to the health centre to catch up on the **schedule**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why might the arm hurt after a **vaccine**? A: The body is busy making **antibodies**.
chunks.source: The body is busy making **antibodies**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Can eating matooke replace a **vaccine**? A: No. Food helps health but cannot give **immunity** like a **vaccine**.
chunks.source: No. Food helps health but cannot give **immunity** like a **vaccine**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Immunisable Diseases. I can name the six immunisable childhood diseases and say how they spread. The six immunisable diseases are **polio**, **measles**, **tuberculosis**, **tetanus**, **whooping cough**, and **diphtheria**. Vaccines on the **schedule** protect against all of them. Keywords: polio: a virus that can cause paralysis; measles: a virus with fever and rash that spreads fast; tuberculosis: a germ that attacks the lungs; tetanus: a germ from soil that enters through cuts; whooping cough: a bacterial cough that makes a whoop sound; diphtheria: a throat infection that can block breathing
chunks.source: The six immunisable diseases are **polio**, **measles**, **tuberculosis**, **tetanus**, **whooping cough**, and **diphtheria**. Vaccines on the **schedule** protect against all of them.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name the six immunisable diseases. A: **Polio**, **measles**, **tuberculosis**, **tetanus**, **whooping cough**, **diphtheria**.
chunks.source: **Polio**, **measles**, **tuberculosis**, **tetanus**, **whooping cough**, **diphtheria**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which disease can cause paralysis? A: **Polio**.
chunks.source: **Polio**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which disease gives a rash and high fever? A: **Measles**.
chunks.source: **Measles**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which disease enters through a dirty cut? A: **Tetanus**.
chunks.source: **Tetanus**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which disease makes a whooping sound when coughing? A: **Whooping cough**.
chunks.source: **Whooping cough**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which disease attacks the lungs and causes long cough? A: **Tuberculosis**.
chunks.source: **Tuberculosis**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which disease makes a thick coat in the throat? A: **Diphtheria**.
chunks.source: **Diphtheria**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How do **measles** and **whooping cough** spread? A: Through the air when a sick person coughs or sneezes.
chunks.source: Through the air when a sick person coughs or sneezes.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: The Immunisation Schedule. I can read the Uganda immunisation schedule and explain the child health card. The Uganda **schedule** gives **BCG** at birth, **OPV** and **DPT** at 6, 10, 14 weeks, **measles** at 9 and 18 months, and **booster** doses at 18 months and 5 years. The **card** records every **dose**. Keywords: BCG: vaccine against tuberculosis given at birth; DPT: vaccine against diphtheria, pertussis, and tetanus; OPV: oral polio vaccine drops given by mouth; measles: vaccine against measles given at 9 months; card: the child health card that records every vaccine; booster: an extra dose to make immunity stronger later
chunks.source: The Uganda **schedule** gives **BCG** at birth, **OPV** and **DPT** at 6, 10, 14 weeks, **measles** at 9 and 18 months, and **booster** doses at 18 months and 5 years. The **card** records every **dose**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What does **BCG** protect against? A: **Tuberculosis**.
chunks.source: **Tuberculosis**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: At what age is **BCG** given? A: At birth.
chunks.source: At birth.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What three diseases does **DPT** cover? A: **Diphtheria**, **whooping cough** (pertussis), and **tetanus**.
chunks.source: **Diphtheria**, **whooping cough** (pertussis), and **tetanus**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How many **DPT** doses are on the infant **schedule**? A: Three — at 6, 10, and 14 weeks.
chunks.source: Three — at 6, 10, and 14 weeks.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What does **OPV** stand for? A: Oral Polio Vaccine.
chunks.source: Oral Polio Vaccine.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How is **OPV** given? A: Two drops in the mouth.
chunks.source: Two drops in the mouth.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: When is the first **measles** **vaccine** given? A: At 9 months.
chunks.source: At 9 months.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is a **booster** dose? A: An extra dose later to make **immunity** stronger.
chunks.source: An extra dose later to make **immunity** stronger.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: The Teeth. I can name the types of teeth and explain how to care for them. We have three tooth types: **incisors** cut, **canines** tear, **molars** grind. **Enamel** protects teeth. Brushing twice daily stops **decay**. Keywords: incisors: front teeth for cutting food; canines: pointed teeth for tearing food; molars: flat back teeth for grinding food; dentition: the arrangement of teeth in the mouth; enamel: hard shiny layer that covers each tooth; decay: rot that makes holes in teeth
chunks.source: We have three tooth types: **incisors** cut, **canines** tear, **molars** grind. **Enamel** protects teeth. Brushing twice daily stops **decay**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name the three types of teeth. A: Incisors, canines, molars
chunks.source: Incisors, canines, molars

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which teeth cut food like a knife? A: Incisors
chunks.source: Incisors

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which teeth tear tough food like meat? A: Canines
chunks.source: Canines

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which teeth grind posho and cassava? A: Molars
chunks.source: Molars

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is the hard shiny layer on a tooth called? A: Enamel
chunks.source: Enamel

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What causes holes in teeth? A: Decay from acid made by bacteria
chunks.source: Decay from acid made by bacteria

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How many times should you brush each day? A: Two times — morning and night
chunks.source: Two times — morning and night

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What should you do if you see a black spot on a tooth? A: Tell a parent and go to the dental clinic
chunks.source: Tell a parent and go to the dental clinic

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Parts of the Digestive System. I can name the main organs of the digestive system and say what each one does. Food travels: **mouth** → **oesophagus** → **stomach** → **intestines**. The **liver** makes bile, the **pancreas** makes enzymes. Nutrients enter blood in the **intestines**. Keywords: mouth: where food enters and chewing starts; oesophagus: tube that carries food to the stomach; stomach: bag that churns food with juices; intestines: long tubes where nutrients enter blood; liver: organ that makes bile for fat digestion; pancreas: organ that makes juices for digestion
chunks.source: Food travels: **mouth** → **oesophagus** → **stomach** → **intestines**. The **liver** makes bile, the **pancreas** makes enzymes. Nutrients enter blood in the **intestines**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Where does digestion begin? A: In the mouth
chunks.source: In the mouth

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which tube carries food from the mouth to the stomach? A: Oesophagus
chunks.source: Oesophagus

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What does the stomach turn food into? A: Chyme, a thick liquid
chunks.source: Chyme, a thick liquid

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Where are most nutrients absorbed into the blood? A: In the small intestines
chunks.source: In the small intestines

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What does the liver make to help digest fat? A: Bile
chunks.source: Bile

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What does the pancreas release into the intestines? A: Enzyme juice
chunks.source: Enzyme juice

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name the organs in order from mouth to intestines. A: Mouth, oesophagus, stomach, intestines
chunks.source: Mouth, oesophagus, stomach, intestines

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What are villi? A: Tiny fingers in the small intestines that absorb nutrients
chunks.source: Tiny fingers in the small intestines that absorb nutrients

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: How Digestion Happens. I can explain the steps of digestion and how nutrients get into the blood. **Digestion** breaks food down. **Saliva** and **enzyme** start in the **mouth**. **Stomach** makes **chyme**. **Enzyme** from **pancreas** and bile from **liver** finish in **intestines**. **Villi** do **absorption** into blood. Keywords: enzyme: a helper protein that breaks down food; saliva: watery fluid in the mouth that softens food; digestion: breaking food into tiny bits the body can use; absorption: nutrients passing through the intestine wall into blood; chyme: thick liquid food mixed with stomach juices; villi: tiny finger shapes in the intestine that catch nutrients
chunks.source: **Digestion** breaks food down. **Saliva** and **enzyme** start in the **mouth**. **Stomach** makes **chyme**. **Enzyme** from **pancreas** and bile from **liver** finish in **intestines**. **Villi** do **absorption** into blood.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What does saliva do to food? A: Wets it and starts starch digestion with enzyme
chunks.source: Wets it and starts starch digestion with enzyme

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is the enzyme in saliva called? A: Amylase
chunks.source: Amylase

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What does the stomach turn food into? A: Chyme
chunks.source: Chyme

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Where does most absorption happen? A: In the small intestines
chunks.source: In the small intestines

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What are villi? A: Tiny fingers that catch nutrients for the blood
chunks.source: Tiny fingers that catch nutrients for the blood

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which organ sends bile to the intestines? A: The liver
chunks.source: The liver

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which organ sends enzyme juice to the intestines? A: The pancreas
chunks.source: The pancreas

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name the four main steps of digestion. A: Mouth: chew and saliva; Stomach: churn to chyme; Small intestines: enzymes finish digestion; Villi absorb nutrients
chunks.source: Mouth: chew and saliva; Stomach: churn to chyme; Small intestines: enzymes finish digestion; Villi absorb nutrients

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Keeping the Digestive System Healthy. I can choose habits that keep my digestive system working well. A **balanced diet** plus **fibre**, **water**, good **chew**, and **hygiene** prevents **constipation** and keeps the digestive system healthy. Keywords: fibre: plant material that helps waste move; water: liquid needed for digestion and soft waste; chew: break food into small pieces with teeth; constipation: hard dry waste that is hard to pass; hygiene: clean habits that stop germs spreading; balanced diet: eating all food groups in right amounts
chunks.source: A **balanced diet** plus **fibre**, **water**, good **chew**, and **hygiene** prevents **constipation** and keeps the digestive system healthy.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name the three food groups in a balanced diet. A: Energy food, body-building food, protective food
chunks.source: Energy food, body-building food, protective food

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What does fibre do in the intestines? A: Adds bulk and keeps waste soft and moving
chunks.source: Adds bulk and keeps waste soft and moving

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How many cups of water should a child drink daily? A: Six to eight cups
chunks.source: Six to eight cups

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why should you chew food well? A: Starts digestion, helps enzymes work, makes swallowing easy

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is constipation? A: Hard dry stool that is painful and rare
chunks.source: Hard dry stool that is painful and rare

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: When should you wash hands with soap? A: After latrine, before cooking, before eating
chunks.source: After latrine, before cooking, before eating

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which foods give fibre? A: Greens, fruit, whole grains, beans
chunks.source: Greens, fruit, whole grains, beans

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What happens if you do not drink enough water? A: Waste becomes hard, constipation risk rises, digestion slows

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Mountains and Highlands of Uganda. I can explain how mountains and highlands in Uganda were formed by volcanicity and faulting. Uganda's mountains formed in two ways: Mount Elgon is a volcano with a wide crater; Mount Rwenzori rose by faulting and has sharp peaks with permanent snow. Keywords: mountain: a very high hill; highland: an area of high land; volcano: a mountain with an opening that can erupt; faulting: cracks in the earth that move up or down; peak: the top point of a mountain; crater: a round hole at the top of a volcano; snow: frozen white flakes that fall like rain
chunks.source: Uganda's mountains formed in two ways: Mount Elgon is a volcano with a wide crater; Mount Rwenzori rose by faulting and has sharp peaks with permanent snow.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Name the two main mountains in Uganda. A: Mount Rwenzori and Mount Elgon
chunks.source: Mount Rwenzori and Mount Elgon

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Which mountain was formed by volcanicity? A: Mount Elgon
chunks.source: Mount Elgon

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Which mountain was formed by faulting? A: Mount Rwenzori
chunks.source: Mount Rwenzori

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: What is the highest peak on Mount Rwenzori? A: Margherita Peak
chunks.source: Margherita Peak

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: What do you find at the top of a volcano? A: A crater
chunks.source: A crater

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Why does snow stay on high peaks? A: It is very cold at high altitude
chunks.source: It is very cold at high altitude

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: What is a highland? A: An area of high land
chunks.source: An area of high land

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Name one difference between a volcano and a block mountain. A: Volcano has a crater; block mountain has sharp peaks from faulting
chunks.source: Volcano has a crater; block mountain has sharp peaks from faulting

chunks.id: L-P5-Social-The Rift Valley, Lakes and Rivers
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: The Rift Valley, Lakes and Rivers
chunks.text: The Rift Valley, Lakes and Rivers. I can describe the Western Rift Valley, major lakes, rivers, and the central plateau of Uganda. The Western Rift Valley was formed by faulting. Lake Victoria sits on the plateau; the River Nile flows north down the plateau into the rift valley to Lake Albert. Keywords: rift valley: a long valley with steep sides formed by faulting; lake victoria: the largest lake in Uganda and Africa; lake albert: a lake in the Western Rift Valley; river nile: the longest river in the world, starts in Uganda; plateau: high flat land; valley: low land between hills or mountains; plain: flat low land
chunks.source: The Western Rift Valley was formed by faulting. Lake Victoria sits on the plateau; the River Nile flows north down the plateau into the rift valley to Lake Albert.

chunks.id: LQ-P5-Social-The Rift Valley, Lakes and Rivers
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: The Rift Valley, Lakes and Rivers
chunks.text: Q: What process formed the Western Rift Valley? A: Faulting
chunks.source: Faulting

chunks.subject: Social

chunks.text: Q: Which lake is the source of the River Nile? A: Lake Victoria
chunks.source: Lake Victoria

chunks.id: LQ-P5-Social-The Rift Valley, Lakes and Rivers
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: The Rift Valley, Lakes and Rivers
chunks.text: Q: Into which lake does the River Nile flow after leaving Lake Victoria? A: Lake Albert
chunks.source: Lake Albert

chunks.id: LQ-P5-Social-The Rift Valley, Lakes and Rivers
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: The Rift Valley, Lakes and Rivers

chunks.source: High flat land

chunks.id: LQ-P5-Social-The Rift Valley, Lakes and Rivers
chunks.subject: Social

chunks.id: LQ-P5-Social-The Rift Valley, Lakes and Rivers
chunks.subject: Social

chunks.text: Q: Name two lakes in the Western Rift Valley. A: Lake Albert, Lake Edward, Lake George (any two)

chunks.id: LQ-P5-Social-The Rift Valley, Lakes and Rivers
chunks.subject: Social

chunks.text: Q: Why does the River Nile flow north? A: The plateau slopes northward; water flows downhill

chunks.id: LQ-P5-Social-The Rift Valley, Lakes and Rivers
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: The Rift Valley, Lakes and Rivers
chunks.text: Q: What is the difference between a valley and a plain? A: A valley is low land between hills; a plain is flat low land
chunks.source: A valley is low land between hills; a plain is flat low land

chunks.id: L-P5-Social-How Features Shape Weather and Life
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: How Features Shape Weather and Life
chunks.text: How Features Shape Weather and Life. I can explain how physical features influence Uganda's climate and activities like farming, fishing, and tourism. Altitude shapes climate: high = cool and wet; low = hot and drier. This decides where people farm, fish, trade, or hike. Mountains catch rain; lakes enable fishing and transport; peaks attract tourists. Keywords: climate: the usual weather in a place over many years; rainfall: the amount of rain that falls; altitude: height above sea level; fishing: catching fish for food or sale; farming: growing crops and keeping animals; tourism: people visiting places for leisure; transport: moving people or goods from place to place
chunks.source: Altitude shapes climate: high = cool and wet; low = hot and drier. This decides where people farm, fish, trade, or hike. Mountains catch rain; lakes enable fishing and transport; peaks attract tourists.

chunks.id: LQ-P5-Social-How Features Shape Weather and Life
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: How Features Shape Weather and Life
chunks.text: Q: How does altitude affect temperature? A: Higher altitude means cooler temperature
chunks.source: Higher altitude means cooler temperature

chunks.id: LQ-P5-Social-How Features Shape Weather and Life
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: How Features Shape Weather and Life
chunks.text: Q: Why do mountains receive more rainfall? A: Moist winds rise, cool, and condense into rain
chunks.source: Moist winds rise, cool, and condense into rain

chunks.id: LQ-P5-Social-How Features Shape Weather and Life
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: How Features Shape Weather and Life

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: How Features Shape Weather and Life
chunks.text: Q: How does the River Nile support transport? A: Boats carry goods and people along the river

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: How Features Shape Weather and Life
chunks.text: Q: What is a rain shadow? A: The dry side of a mountain where less rain falls

chunks.id: LQ-P5-Social-How Features Shape Weather and Life

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Problems and Protecting Our Features. I can identify problems caused by physical features and explain how to protect lakes, rivers, and land. Physical features bring both gifts and dangers. Mountains give rain but cause landslides. Rivers give water and transport but flood. Lakes give fish but suffer pollution. We must protect them — plant trees, treat waste, save water — to keep Uganda healthy. Keywords: flood: water covering land that is usually dry; drought: a long time with no rain; landslide: soil and rock sliding down a slope; erosion: soil being washed or blown away; pollution: dirtying water, air, or land; protect: to keep safe from harm; disease: illness caused by germs
chunks.source: Physical features bring both gifts and dangers. Mountains give rain but cause landslides. Rivers give water and transport but flood. Lakes give fish but suffer pollution. We must protect them — plant trees, treat waste, save water — to keep Uganda healthy.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: What causes a landslide on a mountain slope? A: Heavy rain on steep slopes with no trees
chunks.source: Heavy rain on steep slopes with no trees

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Why does the Nile plain flood? A: Heavy rain upstream fills the river; flat plain cannot drain fast
chunks.source: Heavy rain upstream fills the river; flat plain cannot drain fast

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: What is erosion? A: Soil being washed or blown away
chunks.source: Soil being washed or blown away

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Name two sources of pollution in Lake Victoria. A: Factory waste, sewage, farm chemicals, plastic rubbish (any two)
chunks.source: Factory waste, sewage, farm chemicals, plastic rubbish (any two)

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: How does pollution lead to disease? A: Dirty water carries germs that cause cholera, typhoid
chunks.source: Dirty water carries germs that cause cholera, typhoid

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: What can farmers do to stop erosion? A: Plant trees, use terraces, keep grass cover, contour ploughing
chunks.source: Plant trees, use terraces, keep grass cover, contour ploughing

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: How can communities prepare for drought? A: Store water, plant drought-resistant crops, save food
chunks.source: Store water, plant drought-resistant crops, save food

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Why should we protect lakes and rivers? A: For fishing, clean water, tourism, and to stop disease
chunks.source: For fishing, clean water, tourism, and to stop disease

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: What Climate Means. I can explain the difference between climate and weather and describe Uganda's tropical climate. Weather changes daily. Climate is the long-term pattern. Uganda has a tropical climate because it lies on the equator, giving us steady temperatures and two rainy seasons each year. Keywords: climate: the usual weather in a place over many years; weather: the condition of the air at one time; temperature: how hot or cold the air is; season: a time of year with certain weather; equator: the imaginary line around the middle of the Earth; tropical: hot and often wet, near the equator; sunshine: light and heat from the sun
chunks.source: Weather changes daily. Climate is the long-term pattern. Uganda has a tropical climate because it lies on the equator, giving us steady temperatures and two rainy seasons each year.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: What is the difference between weather and climate? A: Weather is the condition of the air at one time. Climate is the usual weather pattern over many years.
chunks.source: Weather is the condition of the air at one time. Climate is the usual weather pattern over many years.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Why does Uganda have a tropical climate? A: Uganda lies on the equator, so it gets strong sunshine all year and stays warm.
chunks.source: Uganda lies on the equator, so it gets strong sunshine all year and stays warm.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Name the two rainy seasons in Uganda. A: March to May and September to November.
chunks.source: March to May and September to November.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: What does temperature measure? A: How hot or cold the air is.
chunks.source: How hot or cold the air is.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: If today is sunny and hot, is that weather or climate? A: That is weather.
chunks.source: That is weather.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: What word describes Uganda's climate because it is near the equator? A: Tropical.
chunks.source: Tropical.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: How many dry seasons does Uganda have each year? A: Two dry seasons.
chunks.source: Two dry seasons.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: What imaginary line crosses Uganda and affects its climate? A: The equator.
chunks.source: The equator.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Things That Influence Our Climate. I can explain how latitude, altitude, relief, vegetation, wind, and lakes affect Uganda's climate. Six factors shape Uganda's climate: latitude (near equator = warm), altitude (higher = cooler), relief (mountains force rain), vegetation (forests add moisture), wind (brings moist air), and lakes (supply water vapour). Keywords: latitude: distance from the equator measured in degrees; altitude: height of land above sea level; relief: the shape and height of the land; vegetation: plants and trees covering the land; wind: moving air; lakes: large bodies of fresh water
chunks.source: Six factors shape Uganda's climate: latitude (near equator = warm), altitude (higher = cooler), relief (mountains force rain), vegetation (forests add moisture), wind (brings moist air), and lakes (supply water vapour).

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: What is latitude? A: Distance from the equator measured in degrees.
chunks.source: Distance from the equator measured in degrees.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: How does altitude affect temperature? A: Higher altitude means cooler temperature.
chunks.source: Higher altitude means cooler temperature.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: What is relief? A: The shape and height of the land, like mountains and valleys.
chunks.source: The shape and height of the land, like mountains and valleys.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: How does vegetation influence climate? A: Plants release water vapour, making the air moist and bringing more rain.
chunks.source: Plants release water vapour, making the air moist and bringing more rain.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Where does the wind that brings rain to Uganda come from? A: From the Indian Ocean and the Congo Basin.
chunks.source: From the Indian Ocean and the Congo Basin.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Name two large lakes in Uganda that affect climate. A: Lake Victoria and Lake Kyoga (or Lake Albert).
chunks.source: Lake Victoria and Lake Kyoga (or Lake Albert).

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Why are the Rwenzori Mountains wet? A: Wind rises over the relief, cools, and drops rain on the slopes.
chunks.source: Wind rises over the relief, cools, and drops rain on the slopes.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: If you cut down a forest, what might happen to the local climate? A: It may become drier because less water vapour is released.
chunks.source: It may become drier because less water vapour is released.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Rainfall in Uganda. I can describe the three types of rainfall in Uganda and explain the seasonal rainfall pattern. Uganda receives three types of rainfall: convectional (from sun heating ground, falls in afternoon), relief (wind forced up by mountains), and frontal (air masses meeting). The rainfall pattern is bimodal — two rainy seasons each year. Keywords: rainfall: rain that falls on the ground; convectional: rain caused by the sun heating the ground; relief: rain caused by wind rising over mountains; frontal: rain caused when two air masses meet; season: a period of the year with a weather pattern; clouds: masses of water droplets in the sky; pattern: the regular way something happens
chunks.source: Uganda receives three types of rainfall: convectional (from sun heating ground, falls in afternoon), relief (wind forced up by mountains), and frontal (air masses meeting). The rainfall pattern is bimodal — two rainy seasons each year.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: What causes convectional rainfall? A: The sun heats the ground, warm air rises, cools, and forms rain.
chunks.source: The sun heats the ground, warm air rises, cools, and forms rain.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: What is relief rainfall? A: Rain that falls when wind is forced to rise over mountains or hills.
chunks.source: Rain that falls when wind is forced to rise over mountains or hills.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: What is frontal rainfall? A: Rain formed when warm and cool air masses meet and the warm air rises over the cool air.
chunks.source: Rain formed when warm and cool air masses meet and the warm air rises over the cool air.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: When does convectional rain usually fall in Uganda? A: In the afternoon after a hot morning.
chunks.source: In the afternoon after a hot morning.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: What does bimodal rainfall pattern mean? A: Two rainy seasons each year.
chunks.source: Two rainy seasons each year.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Name Uganda's two rainy seasons. A: March to May (long rains) and September to November (short rains).
chunks.source: March to May (long rains) and September to November (short rains).

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Which side of a mountain gets more relief rainfall? A: The windward side (the side the wind hits first).
chunks.source: The windward side (the side the wind hits first).

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: What type of clouds bring convectional rain? A: Tall, dark cumulonimbus clouds.
chunks.source: Tall, dark cumulonimbus clouds.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Climate, Farming and Daily Life. I can explain how climate affects farming in different regions and how people cope with drought. Climate controls farming calendars across Uganda's regions. Central and southern areas have two planting seasons; the north has one. Drought threatens food security, but people cope by storing food, growing tolerant crops, harvesting water, and planting trees. Keywords: farming: growing crops and keeping animals; crops: plants grown for food or sale; harvesting: gathering ripe crops from the field; planting: putting seeds in the ground to grow; drought: a long time with little or no rain; food: what people eat to stay alive; regions: large areas with similar features
chunks.source: Climate controls farming calendars across Uganda's regions. Central and southern areas have two planting seasons; the north has one. Drought threatens food security, but people cope by storing food, growing tolerant crops, harvesting water, and planting trees.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: How does climate determine when farmers plant? A: Farmers plant at the start of the rainy season so crops get water.
chunks.source: Farmers plant at the start of the rainy season so crops get water.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Why does central Uganda have two planting seasons? A: It has a bimodal rainfall pattern with two rainy seasons.
chunks.source: It has a bimodal rainfall pattern with two rainy seasons.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: What crops grow well in the cool western highlands? A: Irish potatoes, cabbages, and tea.
chunks.source: Irish potatoes, cabbages, and tea.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: What is a drought? A: A long period with little or no rain that causes crops to fail.
chunks.source: A long period with little or no rain that causes crops to fail.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Name two drought-tolerant crops grown in Uganda. A: Cassava and sorghum (or millet, groundnuts).
chunks.source: Cassava and sorghum (or millet, groundnuts).

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: How do valley tanks help during drought? A: They store rainwater for crops and animals during dry spells.
chunks.source: They store rainwater for crops and animals during dry spells.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: What happens to food prices during drought? A: Prices rise because food becomes scarce.
chunks.source: Prices rise because food becomes scarce.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Why do northern regions have only one planting season? A: They have a unimodal rainfall pattern with one long rainy season.
chunks.source: They have a unimodal rainfall pattern with one long rainy season.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: The First Peoples of Uganda. I can name the main ethnic groups of pre-colonial Uganda and explain where they came from and where they settled. The Bantu migrated from West Africa and settled in the south near Lake Victoria. The Nilotics came from the Nile valley and settled in the north and east. Their migration and settlement created Uganda's many ethnic groups in pre-colonial times. Keywords: bantu: a large group of people who speak related languages; nilotics: people who came from the Nile area and speak Nilotic languages; ethnic: belonging to a group with shared culture and language; pre-colonial: the time before foreign rulers came; origin: the place where something begins; migration: moving from one place to live in another; settlement: a place where people make their homes
chunks.source: The Bantu migrated from West Africa and settled in the south near Lake Victoria. The Nilotics came from the Nile valley and settled in the north and east. Their migration and settlement created Uganda's many ethnic groups in pre-colonial times.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Name the two main groups who migrated to Uganda in pre-colonial times. A: The Bantu and the Nilotics.
chunks.source: The Bantu and the Nilotics.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: What does 'pre-colonial' mean? A: The time before foreign rulers came.
chunks.source: The time before foreign rulers came.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Where was the origin of the Bantu people? A: West Africa.
chunks.source: West Africa.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Why did the Nilotics settle in the north and east? A: They needed pasture and water for their cattle.
chunks.source: They needed pasture and water for their cattle.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Give the meaning of 'migration'. A: Moving from one place to live in another.
chunks.source: Moving from one place to live in another.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: What is an ethnic group? A: A group with shared culture and language.
chunks.source: A group with shared culture and language.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: What did the Bantu look for in a settlement? A: Fertile soil and water for farming.
chunks.source: Fertile soil and water for farming.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Name one result of the migration and settlement. A: Uganda has many ethnic groups today.
chunks.source: Uganda has many ethnic groups today.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Kingdoms and Chiefdoms. I can explain the difference between a kingdom and a chiefdom and name examples from pre-colonial Uganda. Pre-colonial Uganda had kingdoms (like Buganda and Bunyoro) ruled by kings, and chiefdoms ruled by chiefs. Both systems used clans and totems to organise society. Customs guided the rulers and the people. Keywords: kingdom: a large area ruled by a king; chiefdom: a smaller area ruled by a chief; king: the male ruler of a kingdom; chief: the male ruler of a chiefdom; clan: a group of families with a common ancestor; totem: an animal or plant symbol for a clan; customs: the traditional ways of a group
chunks.source: Pre-colonial Uganda had kingdoms (like Buganda and Bunyoro) ruled by kings, and chiefdoms ruled by chiefs. Both systems used clans and totems to organise society. Customs guided the rulers and the people.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: What is the main difference between a kingdom and a chiefdom? A: A kingdom is larger and ruled by a king; a chiefdom is smaller and ruled by a chief.
chunks.source: A kingdom is larger and ruled by a king; a chiefdom is smaller and ruled by a chief.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Name two kingdoms in pre-colonial Uganda. A: Buganda and Bunyoro.
chunks.source: Buganda and Bunyoro.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Who rules a kingdom? A: A king.
chunks.source: A king.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Who rules a chiefdom? A: A chief.
chunks.source: A chief.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: What is a clan? A: A group of families with a common ancestor.
chunks.source: A group of families with a common ancestor.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: What is a totem? A: An animal or plant symbol for a clan.
chunks.source: An animal or plant symbol for a clan.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Give an example of a custom in a kingdom. A: The king must consult clan elders before big decisions.
chunks.source: The king must consult clan elders before big decisions.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: How did clans connect kingdoms and chiefdoms? A: Clans existed in both; members of the same clan lived in different areas.
chunks.source: Clans existed in both; members of the same clan lived in different areas.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Clans, Customs and Daily Life. I can describe clan life, totems, customs and daily work like farming, herding and crafts in pre-colonial Uganda. In pre-colonial Uganda, clans were the centre of life. Each clan had a totem. Customs guided daily behaviour. The Bantu farmed; the Nilotics herded. Both made crafts. Language carried culture across generations. Keywords: clan: a group of families with a common ancestor; totem: an animal or plant symbol for a clan; customs: the traditional ways of a group; language: the words and speech of a people; farming: growing crops for food; herding: keeping and moving animals for food; crafts: making things by hand like pots or baskets
chunks.source: In pre-colonial Uganda, clans were the centre of life. Each clan had a totem. Customs guided daily behaviour. The Bantu farmed; the Nilotics herded. Both made crafts. Language carried culture across generations.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: What is a clan? A: A group of families with a common ancestor.
chunks.source: A group of families with a common ancestor.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: What is a totem? A: An animal or plant symbol for a clan.
chunks.source: An animal or plant symbol for a clan.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Give one example of a custom in pre-colonial Uganda. A: Elders eat first at meals.
chunks.source: Elders eat first at meals.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: What was the main work of Bantu clans? A: Farming.
chunks.source: Farming.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: What was the main work of Nilotic clans? A: Herding.
chunks.source: Herding.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Name two crafts made by hand. A: Pots and baskets.
chunks.source: Pots and baskets.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: How did language help the clan? A: It bound people together and carried stories.
chunks.source: It bound people together and carried stories.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Why were totems not eaten? A: They were sacred symbols of the clan.
chunks.source: They were sacred symbols of the clan.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Why People Moved and Settled. I can explain the reasons why people migrated and settled in new areas: water, pasture, fertile land, trade and security. People migrated for pasture, water, fertile land, security, and trade. Herders moved for grass and water. Farmers sought good soil. Traders settled at crossroads. Security made hilltops popular. Each settlement began with a reason. Keywords: migration: moving from one place to live in another; pasture: grassland for animals to eat; water: rivers, lakes, rain for drinking and crops; fertile: soil that grows crops well; security: safety from enemies or danger; trade: buying and selling goods; land: the ground people live and work on
chunks.source: People migrated for pasture, water, fertile land, security, and trade. Herders moved for grass and water. Farmers sought good soil. Traders settled at crossroads. Security made hilltops popular. Each settlement began with a reason.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: List three reasons why herders migrated. A: Pasture, water, and security.
chunks.source: Pasture, water, and security.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: List two reasons why farmers migrated. A: Fertile land and water for crops.
chunks.source: Fertile land and water for crops.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: How did trade cause migration? A: Traders settled where trade routes crossed.
chunks.source: Traders settled where trade routes crossed.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Why did people choose hilltops for settlement? A: For security — they could see enemies coming.
chunks.source: For security — they could see enemies coming.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: What does 'fertile' mean? A: Soil that grows crops well.
chunks.source: Soil that grows crops well.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Give an example of a trade good in pre-colonial Uganda. A: Salt from Katwe or iron from Muko.
chunks.source: Salt from Katwe or iron from Muko.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: What is the difference between migration and settlement? A: Migration is the move; settlement is making a new home.
chunks.source: Migration is the move; settlement is making a new home.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Name one thing families carried on a migration journey. A: Seeds, tools, cattle, or water containers.
chunks.source: Seeds, tools, cattle, or water containers.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Traders, Explorers and Missionaries Arrive. I can explain who came to Uganda from the coast and Europe and why they came. Arab and Indian traders came first from the coast. European explorers followed. Then Christian missionaries arrived. All used the same inland route. Keywords: traders: people who buy and sell goods; explorers: people who travel to find new places; missionaries: people who teach their religion; foreigners: people from another country; arab: a person from the Arab world; route: a path for travel; coast: land beside the sea
chunks.source: Arab and Indian traders came first from the coast. European explorers followed. Then Christian missionaries arrived. All used the same inland route.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Who were the first foreigners to reach Uganda from the coast? A: Arab and Indian traders.
chunks.source: Arab and Indian traders.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: What did the traders carry on the caravan route? A: Cloth, beads, guns, and salt.
chunks.source: Cloth, beads, guns, and salt.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Name two European explorers who came to Uganda. A: Speke and Stanley.
chunks.source: Speke and Stanley.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: What did the explorers want to find? A: The source of the Nile and map the lakes.
chunks.source: The source of the Nile and map the lakes.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Which two missionary groups came to Uganda? A: Church Missionary Society (CMS) and White Fathers (Catholics).
chunks.source: Church Missionary Society (CMS) and White Fathers (Catholics).

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: What did missionaries build at Kasubi and Rubaga? A: Schools and a church.
chunks.source: Schools and a church.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Why did traders walk inland from the coast? A: To get ivory and slaves.
chunks.source: To get ivory and slaves.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: What is a caravan route? A: A path used by traders to travel inland.
chunks.source: A path used by traders to travel inland.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Agreements and the Protectorate. I can describe how agreements made Uganda a British Protectorate. Agreements in 1890, 1894 and 1900 made Uganda a British Protectorate. Local kings stayed but a British Governor held real power. Keywords: agreement: a written promise between groups; treaty: a formal agreement between leaders; protectorate: a country controlled by another but keeps local rulers; governor: the top British official in a colony; colonialism: when one country rules another; rule: government control; nation: a people with shared land and history
chunks.source: Agreements in 1890, 1894 and 1900 made Uganda a British Protectorate. Local kings stayed but a British Governor held real power.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: What year was Uganda declared a British Protectorate? A: 1894.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: What was the 1900 Buganda Agreement also called? A: A treaty.
chunks.source: A treaty.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Who was the first British Governor of Uganda? A: Sir Harry Johnston.
chunks.source: Sir Harry Johnston.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Where did the Governor live? A: Entebbe.
chunks.source: Entebbe.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: What is a protectorate? A: A country controlled by another but keeps local rulers.
chunks.source: A country controlled by another but keeps local rulers.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: What did Buganda chiefs gain from the 1900 Agreement? A: Mailo land (freehold land).
chunks.source: Mailo land (freehold land).

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: What is colonialism? A: When one country rules another.
chunks.source: When one country rules another.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: How did the agreements help form a nation? A: They brought different kingdoms under one administration.
chunks.source: They brought different kingdoms under one administration.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Life Under Colonial Rule. I can explain how colonial rule changed daily life in Uganda. Colonial administration built roads, schools and hospitals. Taxation forced men into cash work. Cash crops like cotton and coffee changed farming. Keywords: administration: the system of government offices; taxation: money people pay to the government; crops: plants grown for food or sale; schools: places where children learn; hospitals: places where sick people get care; roads: paths for vehicles; changes: things that become different
chunks.source: Colonial administration built roads, schools and hospitals. Taxation forced men into cash work. Cash crops like cotton and coffee changed farming.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: What was the main reason the administration built roads? A: To transport cash crops to the coast.
chunks.source: To transport cash crops to the coast.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Name two cash crops introduced by the colonial administration. A: Cotton and coffee.
chunks.source: Cotton and coffee.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: What two taxes did men have to pay? A: Hut tax and poll tax.
chunks.source: Hut tax and poll tax.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: How did men earn money to pay taxes? A: They grew cash crops or worked for wages.
chunks.source: They grew cash crops or worked for wages.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Who built the first schools in Uganda? A: Missionaries.
chunks.source: Missionaries.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: What medical help did hospitals give? A: Quinine for malaria and vaccines for smallpox.
chunks.source: Quinine for malaria and vaccines for smallpox.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: What is administration? A: The system of government offices.
chunks.source: The system of government offices.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Give one change that affected women during colonial rule. A: Women did more farm work while men were away earning wages.
chunks.source: Women did more farm work while men were away earning wages.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Ugandans Respond to Foreign Rule. I can describe how Ugandans resisted and cooperated with colonial rule and how culture was affected. Some Ugandans resisted (Kabalega), others cooperated (Buganda chiefs). Traditional culture weakened. New educated leaders used protest to demand rights. Keywords: resistance: fighting against control; cooperation: working together with rulers; culture: the way of life of a people; traditional: belonging to the old customs; weakened: made less strong; protest: showing you disagree; leaders: people who guide others
chunks.source: Some Ugandans resisted (Kabalega), others cooperated (Buganda chiefs). Traditional culture weakened. New educated leaders used protest to demand rights.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Who led the famous resistance in Bunyoro? A: Omukama Kabalega.
chunks.source: Omukama Kabalega.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: What year was Kabalega captured? A: 1899.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Why did Buganda chiefs cooperate with the British? A: They gained mailo land and administration jobs.
chunks.source: They gained mailo land and administration jobs.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Name one political party formed in the 1940s. A: Bataka Party or Uganda African Farmers Union.
chunks.source: Bataka Party or Uganda African Farmers Union.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: What did the 1940s protesters demand? A: Fair cotton prices and African representation.
chunks.source: Fair cotton prices and African representation.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: How was traditional culture weakened? A: Western education, Christianity and English language replaced traditional ways.
chunks.source: Western education, Christianity and English language replaced traditional ways.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: What is a protest? A: Showing you disagree, often publicly.
chunks.source: Showing you disagree, often publicly.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Give an example of a traditional leader whose power was weakened. A: Kabalega of Bunyoro or the Kabaka of Buganda under the Governor.
chunks.source: Kabalega of Bunyoro or the Kabaka of Buganda under the Governor.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: The Three Arms of Government. I can name the three arms of government and explain what each one does. Uganda's government has three arms: the Executive led by the President implements laws, the Legislature (Parliament) makes laws, and the Judiciary (Courts) interprets laws. Keywords: government: the system that runs the country; executive: the arm that puts laws into action; legislature: the arm that makes laws; judiciary: the arm that explains laws; president: the head of the executive arm; parliament: where the legislature meets; courts: places where judges work
chunks.source: Uganda's government has three arms: the Executive led by the President implements laws, the Legislature (Parliament) makes laws, and the Judiciary (Courts) interprets laws.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: What are the three arms of government in Uganda? A: The three arms are the Executive, the Legislature, and the Judiciary.
chunks.source: The three arms are the Executive, the Legislature, and the Judiciary.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Which arm makes laws? A: The Legislature (Parliament) makes laws.
chunks.source: The Legislature (Parliament) makes laws.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Which arm implements laws? A: The Executive implements laws.
chunks.source: The Executive implements laws.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Which arm interprets laws? A: The Judiciary (Courts) interprets laws.
chunks.source: The Judiciary (Courts) interprets laws.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Who heads the Executive arm? A: The President heads the Executive arm.
chunks.source: The President heads the Executive arm.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Where does the Legislature meet? A: The Legislature meets in Parliament.
chunks.source: The Legislature meets in Parliament.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: What is the role of the Courts? A: Courts interpret laws and decide if they are fair.
chunks.source: Courts interpret laws and decide if they are fair.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Our Constitution. I can explain what the Constitution is and why it is important for Uganda. The Constitution of Uganda is the supreme law of the nation. It protects citizens' rights, lists their duties, sets rules for government, and guides how laws are made. Keywords: constitution: the supreme law of the country; laws: rules made by the legislature; rights: things every person deserves; duties: things every person must do; citizens: people who belong to a country; rules: guidelines for how things work; nation: a country with its own government
chunks.source: The Constitution of Uganda is the supreme law of the nation. It protects citizens' rights, lists their duties, sets rules for government, and guides how laws are made.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: What is the Constitution of Uganda? A: The Constitution is the supreme law of the nation.
chunks.source: The Constitution is the supreme law of the nation.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Name two rights protected by the Constitution. A: Right to education and right to health.
chunks.source: Right to education and right to health.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Name two duties of a citizen. A: Paying taxes and voting.
chunks.source: Paying taxes and voting.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Who must follow the Constitution? A: Everyone in Uganda must follow the Constitution.
chunks.source: Everyone in Uganda must follow the Constitution.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: What does the Constitution say about how laws are made? A: It sets rules for how laws are made and changed.
chunks.source: It sets rules for how laws are made and changed.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Why is the Constitution important? A: It protects rights, lists duties, and guides government.
chunks.source: It protects rights, lists duties, and guides government.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: What is a nation? A: A country with its own government.
chunks.source: A country with its own government.

chunks.id: L-P5-Social-How Government Gets and Spends Money
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: How Government Gets and Spends Money
chunks.text: How Government Gets and Spends Money. I can list sources of government revenue and explain how the money is spent. Government gets revenue from taxation, licences, tourism, and grants. It spends this money on salaries, security, development, and social services. Keywords: revenue: money the government collects; taxation: money paid to government as tax; licence: a permit that costs money; tourism: money from visitors; grants: money given by other countries; expenditure: money the government spends; salaries: pay for workers
chunks.source: Government gets revenue from taxation, licences, tourism, and grants. It spends this money on salaries, security, development, and social services.

chunks.id: LQ-P5-Social-How Government Gets and Spends Money
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: How Government Gets and Spends Money
chunks.text: Q: What is government revenue? A: Money the government collects from taxes, licences, tourism, and grants.
chunks.source: Money the government collects from taxes, licences, tourism, and grants.

chunks.id: LQ-P5-Social-How Government Gets and Spends Money
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: How Government Gets and Spends Money
chunks.text: Q: Name three sources of revenue. A: Taxation, licence fees, tourism, and grants.
chunks.source: Taxation, licence fees, tourism, and grants.

chunks.id: LQ-P5-Social-How Government Gets and Spends Money
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: How Government Gets and Spends Money
chunks.text: Q: What is taxation? A: Money paid by citizens and businesses to the government.
chunks.source: Money paid by citizens and businesses to the government.

chunks.id: LQ-P5-Social-How Government Gets and Spends Money
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: How Government Gets and Spends Money
chunks.text: Q: What is a licence? A: A permit that costs money, like a driving licence.
chunks.source: A permit that costs money, like a driving licence.

chunks.id: LQ-P5-Social-How Government Gets and Spends Money
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: How Government Gets and Spends Money
chunks.text: Q: What does the government spend money on? A: Salaries, security, roads, health, and education.
chunks.source: Salaries, security, roads, health, and education.

chunks.id: LQ-P5-Social-How Government Gets and Spends Money
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: How Government Gets and Spends Money
chunks.text: Q: What are salaries? A: Pay for workers like teachers and doctors.
chunks.source: Pay for workers like teachers and doctors.

chunks.id: LQ-P5-Social-How Government Gets and Spends Money
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: How Government Gets and Spends Money
chunks.text: Q: Why does the government need revenue? A: To pay for services and development.
chunks.source: To pay for services and development.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Leaders, Elections and Citizens. I can describe how leaders are chosen and what duties citizens have. Citizens choose leaders through elections and voting. They have the duty to vote and the responsibility to obey laws. Ministers are leaders appointed to serve the nation. Keywords: minister: a leader in charge of a ministry; election: a process to choose leaders; voting: casting a ballot to choose; citizen: a person who belongs to a country; responsibility: something you should do; duty: something you must do; leader: a person who guides others
chunks.source: Citizens choose leaders through elections and voting. They have the duty to vote and the responsibility to obey laws. Ministers are leaders appointed to serve the nation.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: How are leaders chosen in Uganda? A: Through elections where citizens vote.
chunks.source: Through elections where citizens vote.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: What is voting? A: Casting a ballot to choose a leader.
chunks.source: Casting a ballot to choose a leader.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Name one duty of a citizen. A: Paying taxes or obeying laws or voting.
chunks.source: Paying taxes or obeying laws or voting.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Name one responsibility of a citizen. A: Keeping the community clean or helping others.
chunks.source: Keeping the community clean or helping others.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Who is a minister? A: A leader in charge of a ministry.
chunks.source: A leader in charge of a ministry.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: What is an election? A: A process to choose leaders.
chunks.source: A process to choose leaders.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Why should citizens vote? A: It is their duty and right to choose leaders.
chunks.source: It is their duty and right to choose leaders.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Road Users and Signs. I can name road users and signs, and use present, continuous, future and present perfect tenses to talk about them. Road users include **pedestrians**, **cyclists**, and **motorists**. **Traffic** follows **signals** and **signposts**. The **zebra crossing** protects **pedestrians**. **Taxis** and **buses** carry passengers. **Cyclists** must wear **helmets**. Use present for habits, continuous for now, future for plans, present perfect for recent actions. Keywords: pedestrian: a person walking on the road; cyclist: a person riding a bicycle; motorist: a person driving a car or motorcycle; traffic: vehicles moving on the road; signal: a light that tells road users what to do; signpost: a sign giving information or warning; zebra crossing: a marked place for pedestrians to cross; taxi: a minibus that carries passengers; bus: a large vehicle that carries many people; helmet: a hard hat that protects the head
chunks.source: Road users include **pedestrians**, **cyclists**, and **motorists**. **Traffic** follows **signals** and **signposts**. The **zebra crossing** protects **pedestrians**. **Taxis** and **buses** carry passengers. **Cyclists** must wear **helmets**. Use present for habits, continuous for now, future for plans, present perfect for recent actions.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Write a sentence in the present tense about a **pedestrian**. A: The **pedestrian** walks on the pavement.
chunks.source: The **pedestrian** walks on the pavement.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Write a sentence in the present continuous tense about a **cyclist**. A: The **cyclist** is wearing a **helmet**.
chunks.source: The **cyclist** is wearing a **helmet**.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Write a sentence in the future tense about a **motorist**. A: The **motorist** will stop at the red **signal**.
chunks.source: The **motorist** will stop at the red **signal**.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Write a sentence in the present perfect tense about **traffic**. A: The **traffic** has stopped at the **zebra crossing**.
chunks.source: The **traffic** has stopped at the **zebra crossing**.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Change to present perfect: The **bus** arrives at the stage. A: The **bus** has arrived at the stage.
chunks.source: The **bus** has arrived at the stage.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Change to future: The **taxi** stops for passengers. A: The **taxi** will stop for passengers.
chunks.source: The **taxi** will stop for passengers.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Change to present continuous: The **cyclist** wears a **helmet**. A: The **cyclist** is wearing a **helmet**.
chunks.source: The **cyclist** is wearing a **helmet**.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Why do we use present perfect for 'The **signpost** has fallen down'? A: Because it happened recently and affects now.
chunks.source: Because it happened recently and affects now.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Write two sentences: one present, one present perfect, about a **zebra crossing**. A: The **zebra crossing** helps **pedestrians**. The **zebra crossing** has saved many lives.
