A good goat house has a **raised floor**, leak-proof roof, and ventilation. Goats need a **paddock** for **browse** and exercise, or safe **tethering** with rotation. Daily feed: **fodder**, **browse**, **concentrate** for high-need goats, **mineral lick**, and clean **water** always. Keywords: raised floor: a floor built above ground to keep goats dry and clean; paddock: a fenced area where goats graze and exercise; fodder: cut grass or crops carried to goats to eat; browse: leaves, twigs, and shrubs that goats eat from trees and bushes; concentrate: a feed mix rich in energy and protein like maize bran and cottonseed cake; mineral lick: a block or loose salt with minerals that goats lick for health; water: clean drinking water needed every day for digestion and milk; tethering: tying a goat with a rope to a stake so it grazes in one spot
chunks.source: A good goat house has a **raised floor**, leak-proof roof, and ventilation. Goats need a **paddock** for **browse** and exercise, or safe **tethering** with rotation. Daily feed: **fodder**, **browse**, **concentrate** for high-need goats, **mineral lick**, and clean **water** always.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why is a **raised floor** better than a cement floor for goats? A: It lets droppings fall through, keeps goats dry, and prevents foot rot.
chunks.source: It lets droppings fall through, keeps goats dry, and prevents foot rot.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is a **paddock**? A: A fenced area where goats graze, **browse**, and exercise.
chunks.source: A fenced area where goats graze, **browse**, and exercise.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name two examples of **fodder** crops. A: Napier grass, maize stover, banana leaves, sweet potato vines.
chunks.source: Napier grass, maize stover, banana leaves, sweet potato vines.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How does **browse** differ from grass? A: **Browse** is leaves and twigs from trees and shrubs; goats prefer it and it is higher in protein.
chunks.source: **Browse** is leaves and twigs from trees and shrubs; goats prefer it and it is higher in protein.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is **concentrate** and when is it given? A: A high-energy, high-protein feed mix given to pregnant **does**, milking **does**, and breeding **bucks**.
chunks.source: A high-energy, high-protein feed mix given to pregnant **does**, milking **does**, and breeding **bucks**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why do goats need a **mineral lick**? A: For salt, calcium, phosphorus, and trace minerals for bones, milk, and health.
chunks.source: For salt, calcium, phosphorus, and trace minerals for bones, milk, and health.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How much **water** does a milking **doe** need daily? A: Up to 10 litres.
chunks.source: Up to 10 litres.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: When is **tethering** used, and what are two risks? A: Used when no **paddock** exists. Risks: limited feed choice, rope injuries, worm build-up on one spot.
chunks.source: Used when no **paddock** exists. Risks: limited feed choice, rope injuries, worm build-up on one spot.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Application: Design a one-day feed plan for a milking **doe** in the dry season. List feeds and amounts. A: Morning: 2 kg **fodder** (napier), 300 g **concentrate**, free **water** and **mineral lick**. Midday: **browse** (calliandra branches). Evening: 2 kg **fodder**, 300 g **concentrate**, free **water**.
chunks.source: Morning: 2 kg **fodder** (napier), 300 g **concentrate**, free **water** and **mineral lick**. Midday: **browse** (calliandra branches). Evening: 2 kg **fodder**, 300 g **concentrate**, free **water**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Goat Diseases and Parasites. I can identify common goat diseases and parasites and explain prevention and control methods. Main goat health threats: **worms** (internal), **ticks** (external), **coccidiosis** (kids), **pneumonia** (housing). Control: **deworming** quarterly, **spraying** fortnightly/monthly, **vaccination** yearly, **quarantine** for new stock. Clean **raised floor** and dry bedding prevent many diseases. Keywords: worms: internal parasites like roundworms that live in the stomach and intestines; ticks: external parasites that suck blood and spread diseases; coccidiosis: a disease caused by tiny parasites in the gut, common in kids; pneumonia: a lung infection from cold, dust, or germs, causing cough and fast breathing; deworming: giving medicine to kill internal **worms**; spraying: applying acaricide on the goat's skin to kill **ticks**; vaccination: giving a vaccine to prevent specific diseases like CCPP and PPR; quarantine: keeping new or sick goats separate from the herd for at least two weeks
chunks.source: Main goat health threats: **worms** (internal), **ticks** (external), **coccidiosis** (kids), **pneumonia** (housing). Control: **deworming** quarterly, **spraying** fortnightly/monthly, **vaccination** yearly, **quarantine** for new stock. Clean **raised floor** and dry bedding prevent many diseases.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name two signs of heavy **worms** in goats. A: Bottle jaw, pale gums, weight loss, diarrhoea.
chunks.source: Bottle jaw, pale gums, weight loss, diarrhoea.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is **coccidiosis** and which goats are most affected? A: A gut parasite causing bloody diarrhoea, mainly in kids 2–8 weeks old.
chunks.source: A gut parasite causing bloody diarrhoea, mainly in kids 2–8 weeks old.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How often should **deworming** be done in a typical Ugandan farm? A: Every 3 months (quarterly).
chunks.source: Every 3 months (quarterly).

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Describe the correct **spraying** method for **ticks**. A: Spray whole body with acaricide, focus on ears, udder, tail base, under legs. Repeat every 2 weeks in wet season.
chunks.source: Spray whole body with acaricide, focus on ears, udder, tail base, under legs. Repeat every 2 weeks in wet season.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which two diseases are prevented by routine **vaccination** in Uganda? A: CCPP (Contagious Caprine Pleuropneumonia) and PPR (Peste des Petits Ruminants).
chunks.source: CCPP (Contagious Caprine Pleuropneumonia) and PPR (Peste des Petits Ruminants).

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is **quarantine** and how long should it last? A: Keeping new or sick goats separate from the herd for at least 14 days.
chunks.source: Keeping new or sick goats separate from the herd for at least 14 days.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: A farmer stops **deworming** because goats look healthy. Why is this a mistake? A: **Worms** build up silently; by the time signs show, damage is done. Regular **deworming** breaks the cycle.
chunks.source: **Worms** build up silently; by the time signs show, damage is done. Regular **deworming** breaks the cycle.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Reasoning: A kid has **pneumonia**. The farmer treats with antibiotics but does not fix the damp **raised floor**. What will likely happen? A: The kid may recover but will get sick again because the cause (damp, ammonia) remains. Housing must be improved.
chunks.source: The kid may recover but will get sick again because the cause (damp, ammonia) remains. Housing must be improved.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Goat Products and Records. I can list goat products, explain the importance of records, and calculate simple profit. Goats give **meat**, **milk**, **skin**, and **manure**. **Records** of **weight**, health, breeding, feed, and money are essential. **Profit** = total sales - total costs. Monthly **weight** checks and good **records** help choose the best goats and sell at the right **market** time. Keywords: meat: goat flesh sold for food, called chevon; milk: the white liquid from a doe, used for drinking and making ghee; skin: the hide of a goat, used for leather after tanning; manure: goat droppings mixed with bedding, used as fertiliser; records: written notes on breeding, feeding, health, weights, and money; profit: money left after subtracting costs from sales; market: the place where goats and products are bought and sold; weight: how heavy a goat is, measured in kilograms to track growth and price
chunks.source: Goats give **meat**, **milk**, **skin**, and **manure**. **Records** of **weight**, health, breeding, feed, and money are essential. **Profit** = total sales - total costs. Monthly **weight** checks and good **records** help choose the best goats and sell at the right **market** time.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: List the four main products from a goat. A: **Meat**, **milk**, **skin**, **manure**.
chunks.source: **Meat**, **milk**, **skin**, **manure**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is **chevon**? A: Goat **meat**.
chunks.source: Goat **meat**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why are **records** important in goat farming? A: They track **weight**, health, breeding, feed costs, and income to show **profit** and guide decisions.
chunks.source: They track **weight**, health, breeding, feed costs, and income to show **profit** and guide decisions.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name three things a farmer should record for each goat. A: **Weight**, **deworming**/**vaccination** dates, milk yield, kidding dates, feed costs, sales.
chunks.source: **Weight**, **deworming**/**vaccination** dates, milk yield, kidding dates, feed costs, sales.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: A goat is sold at 25 kg for 14,000 shillings per kg. What is the gross income? A: 350,000 shillings.
chunks.source: 350,000 shillings.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: If the same goat cost 120,000 to buy, 60,000 for feed, 15,000 for health, and 5,000 for transport, what is the **profit**? A: 350,000 - 200,000 = 150,000 shillings.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How does recording **weight** monthly help the farmer? A: Shows growth rate, detects illness early, decides sale time, checks feed value.
chunks.source: Shows growth rate, detects illness early, decides sale time, checks feed value.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Application: A farmer has 5 **does**. Each gives 1.5 litres **milk** per day for 180 days. Milk price 2,500/shilling per litre. Total feed and health cost 400,000. Calculate annual milk **profit**. A: 5 × 1.5 × 180 = 1,350 litres. 1,350 × 2,500 = 3,375,000 income. Minus 400,000 = 2,975,000 **profit**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Cattle Breeds. I can identify common cattle breeds in Uganda and explain the difference between beef, dairy, and crossbreed cattle. Cattle breeds are grouped by purpose: beef breeds (ankole, zebu) for meat, dairy breeds (friesian, jersey) for milk, and crossbreeds combine both traits for Ugandan conditions. Keywords: ankole: A local Ugandan cattle breed with very long horns, kept mainly for beef.; friesian: A dairy cattle breed from Europe, black and white, that gives a lot of milk.; jersey: A small dairy cattle breed from Jersey Island, light brown, with high butterfat milk.; zebu: A humped cattle breed common in eastern Uganda, kept for beef and draught work.; beef: Meat from cattle; breeds kept mainly for meat are called beef breeds.; dairy: Relating to milk production; dairy breeds are kept mainly for milk.; breed: A group of animals with similar traits that are passed to their young.; crossbreed: An animal born from parents of two different breeds, combining their traits.
chunks.source: Cattle breeds are grouped by purpose: beef breeds (ankole, zebu) for meat, dairy breeds (friesian, jersey) for milk, and crossbreeds combine both traits for Ugandan conditions.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which breed is known for very long horns and is kept mainly for beef? A: Ankole
chunks.source: Ankole

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name two dairy breeds mentioned in the lesson. A: Friesian and Jersey
chunks.source: Friesian and Jersey

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is a zebu cattle used for besides beef? A: Draught work (pulling ploughs/carts)
chunks.source: Draught work (pulling ploughs/carts)

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Define 'crossbreed' in your own words. A: An animal with parents from two different breeds, combining their traits.
chunks.source: An animal with parents from two different breeds, combining their traits.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why might a Ugandan farmer choose a crossbreed over a pure friesian? A: Crossbreeds handle heat and diseases better and give both milk and beef.
chunks.source: Crossbreeds handle heat and diseases better and give both milk and beef.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which breed gives milk with high butterfat, good for ghee? A: Jersey
chunks.source: Jersey

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: True or false: All cattle breeds are good for both milk and meat. A: False
chunks.source: False

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: If you see a humped cow in Soroti, what breed is it likely to be? A: Zebu
chunks.source: Zebu

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What does 'dairy' mean? A: Relating to milk production.
chunks.source: Relating to milk production.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Explain why a farmer might keep both ankole and friesian on the same farm. A: Ankole for beef sales, friesian for daily milk for family and sale.
chunks.source: Ankole for beef sales, friesian for daily milk for family and sale.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Cattle Housing and Feeding. I can describe proper cattle housing and feeding practices to keep cattle healthy and productive. Good cattle housing uses a dry kraal at night and rotational paddocks by day. Feeding combines fresh pasture, hay, silage, salt, and constant water, with weekly dipping for tick control. Keywords: kraal: An enclosure for keeping cattle, usually made of poles and thorn bushes.; paddock: A fenced area where cattle graze during the day.; pasture: Grass and plants growing in a field that cattle eat.; hay: Dried grass stored to feed cattle when fresh grass is scarce.; silage: Fermented green fodder stored in a pit or silo for dry-season feeding.; salt: A mineral block or loose salt given to cattle for essential nutrients.; dip: A tank of medicated water where cattle walk through to kill ticks.; water: Clean drinking water that cattle must have at all times.
chunks.source: Good cattle housing uses a dry kraal at night and rotational paddocks by day. Feeding combines fresh pasture, hay, silage, salt, and constant water, with weekly dipping for tick control.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is the purpose of a kraal? A: To keep cattle safe at night from thieves and predators.
chunks.source: To keep cattle safe at night from thieves and predators.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why do farmers use rotational paddocks? A: To allow pasture to regrow and prevent overgrazing.
chunks.source: To allow pasture to regrow and prevent overgrazing.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name two dry-season feeds mentioned in the lesson. A: Hay and silage
chunks.source: Hay and silage

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is silage made from? A: Fermented green fodder like maize stalks and napier grass.
chunks.source: Fermented green fodder like maize stalks and napier grass.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why do cattle need a salt lick? A: For essential minerals like sodium and trace elements.
chunks.source: For essential minerals like sodium and trace elements.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How often should cattle go through the dip? A: Weekly (or as recommended by vet).
chunks.source: Weekly (or as recommended by vet).

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How much water can a dairy cow drink in a day? A: Up to 100 litres.
chunks.source: Up to 100 litres.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: True or false: Hay is more nutritious than silage. A: False (silage retains more vitamins).
chunks.source: False (silage retains more vitamins).

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What happens if cattle overgraze one paddock? A: Grass is eaten to roots, pasture degrades, weeds invade.
chunks.source: Grass is eaten to roots, pasture degrades, weeds invade.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Design a simple feeding plan for a farmer with 5 cows during dry season. A: Morning: 5 kg hay + 3 kg silage per cow. Salt lick always available. Clean water ad lib. Dip weekly.
chunks.source: Morning: 5 kg hay + 3 kg silage per cow. Salt lick always available. Clean water ad lib. Dip weekly.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Cattle Diseases and Control. I can identify major cattle diseases in Uganda, explain how they spread, and describe control methods including vaccination, dipping, and quarantine. Major diseases: east coast fever (tick-borne, control by dipping/vaccination), foot and mouth (viral, control by vaccination/quarantine), anthrax (bacterial, sudden death, never open carcass, vaccinate yearly). Always call the vet. Keywords: east coast fever: A deadly tick-borne disease causing high fever, swollen lymph nodes, and death.; foot and mouth: A viral disease causing blisters on the mouth and feet, spreading fast between animals.; anthrax: A bacterial disease that kills suddenly; spores survive in soil for years.; tick: A small blood-sucking parasite that spreads diseases like east coast fever.; vaccination: Giving a vaccine to make cattle immune to a specific disease.; dipping: Walking cattle through a medicated tank to kill ticks on their bodies.; quarantine: Isolating sick or new animals to stop disease spread.; vet: Short for veterinarian — an animal doctor who treats and prevents diseases.
chunks.source: Major diseases: east coast fever (tick-borne, control by dipping/vaccination), foot and mouth (viral, control by vaccination/quarantine), anthrax (bacterial, sudden death, never open carcass, vaccinate yearly). Always call the vet.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which parasite spreads east coast fever? A: Tick (brown ear tick)
chunks.source: Tick (brown ear tick)

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name two methods to control east coast fever. A: Weekly dipping and vaccination
chunks.source: Weekly dipping and vaccination

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What are the signs of foot and mouth disease? A: Blisters on mouth and feet, salivation, lameness.
chunks.source: Blisters on mouth and feet, salivation, lameness.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why is quarantine important for foot and mouth? A: Stops the virus spreading to other farms.
chunks.source: Stops the virus spreading to other farms.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How often should cattle be vaccinated against foot and mouth? A: Every six months.
chunks.source: Every six months.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What should you NEVER do if you suspect anthrax? A: Open the carcass.
chunks.source: Open the carcass.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How long can anthrax spores survive in soil? A: Decades (many years).
chunks.source: Decades (many years).

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: True or false: Dipping treats east coast fever in sick cattle. A: False (dipping prevents by killing ticks; sick cattle need treatment).
chunks.source: False (dipping prevents by killing ticks; sick cattle need treatment).

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Who should you call immediately when cattle show strange signs? A: The vet (veterinarian).
chunks.source: The vet (veterinarian).

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Explain why selling a cow with foot and mouth is dangerous. A: It spreads the highly contagious virus to other farms and markets.
chunks.source: It spreads the highly contagious virus to other farms and markets.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Milk Production and Hygiene. I can explain the process of clean milk production from udder preparation to cooling, and why hygiene matters at every step. Clean milk production requires hygiene throughout: clean milker, washed udder, gentle milking, clean can, straining, and rapid cooling. A cow's lactation lasts ~300 days. Clean milk fetches better price at the dairy. Keywords: udder: The milk-producing organ of a cow, with four teats.; milking: The act of removing milk from the udder by hand or machine.; lactation: The period after calving when a cow produces milk.; straining: Pouring milk through a clean cloth or sieve to remove dirt and hair.; cooling: Lowering milk temperature quickly to slow bacterial growth.; hygiene: Clean practices that prevent contamination and disease.; can: A metal container (usually aluminium) for carrying and storing milk.; dairy: A place where milk is collected, processed, or sold; also relates to milk production.
chunks.source: Clean milk production requires hygiene throughout: clean milker, washed udder, gentle milking, clean can, straining, and rapid cooling. A cow's lactation lasts ~300 days. Clean milk fetches better price at the dairy.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why wash the udder with warm water before milking? A: Stimulates milk let-down and removes bacteria.
chunks.source: Stimulates milk let-down and removes bacteria.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is the purpose of the strip cup? A: To check first streams for clots or blood (mastitis signs).
chunks.source: To check first streams for clots or blood (mastitis signs).

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Describe correct hand milking technique. A: Squeeze teat base gently, do not pull.
chunks.source: Squeeze teat base gently, do not pull.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why must the milk can be scrubbed and sun-dried? A: To kill bacteria and prevent contamination.
chunks.source: To kill bacteria and prevent contamination.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What does straining milk achieve? A: Removes hairs, dirt, and debris.
chunks.source: Removes hairs, dirt, and debris.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why is rapid cooling of milk important? A: Slows bacterial growth; milk at 35°C doubles bacteria every 20 minutes.
chunks.source: Slows bacterial growth; milk at 35°C doubles bacteria every 20 minutes.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How long is a typical lactation period? A: About 300 days (10 months).
chunks.source: About 300 days (10 months).

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What test might a dairy cooperative do on delivery? A: Clot-on-boiling test, smell, temperature check.
chunks.source: Clot-on-boiling test, smell, temperature check.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: True or false: Pulling the teat during milking is correct technique. A: False (causes teat damage and mastitis).
chunks.source: False (causes teat damage and mastitis).

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: List the 5 key hygiene steps from udder to dairy. A: 1. Clean milker 2. Clean udder 3. Clean can 4. Straining 5. Rapid cooling.
chunks.source: 1. Clean milker 2. Clean udder 3. Clean can 4. Straining 5. Rapid cooling.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Science in the Kitchen. I can explain how boiling, filtering, sieving, fermentation, leavening, preservation, mixture and solution are used when we cook at home. In the kitchen we use **boiling**, **filtering**, **sieving**, **fermentation**, **leavening**, **preservation**, **mixture** and **solution** to prepare and keep food safe. Keywords: boiling: heating a liquid until it turns to vapour; filtering: passing a liquid through a cloth or paper to remove small bits; sieving: shaking a dry powder through a mesh to separate big pieces; fermentation: tiny living things change food, making gas or acid; leavening: adding something that makes dough rise; preservation: keeping food safe to eat for a long time; mixture: two or more things put together but not chemically joined; solution: a solid completely dissolves in a liquid
chunks.source: In the kitchen we use **boiling**, **filtering**, **sieving**, **fermentation**, **leavening**, **preservation**, **mixture** and **solution** to prepare and keep food safe.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What happens to water when it is heated until it **boils**? A: It turns into steam.
chunks.source: It turns into steam.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which process uses a cloth to remove tea leaves from hot water? A: **Filtering**.
chunks.source: **Filtering**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What do we call shaking flour through a mesh to remove lumps? A: **Sieving**.
chunks.source: **Sieving**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name the process where yeast makes gas in dough. A: **Fermentation**.
chunks.source: **Fermentation**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is the name of the powder that makes dough rise in the oven? A: **Leavening**.
chunks.source: **Leavening**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why do we dry fish in the sun? A: For **preservation** so it lasts longer.
chunks.source: For **preservation** so it lasts longer.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Rice and beans cooked together are an example of what? A: A **mixture**.
chunks.source: A **mixture**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: When sugar disappears in tea, what has formed? A: A **solution**.
chunks.source: A **solution**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Explain the difference between **fermentation** and **leavening**. A: **Fermentation** uses living yeast to make gas over time; **leavening** uses a chemical like baking powder that releases gas quickly when heated.
chunks.source: **Fermentation** uses living yeast to make gas over time; **leavening** uses a chemical like baking powder that releases gas quickly when heated.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: If you want to keep cooked beans safe for a week, which method would you use? A: **Preservation** by drying or storing in a sealed container.
chunks.source: **Preservation** by drying or storing in a sealed container.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Science in Building and Farming. I can describe how levers, pulleys, cement, compost, mulching, irrigation, tools and machines make work easier at home and on the farm. **Lever**, **pulley**, **cement**, **compost**, **mulching**, **irrigation**, **tool** and **machine** are scientific ideas that make building and farming easier. Keywords: lever: a stiff bar that turns on a fixed point to lift heavy things; pulley: a wheel with a groove that guides a rope to lift loads; cement: a grey powder that hardens when mixed with water and sand; compost: rotted plant and animal waste used to enrich soil; mulching: covering soil with dry grass or leaves to keep moisture; irrigation: supplying water to crops by channels or pipes; tool: a simple hand‑held device for doing work; machine: a device with moving parts that does work
chunks.source: **Lever**, **pulley**, **cement**, **compost**, **mulching**, **irrigation**, **tool** and **machine** are scientific ideas that make building and farming easier.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is a **lever**? A: A stiff bar that turns on a fixed point to lift heavy things.
chunks.source: A stiff bar that turns on a fixed point to lift heavy things.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How does a **pulley** help at a well? A: It guides the rope so the bucket lifts easily.
chunks.source: It guides the rope so the bucket lifts easily.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What happens when **cement** is mixed with water and sand? A: It hardens into strong concrete.
chunks.source: It hardens into strong concrete.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why do farmers add **compost** to the garden? A: To enrich the soil with nutrients.
chunks.source: To enrich the soil with nutrients.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is the purpose of **mulching**? A: To keep soil moisture and reduce weeds.
chunks.source: To keep soil moisture and reduce weeds.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Define **irrigation**. A: Supplying water to crops by channels or pipes.
chunks.source: Supplying water to crops by channels or pipes.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give an example of a **tool** used for digging. A: A hoe.
chunks.source: A hoe.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name a **machine** that ploughs a large field. A: A tractor.
chunks.source: A tractor.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Explain the difference between a **tool** and a **machine**. A: A **tool** is simple and hand‑held; a **machine** has moving parts and often uses power.
chunks.source: A **tool** is simple and hand‑held; a **machine** has moving parts and often uses power.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: If you want to keep the soil moist during a dry spell, which practice would you use? A: **Mulching**.
chunks.source: **Mulching**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Water Purification at Home. I can explain how to make water safe by filtering, boiling, chlorination, sedimentation, proper storage and avoiding contamination. To make water **safe** at home we use **sedimentation**, **filter**, **boil**, **chlorination**, and proper **storage** to remove **contamination** and kill **germs**. Keywords: filter: pass water through a material that traps dirt and germs; boil: heat water until it bubbles to kill germs; chlorination: adding a small amount of chlorine to kill germs; sedimentation: letting heavy particles settle at the bottom of a container; contamination: when germs or dirt get into water; storage: keeping clean water in a covered, clean container; germs: tiny living things that can make us sick; safe: free from harmful germs and dirt
chunks.source: To make water **safe** at home we use **sedimentation**, **filter**, **boil**, **chlorination**, and proper **storage** to remove **contamination** and kill **germs**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is the first step to clear cloudy water? A: **Sedimentation**.
chunks.source: **Sedimentation**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which household item can be used as a **filter**? A: A clean cloth.
chunks.source: A clean cloth.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How long should water **boil** to kill **germs**? A: At least ten minutes.
chunks.source: At least ten minutes.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What does **chlorination** add to water? A: A small amount of chlorine.
chunks.source: A small amount of chlorine.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why must the storage container have a tight lid? A: To prevent **contamination**.
chunks.source: To prevent **contamination**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name two ways to kill **germs** in water. A: **Boiling** and **chlorination**.
chunks.source: **Boiling** and **chlorination**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What happens during **sedimentation**? A: Heavy particles settle at the bottom.
chunks.source: Heavy particles settle at the bottom.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: If water looks clear but you are not sure it is **safe**, what should you do? A: **Boil** it or add chlorine.
chunks.source: **Boil** it or add chlorine.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Explain the correct order of the five steps. A: **Sedimentation**, **filter**, **boil**, **chlorination**, **storage**.
chunks.source: **Sedimentation**, **filter**, **boil**, **chlorination**, **storage**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What could happen if you skip **storage** after cleaning water? A: New **germs** or dirt could cause **contamination**.
chunks.source: New **germs** or dirt could cause **contamination**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Waste Management. I can describe how to sort waste, use a compost pit, recycle, avoid incineration and landfill problems, and prevent sewage pollution. We **sort** waste into **biodegradable** for the **compost pit**, **recycle** plastics and paper, avoid **incineration** that causes **pollution**, use a lined **landfill** for the rest, and treat **sewage** to keep water clean. Keywords: biodegradable: material that rots naturally; compost pit: a hole where organic waste turns into fertilizer; recycle: turn used materials into new products; incineration: burning waste at high temperature; landfill: a large area where waste is buried; sewage: liquid waste from toilets and drains; pollution: harmful substances in air, water or soil; sort: separate waste into different groups
chunks.source: We **sort** waste into **biodegradable** for the **compost pit**, **recycle** plastics and paper, avoid **incineration** that causes **pollution**, use a lined **landfill** for the rest, and treat **sewage** to keep water clean.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What does **biodegradable** mean? A: Material that rots naturally.
chunks.source: Material that rots naturally.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Where do we put fruit peels at school? A: In the **biodegradable** bin for the **compost pit**.
chunks.source: In the **biodegradable** bin for the **compost pit**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name one item that can be **recycled**. A: Plastic bottles.
chunks.source: Plastic bottles.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What harmful effect does **incineration** of plastic have? A: It causes **pollution**.
chunks.source: It causes **pollution**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is a **landfill**? A: A large area where waste is buried.
chunks.source: A large area where waste is buried.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why is **sewage** dangerous if it reaches a river? A: It causes **pollution** and spreads disease.
chunks.source: It causes **pollution** and spreads disease.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What does it mean to **sort** waste? A: Separate waste into different groups.
chunks.source: Separate waste into different groups.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How does a **compost pit** help the garden? A: It turns organic waste into fertilizer.
chunks.source: It turns organic waste into fertilizer.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Explain why we should not burn all waste. A: Burning plastic creates toxic **pollution**; some waste can be **recycled** or composted instead.
chunks.source: Burning plastic creates toxic **pollution**; some waste can be **recycled** or composted instead.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: If a community has no **landfill**, what could happen to waste? A: It may be dumped openly, causing **pollution** and health risks.
chunks.source: It may be dumped openly, causing **pollution** and health risks.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Elements of PHC. I can name and explain the eight elements of Primary Health Care and give Ugandan examples. Primary Health Care has eight elements: immunisation, health education, safe water, sanitation, nutrition, maternal care, treatment, and referral. They work together to keep Ugandan communities healthy. Keywords: immunisation: giving vaccines to prevent diseases; health education: teaching people how to stay healthy; safe water: clean water that does not cause illness; sanitation: safe disposal of human waste and rubbish; nutrition: eating the right foods for growth and health; maternal care: care for pregnant women and new mothers; treatment: medical care given for an illness or injury; referral: sending a patient to a higher level facility
chunks.source: Primary Health Care has eight elements: immunisation, health education, safe water, sanitation, nutrition, maternal care, treatment, and referral. They work together to keep Ugandan communities healthy.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: List the eight elements of Primary Health Care. A: Immunisation, health education, safe water, sanitation, nutrition, maternal care, treatment, referral.
chunks.source: Immunisation, health education, safe water, sanitation, nutrition, maternal care, treatment, referral.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What does UNEPI stand for? A: Uganda National Expanded Programme on Immunisation.
chunks.source: Uganda National Expanded Programme on Immunisation.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give two examples of health education in your village. A: Teaching hand washing at school; VHT showing how to use a mosquito net.
chunks.source: Teaching hand washing at school; VHT showing how to use a mosquito net.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why is a borehole called a safe water source? A: It is protected from contamination and provides clean water without boiling.
chunks.source: It is protected from contamination and provides clean water without boiling.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name the three food groups for good nutrition. A: Body-building (proteins), energy-giving (carbohydrates/fats), protective (vitamins/minerals).
chunks.source: Body-building (proteins), energy-giving (carbohydrates/fats), protective (vitamins/minerals).

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: When should a pregnant woman make her first antenatal visit? A: As soon as she knows she is pregnant, ideally before 12 weeks.
chunks.source: As soon as she knows she is pregnant, ideally before 12 weeks.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is the difference between treatment and referral? A: Treatment is care given at the current facility; referral is sending the patient to a higher-level facility for advanced care.
chunks.source: Treatment is care given at the current facility; referral is sending the patient to a higher-level facility for advanced care.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: A child has watery diarrhoea for two days. The health centre has ORS but no IV fluids. The child is lethargic. What should the health worker do? A: Give ORS, write a referral note, and arrange urgent transport to the hospital for IV fluids.
chunks.source: Give ORS, write a referral note, and arrange urgent transport to the hospital for IV fluids.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Explain how safe water and sanitation work together to prevent cholera. A: Safe water stops germs entering the body; sanitation stops germs leaving the body into the environment. Both are needed to break the cholera cycle.
chunks.source: Safe water stops germs entering the body; sanitation stops germs leaving the body into the environment. Both are needed to break the cholera cycle.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Reasoning: If a village has good immunisation but poor sanitation, what diseases might still spread? A: Diarrhoeal diseases like cholera, typhoid, and worms can still spread because sanitation stops faecal-oral transmission, which vaccines do not cover.
chunks.source: Diarrhoeal diseases like cholera, typhoid, and worms can still spread because sanitation stops faecal-oral transmission, which vaccines do not cover.

chunks.id: L-P6-Science-The Role of a Health Worker
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: The Role of a Health Worker
chunks.text: The Role of a Health Worker. I can describe the roles of community health workers including VHTs, nurses, and clinical officers. Community health workers include VHTs, nurses, and clinical officers. VHTs educate, give first aid, keep records, and mobilise. Nurses and clinical officers diagnose, treat, counsel, and run outreach. Good records and teamwork make the system work. Keywords: VHT: Village Health Team member, a volunteer who promotes health in the village; diagnosis: identifying a disease from its signs and symptoms; first aid: immediate help given before full medical treatment; outreach: health services taken to the community instead of waiting at the clinic; record: written information about a patient's health; counselling: talking with someone to help them make healthy decisions; mobilise: organise people to take part in a health activity; clinic: a place where health workers see patients
chunks.source: Community health workers include VHTs, nurses, and clinical officers. VHTs educate, give first aid, keep records, and mobilise. Nurses and clinical officers diagnose, treat, counsel, and run outreach. Good records and teamwork make the system work.

chunks.id: LQ-P6-Science-The Role of a Health Worker
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: The Role of a Health Worker
chunks.text: Q: What does VHT stand for? A: Village Health Team.
chunks.source: Village Health Team.

chunks.id: LQ-P6-Science-The Role of a Health Worker
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: The Role of a Health Worker
chunks.text: Q: List three tasks a VHT does in the village. A: Health education, first aid for minor injuries, refer danger signs, keep household records, mobilise for health activities.
chunks.source: Health education, first aid for minor injuries, refer danger signs, keep household records, mobilise for health activities.

chunks.id: LQ-P6-Science-The Role of a Health Worker
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: The Role of a Health Worker
chunks.text: Q: Who makes a medical diagnosis in Uganda's health system? A: A nurse, clinical officer, or doctor — not a VHT.
chunks.source: A nurse, clinical officer, or doctor — not a VHT.

chunks.id: LQ-P6-Science-The Role of a Health Worker
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: The Role of a Health Worker
chunks.text: Q: Give two examples of first aid a VHT can give. A: Clean and bandage a small cut; cool a burn with clean water; stop a nosebleed by pinching the nose.
chunks.source: Clean and bandage a small cut; cool a burn with clean water; stop a nosebleed by pinching the nose.

chunks.id: LQ-P6-Science-The Role of a Health Worker
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: The Role of a Health Worker
chunks.text: Q: What is outreach and why is it done? A: Taking health services (vaccines, vitamin A, deworming) to the community because distance and bad roads prevent access.
chunks.source: Taking health services (vaccines, vitamin A, deworming) to the community because distance and bad roads prevent access.

chunks.id: LQ-P6-Science-The Role of a Health Worker
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: The Role of a Health Worker
chunks.text: Q: What information is in a VHT's household record? A: Number of under-fives, pregnant women, latrine presence, mosquito net use, vaccination status.
chunks.source: Number of under-fives, pregnant women, latrine presence, mosquito net use, vaccination status.

chunks.id: LQ-P6-Science-The Role of a Health Worker
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: The Role of a Health Worker
chunks.text: Q: How does counselling differ from health education? A: Health education gives general information to groups; counselling is a private conversation to help one person make a personal health decision.
chunks.source: Health education gives general information to groups; counselling is a private conversation to help one person make a personal health decision.

chunks.id: LQ-P6-Science-The Role of a Health Worker
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: The Role of a Health Worker
chunks.text: Q: A clinical officer sees a patient with suspected TB. What steps should follow? A: Confirm **diagnosis** with sputum test, start **treatment** per guidelines, give **counselling** on adherence, record in TB register, **refer** if complications.
chunks.source: Confirm **diagnosis** with sputum test, start **treatment** per guidelines, give **counselling** on adherence, record in TB register, **refer** if complications.

chunks.id: LQ-P6-Science-The Role of a Health Worker
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: The Role of a Health Worker
chunks.text: Q: Reasoning: If VHTs do not keep records, how would outreach planning suffer? A: Without records, health workers would not know which villages have low immunisation, many pregnant women, or poor sanitation. Outreach would miss the neediest areas.
chunks.source: Without records, health workers would not know which villages have low immunisation, many pregnant women, or poor sanitation. Outreach would miss the neediest areas.

chunks.id: LQ-P6-Science-The Role of a Health Worker
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: The Role of a Health Worker
chunks.text: Q: Common mistake: Some people think VHTs can prescribe medicine. Why is this wrong? A: VHTs are volunteers with basic training. Prescribing requires clinical **diagnosis** and knowledge of drug interactions, which only qualified health workers have.
chunks.source: VHTs are volunteers with basic training. Prescribing requires clinical **diagnosis** and knowledge of drug interactions, which only qualified health workers have.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Healthy Homes. I can identify features of a healthy home and explain how each prevents disease. A healthy home has eight features: ventilation, lighting, latrine, bathroom, kitchen, drainage, clean compound, and vector control. Each stops specific diseases — together they protect the whole family. Keywords: ventilation: fresh air moving through a room; lighting: enough natural or artificial light to see clearly; latrine: a toilet for safe disposal of faeces; bathroom: a place for bathing and washing; kitchen: a place for cooking and storing food; drainage: system to carry away waste water; compound: the yard around the house; vector: an animal that carries disease germs
chunks.source: A healthy home has eight features: ventilation, lighting, latrine, bathroom, kitchen, drainage, clean compound, and vector control. Each stops specific diseases — together they protect the whole family.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Define ventilation in a healthy home. A: Fresh air moving through a room via openings on opposite walls (at least 10% of floor area).
chunks.source: Fresh air moving through a room via openings on opposite walls (at least 10% of floor area).

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why is a vent pipe with a fly screen important on a latrine? A: It removes bad smells and prevents flies from entering or leaving the pit.
chunks.source: It removes bad smells and prevents flies from entering or leaving the pit.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is the purpose of a soak pit for bathroom water? A: To absorb waste water so it does not create stagnant pools for mosquito breeding.
chunks.source: To absorb waste water so it does not create stagnant pools for mosquito breeding.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: List three vector control measures for the compound. A: Clear drainage, cover rubbish pit, cut tall grass, remove containers holding water.
chunks.source: Clear drainage, cover rubbish pit, cut tall grass, remove containers holding water.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why should the kitchen be separate from the sleeping room? A: To keep smoke, burns, and food contamination away from where people sleep.
chunks.source: To keep smoke, burns, and food contamination away from where people sleep.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How does good lighting improve health? A: Prevents accidents, allows thorough cleaning, reduces eye strain, enables reading at night.
chunks.source: Prevents accidents, allows thorough cleaning, reduces eye strain, enables reading at night.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: A family has a latrine but no hand-washing facility. What disease risk remains high? A: Diarrhoea and cholera because faecal germs stay on hands and contaminate food.
chunks.source: Diarrhoea and cholera because faecal germs stay on hands and contaminate food.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Explain how drainage, compound cleanliness, and vector control work together. A: Drainage removes standing water (mosquito breeding); clean compound removes rubbish (fly/rat breeding); together they cut vector life cycles.
chunks.source: Drainage removes standing water (mosquito breeding); clean compound removes rubbish (fly/rat breeding); together they cut vector life cycles.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Reasoning: If a home has perfect ventilation but no latrine, which diseases are still likely? A: Diarrhoeal diseases, cholera, typhoid, worms — because faecal-oral transmission continues without sanitation.
chunks.source: Diarrhoeal diseases, cholera, typhoid, worms — because faecal-oral transmission continues without sanitation.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Common mistake: People think a bathroom soak pit can be the same as the latrine pit. Why is this wrong? A: A latrine pit holds faeces and pathogens; a soak pit only handles grey water. Mixing them overloads the pit and spreads contamination.
chunks.source: A latrine pit holds faeces and pathogens; a soak pit only handles grey water. Mixing them overloads the pit and spreads contamination.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Disease Prevention in the Community. I can describe community activities that prevent disease outbreaks and explain how each works. Community disease prevention uses seven tools: vaccination, drainage, health parade, clean-up, net use, surveillance, and quarantine. Together they stop epidemics before they start. Every person's action counts. Keywords: vaccination: giving a vaccine to protect against a specific disease; drainage: clearing channels so water flows away; health parade: a community walk with health messages and inspections; clean-up: collecting rubbish and clearing bushes in the community; net: insecticide-treated mosquito net for sleeping under; surveillance: watching for disease signs and reporting them quickly; epidemic: a sudden increase in disease cases above normal; quarantine: separating sick or exposed people to stop spread
chunks.source: Community disease prevention uses seven tools: vaccination, drainage, health parade, clean-up, net use, surveillance, and quarantine. Together they stop epidemics before they start. Every person's action counts.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is a health parade? A: A community walk with health inspections, education, and collective action like clean-up.
chunks.source: A community walk with health inspections, education, and collective action like clean-up.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How does drainage prevent malaria? A: It removes stagnant water where mosquitoes breed.
chunks.source: It removes stagnant water where mosquitoes breed.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why is vaccination called a shield against epidemics? A: It creates herd immunity so diseases cannot spread easily.
chunks.source: It creates herd immunity so diseases cannot spread easily.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What should you do if your mosquito net has holes? A: Repair it or replace it; a torn net does not protect.
chunks.source: Repair it or replace it; a torn net does not protect.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Define surveillance in your own words. A: Actively watching for disease signs in the community and reporting immediately.
chunks.source: Actively watching for disease signs in the community and reporting immediately.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: When is quarantine necessary? A: For highly infectious, outbreak-prone diseases (Ebola, cholera, COVID-19) to stop transmission.
chunks.source: For highly infectious, outbreak-prone diseases (Ebola, cholera, COVID-19) to stop transmission.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: A village has low vaccination coverage. What epidemic risk is highest? A: Measles, because it spreads fast and needs 95% coverage to stop outbreaks.
chunks.source: Measles, because it spreads fast and needs 95% coverage to stop outbreaks.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: List the steps when a VHT finds a suspected cholera case. A: Report immediately, give ORS, refer to clinic, set up quarantine, disinfect home, trace contacts.
chunks.source: Report immediately, give ORS, refer to clinic, set up quarantine, disinfect home, trace contacts.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Reasoning: If a community does clean-ups but ignores drainage, what problem remains? A: Mosquito breeding continues in stagnant water, so malaria risk stays high despite clean surroundings.
chunks.source: Mosquito breeding continues in stagnant water, so malaria risk stays high despite clean surroundings.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Common mistake: People think quarantine means abandoning the sick. Explain the difference. A: Quarantine means separating with care — the patient gets treatment, food, and monitoring. Abandonment is neglect; quarantine is protection with support.
chunks.source: Quarantine means separating with care — the patient gets treatment, food, and monitoring. Abandonment is neglect; quarantine is protection with support.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Nutrients and Their Functions. I can name the main nutrients and explain what each does in my body. The eight main nutrients each have a special job: carbohydrate gives quick energy, protein builds muscles, vitamin and mineral keep the body working, fats store energy, water carries nutrients, roughage aids digestion, and enzymes break down food. Keywords: carbohydrate: gives quick energy; protein: builds and repairs body parts; vitamin: helps the body work properly; mineral: keeps bones and teeth strong; fats: stores energy and protects organs; water: carries nutrients and removes waste; roughage: helps food move through the gut; enzyme: breaks down food so the body can use it
chunks.source: The eight main nutrients each have a special job: carbohydrate gives quick energy, protein builds muscles, vitamin and mineral keep the body working, fats store energy, water carries nutrients, roughage aids digestion, and enzymes break down food.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What nutrient gives quick energy? A: Carbohydrate
chunks.source: Carbohydrate

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which nutrient builds and repairs muscles? A: Protein
chunks.source: Protein

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name a nutrient that helps keep bones strong. A: Mineral
chunks.source: Mineral

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What does water do in the body? A: Carries nutrients and removes waste
chunks.source: Carries nutrients and removes waste

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which nutrient helps food move through the gut? A: Roughage
chunks.source: Roughage

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is the role of an enzyme? A: Breaks down food so the body can use it
chunks.source: Breaks down food so the body can use it

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give an example of a food rich in carbohydrate. A: Posho or cassava
chunks.source: Posho or cassava

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give an example of a food rich in protein. A: Beans or fish
chunks.source: Beans or fish

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Reasoning: If a child eats only rice and no vegetables, which two nutrients might be low? A: Vitamin and roughage
chunks.source: Vitamin and roughage

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Balanced Diet for Different People. I can plan a balanced meal for an infant, adolescent, pregnant woman, elderly person, invalid, and athlete. Different people have different nutrient requirements; portion sizes and food choices must match age, health, and activity level. Keywords: infant: baby under one year; adolescent: teenager growing fast; pregnant: woman expecting a baby; elderly: older person; invalid: person who is sick and cannot move much; athlete: person who trains hard in sport; portion: amount of food served at one time; requirement: what the body needs each day
chunks.source: Different people have different nutrient requirements; portion sizes and food choices must match age, health, and activity level.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which group needs the smallest portion size? A: Infant
chunks.source: Infant

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What nutrient is especially important for a pregnant woman? A: Iron and folic acid
chunks.source: Iron and folic acid

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: An athlete needs large portions of which nutrient for energy? A: Carbohydrate
chunks.source: Carbohydrate

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why should an elderly person avoid very large portions? A: Lower activity can lead to obesity
chunks.source: Lower activity can lead to obesity

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What type of food is best for an invalid who cannot chew well? A: Soft, easy‑to‑digest meals
chunks.source: Soft, easy‑to‑digest meals

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Define 'requirement' in the context of nutrition. A: What the body needs each day
chunks.source: What the body needs each day

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give an example of a nutrient‑dense snack for an adolescent. A: Groundnut paste on bread
chunks.source: Groundnut paste on bread

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: If a pregnant woman eats only rice, which two nutrients might be low? A: Iron and folic acid
chunks.source: Iron and folic acid

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Reasoning: Plan a one‑day menu for an adolescent and list the portion for each meal. A: Breakfast: 1 cup millet porridge + ½ cup milk; Lunch: 2 cups posho + 1 cup beans + 1 cup greens; Snack: 2 tbsp groundnut paste; Dinner: 1 cup fish stew + 1 cup matooke + 1 fruit
chunks.source: Breakfast: 1 cup millet porridge + ½ cup milk; Lunch: 2 cups posho + 1 cup beans + 1 cup greens; Snack: 2 tbsp groundnut paste; Dinner: 1 cup fish stew + 1 cup matooke + 1 fruit

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Malnutrition. I can identify causes, signs, and prevention of malnutrition. Malnutrition includes kwashiorkor, marasmus, underweight, stunted growth, and obesity; each has distinct signs, causes, and requires proper rehabilitation and prevention. Keywords: kwashiorkor: protein deficiency with swelling; marasmus: severe energy deficiency, very thin; underweight: weight too low for age; stunted: height too low for age; obesity: excess body fat; deficiency: lack of a needed nutrient; sign: observable clue of a condition; rehabilitation: process of restoring health
chunks.source: Malnutrition includes kwashiorkor, marasmus, underweight, stunted growth, and obesity; each has distinct signs, causes, and requires proper rehabilitation and prevention.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which condition shows swelling of feet and belly? A: Kwashiorkor
chunks.source: Kwashiorkor

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is marasmus? A: Severe energy deficiency causing extreme thinness
chunks.source: Severe energy deficiency causing extreme thinness

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How is underweight detected? A: Weight‑for‑age chart
chunks.source: Weight‑for‑age chart

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What does stunted mean? A: Height too low for age
chunks.source: Height too low for age

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name one cause of obesity in children. A: Too many fried foods and sugary drinks with little activity
chunks.source: Too many fried foods and sugary drinks with little activity

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is a deficiency? A: Lack of a needed nutrient
chunks.source: Lack of a needed nutrient

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give an example of a sign of kwashiorkor. A: Swollen belly
chunks.source: Swollen belly

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What does rehabilitation involve for severe malnutrition? A: Small frequent therapeutic feeds, then gradual normal diet
chunks.source: Small frequent therapeutic feeds, then gradual normal diet

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Reasoning: If a child eats only cassava every day, which two malnutrition types are most likely? A: Kwashiorkor (protein deficiency) and underweight
chunks.source: Kwashiorkor (protein deficiency) and underweight

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Food Hygiene and Preservation. I can keep food safe from farm to plate by practicing hygiene and preservation. Food safety depends on preventing contamination, avoiding adulteration, reading labels, respecting expiry dates, and using proper preservation like refrigeration and drying. Keywords: contamination: harmful germs getting into food; adulteration: adding unsafe substances to food; expiry: date after which food may be unsafe; refrigeration: keeping food cold to slow germs; drying: removing moisture to preserve food; clean: free from dirt and germs; label: information on a food package; storage: how and where food is kept
chunks.source: Food safety depends on preventing contamination, avoiding adulteration, reading labels, respecting expiry dates, and using proper preservation like refrigeration and drying.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is contamination? A: Harmful germs getting into food
chunks.source: Harmful germs getting into food

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give an example of adulteration. A: Adding water to milk
chunks.source: Adding water to milk

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What does the expiry date tell you? A: When the food may become unsafe
chunks.source: When the food may become unsafe

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How does refrigeration keep food safe? A: Slows germ growth by keeping food cold
chunks.source: Slows germ growth by keeping food cold

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Describe proper drying of fish. A: Clean, salt, and dry on a raised rack
chunks.source: Clean, salt, and dry on a raised rack

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why should raw meat be stored on the bottom fridge shelf? A: To prevent drips onto other foods
chunks.source: To prevent drips onto other foods

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What information is found on a food label? A: Ingredients, expiry date, storage instructions
chunks.source: Ingredients, expiry date, storage instructions

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What does 'first in, first out' mean for storage? A: Use older stock before newer stock
chunks.source: Use older stock before newer stock

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Reasoning: If you find a packet of flour with no label and a strange smell, what should you do? A: Do not use it; discard and tell an adult
chunks.source: Do not use it; discard and tell an adult

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Components of a Clean Home. I can identify the main sanitation facilities in a home and explain why each one is needed. A clean home needs a **latrine**, **bathroom**, **kitchen**, **dustbin**, **rubbish pit**, **rack**, and tidy **compound** working together. Each part stops germs in a different way — miss one, and disease can enter. Keywords: latrine: a toilet built outside the house for human waste; bathroom: a room for washing the body; kitchen: a room where food is cooked and stored; dustbin: a small container for collecting daily rubbish inside the house; rubbish pit: a hole dug in the ground for burning or burying solid waste; rack: a raised stand for drying plates, cups and utensils; compound: the whole area around the house including the garden and paths; utensil: a tool or container used in the kitchen like a plate, cup or spoon
chunks.source: A clean home needs a **latrine**, **bathroom**, **kitchen**, **dustbin**, **rubbish pit**, **rack**, and tidy **compound** working together. Each part stops germs in a different way — miss one, and disease can enter.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name the part of the home where human waste is safely stored. A: **latrine**
chunks.source: **latrine**

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What do we call the raised stand for drying plates and cups? A: **rack**
chunks.source: **rack**

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Where should daily kitchen rubbish go first before the **rubbish pit**? A: **dustbin**
chunks.source: **dustbin**

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why must the **compound** have no stagnant water? A: Stagnant water breeds mosquitoes that spread malaria.
chunks.source: Stagnant water breeds mosquitoes that spread malaria.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is the purpose of a **vent pipe** on a **latrine**? A: It carries smells up and away from the **superstructure**.
chunks.source: It carries smells up and away from the **superstructure**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: If **utensil**s are dried on the ground, name two risks. A: Chickens walk on them; rain splashes mud and germs onto them.
chunks.source: Chickens walk on them; rain splashes mud and germs onto them.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why is a fence around the **rubbish pit** important? A: It keeps children and animals from falling in or scattering waste.
chunks.source: It keeps children and animals from falling in or scattering waste.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Explain how the **latrine**, **kitchen**, and **compound** work together to stop the faecal-oral route. A: The **latrine** traps faeces so flies cannot carry germs to the **kitchen**; a clean **compound** stops flies breeding and keeps paths safe.
chunks.source: The **latrine** traps faeces so flies cannot carry germs to the **kitchen**; a clean **compound** stops flies breeding and keeps paths safe.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Types of Latrines. I can describe the main types of latrines used in Uganda and explain how each one works. Uganda uses four main **latrine** types: **pit latrine** (simple pit), **VIP latrine** (adds **vent pipe** and **fly screen**), **ecosan** (separates urine/faeces for compost), **flush toilet** (needs water and **septic tank**). Choose based on water, cost, and whether you want fertiliser. Keywords: pit latrine: a simple toilet with a hole dug in the ground and a slab on top; VIP latrine: a ventilated improved pit latrine with a vent pipe and fly screen; ecosan: an ecological sanitation toilet that separates urine and faeces for composting; flush toilet: a toilet that uses water to wash waste into a pipe or septic tank; squat: to sit low with knees bent and heels on the ground; vent pipe: a vertical pipe that carries smells up and out of the latrine; fly screen: a fine mesh covering the top of the vent pipe to keep flies out; superstructure: the walls, roof and door that give privacy and shelter
chunks.source: Uganda uses four main **latrine** types: **pit latrine** (simple pit), **VIP latrine** (adds **vent pipe** and **fly screen**), **ecosan** (separates urine/faeces for compost), **flush toilet** (needs water and **septic tank**). Choose based on water, cost, and whether you want fertiliser.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which latrine type uses a **vent pipe** and **fly screen** to control smells and flies? A: **VIP latrine**
chunks.source: **VIP latrine**

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What does **ecosan** stand for? A: ecological sanitation
chunks.source: ecological sanitation

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name the part that gives a latrine privacy and shelter. A: **superstructure**
chunks.source: **superstructure**

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why does a **flush toilet** need a U-bend water seal? A: To block smells from coming back up the pipe.
chunks.source: To block smells from coming back up the pipe.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How does the **vent pipe** on a **VIP latrine** work? A: Sun heats the pipe, air rises, pulling odours up and out; **fly screen** traps flies.
chunks.source: Sun heats the pipe, air rises, pulling odours up and out; **fly screen** traps flies.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is added to faeces in an **ecosan** after each use? A: Ash or dry soil to dry the waste and kill germs.
chunks.source: Ash or dry soil to dry the waste and kill germs.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why can a **flush toilet** be difficult in a rural Ugandan village? A: It needs a reliable piped water supply and a **septic tank** or sewerage system.
chunks.source: It needs a reliable piped water supply and a **septic tank** or sewerage system.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Compare **pit latrine** and **VIP latrine**: what two extra parts does the **VIP latrine** have? A: **vent pipe** and **fly screen**
chunks.source: **vent pipe** and **fly screen**

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Reasoning: A school has 500 pupils and no water pipe. Which latrine type would you recommend and why? A: **VIP latrine** — no water needed, **vent pipe** reduces smells for many users, **fly screen** stops flies spreading germs to food areas.
chunks.source: **VIP latrine** — no water needed, **vent pipe** reduces smells for many users, **fly screen** stops flies spreading germs to food areas.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Disposal of Faeces and Rubbish. I can explain safe methods for disposing of human faeces and solid rubbish to protect water sources and health. Safe disposal: **faeces** in **latrine**/**septic tank**/**sewage**; kitchen waste to **composting** or **rubbish pit**; waste water to **leach pit**; plastics/toxics buried deep; **burning** only for dry paper. All pits downhill and 30+ metres from **ground water** sources. Keywords: faeces: solid human waste from the body; sewage: waste water and faeces carried away in pipes; composting: breaking down organic waste into fertiliser using air and moisture; burying: putting waste deep in the ground and covering it with soil; burning: destroying dry waste by fire in a controlled place; leach pit: a lined pit where liquid waste soaks into the ground safely; contamination: making something dirty or dangerous by adding germs or chemicals; ground water: water stored underground in rocks and soil, used for wells and boreholes
chunks.source: Safe disposal: **faeces** in **latrine**/**septic tank**/**sewage**; kitchen waste to **composting** or **rubbish pit**; waste water to **leach pit**; plastics/toxics buried deep; **burning** only for dry paper. All pits downhill and 30+ metres from **ground water** sources.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is the minimum safe distance between a **latrine** and a water source? A: At least 30 metres, and the **latrine** must be downhill.
chunks.source: At least 30 metres, and the **latrine** must be downhill.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name two things that must NEVER be burned in a **rubbish pit**. A: Plastic and batteries (also aerosols, tyres).
chunks.source: Plastic and batteries (also aerosols, tyres).

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is a **leach pit** and what does it receive? A: A stone-filled lined pit that safely soaks up **bathroom** and **kitchen** waste water.
chunks.source: A stone-filled lined pit that safely soaks up **bathroom** and **kitchen** waste water.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why is open defecation dangerous for **ground water**? A: **Faeces** on the ground wash or seep into **ground water**, causing **contamination**.
chunks.source: **Faeces** on the ground wash or seep into **ground water**, causing **contamination**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: List the four ingredients for good **composting**. A: Green waste, brown waste, soil, water — plus air from turning.
chunks.source: Green waste, brown waste, soil, water — plus air from turning.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Where should baby **faeces** be disposed? A: In the **latrine** — never in the bush or **rubbish pit**.
chunks.source: In the **latrine** — never in the bush or **rubbish pit**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What happens if **sewage** pipes leak near a borehole? A: **Contamination** of **ground water** with pathogens — report leaks immediately.
chunks.source: **Contamination** of **ground water** with pathogens — report leaks immediately.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Reasoning: A family composts well but puts the heap 5 metres uphill from their shallow well. Is this safe? Why or why not? A: Unsafe. Liquid from the compost (leachate) can seep downhill into the well, carrying bacteria. Compost heap must be downhill and at least 15 metres from water sources.
chunks.source: Unsafe. Liquid from the compost (leachate) can seep downhill into the well, carrying bacteria. Compost heap must be downhill and at least 15 metres from water sources.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Sanitation Diseases. I can name diseases caused by poor sanitation, explain how they spread, and describe how to prevent them. Poor sanitation causes **cholera**, **typhoid**, **dysentery**, **worms**, **trachoma**, **scabies**. Most spread by the **faecal-oral** route (**Faeces** → **Fingers**/ **Flies**/ **Fields**/ **Fluids**/ **Food** → Mouth). **Prevention**: **latrine**, handwashing, safe water, shoes, face washing, deworming, clean **compound**. Facilities + behaviour = health. Keywords: cholera: a severe diarrhoea disease from contaminated water or food; typhoid: a fever disease from bacteria in contaminated food or water; dysentery: diarrhoea with blood and mucus caused by bacteria or amoeba; worms: parasites like roundworm, hookworm, whipworm living in the intestines; trachoma: an eye infection spread by flies and dirty faces; scabies: a skin disease caused by tiny mites that burrow and cause itching; faecal-oral: the route where germs from faeces enter the mouth via water, food, fingers, flies, fields; prevention: actions that stop disease before it starts
chunks.source: Poor sanitation causes **cholera**, **typhoid**, **dysentery**, **worms**, **trachoma**, **scabies**. Most spread by the **faecal-oral** route (**Faeces** → **Fingers**/ **Flies**/ **Fields**/ **Fluids**/ **Food** → Mouth). **Prevention**: **latrine**, handwashing, safe water, shoes, face washing, deworming, clean **compound**. Facilities + behaviour = health.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which disease causes 'rice water' diarrhoea and can kill in hours? A: **cholera**
chunks.source: **cholera**

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name the disease spread by flies landing on faces after **faeces**. A: **trachoma**
chunks.source: **trachoma**

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How do hookworms enter the body? A: Larvae penetrate bare feet from contaminated soil.
chunks.source: Larvae penetrate bare feet from contaminated soil.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is the **faecal-oral** route? A: Germs from **faeces** reach the mouth via water, food, fingers, flies, fields.
chunks.source: Germs from **faeces** reach the mouth via water, food, fingers, flies, fields.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: List three **prevention** steps for **typhoid**. A: Use **latrine**, wash hands with soap, drink safe water (boil/treat), cover food.
chunks.source: Use **latrine**, wash hands with soap, drink safe water (boil/treat), cover food.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why is handwashing the most powerful **prevention** for **faecal-oral** diseases? A: It blocks the **Fingers** path in the **F-diagram** — stops germs moving from **faeces** to food/mouth.
chunks.source: It blocks the **Fingers** path in the **F-diagram** — stops germs moving from **faeces** to food/mouth.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which disease is NOT spread by the **faecal-oral** route? A: **scabies** (spread by skin contact and shared items).
chunks.source: **scabies** (spread by skin contact and shared items).

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: A child has bloody diarrhoea. Name two possible causes. A: **Dysentery** (Shigella or amoeba) or severe **worms**.
chunks.source: **Dysentery** (Shigella or amoeba) or severe **worms**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Reasoning: A village builds **VIP latrine**s for every home but **cholera** still breaks out. Give two possible reasons. A: 1) People don't use **latrine**s consistently (open defecation continues). 2) Handwashing with soap is not practised. 3) Water source is contaminated upstream. 4) Food handled by carriers.
chunks.source: 1) People don't use **latrine**s consistently (open defecation continues). 2) Handwashing with soap is not practised. 3) Water source is contaminated upstream. 4) Food handled by carriers.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: First Aid Basics. I can explain the principles of first aid, name the contents of a first aid kit, and describe the recovery position and emergency numbers in Uganda. First aid is immediate help for a casualty using DR ABC; every home and school needs a stocked kit and emergency numbers. Keywords: first aid: immediate help given to an injured person before medical care arrives; casualty: a person who is injured or ill and needs help; airway: the passage for air to reach the lungs; breathing: the process of taking air in and out of the lungs; circulation: the flow of blood through the body; recovery position: lying an unconscious breathing person on their side to keep the airway open; kit: a box or bag with medical supplies for first aid; emergency: a sudden dangerous situation needing immediate action
chunks.source: First aid is immediate help for a casualty using DR ABC; every home and school needs a stocked kit and emergency numbers.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What does DR ABC stand for? A: Danger, Response, Airway, Breathing, Circulation
chunks.source: Danger, Response, Airway, Breathing, Circulation

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name three items that should be in a first aid kit. A: Gauze, bandages, antiseptic wipes, scissors, safety pins, gloves (any three)
chunks.source: Gauze, bandages, antiseptic wipes, scissors, safety pins, gloves (any three)

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: When do you place a casualty in the recovery position? A: When they are unconscious but breathing normally
chunks.source: When they are unconscious but breathing normally

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What are the two main emergency numbers in Uganda? A: 999 for police and 112 for ambulance
chunks.source: 999 for police and 112 for ambulance

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why should you check for danger before helping a casualty? A: To avoid becoming a second casualty
chunks.source: To avoid becoming a second casualty

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: A classmate faints during assembly and wakes up after 30 seconds. Should you put them in the recovery position? Why or why not? A: No, because they are now conscious. Recovery position is only for unconscious breathing casualties.
chunks.source: No, because they are now conscious. Recovery position is only for unconscious breathing casualties.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: If you find a casualty not breathing, what should you do after checking danger and response? A: Open airway, check breathing, then start CPR (chest compressions and rescue breaths)
chunks.source: Open airway, check breathing, then start CPR (chest compressions and rescue breaths)

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why is it important to keep emergency numbers written down near the phone? A: So anyone can call quickly without wasting time searching for numbers
chunks.source: So anyone can call quickly without wasting time searching for numbers

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Fractures and Bleeding. I can identify a fracture, explain how to immobilise it with a splint and sling, and describe how to control severe bleeding with pressure and when to use a tourniquet. For fractures: immobilise with splint and sling. For severe bleeding: apply direct pressure first; tourniquet only as a last resort. Always seek hospital care.
