Keywords: fracture: a broken bone; splint: a rigid support used to keep a broken bone from moving; sling: a cloth bandage used to support an injured arm; haemorrhage: severe bleeding that can be life-threatening; pressure: pressing firmly on a wound to stop bleeding; tourniquet: a tight band used to stop all blood flow to a limb as a last resort; wound: an injury where the skin is cut or broken; immobilise: to keep a body part from moving
chunks.source: For fractures: immobilise with splint and sling. For severe bleeding: apply direct pressure first; tourniquet only as a last resort. Always seek hospital care.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is a fracture? A: A broken bone
chunks.source: A broken bone

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name two things used to immobilise a broken arm. A: A splint and a sling
chunks.source: A splint and a sling

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why should you not straighten a fractured limb? A: Moving bone ends can damage nerves and blood vessels
chunks.source: Moving bone ends can damage nerves and blood vessels

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is the first step to control severe bleeding? A: Apply direct pressure with a clean pad
chunks.source: Apply direct pressure with a clean pad

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: When should a tourniquet be used? A: Only as a last resort for severe limb bleeding that direct pressure cannot stop
chunks.source: Only as a last resort for severe limb bleeding that direct pressure cannot stop

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: If blood soaks through the first pad on a wound, what should you do? A: Add another pad on top; do not remove the first pad
chunks.source: Add another pad on top; do not remove the first pad

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: A boy falls from a mango tree and his leg is bent strangely. He is in pain. What are the first three steps you would take? A: 1. Tell him not to move. 2. Call for help. 3. Immobilise the leg with a splint if trained, otherwise keep it still until help arrives.
chunks.source: 1. Tell him not to move. 2. Call for help. 3. Immobilise the leg with a splint if trained, otherwise keep it still until help arrives.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why is it important to note the time a tourniquet is applied? A: Because leaving it on too long can cause permanent damage to the limb; medical staff need to know how long it has been on.
chunks.source: Because leaving it on too long can cause permanent damage to the limb; medical staff need to know how long it has been on.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Burns, Scalds and Drowning. I can explain first aid for burns and scalds including cooling and blister care, and describe the rescue steps and artificial respiration for drowning. Cool burns and scalds with running water for 20 minutes; never burst blisters. For drowning: Shout, Reach, Throw, Row, Go — never jump in. Give artificial respiration if not breathing. All drowning casualties need hospital. Keywords: burn: injury caused by dry heat like fire or hot metal; scald: injury caused by wet heat like boiling water or steam; blister: a bubble of fluid under the skin from a burn; cool: to lower the temperature of a burn with running water; drowning: suffocation in water; rescue: saving someone from danger; artificial respiration: giving rescue breaths to someone not breathing; shock: a life-threatening condition where circulation fails
chunks.source: Cool burns and scalds with running water for 20 minutes; never burst blisters. For drowning: Shout, Reach, Throw, Row, Go — never jump in. Give artificial respiration if not breathing. All drowning casualties need hospital.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is the difference between a burn and a scald? A: A burn is from dry heat (fire, hot metal); a scald is from wet heat (boiling water, steam)
chunks.source: A burn is from dry heat (fire, hot metal); a scald is from wet heat (boiling water, steam)

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How long should you cool a burn or scald under running water? A: At least 20 minutes
chunks.source: At least 20 minutes

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why should you not put butter, oil, or toothpaste on a burn? A: They trap heat and increase risk of infection
chunks.source: They trap heat and increase risk of infection

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What should you do if a blister forms on a burn? A: Leave it intact; cover loosely with a sterile non-stick dressing
chunks.source: Leave it intact; cover loosely with a sterile non-stick dressing

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: List the rescue order for drowning. A: Shout, Reach, Throw, Row, Go
chunks.source: Shout, Reach, Throw, Row, Go

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why should you not jump into water to rescue a drowning person? A: A panicked casualty can pull you under and drown you too
chunks.source: A panicked casualty can pull you under and drown you too

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is artificial respiration? A: Giving rescue breaths to a person who is not breathing
chunks.source: Giving rescue breaths to a person who is not breathing

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why must all drowning casualties go to hospital even if they seem fine? A: Water in the lungs can cause complications hours later (secondary drowning)
chunks.source: Water in the lungs can cause complications hours later (secondary drowning)

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Fainting, Fever and Poisoning. I can describe first aid for fainting and convulsions, manage fever with sponging and medication, and explain the correct action for poisoning including why not to induce vomiting. Fainting: lie down, raise legs. Convulsion: protect head, no objects in mouth. Fever: tepid sponge, fluids, paracetamol, hospital if high/drowsy. Poison: hospital with container, never induce vomiting, no home antidotes. Keywords: fainting: sudden brief loss of consciousness from reduced blood flow to the brain; convulsion: involuntary jerking of muscles, often with loss of consciousness; poison: a substance that causes harm if swallowed, inhaled, or absorbed; antidote: a substance that counteracts a specific poison; vomiting: forcefully bringing stomach contents up through the mouth; temperature: measure of body heat; high temperature means fever; sponge: to wipe the body with a damp cloth to lower temperature; hospital: a medical facility for serious illness or injury
chunks.source: Fainting: lie down, raise legs. Convulsion: protect head, no objects in mouth. Fever: tepid sponge, fluids, paracetamol, hospital if high/drowsy. Poison: hospital with container, never induce vomiting, no home antidotes.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is the first aid for fainting? A: Lay the person down, raise their legs, loosen tight clothing, ensure fresh air
chunks.source: Lay the person down, raise their legs, loosen tight clothing, ensure fresh air

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: If a person does not wake up after fainting for 2 minutes, what should you do? A: Place them in the recovery position and call emergency services
chunks.source: Place them in the recovery position and call emergency services

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: During a convulsion, why should you not put anything in the person's mouth? A: It can break teeth, block the airway, and you cannot stop the jaw clenching
chunks.source: It can break teeth, block the airway, and you cannot stop the jaw clenching

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How should you sponge a child with high fever? A: Use tepid (lukewarm) water, not cold water; wipe the body and let it evaporate
chunks.source: Use tepid (lukewarm) water, not cold water; wipe the body and let it evaporate

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: A child drinks bleach. Should you make them vomit? Why or why not? A: No. Bleach is corrosive; vomiting burns the oesophagus and throat again. Rush to hospital with the container.
chunks.source: No. Bleach is corrosive; vomiting burns the oesophagus and throat again. Rush to hospital with the container.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What information should you take to the hospital for a poisoning case? A: The container or label of the poison, amount taken, time taken, and the child's weight
chunks.source: The container or label of the poison, amount taken, time taken, and the child's weight

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why is it dangerous to give salt water to induce vomiting? A: It can cause salt poisoning (hypernatremia) which is life-threatening
chunks.source: It can cause salt poisoning (hypernatremia) which is life-threatening

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: If a child has a temperature of 40°C and is very drowsy, what should you do? A: Give paracetamol, sponge with tepid water, and take to hospital immediately
chunks.source: Give paracetamol, sponge with tepid water, and take to hospital immediately

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Types of Alcoholic Drinks. I can name local and factory alcoholic drinks in Uganda and explain how they are made. Factory **beer** is **brew**ed and labelled with **alcohol content**. Local drinks like **tonto** and **malwa** are **brew**ed at home by **ferment**ing. **Waragi** is **distil**led to make a strong spirit. All contain alcohol but strengths differ. Keywords: beer: a factory-made alcoholic drink from barley or sorghum; waragi: a strong local spirit distilled from banana or millet; tonto: a traditional banana beer brewed in Uganda; malwa: a millet or sorghum beer shared in a pot; brew: to make beer or alcohol by soaking and fermenting grain; distil: to heat a liquid and collect the vapour to make a stronger drink; ferment: when yeast turns sugar into alcohol over time; alcohol content: the percentage of pure alcohol in a drink
chunks.source: Factory **beer** is **brew**ed and labelled with **alcohol content**. Local drinks like **tonto** and **malwa** are **brew**ed at home by **ferment**ing. **Waragi** is **distil**led to make a strong spirit. All contain alcohol but strengths differ.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name two factory-made alcoholic drinks sold in Uganda. A: Beer, spirits like vodka or whisky (factory-made).
chunks.source: Beer, spirits like vodka or whisky (factory-made).

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name three traditional Ugandan alcoholic drinks. A: **Tonto**, **malwa**, **waragi**.
chunks.source: **Tonto**, **malwa**, **waragi**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What does **ferment** mean? A: Yeast turns sugar into alcohol over time.
chunks.source: Yeast turns sugar into alcohol over time.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What does **distil** mean? A: Heating a fermented liquid and collecting the vapour to make a stronger drink.
chunks.source: Heating a fermented liquid and collecting the vapour to make a stronger drink.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which has higher alcohol content: **beer** or **waragi**? A: **Waragi** (up to 40%) has higher alcohol content than **beer** (4-6%).
chunks.source: **Waragi** (up to 40%) has higher alcohol content than **beer** (4-6%).

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why is the alcohol content of **malwa** hard to know? A: It is home-brewed without labels or machines to measure it.
chunks.source: It is home-brewed without labels or machines to measure it.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: If a label says 5% alcohol content, how much pure alcohol is in 100ml? A: 5ml of pure alcohol.
chunks.source: 5ml of pure alcohol.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Peter thinks all local drinks are the same. Explain why he is wrong. A: **Tonto** and **malwa** are **brew**ed (fermented). **Waragi** is **distil**led, making it much stronger. They are made differently and have different alcohol content.
chunks.source: **Tonto** and **malwa** are **brew**ed (fermented). **Waragi** is **distil**led, making it much stronger. They are made differently and have different alcohol content.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Reasoning: A man drinks two bottles of **beer** (5% each, 500ml per bottle) and a small glass of **waragi** (40%, 50ml). Which gives more pure alcohol? Show your work. A: Beer: 2 bottles × 500ml × 5% = 50ml alcohol. Waragi: 50ml × 40% = 20ml alcohol. The beer gives more pure alcohol in this case.
chunks.source: Beer: 2 bottles × 500ml × 5% = 50ml alcohol. Waragi: 50ml × 40% = 20ml alcohol. The beer gives more pure alcohol in this case.

chunks.id: L-P6-Science-Effects of Alcohol on the Body
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: Effects of Alcohol on the Body
chunks.text: Effects of Alcohol on the Body. I can explain the short-term and long-term effects of alcohol on the liver, brain, and body. Alcohol slows the **brain** — causing **intoxication**, poor **judgement**, bad **coordination**. It damages the **liver** — leading to **cirrhosis**. Regular use causes **dependence** and **addiction**. Children should never drink. Keywords: liver: the organ that cleans blood and breaks down alcohol; brain: the organ that controls thinking, memory, and movement; addiction: a strong need to keep drinking even when it causes harm; cirrhosis: serious liver scarring caused by long-term heavy drinking; intoxication: being drunk — slurred speech, poor balance, slow reactions; coordination: the ability to move different body parts together smoothly; judgement: the ability to make good decisions; dependence: when the body gets used to alcohol and needs it to feel normal
chunks.source: Alcohol slows the **brain** — causing **intoxication**, poor **judgement**, bad **coordination**. It damages the **liver** — leading to **cirrhosis**. Regular use causes **dependence** and **addiction**. Children should never drink.

chunks.id: LQ-P6-Science-Effects of Alcohol on the Body
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: Effects of Alcohol on the Body
chunks.text: Q: Which organ breaks down alcohol in the body? A: The **liver**.
chunks.source: The **liver**.

chunks.id: LQ-P6-Science-Effects of Alcohol on the Body
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: Effects of Alcohol on the Body
chunks.text: Q: What is **intoxication**? A: Being drunk — slurred speech, poor balance, slow reactions.
chunks.source: Being drunk — slurred speech, poor balance, slow reactions.

chunks.id: LQ-P6-Science-Effects of Alcohol on the Body
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: Effects of Alcohol on the Body
chunks.text: Q: How does alcohol affect **judgement**? A: It makes decision-making poor, leading to risky choices.
chunks.source: It makes decision-making poor, leading to risky choices.

chunks.id: LQ-P6-Science-Effects of Alcohol on the Body
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: Effects of Alcohol on the Body
chunks.text: Q: What is **cirrhosis**? A: Serious scarring of the **liver** from long-term heavy drinking.
chunks.source: Serious scarring of the **liver** from long-term heavy drinking.

chunks.id: LQ-P6-Science-Effects of Alcohol on the Body
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: Effects of Alcohol on the Body
chunks.text: Q: What is the difference between **dependence** and **addiction**? A: **Dependence** is physical — body needs alcohol. **Addiction** is behavioural — cannot stop despite harm.
chunks.source: **Dependence** is physical — body needs alcohol. **Addiction** is behavioural — cannot stop despite harm.

chunks.id: LQ-P6-Science-Effects of Alcohol on the Body
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: Effects of Alcohol on the Body
chunks.text: Q: Why is drinking and riding a boda boda dangerous? A: Alcohol ruins **coordination** and **judgement**, causing **accidents**.
chunks.source: Alcohol ruins **coordination** and **judgement**, causing **accidents**.

chunks.id: LQ-P6-Science-Effects of Alcohol on the Body
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: Effects of Alcohol on the Body
chunks.text: Q: If someone has **dependence**, what happens when they stop drinking? A: They may shake, sweat, feel anxious — withdrawal symptoms.
chunks.source: They may shake, sweat, feel anxious — withdrawal symptoms.

chunks.id: LQ-P6-Science-Effects of Alcohol on the Body
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: Effects of Alcohol on the Body
chunks.text: Q: Name two long-term effects of heavy alcohol use. A: **Cirrhosis** of the **liver**, brain damage, **addiction**, memory loss.
chunks.source: **Cirrhosis** of the **liver**, brain damage, **addiction**, memory loss.

chunks.id: LQ-P6-Science-Effects of Alcohol on the Body
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: Effects of Alcohol on the Body
chunks.text: Q: Reasoning: A man says, 'I only drink **malwa**, it's weak, so my **liver** is safe.' Is he right? Explain. A: No. **Malwa** still contains alcohol. Daily drinking of any alcohol overworks the **liver**. **Cirrhosis** comes from total alcohol over time, not just strong drinks.
chunks.source: No. **Malwa** still contains alcohol. Daily drinking of any alcohol overworks the **liver**. **Cirrhosis** comes from total alcohol over time, not just strong drinks.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Alcohol and Society. I can describe how alcohol abuse affects families, communities, and the nation. **Alcohol abuse** harms society: **violence**, **poverty**, **accidents**, **neglect**, **divorce**, **crime**, low **productivity**. The drinker is not the only victim — families and the nation pay the price. Keywords: violence: hurting others physically or emotionally; poverty: being very poor, lacking basic needs; accidents: unplanned events causing injury or death; neglect: failing to care for those who depend on you; divorce: legal end of a marriage; crime: breaking the law; productivity: how much useful work a person or country does; abuse: using something in a harmful way
chunks.source: **Alcohol abuse** harms society: **violence**, **poverty**, **accidents**, **neglect**, **divorce**, **crime**, low **productivity**. The drinker is not the only victim — families and the nation pay the price.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name three social problems caused by alcohol abuse. A: **Violence**, **poverty**, **accidents**, **neglect**, **divorce**, **crime** (any three).
chunks.source: **Violence**, **poverty**, **accidents**, **neglect**, **divorce**, **crime** (any three).

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How does alcohol abuse cause **poverty**? A: Money spent on drink instead of food, rent, school fees.
chunks.source: Money spent on drink instead of food, rent, school fees.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is **neglect** in a family? A: Failing to care for dependents — not feeding, clothing, or supervising children.
chunks.source: Failing to care for dependents — not feeding, clothing, or supervising children.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why do drunk drivers cause **accidents**? A: Alcohol ruins **coordination** and **judgement**.
chunks.source: Alcohol ruins **coordination** and **judgement**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How does **alcohol abuse** lead to **crime**? A: People steal to buy drink; drunk people fight; youth with no hope turn to theft.
chunks.source: People steal to buy drink; drunk people fight; youth with no hope turn to theft.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What happens to **productivity** when workers drink heavily? A: They miss work, work poorly, get sick, have **accidents**.
chunks.source: They miss work, work poorly, get sick, have **accidents**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: If a mother drinks **tonto** all day and her baby is unfed, what is this? A: **Neglect** caused by **alcohol abuse**.
chunks.source: **Neglect** caused by **alcohol abuse**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name two ways alcohol abuse affects children in a home. A: **Neglect**, **violence**, hunger, poor school attendance, emotional trauma, copying the habit.
chunks.source: **Neglect**, **violence**, hunger, poor school attendance, emotional trauma, copying the habit.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Reasoning: A village passes a bylaw closing bars at 10pm. After six months, **accidents** drop 30% and school attendance rises. Explain the link. A: Less drinking time → less **intoxication** → fewer drunk drivers (**accidents** down). Parents home earlier → less **neglect**, more money for school → attendance up. Bylaws reduce **abuse**, helping families and **productivity**.
chunks.source: Less drinking time → less **intoxication** → fewer drunk drivers (**accidents** down). Parents home earlier → less **neglect**, more money for school → attendance up. Bylaws reduce **abuse**, helping families and **productivity**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Preventing Alcohol Abuse. I can explain laws, strategies, and personal choices that prevent alcohol abuse in Uganda. Prevention uses many tools: **law** (**age limit** 18), **education**, **religion**, **alternative** activities, resisting **peer pressure**, **counselling**, **rehabilitation**. Together they protect individuals and communities from **alcohol abuse**. Keywords: law: official rules made by parliament; age limit: the minimum legal age to buy or drink alcohol; counselling: talking with a trained person to solve problems; rehabilitation: a programme to help someone recover from addiction; alternative: something you do instead of a harmful habit; peer pressure: when friends push you to do something you may not want; religion: faith teachings that guide behaviour; education: learning facts to make wise choices
chunks.source: Prevention uses many tools: **law** (**age limit** 18), **education**, **religion**, **alternative** activities, resisting **peer pressure**, **counselling**, **rehabilitation**. Together they protect individuals and communities from **alcohol abuse**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is Uganda's legal **age limit** for buying alcohol? A: 18 years.
chunks.source: 18 years.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name two things the **law** does to control alcohol. A: Sets **age limit**, licenses sellers, taxes drinks, bans sales to children, regulates hours.
chunks.source: Sets **age limit**, licenses sellers, taxes drinks, bans sales to children, regulates hours.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How does **education** prevent alcohol abuse? A: Teaches facts about harm, builds decision-making skills, counters myths.
chunks.source: Teaches facts about harm, builds decision-making skills, counters myths.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is **peer pressure**? A: Friends pushing you to do something you may not want, like drinking.
chunks.source: Friends pushing you to do something you may not want, like drinking.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give two examples of healthy **alternative** activities for youth. A: Sports, music, drama, farming, clubs, volunteering, reading.
chunks.source: Sports, music, drama, farming, clubs, volunteering, reading.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is the role of **counselling** in treating alcohol problems? A: Helps person understand triggers, develop coping skills, change thinking.
chunks.source: Helps person understand triggers, develop coping skills, change thinking.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How is **rehabilitation** different from **counselling**? A: **Rehabilitation** is a full programme (detox, **counselling**, skills, group, aftercare); **counselling** is talk therapy within it.
chunks.source: **Rehabilitation** is a full programme (detox, **counselling**, skills, group, aftercare); **counselling** is talk therapy within it.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name two ways **religion** helps prevent alcohol abuse. A: Teaches moderation/abstinence, provides community support, gives moral framework.
chunks.source: Teaches moderation/abstinence, provides community support, gives moral framework.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Reasoning: A village has strict **law** enforcement but no youth centre. Another has a great youth centre but ignores the **age limit**. Which approach is better? Explain. A: Both are needed. **Law** without **alternative** activities leaves youth bored and tempted. **Alternative** activities without **law** allow easy access. Best: enforce **age limit** AND provide sports, clubs, **education**, **counselling**. Prevention works in layers.
chunks.source: Both are needed. **Law** without **alternative** activities leaves youth bored and tempted. **Alternative** activities without **law** allow easy access. Best: enforce **age limit** AND provide sports, clubs, **education**, **counselling**. Prevention works in layers.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: The Heart. I can name the parts of the heart and explain how they work together to pump blood. The heart has four chambers (two atria, two ventricles) separated by a septum. Valves keep blood moving one way. The pericardium protects the heart. Each beat makes a pulse you can feel. Keywords: heart: the muscular pump in your chest that moves blood; atrium: an upper chamber of the heart that receives blood; ventricle: a lower chamber of the heart that pumps blood out; valve: a flap that opens and closes to keep blood moving one way; septum: the thick wall that separates the left and right sides of the heart; pericardium: the tough sac that surrounds and protects the heart; beat: one complete squeeze and relax of the heart; pulse: the throb you feel in an artery each time the heart beats
chunks.source: The heart has four chambers (two atria, two ventricles) separated by a septum. Valves keep blood moving one way. The pericardium protects the heart. Each beat makes a pulse you can feel.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name the four chambers of the heart. A: Right atrium, left atrium, right ventricle, left ventricle.
chunks.source: Right atrium, left atrium, right ventricle, left ventricle.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is the job of the pericardium? A: It protects the heart and holds it in place.
chunks.source: It protects the heart and holds it in place.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which valve sound is 'lub' and which is 'dub'? A: Lub = valves between atria and ventricles close. Dub = valves at artery exits close.
chunks.source: Lub = valves between atria and ventricles close. Dub = valves at artery exits close.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: If the septum has a hole, what happens? A: Oxygen-rich and oxygen-poor blood mix.
chunks.source: Oxygen-rich and oxygen-poor blood mix.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How do you measure your pulse rate per minute? A: Count beats at wrist for 15 seconds, multiply by 4.
chunks.source: Count beats at wrist for 15 seconds, multiply by 4.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why does the left ventricle have a thicker wall than the right? A: It pumps blood to the whole body, needing more force.
chunks.source: It pumps blood to the whole body, needing more force.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What would happen if a valve let blood leak backwards? A: The heart works harder and you get tired easily.
chunks.source: The heart works harder and you get tired easily.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Draw a simple heart and label: atrium, ventricle, valve, septum, pericardium. A: Drawing shows four chambers, valves between them, septum down middle, pericardium outside.
chunks.source: Drawing shows four chambers, valves between them, septum down middle, pericardium outside.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Reasoning: A doctor hears a 'whoosh' sound between lub and dub. Which valve might be leaky? A: The valve between atrium and ventricle (mitral or tricuspid) because lub is those valves closing.
chunks.source: The valve between atrium and ventricle (mitral or tricuspid) because lub is those valves closing.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Blood Vessels. I can explain the differences between arteries, veins and capillaries and how they work together. Arteries have thick muscular walls for high pressure; veins have thinner walls, valves, and low pressure; capillaries have one-cell walls for exchange. The aorta and vena cava are the largest vessels. Keywords: artery: a thick-walled vessel that carries fresh blood away from the heart; vein: a thinner-walled vessel that carries used blood back to the heart; capillary: a tiny vessel with walls one cell thick where oxygen swaps with tissues; aorta: the main artery leaving the left ventricle to the body; vena cava: the main vein bringing used blood to the right atrium; pressure: the force of blood pushing against vessel walls; wall: the layers of tissue that make up a blood vessel; valve: a flap inside veins that keeps blood moving toward the heart
chunks.source: Arteries have thick muscular walls for high pressure; veins have thinner walls, valves, and low pressure; capillaries have one-cell walls for exchange. The aorta and vena cava are the largest vessels.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: List the three main types of blood vessels. A: Artery, vein, capillary.
chunks.source: Artery, vein, capillary.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which vessel has the thickest wall and why? A: Artery, because it withstands high pressure from the heart.
chunks.source: Artery, because it withstands high pressure from the heart.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is the function of the aorta? A: Main artery carrying fresh blood from left ventricle to the body.
chunks.source: Main artery carrying fresh blood from left ventricle to the body.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is the function of the vena cava? A: Main vein bringing used blood to right atrium.
chunks.source: Main vein bringing used blood to right atrium.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why are capillary walls only one cell thick? A: To allow oxygen and nutrients to pass easily to cells.
chunks.source: To allow oxygen and nutrients to pass easily to cells.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How do valves in veins work? A: They open when blood moves toward the heart and close to prevent backflow.
chunks.source: They open when blood moves toward the heart and close to prevent backflow.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Compare pressure in arteries vs veins. A: Arteries have high pressure; veins have low pressure.
chunks.source: Arteries have high pressure; veins have low pressure.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Worked example: A runner's leg muscles help blood return to the heart. Explain how. A: Muscle contractions squeeze veins, pushing blood upward past valves.
chunks.source: Muscle contractions squeeze veins, pushing blood upward past valves.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: If a person stands still for a long time, blood may pool in legs. Why? A: Without muscle squeezes, valves cannot push blood up against gravity.
chunks.source: Without muscle squeezes, valves cannot push blood up against gravity.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Reasoning: Why don't capillaries have valves? A: Blood flows slowly and pressure is very low; valves are not needed to prevent backflow.
chunks.source: Blood flows slowly and pressure is very low; valves are not needed to prevent backflow.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Blood and Its Functions. I can name the components of blood and describe what each one does. Blood has four parts: red cells carry oxygen with haemoglobin; white cells make antibodies to fight germs; platelets start clotting; plasma is the liquid that transports everything. Keywords: red cells: disc-shaped cells that carry oxygen using haemoglobin; white cells: cells that fight germs and make antibodies; platelets: tiny cell fragments that help blood clot; plasma: the yellow liquid part of blood that carries everything; haemoglobin: the protein in red cells that grabs oxygen; clotting: the process where platelets and proteins form a plug to stop bleeding; antibodies: proteins made by white cells that target specific germs; transport: the job of blood to carry oxygen, nutrients, waste and heat around the body
chunks.source: Blood has four parts: red cells carry oxygen with haemoglobin; white cells make antibodies to fight germs; platelets start clotting; plasma is the liquid that transports everything.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What are the four main components of blood? A: Red cells, white cells, platelets, plasma.
chunks.source: Red cells, white cells, platelets, plasma.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What protein in red cells carries oxygen? A: Haemoglobin.
chunks.source: Haemoglobin.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which component fights infection and makes antibodies? A: White cells.
chunks.source: White cells.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What starts the clotting process when you cut yourself? A: Platelets stick to the wound and release clotting chemicals.
chunks.source: Platelets stick to the wound and release clotting chemicals.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is plasma mostly made of? A: Water (about 90%).
chunks.source: Water (about 90%).

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why are red cells shaped like discs with a dent? A: Increases surface area for oxygen exchange and allows flexibility in capillaries.
chunks.source: Increases surface area for oxygen exchange and allows flexibility in capillaries.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How do antibodies help immunity? A: They bind to specific germs, marking them for destruction and remembering them for faster response next time.
chunks.source: They bind to specific germs, marking them for destruction and remembering them for faster response next time.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Worked example: Trace glucose from mouth to muscle cell. A: Mouth → stomach → intestine → plasma (in capillary) → muscle cell.
chunks.source: Mouth → stomach → intestine → plasma (in capillary) → muscle cell.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: If plasma leaked out of capillaries into tissues, what would happen? A: Swelling (oedema) because fluid builds up; blood volume drops.
chunks.source: Swelling (oedema) because fluid builds up; blood volume drops.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Reasoning: A person has normal red cells but low haemoglobin. What condition? Why tired? A: Iron deficiency anaemia. Haemoglobin needs iron; without it, red cells carry less oxygen.
chunks.source: Iron deficiency anaemia. Haemoglobin needs iron; without it, red cells carry less oxygen.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Diseases of the Circulatory System. I can name common circulatory diseases, explain their causes, and list healthy habits to prevent them. Hypertension (high pressure), anaemia (low iron), sickle cell (inherited), leukaemia (white cell cancer), heart attack and stroke (vessel blockage) are major circulatory diseases. Prevention: healthy diet, exercise, no smoking, regular check-ups. Keywords: hypertension: high blood pressure that strains the heart and vessels; anaemia: too few red cells or too little haemoglobin, causing tiredness; leukaemia: cancer of white blood cells that crowds out healthy cells; heart attack: blockage of blood flow to heart muscle, causing damage; sickle cell: inherited condition where red cells become crescent-shaped and block vessels; clot: a solid lump of blood that can block a vessel; stroke: brain damage from blocked or burst blood vessel in the brain; prevention: healthy habits that lower risk of circulatory diseases
chunks.source: Hypertension (high pressure), anaemia (low iron), sickle cell (inherited), leukaemia (white cell cancer), heart attack and stroke (vessel blockage) are major circulatory diseases. Prevention: healthy diet, exercise, no smoking, regular check-ups.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is hypertension and one main cause? A: High blood pressure; main cause: too much salt.
chunks.source: High blood pressure; main cause: too much salt.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: List three signs of anaemia. A: Pale palms, tiredness, shortness of breath.
chunks.source: Pale palms, tiredness, shortness of breath.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How does sickle cell disease affect red cells? A: Red cells become crescent-shaped, block vessels, cause pain crises.
chunks.source: Red cells become crescent-shaped, block vessels, cause pain crises.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is leukaemia? A: Cancer of white blood cells that crowds out healthy blood cells.
chunks.source: Cancer of white blood cells that crowds out healthy blood cells.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Compare heart attack and stroke. A: Heart attack: clot blocks heart artery. Stroke: clot or burst vessel in brain.
chunks.source: Heart attack: clot blocks heart artery. Stroke: clot or burst vessel in brain.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why is hypertension called the 'silent killer'? A: Often has no symptoms until damage is done.
chunks.source: Often has no symptoms until damage is done.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name three prevention habits for circulatory diseases. A: Eat less salt, exercise daily, don't smoke, sleep under mosquito net, check blood pressure.
chunks.source: Eat less salt, exercise daily, don't smoke, sleep under mosquito net, check blood pressure.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Worked example: A 50-year-old trader smokes, eats fried food, never checks pressure. He gets chest pain. What likely happened? What should he do? A: Heart attack. Call for help, get to hospital immediately.
chunks.source: Heart attack. Call for help, get to hospital immediately.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: If a child has frequent infections and bruises easily, what might the doctor suspect? A: Leukaemia — abnormal white cells crowd out platelets and healthy white cells.
chunks.source: Leukaemia — abnormal white cells crowd out platelets and healthy white cells.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Reasoning: Why does dehydration trigger sickle cell crisis? A: Less water makes blood thicker; red cells sickle more easily and block capillaries.
chunks.source: Less water makes blood thicker; red cells sickle more easily and block capillaries.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Parts of the Respiratory System. I can name and locate the main parts of the respiratory system and explain their functions. The respiratory system includes the **nose**, **trachea**, **bronchi**, **lungs**, **alveoli**, **pleura**, **ribs**, and **diaphragm**. Air travels through passages to reach the **alveoli** where **gaseous exchange** occurs. The **diaphragm** and **ribs** create the movements for breathing. Keywords: nose: the opening where air enters the body; trachea: the windpipe that carries air to the lungs; bronchi: two tubes that branch from the trachea into each lung; lungs: the main organs where gas exchange happens; diaphragm: a dome-shaped muscle below the lungs that moves to help breathing; ribs: bones that form a cage protecting the lungs and heart; alveoli: tiny air sacs in the lungs where oxygen enters the blood; pleura: a thin membrane that covers the lungs and lines the chest cavity
chunks.source: The respiratory system includes the **nose**, **trachea**, **bronchi**, **lungs**, **alveoli**, **pleura**, **ribs**, and **diaphragm**. Air travels through passages to reach the **alveoli** where **gaseous exchange** occurs. The **diaphragm** and **ribs** create the movements for breathing.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name the part where air enters the body. A: The **nose**.
chunks.source: The **nose**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is the windpipe called? A: The **trachea**.
chunks.source: The **trachea**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Into what two tubes does the trachea divide? A: The **bronchi**.
chunks.source: The **bronchi**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Where does oxygen enter the blood? A: In the **alveoli**.
chunks.source: In the **alveoli**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What membrane covers the lungs? A: The **pleura**.
chunks.source: The **pleura**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which bones protect the lungs? A: The **ribs**.
chunks.source: The **ribs**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What muscle lies below the lungs? A: The **diaphragm**.
chunks.source: The **diaphragm**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: List the path of air from nose to alveoli. A: **Nose** → **trachea** → **bronchi** → **lungs** → **alveoli**.
chunks.source: **Nose** → **trachea** → **bronchi** → **lungs** → **alveoli**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why are alveoli walls so thin? A: To allow **diffusion** of oxygen into blood.
chunks.source: To allow **diffusion** of oxygen into blood.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What would happen if the pleura were damaged? A: The **lungs** would not slide smoothly; breathing would be painful.
chunks.source: The **lungs** would not slide smoothly; breathing would be painful.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: How Breathing Happens. I can explain the mechanism of inhalation and exhalation using volume and pressure changes. **Inhalation**: **diaphragm** contracts, **rib cage** expands, **volume** increases, **pressure** drops, air enters. **Exhalation**: **diaphragm** relaxes, **rib cage** falls, **volume** decreases, **pressure** rises, air leaves. **Gaseous exchange** by **diffusion** at the **alveoli**. Keywords: inhalation: breathing in; taking air into the lungs; exhalation: breathing out; pushing air out of the lungs; diaphragm: the main breathing muscle that contracts and flattens; rib cage: the bony structure formed by ribs that protects the lungs; volume: the amount of space inside the chest cavity; pressure: the force of air pushing on surfaces; gaseous exchange: the swap of oxygen and carbon dioxide in the alveoli; diffusion: movement of gas from high concentration to low concentration
chunks.source: **Inhalation**: **diaphragm** contracts, **rib cage** expands, **volume** increases, **pressure** drops, air enters. **Exhalation**: **diaphragm** relaxes, **rib cage** falls, **volume** decreases, **pressure** rises, air leaves. **Gaseous exchange** by **diffusion** at the **alveoli**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is inhalation? A: Breathing in; active process where the **diaphragm** contracts and **rib cage** expands.
chunks.source: Breathing in; active process where the **diaphragm** contracts and **rib cage** expands.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is exhalation? A: Breathing out; usually passive where the **diaphragm** relaxes and **rib cage** falls.
chunks.source: Breathing out; usually passive where the **diaphragm** relaxes and **rib cage** falls.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What happens to chest volume during inhalation? A: Chest **volume** increases.
chunks.source: Chest **volume** increases.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What happens to pressure inside the lungs during inhalation? A: **Pressure** decreases below atmospheric **pressure**.
chunks.source: **Pressure** decreases below atmospheric **pressure**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why does air flow into the lungs? A: Air moves from high **pressure** outside to low **pressure** inside.
chunks.source: Air moves from high **pressure** outside to low **pressure** inside.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is the main muscle of breathing? A: The **diaphragm**.
chunks.source: The **diaphragm**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How does oxygen enter the blood? A: By **diffusion** from high concentration in **alveoli** to low concentration in blood.
chunks.source: By **diffusion** from high concentration in **alveoli** to low concentration in blood.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is gaseous exchange? A: The swap of oxygen and carbon dioxide in the **alveoli**.
chunks.source: The swap of oxygen and carbon dioxide in the **alveoli**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Describe the syringe model of breathing. A: Pull plunger → **volume** up, **pressure** down → air in (**inhalation**). Push plunger → **volume** down, **pressure** up → air out (**exhalation**).
chunks.source: Pull plunger → **volume** up, **pressure** down → air in (**inhalation**). Push plunger → **volume** down, **pressure** up → air out (**exhalation**).

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why is exhalation usually passive? A: The **diaphragm** and **rib cage** relax due to elasticity; no muscle contraction needed.
chunks.source: The **diaphragm** and **rib cage** relax due to elasticity; no muscle contraction needed.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Diseases of the Respiratory System. I can identify common respiratory diseases, their causes, symptoms, and prevention methods. **Pneumonia**, **tuberculosis**, **influenza**, **bronchitis** are **infections**. **Asthma** is a chronic condition triggered by **dust** and **smoking**. **Smoking** and **dust** damage airways. Prevention: **ventilation**, **vaccination**, no **smoking**, reduce **dust**, cover coughs, seek early treatment. Keywords: pneumonia: infection causing lung inflammation and fluid in alveoli; tuberculosis: bacterial infection that mainly attacks the lungs; asthma: condition where airways narrow and swell, making breathing hard; influenza: viral infection of the nose, throat, and lungs; bronchitis: inflammation of the bronchial tubes; smoking: inhaling tobacco smoke which damages lungs; dust: fine particles that irritate the airways; infection: invasion by germs like bacteria or viruses
chunks.source: **Pneumonia**, **tuberculosis**, **influenza**, **bronchitis** are **infections**. **Asthma** is a chronic condition triggered by **dust** and **smoking**. **Smoking** and **dust** damage airways. Prevention: **ventilation**, **vaccination**, no **smoking**, reduce **dust**, cover coughs, seek early treatment.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name two diseases caused by bacterial infection. A: **Tuberculosis** and bacterial **pneumonia**.
chunks.source: **Tuberculosis** and bacterial **pneumonia**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name a viral respiratory disease. A: **Influenza** (or viral **pneumonia**).
chunks.source: **Influenza** (or viral **pneumonia**).

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What triggers asthma attacks? A: **Dust**, **smoking**, cold air, exercise, allergens.
chunks.source: **Dust**, **smoking**, cold air, exercise, allergens.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How does smoking damage the respiratory system? A: Damages **trachea**, **bronchi**, **alveoli**; causes chronic **bronchitis**, cancer.
chunks.source: Damages **trachea**, **bronchi**, **alveoli**; causes chronic **bronchitis**, cancer.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What are the main symptoms of tuberculosis? A: Cough >2 weeks, night sweats, weight loss, fever.
chunks.source: Cough >2 weeks, night sweats, weight loss, fever.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How does influenza spread? A: Through cough/sneeze droplets; crowded places.
chunks.source: Through cough/sneeze droplets; crowded places.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why is ventilation important? A: Removes **infection** droplets; reduces **dust** concentration.
chunks.source: Removes **infection** droplets; reduces **dust** concentration.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What vaccination prevents tuberculosis? A: BCG vaccine given at birth.
chunks.source: BCG vaccine given at birth.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Compare bronchitis and asthma. A: **Bronchitis**: inflamed **bronchi**, mucus cough, often from **infection**. **Asthma**: narrowed **bronchi**, wheezing, triggered by **dust**/**smoking**, not an **infection**.
chunks.source: **Bronchitis**: inflamed **bronchi**, mucus cough, often from **infection**. **Asthma**: narrowed **bronchi**, wheezing, triggered by **dust**/**smoking**, not an **infection**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: A child has sudden fever, body aches, sore throat. What is the likely disease? A: **Influenza** — viral **infection** with sudden onset.
chunks.source: **Influenza** — viral **infection** with sudden onset.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Keeping Lungs Healthy. I can describe habits that protect the respiratory system and demonstrate healthy breathing practices. Healthy lungs need: **exercise** to strengthen muscles, no **smoking**, **ventilation** for **clean air**, **dust mask** in dusty places, **vaccination** against **infection**, good **posture** for maximum **volume**, and daily **deep breathing** to clear **alveoli** and boost **gaseous exchange**. Keywords: exercise: physical activity that strengthens the heart and lungs; smoking: inhaling tobacco smoke which damages the respiratory system; ventilation: fresh air moving through a space; dust mask: a mask that filters out dust particles; vaccination: getting vaccines to prevent infectious diseases; clean air: air free from smoke, dust, and pollutants; posture: the position of the body when sitting or standing; deep breathing: slow, full breaths that use the whole lung capacity
chunks.source: Healthy lungs need: **exercise** to strengthen muscles, no **smoking**, **ventilation** for **clean air**, **dust mask** in dusty places, **vaccination** against **infection**, good **posture** for maximum **volume**, and daily **deep breathing** to clear **alveoli** and boost **gaseous exchange**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How does exercise help the respiratory system? A: Strengthens **diaphragm** and **rib cage** muscles; increases **lung** capacity; improves **gaseous exchange**.
chunks.source: Strengthens **diaphragm** and **rib cage** muscles; increases **lung** capacity; improves **gaseous exchange**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why is smoking harmful to lungs? A: Destroys **alveoli**; paralyses cilia in **trachea**/**bronchi**; causes cancer, **bronchitis**.
chunks.source: Destroys **alveoli**; paralyses cilia in **trachea**/**bronchi**; causes cancer, **bronchitis**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What does ventilation do? A: Brings **clean air** in; removes **infection** droplets, **dust**, smoke.
chunks.source: Brings **clean air** in; removes **infection** droplets, **dust**, smoke.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: When should you wear a dust mask? A: During dusty work: quarry, dry garden, sweeping, threshing.
chunks.source: During dusty work: quarry, dry garden, sweeping, threshing.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which vaccinations protect the respiratory system? A: BCG for **tuberculosis**; **influenza** vaccine; pneumococcal vaccine.
chunks.source: BCG for **tuberculosis**; **influenza** vaccine; pneumococcal vaccine.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How does posture affect breathing? A: Good **posture** allows full **rib cage** expansion and **diaphragm** descent; slouching restricts **volume**.
chunks.source: Good **posture** allows full **rib cage** expansion and **diaphragm** descent; slouching restricts **volume**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is deep breathing? A: Slow, full **inhalation** through **nose**, complete **exhalation**; uses full **lung** capacity.
chunks.source: Slow, full **inhalation** through **nose**, complete **exhalation**; uses full **lung** capacity.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: List five habits for healthy lungs. A: **Exercise**, no **smoking**, good **ventilation**, **dust mask** when needed, **vaccination**, good **posture**, **deep breathing**, **clean air**.
chunks.source: **Exercise**, no **smoking**, good **ventilation**, **dust mask** when needed, **vaccination**, good **posture**, **deep breathing**, **clean air**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: A farmer works in a dusty maize store. What three things protect his lungs? A: Wear **dust mask**, ensure **ventilation**, wet-sweep to reduce **dust**, no **smoking**.
chunks.source: Wear **dust mask**, ensure **ventilation**, wet-sweep to reduce **dust**, no **smoking**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why is deep breathing better than shallow breathing? A: **Deep breathing** reaches lower **alveoli**, clears stale air, improves **gaseous exchange**, calms the nervous system.
chunks.source: **Deep breathing** reaches lower **alveoli**, clears stale air, improves **gaseous exchange**, calms the nervous system.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: The Male Reproductive System. I can name the male reproductive organs and explain their functions. The male reproductive system includes the testes, scrotum, penis, urethra, and prostate. The testes make sperm and testosterone. The scrotum keeps testes cool. The prostate adds fluid to make semen. The urethra carries semen out through the penis. These changes start at puberty. Keywords: testes: two oval organs that make sperm and hormones; sperm: tiny cells made in the testes that can join with an egg; penis: the outside organ used for passing urine and delivering sperm; scrotum: the loose bag of skin that holds the testes; urethra: the tube inside the penis that carries urine and semen out; prostate: a gland that adds fluid to sperm to make semen; semen: the whitish fluid that carries sperm out of the body; puberty: the time when a child's body changes into an adult body
chunks.source: The male reproductive system includes the testes, scrotum, penis, urethra, and prostate. The testes make sperm and testosterone. The scrotum keeps testes cool. The prostate adds fluid to make semen. The urethra carries semen out through the penis. These changes start at puberty.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name the organ that makes sperm and testosterone. A: The testes.
chunks.source: The testes.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is the function of the scrotum? A: It holds the testes and keeps them cool for sperm production.
chunks.source: It holds the testes and keeps them cool for sperm production.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which gland adds fluid to sperm to form semen? A: The prostate gland.
chunks.source: The prostate gland.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Through which tube does semen leave the body? A: The urethra inside the penis.
chunks.source: The urethra inside the penis.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is semen made of? A: Sperm and fluids from the prostate and other glands.
chunks.source: Sperm and fluids from the prostate and other glands.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: At what life stage do the male reproductive organs mature? A: Puberty.
chunks.source: Puberty.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why must the testes be kept cooler than body temperature? A: Cool temperature is needed for healthy sperm production.
chunks.source: Cool temperature is needed for healthy sperm production.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Peter notices his voice is deepening and hair is growing on his face. What is happening? A: He is going through puberty.
chunks.source: He is going through puberty.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Explain the journey of sperm from production to leaving the body. A: Sperm are made in the testes, travel through the vas deferens, mix with fluids from the prostate and other glands to become semen, then pass through the urethra in the penis during ejaculation.
chunks.source: Sperm are made in the testes, travel through the vas deferens, mix with fluids from the prostate and other glands to become semen, then pass through the urethra in the penis during ejaculation.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: A boy thinks urine and semen come out together. Is he correct? Why or why not? A: No. A muscle closes the bladder opening when semen passes, so urine and semen never mix or come out at the same time.
chunks.source: No. A muscle closes the bladder opening when semen passes, so urine and semen never mix or come out at the same time.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: The Female Reproductive System. I can name the female reproductive organs and explain their functions. The female reproductive system includes two ovaries that release eggs, two oviducts that carry eggs to the uterus, the uterus where a baby grows, the cervix at the bottom of the uterus, and the vagina leading outside. Menstruation is the monthly shedding of the uterus lining when no egg is fertilised. These changes begin at puberty. Keywords: ovary: one of two organs that store and release eggs; egg: the female reproductive cell that can join with sperm; uterus: the hollow muscular organ where a baby grows; oviduct: the tube that carries the egg from the ovary to the uterus; vagina: the muscular canal leading from the uterus to the outside; cervix: the narrow lower part of the uterus that opens into the vagina; menstruation: the monthly flow of blood and tissue from the uterus; puberty: the time when a girl's body changes into a woman's body
chunks.source: The female reproductive system includes two ovaries that release eggs, two oviducts that carry eggs to the uterus, the uterus where a baby grows, the cervix at the bottom of the uterus, and the vagina leading outside. Menstruation is the monthly shedding of the uterus lining when no egg is fertilised. These changes begin at puberty.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name the organ that stores and releases eggs. A: The ovary.
chunks.source: The ovary.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is the name of the tube that carries the egg to the uterus? A: The oviduct (fallopian tube).
chunks.source: The oviduct (fallopian tube).

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Where does a baby grow during pregnancy? A: In the uterus.
chunks.source: In the uterus.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is the cervix? A: The narrow lower part of the uterus that opens into the vagina.
chunks.source: The narrow lower part of the uterus that opens into the vagina.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is menstruation? A: The monthly flow of blood and tissue from the uterus when no egg is fertilised.
chunks.source: The monthly flow of blood and tissue from the uterus when no egg is fertilised.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How often does an ovary usually release an egg? A: Once a month.
chunks.source: Once a month.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is the function of the vagina? A: It is the passage for menstruation flow and for a baby during birth.
chunks.source: It is the passage for menstruation flow and for a baby during birth.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Amina is 12 and has not started menstruation. Her friend has. Should she worry? A: No. Puberty starts at different ages for different girls, usually between 10 and 15.
chunks.source: No. Puberty starts at different ages for different girls, usually between 10 and 15.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Trace the path of an egg from the ovary to outside the body if it is not fertilised. A: Ovary → oviduct → uterus → cervix → vagina (as part of menstruation).
chunks.source: Ovary → oviduct → uterus → cervix → vagina (as part of menstruation).

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why does the uterus lining thicken each month? A: To prepare for a possible fertilised egg to implant and grow.
chunks.source: To prepare for a possible fertilised egg to implant and grow.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Fertilisation and Pregnancy. I can explain how fertilisation happens and describe the stages of pregnancy until birth. Fertilisation joins sperm and egg in the oviduct to form a zygote. The zygote divides, moves to the uterus, and implants. The placenta and umbilical cord feed the baby during gestation (about 40 weeks). Antenatal care keeps mother and baby healthy. Delivery is the birth of the baby. Keywords: fertilisation: the joining of a sperm and an egg; zygote: the single cell formed when sperm and egg join; implantation: the attachment of the developing embryo to the uterus lining; placenta: the organ that grows in the uterus to feed the baby; umbilical cord: the rope-like cord connecting the baby to the placenta; gestation: the time the baby develops inside the uterus, about nine months; antenatal: care and check-ups for a pregnant woman before birth; delivery: the process of giving birth to the baby
chunks.source: Fertilisation joins sperm and egg in the oviduct to form a zygote. The zygote divides, moves to the uterus, and implants. The placenta and umbilical cord feed the baby during gestation (about 40 weeks). Antenatal care keeps mother and baby healthy. Delivery is the birth of the baby.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is fertilisation? A: The joining of a sperm and an egg.
chunks.source: The joining of a sperm and an egg.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Where does fertilisation usually occur? A: In the oviduct (fallopian tube).
chunks.source: In the oviduct (fallopian tube).

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is a zygote? A: The single cell formed when sperm and egg join.
chunks.source: The single cell formed when sperm and egg join.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is implantation? A: The attachment of the developing embryo to the uterus lining.
chunks.source: The attachment of the developing embryo to the uterus lining.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What does the placenta do? A: Passes oxygen and nutrients from mother to baby and removes waste.
chunks.source: Passes oxygen and nutrients from mother to baby and removes waste.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is the umbilical cord? A: The cord connecting the baby to the placenta, carrying blood vessels.
chunks.source: The cord connecting the baby to the placenta, carrying blood vessels.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How long is human gestation? A: About 40 weeks (nine months).
chunks.source: About 40 weeks (nine months).

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why are antenatal visits important? A: To check the baby's growth, heartbeat, and the mother's health.
chunks.source: To check the baby's growth, heartbeat, and the mother's health.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Describe the journey from fertilisation to implantation. A: Sperm meets egg in oviduct → forms zygote → zygote divides → travels to uterus → implants in uterus lining about 6 days later.
chunks.source: Sperm meets egg in oviduct → forms zygote → zygote divides → travels to uterus → implants in uterus lining about 6 days later.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: A pregnant woman skips antenatal visits because she feels fine. Is this wise? Explain. A: No. Antenatal visits catch problems early, monitor baby's growth, and give the mother iron/folic acid. Feeling fine does not mean everything is fine.
chunks.source: No. Antenatal visits catch problems early, monitor baby's growth, and give the mother iron/folic acid. Feeling fine does not mean everything is fine.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: STIs and HIV Prevention. I can name common STIs, explain how HIV spreads, and describe ways to prevent infection. STIs spread through sex. HIV causes AIDS and has no cure, but medicine controls it. Syphilis and gonorrhoea are bacterial and curable. Prevention: abstinence (best for youth), faithfulness to one tested partner, condoms used correctly every time. Regular testing finds infections early. No shame in protecting your health. Keywords: HIV: a virus that attacks the body's defence system; AIDS: the late stage of HIV infection when the body cannot fight diseases; syphilis: a bacterial STI that causes sores and can damage organs if untreated; gonorrhoea: a bacterial STI that causes discharge and pain when urinating; abstinence: choosing not to have sex until ready, usually after marriage; faithfulness: having sex with only one uninfected partner who also has only you; condom: a thin rubber sheath worn on the penis during sex to block fluids; testing: checking your blood for HIV and other STIs at a health centre
chunks.source: STIs spread through sex. HIV causes AIDS and has no cure, but medicine controls it. Syphilis and gonorrhoea are bacterial and curable. Prevention: abstinence (best for youth), faithfulness to one tested partner, condoms used correctly every time. Regular testing finds infections early. No shame in protecting your health.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What does HIV stand for? A: Human Immunodeficiency Virus.
chunks.source: Human Immunodeficiency Virus.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is AIDS? A: The late stage of HIV infection when the body cannot fight diseases.
chunks.source: The late stage of HIV infection when the body cannot fight diseases.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name two bacterial STIs that can be cured with antibiotics. A: Syphilis and gonorrhoea.
chunks.source: Syphilis and gonorrhoea.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How is HIV mainly transmitted? A: Through unprotected sex, mother to baby, and shared needles.
chunks.source: Through unprotected sex, mother to baby, and shared needles.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Can you get HIV from mosquito bites? Explain. A: No. HIV does not survive in mosquitoes. It spreads through blood, semen, vaginal fluids, and breast milk.
chunks.source: No. HIV does not survive in mosquitoes. It spreads through blood, semen, vaginal fluids, and breast milk.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is abstinence? A: Choosing not to have sex until ready, usually after marriage.
chunks.source: Choosing not to have sex until ready, usually after marriage.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How does a condom prevent STIs? A: It blocks contact with semen and vaginal fluids that carry viruses and bacteria.
chunks.source: It blocks contact with semen and vaginal fluids that carry viruses and bacteria.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why should a person get tested for HIV even if they feel fine? A: HIV can have no symptoms for years. Testing finds it early for treatment.
chunks.source: HIV can have no symptoms for years. Testing finds it early for treatment.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Peter hears a friend say: 'I trust my girlfriend, so we don't need condoms.' What should Peter say? A: Trust is good, but one partner could have an STI from before without knowing. Testing together and faithfulness protect both. Condoms add extra safety.
chunks.source: Trust is good, but one partner could have an STI from before without knowing. Testing together and faithfulness protect both. Condoms add extra safety.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: List three ways to prevent STIs. A: Abstinence, faithfulness to one tested partner, correct condom use every time.
chunks.source: Abstinence, faithfulness to one tested partner, correct condom use every time.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: How Sound Is Produced. I can explain how sound is produced by vibrations and name the parts of a sound wave. Sound starts with a vibration at a source. The vibration creates a sound wave that needs a medium to travel. Frequency decides pitch; vibration size decides volume. Echoes are reflected sound waves. Keywords: vibration: a quick back-and-forth movement; sound wave: a pattern of moving energy through a medium; medium: the material that carries sound waves; pitch: how high or low a sound is; volume: how loud or soft a sound is; frequency: the number of vibrations per second; echo: a sound heard again after bouncing off a surface; source: the place where sound starts
chunks.source: Sound starts with a vibration at a source. The vibration creates a sound wave that needs a medium to travel. Frequency decides pitch; vibration size decides volume. Echoes are reflected sound waves.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is the starting point of every sound called? A: The source.
chunks.source: The source.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is a vibration? A: A quick back-and-forth movement.
chunks.source: A quick back-and-forth movement.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What carries sound waves from one place to another? A: A medium, such as air, water, or solids.
chunks.source: A medium, such as air, water, or solids.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: If a vibration is faster, what happens to the pitch? A: The pitch becomes higher.
chunks.source: The pitch becomes higher.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What do we call the loudness of a sound? A: Volume.
chunks.source: Volume.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is frequency? A: The number of vibrations per second.
chunks.source: The number of vibrations per second.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why can we not hear sound in a vacuum? A: There is no medium to carry the sound wave.
chunks.source: There is no medium to carry the sound wave.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What causes an echo? A: A sound wave reflects off a hard surface and returns to the listener.
chunks.source: A sound wave reflects off a hard surface and returns to the listener.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: A guitarist plucks a thick string and then a thin string. Which has a higher pitch? A: The thin string vibrates faster, so it has a higher pitch.
chunks.source: The thin string vibrates faster, so it has a higher pitch.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Explain how a drum produces sound when hit. A: The drum skin vibrates. The vibration pushes air molecules, creating a sound wave that travels to the ear.
chunks.source: The drum skin vibrates. The vibration pushes air molecules, creating a sound wave that travels to the ear.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: How Sound Travels. I can describe how sound travels through solids, liquids, and gases, and explain why it cannot travel in a vacuum. Sound travels fastest in solids, slower in liquids, and slowest in gases. It cannot travel in a vacuum because there are no particles to carry the vibrations. Echoes are caused by reflection of sound waves off hard surfaces. Keywords: solid: a hard material with tightly packed particles; liquid: a material that flows, like water; gas: a material like air that fills space; speed: how fast something moves; vacuum: empty space with no particles; echo: a reflected sound heard again; reflection: bouncing back of a wave from a surface; ear: the organ that detects sound waves
chunks.source: Sound travels fastest in solids, slower in liquids, and slowest in gases. It cannot travel in a vacuum because there are no particles to carry the vibrations. Echoes are caused by reflection of sound waves off hard surfaces.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Through which medium does sound travel fastest: solid, liquid, or gas? A: Solid.
chunks.source: Solid.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why does sound travel faster in solids than in gases? A: Particles in solids are tightly packed, so vibrations pass quickly from one to the next.
chunks.source: Particles in solids are tightly packed, so vibrations pass quickly from one to the next.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Can sound travel through water? A: Yes, sound travels well through liquids like water.
chunks.source: Yes, sound travels well through liquids like water.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is a vacuum? A: Empty space with no particles.
chunks.source: Empty space with no particles.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why can sound not travel in a vacuum? A: There are no particles to carry the vibrations.
chunks.source: There are no particles to carry the vibrations.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is the speed of sound in air at room temperature? A: About 340 metres per second.
chunks.source: About 340 metres per second.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What causes an echo? A: Reflection of a sound wave off a hard surface.
chunks.source: Reflection of a sound wave off a hard surface.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which surface reflects sound better: a smooth wall or a curtain? A: A smooth wall.
chunks.source: A smooth wall.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: If you put your ear to a metal fence, you hear a distant knock sooner than through air. Why? A: Metal is a solid; sound travels faster in solids than in gases.
chunks.source: Metal is a solid; sound travels faster in solids than in gases.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Explain why astronauts on the Moon use radios to talk, even when standing next to each other. A: The Moon has no atmosphere (vacuum). Sound needs a medium to travel, so their voices cannot carry through the vacuum.
chunks.source: The Moon has no atmosphere (vacuum). Sound needs a medium to travel, so their voices cannot carry through the vacuum.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Musical Instruments. I can group musical instruments into strings, wind, and percussion, and explain how each produces sound. Instruments are grouped by how they vibrate: strings vibrate strings, wind vibrates air columns, percussion vibrates by being hit. Pitch depends on length, tension, or air column size. Keywords: string: a thin wire or cord that vibrates to make sound; wind: instruments played by blowing air through them; percussion: instruments hit or shaken to make sound; drum: a hollow body with a stretched skin hit to make sound; flute: a tube with holes, played by blowing across the top; tube fiddle: a one-string Ugandan instrument played with a bow; xylophone: wooden bars of different lengths hit with sticks; pitch: how high or low a sound is
chunks.source: Instruments are grouped by how they vibrate: strings vibrate strings, wind vibrates air columns, percussion vibrates by being hit. Pitch depends on length, tension, or air column size.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name the three main groups of musical instruments. A: String, wind, percussion.
chunks.source: String, wind, percussion.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How does a string instrument make sound? A: A stretched string vibrates when plucked, bowed, or struck.
chunks.source: A stretched string vibrates when plucked, bowed, or struck.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give an example of a Ugandan string instrument. A: Tube fiddle (endingidi).
chunks.source: Tube fiddle (endingidi).

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How does a wind instrument make sound? A: Air vibrates inside a tube when blown across or into it.
chunks.source: Air vibrates inside a tube when blown across or into it.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What changes the pitch on a flute? A: Covering or uncovering holes changes the length of the vibrating air column.
chunks.source: Covering or uncovering holes changes the length of the vibrating air column.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How does a percussion instrument make sound? A: It is hit, shaken, or scraped, causing vibration.
chunks.source: It is hit, shaken, or scraped, causing vibration.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why does a shorter xylophone bar give a higher pitch? A: A shorter bar vibrates faster, producing a higher frequency.
chunks.source: A shorter bar vibrates faster, producing a higher frequency.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What happens to the pitch of a drum if you tighten its skin? A: The pitch becomes higher.
chunks.source: The pitch becomes higher.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Classify these instruments: drum, flute, tube fiddle, xylophone. A: Drum = percussion; Flute = wind; Tube fiddle = string; Xylophone = percussion.
chunks.source: Drum = percussion; Flute = wind; Tube fiddle = string; Xylophone = percussion.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Explain how the tube fiddle produces different pitches. A: The player presses the string at different points, shortening the vibrating length. Shorter length = higher pitch.
chunks.source: The player presses the string at different points, shortening the vibrating length. Shorter length = higher pitch.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: The Ear and Hearing. I can name the parts of the ear, describe how we hear, and explain how to care for our ears. The ear has three parts: outer (pinna, canal), middle (ear drum, ossicles), inner (cochlea, auditory nerve). Sound waves vibrate the ear drum; ossicles amplify; cochlea converts to nerve signals. Protect ears from loud noise and never insert objects. Keywords: pinna: the outer visible part of the ear that collects sound; ear drum: a thin membrane that vibrates when sound hits it; ossicles: three tiny bones that amplify vibrations; cochlea: a spiral, fluid-filled organ that turns vibrations into nerve signals; auditory nerve: the nerve that carries hearing signals to the brain; deafness: partial or total inability to hear; wax: a sticky substance that protects the ear canal; care: actions to keep ears healthy and safe
chunks.source: The ear has three parts: outer (pinna, canal), middle (ear drum, ossicles), inner (cochlea, auditory nerve). Sound waves vibrate the ear drum; ossicles amplify; cochlea converts to nerve signals. Protect ears from loud noise and never insert objects.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is the function of the pinna? A: It collects sound waves and directs them into the ear canal.
chunks.source: It collects sound waves and directs them into the ear canal.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What happens when sound waves hit the ear drum? A: The ear drum vibrates.
chunks.source: The ear drum vibrates.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name the three ossicles. A: Hammer, anvil, stirrup.
chunks.source: Hammer, anvil, stirrup.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What do the ossicles do? A: They amplify vibrations from the ear drum and pass them to the cochlea.
chunks.source: They amplify vibrations from the ear drum and pass them to the cochlea.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is the cochlea? A: A spiral, fluid-filled organ that converts vibrations into nerve signals.
chunks.source: A spiral, fluid-filled organ that converts vibrations into nerve signals.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which nerve carries hearing signals to the brain? A: The auditory nerve.
chunks.source: The auditory nerve.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is deafness? A: Partial or total inability to hear.
chunks.source: Partial or total inability to hear.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why is ear wax useful? A: It traps dust and germs, protecting the ear drum.
chunks.source: It traps dust and germs, protecting the ear drum.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: List two ways to care for your ears. A: Keep volume low; wear ear protection in loud places; do not insert objects; dry ears after swimming.
chunks.source: Keep volume low; wear ear protection in loud places; do not insert objects; dry ears after swimming.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Explain the path of a sound wave from the pinna to the brain. A: Pinna collects sound → ear canal → ear drum vibrates → ossicles amplify → cochlea converts to signals → auditory nerve → brain.
chunks.source: Pinna collects sound → ear canal → ear drum vibrates → ossicles amplify → cochlea converts to signals → auditory nerve → brain.

chunks.id: L-P6-Social-The Land and Its Living Resources
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: The Land and Its Living Resources
chunks.text: The Land and Its Living Resources. I can explain how land, forests, plants, animals and game parks are used as resources in East Africa.
