chunks.source: Write a **timetable** – it organises study time.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Why is **revision** important? A: It prevents forgetting facts **or else** marks are lost.
chunks.source: It prevents forgetting facts **or else** marks are lost.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: What does a **candidate** need to set to stay focused? A: A clear **goal** – it guides daily work.
chunks.source: A clear **goal** – it guides daily work.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: How does a **plan** help a student? A: It breaks the syllabus into manageable parts.
chunks.source: It breaks the syllabus into manageable parts.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: What should a student do **or else** they waste time? A: Follow the **timetable** – without it time is wasted.
chunks.source: Follow the **timetable** – without it time is wasted.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Which of these shows good **notes**? A: Bullet points with key words – they aid **revision**.
chunks.source: Bullet points with key words – they aid **revision**.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: If a student skips **revision**, what is the consequence? A: They may forget facts **or else** lose marks.
chunks.source: They may forget facts **or else** lose marks.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: What leads to **success** in examinations? A: Consistent **preparation**, **revision**, and a strong **goal**.
chunks.source: Consistent **preparation**, **revision**, and a strong **goal**.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Sitting an Examination. I can describe what happens in the examination room and how to follow instructions. Follow the invigilator's instructions, write your index number, keep silence, and check your answers for a fair examination. Keywords: invigilator: exam supervisor; index number: candidate ID; register: attendance list; examination: formal test; instructions: directions given; paper: exam question sheet; answer: written response; silence: quietness
chunks.source: Follow the invigilator's instructions, write your index number, keep silence, and check your answers for a fair examination.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Who reads the **instructions** in the exam hall? A: The **invigilator** – they give oral and written directions.
chunks.source: The **invigilator** – they give oral and written directions.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: What must a candidate write on the **paper** first? A: Their **index number** – it identifies the script.
chunks.source: Their **index number** – it identifies the script.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Why is **silence** required during the **examination**? A: To keep the exam **fair** and avoid disturbance.
chunks.source: To keep the exam **fair** and avoid disturbance.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: What should a candidate do if they finish early? A: Review their **answer** sheet – do not leave the hall.
chunks.source: Review their **answer** sheet – do not leave the hall.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: What is the **register** used for? A: To record attendance of each **candidate**.
chunks.source: To record attendance of each **candidate**.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: If a candidate talks during the exam, what rule is broken? A: The rule of **silence** – the **invigilator** will warn them.
chunks.source: The rule of **silence** – the **invigilator** will warn them.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: What must a candidate **must not** do during the exam? A: Must not communicate with others – it is **malpractice**.
chunks.source: Must not communicate with others – it is **malpractice**.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: How does following **instructions** help the candidate? A: It ensures the **paper** is completed correctly and avoids penalties.
chunks.source: It ensures the **paper** is completed correctly and avoids penalties.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Results and Performance. I can interpret examination results and compare performance using 'whereas'. Results show marks, grade, aggregate and division; whereas helps compare performance to improve. Keywords: results: exam outcomes; performance: how well someone does; certificate: official document; failure: not succeeding; marks: scores; grade: letter showing level; aggregate: total marks; division: ranking group
chunks.source: Results show marks, grade, aggregate and division; whereas helps compare performance to improve.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: What does **aggregate** mean in PLE results? A: The total of all **marks** obtained.
chunks.source: The total of all **marks** obtained.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: How is **division** different from **grade**? A: **Division** ranks candidates nationally; **grade** shows subject level.
chunks.source: **Division** ranks candidates nationally; **grade** shows subject level.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Write a sentence using **whereas** to compare two results. A: **Whereas** her **aggregate** was 20 last year, this year it is 15.
chunks.source: **Whereas** her **aggregate** was 20 last year, this year it is 15.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: What does a **certificate** show? A: It shows the **division** and **grade** earned.
chunks.source: It shows the **division** and **grade** earned.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: If a student gets low **marks**, what might they feel? A: They may feel **failure**, but it can motivate improvement.
chunks.source: They may feel **failure**, but it can motivate improvement.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: How can a student improve **performance**? A: By reviewing weak subjects and practising past papers.
chunks.source: By reviewing weak subjects and practising past papers.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: What is the purpose of **results**? A: To inform the candidate of their **marks**, **grade**, **aggregate**, and **division**.
chunks.source: To inform the candidate of their **marks**, **grade**, **aggregate**, and **division**.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Why is **whereas** useful in writing about results? A: It clearly shows contrast between two sets of data.
chunks.source: It clearly shows contrast between two sets of data.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Examination Rules and Honesty. I can state the PLE examination rules and explain why honesty matters. Exam rules are strict; cheating leads to penalty or disqualification; honesty keeps exams fair. Keywords: rules: official guidelines; cheating: copying dishonestly; honesty: truthfulness; malpractice: wrongdoing in exam; penalty: punishment; fair: just; strict: firm; disqualify: remove from exam
chunks.source: Exam rules are strict; cheating leads to penalty or disqualification; honesty keeps exams fair.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: What is **cheating** in an examination? A: Copying or using unauthorised material – it is **malpractice**.
chunks.source: Copying or using unauthorised material – it is **malpractice**.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: What **penalty** can a candidate face for **cheating**? A: They may be **disqualify** from the exam.
chunks.source: They may be **disqualify** from the exam.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Why are exam **rules** described as **strict**? A: To ensure the exam is **fair** for all candidates.
chunks.source: To ensure the exam is **fair** for all candidates.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: What must a candidate **must not** do during the exam? A: Must not talk, copy, or bring forbidden items.
chunks.source: Must not talk, copy, or bring forbidden items.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: How does **honesty** affect the value of a **certificate**? A: An honest **certificate** proves true ability.
chunks.source: An honest **certificate** proves true ability.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: What is **malpractice**? A: Any dishonest act like cheating, impersonation, or leaking papers.
chunks.source: Any dishonest act like cheating, impersonation, or leaking papers.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: If a candidate is caught **cheating**, what happens to their **results**? A: Their **results** may be cancelled and they are **disqualify**.
chunks.source: Their **results** may be cancelled and they are **disqualify**.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Why is it important to follow **rules** even when no one watches? A: Because **honesty** is personal integrity, not just fear of **penalty**.
chunks.source: Because **honesty** is personal integrity, not just fear of **penalty**.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Radio and Television. I can talk about radio and television and say what I prefer. Radio and television are electronic media that broadcast programmes. We can say what we prefer using 'more interested in ... than in'. Keywords: radio: a device that plays sound from the air; television: a device that shows moving pictures and sound; broadcast: to send out a programme over the air; programme: a show on radio or television; news: new information about events; channel: a station on radio or television; listener: a person who hears a radio programme; viewer: a person who watches a television programme
chunks.source: Radio and television are electronic media that broadcast programmes. We can say what we prefer using 'more interested in ... than in'.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Choose the correct word: The ______ sends out the programme to many homes. A: broadcast – because broadcast means to send out a programme over the air.
chunks.source: broadcast – because broadcast means to send out a programme over the air.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Amina says: 'I am more interested in news than in music.' Which structure does she use? A: more interested in ... than in – this shows preference.
chunks.source: more interested in ... than in – this shows preference.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: What is a person who watches television called? A: viewer – a viewer watches television.
chunks.source: viewer – a viewer watches television.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Which word means a station on radio or television? A: channel – a channel is a station.
chunks.source: channel – a channel is a station.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Fill the gap: The ______ on the wall shows moving pictures. A: television – television shows pictures and sound.
chunks.source: television – television shows pictures and sound.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: What does a listener do? A: listens to the radio – a listener hears radio programmes.
chunks.source: listens to the radio – a listener hears radio programmes.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Identify the word that means new information about events. A: news – news gives current information.
chunks.source: news – news gives current information.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Write a sentence using 'programme' and 'channel'. A: Any correct sentence, e.g., 'My favourite programme is on channel 5.'
chunks.source: Any correct sentence, e.g., 'My favourite programme is on channel 5.'

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Which sentence correctly uses the preference pattern? A: I am more interested in sports than in drama. – uses 'more interested in ... than in'.
chunks.source: I am more interested in sports than in drama. – uses 'more interested in ... than in'.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Other Electronic Media. I can name other electronic media and join ideas to show results. Media such as mobile phones, computers, cassette players and videos are electronic. We join cause and result with 'and so'. Keywords: media: ways of sharing information like radio, TV, phone; electronic: working with electricity; mobile phone: a small phone you carry; video: a recording of moving pictures; record: to store sound or pictures for later; cassette: a small plastic box with magnetic tape; tape player: a machine that plays cassettes; computer: an electronic machine for processing data
chunks.source: Media such as mobile phones, computers, cassette players and videos are electronic. We join cause and result with 'and so'.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Choose the word that means ways of sharing information: ______. A: media – media are ways like radio, TV, phone.
chunks.source: media – media are ways like radio, TV, phone.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Which word describes something that works with electricity? A: electronic – electronic devices need power.
chunks.source: electronic – electronic devices need power.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: What do you call a small phone you carry? A: mobile phone – a mobile phone fits in your pocket.
chunks.source: mobile phone – a mobile phone fits in your pocket.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: A recording of moving pictures is called a ______. A: video – video shows moving pictures.
chunks.source: video – video shows moving pictures.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: To keep sound for later you ______ it. A: record – record means store sound or pictures.
chunks.source: record – record means store sound or pictures.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: A small plastic box with magnetic tape is a ______. A: cassette – cassette holds tape.
chunks.source: cassette – cassette holds tape.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: The machine that plays cassettes is a ______. A: tape player – tape player plays cassettes.
chunks.source: tape player – tape player plays cassettes.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: An electronic machine for processing data is a ______. A: computer – computer processes data.
chunks.source: computer – computer processes data.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Join the two ideas with 'and so': He saved the file. We opened it later. A: He saved the file, and so we opened it later. – 'and so' shows result.
chunks.source: He saved the file, and so we opened it later. – 'and so' shows result.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Understanding News Reports. I can find the main idea in news reports and other media texts. In media texts the headline shows the main idea; the article gives details. Adverts sell, while news informs. Keywords: news: new information about events; advert: a notice that tries to sell something; announce: to tell people something officially; report: a written or spoken account of an event; message: a piece of information sent to someone; information: facts or details about something; headline: the title of a news story; article: a piece of writing in a newspaper or magazine
chunks.source: In media texts the headline shows the main idea; the article gives details. Adverts sell, while news informs.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: What does the **headline** do in a news story? A: It gives the main idea in a few words.
chunks.source: It gives the main idea in a few words.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Which word means a notice that tries to sell something? A: advert – an advert promotes a product.
chunks.source: advert – an advert promotes a product.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Choose the correct verb: The teacher will ______ the exam results tomorrow. A: announce – announce means to tell officially.
chunks.source: announce – announce means to tell officially.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: A written account of an event is called a ______. A: report – a report describes what happened.
chunks.source: report – a report describes what happened.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: A piece of information sent to someone is a ______. A: message – a message carries information.
chunks.source: message – a message carries information.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Facts or details about something are called ______. A: information – information is facts.
chunks.source: information – information is facts.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: The title of a news story is the ______. A: headline – headline is the title.
chunks.source: headline – headline is the title.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: A piece of writing in a newspaper is an ______. A: article – article is a story in a paper.
chunks.source: article – article is a story in a paper.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Identify the main idea of this short text: 'Heavy rain caused floods in Kampala. Many roads are closed.' A: Heavy rain caused floods – the first sentence is the main idea.
chunks.source: Heavy rain caused floods – the first sentence is the main idea.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Which of these is NOT a news text? A: An advert for a new phone – adverts sell, they are not news.
chunks.source: An advert for a new phone – adverts sell, they are not news.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Writing About My Favourite Programme. I can write a paragraph about my favourite TV or radio programme. When writing about a favourite programme, use words like favourite, prefer, daily, weekly, habit, watch, listen to give clear details. Keywords: favourite: liked most; prefer: like one thing more than another; programme: a show on radio or television; watch: to look at a television programme; listen: to hear a radio programme; daily: happening every day; weekly: happening every week; habit: something you do regularly
chunks.source: When writing about a favourite programme, use words like favourite, prefer, daily, weekly, habit, watch, listen to give clear details.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Choose the correct word: My ______ programme is the evening news. A: favourite – favourite means liked most.
chunks.source: favourite – favourite means liked most.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Complete the sentence: I ______ listening to the radio than watching TV. A: prefer – prefer shows you like one thing more.
chunks.source: prefer – prefer shows you like one thing more.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: What does **daily** mean? A: Happening every day.
chunks.source: Happening every day.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: What does **weekly** mean? A: Happening every week.
chunks.source: Happening every week.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Write a sentence using **watch** and **programme**. A: Any correct sentence, e.g., 'I watch the programme at seven.'
chunks.source: Any correct sentence, e.g., 'I watch the programme at seven.'

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Write a sentence using **listen** and **habit**. A: Any correct sentence, e.g., 'Listening to the radio is my habit.'
chunks.source: Any correct sentence, e.g., 'Listening to the radio is my habit.'

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Identify the topic sentence in this paragraph: 'My favourite programme is the daily news. I prefer it because it gives information. I watch it every evening.' A: My favourite programme is the daily news. – it introduces the topic.
chunks.source: My favourite programme is the daily news. – it introduces the topic.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Which word means something you do regularly? A: habit – a habit is a regular action.
chunks.source: habit – a habit is a regular action.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Rewrite using **prefer**: I like news more than music. A: I prefer news to music. – prefer takes 'to'.
chunks.source: I prefer news to music. – prefer takes 'to'.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: What should a good paragraph about a favourite programme include? A: A topic sentence, supporting details, and a closing sentence.
chunks.source: A topic sentence, supporting details, and a closing sentence.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Children's Rights. I can state children's rights using 'has a right to' and explain what each right means in Uganda. Every Ugandan child has rights to education, health, food, play, protection, freedom, and a name. These are guaranteed by the Constitution and the Children Act. The government and parents have duties to fulfil them. Keywords: right: something you are allowed to have or do; education: learning at school; health: being well and not sick; food: what you eat to stay strong; play: games and fun activities; protection: being kept safe from harm; freedom: being able to choose and speak; name: what you are called
chunks.source: Every Ugandan child has rights to education, health, food, play, protection, freedom, and a name. These are guaranteed by the Constitution and the Children Act. The government and parents have duties to fulfil them.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: State the right that guarantees free primary schooling in Uganda. A: Right to education — Universal Primary Education (UPE) provides free primary schooling.
chunks.source: Right to education — Universal Primary Education (UPE) provides free primary schooling.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: What does the right to health include for a Ugandan child? A: Access to medical care, immunisation, clean water, and nutritious food.
chunks.source: Access to medical care, immunisation, clean water, and nutritious food.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Name the document that gives Ugandan children the right to a name. A: The Constitution of Uganda and the Children Act guarantee the right to a name and birth registration.
chunks.source: The Constitution of Uganda and the Children Act guarantee the right to a name and birth registration.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Explain why the right to protection is important. A: It keeps children safe from abuse, neglect, exploitation, and violence.
chunks.source: It keeps children safe from abuse, neglect, exploitation, and violence.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Complete: Every child has a right to ______ so they can grow strong. A: food — nutritious meals like posho, beans, and matooke.
chunks.source: food — nutritious meals like posho, beans, and matooke.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Which right allows Amina to sing in church or mosque? A: Freedom of religion / freedom of worship.
chunks.source: Freedom of religion / freedom of worship.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Give one government action that fulfils the right to education. A: Building schools, training teachers, or providing UPE capitation grants.
chunks.source: Building schools, training teachers, or providing UPE capitation grants.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Why is a birth certificate important for a child's rights? A: It proves identity, allows school enrolment, and helps claim other rights.
chunks.source: It proves identity, allows school enrolment, and helps claim other rights.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Match: 'Right to play' — what does it mean? A: Time for rest, leisure, and recreational activities like football or netball.
chunks.source: Time for rest, leisure, and recreational activities like football or netball.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Write a PLE-style sentence for the right to freedom of expression. A: Every child has a right to freedom of expression, including the freedom to seek, receive, and share ideas.
chunks.source: Every child has a right to freedom of expression, including the freedom to seek, receive, and share ideas.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Responsibilities at Home and School. I can use 'must' and 'should' to talk about duties and responsibilities at home and school. Responsibilities at home and school use 'must' for strong obligations (rules, laws) and 'should' for moral duties (advice, good behaviour). Key duties: attend, obey, respect, help, do chores, show discipline. Keywords: responsibility: a duty to do something; duty: something you must do; obey: follow rules or orders; respect: treat others well; discipline: self-control and good behaviour; attend: be present at; help: assist someone; chore: a regular small job
chunks.source: Responsibilities at home and school use 'must' for strong obligations (rules, laws) and 'should' for moral duties (advice, good behaviour). Key duties: attend, obey, respect, help, do chores, show discipline.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Rewrite using 'must': It is necessary to do homework. A: We must do homework.
chunks.source: We must do homework.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Rewrite using 'should': It is a good idea to help parents. A: We should help parents.
chunks.source: We should help parents.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: State one responsibility of a child at home using 'must'. A: A child must fetch water / wash utensils / sweep the compound.
chunks.source: A child must fetch water / wash utensils / sweep the compound.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: State one responsibility of a pupil at school using 'should'. A: A pupil should revise notes daily / respect prefects / keep the compound clean.
chunks.source: A pupil should revise notes daily / respect prefects / keep the compound clean.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Complete: ______ means treating elders with kindness. A: Respect
chunks.source: Respect

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Complete: ______ is a daily task like fetching water. A: Chore
chunks.source: Chore

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Choose the correct modal: Pupils ______ attend assembly. (must/should) A: must — it is a school rule.
chunks.source: must — it is a school rule.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Choose the correct modal: Children ______ share with siblings. (must/should) A: should — it is a moral duty.
chunks.source: should — it is a moral duty.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Why is discipline needed for a P.7 candidate? A: Discipline ensures regular attendance, obedience to rules, and respect, leading to success in PLE.
chunks.source: Discipline ensures regular attendance, obedience to rules, and respect, leading to success in PLE.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Write a sentence using 'obey' about school rules. A: We must obey the school rules to maintain order and learn well.
chunks.source: We must obey the school rules to maintain order and learn well.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Animal Needs and Freedoms. I can explain animal freedoms using 'should' and 'need to' and describe what animals require to live well. Animals have needs: food, water, shelter, care, and freedom to behave naturally. The Five Freedoms guide us. 'Animals should not suffer' means we must protect them from unnecessary pain. Care is a duty. Keywords: animal: a living creature like a cow, goat, or dog; freedom: the ability to live naturally; food: what animals eat; water: liquid animals drink; shelter: a safe place to stay; care: looking after well-being; suffer: feel pain or distress; protect: keep safe from harm
chunks.source: Animals have needs: food, water, shelter, care, and freedom to behave naturally. The Five Freedoms guide us. 'Animals should not suffer' means we must protect them from unnecessary pain. Care is a duty.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: List the Five Freedoms for animals. A: 1. Freedom from hunger/thirst. 2. Freedom from discomfort. 3. Freedom from pain/injury/disease. 4. Freedom to express normal behaviour. 5. Freedom from fear/distress.
chunks.source: 1. Freedom from hunger/thirst. 2. Freedom from discomfort. 3. Freedom from pain/injury/disease. 4. Freedom to express normal behaviour. 5. Freedom from fear/distress.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: State two needs of a cow. A: Food (grass, hay) and clean water daily.
chunks.source: Food (grass, hay) and clean water daily.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Explain 'freedom to express normal behaviour' for a chicken. A: Chickens must scratch ground, dust-bathe, perch, and flap wings — not be confined in a small cage.
chunks.source: Chickens must scratch ground, dust-bathe, perch, and flap wings — not be confined in a small cage.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Why should farmers vaccinate their animals? A: To protect them from disease, prevent suffering, and ensure good production (milk, meat, eggs).
chunks.source: To protect them from disease, prevent suffering, and ensure good production (milk, meat, eggs).

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Complete: Animals ______ not suffer unnecessarily. A: should — moral duty to prevent suffering.
chunks.source: should — moral duty to prevent suffering.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Give one way to protect a dog from disease. A: Vaccinate against rabies and deworm regularly.
chunks.source: Vaccinate against rabies and deworm regularly.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: What does 'shelter' mean for a goat? A: A raised, dry, ventilated house that protects from rain, sun, and predators.
chunks.source: A raised, dry, ventilated house that protects from rain, sun, and predators.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Rewrite using 'should': It is right to give animals clean water. A: Animals should have clean water daily.
chunks.source: Animals should have clean water daily.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Name the Ugandan law that prevents cruelty to animals. A: The Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act.
chunks.source: The Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Write a PLE sentence: 'State one responsibility of a farmer towards animals.' A: A farmer must provide food, water, shelter, and medical care to prevent suffering.
chunks.source: A farmer must provide food, water, shelter, and medical care to prevent suffering.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Imagining a Fair World. I can use the second conditional to imagine a fairer world and express wishes for equality. The second conditional (If + past simple, would + base verb) expresses imaginary situations and wishes. It is the grammar of hope: 'If the world were fair, everyone would have rights.' Use 'were' for all persons. It lets us speak about justice. Keywords: freedom: the right to act and speak; choose: pick what you want; speak: say what you think; learn: gain knowledge; fair: just and equal; equal: the same for everyone; right: what you are entitled to; voice: your opinion expressed
chunks.source: The second conditional (If + past simple, would + base verb) expresses imaginary situations and wishes. It is the grammar of hope: 'If the world were fair, everyone would have rights.' Use 'were' for all persons. It lets us speak about justice.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Complete the second conditional: If I ______ (be) a teacher, I ______ (listen) to every child. A: If I **were** a teacher, I **would listen** to every child.
chunks.source: If I **were** a teacher, I **would listen** to every child.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Rewrite using second conditional: Girls do not have equal chances. They cannot become leaders. A: If girls **had** equal chances, they **would become** leaders.
chunks.source: If girls **had** equal chances, they **would become** leaders.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Make a sentence about education using 'If every child... would...' A: If every child **had** the **right** to **education**, they **would learn** to read and write.
chunks.source: If every child **had** the **right** to **education**, they **would learn** to read and write.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Choose correct form: If we ______ (respect) each other, there ______ (be) no fights. A: **respected** ... **would be**
chunks.source: **respected** ... **would be**

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Why do we use 'were' not 'was' in 'If I were you'? A: Formal second conditional uses 'were' for all persons (I, he, she, it) to show imaginary situation.
chunks.source: Formal second conditional uses 'were' for all persons (I, he, she, it) to show imaginary situation.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Write a second conditional sentence about freedom of speech. A: If everyone **had** **freedom** of **speech**, they **would** **speak** their **voice** without fear.
chunks.source: If everyone **had** **freedom** of **speech**, they **would** **speak** their **voice** without fear.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Complete: If leaders ______ (listen) to children, laws ______ (be) better. A: **listened** ... **would be**
chunks.source: **listened** ... **would be**

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Transform to second conditional: We don't have enough books. We cannot read widely. A: If we **had** enough books, we **would read** widely.
chunks.source: If we **had** enough books, we **would read** widely.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: What does the second conditional show in a composition about rights? A: It shows the gap between reality and the imagined fair world; expresses wishes for justice and equality.
chunks.source: It shows the gap between reality and the imagined fair world; expresses wishes for justice and equality.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Write a PLE-style sentence: 'If all children ______, the country ______.' A: If all children **went** to school, the country **would develop**.
chunks.source: If all children **went** to school, the country **would develop**.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Why Our Environment Matters. I can explain why we must protect our environment using necessity and obligation language. We must protect our environment to stop pollution, erosion, drought and floods. Garbage and refuse block drains. Flora and fauna need their habitat. Use 'must' and 'have to' for obligation. Keywords: pollution: dirty air, water or land; garbage: rubbish or waste; refuse: rubbish that is thrown away; erosion: soil being washed or blown away; drought: long time without rain; floods: too much water covering land; habitat: natural home of plants and animals; flora: plants of a place; fauna: animals of a place
chunks.source: We must protect our environment to stop pollution, erosion, drought and floods. Garbage and refuse block drains. Flora and fauna need their habitat. Use 'must' and 'have to' for obligation.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Fill the gap with an abstract noun: The ______ from the lorry made the air dirty. A: pollution — abstract noun for dirty air/water/land
chunks.source: pollution — abstract noun for dirty air/water/land

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Rewrite using 'must': It is necessary to protect the habitat of flora and fauna. A: We must protect the habitat of flora and fauna. — 'must' shows obligation
chunks.source: We must protect the habitat of flora and fauna. — 'must' shows obligation

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Choose the correct word: The long dry season is called ______. A: drought — long time without rain
chunks.source: drought — long time without rain

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Fill the gap: Heavy rain on bare ground causes ______. A: erosion — soil washed or blown away
chunks.source: erosion — soil washed or blown away

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Rewrite using 'have to': It is necessary to stop dumping garbage in the river. A: We have to stop dumping garbage in the river. — 'have to' shows obligation
chunks.source: We have to stop dumping garbage in the river. — 'have to' shows obligation

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: What is the natural home of plants and animals called? A: habitat — natural home of flora and fauna
chunks.source: habitat — natural home of flora and fauna

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Fill the gap: The ______ of Uganda includes mvule trees and elephants. A: flora and fauna — plants and animals of a place
chunks.source: flora and fauna — plants and animals of a place

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Rewrite: 'We are obliged to conserve water.' (Use 'must') A: We must conserve water. — 'must' replaces 'are obliged to'
chunks.source: We must conserve water. — 'must' replaces 'are obliged to'

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Choose the correct word: Too much water covering the land is ______. A: floods — too much water covering land
chunks.source: floods — too much water covering land

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Write one sentence using 'must' and 'erosion'. A: We must build terraces to stop erosion. — shows obligation + correct use of target word
chunks.source: We must build terraces to stop erosion. — shows obligation + correct use of target word

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Since the Trees Were Cut. I can use 'since' and 'so' to explain cause and effect about deforestation. Since shows cause. So shows effect. Since the trees were cut, so the soil erodes. Since overgrazing, so the land degrades. Since draining wetlands, so water tables drop. We must reverse the causes. Keywords: source: where something comes from; raw materials: natural things used to make products; storms: violent weather with wind and rain; manure: animal or plant waste used to fertilise soil; draining: removing water from land; overgrazing: too many animals eating grass; burning: setting fire to land or waste; smoking: preserving fish or meat with smoke
chunks.source: Since shows cause. So shows effect. Since the trees were cut, so the soil erodes. Since overgrazing, so the land degrades. Since draining wetlands, so water tables drop. We must reverse the causes.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Rewrite using 'since' at the end: Since the trees were cut, the soil eroded. A: The soil eroded since the trees were cut. — effect + since + cause
chunks.source: The soil eroded since the trees were cut. — effect + since + cause

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Fill the gap: ______ the wetland was drained, the water table dropped. A: Since — introduces the cause
chunks.source: Since — introduces the cause

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Choose the correct completion: Since overgrazing left the ground bare, ______. A: so the rain washed the soil away. — cause (overgrazing) → effect (erosion)
chunks.source: so the rain washed the soil away. — cause (overgrazing) → effect (erosion)

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Rewrite: The stream dried up because the source was exposed. (Start with 'Since') A: Since the source was exposed, the stream dried up. — 'since' replaces 'because' at start
chunks.source: Since the source was exposed, the stream dried up. — 'since' replaces 'because' at start

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Fill the gap: ______ people burn bush every dry season, ______ the soil loses nutrients. A: Since ... so ... — cause-effect pair
chunks.source: Since ... so ... — cause-effect pair

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: What are 'raw materials'? A: Natural things used to make products, e.g. trees for timber.
chunks.source: Natural things used to make products, e.g. trees for timber.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Rewrite: Since the storms are fierce, the roof leaks. (Use 'so') A: Since the storms are fierce, so the roof leaks. — keep 'since', add 'so' before effect
chunks.source: Since the storms are fierce, so the roof leaks. — keep 'since', add 'so' before effect

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Choose the correct word: Preserving fish with smoke is called ______. A: smoking — preserving fish or meat with smoke
chunks.source: smoking — preserving fish or meat with smoke

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Write a sentence using 'since' and 'manure'. A: Since the soil is poor, we add manure. — correct structure + target word
chunks.source: Since the soil is poor, we add manure. — correct structure + target word

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Rewrite: The fish died since the factory polluted the river. (Start with 'Since') A: Since the factory polluted the river, the fish died. — cause first, then effect
chunks.source: Since the factory polluted the river, the fish died. — cause first, then effect

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Protecting Our Environment. I can use conditionals to explain environmental protection methods. First conditional: If + present, will + verb — for real plans. If we build terraces, soil will not erode. If we mulch, soil keeps moisture. If we use incinerators, air stays clean. Second conditional: If + past, would + verb — for unreal dreams. Keywords: terraces: level steps on a hillside; crop rotation: changing crops each season; mulching: covering soil with dry grass; dumping: throwing waste carelessly; dust bin: container for household waste; dispose: get rid of waste properly; incinerator: furnace for burning waste safely; waste basket: small bin for paper and light waste
chunks.source: First conditional: If + present, will + verb — for real plans. If we build terraces, soil will not erode. If we mulch, soil keeps moisture. If we use incinerators, air stays clean. Second conditional: If + past, would + verb — for unreal dreams.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Complete the first conditional: If we ______ (build) terraces, the soil ______ (not erode). A: build / will not erode — present simple + will + verb
chunks.source: build / will not erode — present simple + will + verb

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Rewrite using 'unless': If we do not mulch, the crops will wilt. A: Unless we mulch, the crops will wilt. — 'unless' = 'if not'
chunks.source: Unless we mulch, the crops will wilt. — 'unless' = 'if not'

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Choose the correct form: If we ______ (dispose) of waste in the incinerator, smoke ______ (not spread). A: dispose / will not spread — first conditional
chunks.source: dispose / will not spread — first conditional

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Identify the conditional type: If we had more dust bins, the compound would be clean. A: Second conditional — unreal present (past simple + would)
chunks.source: Second conditional — unreal present (past simple + would)

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Rewrite: Without crop rotation, the soil loses fertility. (Start with 'If') A: If we do not practise crop rotation, the soil will lose fertility. — first conditional
chunks.source: If we do not practise crop rotation, the soil will lose fertility. — first conditional

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Fill the gap: If every home ______ a waste basket, litter ______ reduce. A: has / will — first conditional
chunks.source: has / will — first conditional

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Rewrite as second conditional: If we build an incinerator, pollution decreases. (Make it unreal) A: If we built an incinerator, pollution would decrease. — past simple + would
chunks.source: If we built an incinerator, pollution would decrease. — past simple + would

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Choose the correct word: Level steps on a hillside to stop erosion are called ______. A: terraces — level steps on a hillside
chunks.source: terraces — level steps on a hillside

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Write a first conditional sentence using 'mulching' and 'moisture'. A: If we mulch the garden, the soil will keep moisture. — correct structure + target words
chunks.source: If we mulch the garden, the soil will keep moisture. — correct structure + target words

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Rewrite: 'Dumping garbage causes floods.' (Use 'If... will...') A: If we dump garbage, floods will occur. — first conditional showing cause-effect
chunks.source: If we dump garbage, floods will occur. — first conditional showing cause-effect

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Writing to Protect Our Environment. I can write a PLE-style composition using target vocabulary and 'as well as', 'had to'. PLE composition: Plan 4 paragraphs. Use past tense (degraded, polluted). Use 'had to' for past obligation. Use 'as well as' to add points. Include keywords: degrade, reserve, conserve, conservation, pollute, protect, as well as, had to. End exactly as instructed. Keywords: degrade: make worse or lower quality; reserve: protected area for nature; conserve: protect from harm or loss; conservation: the act of protecting nature; pollute: make dirty or harmful; protect: keep safe from damage; as well as: in addition to; had to: was obliged to (past)
chunks.source: PLE composition: Plan 4 paragraphs. Use past tense (degraded, polluted). Use 'had to' for past obligation. Use 'as well as' to add points. Include keywords: degrade, reserve, conserve, conservation, pollute, protect, as well as, had to. End exactly as instructed.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Fill the gap with the correct past tense: The factory ______ (pollute) the river last year. A: polluted — regular verb, add -d
chunks.source: polluted — regular verb, add -d

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Rewrite using 'as well as': We planted trees. We planted grass. A: We planted trees as well as grass. — adds second noun
chunks.source: We planted trees as well as grass. — adds second noun

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Choose the correct form: We ______ (have to) boil water during the cholera outbreak. A: had to — past obligation
chunks.source: had to — past obligation

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Fill the gap: The forest ______ is a protected area for wildlife. A: reserve — protected area for nature
chunks.source: reserve — protected area for nature

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Rewrite: 'We were obliged to build an incinerator.' (Use 'had to') A: We had to build an incinerator. — past obligation
chunks.source: We had to build an incinerator. — past obligation

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Write a sentence using 'conservation' and 'protect'. A: Conservation helps protect the environment. — both target words used correctly
chunks.source: Conservation helps protect the environment. — both target words used correctly

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Complete: The soil ______ (degrade) because of overgrazing. A: degraded — past tense of degrade
chunks.source: degraded — past tense of degrade

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Rewrite using 'as well as': They conserve water. They conserve soil. A: They conserve water as well as soil. — links two objects
chunks.source: They conserve water as well as soil. — links two objects

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Write a composition opening (2 sentences) using 'degrade' and 'pollute'. A: Our lake degraded quickly. Factories pollute it with waste. — past + present for ongoing problem
chunks.source: Our lake degraded quickly. Factories pollute it with waste. — past + present for ongoing problem

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: End a story with: '...so we had to protect our environment.' Write the sentence before it. A: We realised the damage was serious, so we had to protect our environment. — leads naturally to required ending
chunks.source: We realised the damage was serious, so we had to protect our environment. — leads naturally to required ending

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: A Wedding Day. I can describe a wedding ceremony using relative pronouns. A Ugandan wedding includes a bride, bridegroom, best man, maid, ring, bouquet, and a signed certificate; relative pronouns like who describe the people. Keywords: bride: the woman getting married; bridegroom: the man getting married; wedding: the marriage ceremony; couple: two people who are married; spouse: husband or wife; best man: the groom's main helper; maid: the bride's main helper; ring: a circular band for marriage; bouquet: a bunch of flowers; certificate: legal paper showing marriage
chunks.source: A Ugandan wedding includes a bride, bridegroom, best man, maid, ring, bouquet, and a signed certificate; relative pronouns like who describe the people.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Fill in the blank: The ______ is the woman who wore the gomesi. A: bride – the word refers to the woman getting married.
chunks.source: bride – the word refers to the woman getting married.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Choose the correct relative pronoun: The ______ is the man who wore the kanzu. A: bridegroom – who refers to a person.
chunks.source: bridegroom – who refers to a person.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: What does the best man give to the bridegroom? A: ring – the best man presents the ring.
chunks.source: ring – the best man presents the ring.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Which item does the maid carry? A: bouquet – the maid holds the flowers.
chunks.source: bouquet – the maid holds the flowers.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: What document is signed to make the marriage legal? A: certificate – it is the legal proof of marriage.
chunks.source: certificate – it is the legal proof of marriage.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Write a sentence using a relative pronoun about the couple. A: The couple who signed the certificate are now husband and wife. – uses who for people.
chunks.source: The couple who signed the certificate are now husband and wife. – uses who for people.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Identify the spouse in this sentence: After the wedding, she became his spouse. A: spouse – means husband or wife.
chunks.source: spouse – means husband or wife.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: What is the function of the ring in the ceremony? A: ring – a symbol of the marriage bond.
chunks.source: ring – a symbol of the marriage bond.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Which word completes: The ______ threw the bouquet to her friends? A: bride – she is the one who throws the bouquet.
chunks.source: bride – she is the one who throws the bouquet.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Marriages in Our Culture. I can explain types of marriage and use the future perfect tense. Uganda recognises religious, cultural, and civil marriages; each has introduction, engagement, bride price, dowry, and a function; future perfect shows actions finished by a future time. Keywords: marriage: the union of two people; religious: connected to faith; cultural: based on traditions; civil: performed by government officials; introduction: formal meeting of families; engagement: promise to marry; fiancé: man engaged to be married; bride price: gifts given to the bride's family; dowry: property a bride brings; function: a formal gathering
chunks.source: Uganda recognises religious, cultural, and civil marriages; each has introduction, engagement, bride price, dowry, and a function; future perfect shows actions finished by a future time.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Fill in the blank: A ______ marriage is registered at the town hall. A: civil – performed by government officials.
chunks.source: civil – performed by government officials.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Choose the correct term: The meeting of families before marriage is called ______. A: introduction – formal family meeting.
chunks.source: introduction – formal family meeting.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: What does the fiancé do during the engagement? A: visits the bride's family – shows commitment.
chunks.source: visits the bride's family – shows commitment.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Which item is part of the bride price? A: cows – typical livestock gift.
chunks.source: cows – typical livestock gift.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: What does the bride bring as dowry? A: land or household goods – property from her family.
chunks.source: land or household goods – property from her family.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Write a future perfect sentence: By next year, the couple ______. A: will have married – action completed before next year.
chunks.source: will have married – action completed before next year.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Identify the marriage type: A ceremony led by a priest in a church. A: religious – church ceremony.
chunks.source: religious – church ceremony.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: What is a function in marriage context? A: a formal gathering – celebration after marriage.
chunks.source: a formal gathering – celebration after marriage.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Complete: The ______ includes the exchange of gifts between families. A: introduction – where bride price is discussed.
chunks.source: introduction – where bride price is discussed.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: A Funeral in Our Community. I can describe a funeral using emphatic pronouns. A funeral includes burial, coffin, cemetery, grave; the widow, widower, orphan, mourners, and heir take part; emphatic pronouns like himself stress personal action. Keywords: burial: the act of placing a body in the ground; widow: woman whose husband has died; widower: man whose wife has died; orphan: child whose parents have died; mourner: person who expresses grief; coffin: box for the dead body; condolences: expressions of sympathy; cemetery: place where bodies are buried; grave: the hole where a coffin is placed; heir: person who inherits property
chunks.source: A funeral includes burial, coffin, cemetery, grave; the widow, widower, orphan, mourners, and heir take part; emphatic pronouns like himself stress personal action.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Fill in the blank: The ______ himself read the condolence messages. A: widower – emphatic pronoun himself refers to widower.
chunks.source: widower – emphatic pronoun himself refers to widower.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: What is the meaning of 'widow'? A: woman whose husband has died – definition.
chunks.source: woman whose husband has died – definition.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Which word refers to the place of burial? A: cemetery – where bodies are buried.
chunks.source: cemetery – where bodies are buried.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Identify the emphatic pronoun: The orphan herself sang a hymn. A: herself – emphasises the orphan.
chunks.source: herself – emphasises the orphan.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: What does the heir receive? A: property – land and belongings of the deceased.
chunks.source: property – land and belongings of the deceased.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Complete: The ______ was carried by six men. A: coffin – box for the dead body.
chunks.source: coffin – box for the dead body.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Write a sentence with an emphatic pronoun about the widow. A: The widow herself placed flowers on the grave. – herself emphasises widow.
chunks.source: The widow herself placed flowers on the grave. – herself emphasises widow.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: What are condolences? A: expressions of sympathy – sent to grieving family.
chunks.source: expressions of sympathy – sent to grieving family.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Which term describes a person who expresses grief at a funeral? A: mourner – attends to show sorrow.
chunks.source: mourner – attends to show sorrow.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Despite the Fact That…. I can write sentences with concession clauses and adjectives of number. Concession clauses with 'Despite the fact that' show contrast; adjectives of number like few, several, many quantify nouns; key funeral terms include shroud, barkcloth, respects, will, heiress, ancestral, mourn, funeral service. Keywords: shroud: cloth covering a dead body; barkcloth: traditional cloth from tree bark; respects: acts of honour; will: legal document for inheritance; heiress: female heir; ancestral: belonging to ancestors; mourn: to feel or show grief; funeral service: ceremony for the dead
chunks.source: Concession clauses with 'Despite the fact that' show contrast; adjectives of number like few, several, many quantify nouns; key funeral terms include shroud, barkcloth, respects, will, heiress, ancestral, mourn, funeral service.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Complete the sentence: Despite the fact that ______, the funeral service went on. A: it rained – concession clause needs a subject and verb.
chunks.source: it rained – concession clause needs a subject and verb.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Choose the correct adjective of number: ______ mourners stood by the grave. A: few – indicates a small number of countable nouns.
chunks.source: few – indicates a small number of countable nouns.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: What is a shroud? A: cloth covering a dead body – used in burial.
chunks.source: cloth covering a dead body – used in burial.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Identify the concession clause in: Despite the fact that she was tired, she spoke. Answer: Despite the fact that she was tired. – introduces contrast. A: undefined

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Which word means a female heir? A: heiress – female who inherits.
chunks.source: heiress – female who inherits.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: What material is barkcloth made from? A: tree bark – traditional Ugandan cloth.
chunks.source: tree bark – traditional Ugandan cloth.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Write a sentence using 'Despite the fact that' and 'few'. A: Despite the fact that few people arrived early, the service started on time. – combines both structures.
chunks.source: Despite the fact that few people arrived early, the service started on time. – combines both structures.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: What does 'ancestral' describe? A: belonging to ancestors – e.g., ancestral land.
chunks.source: belonging to ancestors – e.g., ancestral land.

chunks.subject: English
chunks.text: Q: Fill in: The ______ named the heiress. A: will – legal document for inheritance.
chunks.source: will – legal document for inheritance.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Venn Diagrams: Two Sets. I can interpret and shade Venn diagrams of two sets. A Venn diagram shows two sets with circles; the union is all members, the intersection is common members, and shading a region highlights a specific set. Keywords: venn diagram: a diagram with overlapping circles to show sets; union: all members in either set; intersection: members common to both sets; shade: to colour a region to show a set; region: a part of the diagram
chunks.source: A Venn diagram shows two sets with circles; the union is all members, the intersection is common members, and shading a region highlights a specific set.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: In a class, 18 pupils like matooke, 15 like posho, and 7 like both. How many pupils like matooke or posho? A: 26; Reason: union = 18 + 15 - 7 = 26.
chunks.source: 26; Reason: union = 18 + 15 - 7 = 26.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: If 20 pupils like only matooke, 12 like only posho, and 8 like both, what is the total number of pupils? A: 40; Reason: total = only matooke + only posho + both = 20+12+8 = 40.
chunks.source: 40; Reason: total = only matooke + only posho + both = 20+12+8 = 40.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Shade the union of two sets where set A has 10 members, set B has 12 members, and intersection has 4 members. How many members are in the union? A: 18; Reason: union = 10 + 12 - 4 = 18.
chunks.source: 18; Reason: union = 10 + 12 - 4 = 18.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Which region represents the intersection in a Venn diagram? A: The overlapping part of the two circles; Reason: intersection shows common members.
chunks.source: The overlapping part of the two circles; Reason: intersection shows common members.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: If you shade the whole of both circles, which set are you showing? A: The union; Reason: shading both circles completely shows the union.
chunks.source: The union; Reason: shading both circles completely shows the union.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: A Venn diagram has two circles. The region only in the left circle represents? A: Members only in the left set; Reason: that region excludes the intersection.
chunks.source: Members only in the left set; Reason: that region excludes the intersection.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: How many members are in the intersection if set A has 14, set B has 16, and union has 25? A: 5; Reason: intersection = A + B - union = 14+16-25 = 5.
chunks.source: 5; Reason: intersection = A + B - union = 14+16-25 = 5.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Draw a Venn diagram for sets: {1,2,3} and {3,4,5}. What is the intersection? A: {3}; Reason: only 3 appears in both sets.
chunks.source: {3}; Reason: only 3 appears in both sets.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Finding Unknown Members. I can find unknown numbers of members in Venn diagrams using equations. Use an equation: total = only A + only B + both, or union = A + B - intersection, to find unknown members in a Venn diagram. Keywords: unknown: not known yet; both: the two together; only: just one and not the other; equation: a maths sentence with an equals sign; members: the people or items in a set
chunks.source: Use an equation: total = only A + only B + both, or union = A + B - intersection, to find unknown members in a Venn diagram.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Total = 50, only A = 20, only B = 15. Find both. A: 15; Reason: both = total - only A - only B = 50 - 20 - 15 = 15.
chunks.source: 15; Reason: both = total - only A - only B = 50 - 20 - 15 = 15.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Set A = 30, set B = 25, union = 40. Find intersection. A: 15; Reason: intersection = A + B - union = 30 + 25 - 40 = 15.
chunks.source: 15; Reason: intersection = A + B - union = 30 + 25 - 40 = 15.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: In a survey, 60 people like tea, 40 like coffee, 20 like both. How many like at least one? A: 80; Reason: union = 60 + 40 - 20 = 80.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Only matooke = 18, only posho = 12, both = 10. Total members? A: 40; Reason: total = only A + only B + both = 18+12+10 = 40.
chunks.source: 40; Reason: total = only A + only B + both = 18+12+10 = 40.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: A Venn diagram shows only A = 5, only B = 7, both = 3. What is the total? A: 15; Reason: total = 5+7+3 = 15.
chunks.source: 15; Reason: total = 5+7+3 = 15.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: If total = 100, only A = 40, only B = 35, find both. A: 25; Reason: both = 100 - 40 - 35 = 25.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Set A has 22 members, set B has 18 members, intersection = 8. Find union. A: 32; Reason: union = 22 + 18 - 8 = 32.
chunks.source: 32; Reason: union = 22 + 18 - 8 = 32.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: A class has 45 pupils. 28 like maths, 20 like English, 12 like both. How many like at least one? A: 36; Reason: union = 28 + 20 - 12 = 36.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Sets and Probability. I can use sets to find probabilities of events. Probability is the fraction of favourable outcomes over total outcomes. Use sets to count them. Keywords: probability: the chance something happens; favourable: the outcomes we want; total outcomes: all possible outcomes; fraction: a part of a whole written as numerator/denominator; chance: the likelihood of an event
chunks.source: Probability is the fraction of favourable outcomes over total outcomes. Use sets to count them.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: A die is rolled. What is the probability of getting a number greater than 4? A: 2/6 = 1/3; Reason: favourable outcomes (5,6) = 2, total outcomes = 6.
chunks.source: 2/6 = 1/3; Reason: favourable outcomes (5,6) = 2, total outcomes = 6.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: A bag has 7 green and 3 yellow marbles. Probability of green? A: 7/10; Reason: favourable = 7, total = 10.
chunks.source: 7/10; Reason: favourable = 7, total = 10.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: A spinner has 4 equal sections: 1 red, 2 blue, 1 yellow. Probability of blue? A: 2/4 = 1/2; Reason: favourable = 2, total = 4.
chunks.source: 2/4 = 1/2; Reason: favourable = 2, total = 4.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: In a class of 40, 25 are boys. Probability of picking a girl? A: 15/40 = 3/8; Reason: favourable = 15 girls, total = 40.
chunks.source: 15/40 = 3/8; Reason: favourable = 15 girls, total = 40.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: A box contains 8 apples and 4 oranges. Probability of picking an apple? A: 8/12 = 2/3; Reason: favourable = 8, total = 12.
chunks.source: 8/12 = 2/3; Reason: favourable = 8, total = 12.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: A coin is tossed. What is the chance of heads? A: 1/2; Reason: favourable = 1, total outcomes = 2.
chunks.source: 1/2; Reason: favourable = 1, total outcomes = 2.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: A bag has 5 red, 5 blue, 5 green balls. Probability of red? A: 5/15 = 1/3; Reason: favourable = 5, total = 15.
chunks.source: 5/15 = 1/3; Reason: favourable = 5, total = 15.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: A deck of 52 cards has 4 aces. Probability of drawing an ace? A: 4/52 = 1/13; Reason: favourable = 4, total = 52.
chunks.source: 4/52 = 1/13; Reason: favourable = 4, total = 52.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: PLE Word Problems with Sets. I can solve PLE-style word problems using Venn diagrams. Draw a Venn diagram, fill in known numbers, then use union = A + B - intersection or total = only A + only B + both to solve PLE word problems. Keywords: word problem: a maths question written in words; venn diagram: a diagram with overlapping circles; total: the whole amount; find: to work out the answer; members: the people or items in a set
chunks.source: Draw a Venn diagram, fill in known numbers, then use union = A + B - intersection or total = only A + only B + both to solve PLE word problems.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: In a village, 50 people like maize, 40 like beans, 20 like both. How many like at least one? A: 70; Reason: union = 50 + 40 - 20 = 70.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: A survey: 60 like tea, 35 like coffee, 15 like both. Find total who like tea or coffee. A: 80; Reason: union = 60 + 35 - 15 = 80.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Only football = 18, only netball = 12, both = 10. Total members? A: 40; Reason: total = 18+12+10 = 40.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Set A = 30, set B = 25, intersection = 10. Find union. A: 45; Reason: union = 30 + 25 - 10 = 45.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Total = 100, only A = 40, only B = 30. Find both. A: 30; Reason: both = 100 - 40 - 30 = 30.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: A class has 45 pupils. 28 like maths, 22 like English, 12 like both. How many like at least one? A: 38; Reason: union = 28 + 22 - 12 = 38.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: In a market, 70 buyers. 35 buy only tomatoes, 20 buy only onions. How many buy both? A: 15; Reason: both = 70 - 35 - 20 = 15.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: A word problem: 55 like matooke, 45 like posho, 25 like both. Find the total who like at least one. A: 75; Reason: union = 55 + 45 - 25 = 75.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Large Numbers and Place Value. I can read, write and expand numbers up to billions using place value. Every **digit** has a **place value** that tells its **value**. To **expand** a number, write each **digit** times its **place value** and add. Numbers up to **billion** have ten **digits**. Keywords: billion: a thousand million (1,000,000,000); place value: the value of a digit based on its position; value: what a digit is worth in a number; expand: write a number as the sum of its place values; digits: the symbols 0 to 9 used to write numbers
chunks.source: Every **digit** has a **place value** that tells its **value**. To **expand** a number, write each **digit** times its **place value** and add. Numbers up to **billion** have ten **digits**.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Write 4,000,000,000 in words. A: Four **billion** — the **digit** 4 is in the **billions** **place value**.
chunks.source: Four **billion** — the **digit** 4 is in the **billions** **place value**.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: **Expand** 6,070,005. A: 6,000,000 + 70,000 + 5 — zeros hold empty **place value** columns.
chunks.source: 6,000,000 + 70,000 + 5 — zeros hold empty **place value** columns.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: What is the **value** of 8 in 8,450,000? A: 8,000,000 — the **digit** 8 is in the millions **place value**.
chunks.source: 8,000,000 — the **digit** 8 is in the millions **place value**.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Write 2 **billion** 50 million 3 thousand in figures. A: 2,050,003,000 — group **digits** in threes from right.
chunks.source: 2,050,003,000 — group **digits** in threes from right.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: **Expand** 90,000,000 + 400,000 + 60 + 2 as a single number. A: 90,400,062 — add each **place value**.
chunks.source: 90,400,062 — add each **place value**.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: How many **digits** in 1,000,000,000? A: Ten **digits** — one **billion** has 1 followed by nine zeros.
chunks.source: Ten **digits** — one **billion** has 1 followed by nine zeros.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Write 7,000,000 + 20,000 + 500 + 3 in standard form. A: 7,020,503 — fill empty **place value** columns with zeros.
chunks.source: 7,020,503 — fill empty **place value** columns with zeros.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: The **value** of 5 in 5,600,000 is? A: 5,000,000 — 5 is in the millions **place value**.
chunks.source: 5,000,000 — 5 is in the millions **place value**.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: **Expand** 100,000,005. A: 100,000,000 + 5 — zeros show empty **place value**.
chunks.source: 100,000,000 + 5 — zeros show empty **place value**.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Which **digit** is in the ten millions place in 45,678,901? A: 4 — count **place value** columns from right.
chunks.source: 4 — count **place value** columns from right.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Number Bases. I can convert numbers between base ten, base two and base five. Each base has its own **digits** and place values (×base each step). To **convert** to **base ten**, multiply each **digit** by its place value and add. To **convert** from **base ten**, divide by the base and read remainders bottom to top. Keywords: base ten: our usual counting system using digits 0-9; base two: counting system using only digits 0 and 1; base five: counting system using digits 0-4; convert: change a number from one base to another; digits: the symbols used to write numbers in a base
chunks.source: Each base has its own **digits** and place values (×base each step). To **convert** to **base ten**, multiply each **digit** by its place value and add. To **convert** from **base ten**, divide by the base and read remainders bottom to top.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: **Convert** 25₁₀ to **base two**. A: 11001₂ — divide by 2: remainders 1,0,0,1,1 read up.
chunks.source: 11001₂ — divide by 2: remainders 1,0,0,1,1 read up.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: **Convert** 37₁₀ to **base five**. A: 122₅ — 37÷5=7 rem2, 7÷5=2 rem2, 2÷5=0 rem2 → 122₅.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Write 15 in **base two**. A: 1111₂ — 8+4+2+1=15.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Write 28 in **base five**. A: 103₅ — 25+0+3=28.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: **Convert** 11100₂ to **base ten**. A: 28 — headings 16,8,4,2,1: 16+8+4=28.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: **Convert** 124₁₀ to **base five**. A: 444₅ — 124÷5=24 rem4, 24÷5=4 rem4, 4÷5=0 rem4.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Indices and Powers. I can use index notation, calculate powers and write numbers in standard form. The **index** shows how many times the **base** is multiplied. **Squared** means **index** 2. **Standard form** writes numbers as A × 10ⁿ where 1 ≤ A < 10 and n is the **index**. Keywords: index: the small number showing how many times to multiply; power: the result of multiplying a number by itself; base: the number that is multiplied by itself; squared: raised to the power of 2 (× itself once); standard form: writing a number as A × 10ⁿ where 1 ≤ A < 10
chunks.source: The **index** shows how many times the **base** is multiplied. **Squared** means **index** 2. **Standard form** writes numbers as A × 10ⁿ where 1 ≤ A < 10 and n is the **index**.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Write 4 × 4 × 4 × 4 × 4 in index notation. A: 4⁵ — **base** 4 appears 5 times.
chunks.source: 4⁵ — **base** 4 appears 5 times.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Calculate 3⁴. A: 81 — 3×3×3×3 = 81.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Write 8,000,000 in **standard form**. A: 8 × 10⁶ — decimal moves 6 places.
chunks.source: 8 × 10⁶ — decimal moves 6 places.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Write 0.0003 in **standard form**. A: 3 × 10⁻⁴ — decimal moves 4 places right.
chunks.source: 3 × 10⁻⁴ — decimal moves 4 places right.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: **Standard form** of 450,000. A: 4.5 × 10⁵ — one digit before decimal.
chunks.source: 4.5 × 10⁵ — one digit before decimal.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: **Standard form** of 0.0062. A: 6.2 × 10⁻³ — decimal right 3 places.
chunks.source: 6.2 × 10⁻³ — decimal right 3 places.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Simplify (3²)³. A: 729 — 3⁶ = 729.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Write 5.6 × 10³ as ordinary number. A: 5,600 — move decimal 3 places right.
chunks.source: 5,600 — move decimal 3 places right.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Prime Factorisation, LCM and GCF. I can find prime factors, LCM and GCF using factor trees. A **factor tree** breaks a number into **prime factor**s. **GCF** uses **common** **prime factor**s with lowest powers. **LCM** uses all **prime factor**s with highest powers. **GCF** × **LCM** = product of the two numbers. Keywords: prime factor: a factor that is a prime number; lcm: lowest common multiple — smallest number divisible by both; gcf: greatest common factor — largest number dividing both; factor tree: diagram breaking a number into prime factors; common: shared by two or more numbers
chunks.source: A **factor tree** breaks a number into **prime factor**s. **GCF** uses **common** **prime factor**s with lowest powers. **LCM** uses all **prime factor**s with highest powers. **GCF** × **LCM** = product of the two numbers.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Find the **prime factor**s of 56. A: 2³ × 7 — **factor tree**: 56=2×28=2×2×14=2×2×2×7.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: **GCF** of 24 and 36. A: 12 — **common** **prime factor**s: 2² × 3 = 12.
chunks.source: 12 — **common** **prime factor**s: 2² × 3 = 12.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: **LCM** of 8 and 12. A: 24 — 8=2³, 12=2²×3. Highest powers: 2³×3=24.
chunks.source: 24 — 8=2³, 12=2²×3. Highest powers: 2³×3=24.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Two numbers have **gcf** 4 and **lcm** 48. One is 16. Find the other. A: 12 — 4×48=192. 192÷16=12.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Write 84 as product of **prime factor**s. A: 2² × 3 × 7 — **factor tree** gives 2,2,3,7.
chunks.source: 2² × 3 × 7 — **factor tree** gives 2,2,3,7.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Find the **gcf** of 100 and 125. A: 25 — 100=2²×5², 125=5³. **Common**: 5²=25.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: BODMAS in Full. I can solve mixed operations using the full BODMAS order including brackets and indices. BODMAS gives the fixed order: brackets, indices, divide/multiply, add/subtract. Follow it every time to get the right answer. Keywords: bodmas: the rule that tells us which operation to do first; brackets: round, square or curly signs that group numbers; indices: small numbers written up high that show powers; order: the fixed sequence we follow in BODMAS; operations: the four calculations: add, subtract, multiply, divide
chunks.source: BODMAS gives the fixed order: brackets, indices, divide/multiply, add/subtract. Follow it every time to get the right answer.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Evaluate 15 + 6 × 2 using BODMAS. A: 27 — Multiply first: 6 × 2 = 12, then add 15 + 12 = 27.
chunks.source: 27 — Multiply first: 6 × 2 = 12, then add 15 + 12 = 27.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Evaluate (12 + 8) ÷ 4. A: 5 — Brackets first: 12 + 8 = 20, then divide 20 ÷ 4 = 5.
chunks.source: 5 — Brackets first: 12 + 8 = 20, then divide 20 ÷ 4 = 5.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Evaluate 3² + 4 × 5. A: 29 — Indices first: 3² = 9, then multiply 4 × 5 = 20, then add 9 + 20 = 29.
chunks.source: 29 — Indices first: 3² = 9, then multiply 4 × 5 = 20, then add 9 + 20 = 29.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Evaluate 30 − (5 + 3) × 2. A: 14 — Brackets first: 5 + 3 = 8, then multiply 8 × 2 = 16, then subtract 30 − 16 = 14.
chunks.source: 14 — Brackets first: 5 + 3 = 8, then multiply 8 × 2 = 16, then subtract 30 − 16 = 14.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Evaluate 18 ÷ 3 + 2³. A: 14 — Indices: 2³ = 8, divide: 18 ÷ 3 = 6, add: 6 + 8 = 14.
chunks.source: 14 — Indices: 2³ = 8, divide: 18 ÷ 3 = 6, add: 6 + 8 = 14.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Evaluate 4 × (6 + 2) − 5. A: 27 — Brackets: 6 + 2 = 8, multiply: 4 × 8 = 32, subtract: 32 − 5 = 27.
chunks.source: 27 — Brackets: 6 + 2 = 8, multiply: 4 × 8 = 32, subtract: 32 − 5 = 27.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Evaluate 50 − 10 ÷ 2 + 3. A: 48 — Divide first: 10 ÷ 2 = 5, then subtract and add left to right: 50 − 5 = 45, 45 + 3 = 48.
chunks.source: 48 — Divide first: 10 ÷ 2 = 5, then subtract and add left to right: 50 − 5 = 45, 45 + 3 = 48.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Evaluate (7 + 3)² ÷ 5. A: 20 — Brackets: 7 + 3 = 10, indices: 10² = 100, divide: 100 ÷ 5 = 20.
chunks.source: 20 — Brackets: 7 + 3 = 10, indices: 10² = 100, divide: 100 ÷ 5 = 20.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Evaluate 100 − 4 × (5 + 3). A: 68 — Brackets: 5 + 3 = 8, multiply: 4 × 8 = 32, subtract: 100 − 32 = 68.
chunks.source: 68 — Brackets: 5 + 3 = 8, multiply: 4 × 8 = 32, subtract: 100 − 32 = 68.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Evaluate 2³ × 3 + 4. A: 28 — Indices: 2³ = 8, multiply: 8 × 3 = 24, add: 24 + 4 = 28.
chunks.source: 28 — Indices: 2³ = 8, multiply: 8 × 3 = 24, add: 24 + 4 = 28.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Squares and Square Roots. I can find squares and square roots of numbers and identify perfect squares. Square = number × itself. Square root = the number that gives the square. Perfect squares have whole roots; others we estimate. Keywords: square: a number multiplied by itself; square root: the number that gives the square when multiplied by itself; perfect square: a number that has a whole number square root; root: short for square root; estimate: find a close value when the exact root is not whole
chunks.source: Square = number × itself. Square root = the number that gives the square. Perfect squares have whole roots; others we estimate.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Find the square of 14. A: 196 — 14 × 14 = 196.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Is 200 a perfect square? Explain. A: No — 14² = 196, 15² = 225, 200 is between them, no whole root.
chunks.source: No — 14² = 196, 15² = 225, 200 is between them, no whole root.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Estimate √30 to one decimal place. A: 5.5 — 5² = 25, 6² = 36, 30 is halfway, so √30 ≈ 5.5.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: A square tile has area 64 cm². Find its side length. A: 8 cm — √64 = 8.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Find the square of 23. A: 529 — 23 × 23 = 529.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Which perfect square is closest to 150? A: 144 — 12² = 144, 13² = 169, 150 − 144 = 6, 169 − 150 = 19.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Estimate √80 to the nearest whole number. A: 9 — 9² = 81, 8² = 64, 80 is closer to 81.
chunks.source: 9 — 9² = 81, 8² = 64, 80 is closer to 81.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Cubes and Cube Roots. I can find cubes and cube roots of numbers and link them to volume. Cube = n × n × n. Cube root = the number that makes the cube. Perfect cubes have whole roots.
