chunks.text: Q: A motorist drives 2 hours at 60 km/h and 3 hours at 80 km/h. Find average speed. A: 72 km/h — total distance = 120+240 = 360 km, total time = 5 h, average = 360÷5
chunks.source: 72 km/h — total distance = 120+240 = 360 km, total time = 5 h, average = 360÷5

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: A journey of 300 km takes 5 hours. First 180 km at 45 km/h. Speed for the rest? A: 60 km/h — time₁ = 4 h, time₂ = 1 h, distance₂ = 120 km, speed = 120÷1
chunks.source: 60 km/h — time₁ = 4 h, time₂ = 1 h, distance₂ = 120 km, speed = 120÷1

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: A lorry covers 240 km. First 4 hours at 40 km/h, then 2 hours at 60 km/h. Average speed? A: 46.7 km/h — total distance = 160+120 = 280 km, total time = 6 h, average = 280÷6
chunks.source: 46.7 km/h — total distance = 160+120 = 280 km, total time = 6 h, average = 280÷6

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: A car travels at 50 km/h for 2.5 hours, then 70 km/h for 1.5 hours. Average speed? A: 57.5 km/h — total distance = 125+105 = 230 km, total time = 4 h, average = 230÷4
chunks.source: 57.5 km/h — total distance = 125+105 = 230 km, total time = 4 h, average = 230÷4

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: PLE 2022: A bus goes from Kampala to Masaka (130 km) at 65 km/h and returns at 50 km/h. Average speed? A: 56.5 km/h — total distance = 260 km, total time = 2+2.6 = 4.6 h, average = 260÷4.6
chunks.source: 56.5 km/h — total distance = 260 km, total time = 2+2.6 = 4.6 h, average = 260÷4.6

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: PLE 2021: A journey has three equal distances at 20, 30, 60 km/h. Average speed? A: 30 km/h — let each be d. total distance = 3d. total time = d/20+d/30+d/60 = 6d/60 = d/10. average = 3d ÷ (d/10) = 30
chunks.source: 30 km/h — let each be d. total distance = 3d. total time = d/20+d/30+d/60 = 6d/60 = d/10. average = 3d ÷ (d/10) = 30

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Timetables and Time Zones. I can read timetables, calculate durations, and convert between time zones. Read **timetables** in **24-hour** clock. **Duration** = finish − start (borrow 60 min if needed). For **time zone** changes: find UTC difference, add if destination is ahead, subtract if behind. Always show steps for **PLE**. Keywords: timetable: a schedule showing departure and arrival times; 24-hour: time written from 00:00 to 23:59; time zone: a region with the same standard time; duration: the length of time something lasts; arrive: to reach a destination
chunks.source: Read **timetables** in **24-hour** clock. **Duration** = finish − start (borrow 60 min if needed). For **time zone** changes: find UTC difference, add if destination is ahead, subtract if behind. Always show steps for **PLE**.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: A bus departs at 06:45 and arrives at 11:20. Find the duration. A: 4 hours 35 minutes — 11:20 − 06:45 = 4 h 35 min
chunks.source: 4 hours 35 minutes — 11:20 − 06:45 = 4 h 35 min

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: A train leaves at 14:30 and arrives at 19:15. Duration? A: 4 hours 45 minutes — 19:15 − 14:30 = 4 h 45 min
chunks.source: 4 hours 45 minutes — 19:15 − 14:30 = 4 h 45 min

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: A flight departs at 22:40 and lands at 02:10 next day. Duration? A: 3 hours 30 minutes — 26:10 − 22:40 = 3 h 30 min
chunks.source: 3 hours 30 minutes — 26:10 − 22:40 = 3 h 30 min

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Convert 3:45 pm to 24-hour clock. A: 15:45 — add 12 to pm hours
chunks.source: 15:45 — add 12 to pm hours

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Convert 00:30 to 12-hour clock. A: 12:30 am — 00:00 is midnight
chunks.source: 12:30 am — 00:00 is midnight

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Kampala (UTC+3) is 14:00. Time in London (UTC+0)? A: 11:00 — subtract 3 hours
chunks.source: 11:00 — subtract 3 hours

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Nairobi (UTC+3) is 09:00. Time in Mumbai (UTC+5:30)? A: 11:30 — add 2.5 hours
chunks.source: 11:30 — add 2.5 hours

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Plane leaves Accra (UTC+0) at 15:00, arrives Kampala (UTC+3) at 21:00. Duration? A: 3 hours — Kampala 21:00 = Accra 18:00. 18:00 − 15:00 = 3 h
chunks.source: 3 hours — Kampala 21:00 = Accra 18:00. 18:00 − 15:00 = 3 h

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: PLE: Bus leaves Kampala 08:00, reaches border 12:30, leaves 13:00, reaches Kigali 16:00. Total travel time? A: 7 hours 30 minutes — (12:30−08:00)+(16:00−13:00) = 4:30+3:00 = 7:30

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: PLE: Flight from Dubai (UTC+4) 02:00 to Entebbe (UTC+3) takes 5h 20min. Local arrival? A: 06:20 — Dubai 02:00+5:20=07:20 Dubai. Entebbe = 07:20−1h = 06:20

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Time Word Problems. I can solve mixed word problems involving time, speed, and timetables. For mixed **time word problems**: (1) List all given numbers with units. (2) Break into parts. (3) Use **speed** = **distance** ÷ **time** for moving parts. (4) Add **duration** of stops. (5) Add total time to **start** to get **finish**. (6) Check answer makes sense. Show all steps for **PLE**. Keywords: problem: a question that needs a solution; duration: the length of time an event lasts; start: the beginning time; finish: the ending time; calculate: to work out using mathematics
chunks.source: For mixed **time word problems**: (1) List all given numbers with units. (2) Break into parts. (3) Use **speed** = **distance** ÷ **time** for moving parts. (4) Add **duration** of stops. (5) Add total time to **start** to get **finish**. (6) Check answer makes sense. Show all steps for **PLE**.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: A lorry leaves at 05:30. Travels 200 km at 50 km/h. Stops 45 min. Travels 150 km at 60 km/h. Arrival time? A: 12:45 — time₁=4h, stop=0.75h, time₂=2.5h, total=7.25h=7h15m, 05:30+7:15=12:45

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: A student starts revising at 18:45. Studies 1h20m, break 15m, studies 50m. Finish time? A: 21:10 — total=145m=2h25m, 18:45+2:25=21:10

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: A flight leaves at 23:30, lands at 03:15 next day. Duration? A: 3 hours 45 minutes — 27:15−23:30=3h45m
chunks.source: 3 hours 45 minutes — 27:15−23:30=3h45m

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Kampala to Gulu 330 km. Bus at 60 km/h, stops 30 min at 200 km mark. Leaves 08:00. Arrival? A: 14:00 — time₁=200÷60=3.333h=3h20m, stop=30m, time₂=130÷60=2.167h=2h10m, total=6h, 08:00+6h=14:00

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: PLE: Car travels 180 km at 60 km/h, then 120 km at 40 km/h. Total time? A: 6 hours — 180÷60=3h, 120÷40=3h, total=6h

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: PLE: Meeting starts 14:30, ends 17:15. Tea break 20 min. Working duration? A: 2 hours 25 minutes — total=2h45m, minus 20m = 2h25m
chunks.source: 2 hours 25 minutes — total=2h45m, minus 20m = 2h25m

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: PLE: Athlete runs 10 km at 12 km/h, walks 2 km at 5 km/h. Total time? A: 1 hour 4 minutes — run=10÷12=0.833h=50m, walk=2÷5=0.4h=24m, total=74m=1h14m? Wait: 50+24=74 min = 1h14m. Let me recheck: 10/12=5/6 h=50 min. 2/5=0.4h=24 min. Total 74 min = 1h14m.
chunks.source: 1 hour 4 minutes — run=10÷12=0.833h=50m, walk=2÷5=0.4h=24m, total=74m=1h14m? Wait: 50+24=74 min = 1h14m. Let me recheck: 10/12=5/6 h=50 min. 2/5=0.4h=24 min. Total 74 min = 1h14m.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: A watch gains 5 minutes every hour. Set correctly at 06:00. What does it show at 12:00 real time? A: 12:30 — 6 hours × 5 min = 30 min gained. 12:00 + 30 min = 12:30
chunks.source: 12:30 — 6 hours × 5 min = 30 min gained. 12:00 + 30 min = 12:30

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Two buses leave same station. Bus A at 08:00, 60 km/h. Bus B at 09:00, 80 km/h. When does B catch A? A: 12:00 — A has 60 km head start. Relative speed = 20 km/h. Catch up time = 60÷20=3h. 09:00+3h=12:00
chunks.source: 12:00 — A has 60 km head start. Relative speed = 20 km/h. Catch up time = 60÷20=3h. 09:00+3h=12:00

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Units of Length Review. I can convert between kilometres, metres and centimetres in multi-step problems. To change between kilometres, metres and centimetres, multiply or divide by 1000 and 100 in the correct order. Keywords: convert: to change from one unit to another; kilometre: a unit of length equal to 1000 metres; metre: a unit of length equal to 100 centimetres; centimetre: a unit of length equal to 10 millimetres; units: standard measures used for length
chunks.source: To change between kilometres, metres and centimetres, multiply or divide by 1000 and 100 in the correct order.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Convert 4.5 km to metres. A: 4500 m (multiply by 1000).
chunks.source: 4500 m (multiply by 1000).

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Change 3200 cm to metres. A: 32 m (divide by 100).
chunks.source: 32 m (divide by 100).

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: If a road is 0.75 km, how many metres? A: 750 m (0.75 × 1000).

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Express 12000 cm in kilometres. A: 0.12 km (divide by 100 then 1000).
chunks.source: 0.12 km (divide by 100 then 1000).

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Amina walks 2 km 300 m. Write the distance in metres. A: 2300 m (2 km = 2000 m + 300 m).

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: A rope is 1500 cm long. How many metres? A: 15 m (1500 ÷ 100).

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Convert 0.03 km to centimetres. A: 3000 cm (0.03 × 1000 × 100).

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Which is longer: 500 m or 0.6 km? A: 0.6 km = 600 m, so 0.6 km is longer.
chunks.source: 0.6 km = 600 m, so 0.6 km is longer.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Circles: Circumference and Area. I can calculate the circumference and area of a circle using radius or diameter. Circumference uses 2πr or πd; area uses πr². Always identify radius or diameter first. Keywords: circumference: the distance around a circle; area: the space inside a flat shape; radius: the distance from the centre to the edge; diameter: the distance across the circle through the centre; pi: a constant approximately 3.14 used in circle formulas
chunks.source: Circumference uses 2πr or πd; area uses πr². Always identify radius or diameter first.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Find the circumference of a circle with radius 10 cm. A: 62.8 cm (2 × 3.14 × 10).

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Calculate the area of a circle with diameter 12 cm. A: 113.04 cm² (radius 6 cm, π × 6²).
chunks.source: 113.04 cm² (radius 6 cm, π × 6²).

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: If the circumference is 31.4 cm, what is the radius? A: 5 cm (C = 2πr → r = C/(2π)).
chunks.source: 5 cm (C = 2πr → r = C/(2π)).

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: A circular garden has diameter 20 m. What is its area? A: 314 m² (radius 10 m, π × 10²).
chunks.source: 314 m² (radius 10 m, π × 10²).

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Which is larger: circumference of radius 5 cm or diameter 12 cm? A: Diameter 12 cm gives C = 37.68 cm, radius 5 cm gives 31.4 cm, so diameter 12 cm larger.
chunks.source: Diameter 12 cm gives C = 37.68 cm, radius 5 cm gives 31.4 cm, so diameter 12 cm larger.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Use π = 22/7 to find circumference of radius 7 cm. A: 44 cm (2 × 22/7 × 7).

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Find the radius if area = 154 cm² (π = 22/7). A: 7 cm (πr² = 154 → r² = 49).

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: A wheel has circumference 66 cm. What is its diameter? A: 21 cm (C = πd → d = C/π = 66 ÷ (22/7) = 21).

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Area of Combined Shapes. I can find the total area of shapes made by joining rectangles, triangles and circles. Break combined shapes into rectangles, triangles and circles; find each area then add or subtract. Keywords: area: the space inside a flat shape; combined: put together from two or more parts; rectangle: a four-sided shape with opposite sides equal; triangle: a three-sided shape; circle: a round shape with all points equal distance from centre
chunks.source: Break combined shapes into rectangles, triangles and circles; find each area then add or subtract.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Find total area of a rectangle 8 m × 5 m with a triangle on top (base 8 m, height 3 m). A: 40 + 12 = 52 m² (rectangle 40, triangle ½×8×3=12).
chunks.source: 40 + 12 = 52 m² (rectangle 40, triangle ½×8×3=12).

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: A square 6 m side has a quarter circle of radius 6 m cut out. Find shaded area (π=3.14). A: 36 − 28.26 = 7.74 m² (square 36, quarter circle ¼×π×36=28.26).
chunks.source: 36 − 28.26 = 7.74 m² (square 36, quarter circle ¼×π×36=28.26).

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Combined shape: rectangle 10×4 m and triangle base 10 m height 5 m. Total area? A: 40 + 25 = 65 m².

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: A rectangle 15×10 m has a circular pond radius 3 m. Find grass area. A: 150 − 28.26 = 121.74 m².

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Two rectangles 5×3 m and 4×3 m joined side by side. Total area? A: 15 + 12 = 27 m².

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Triangle base 12 m height 6 m attached to rectangle 12×4 m. Total area? A: 36 + 48 = 84 m².

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Circle radius 5 m inside a square 10×10 m. Find area outside circle. A: 100 − 78.5 = 21.5 m².

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Shape: rectangle 9×6 m, triangle on one 9 m side height 4 m, semicircle on opposite 9 m side radius 4.5 m. Find total area (π=3.14). A: 54 + 18 + 31.79 = 103.79 m².

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Volume and Capacity. I can calculate the volume of cuboids and cylinders and change cubic metres to litres. Volume of cuboid = length × width × height; volume of cylinder = π × radius² × height. 1 m³ = 1000 litres. Keywords: volume: the amount of space inside a 3D object; cuboid: a 3D shape with six rectangular faces; cylinder: a 3D shape with circular ends and curved side; litres: a unit of capacity equal to 1000 cm³; capacity: the maximum amount a container can hold
chunks.source: Volume of cuboid = length × width × height; volume of cylinder = π × radius² × height. 1 m³ = 1000 litres.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Find the volume of a cuboid 3 m × 2 m × 1.5 m. A: 9 m³ (3×2×1.5).

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Convert 4.5 m³ to litres. A: 4500 litres (×1000).

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: A cylinder has radius 0.3 m and height 1 m. Find its volume (π=3.14). A: 0.2826 m³ (π×0.09×1).

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: What is the capacity in litres of a cylinder with volume 0.75 m³? A: 750 litres (0.75×1000).

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: A rectangular tank 2.5 m long, 1.2 m wide, 1 m high. How many litres of water can it hold? A: 3000 litres (2.5×1.2×1=3 m³ → 3000 L).

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Cylinder radius 0.4 m, height 2.5 m. Volume? A: 1.256 m³ (π×0.16×2.5).

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: If a container holds 2500 litres, what is its volume in m³? A: 2.5 m³ (÷1000).

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Compare: cuboid 2×2×2 m vs cylinder radius 1 m height 2 m. Which has larger volume? A: Cuboid 8 m³, cylinder 6.28 m³ → cuboid larger.
chunks.source: Cuboid 8 m³, cylinder 6.28 m³ → cuboid larger.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Simplifying and Expanding. I can simplify algebraic expressions and expand brackets. Simplifying joins like terms; expanding multiplies each term inside brackets. Keywords: simplify: to make an expression shorter by combining like terms; expand: to multiply out brackets so every term is shown; brackets: symbols ( ) that group terms together; like terms: terms that have the same variable and power; expression: a mathematical phrase with numbers, variables and operations
chunks.source: Simplifying joins like terms; expanding multiplies each term inside brackets.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Simplify 6a + 4a - 2a. A: 12a - 2a = 10a. Combine like terms.
chunks.source: 12a - 2a = 10a. Combine like terms.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Expand 4(b - 2). A: 4b - 8. Multiply 4 by each term inside brackets.
chunks.source: 4b - 8. Multiply 4 by each term inside brackets.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Simplify 7m + 3n - 2m + 5n. A: (7m-2m)+(3n+5n)=5m+8n. Group like terms.
chunks.source: (7m-2m)+(3n+5n)=5m+8n. Group like terms.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Expand and simplify 3(x+2)+2(x-1). A: 3x+6+2x-2 = 5x+4. Expand then combine like terms.
chunks.source: 3x+6+2x-2 = 5x+4. Expand then combine like terms.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Simplify 9k - 4k + k. A: 9k-4k=5k; 5k+k=6k. Add and subtract like terms.
chunks.source: 9k-4k=5k; 5k+k=6k. Add and subtract like terms.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Expand 5(2y+3). A: 10y+15. Distribute 5 to both terms.
chunks.source: 10y+15. Distribute 5 to both terms.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Simplify 8p + 3q - 5p - q. A: (8p-5p)+(3q-q)=3p+2q. Collect like terms.
chunks.source: (8p-5p)+(3q-q)=3p+2q. Collect like terms.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Expand and simplify 2(3r-4)+r. A: 6r-8+r = 7r-8. Expand then combine like terms.
chunks.source: 6r-8+r = 7r-8. Expand then combine like terms.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Simplify 10t - 3t + 2t - t. A: 10t-3t=7t; 7t+2t=9t; 9t-t=8t. Stepwise combine.
chunks.source: 10t-3t=7t; 7t+2t=9t; 9t-t=8t. Stepwise combine.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Equations and Inequalities. I can solve simple equations and represent inequalities on a number line. Solving an equation finds the unknown; inequalities show a range of values on a number line. Keywords: equation: a statement that two expressions are equal; inequality: a statement that one expression is greater or less than another; solve: to find the value of the unknown that makes the equation true; unknown: the variable we need to find; number line: a line with numbers used to show solutions of inequalities
chunks.source: Solving an equation finds the unknown; inequalities show a range of values on a number line.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Solve 3x + 6 = 18. A: Subtract 6: 3x=12. Divide 3: x=4. Balanced steps.
chunks.source: Subtract 6: 3x=12. Divide 3: x=4. Balanced steps.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Solve 5y - 10 = 15. A: Add 10: 5y=25. Divide 5: y=5. Keep equation balanced.
chunks.source: Add 10: 5y=25. Divide 5: y=5. Keep equation balanced.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Show x < 4 on a number line. A: Open circle at 4, arrow left. Open circle means 4 not included.
chunks.source: Open circle at 4, arrow left. Open circle means 4 not included.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Show x ≥ -2 on a number line. A: Closed circle at -2, arrow right. Closed circle means -2 included.
chunks.source: Closed circle at -2, arrow right. Closed circle means -2 included.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Solve 2z + 3 = 3z - 4. A: Subtract 2z: 3 = z - 4. Add 4: z = 7. Collect variable terms.
chunks.source: Subtract 2z: 3 = z - 4. Add 4: z = 7. Collect variable terms.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Solve 4w - 8 = 0. A: Add 8: 4w=8. Divide 4: w=2. Simple two-step.
chunks.source: Add 8: 4w=8. Divide 4: w=2. Simple two-step.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Solve 6k + 2 = 4k + 10. A: Subtract 4k: 2k+2=10. Subtract 2: 2k=8. Divide 2: k=4.
chunks.source: Subtract 4k: 2k+2=10. Subtract 2: 2k=8. Divide 2: k=4.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Represent 3 < x ≤ 7 on a number line. A: Open circle at 3, closed at 7, shade between. Mixed inequality.
chunks.source: Open circle at 3, closed at 7, shade between. Mixed inequality.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Solve 7m - 5 = 2m + 20. A: Subtract 2m: 5m-5=20. Add 5: 5m=25. Divide 5: m=5.
chunks.source: Subtract 2m: 5m-5=20. Add 5: 5m=25. Divide 5: m=5.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Solve 9 - 2n = 3. A: Subtract 9: -2n = -6. Divide -2: n = 3. Watch signs.
chunks.source: Subtract 9: -2n = -6. Divide -2: n = 3. Watch signs.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Substitution in Formulae. I can substitute values into formulae and evaluate the result. Substitution replaces each variable with its value; then evaluate following the order of operations. Keywords: substitute: to replace a variable with a given number; formula: a rule written with symbols that shows a relationship; value: the number that a variable stands for; evaluate: to work out the numerical answer after substitution; replace: same as substitute; put a number in place of a letter
chunks.source: Substitution replaces each variable with its value; then evaluate following the order of operations.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Substitute x = 3 into 4x + 7. A: 4×3+7 = 12+7 = 19. Replace x then calculate.
chunks.source: 4×3+7 = 12+7 = 19. Replace x then calculate.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Evaluate A = πr² with r = 2 (use π = 3.14). A: 3.14×2² = 3.14×4 = 12.56. Square radius first.
chunks.source: 3.14×2² = 3.14×4 = 12.56. Square radius first.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Replace y = -1 in 2y² - 3y. A: 2×(-1)² - 3×(-1) = 2×1 + 3 = 5. Square before multiply.
chunks.source: 2×(-1)² - 3×(-1) = 2×1 + 3 = 5. Square before multiply.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Evaluate P = 2(a+b) when a = 4, b = 6. A: 2(4+6)=2×10=20. Brackets first.
chunks.source: 2(4+6)=2×10=20. Brackets first.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Substitute m = 5, n = 2 into M = m² - n². A: 5² - 2² = 25 - 4 = 21. Square each then subtract.
chunks.source: 5² - 2² = 25 - 4 = 21. Square each then subtract.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Evaluate V = (1/3)πr²h with r=3, h=4 (π=3.14). A: (1/3)×3.14×9×4 = 37.68. Follow order.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Replace p = 7 in 3p - 4p + 2. A: 3×7 - 4×7 + 2 = 21 - 28 + 2 = -5. Combine like terms after substitution.
chunks.source: 3×7 - 4×7 + 2 = 21 - 28 + 2 = -5. Combine like terms after substitution.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Evaluate K = (x+y)/2 when x=8, y=12. A: (8+12)/2 = 20/2 = 10. Add then divide.
chunks.source: (8+12)/2 = 20/2 = 10. Add then divide.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Substitute t = -3 in 5t + 2t². A: 5(-3)+2(-3)² = -15+2×9 = -15+18 = 3. Square first.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: Evaluate R = 2πr with r=5 (π=22/7). A: 2×22/7×5 = 220/7 ≈ 31.43. Multiply stepwise.
chunks.source: 2×22/7×5 = 220/7 ≈ 31.43. Multiply stepwise.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: PLE Algebra Problems. I can solve PLE‑style algebra word problems. PLE algebra problems need: identify unknown, form equation, solve, give answer with units. Keywords: algebra: the branch of mathematics using letters for numbers; word problem: a question written in sentences that needs mathematics; equation: a mathematical statement with an equals sign; solve: to find the unknown value; answer: the final result with correct units
chunks.source: PLE algebra problems need: identify unknown, form equation, solve, give answer with units.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: A box contains 5 red pens and 3 blue pens. Each red pen costs 200 UGX more than a blue pen. Total cost is 4,600 UGX. Find the cost of a blue pen. A: Let b = blue pen cost. Red = b+200. Equation: 5(b+200)+3b=4600 → 5b+1000+3b=4600 → 8b=3600 → b=450 UGX. Form equation from story.
chunks.source: Let b = blue pen cost. Red = b+200. Equation: 5(b+200)+3b=4600 → 5b+1000+3b=4600 → 8b=3600 → b=450 UGX. Form equation from story.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: The sum of two numbers is 45. One number is 7 more than the other. Find the numbers. A: Let x = smaller. Larger = x+7. Equation: x+(x+7)=45 → 2x+7=45 → 2x=38 → x=19, larger=26. Two‑step equation.
chunks.source: Let x = smaller. Larger = x+7. Equation: x+(x+7)=45 → 2x+7=45 → 2x=38 → x=19, larger=26. Two‑step equation.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: A matatu carries 14 passengers. 3 matatus carry the same as 5 boda bodas. How many passengers per boda boda? A: Let x = passengers per boda. Equation: 5x = 3×14 = 42 → x = 8.4. Model may give fraction. Set up proportion.
chunks.source: Let x = passengers per boda. Equation: 5x = 3×14 = 42 → x = 8.4. Model may give fraction. Set up proportion.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: A rectangle's length is twice its width. Perimeter = 36 cm. Find width. A: Let w = width. Length = 2w. Perimeter 2(w+2w)=36 → 6w=36 → w=6 cm. Use perimeter formula.
chunks.source: Let w = width. Length = 2w. Perimeter 2(w+2w)=36 → 6w=36 → w=6 cm. Use perimeter formula.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: John has 3 times as many books as Mary. Together they have 48 books. How many does Mary have? A: Let m = Mary's books. John = 3m. Equation: m+3m=48 → 4m=48 → m=12. Simple ratio.
chunks.source: Let m = Mary's books. John = 3m. Equation: m+3m=48 → 4m=48 → m=12. Simple ratio.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: A shirt costs 1,500 UGX more than a pair of shorts. 2 shirts and 3 shorts cost 13,500 UGX. Find shorts price. A: Let s = shorts. Shirt = s+1500. Equation: 2(s+1500)+3s=13500 → 2s+3000+3s=13500 → 5s=10500 → s=2100 UGX. Two‑variable substitution.
chunks.source: Let s = shorts. Shirt = s+1500. Equation: 2(s+1500)+3s=13500 → 2s+3000+3s=13500 → 5s=10500 → s=2100 UGX. Two‑variable substitution.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: The product of a number and 4 is 28. Find the number. A: Let n = number. Equation: 4n=28 → n=7. Direct translation.
chunks.source: Let n = number. Equation: 4n=28 → n=7. Direct translation.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: A farmer has chickens and goats. Total heads = 30, total legs = 88. How many chickens? A: Let c = chickens, g = goats. Heads: c+g=30. Legs: 2c+4g=88. Solve: from first g=30-c. Substitute: 2c+4(30-c)=88 → 2c+120-4c=88 → -2c=-32 → c=16. Simultaneous equations.
chunks.source: Let c = chickens, g = goats. Heads: c+g=30. Legs: 2c+4g=88. Solve: from first g=30-c. Substitute: 2c+4(30-c)=88 → 2c+120-4c=88 → -2c=-32 → c=16. Simultaneous equations.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: A taxi charges 2,000 UGX per km plus a fixed 500 UGX. A trip costs 9,500 UGX. How many km? A: Let k = km. Equation: 2000k+500=9500 → 2000k=9000 → k=4.5 km. Linear equation with fixed charge.
chunks.source: Let k = km. Equation: 2000k+500=9500 → 2000k=9000 → k=4.5 km. Linear equation with fixed charge.

chunks.subject: Math
chunks.text: Q: A school buys 10 desks and 5 chairs for 2,500,000 UGX. A desk costs 150,000 UGX more than a chair. Find chair price. A: Let c = chair. Desk = c+150000. Equation: 10(c+150000)+5c=2500000 → 10c+1500000+5c=2500000 → 15c=1000000 → c=66,666.67 UGX. Large numbers, same method.
chunks.source: Let c = chair. Desk = c+150000. Equation: 10(c+150000)+5c=2500000 → 10c+1500000+5c=2500000 → 15c=1000000 → c=66,666.67 UGX. Large numbers, same method.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Principles of First Aid. I can explain the aims of first aid and follow the ABC steps to help a casualty in an emergency. First aid aims: preserve life, prevent worsening, promote recovery. Follow ABC — Airway, Breathing, Circulation. Unconscious but breathing? Use recovery position. Every home and school needs a stocked first aid kit. Keywords: first aid: help given at once to an injured person before a doctor arrives; casualty: a person who is hurt or ill and needs help; airway: the passage for air to reach the lungs; breathing: taking air in and out of the lungs; circulation: the movement of blood around the body; recovery position: a safe way to lay an unconscious person on their side; emergency: a sudden dangerous situation that needs quick action; first aid kit: a box with bandages, plasters, antiseptic and other items for treating injuries
chunks.source: First aid aims: preserve life, prevent worsening, promote recovery. Follow ABC — Airway, Breathing, Circulation. Unconscious but breathing? Use recovery position. Every home and school needs a stocked first aid kit.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State the three aims of first aid in the correct order. A: 1. Preserve life. 2. Prevent worsening. 3. Promote recovery. — PLE requires exact order.
chunks.source: 1. Preserve life. 2. Prevent worsening. 3. Promote recovery. — PLE requires exact order.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What does ABC stand for in first aid? A: Airway, Breathing, Circulation. — Always check in this sequence.
chunks.source: Airway, Breathing, Circulation. — Always check in this sequence.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: A casualty is unconscious but breathing. What position should you place them in? A: Recovery position. — Keeps airway open and prevents choking.
chunks.source: Recovery position. — Keeps airway open and prevents choking.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: List four essential items in a first aid kit. A: Sterile dressing, bandage, antiseptic, gloves (or plasters, scissors, safety pins, triangular bandage). — Examiner wants specific items.
chunks.source: Sterile dressing, bandage, antiseptic, gloves (or plasters, scissors, safety pins, triangular bandage). — Examiner wants specific items.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why should you not move a casualty unless there is immediate danger? A: Moving may worsen spinal or internal injuries. — Only move if fire, traffic, or collapsing building.
chunks.source: Moving may worsen spinal or internal injuries. — Only move if fire, traffic, or collapsing building.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How long should you check for breathing? A: 10 seconds. — Look, listen, feel for up to 10 seconds.
chunks.source: 10 seconds. — Look, listen, feel for up to 10 seconds.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is the first thing to do when you arrive at an emergency scene? A: Check for danger to yourself and the casualty. — Your safety comes first.
chunks.source: Check for danger to yourself and the casualty. — Your safety comes first.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Define the term 'casualty' in first aid. A: A person who is injured or ill and needs help. — Not just 'victim', but anyone needing first aid.
chunks.source: A person who is injured or ill and needs help. — Not just 'victim', but anyone needing first aid.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name the three Ps of first aid. A: Preserve life, Prevent worsening, Promote recovery. — Same as the three aims.
chunks.source: Preserve life, Prevent worsening, Promote recovery. — Same as the three aims.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: If a casualty is not breathing, what should you do after opening the airway? A: Give rescue breaths (or start CPR if no pulse). — Breathing check comes before circulation.
chunks.source: Give rescue breaths (or start CPR if no pulse). — Breathing check comes before circulation.

chunks.id: L-P7-Science-First Aid for Fractures and Sprains
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: First Aid for Fractures and Sprains
chunks.text: First Aid for Fractures and Sprains. I can identify fractures, sprains, and dislocations and give correct first aid using splints and slings. Fracture = broken bone. Signs: pain, swelling, deformity, can't move. Immobilise with padded splint above and below the break. Check circulation. Sprain = ligament twist. Use RICE: Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation. Never massage a fresh sprain. Dislocation = bone out of joint — immobilise as found. Keywords: fracture: a break or crack in a bone; sprain: an injury to a ligament when a joint is twisted; splint: a rigid support used to keep a broken bone still; sling: a cloth triangle used to support an injured arm; dislocation: a bone forced out of its normal joint position; immobilise: to keep a body part completely still to prevent further damage; swelling: puffiness caused by fluid collecting in injured tissues; strain: an injury to a muscle or tendon from overstretching
chunks.source: Fracture = broken bone. Signs: pain, swelling, deformity, can't move. Immobilise with padded splint above and below the break. Check circulation. Sprain = ligament twist. Use RICE: Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation. Never massage a fresh sprain. Dislocation = bone out of joint — immobilise as found.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Science-First Aid for Fractures and Sprains
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: First Aid for Fractures and Sprains
chunks.text: Q: State four signs of a fracture. A: Pain, swelling, deformity, inability to move, grating sound, tenderness. — Any four. Examiner wants specific signs.
chunks.source: Pain, swelling, deformity, inability to move, grating sound, tenderness. — Any four. Examiner wants specific signs.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Science-First Aid for Fractures and Sprains
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: First Aid for Fractures and Sprains
chunks.text: Q: What does RICE stand for in sprain management? A: Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation. — Standard first aid for sprains and strains.
chunks.source: Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation. — Standard first aid for sprains and strains.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Science-First Aid for Fractures and Sprains
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: First Aid for Fractures and Sprains
chunks.text: Q: Why should a splint be padded before applying? A: To prevent pressure sores and increase comfort. — Examiner wants 'comfort' or 'prevent pressure'.
chunks.source: To prevent pressure sores and increase comfort. — Examiner wants 'comfort' or 'prevent pressure'.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Science-First Aid for Fractures and Sprains
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: First Aid for Fractures and Sprains
chunks.text: Q: Where should you tie the bandages when splinting a fractured forearm? A: Above and below the fracture site, NOT on the fracture. — Examiner wants 'above and below'.
chunks.source: Above and below the fracture site, NOT on the fracture. — Examiner wants 'above and below'.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Science-First Aid for Fractures and Sprains
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: First Aid for Fractures and Sprains
chunks.text: Q: What should you check after applying a splint? A: Circulation beyond the splint (capillary refill, colour, warmth, sensation). — Examiner wants 'circulation'.
chunks.source: Circulation beyond the splint (capillary refill, colour, warmth, sensation). — Examiner wants 'circulation'.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Science-First Aid for Fractures and Sprains
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: First Aid for Fractures and Sprains
chunks.text: Q: How does a dislocation differ from a fracture? A: Dislocation: bone out of joint. Fracture: bone broken. Both need immobilisation. — Examiner wants the distinction.
chunks.source: Dislocation: bone out of joint. Fracture: bone broken. Both need immobilisation. — Examiner wants the distinction.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Science-First Aid for Fractures and Sprains
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: First Aid for Fractures and Sprains
chunks.text: Q: Why should you not massage a fresh sprain? A: Massage increases swelling and internal bleeding. — Use ice, not heat or massage, for first 48 hours.
chunks.source: Massage increases swelling and internal bleeding. — Use ice, not heat or massage, for first 48 hours.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Science-First Aid for Fractures and Sprains
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: First Aid for Fractures and Sprains
chunks.text: Q: What is the purpose of a sling for an arm fracture? A: Supports the weight of the arm, reduces pain, keeps hand slightly elevated. — Examiner wants 'support' and 'elevation'.
chunks.source: Supports the weight of the arm, reduces pain, keeps hand slightly elevated. — Examiner wants 'support' and 'elevation'.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Science-First Aid for Fractures and Sprains
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: First Aid for Fractures and Sprains
chunks.text: Q: Define 'strain' and give one cause. A: Injury to muscle or tendon from overstretching. Cause: sprinting, lifting heavy load. — Examiner wants 'muscle/tendon' and 'overstretching'.
chunks.source: Injury to muscle or tendon from overstretching. Cause: sprinting, lifting heavy load. — Examiner wants 'muscle/tendon' and 'overstretching'.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Science-First Aid for Fractures and Sprains
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: First Aid for Fractures and Sprains
chunks.text: Q: If fingers become cold and blue after splinting, what should you do? A: Loosen the splint immediately. — Tight splint cuts off circulation. Check every 10 minutes.
chunks.source: Loosen the splint immediately. — Tight splint cuts off circulation. Check every 10 minutes.

chunks.id: L-P7-Science-First Aid for Bleeding and Wounds
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: First Aid for Bleeding and Wounds
chunks.text: First Aid for Bleeding and Wounds. I can control severe bleeding, dress wounds, and prevent infection and tetanus. Severe bleeding: Direct pressure first. Elevate. Pressure point (brachial/femoral). Tourniquet LAST RESORT. Arterial = bright red spurts. Clean wounds with antiseptic, dress sterilely. Watch for infection: redness, heat, pus, red streaks. Deep dirty wounds = tetanus risk — check immunisation. Keywords: haemorrhage: severe bleeding that can be life-threatening; artery: a blood vessel carrying oxygen-rich blood from the heart; pressure point: a place where an artery can be pressed against a bone to slow bleeding; tourniquet: a tight band used only as a last resort to stop extreme limb bleeding; antiseptic: a substance that kills germs on skin or wounds; dressing: a sterile pad placed on a wound to absorb blood and protect it; tetanus: a deadly disease from germs entering deep wounds, prevented by vaccination; infection: harmful germs growing in a wound, causing pus, heat, redness
chunks.source: Severe bleeding: Direct pressure first. Elevate. Pressure point (brachial/femoral). Tourniquet LAST RESORT. Arterial = bright red spurts. Clean wounds with antiseptic, dress sterilely. Watch for infection: redness, heat, pus, red streaks. Deep dirty wounds = tetanus risk — check immunisation.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Science-First Aid for Bleeding and Wounds
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: First Aid for Bleeding and Wounds
chunks.text: Q: What is the first step to control severe bleeding? A: Direct pressure on the wound with a clean dressing. — Examiner wants 'direct pressure first'.
chunks.source: Direct pressure on the wound with a clean dressing. — Examiner wants 'direct pressure first'.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Science-First Aid for Bleeding and Wounds
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: First Aid for Bleeding and Wounds
chunks.text: Q: How does arterial bleeding differ from venous bleeding? A: Arterial: bright red, spurts with heartbeat. Venous: dark red, steady flow. — Examiner wants colour and pattern.
chunks.source: Arterial: bright red, spurts with heartbeat. Venous: dark red, steady flow. — Examiner wants colour and pattern.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Science-First Aid for Bleeding and Wounds
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: First Aid for Bleeding and Wounds
chunks.text: Q: When should a tourniquet be used? A: Only as a last resort when direct pressure, elevation, and pressure points fail and life is at risk. — Examiner wants 'last resort'.
chunks.source: Only as a last resort when direct pressure, elevation, and pressure points fail and life is at risk. — Examiner wants 'last resort'.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Science-First Aid for Bleeding and Wounds
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: First Aid for Bleeding and Wounds
chunks.text: Q: Name two pressure points for limb bleeding. A: Brachial artery (inner upper arm) for arm; Femoral artery (groin) for leg. — Examiner wants specific locations.
chunks.source: Brachial artery (inner upper arm) for arm; Femoral artery (groin) for leg. — Examiner wants specific locations.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Science-First Aid for Bleeding and Wounds
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: First Aid for Bleeding and Wounds
chunks.text: Q: Why should you not remove a blood-soaked dressing? A: Removing it disturbs the clot. Add another dressing on top. — Examiner wants 'do not disturb clot'.
chunks.source: Removing it disturbs the clot. Add another dressing on top. — Examiner wants 'do not disturb clot'.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Science-First Aid for Bleeding and Wounds
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: First Aid for Bleeding and Wounds
chunks.text: Q: List four signs of wound infection. A: Redness, heat, swelling, pus, red streaks, foul smell. Any four. — Examiner wants specific signs.
chunks.source: Redness, heat, swelling, pus, red streaks, foul smell. Any four. — Examiner wants specific signs.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Science-First Aid for Bleeding and Wounds
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: First Aid for Bleeding and Wounds
chunks.text: Q: What disease is prevented by a tetanus booster after a dirty wound? A: Tetanus (lockjaw). — Caused by Clostridium tetani in soil, dust, animal faeces.
chunks.source: Tetanus (lockjaw). — Caused by Clostridium tetani in soil, dust, animal faeces.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Science-First Aid for Bleeding and Wounds
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: First Aid for Bleeding and Wounds
chunks.text: Q: How should you clean a wound before dressing? A: Wash hands, wear gloves, clean with water and antiseptic, wipe from centre outward. — Examiner wants 'centre outward'.
chunks.source: Wash hands, wear gloves, clean with water and antiseptic, wipe from centre outward. — Examiner wants 'centre outward'.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Science-First Aid for Bleeding and Wounds
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: First Aid for Bleeding and Wounds
chunks.text: Q: Why elevate a bleeding limb? A: Reduces blood pressure in the limb, slows bleeding. — Only if no fracture suspected.
chunks.source: Reduces blood pressure in the limb, slows bleeding. — Only if no fracture suspected.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Science-First Aid for Bleeding and Wounds
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: First Aid for Bleeding and Wounds
chunks.text: Q: What should you do if a casualty has a deep cut from a rusty hoe? A: Clean wound, apply antiseptic, sterile dressing, check tetanus immunisation, give booster if needed. — Examiner wants 'tetanus booster'.
chunks.source: Clean wound, apply antiseptic, sterile dressing, check tetanus immunisation, give booster if needed. — Examiner wants 'tetanus booster'.

chunks.id: L-P7-Science-First Aid for Animal Bites and Stings
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: First Aid for Animal Bites and Stings
chunks.text: First Aid for Animal Bites and Stings. I can give correct first aid for animal bites, snake bites, and insect stings, and explain the danger of rabies. Animal bite: Wash 15 mins with soap and water → antiseptic → dressing → hospital for rabies vaccine. Snake bite: Immobilise with splint, keep still, carry to hospital for antivenom. NO cutting, sucking, tourniquet. Bee sting: Scrape stinger sideways, ice, watch for allergy. Scorpion sting: Ice, calm, hospital. Rabies kills — vaccine prevents. Keywords: rabies: a deadly viral disease from animal bites, preventable by vaccine; snake venom: poison injected by a snake bite that can kill or disable; bee sting: a painful puncture from a bee leaving a stinger and venom sac; scorpion: a small creature with a stinging tail, common in dry areas; antivenom: a medicine that neutralises snake or scorpion venom, given in hospital; wash: to clean a wound thoroughly with soap and running water; immobilise: to keep a bitten limb completely still to slow venom spread; hospital: a medical facility where antivenom and rabies vaccine are given
chunks.source: Animal bite: Wash 15 mins with soap and water → antiseptic → dressing → hospital for rabies vaccine. Snake bite: Immobilise with splint, keep still, carry to hospital for antivenom. NO cutting, sucking, tourniquet. Bee sting: Scrape stinger sideways, ice, watch for allergy. Scorpion sting: Ice, calm, hospital. Rabies kills — vaccine prevents.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Science-First Aid for Animal Bites and Stings
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: First Aid for Animal Bites and Stings
chunks.text: Q: What is the single most important first aid step for any animal bite? A: Wash the wound with soap and running water for 15 minutes. — Removes rabies virus and bacteria.
chunks.source: Wash the wound with soap and running water for 15 minutes. — Removes rabies virus and bacteria.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Science-First Aid for Animal Bites and Stings
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: First Aid for Animal Bites and Stings
chunks.text: Q: Why is rabies vaccine given after a dog bite? A: Rabies virus travels nerves to brain; once symptoms start, death is certain. Vaccine stops it if given early. — Examiner wants 'prevents rabies'.
chunks.source: Rabies virus travels nerves to brain; once symptoms start, death is certain. Vaccine stops it if given early. — Examiner wants 'prevents rabies'.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Science-First Aid for Animal Bites and Stings
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: First Aid for Animal Bites and Stings
chunks.text: Q: List three things you must NOT do for a snake bite. A: Do not cut, do not suck, do not apply tourniquet, do not let walk, do not give alcohol. Any three. — Examiner wants the prohibitions.
chunks.source: Do not cut, do not suck, do not apply tourniquet, do not let walk, do not give alcohol. Any three. — Examiner wants the prohibitions.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Science-First Aid for Animal Bites and Stings
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: First Aid for Animal Bites and Stings
chunks.text: Q: How should you remove a bee stinger? A: Scrape sideways with a card or fingernail. Do not pinch or pull. — Pinching injects more venom.
chunks.source: Scrape sideways with a card or fingernail. Do not pinch or pull. — Pinching injects more venom.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Science-First Aid for Animal Bites and Stings
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: First Aid for Animal Bites and Stings
chunks.text: Q: Why should a snake bite victim not walk? A: Walking increases circulation and muscle pump, spreading venom faster. — Carry the casualty.
chunks.source: Walking increases circulation and muscle pump, spreading venom faster. — Carry the casualty.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Science-First Aid for Animal Bites and Stings
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: First Aid for Animal Bites and Stings
chunks.text: Q: What is antivenom and where is it given? A: Medicine that neutralises snake/scorpion venom. Given only in hospital. — Examiner wants 'hospital'.
chunks.source: Medicine that neutralises snake/scorpion venom. Given only in hospital. — Examiner wants 'hospital'.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Science-First Aid for Animal Bites and Stings
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: First Aid for Animal Bites and Stings
chunks.text: Q: How long should you wash an animal bite? A: 15 minutes with soap and running water. — Examiner wants '15 minutes'.
chunks.source: 15 minutes with soap and running water. — Examiner wants '15 minutes'.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Science-First Aid for Animal Bites and Stings
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: First Aid for Animal Bites and Stings
chunks.text: Q: What are the signs of a severe allergic reaction to a bee sting? A: Difficulty breathing, swelling of face/lips/tongue, dizziness, widespread rash. — Go to hospital immediately.
chunks.source: Difficulty breathing, swelling of face/lips/tongue, dizziness, widespread rash. — Go to hospital immediately.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Science-First Aid for Animal Bites and Stings
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: First Aid for Animal Bites and Stings
chunks.text: Q: Why keep a snake-bitten limb below heart level? A: Recent guidance: reduces venom spread to heart. (Old guidance said elevate — now immobilise below heart). — Examiner may accept either with explanation.
chunks.source: Recent guidance: reduces venom spread to heart. (Old guidance said elevate — now immobilise below heart). — Examiner may accept either with explanation.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Science-First Aid for Animal Bites and Stings
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: First Aid for Animal Bites and Stings
chunks.text: Q: What two injections may be needed after a deep dirty animal bite? A: Rabies vaccine and tetanus booster. — Both are life-saving.
chunks.source: Rabies vaccine and tetanus booster. — Both are life-saving.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Science in Food Preparation. I can explain the scientific processes used when we prepare and keep food at home. Cooking uses science: mixtures combine ingredients; fermentation and leavening use microorganisms; emulsification mixes oil and water; pasteurisation makes milk safe; preservation removes water to stop germs; separation divides mixtures; energy from fuel cooks our food. Keywords: fermentation: when tiny living things change food over time; leavening: making dough rise by adding gas bubbles; emulsification: mixing two liquids that usually separate, like oil and water; preservation: keeping food safe to eat for a longer time; pasteurisation: heating liquid to kill harmful germs then cooling it fast; mixture: two or more substances put together but not chemically joined; separation: dividing a mixture into its different parts; energy: the power to do work or cause change
chunks.source: Cooking uses science: mixtures combine ingredients; fermentation and leavening use microorganisms; emulsification mixes oil and water; pasteurisation makes milk safe; preservation removes water to stop germs; separation divides mixtures; energy from fuel cooks our food.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Define fermentation and give one Ugandan food made by fermentation. A: Fermentation is the breakdown of sugar by yeast or bacteria into alcohol or acid and gas. Example: **kwete** from millet. Reason: PLE tests definition and local example.
chunks.source: Fermentation is the breakdown of sugar by yeast or bacteria into alcohol or acid and gas. Example: **kwete** from millet. Reason: PLE tests definition and local example.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State the purpose of leavening in baking. A: Leavening makes dough rise by producing gas bubbles, giving a light texture. Reason: PLE asks for function of leavening agents.
chunks.source: Leavening makes dough rise by producing gas bubbles, giving a light texture. Reason: PLE asks for function of leavening agents.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Explain how emulsification works in making mayonnaise. A: Egg yolk contains lecithin; one end attracts oil, the other water, holding them together. Reason: PLE tests understanding of emulsifier action.
chunks.source: Egg yolk contains lecithin; one end attracts oil, the other water, holding them together. Reason: PLE tests understanding of emulsifier action.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name two methods of food preservation used in Uganda and explain how one works. A: Drying and salting. Drying removes water so germs cannot grow. Reason: PLE requires method plus scientific explanation.
chunks.source: Drying and salting. Drying removes water so germs cannot grow. Reason: PLE requires method plus scientific explanation.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Describe pasteurisation of milk. Include temperature and time. A: Heating milk to 72°C for 15 seconds then cooling rapidly to kill germs. Reason: PLE asks for specific conditions of pasteurisation.
chunks.source: Heating milk to 72°C for 15 seconds then cooling rapidly to kill germs. Reason: PLE asks for specific conditions of pasteurisation.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is a mixture? Give an example from the kitchen. A: A mixture is two or more substances combined without chemical reaction. Example: flour and water for posho. Reason: PLE tests definition and everyday example.
chunks.source: A mixture is two or more substances combined without chemical reaction. Example: flour and water for posho. Reason: PLE tests definition and everyday example.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How is cream separated from fresh milk? A: Milk is left to stand; cream, being less dense, rises to the top and is skimmed off. Reason: PLE tests separation by density difference.
chunks.source: Milk is left to stand; cream, being less dense, rises to the top and is skimmed off. Reason: PLE tests separation by density difference.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Identify the main source of heat energy for cooking in rural Uganda. A: Firewood (biomass). Reason: PLE often asks about common energy sources in Ugandan context.
chunks.source: Firewood (biomass). Reason: PLE often asks about common energy sources in Ugandan context.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why is salt effective in preserving meat? A: Salt draws water out of cells by osmosis; germs cannot grow without water. Reason: PLE tests osmosis principle in preservation.
chunks.source: Salt draws water out of cells by osmosis; germs cannot grow without water. Reason: PLE tests osmosis principle in preservation.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What happens to the nutrients in milk during pasteurisation? A: Most nutrients remain because the heat treatment is brief; only some vitamin C is slightly reduced. Reason: PLE distinguishes pasteurisation from boiling.
chunks.source: Most nutrients remain because the heat treatment is brief; only some vitamin C is slightly reduced. Reason: PLE distinguishes pasteurisation from boiling.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Science in Construction. I can describe how scientific principles are used when building houses and structures in our community. Building uses science: foundation spreads load; mixture ratio gives concrete strength; curing completes cement reaction; plumb line and levelling keep walls vertical and horizontal for stability; triangles make rigid roof shapes. Keywords: cement: a grey powder that binds sand and stones when mixed with water; curing: keeping concrete wet so it gains full strength slowly; levelling: making a surface flat and even using a spirit level; plumb line: a string with a weight that shows a perfectly vertical line; foundation: the strong base of a building that carries the load to the ground; mixture ratio: the correct proportions of cement, sand, and aggregate; load: the weight or force that a structure must carry; stability: the ability of a structure to stand firm and not fall over
chunks.source: Building uses science: foundation spreads load; mixture ratio gives concrete strength; curing completes cement reaction; plumb line and levelling keep walls vertical and horizontal for stability; triangles make rigid roof shapes.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State the standard mixture ratio for foundation concrete and explain what each number means. A: 1:2:4 means 1 part cement, 2 parts sand, 4 parts aggregate by volume. Reason: PLE tests knowledge of standard mix proportions.
chunks.source: 1:2:4 means 1 part cement, 2 parts sand, 4 parts aggregate by volume. Reason: PLE tests knowledge of standard mix proportions.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why is curing of concrete necessary? Explain the science. A: Curing keeps concrete wet so cement hydration continues, giving full strength. Without water, reaction stops early. Reason: PLE asks for the chemical reason behind curing.
chunks.source: Curing keeps concrete wet so cement hydration continues, giving full strength. Without water, reaction stops early. Reason: PLE asks for the chemical reason behind curing.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Describe how a plumb line works and why it is used. A: A weight on a string uses gravity to show a true vertical line. It ensures walls are vertical for proper load transfer. Reason: PLE tests understanding of gravity as a vertical reference.
chunks.source: A weight on a string uses gravity to show a true vertical line. It ensures walls are vertical for proper load transfer. Reason: PLE tests understanding of gravity as a vertical reference.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is the purpose of levelling in bricklaying? A: Levelling keeps each course horizontal so load transfers vertically and walls stay stable. Reason: PLE connects levelling to structural stability.
chunks.source: Levelling keeps each course horizontal so load transfers vertically and walls stay stable. Reason: PLE connects levelling to structural stability.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Define foundation and state its function in a building. A: The foundation is the base that spreads the building's load to the ground safely. Reason: PLE requires definition and function.
chunks.source: The foundation is the base that spreads the building's load to the ground safely. Reason: PLE requires definition and function.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Explain why a triangular roof truss is more stable than a rectangular frame. A: A triangle cannot deform without bending its sides; it directs loads along members to supports. Reason: PLE tests geometric stability principles.
chunks.source: A triangle cannot deform without bending its sides; it directs loads along members to supports. Reason: PLE tests geometric stability principles.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: If a mason uses a 1:1:2 mixture ratio for a foundation, what is the likely result? A: Too much cement causes shrinkage cracks and waste; too little aggregate reduces bulk strength. Reason: PLE tests consequences of incorrect mix ratios.
chunks.source: Too much cement causes shrinkage cracks and waste; too little aggregate reduces bulk strength. Reason: PLE tests consequences of incorrect mix ratios.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How does the width of a foundation affect stability? A: A wider foundation spreads the load over more soil area, reducing pressure and increasing stability. Reason: PLE links foundation dimensions to load distribution.
chunks.source: A wider foundation spreads the load over more soil area, reducing pressure and increasing stability. Reason: PLE links foundation dimensions to load distribution.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What happens to cement hydration if concrete dries in hot sun without curing? A: Hydration stops prematurely; concrete reaches only 50-60% strength and develops micro-cracks. Reason: PLE tests the effect of water loss on chemical reaction.
chunks.source: Hydration stops prematurely; concrete reaches only 50-60% strength and develops micro-cracks. Reason: PLE tests the effect of water loss on chemical reaction.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name two tools used to ensure a wall is vertical and horizontal. A: Plumb line (vertical) and spirit level (horizontal). Reason: PLE asks for specific tools and their purposes.
chunks.source: Plumb line (vertical) and spirit level (horizontal). Reason: PLE asks for specific tools and their purposes.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Science in Agriculture. I can explain how scientific methods improve crop and animal farming in our community. Scientific farming: soil testing guides fertiliser; pruning manages light and air; grafting combines best traits; irrigation delivers water efficiently; spacing optimises plant population; mulching conserves moisture and builds soil; pest control uses multiple methods together. Keywords: soil testing: checking soil to know its nutrients and pH before planting; fertiliser: substance added to soil to supply nutrients for plant growth; pruning: cutting off unwanted branches to improve growth and yield; grafting: joining a shoot from a good variety onto a strong rootstock; irrigation: supplying water to crops artificially when rain is not enough; pest control: managing insects and diseases that damage crops; spacing: planting at the correct distance between plants and rows; mulching: covering soil with dry grass or leaves to keep moisture and stop weeds
chunks.source: Scientific farming: soil testing guides fertiliser; pruning manages light and air; grafting combines best traits; irrigation delivers water efficiently; spacing optimises plant population; mulching conserves moisture and builds soil; pest control uses multiple methods together.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why is soil testing the first step before applying fertiliser? A: Soil testing reveals pH and nutrient deficiencies, allowing targeted fertiliser choice and rate. Reason: PLE tests the logical sequence: test → diagnose → treat.
chunks.source: Soil testing reveals pH and nutrient deficiencies, allowing targeted fertiliser choice and rate. Reason: PLE tests the logical sequence: test → diagnose → treat.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State the meaning of NPK 20:10:10 on a fertiliser bag. A: 20% nitrogen (leaves), 10% phosphorus (roots), 10% potassium (fruit/quality). Reason: PLE asks for interpretation of fertiliser grade.
chunks.source: 20% nitrogen (leaves), 10% phosphorus (roots), 10% potassium (fruit/quality). Reason: PLE asks for interpretation of fertiliser grade.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Explain how pruning increases crop yield. A: Pruning removes unproductive wood, improves light penetration and air circulation, reduces disease, and redirects energy to fruiting wood. Reason: PLE links pruning to photosynthesis and pest control.
chunks.source: Pruning removes unproductive wood, improves light penetration and air circulation, reduces disease, and redirects energy to fruiting wood. Reason: PLE links pruning to photosynthesis and pest control.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Describe the process of grafting and give one advantage. A: Joining a scion (desired variety) to a rootstock (strong roots) so cambium layers fuse. Advantage: early fruiting, true-to-type fruit, disease resistance. Reason: PLE tests grafting principle and benefits.
chunks.source: Joining a scion (desired variety) to a rootstock (strong roots) so cambium layers fuse. Advantage: early fruiting, true-to-type fruit, disease resistance. Reason: PLE tests grafting principle and benefits.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is drip irrigation and why is it better than flooding for vegetables? A: Drip irrigation delivers water slowly to root zone via pipes; saves water, keeps leaves dry (less disease), reduces weed growth. Reason: PLE compares irrigation methods on efficiency and crop health.
chunks.source: Drip irrigation delivers water slowly to root zone via pipes; saves water, keeps leaves dry (less disease), reduces weed growth. Reason: PLE compares irrigation methods on efficiency and crop health.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State the recommended spacing for maize and explain why it matters. A: 75 cm x 30 cm, two seeds per hole. Correct spacing prevents competition for light, water, nutrients; optimises plant population. Reason: PLE tests specific spacing and its scientific basis.
chunks.source: 75 cm x 30 cm, two seeds per hole. Correct spacing prevents competition for light, water, nutrients; optimises plant population. Reason: PLE tests specific spacing and its scientific basis.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: List three benefits of mulching in a banana plantation. A: Conserves moisture, suppresses weeds, adds organic matter/fertiliser as it decomposes. Reason: PLE asks for multiple benefits of a practice.
chunks.source: Conserves moisture, suppresses weeds, adds organic matter/fertiliser as it decomposes. Reason: PLE asks for multiple benefits of a practice.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How does proper spacing help in pest control? A: Good spacing improves air flow, reducing humidity and fungal diseases; allows spray penetration if needed. Reason: PLE links cultural practices to pest management.
chunks.source: Good spacing improves air flow, reducing humidity and fungal diseases; allows spray penetration if needed. Reason: PLE links cultural practices to pest management.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why are grafted fruit trees preferred over seedlings? A: Grafted trees fruit earlier (2-3 years vs 7-10), have known fruit quality, and inherit rootstock disease resistance. Reason: PLE compares propagation methods.
chunks.source: Grafted trees fruit earlier (2-3 years vs 7-10), have known fruit quality, and inherit rootstock disease resistance. Reason: PLE compares propagation methods.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: If a farmer applies nitrogen fertiliser to a crop with yellow leaves but soil test shows high nitrogen, what is the likely problem? A: The yellowing may be due to poor drainage, root damage, or pH locking up nutrients — not nitrogen lack. Reason: PLE tests diagnosis beyond symptoms using soil test data.
chunks.source: The yellowing may be due to poor drainage, root damage, or pH locking up nutrients — not nitrogen lack. Reason: PLE tests diagnosis beyond symptoms using soil test data.

chunks.id: L-P7-Science-Science in Health Care at Home
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: Science in Health Care at Home
chunks.text: Science in Health Care at Home. I can apply scientific knowledge to manage common health situations safely at home. Home health care uses science: oral rehydration saves lives from diarrhoea; exact dosage needs the right measure; thermometer gives numbers not guesses; disinfectant kills germs on cuts; diagnosis follows history-examination-test; hygiene stops spread; expiry and storage keep medicine safe and effective. Keywords: dosage: the correct amount of medicine to take at one time; thermometer: an instrument for measuring body temperature; disinfectant: a chemical that kills germs on surfaces and skin; oral rehydration: giving water with salt and sugar to replace lost fluids; diagnosis: identifying an illness from its signs and symptoms; hygiene: practices that keep us clean and prevent disease spread; expiry: the date after which medicine may not work or may be harmful; storage: keeping medicines correctly so they stay effective
chunks.source: Home health care uses science: oral rehydration saves lives from diarrhoea; exact dosage needs the right measure; thermometer gives numbers not guesses; disinfectant kills germs on cuts; diagnosis follows history-examination-test; hygiene stops spread; expiry and storage keep medicine safe and effective.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Science-Science in Health Care at Home
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: Science in Health Care at Home
chunks.text: Q: Prepare oral rehydration solution (ORS) correctly. Give the recipe. A: 1 litre boiled cooled water + ½ level teaspoon salt + 6 level teaspoons sugar. Stir until dissolved. Reason: PLE tests exact ORS recipe for home management of diarrhoea.
chunks.source: 1 litre boiled cooled water + ½ level teaspoon salt + 6 level teaspoons sugar. Stir until dissolved. Reason: PLE tests exact ORS recipe for home management of diarrhoea.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Science-Science in Health Care at Home
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: Science in Health Care at Home
chunks.text: Q: Why is it dangerous to use a kitchen spoon to measure liquid medicine? A: Kitchen spoons vary (2.5-7 ml); dosage must be precise to avoid under/overdose. Use the cup/syringe provided. Reason: PLE emphasises accurate dosage measurement.
chunks.source: Kitchen spoons vary (2.5-7 ml); dosage must be precise to avoid under/overdose. Use the cup/syringe provided. Reason: PLE emphasises accurate dosage measurement.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Science-Science in Health Care at Home
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: Science in Health Care at Home
chunks.text: Q: State the normal human body temperature and the fever threshold. A: Normal: 36.5-37.5°C. Fever: above 37.5°C (axillary) or 38°C (rectal). Reason: PLE asks for normal range and fever definition.
chunks.source: Normal: 36.5-37.5°C. Fever: above 37.5°C (axillary) or 38°C (rectal). Reason: PLE asks for normal range and fever definition.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Science-Science in Health Care at Home
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: Science in Health Care at Home
chunks.text: Q: Explain the difference between disinfectant and antiseptic. A: Disinfectant kills germs on non-living surfaces; antiseptic kills germs on living tissue (skin). Both reduce infection. Reason: PLE distinguishes use on surfaces vs skin.
chunks.source: Disinfectant kills germs on non-living surfaces; antiseptic kills germs on living tissue (skin). Both reduce infection. Reason: PLE distinguishes use on surfaces vs skin.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Science-Science in Health Care at Home
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: Science in Health Care at Home
chunks.text: Q: List the three steps of clinical diagnosis in order. A: 1) History taking, 2) Physical examination, 3) Investigations/tests if needed. Reason: PLE tests the systematic diagnostic process.
chunks.source: 1) History taking, 2) Physical examination, 3) Investigations/tests if needed. Reason: PLE tests the systematic diagnostic process.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Science-Science in Health Care at Home
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: Science in Health Care at Home
chunks.text: Q: Why must medicines be stored in a cool, dry place? A: Heat and moisture accelerate chemical breakdown, reducing potency or creating harmful products. Reason: PLE links storage conditions to medicine stability.
chunks.source: Heat and moisture accelerate chemical breakdown, reducing potency or creating harmful products. Reason: PLE links storage conditions to medicine stability.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Science-Science in Health Care at Home
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: Science in Health Care at Home
chunks.text: Q: What should you do with medicine past its expiry date? A: Dispose of it safely (mix with dirt/coffee grounds, seal, bin). Do not use. Do not flush. Reason: PLE tests safe disposal of expired medicines.
chunks.source: Dispose of it safely (mix with dirt/coffee grounds, seal, bin). Do not use. Do not flush. Reason: PLE tests safe disposal of expired medicines.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Science-Science in Health Care at Home
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: Science in Health Care at Home
chunks.text: Q: How does hand hygiene with soap stop diarrhoea spread? A: Soap breaks down germ membranes and removes them mechanically; running water washes them away. Breaks faecal-oral route. Reason: PLE asks for mechanism of handwashing.
chunks.source: Soap breaks down germ membranes and removes them mechanically; running water washes them away. Breaks faecal-oral route. Reason: PLE asks for mechanism of handwashing.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Science-Science in Health Care at Home
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: Science in Health Care at Home
chunks.text: Q: A child takes paracetamol syrup 120 mg/5 ml. The dose is 15 mg/kg. Child weighs 10 kg. What volume to give? A: 15 mg/kg × 10 kg = 150 mg needed. 120 mg in 5 ml → 150 mg in (150/120)×5 = 6.25 ml. Reason: PLE tests dosage calculation from concentration and weight.
chunks.source: 15 mg/kg × 10 kg = 150 mg needed. 120 mg in 5 ml → 150 mg in (150/120)×5 = 6.25 ml. Reason: PLE tests dosage calculation from concentration and weight.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Science-Science in Health Care at Home
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: Science in Health Care at Home
chunks.text: Q: Why is it important to complete the full course of antibiotics even if the child feels better? A: Stopping early allows resistant bacteria to survive and multiply, making future infections harder to treat. Reason: PLE tests antibiotic resistance concept.
chunks.source: Stopping early allows resistant bacteria to survive and multiply, making future infections harder to treat. Reason: PLE tests antibiotic resistance concept.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: The Human Skeleton. I can name the main parts of the skeleton and explain how they protect, support and allow movement. The human skeleton is made of bones like the skull, ribcage, backbone and limbs. It protects organs, supports the body and allows movement through joints, cartilage and ligaments. Keywords: skull: the bone that covers the brain; ribcage: the set of ribs that surrounds the chest; backbone: the column of bones down the back; limb: an arm or a leg; joint: a place where two bones meet; cartilage: smooth tissue that covers bone ends; ligament: strong band that joins bone to bone; support: to hold up the body
chunks.source: The human skeleton is made of bones like the skull, ribcage, backbone and limbs. It protects organs, supports the body and allows movement through joints, cartilage and ligaments.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name the bone that protects the brain. A: Skull – it forms a hard case around the brain.
chunks.source: Skull – it forms a hard case around the brain.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which structure shields the heart and lungs? A: Ribcage – it forms a cage around the chest.
chunks.source: Ribcage – it forms a cage around the chest.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is the function of the backbone? A: Support – it holds the body upright.
chunks.source: Support – it holds the body upright.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What do we call an arm or a leg? A: Limb – each limb contains many bones.
chunks.source: Limb – each limb contains many bones.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Where do two bones meet? A: Joint – a place where bones connect.
chunks.source: Joint – a place where bones connect.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What covers the ends of bones to reduce friction? A: Cartilage – smooth tissue on bone ends.
chunks.source: Cartilage – smooth tissue on bone ends.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which tissue joins bone to bone at a joint? A: Ligament – strong bands that hold bones together.
chunks.source: Ligament – strong bands that hold bones together.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give one way the skeleton helps movement. A: Bones act as levers that muscles pull on.
chunks.source: Bones act as levers that muscles pull on.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Types of Joints. I can identify hinge, ball-and-socket, pivot, gliding and immovable joints and explain their movements. Joints are places where bones meet. Hinge joints bend like a door, ball-and-socket joints move in many directions, pivot joints rotate, gliding joints slide, and immovable joints do not move. Synovial fluid keeps them smooth. Keywords: hinge: joint that moves like a door; ball and socket: joint that allows movement in many directions; pivot: joint that allows rotation; gliding: joint where bones slide over each other; immovable: joint that does not move; synovial fluid: oil-like liquid that lubricates joints; movement: the act of changing position; flexibility: ability to bend easily
chunks.source: Joints are places where bones meet. Hinge joints bend like a door, ball-and-socket joints move in many directions, pivot joints rotate, gliding joints slide, and immovable joints do not move. Synovial fluid keeps them smooth.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which joint works like a door hinge? A: Hinge – it moves back and forth in one plane.
chunks.source: Hinge – it moves back and forth in one plane.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What type of joint is the shoulder? A: Ball and socket – it allows movement in many directions.
chunks.source: Ball and socket – it allows movement in many directions.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which joint lets you turn your head side to side? A: Pivot – it allows rotation.
chunks.source: Pivot – it allows rotation.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Where do you find gliding joints? A: Wrist and ankle – bones slide over each other.
chunks.source: Wrist and ankle – bones slide over each other.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give an example of an immovable joint. A: Skull sutures – bones are fused together.
chunks.source: Skull sutures – bones are fused together.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What fluid reduces friction in movable joints? A: Synovial fluid – it lubricates the joint.
chunks.source: Synovial fluid – it lubricates the joint.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Define flexibility. A: Flexibility is the ability to bend easily.
chunks.source: Flexibility is the ability to bend easily.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why are hinge joints important for walking? A: They allow the knee and ankle to bend and straighten.
chunks.source: They allow the knee and ankle to bend and straighten.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Muscles and Movement. I can explain how skeletal muscles work in antagonistic pairs using the biceps and triceps as examples. Skeletal muscles are voluntary and work in antagonistic pairs like the biceps and triceps. Tendons attach muscles to bones. Contraction pulls the bone; relaxation returns it. This teamwork creates movement. Keywords: voluntary: muscles we control consciously; involuntary: muscles that work without our control; biceps: muscle on the front of the upper arm; triceps: muscle on the back of the upper arm; tendon: strong cord that attaches muscle to bone; contraction: muscle shortening to pull a bone; relaxation: muscle lengthening after contraction; antagonistic: muscles that work in opposite pairs
chunks.source: Skeletal muscles are voluntary and work in antagonistic pairs like the biceps and triceps. Tendons attach muscles to bones. Contraction pulls the bone; relaxation returns it. This teamwork creates movement.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which muscle bends the elbow? A: Biceps – it contracts to flex the arm.
chunks.source: Biceps – it contracts to flex the arm.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which muscle straightens the elbow? A: Triceps – it contracts to extend the arm.
chunks.source: Triceps – it contracts to extend the arm.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What attaches muscle to bone? A: Tendon – a strong fibrous cord.
chunks.source: Tendon – a strong fibrous cord.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Define contraction. A: Contraction is the shortening of a muscle to pull a bone.
chunks.source: Contraction is the shortening of a muscle to pull a bone.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Define relaxation. A: Relaxation is the lengthening of a muscle after contraction.
chunks.source: Relaxation is the lengthening of a muscle after contraction.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give an example of antagonistic muscles. A: Biceps and triceps – one flexes, the other extends.
chunks.source: Biceps and triceps – one flexes, the other extends.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Are skeletal muscles voluntary or involuntary? A: Voluntary – we control them consciously.
chunks.source: Voluntary – we control them consciously.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What type of muscle is the heart? A: Involuntary – it beats without conscious control.
chunks.source: Involuntary – it beats without conscious control.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Disorders of Bones and Muscles. I can name common disorders of the muscular-skeletal system and explain how to prevent some of them. Common muscular-skeletal disorders include fracture, rickets, arthritis, polio, cramp and sprain. Good nutrition (calcium, vitamin D), safe play, warm-up exercises and vaccination keep bones and muscles healthy. Keywords: fracture: a broken bone; rickets: soft bones due to lack of vitamin D; arthritis: painful swelling of joints; polio: a viral disease that can paralyse muscles; cramp: sudden painful muscle tightening; sprain: stretched or torn ligament; calcium: mineral that makes bones strong; vitamin D: helps the body absorb calcium
chunks.source: Common muscular-skeletal disorders include fracture, rickets, arthritis, polio, cramp and sprain. Good nutrition (calcium, vitamin D), safe play, warm-up exercises and vaccination keep bones and muscles healthy.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is a fracture? A: A broken bone – caused by trauma like a fall.
chunks.source: A broken bone – caused by trauma like a fall.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name the disorder caused by vitamin D deficiency. A: Rickets – bones become soft and deformed.
chunks.source: Rickets – bones become soft and deformed.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is arthritis? A: Painful swelling of joints, common in older age.
chunks.source: Painful swelling of joints, common in older age.
