chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How is polio prevented? A: By vaccination – the polio vaccine gives immunity.
chunks.source: By vaccination – the polio vaccine gives immunity.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Define a cramp. A: A sudden, painful, involuntary muscle contraction.
chunks.source: A sudden, painful, involuntary muscle contraction.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is a sprain? A: A stretched or torn ligament, often at the ankle.
chunks.source: A stretched or torn ligament, often at the ankle.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which mineral makes bones strong? A: Calcium – found in milk, greens, small fish.
chunks.source: Calcium – found in milk, greens, small fish.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which vitamin helps absorb calcium? A: Vitamin D – made in skin with sunlight.
chunks.source: Vitamin D – made in skin with sunlight.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: The Breathing System. I can name the parts of the breathing system and explain what each part does. Air travels: nose → epiglottis → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli. The diaphragm and intercostal muscles move the chest. The pleural cavity lets lungs slide smoothly. Keywords: trachea: the windpipe that carries air to the lungs; bronchi: two tubes that branch from the trachea into each lung; bronchioles: tiny tubes inside the lungs that carry air to air sacs; alveoli: tiny air sacs where gas exchange happens; diaphragm: a dome-shaped muscle under the lungs that helps breathing; intercostal: muscles between the ribs that help the chest move; pleural cavity: the space around the lungs lined with a slippery membrane; epiglottis: a flap that covers the windpipe when we swallow
chunks.source: Air travels: nose → epiglottis → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli. The diaphragm and intercostal muscles move the chest. The pleural cavity lets lungs slide smoothly.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name the tube that carries air from the throat to the bronchi. A: trachea — the windpipe that connects the larynx to the bronchi.
chunks.source: trachea — the windpipe that connects the larynx to the bronchi.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What does the epiglottis do when you swallow food? A: It closes over the trachea to prevent food from entering the airway.
chunks.source: It closes over the trachea to prevent food from entering the airway.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which muscles are found between the ribs? A: intercostal muscles — they lift and lower the rib cage during breathing.
chunks.source: intercostal muscles — they lift and lower the rib cage during breathing.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Where does gaseous exchange take place in the lungs? A: In the alveoli — tiny air sacs surrounded by capillaries.
chunks.source: In the alveoli — tiny air sacs surrounded by capillaries.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is the function of the pleural cavity? A: It contains lubricating fluid that allows the lungs to move smoothly against the chest wall.
chunks.source: It contains lubricating fluid that allows the lungs to move smoothly against the chest wall.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which part divides into two branches, one for each lung? A: The trachea divides into the left and right bronchi.
chunks.source: The trachea divides into the left and right bronchi.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What happens to the bronchioles as they go deeper into the lung? A: They become narrower and end in clusters of alveoli.
chunks.source: They become narrower and end in clusters of alveoli.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why is the diaphragm described as dome-shaped? A: It curves upward into the chest cavity when relaxed, forming a dome under the lungs.
chunks.source: It curves upward into the chest cavity when relaxed, forming a dome under the lungs.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Gaseous Exchange. I can explain how oxygen and carbon dioxide move in the alveoli and why alveoli are adapted for this job. Diffusion moves oxygen from alveoli to blood and carbon dioxide from blood to alveoli. Alveoli are adapted: huge surface area, thin wall, moist lining, rich capillary supply. Keywords: diffusion: movement of gas from high concentration to low concentration; oxygen: gas needed by cells for respiration; carbon dioxide: waste gas produced by cells; alveoli: tiny air sacs where gas exchange happens; capillary: tiny blood vessel around the alveoli; surface area: total area available for gas exchange; moist: wet or damp; thin wall: a wall only one cell thick
chunks.source: Diffusion moves oxygen from alveoli to blood and carbon dioxide from blood to alveoli. Alveoli are adapted: huge surface area, thin wall, moist lining, rich capillary supply.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Define diffusion as used in gaseous exchange. A: Movement of gas particles from an area of high concentration to an area of low concentration.
chunks.source: Movement of gas particles from an area of high concentration to an area of low concentration.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name the gas that diffuses from the alveoli into the blood. A: Oxygen — it is at higher concentration in the alveolar air than in deoxygenated blood.
chunks.source: Oxygen — it is at higher concentration in the alveolar air than in deoxygenated blood.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name the waste gas that diffuses from the blood into the alveoli. A: Carbon dioxide — it is at higher concentration in deoxygenated blood than in alveolar air.
chunks.source: Carbon dioxide — it is at higher concentration in deoxygenated blood than in alveolar air.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State two adaptations of the alveolus that increase the rate of diffusion. A: Any two: large surface area, thin wall (one cell thick), moist lining, dense capillary network.
chunks.source: Any two: large surface area, thin wall (one cell thick), moist lining, dense capillary network.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why must the lining of the alveolus be moist? A: Gases must dissolve in water before they can diffuse across the membrane.
chunks.source: Gases must dissolve in water before they can diffuse across the membrane.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is the function of the capillary network around the alveolus? A: It brings deoxygenated blood close to the alveolar air so oxygen can diffuse in and carbon dioxide can diffuse out.
chunks.source: It brings deoxygenated blood close to the alveolar air so oxygen can diffuse in and carbon dioxide can diffuse out.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: If the walls of the alveoli break down and merge, what happens to surface area? A: Surface area decreases, reducing the rate of gaseous exchange.
chunks.source: Surface area decreases, reducing the rate of gaseous exchange.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: In which direction does carbon dioxide diffuse during gaseous exchange? A: From the capillary blood (high concentration) into the alveolus (low concentration).
chunks.source: From the capillary blood (high concentration) into the alveolus (low concentration).

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Breathing Mechanism. I can explain how the diaphragm and intercostal muscles change chest volume and pressure to cause inhalation and exhalation. Inhalation: diaphragm contracts (flattens), intercostal muscles contract (rib cage up/out), volume ↑, pressure ↓, air enters. Exhalation: diaphragm relaxes (domes up), intercostal muscles relax (rib cage down/in), volume ↓, pressure ↑, air leaves. Keywords: inhalation: breathing in — chest volume increases, pressure decreases; exhalation: breathing out — chest volume decreases, pressure increases; rib cage: the bony structure protecting the lungs; diaphragm: dome-shaped muscle separating chest from abdomen; pressure: force exerted by gas particles; volume: amount of space inside the chest; intercostal muscles: muscles between the ribs; ventilation: the process of moving air in and out of the lungs
chunks.source: Inhalation: diaphragm contracts (flattens), intercostal muscles contract (rib cage up/out), volume ↑, pressure ↓, air enters. Exhalation: diaphragm relaxes (domes up), intercostal muscles relax (rib cage down/in), volume ↓, pressure ↑, air leaves.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State the action of the diaphragm during inhalation. A: It contracts and flattens, moving downward.
chunks.source: It contracts and flattens, moving downward.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What happens to the rib cage during inhalation? A: It moves up and out as the external intercostal muscles contract.
chunks.source: It moves up and out as the external intercostal muscles contract.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How does chest volume change during inhalation? A: Volume increases because the diaphragm flattens and the rib cage expands.
chunks.source: Volume increases because the diaphragm flattens and the rib cage expands.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What happens to pressure inside the chest when volume increases? A: Pressure decreases below atmospheric pressure.
chunks.source: Pressure decreases below atmospheric pressure.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why does air enter the lungs during inhalation? A: Air moves from higher atmospheric pressure to lower pressure inside the chest.
chunks.source: Air moves from higher atmospheric pressure to lower pressure inside the chest.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Describe the movement of the diaphragm during exhalation. A: It relaxes and returns to its dome shape, moving upward.
chunks.source: It relaxes and returns to its dome shape, moving upward.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What happens to chest volume during exhalation? A: Volume decreases as the diaphragm domes up and the rib cage moves down and in.
chunks.source: Volume decreases as the diaphragm domes up and the rib cage moves down and in.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Is exhalation usually active or passive? Explain. A: Passive — it occurs when the diaphragm and intercostal muscles relax, and the elastic lungs recoil.
chunks.source: Passive — it occurs when the diaphragm and intercostal muscles relax, and the elastic lungs recoil.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Respiratory Diseases and Smoking. I can name common respiratory diseases, explain how smoking damages the lungs, and state ways to keep lungs healthy. Smoking damages lungs: tar coats alveoli and paralyses cilia → bronchitis, emphysema, lung cancer. Nicotine narrows vessels, raises blood pressure. TB, pneumonia, asthma are other respiratory diseases. Prevention: no smoking, vaccines, hygiene, ventilation. Keywords: lung cancer: uncontrolled growth of abnormal cells in the lung; bronchitis: inflammation of the bronchi causing cough and mucus; emphysema: destruction of alveoli walls reducing surface area; tar: sticky brown substance in tobacco smoke; nicotine: addictive drug in tobacco that narrows blood vessels; tuberculosis: bacterial infection that mainly attacks the lungs; asthma: condition where airways narrow and swell, making breathing hard; pneumonia: infection that inflames the alveoli and fills them with fluid
chunks.source: Smoking damages lungs: tar coats alveoli and paralyses cilia → bronchitis, emphysema, lung cancer. Nicotine narrows vessels, raises blood pressure. TB, pneumonia, asthma are other respiratory diseases. Prevention: no smoking, vaccines, hygiene, ventilation.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name the sticky substance in cigarette smoke that coats the lungs. A: Tar — it coats the trachea, bronchi, and alveoli, paralysing cilia.
chunks.source: Tar — it coats the trachea, bronchi, and alveoli, paralysing cilia.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which drug in tobacco makes smoking addictive? A: Nicotine — it is a stimulant that causes dependence.
chunks.source: Nicotine — it is a stimulant that causes dependence.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State two effects of tar on the respiratory system. A: Any two: coats alveoli reducing gas exchange, paralyses cilia causing mucus buildup, causes cancer, irritates bronchi leading to bronchitis.
chunks.source: Any two: coats alveoli reducing gas exchange, paralyses cilia causing mucus buildup, causes cancer, irritates bronchi leading to bronchitis.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What happens to the alveoli in emphysema? A: The walls between alveoli break down, reducing surface area for diffusion.
chunks.source: The walls between alveoli break down, reducing surface area for diffusion.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How does carbon monoxide from smoke affect the blood? A: It binds to haemoglobin more strongly than oxygen, reducing oxygen transport.
chunks.source: It binds to haemoglobin more strongly than oxygen, reducing oxygen transport.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name the bacterial disease that spreads through cough droplets and mainly affects the lungs. A: Tuberculosis (TB) — caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
chunks.source: Tuberculosis (TB) — caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What happens in the alveoli during pneumonia? A: They become inflamed and fill with pus and fluid, blocking diffusion of oxygen.
chunks.source: They become inflamed and fill with pus and fluid, blocking diffusion of oxygen.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State two ways to prevent the spread of tuberculosis. A: Cover mouth when coughing, ensure good ventilation, complete full course of treatment if infected, BCG vaccination at birth.
chunks.source: Cover mouth when coughing, ensure good ventilation, complete full course of treatment if infected, BCG vaccination at birth.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Male Reproductive System. I can name the parts of the male reproductive system and explain the function of each part. The male reproductive system makes and delivers sperm. Testes produce sperm and testosterone; scrotum keeps testes cool; sperm duct carries sperm; prostate gland adds fluid; urethra carries semen and urine through the penis. Keywords: testes: two oval organs that make sperm and testosterone; scrotum: a loose skin bag that holds the testes outside the body; sperm duct: a tube that carries sperm from the testes to the urethra; prostate gland: a gland that adds fluid to sperm to make semen; urethra: a tube that carries urine and semen out of the body; penis: the male organ used for passing urine and delivering semen; semen: the whitish fluid made of sperm and gland fluids; testosterone: the male hormone that controls sperm production and body changes at puberty
chunks.source: The male reproductive system makes and delivers sperm. Testes produce sperm and testosterone; scrotum keeps testes cool; sperm duct carries sperm; prostate gland adds fluid; urethra carries semen and urine through the penis.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name the organ that produces sperm. A: Testes — they contain seminiferous tubules where sperm are made.
chunks.source: Testes — they contain seminiferous tubules where sperm are made.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State the function of the scrotum. A: It holds the testes outside the body to keep them cooler than body temperature for sperm production.
chunks.source: It holds the testes outside the body to keep them cooler than body temperature for sperm production.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which tube transports sperm from the testes to the urethra? A: Sperm duct (vas deferens) — it connects the epididymis to the urethra.
chunks.source: Sperm duct (vas deferens) — it connects the epididymis to the urethra.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name the gland that adds alkaline fluid to semen. A: Prostate gland — its fluid neutralises vaginal acidity and activates sperm motility.
chunks.source: Prostate gland — its fluid neutralises vaginal acidity and activates sperm motility.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Through which tube do both urine and semen pass? A: Urethra — it serves both urinary and reproductive systems in males.
chunks.source: Urethra — it serves both urinary and reproductive systems in males.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is the male hormone called? A: Testosterone — produced by Leydig cells in the testes; controls secondary sexual characteristics.
chunks.source: Testosterone — produced by Leydig cells in the testes; controls secondary sexual characteristics.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Define semen. A: A whitish fluid composed of sperm and secretions from the prostate gland, seminal vesicles, and bulbourethral glands.
chunks.source: A whitish fluid composed of sperm and secretions from the prostate gland, seminal vesicles, and bulbourethral glands.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why are the testes located outside the abdominal cavity? A: Spermatogenesis requires a temperature 2–3°C below core body temperature; the scrotum provides this.
chunks.source: Spermatogenesis requires a temperature 2–3°C below core body temperature; the scrotum provides this.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which part becomes erect during sexual arousal? A: Penis — it contains erectile tissue that fills with blood.
chunks.source: Penis — it contains erectile tissue that fills with blood.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State one function of testosterone. A: It stimulates sperm production, deepens the voice, grows facial hair, and increases muscle mass at puberty.
chunks.source: It stimulates sperm production, deepens the voice, grows facial hair, and increases muscle mass at puberty.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Female Reproductive System. I can name the parts of the female reproductive system, explain the menstrual cycle, and describe the role of oestrogen. The female system produces ova and supports pregnancy. Ovaries release ova and make oestrogen; oviduct is where fertilisation happens; uterus grows the baby; cervix opens to vagina; menstrual cycle is driven by oestrogen and progesterone. Keywords: ovaries: two small organs that store and release ova and make oestrogen; oviduct: a tube that carries the ovum from the ovary to the uterus; fertilisation happens here; uterus: a muscular hollow organ where a baby grows during pregnancy; cervix: the narrow lower part of the uterus that opens into the vagina; vagina: a muscular canal from the cervix to the outside; receives the penis and is the birth canal; ovum: the female sex cell (egg) released by the ovary once a month; menstrual cycle: the monthly cycle of changes in the uterus and ovaries, lasting about 28 days; oestrogen: the main female hormone that controls the menstrual cycle and body changes at puberty
chunks.source: The female system produces ova and supports pregnancy. Ovaries release ova and make oestrogen; oviduct is where fertilisation happens; uterus grows the baby; cervix opens to vagina; menstrual cycle is driven by oestrogen and progesterone.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name the organ that produces ova and oestrogen. A: Ovaries — they contain follicles that release ova and secrete oestrogen.
chunks.source: Ovaries — they contain follicles that release ova and secrete oestrogen.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Where does fertilisation usually take place? A: Oviduct (fallopian tube) — the ovum meets sperm in the ampulla of the tube.
chunks.source: Oviduct (fallopian tube) — the ovum meets sperm in the ampulla of the tube.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is the function of the uterus? A: It houses and nourishes the developing embryo and foetus; its muscular wall contracts during labour.
chunks.source: It houses and nourishes the developing embryo and foetus; its muscular wall contracts during labour.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Describe the cervix. A: The narrow lower part of the uterus that opens into the vagina; dilates during childbirth.
chunks.source: The narrow lower part of the uterus that opens into the vagina; dilates during childbirth.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State the role of the vagina in reproduction. A: Receives the penis and semen during intercourse; serves as the birth canal during delivery.
chunks.source: Receives the penis and semen during intercourse; serves as the birth canal during delivery.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Define ovum. A: The female gamete (egg cell); large, non-motile, released once per menstrual cycle at ovulation.
chunks.source: The female gamete (egg cell); large, non-motile, released once per menstrual cycle at ovulation.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is the menstrual cycle? A: A roughly 28-day cycle of hormonal and uterine changes preparing for pregnancy; includes menstruation, follicular phase, ovulation, luteal phase.
chunks.source: A roughly 28-day cycle of hormonal and uterine changes preparing for pregnancy; includes menstruation, follicular phase, ovulation, luteal phase.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which hormone thickens the uterus lining in the first half of the cycle? A: Oestrogen — secreted by the developing ovarian follicle; causes proliferative phase.
chunks.source: Oestrogen — secreted by the developing ovarian follicle; causes proliferative phase.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: When does ovulation occur in a 28-day cycle? A: Around day 14 — triggered by an LH surge; the mature follicle ruptures and releases the ovum.
chunks.source: Around day 14 — triggered by an LH surge; the mature follicle ruptures and releases the ovum.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why does menstruation happen if pregnancy does not occur? A: The corpus luteum degenerates, progesterone falls, and the thickened uterus lining is shed through the vagina.
chunks.source: The corpus luteum degenerates, progesterone falls, and the thickened uterus lining is shed through the vagina.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Fertilisation, Pregnancy and Birth. I can explain fertilisation, describe the stages from zygote to foetus, and state the functions of the placenta, umbilical cord, and antenatal care. Fertilisation in the oviduct forms a zygote (46 chromosomes). It divides, implants as an embryo, becomes a foetus at 9 weeks. The placenta and umbilical cord exchange substances. Labour delivers the baby and placenta. Antenatal care keeps mother and baby healthy. Keywords: fertilisation: the fusion of a sperm nucleus with an ovum nucleus to form a zygote; zygote: the single cell formed when sperm and ovum fuse; it divides by mitosis; embryo: the developing organism from the 2-cell stage to 8 weeks; foetus: the developing baby from 9 weeks until birth; placenta: an organ that grows from the embryo and uterine lining; exchanges nutrients, oxygen, and waste; umbilical cord: a rope-like structure connecting the foetus to the placenta; contains two arteries and one vein; labour: the process of childbirth: contractions, cervical dilation, delivery of baby and placenta; antenatal: care given to a pregnant woman before birth to monitor health of mother and baby
chunks.source: Fertilisation in the oviduct forms a zygote (46 chromosomes). It divides, implants as an embryo, becomes a foetus at 9 weeks. The placenta and umbilical cord exchange substances. Labour delivers the baby and placenta. Antenatal care keeps mother and baby healthy.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Define fertilisation. A: Fusion of a sperm nucleus with an ovum nucleus to form a diploid zygote.
chunks.source: Fusion of a sperm nucleus with an ovum nucleus to form a diploid zygote.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How many chromosomes are in a human zygote? A: 46 (23 pairs) — 23 from sperm, 23 from ovum.
chunks.source: 46 (23 pairs) — 23 from sperm, 23 from ovum.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is the difference between an embryo and a foetus? A: Embryo: from fertilisation to 8 weeks; foetus: from 9 weeks to birth.
chunks.source: Embryo: from fertilisation to 8 weeks; foetus: from 9 weeks to birth.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State two functions of the placenta. A: Allows exchange of oxygen/nutrients from mother to foetus and waste (CO2, urea) from foetus to mother; produces progesterone to maintain pregnancy.
chunks.source: Allows exchange of oxygen/nutrients from mother to foetus and waste (CO2, urea) from foetus to mother; produces progesterone to maintain pregnancy.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How many blood vessels are in the umbilical cord, and what does each carry? A: Three vessels: one vein carries oxygenated blood to the foetus; two arteries carry deoxygenated blood and waste from the foetus.
chunks.source: Three vessels: one vein carries oxygenated blood to the foetus; two arteries carry deoxygenated blood and waste from the foetus.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Describe what happens during labour. A: Uterine contractions dilate the cervix to 10 cm; baby is pushed through the vagina; placenta is delivered after the baby.
chunks.source: Uterine contractions dilate the cervix to 10 cm; baby is pushed through the vagina; placenta is delivered after the baby.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why is antenatal care important? Give two reasons. A: Detects maternal complications (e.g., high blood pressure, anaemia); monitors foetal growth and heartbeat; provides tetanus immunisation and iron/folic acid supplements.
chunks.source: Detects maternal complications (e.g., high blood pressure, anaemia); monitors foetal growth and heartbeat; provides tetanus immunisation and iron/folic acid supplements.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Where does the zygote implant? A: In the endometrium (lining) of the uterus.
chunks.source: In the endometrium (lining) of the uterus.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What triggers the start of labour? A: Hormonal changes — oxytocin causes uterine contractions; progesterone drops; baby's lungs release surfactant signalling readiness.
chunks.source: Hormonal changes — oxytocin causes uterine contractions; progesterone drops; baby's lungs release surfactant signalling readiness.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name the stage when all major organs have formed. A: Foetus (from 9 weeks onwards).
chunks.source: Foetus (from 9 weeks onwards).

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Reproductive Health and STIs. I can name common STIs, explain how HIV leads to AIDS, and describe prevention methods including abstinence, condoms, and family planning. HIV attacks the immune system; untreated leads to AIDS. Bacterial STIs (gonorrhoea, syphilis) are curable; candidiasis is fungal. Abstinence is 100% protection. Condoms give dual protection. Family planning spaces births. Test for HIV, treat STIs early, plan your family. Keywords: HIV: Human Immunodeficiency Virus; a virus that attacks the immune system (CD4 cells); AIDS: Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome; the late stage of HIV infection when the immune system is severely damaged; gonorrhoea: a bacterial STI causing discharge and pain when urinating; syphilis: a bacterial STI with stages: sore, rash, then serious organ damage if untreated; candidiasis: a fungal infection (yeast) causing itching and white discharge; not always sexually transmitted; abstinence: choosing not to have sexual intercourse; 100% effective against STIs and pregnancy; condom: a barrier worn on the penis or inside the vagina during sex to block fluids; family planning: methods to decide when and how many children to have; includes pills, implants, condoms
chunks.source: HIV attacks the immune system; untreated leads to AIDS. Bacterial STIs (gonorrhoea, syphilis) are curable; candidiasis is fungal. Abstinence is 100% protection. Condoms give dual protection. Family planning spaces births. Test for HIV, treat STIs early, plan your family.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What does HIV stand for? A: Human Immunodeficiency Virus — a retrovirus that attacks CD4+ T cells.
chunks.source: Human Immunodeficiency Virus — a retrovirus that attacks CD4+ T cells.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is AIDS? A: Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome — the advanced stage of HIV infection with severe immune suppression (CD4 < 200) and opportunistic infections.
chunks.source: Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome — the advanced stage of HIV infection with severe immune suppression (CD4 < 200) and opportunistic infections.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name three body fluids that transmit HIV. A: Blood, semen, vaginal fluids, breast milk (any three).
chunks.source: Blood, semen, vaginal fluids, breast milk (any three).

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which STI is caused by a bacterium and causes a painless sore? A: Syphilis — primary stage chancre is painless; caused by Treponema pallidum.
chunks.source: Syphilis — primary stage chancre is painless; caused by Treponema pallidum.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State one symptom of gonorrhoea in males. A: Yellowish pus discharge from the penis and painful urination.
chunks.source: Yellowish pus discharge from the penis and painful urination.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why is candidiasis not strictly an STI? A: Candida yeast lives normally in the body; overgrowth can occur due to antibiotics, diabetes, pregnancy, weakened immunity — not only sexual contact.
chunks.source: Candida yeast lives normally in the body; overgrowth can occur due to antibiotics, diabetes, pregnancy, weakened immunity — not only sexual contact.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is the only 100% effective method to prevent both STIs and pregnancy? A: Abstinence — not engaging in sexual intercourse.
chunks.source: Abstinence — not engaging in sexual intercourse.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which contraceptive method provides dual protection (pregnancy and STIs)? A: Condom (male or female) — it is a physical barrier to fluids.
chunks.source: Condom (male or female) — it is a physical barrier to fluids.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name two hormonal family planning methods. A: Contraceptive pill, injectable (Depo-Provera), implant (Implanon), hormonal IUD (any two).
chunks.source: Contraceptive pill, injectable (Depo-Provera), implant (Implanon), hormonal IUD (any two).

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why should a pregnant woman test for HIV? A: To start ARVs early if positive, preventing mother-to-child transmission during pregnancy, birth, and breastfeeding.
chunks.source: To start ARVs early if positive, preventing mother-to-child transmission during pregnancy, birth, and breastfeeding.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: What Is Excretion?. I can explain what excretion is and name the main excretory products. Excretion removes toxic metabolic waste such as urea, carbon dioxide, and sweat to keep the body healthy. Keywords: excretion: the process of removing metabolic waste from the body; waste: unwanted substances produced during metabolism; urea: a nitrogenous waste from protein breakdown; urine: liquid waste produced by the kidneys; carbon dioxide: a waste gas from respiration; sweat: fluid released by skin glands to cool the body; metabolism: chemical processes that provide energy; toxic: poisonous or harmful if it builds up
chunks.source: Excretion removes toxic metabolic waste such as urea, carbon dioxide, and sweat to keep the body healthy.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is excretion? A: Excretion is the removal of metabolic waste like urea, carbon dioxide, and sweat from the body. Reason: Excretion gets rid of toxic substances produced during metabolism.
chunks.source: Excretion is the removal of metabolic waste like urea, carbon dioxide, and sweat from the body. Reason: Excretion gets rid of toxic substances produced during metabolism.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name two excretory products in humans. A: Urea and carbon dioxide are excretory products. Reason: They are waste from metabolism excreted by kidneys and lungs.
chunks.source: Urea and carbon dioxide are excretory products. Reason: They are waste from metabolism excreted by kidneys and lungs.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which organ produces urine? A: The kidneys produce urine by filtering urea from blood. Reason: Kidneys are the main excretory organs for nitrogenous waste.
chunks.source: The kidneys produce urine by filtering urea from blood. Reason: Kidneys are the main excretory organs for nitrogenous waste.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What waste gas is removed by the lungs? A: Carbon dioxide is removed by the lungs. Reason: It is a product of cellular respiration.
chunks.source: Carbon dioxide is removed by the lungs. Reason: It is a product of cellular respiration.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How does sweat help the body? A: Sweat cools the body and excretes water, salts, and urea. Reason: Evaporation of sweat lowers temperature and removes waste.
chunks.source: Sweat cools the body and excretes water, salts, and urea. Reason: Evaporation of sweat lowers temperature and removes waste.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is the difference between excretion and egestion? A: Excretion removes metabolic waste; egestion removes undigested food as faeces. Reason: They involve different systems and waste types.
chunks.source: Excretion removes metabolic waste; egestion removes undigested food as faeces. Reason: They involve different systems and waste types.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why is urea toxic if it builds up? A: High urea levels damage cells and organs. Reason: Urea is a nitrogenous waste that must be excreted.
chunks.source: High urea levels damage cells and organs. Reason: Urea is a nitrogenous waste that must be excreted.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which process in the kidney filters blood to form urine? A: Filtration in the nephron filters blood to form urine. Reason: Filtration is the first step of urine formation.
chunks.source: Filtration in the nephron filters blood to form urine. Reason: Filtration is the first step of urine formation.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: The Kidneys and Urinary System. I can describe the structure of the kidney and how urine is formed. The kidney filters blood in nephrons through filtration and reabsorption to form urine, which travels via ureters to the bladder and out through the urethra. Keywords: kidney: bean-shaped organ that filters blood; ureter: tube that carries urine from kidney to bladder; bladder: muscular sac that stores urine; urethra: tube that carries urine out of the body; nephron: tiny filtering unit inside the kidney; filtration: first step where blood plasma is filtered; reabsorption: return of useful substances from filtrate to blood; urine: liquid waste formed after filtration and reabsorption
chunks.source: The kidney filters blood in nephrons through filtration and reabsorption to form urine, which travels via ureters to the bladder and out through the urethra.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is the function of the kidney? A: The kidney filters blood to remove waste and form urine. Reason: Kidneys contain nephrons that perform filtration and reabsorption.
chunks.source: The kidney filters blood to remove waste and form urine. Reason: Kidneys contain nephrons that perform filtration and reabsorption.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name the tube that carries urine from the kidney to the bladder. A: The ureter carries urine from the kidney to the bladder. Reason: Ureters are muscular tubes connecting kidneys to bladder.
chunks.source: The ureter carries urine from the kidney to the bladder. Reason: Ureters are muscular tubes connecting kidneys to bladder.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Where is urine stored before it leaves the body? A: Urine is stored in the bladder. Reason: The bladder is a muscular sac that holds urine until urination.
chunks.source: Urine is stored in the bladder. Reason: The bladder is a muscular sac that holds urine until urination.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is the first step of urine formation in the nephron? A: Filtration of blood in the glomerulus is the first step. Reason: Filtration creates the initial filtrate.
chunks.source: Filtration of blood in the glomerulus is the first step. Reason: Filtration creates the initial filtrate.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What happens during reabsorption? A: Useful substances like glucose and water are returned to the blood. Reason: Reabsorption prevents loss of valuable nutrients.
chunks.source: Useful substances like glucose and water are returned to the blood. Reason: Reabsorption prevents loss of valuable nutrients.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which structure carries urine from the bladder to the outside? A: The urethra carries urine out of the body. Reason: The urethra is the final passage for urine excretion.
chunks.source: The urethra carries urine out of the body. Reason: The urethra is the final passage for urine excretion.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What can block the ureter and cause severe pain? A: Kidney stones can block the ureter. Reason: Stones often pass from kidney into the narrow ureter.
chunks.source: Kidney stones can block the ureter. Reason: Stones often pass from kidney into the narrow ureter.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Describe the path of urine from formation to excretion. A: Urine forms in nephron → passes to ureter → stored in bladder → expelled via urethra. Reason: This sequence follows the urinary tract anatomy.
chunks.source: Urine forms in nephron → passes to ureter → stored in bladder → expelled via urethra. Reason: This sequence follows the urinary tract anatomy.

chunks.id: L-P7-Science-The Skin as an Excretory Organ
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: The Skin as an Excretory Organ
chunks.text: The Skin as an Excretory Organ. I can explain how the skin excretes waste and controls temperature. The skin excretes sweat through sweat glands and pores, helping temperature control, while the dermis contains glands, hair follicles, and nerve endings. Keywords: epidermis: outer layer of the skin; dermis: inner layer containing glands and nerves; sweat gland: gland that produces sweat; sweat pore: tiny opening on the skin surface for sweat; sebum: oily substance that waterproofs skin and hair; temperature control: regulation of body heat; hair follicle: structure that anchors hair in the skin; nerve endings: sensory receptors in the skin
chunks.source: The skin excretes sweat through sweat glands and pores, helping temperature control, while the dermis contains glands, hair follicles, and nerve endings.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Science-The Skin as an Excretory Organ
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: The Skin as an Excretory Organ
chunks.text: Q: What are the two main layers of the skin? A: The epidermis (outer) and dermis (inner). Reason: These layers have different structures and functions.
chunks.source: The epidermis (outer) and dermis (inner). Reason: These layers have different structures and functions.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Science-The Skin as an Excretory Organ
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: The Skin as an Excretory Organ
chunks.text: Q: Where are sweat glands located? A: Sweat glands are in the dermis. Reason: The dermis contains glands, hair follicles, and nerves.
chunks.source: Sweat glands are in the dermis. Reason: The dermis contains glands, hair follicles, and nerves.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Science-The Skin as an Excretory Organ
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: The Skin as an Excretory Organ
chunks.text: Q: What is the function of sweat pores? A: Sweat pores allow sweat to reach the skin surface. Reason: They are openings of sweat gland ducts.
chunks.source: Sweat pores allow sweat to reach the skin surface. Reason: They are openings of sweat gland ducts.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Science-The Skin as an Excretory Organ
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: The Skin as an Excretory Organ
chunks.text: Q: Name two substances excreted in sweat. A: Water and salts (also urea). Reason: Sweat carries waste and helps cooling.
chunks.source: Water and salts (also urea). Reason: Sweat carries waste and helps cooling.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Science-The Skin as an Excretory Organ
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: The Skin as an Excretory Organ
chunks.text: Q: What does sebum do? A: Sebum waterproofs the epidermis and lubricates hair. Reason: It prevents drying and keeps skin flexible.
chunks.source: Sebum waterproofs the epidermis and lubricates hair. Reason: It prevents drying and keeps skin flexible.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Science-The Skin as an Excretory Organ
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: The Skin as an Excretory Organ
chunks.text: Q: Which layer contains nerve endings? A: The dermis contains nerve endings. Reason: Sensory receptors are located in the dermis.
chunks.source: The dermis contains nerve endings. Reason: Sensory receptors are located in the dermis.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Science-The Skin as an Excretory Organ
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: The Skin as an Excretory Organ
chunks.text: Q: How does the skin help temperature control? A: Sweat evaporates and cools the body. Reason: Evaporation removes heat from the skin surface.
chunks.source: Sweat evaporates and cools the body. Reason: Evaporation removes heat from the skin surface.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Science-The Skin as an Excretory Organ
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: The Skin as an Excretory Organ
chunks.text: Q: What is the role of hair follicles? A: Hair follicles anchor hairs and have associated sebaceous glands. Reason: They are structures in the dermis.
chunks.source: Hair follicles anchor hairs and have associated sebaceous glands. Reason: They are structures in the dermis.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Excretory Disorders and Care. I can identify common excretory disorders and explain how to care for the urinary system. Kidney stones, urinary infections, and diabetes affect the excretory system; drinking water, reducing salt, and good hygiene keep kidneys healthy. Keywords: kidney stones: hard deposits of salts in the kidney; dialysis: machine filtering of blood when kidneys fail; urinary infection: bacterial infection of the urinary tract; dehydration: lack of enough water in the body; salt: mineral that can form crystals in urine; water: essential fluid for diluting urine; hygiene: clean habits to prevent infection; diabetes: disease with high blood sugar that can damage kidneys
chunks.source: Kidney stones, urinary infections, and diabetes affect the excretory system; drinking water, reducing salt, and good hygiene keep kidneys healthy.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is a kidney stone? A: A hard deposit of salts and minerals in the kidney. Reason: Stones form when urine is concentrated.
chunks.source: A hard deposit of salts and minerals in the kidney. Reason: Stones form when urine is concentrated.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is dialysis used for? A: Dialysis filters blood when kidneys fail. Reason: It replaces the excretory function of kidneys.
chunks.source: Dialysis filters blood when kidneys fail. Reason: It replaces the excretory function of kidneys.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name a symptom of urinary infection. A: Pain or burning when urinating. Reason: Bacteria irritate the urinary tract lining.
chunks.source: Pain or burning when urinating. Reason: Bacteria irritate the urinary tract lining.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How does dehydration contribute to kidney stones? A: Dehydration concentrates urine, increasing crystal formation. Reason: Less water means higher salt concentration.
chunks.source: Dehydration concentrates urine, increasing crystal formation. Reason: Less water means higher salt concentration.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why is high salt intake a risk for kidney stones? A: Excess salt increases calcium in urine, promoting stones. Reason: Salt affects mineral balance in urine.
chunks.source: Excess salt increases calcium in urine, promoting stones. Reason: Salt affects mineral balance in urine.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How does drinking water prevent urinary infections? A: Water flushes bacteria from the urinary tract. Reason: Frequent urination reduces bacterial growth.
chunks.source: Water flushes bacteria from the urinary tract. Reason: Frequent urination reduces bacterial growth.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What hygiene practice helps prevent urinary infections? A: Wiping front to back after using the toilet. Reason: Prevents bacteria from anus reaching urethra.
chunks.source: Wiping front to back after using the toilet. Reason: Prevents bacteria from anus reaching urethra.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How can diabetes affect the kidneys? A: High blood sugar damages kidney filters over time. Reason: Diabetes leads to diabetic nephropathy.
chunks.source: High blood sugar damages kidney filters over time. Reason: Diabetes leads to diabetic nephropathy.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Sources and Properties of Light. I can identify light sources, describe how light travels, and classify materials by how they let light pass. Luminous objects make light; non-luminous objects reflect it. Light travels in straight lines as rays. Transparent materials let all light through, translucent scatter light, opaque block light. Keywords: luminous: giving out its own light; non-luminous: not giving out its own light; ray: a narrow line of light; beam: a group of rays travelling together; straight line: the path light follows in one medium; transparent: letting all light pass through; opaque: blocking all light; translucent: letting some light pass but scattering it
chunks.source: Luminous objects make light; non-luminous objects reflect it. Light travels in straight lines as rays. Transparent materials let all light through, translucent scatter light, opaque block light.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Define 'luminous' and give two examples from a Ugandan home. A: Luminous means giving out its own light. Examples: candle, charcoal fire, paraffin lamp, electric bulb.
chunks.source: Luminous means giving out its own light. Examples: candle, charcoal fire, paraffin lamp, electric bulb.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why is the moon classified as non-luminous? A: The moon does not produce its own light; it reflects light from the sun.
chunks.source: The moon does not produce its own light; it reflects light from the sun.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Draw a diagram showing a ray, a beam, and straight line propagation. A: A ray is a single line with arrow. A beam is multiple parallel rays. Straight line shown by rays not bending.
chunks.source: A ray is a single line with arrow. A beam is multiple parallel rays. Straight line shown by rays not bending.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: A material lets light through but you cannot see clearly through it. What is it? A: Translucent.
chunks.source: Translucent.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: List one transparent, one translucent, and one opaque material found in a classroom. A: Transparent: window pane. Translucent: frosted glass or oiled paper. Opaque: wooden desk, chalkboard.
chunks.source: Transparent: window pane. Translucent: frosted glass or oiled paper. Opaque: wooden desk, chalkboard.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Explain how you would prove light travels in a straight line using three cardboards. A: Make a hole in each cardboard. Align holes in a straight line. Shine a torch through. Light passes only when aligned.
chunks.source: Make a hole in each cardboard. Align holes in a straight line. Shine a torch through. Light passes only when aligned.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: A beam of light hits a clear glass window. What happens to the light? A: It passes through because glass is transparent.
chunks.source: It passes through because glass is transparent.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: A beam of light hits a wooden door. What happens? A: It is blocked because wood is opaque; a shadow forms.
chunks.source: It is blocked because wood is opaque; a shadow forms.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: PLE-style: Which of these is a luminous source? A) Moon B) Candle C) Mirror D) Book A: B) Candle — it produces its own light by burning.
chunks.source: B) Candle — it produces its own light by burning.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: PLE-style: Light travels in a straight line. This property is called: A: Rectilinear propagation of light.
chunks.source: Rectilinear propagation of light.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Shadows and Eclipses. I can explain how shadows form, name the parts of a shadow, describe solar and lunar eclipses, and explain how a pinhole camera works. Shadows form when opaque objects block light. Umbra = total darkness, penumbra = partial. Solar eclipse: moon blocks sun. Lunar eclipse: earth blocks sun from moon. Pinhole camera uses straight-line light to form inverted images. Keywords: shadow: dark area where light is blocked; umbra: dark central part of a shadow where all light is blocked; penumbra: lighter outer part of a shadow where some light reaches; solar eclipse: moon blocks sun's light from reaching earth; lunar eclipse: earth blocks sun's light from reaching moon; opaque: blocking all light; pinhole camera: simple camera using a small hole to form an image; image: likeness of an object formed by light
chunks.source: Shadows form when opaque objects block light. Umbra = total darkness, penumbra = partial. Solar eclipse: moon blocks sun. Lunar eclipse: earth blocks sun from moon. Pinhole camera uses straight-line light to form inverted images.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Define 'shadow' and state the condition needed for its formation. A: A shadow is a dark area formed when an opaque object blocks light. Light must travel in straight lines.
chunks.source: A shadow is a dark area formed when an opaque object blocks light. Light must travel in straight lines.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Distinguish between umbra and penumbra. A: Umbra is the dark central part where all light is blocked. Penumbra is the lighter outer part where only some light is blocked.
chunks.source: Umbra is the dark central part where all light is blocked. Penumbra is the lighter outer part where only some light is blocked.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Explain why shadows are longer in the morning and evening but shorter at noon. A: The sun is low in the morning/evening, so rays hit objects at a shallow angle, stretching the shadow. At noon, the sun is overhead, rays are steep, shadow is short.
chunks.source: The sun is low in the morning/evening, so rays hit objects at a shallow angle, stretching the shadow. At noon, the sun is overhead, rays are steep, shadow is short.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Describe how a solar eclipse occurs. Include the positions of the sun, moon, and earth. A: The moon passes directly between the sun and the earth. The moon's umbra falls on the earth's surface.
chunks.source: The moon passes directly between the sun and the earth. The moon's umbra falls on the earth's surface.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Describe how a lunar eclipse occurs. A: The earth passes directly between the sun and the moon. The earth's umbra falls on the moon.
chunks.source: The earth passes directly between the sun and the moon. The earth's umbra falls on the moon.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why is a lunar eclipse visible from more places than a solar eclipse? A: Earth's umbra is much larger than the moon's umbra, covering the whole moon. Anyone on the night side of earth can see it.
chunks.source: Earth's umbra is much larger than the moon's umbra, covering the whole moon. Anyone on the night side of earth can see it.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Explain how a pinhole camera forms an inverted image. Use the term 'straight line'. A: Light from each point on the object travels in a straight line through the pinhole. Rays from the top go to the bottom of the screen, and vice versa, causing inversion.
chunks.source: Light from each point on the object travels in a straight line through the pinhole. Rays from the top go to the bottom of the screen, and vice versa, causing inversion.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State two differences between a pinhole camera image and a plane mirror image. A: Pinhole image: inverted, real, formed on a screen. Plane mirror image: upright, virtual, appears behind the mirror.
chunks.source: Pinhole image: inverted, real, formed on a screen. Plane mirror image: upright, virtual, appears behind the mirror.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: PLE-style: During a solar eclipse, the dark part of the shadow on earth is called: A: The umbra.
chunks.source: The umbra.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: PLE-style: If the pinhole in a pinhole camera is made larger, the image becomes: A: Brighter but blurred (less sharp).
chunks.source: Brighter but blurred (less sharp).

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Reflection of Light. I can state the laws of reflection, draw ray diagrams for plane mirrors, explain how a periscope works, and describe the nature of mirror images. Laws of reflection: angle i = angle r; incident ray, reflected ray, normal in same plane. Plane mirror image: upright, same size, laterally inverted, virtual. Periscope uses two mirrors at 45° to turn light 90° twice. Keywords: incident ray: ray hitting a surface; reflected ray: ray bouncing off a surface; normal: imaginary line at 90 degrees to the surface; angle: measure of turn between two lines; plane mirror: flat reflecting surface; periscope: device using two mirrors to see over obstacles; image: likeness formed by reflected rays; virtual: cannot be formed on a screen; rays only appear to come from it
chunks.source: Laws of reflection: angle i = angle r; incident ray, reflected ray, normal in same plane. Plane mirror image: upright, same size, laterally inverted, virtual. Periscope uses two mirrors at 45° to turn light 90° twice.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State the two laws of reflection. A: 1. Angle of incidence equals angle of reflection. 2. Incident ray, reflected ray, and normal all lie in the same plane.
chunks.source: 1. Angle of incidence equals angle of reflection. 2. Incident ray, reflected ray, and normal all lie in the same plane.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Define 'normal' in reflection. A: An imaginary line drawn at 90° (perpendicular) to the reflecting surface at the point of incidence.
chunks.source: An imaginary line drawn at 90° (perpendicular) to the reflecting surface at the point of incidence.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: An incident ray makes an angle of 40° with the mirror surface. What is the angle of reflection? A: Angle of incidence = 90° - 40° = 50°. Angle of reflection = 50° (measured from normal).
chunks.source: Angle of incidence = 90° - 40° = 50°. Angle of reflection = 50° (measured from normal).

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: List four characteristics of an image formed by a plane mirror. A: Upright, same size, laterally inverted, virtual.
chunks.source: Upright, same size, laterally inverted, virtual.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Explain why a plane mirror image is called virtual. A: The reflected rays only appear to diverge from behind the mirror; they do not actually meet there. The image cannot be formed on a screen.
chunks.source: The reflected rays only appear to diverge from behind the mirror; they do not actually meet there. The image cannot be formed on a screen.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Draw a ray diagram to show how a periscope works. Label incident ray, reflected ray, normal, and angles. A: Two mirrors at 45°. Ray from top hits first mirror, reflects down 90°. Hits second mirror, reflects 90° to eye. All angles 45° to normals.
chunks.source: Two mirrors at 45°. Ray from top hits first mirror, reflects down 90°. Hits second mirror, reflects 90° to eye. All angles 45° to normals.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: A boy stands 2 m from a plane mirror. How far is his image from him? A: 4 m (2 m to mirror + 2 m behind mirror).
chunks.source: 4 m (2 m to mirror + 2 m behind mirror).

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: PLE-style: The angle between the incident ray and the reflected ray is 60°. What is the angle of incidence? A: 30° (since angle of incidence = angle of reflection, and their sum is 60°).
chunks.source: 30° (since angle of incidence = angle of reflection, and their sum is 60°).

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: PLE-style: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of a plane mirror image? A) Virtual B) Inverted C) Same size D) Laterally inverted A: B) Inverted — plane mirror images are upright.
chunks.source: B) Inverted — plane mirror images are upright.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: PLE-style: A periscope uses two plane mirrors. The angle between each mirror and the horizontal is: A: 45°.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Refraction and Lenses. I can explain refraction, describe how convex and concave lenses bend light, define focus and focal length, and explain dispersion and rainbow formation. Refraction bends light at media boundaries. Convex lenses converge rays to a focus; concave lenses diverge rays. Dispersion splits white light into a spectrum. Rainbows form by refraction, reflection, and dispersion in raindrops. Keywords: refraction: bending of light when it passes from one medium to another; lens: transparent material with curved surfaces that bends light; convex: thicker at the centre than at the edges; converges light; concave: thinner at the centre than at the edges; diverges light; focus: point where parallel rays meet after passing through a convex lens; spectrum: band of colours produced when white light splits; rainbow: natural spectrum formed by sunlight and rain droplets; dispersion: splitting of white light into its component colours
chunks.source: Refraction bends light at media boundaries. Convex lenses converge rays to a focus; concave lenses diverge rays. Dispersion splits white light into a spectrum. Rainbows form by refraction, reflection, and dispersion in raindrops.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Define 'refraction' and state its cause. A: Refraction is the bending of light when it passes from one medium to another of different density. Cause: change in speed of light.
chunks.source: Refraction is the bending of light when it passes from one medium to another of different density. Cause: change in speed of light.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: A ray of light passes from air into water. Does it bend towards or away from the normal? A: Towards the normal (water is denser than air, light slows down).
chunks.source: Towards the normal (water is denser than air, light slows down).

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Distinguish between a convex lens and a concave lens. A: Convex: thicker at centre, converges rays. Concave: thinner at centre, diverges rays.
chunks.source: Convex: thicker at centre, converges rays. Concave: thinner at centre, diverges rays.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Define 'focus' and 'focal length' of a convex lens. A: Focus: point where parallel rays converge after refraction. Focal length: distance from lens centre to focus.
chunks.source: Focus: point where parallel rays converge after refraction. Focal length: distance from lens centre to focus.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State one use of a convex lens and one use of a concave lens. A: Convex: magnifying glass, projector, camera, correcting long sight. Concave: correcting short sight, peephole.
chunks.source: Convex: magnifying glass, projector, camera, correcting long sight. Concave: correcting short sight, peephole.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Explain how a rainbow is formed. Use the words: refraction, reflection, dispersion, raindrop. A: Sunlight enters a raindrop, refracts and disperses into colours, reflects off the back, refracts again on exit. Each colour emerges at a fixed angle.
chunks.source: Sunlight enters a raindrop, refracts and disperses into colours, reflects off the back, refracts again on exit. Each colour emerges at a fixed angle.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why does red appear on the outer edge of a primary rainbow? A: Red light is deviated least (42°), violet most (40°). Drops at 42° send red to the eye; they form the outer arc.
chunks.source: Red light is deviated least (42°), violet most (40°). Drops at 42° send red to the eye; they form the outer arc.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: PLE-style: A convex lens forms a real, inverted image. The object is placed between F and 2F. Where is the image? A: Beyond 2F, real, inverted, magnified.
chunks.source: Beyond 2F, real, inverted, magnified.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: PLE-style: White light passes through a prism. Which colour is deviated the most? A: Violet.
chunks.source: Violet.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: PLE-style: The splitting of white light into its component colours is called: A: Dispersion.
chunks.source: Dispersion.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: The Eye and Its Care. I can label parts of the eye, explain how we see, describe short sight and long sight, and state how to care for eyes. Eye parts: cornea, iris, pupil, lens, retina, optic nerve. Cornea + lens focus light on retina. Short sight = focus in front of retina (concave lens). Long sight = focus behind retina (convex lens). Care: vitamin A, good light, clean water, no rubbing, check-ups. Keywords: cornea: transparent front layer that refracts light into the eye; iris: coloured part that controls pupil size; pupil: dark opening that lets light into the eye; lens: flexible transparent structure that fine-tunes focus; retina: light-sensitive layer at the back of the eye; optic nerve: nerve that carries signals from retina to brain; short sight: cannot see distant objects clearly; focus falls in front of retina; long sight: cannot see near objects clearly; focus falls behind retina
chunks.source: Eye parts: cornea, iris, pupil, lens, retina, optic nerve. Cornea + lens focus light on retina. Short sight = focus in front of retina (concave lens). Long sight = focus behind retina (convex lens). Care: vitamin A, good light, clean water, no rubbing, check-ups.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Label a diagram of the eye: cornea, iris, pupil, lens, retina, optic nerve. A: Cornea: transparent front. Iris: coloured muscle. Pupil: opening. Lens: flexible focuser. Retina: light sensor. Optic nerve: signal cable.
chunks.source: Cornea: transparent front. Iris: coloured muscle. Pupil: opening. Lens: flexible focuser. Retina: light sensor. Optic nerve: signal cable.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State the function of the iris. A: Controls the size of the pupil to regulate the amount of light entering the eye.
chunks.source: Controls the size of the pupil to regulate the amount of light entering the eye.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Explain how the eye focuses on near and far objects. A: Ciliary muscles change the lens shape: fat/thick for near objects, thin/flat for far objects (accommodation).
chunks.source: Ciliary muscles change the lens shape: fat/thick for near objects, thin/flat for far objects (accommodation).

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Describe short sight (myopia) and its correction. A: Eyeball too long or cornea too curved. Focus falls in front of retina. Corrected with concave (diverging) lens.
chunks.source: Eyeball too long or cornea too curved. Focus falls in front of retina. Corrected with concave (diverging) lens.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Describe long sight (hyperopia) and its correction. A: Eyeball too short or lens too weak. Focus falls behind retina. Corrected with convex (converging) lens.
chunks.source: Eyeball too short or lens too weak. Focus falls behind retina. Corrected with convex (converging) lens.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: A student squeezes eyes to see the board. What defect? What should be done? A: Likely short sight. Should get eyes tested and wear prescribed concave lenses.
chunks.source: Likely short sight. Should get eyes tested and wear prescribed concave lenses.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: List four ways to care for the eyes. A: 1. Eat vitamin A foods (carrots, mangoes, greens). 2. Read in good light. 3. Wash face with clean water. 4. Avoid rubbing eyes. 5. Take screen breaks. 6. Wear UV protection. 7. Regular check-ups.
chunks.source: 1. Eat vitamin A foods (carrots, mangoes, greens). 2. Read in good light. 3. Wash face with clean water. 4. Avoid rubbing eyes. 5. Take screen breaks. 6. Wear UV protection. 7. Regular check-ups.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: PLE-style: The part of the eye that controls the amount of light entering is the: A: Iris.
chunks.source: Iris.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: PLE-style: The image formed on the retina is: A: Real, inverted, and diminished.
chunks.source: Real, inverted, and diminished.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: PLE-style: A person with long sight needs a lens that: A: Converges light rays (convex lens).
chunks.source: Converges light rays (convex lens).

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Static and Current Electricity. I can explain the difference between static and current electricity and name the parts of a simple circuit. **Static** electricity is charge at rest. **Current** electricity flows in a closed **circuit**. A **cell** gives energy; a **battery** joins **cells**. **Conductors** allow flow; **insulators** block it. Learn the circuit symbols for PLE. Keywords: static: electricity that stays in one place; charge: the amount of electricity an object holds; current: the flow of electricity through a wire; circuit: a complete path for electricity to flow; cell: a single source of electric energy; battery: two or more cells joined together; conductor: a material that lets electricity pass through; insulator: a material that stops electricity from passing
chunks.source: **Static** electricity is charge at rest. **Current** electricity flows in a closed **circuit**. A **cell** gives energy; a **battery** joins **cells**. **Conductors** allow flow; **insulators** block it. Learn the circuit symbols for PLE.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Define **static** electricity. A: **Static** electricity is electric **charge** that stays on an object and does not flow. Reason: PLE defines it as charge at rest.
chunks.source: **Static** electricity is electric **charge** that stays on an object and does not flow. Reason: PLE defines it as charge at rest.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is the difference between a **cell** and a **battery**? A: A **cell** is a single unit (1.5 V). A **battery** is two or more **cells** joined together. Reason: PLE tests symbols and definitions.
chunks.source: A **cell** is a single unit (1.5 V). A **battery** is two or more **cells** joined together. Reason: PLE tests symbols and definitions.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why does a bulb not light when the **switch** is open? A: The **circuit** is broken, so **current** cannot flow. Reason: PLE asks for 'open circuit' or 'incomplete circuit'.
chunks.source: The **circuit** is broken, so **current** cannot flow. Reason: PLE asks for 'open circuit' or 'incomplete circuit'.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name the symbol for a **cell** in a circuit diagram. A: One long line and one short line. Reason: PLE diagram questions use standard symbols.
chunks.source: One long line and one short line. Reason: PLE diagram questions use standard symbols.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give two examples of **conductors** and two of **insulators**. A: **Conductors**: copper, aluminium, iron. **Insulators**: plastic, rubber, dry wood, glass. Reason: PLE lists common materials.
chunks.source: **Conductors**: copper, aluminium, iron. **Insulators**: plastic, rubber, dry wood, glass. Reason: PLE lists common materials.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What happens to electrons when you rub a pen on wool? A: Electrons move from wool to pen. The pen gains a negative **charge**. Reason: PLE explains **static** by electron transfer.
chunks.source: Electrons move from wool to pen. The pen gains a negative **charge**. Reason: PLE explains **static** by electron transfer.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: A torch uses two dry **cells**. What is the total voltage? A: 3.0 volts (1.5 V + 1.5 V). Reason: PLE calculates voltage in series **cells**.
chunks.source: 3.0 volts (1.5 V + 1.5 V). Reason: PLE calculates voltage in series **cells**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why are electric wires covered with plastic? A: Plastic is an **insulator**. It prevents electric shock and short circuits. Reason: PLE links safety to **insulators**.
chunks.source: Plastic is an **insulator**. It prevents electric shock and short circuits. Reason: PLE links safety to **insulators**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Draw a simple **circuit** with a **battery**, **switch**, and bulb. Label all parts. A: Diagram: two pairs of lines (**battery**), gap with lever (**switch**), circle with cross (bulb), straight lines (wires). Labels correct. Reason: PLE awards marks for correct symbols and labels.
chunks.source: Diagram: two pairs of lines (**battery**), gap with lever (**switch**), circle with cross (bulb), straight lines (wires). Labels correct. Reason: PLE awards marks for correct symbols and labels.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: If a **circuit** has a **conductor** and an **insulator** in series, will the bulb light? A: No. The **insulator** breaks the **circuit**. **Current** cannot flow. Reason: PLE tests understanding of complete **circuit**.
chunks.source: No. The **insulator** breaks the **circuit**. **Current** cannot flow. Reason: PLE tests understanding of complete **circuit**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Electric Circuits. I can describe series and parallel circuits, explain the function of a fuse, and use ammeter and voltmeter correctly. **Series** = one path, same **current**, **voltage** divides. **Parallel** = many paths, same **voltage**, **current** divides. **Ammeter** in **series** (low **resistance**). **Voltmeter** in **parallel** (high **resistance**). **Fuse** protects against excess **current**. **Short circuit** = danger. Keywords: series: components connected one after another in a single path; parallel: components connected across the same two points, giving multiple paths; switch: a device that opens or closes a circuit; fuse: a safety device that melts and breaks the circuit if current is too high; ammeter: an instrument that measures electric current in amperes; voltmeter: an instrument that measures potential difference in volts; resistance: the opposition to the flow of current; short circuit: a path of very low resistance that bypasses the load
chunks.source: **Series** = one path, same **current**, **voltage** divides. **Parallel** = many paths, same **voltage**, **current** divides. **Ammeter** in **series** (low **resistance**). **Voltmeter** in **parallel** (high **resistance**). **Fuse** protects against excess **current**. **Short circuit** = danger.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State the difference between a **series** and a **parallel** circuit. A: **Series**: one path, same **current** throughout. **Parallel**: multiple paths, same **voltage** across each branch. Reason: PLE compares current and voltage behaviour.
chunks.source: **Series**: one path, same **current** throughout. **Parallel**: multiple paths, same **voltage** across each branch. Reason: PLE compares current and voltage behaviour.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why is an **ammeter** connected in **series**? A: It has very low **resistance** and must carry the same **current** as the component. Reason: PLE tests instrument connection rules.
chunks.source: It has very low **resistance** and must carry the same **current** as the component. Reason: PLE tests instrument connection rules.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why is a **voltmeter** connected in **parallel**? A: It has very high **resistance** and measures potential difference across a component without drawing significant **current**. Reason: PLE requires 'high resistance' and 'parallel'.
chunks.source: It has very high **resistance** and measures potential difference across a component without drawing significant **current**. Reason: PLE requires 'high resistance' and 'parallel'.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is the function of a **fuse** in a circuit? A: It melts and breaks the **circuit** when **current** exceeds a safe value, protecting wiring and appliances. Reason: PLE asks for 'melts', 'breaks circuit', 'protects'.
chunks.source: It melts and breaks the **circuit** when **current** exceeds a safe value, protecting wiring and appliances. Reason: PLE asks for 'melts', 'breaks circuit', 'protects'.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: A **short circuit** occurs when a wire connects the two terminals of a **battery** directly. Why is this dangerous? A: Very low **resistance** allows a huge **current** to flow, causing overheating, fire, or **battery** damage. Reason: PLE links **short circuit** to low **resistance** and high **current**.
chunks.source: Very low **resistance** allows a huge **current** to flow, causing overheating, fire, or **battery** damage. Reason: PLE links **short circuit** to low **resistance** and high **current**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: In a **series** circuit with two identical bulbs, one bulb is removed. What happens to the other bulb? A: It goes out because the **circuit** is broken. Reason: PLE tests that **series** circuit fails if any part opens.
chunks.source: It goes out because the **circuit** is broken. Reason: PLE tests that **series** circuit fails if any part opens.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: In a **parallel** circuit with two identical bulbs, one bulb is removed. What happens to the other bulb? A: It stays lit with the same brightness. Reason: Each branch is independent; **voltage** across remaining bulb unchanged.
chunks.source: It stays lit with the same brightness. Reason: Each branch is independent; **voltage** across remaining bulb unchanged.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: A pupil connects an **ammeter** in **parallel** across a bulb. State two consequences. A: 1. **Short circuit** through **ammeter** (low **resistance**). 2. **Ammeter** may be damaged by large **current**. Reason: PLE penalises wrong connections.
chunks.source: 1. **Short circuit** through **ammeter** (low **resistance**). 2. **Ammeter** may be damaged by large **current**. Reason: PLE penalises wrong connections.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Calculate the total resistance of two 4 Ω resistors in **series**. A: 8 Ω (R_total = R1 + R2). Reason: PLE uses simple addition for **series** resistance.
chunks.source: 8 Ω (R_total = R1 + R2). Reason: PLE uses simple addition for **series** resistance.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Calculate the total resistance of two 4 Ω resistors in **parallel**. A: 2 Ω (1/R_total = 1/4 + 1/4 = 1/2). Reason: PLE uses reciprocal formula for **parallel** resistance.
chunks.source: 2 Ω (1/R_total = 1/4 + 1/4 = 1/2). Reason: PLE uses reciprocal formula for **parallel** resistance.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Magnetism. I can describe magnetic poles, fields, attraction and repulsion, and explain how to make an electromagnet. **Magnet** has north and south **pole**. Like **poles** repel (**repulsion**), unlike attract (**attraction**). **Magnetic field** lines go N→S. **Compass** aligns with Earth's field. **Electromagnet** = **current** + coil + iron core. **Lodestone** = natural **magnet**. Demagnetise by heat, hammer, or AC. Keywords: magnet: an object that produces a magnetic field and attracts magnetic materials; pole: the end of a magnet where the magnetic force is strongest; attraction: the pull between unlike poles or between a magnet and magnetic material; repulsion: the push between like poles; magnetic field: the region around a magnet where magnetic force acts; compass: a small pivoted magnet that points to Earth's magnetic north; electromagnet: a temporary magnet made by passing current through a coil of wire; lodestone: a naturally occurring magnetic form of iron oxide
chunks.source: **Magnet** has north and south **pole**. Like **poles** repel (**repulsion**), unlike attract (**attraction**). **Magnetic field** lines go N→S. **Compass** aligns with Earth's field. **Electromagnet** = **current** + coil + iron core. **Lodestone** = natural **magnet**. Demagnetise by heat, hammer, or AC.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State the law of magnetic poles. A: Like **poles** repel; unlike **poles** attract. Reason: PLE requires exact wording.
chunks.source: Like **poles** repel; unlike **poles** attract. Reason: PLE requires exact wording.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why is **repulsion** the only sure test for a **magnet**? A: **Attraction** happens with any magnetic material. **Repulsion** only occurs between two **magnets** with like **poles**. Reason: PLE distinguishes attraction from repulsion.
chunks.source: **Attraction** happens with any magnetic material. **Repulsion** only occurs between two **magnets** with like **poles**. Reason: PLE distinguishes attraction from repulsion.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Draw the **magnetic field** pattern of a bar **magnet**. A: Curved lines from north to south **pole**. Arrows from N to S. Lines denser at **poles**. Reason: PLE awards marks for direction, shape, and labels.
chunks.source: Curved lines from north to south **pole**. Arrows from N to S. Lines denser at **poles**. Reason: PLE awards marks for direction, shape, and labels.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is a **compass** and how does it work? A: A **compass** is a freely pivoted **magnet**. Its north-seeking **pole** points to Earth's magnetic south **pole** (geographic north). Reason: PLE links **compass** to Earth's **magnetic field**.
chunks.source: A **compass** is a freely pivoted **magnet**. Its north-seeking **pole** points to Earth's magnetic south **pole** (geographic north). Reason: PLE links **compass** to Earth's **magnetic field**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Describe how to make an **electromagnet**. A: Wind insulated copper wire on a soft iron core. Connect to a **cell**/**battery**. **Current** creates **magnetic field**. Reason: PLE requires core, wire, **current**, insulation.
chunks.source: Wind insulated copper wire on a soft iron core. Connect to a **cell**/**battery**. **Current** creates **magnetic field**. Reason: PLE requires core, wire, **current**, insulation.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State two ways to increase the strength of an **electromagnet**. A: 1. Increase number of turns. 2. Increase **current** (more **cells**). 3. Use soft iron core. (Any two). Reason: PLE lists these factors.
