chunks.source: 1. Increase number of turns. 2. Increase **current** (more **cells**). 3. Use soft iron core. (Any two). Reason: PLE lists these factors.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is **lodestone**? A: A naturally occurring magnetic form of iron oxide (Fe3O4). It was the first **compass**. Reason: PLE asks for natural **magnet** and historical use.
chunks.source: A naturally occurring magnetic form of iron oxide (Fe3O4). It was the first **compass**. Reason: PLE asks for natural **magnet** and historical use.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State two methods to demagnetise a **magnet**. A: Heat strongly; hammer repeatedly; place in AC coil and withdraw slowly. (Any two). Reason: PLE tests domain theory application.
chunks.source: Heat strongly; hammer repeatedly; place in AC coil and withdraw slowly. (Any two). Reason: PLE tests domain theory application.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: A steel needle is stroked with a **magnet** in one direction. Explain why it becomes a **magnet**. A: Stroking aligns the magnetic domains in the steel. They stay aligned, making a permanent **magnet**. Reason: PLE uses domain theory.
chunks.source: Stroking aligns the magnetic domains in the steel. They stay aligned, making a permanent **magnet**. Reason: PLE uses domain theory.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: The north-seeking **pole** of a **compass** points to the geographic north. Explain. A: Earth's magnetic south **pole** is near geographic north. Unlike **poles** attract. Reason: PLE tests Earth's magnetism model.
chunks.source: Earth's magnetic south **pole** is near geographic north. Unlike **poles** attract. Reason: PLE tests Earth's magnetism model.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Electricity at Home and Safety. I can explain how mains electricity reaches our homes, name the parts of a plug, and state safety rules including earthing and lightning protection. **Mains** = 240 V a.c. from grid. **Socket** (wall) → **Plug** (appliance). Wires: Brown=live, Blue=neutral, Green/yellow=**earth wire**. **Fuse** in live wire. **Transformer** steps voltage down. **Lightning** = giant **static** discharge. **Safety**: earthing, correct **fuse**, dry hands, no overload, unplug in storms. Keywords: mains: the public electricity supply from the grid; socket: the fixed outlet on the wall where you insert a plug; plug: the movable connector on an appliance cable; earth wire: a safety wire that carries fault current to ground; lightning: a massive natural electric discharge during thunderstorms; conductor: a material that allows electricity to flow; safety: practices that prevent injury from electricity; transformer: a device that changes the voltage of an alternating current
chunks.source: **Mains** = 240 V a.c. from grid. **Socket** (wall) → **Plug** (appliance). Wires: Brown=live, Blue=neutral, Green/yellow=**earth wire**. **Fuse** in live wire. **Transformer** steps voltage down. **Lightning** = giant **static** discharge. **Safety**: earthing, correct **fuse**, dry hands, no overload, unplug in storms.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State the colour code for the three wires in a Ugandan **plug**. A: Live = brown. Neutral = blue. Earth = green/yellow. Reason: PLE requires exact colours.
chunks.source: Live = brown. Neutral = blue. Earth = green/yellow. Reason: PLE requires exact colours.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why is the **fuse** connected to the live wire? A: So that when it blows, the appliance is disconnected from the high voltage supply. Reason: PLE tests safety logic.
chunks.source: So that when it blows, the appliance is disconnected from the high voltage supply. Reason: PLE tests safety logic.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is the function of the **earth wire**? A: It provides a low resistance path to ground for fault current, causing the **fuse** to blow and preventing shock. Reason: PLE links **earth wire** and **fuse** action.
chunks.source: It provides a low resistance path to ground for fault current, causing the **fuse** to blow and preventing shock. Reason: PLE links **earth wire** and **fuse** action.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name the device that steps down voltage for home **mains** supply. A: A step-down **transformer** at the substation. Reason: PLE asks for **transformer** role in distribution.
chunks.source: A step-down **transformer** at the substation. Reason: PLE asks for **transformer** role in distribution.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State two safety rules for using **sockets**. A: 1. Do not overload. 2. Do not touch with wet hands. 3. Switch off before plugging/unplugging. 4. Use child covers. (Any two). Reason: PLE lists common **safety** rules.
chunks.source: 1. Do not overload. 2. Do not touch with wet hands. 3. Switch off before plugging/unplugging. 4. Use child covers. (Any two). Reason: PLE lists common **safety** rules.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Explain how a lightning **conductor** protects a building. A: It provides a preferred **conductor** path for **lightning** to reach earth safely, bypassing the structure. Reason: PLE requires 'safe path to earth'.
chunks.source: It provides a preferred **conductor** path for **lightning** to reach earth safely, bypassing the structure. Reason: PLE requires 'safe path to earth'.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why is electricity transmitted at high voltage? A: To reduce **current** and thus reduce I²R heat losses in the lines. Reason: PLE uses P=VI and power loss formula.
chunks.source: To reduce **current** and thus reduce I²R heat losses in the lines. Reason: PLE uses P=VI and power loss formula.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: A **plug** has a 13 A **fuse**. The appliance draws 10 A. Is this **fuse** suitable? A: Yes. The **fuse** rating should be slightly above the normal working **current** (e.g., 13 A for 10 A load). Reason: PLE tests **fuse** selection.
chunks.source: Yes. The **fuse** rating should be slightly above the normal working **current** (e.g., 13 A for 10 A load). Reason: PLE tests **fuse** selection.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is the voltage of Uganda **mains** electricity? A: 240 V a.c. (alternating current). Reason: PLE states standard **mains** voltage.
chunks.source: 240 V a.c. (alternating current). Reason: PLE states standard **mains** voltage.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: List three differences between **mains** electricity and a **cell**/**battery**. A: 1. **Mains** is a.c. (alternating); **cell** is d.c. (direct). 2. **Mains** is 240 V; **cell** is 1.5 V. 3. **Mains** comes from grid; **cell** is portable. Reason: PLE compares sources.
chunks.source: 1. **Mains** is a.c. (alternating); **cell** is d.c. (direct). 2. **Mains** is 240 V; **cell** is 1.5 V. 3. **Mains** comes from grid; **cell** is portable. Reason: PLE compares sources.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Levers. I can identify the three classes of levers and calculate mechanical advantage. A lever turns about a fulcrum; first class has fulcrum in middle, second class has load in middle, third class has effort in middle. Mechanical advantage = load ÷ effort. Keywords: lever: a rigid bar that turns around a point; fulcrum: the fixed point on which a lever turns; effort: the force applied to a lever; load: the weight that a lever lifts; first class: fulcrum between effort and load; second class: load between fulcrum and effort; third class: effort between fulcrum and load; mechanical advantage: how many times a lever multiplies force
chunks.source: A lever turns about a fulcrum; first class has fulcrum in middle, second class has load in middle, third class has effort in middle. Mechanical advantage = load ÷ effort.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is a **lever**? A: A rigid bar that turns around a fixed point called the fulcrum.
chunks.source: A rigid bar that turns around a fixed point called the fulcrum.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Define **fulcrum**. A: The fixed point on which a lever pivots.
chunks.source: The fixed point on which a lever pivots.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: If a **first class** **lever** has a **load** of 20 N and an **effort** of 5 N, what is its **mechanical advantage**? A: 4; mechanical advantage = load ÷ effort = 20 ÷ 5 = 4.
chunks.source: 4; mechanical advantage = load ÷ effort = 20 ÷ 5 = 4.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which class of **lever** has the **load** between the **fulcrum** and the **effort**? A: Second class; the load is in the middle.
chunks.source: Second class; the load is in the middle.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give an everyday example of a **third class** **lever**. A: Tongs or a fishing rod; effort is between fulcrum and load.
chunks.source: Tongs or a fishing rod; effort is between fulcrum and load.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: A wheelbarrow is an example of which class of **lever**? A: Second class; the wheel is the fulcrum, load in the bucket, effort at handles.
chunks.source: Second class; the wheel is the fulcrum, load in the bucket, effort at handles.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How does increasing the distance from the **fulcrum** to the **effort** affect **mechanical advantage**? A: It increases mechanical advantage because effort arm becomes longer.
chunks.source: It increases mechanical advantage because effort arm becomes longer.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why is a seesaw a **first class** **lever**? A: The fulcrum is in the centre with effort and load on opposite sides.
chunks.source: The fulcrum is in the centre with effort and load on opposite sides.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State the formula for **mechanical advantage** of a lever. A: Mechanical advantage = load ÷ effort.
chunks.source: Mechanical advantage = load ÷ effort.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Pulleys and Inclined Planes. I can name types of pulleys, inclined planes, screws, wedges and wheel‑and‑axle and explain how they reduce effort. Pulleys (fixed and movable), inclined planes (ramps), screws, wedges and wheel‑and‑axle are simple machines that trade distance for reduced effort. Keywords: pulley: a wheel with a groove for a rope; fixed: attached firmly so it does not move; movable: able to move with the load; inclined plane: a flat surface set at an angle; ramp: an inclined plane used for moving loads; screw: an inclined plane wrapped around a cylinder; wheel and axle: a wheel fixed to a rod that turns together; wedge: two inclined planes joined back to back
chunks.source: Pulleys (fixed and movable), inclined planes (ramps), screws, wedges and wheel‑and‑axle are simple machines that trade distance for reduced effort.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name the two main types of **pulley**. A: Fixed pulley and movable pulley.
chunks.source: Fixed pulley and movable pulley.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What does a **fixed** pulley change? A: It changes the direction of the applied force.
chunks.source: It changes the direction of the applied force.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How does a **movable** pulley affect the **effort** needed to lift a load? A: It halves the effort; mechanical advantage = 2.
chunks.source: It halves the effort; mechanical advantage = 2.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Define **inclined plane**. A: A flat surface set at an angle to the horizontal.
chunks.source: A flat surface set at an angle to the horizontal.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give an example of a **ramp** used in daily life. A: Loading a wheelchair into a van or a truck loading dock.
chunks.source: Loading a wheelchair into a van or a truck loading dock.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Explain how a **screw** works as a simple machine. A: It converts rotational effort into linear motion, multiplying force.
chunks.source: It converts rotational effort into linear motion, multiplying force.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Identify a **wheel and axle** in the home. A: A doorknob, a steering wheel, or a rolling pin.
chunks.source: A doorknob, a steering wheel, or a rolling pin.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is a **wedge** and how does it help? A: Two inclined planes joined; it splits or holds objects with less effort.
chunks.source: Two inclined planes joined; it splits or holds objects with less effort.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: If an inclined plane is 5 m long and 1 m high, what is its mechanical advantage? A: 5; MA = length ÷ height = 5 ÷ 1 = 5.
chunks.source: 5; MA = length ÷ height = 5 ÷ 1 = 5.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why does a longer ramp require less effort than a shorter one for the same height? A: Because the effort distance increases, reducing the force needed.
chunks.source: Because the effort distance increases, reducing the force needed.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Friction: Uses and Disadvantages. I can explain the advantages and disadvantages of friction and describe ways to reduce unwanted friction. Friction is useful for grip but causes wear and heat; we reduce unwanted friction with lubrication, ball bearings, polishing and streamlining. Keywords: friction: a force that opposes motion between surfaces; grip: the ability to hold or prevent slipping; lubrication: applying a substance to reduce friction; wear: damage caused by rubbing surfaces; heat: thermal energy produced by friction; streamlining: shaping an object to reduce air resistance; ball bearing: small balls that reduce friction between moving parts; polish: making a surface smooth to lower friction
chunks.source: Friction is useful for grip but causes wear and heat; we reduce unwanted friction with lubrication, ball bearings, polishing and streamlining.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Define **friction**. A: A force that opposes relative motion between two surfaces in contact.
chunks.source: A force that opposes relative motion between two surfaces in contact.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State one advantage of **friction** in daily life. A: It provides **grip** for walking, driving and holding objects.
chunks.source: It provides **grip** for walking, driving and holding objects.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name two disadvantages of **friction**. A: **Wear** of parts and production of **heat**.
chunks.source: **Wear** of parts and production of **heat**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is **lubrication** and how does it help? A: Applying oil or grease to reduce **friction**, **heat** and **wear**.
chunks.source: Applying oil or grease to reduce **friction**, **heat** and **wear**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Explain how a **ball bearing** reduces **friction**. A: Small balls roll between surfaces, replacing sliding friction with rolling friction.
chunks.source: Small balls roll between surfaces, replacing sliding friction with rolling friction.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give an example of **streamlining** in transport. A: A streamlined lorry or a fish shape reduces air resistance.
chunks.source: A streamlined lorry or a fish shape reduces air resistance.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why does polishing a floor reduce **friction**? A: **Polish** makes the surface smoother, lowering the contact resistance.
chunks.source: **Polish** makes the surface smoother, lowering the contact resistance.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: If a machine part shows excessive **wear**, what should be done? A: Apply **lubrication** or replace with a **ball bearing**.
chunks.source: Apply **lubrication** or replace with a **ball bearing**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Describe how **heat** is produced by **friction**. A: Work done against friction converts mechanical energy into thermal energy.
chunks.source: Work done against friction converts mechanical energy into thermal energy.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: List three methods to reduce unwanted **friction**. A: **Lubrication**, **ball bearing**, **polish**, and **streamlining**.
chunks.source: **Lubrication**, **ball bearing**, **polish**, and **streamlining**.

chunks.id: L-P7-Science-Machines at Home and in Agriculture
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: Machines at Home and in Agriculture
chunks.text: Machines at Home and in Agriculture. I can identify common simple machines used at home and on the farm and explain how they improve effort and efficiency. Common machines at home and on the farm – wheelbarrow, spanner, crowbar, jack, bicycle, sewing machine – are built from levers, screws, wheels and axles; they reduce effort and improve efficiency when friction is low. Keywords: wheelbarrow: a small cart with one wheel used for carrying loads; spanner: a tool for turning nuts and bolts; crowbar: a heavy iron bar used as a lever; jack: a device for lifting heavy loads; bicycle: a two‑wheeled vehicle powered by pedals; sewing machine: a machine that stitches fabric; effort: the force applied to a machine; efficiency: the ratio of useful work output to work input
chunks.source: Common machines at home and on the farm – wheelbarrow, spanner, crowbar, jack, bicycle, sewing machine – are built from levers, screws, wheels and axles; they reduce effort and improve efficiency when friction is low.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Science-Machines at Home and in Agriculture
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: Machines at Home and in Agriculture
chunks.text: Q: Identify the class of lever for a **wheelbarrow**. A: Second class lever; load between fulcrum and effort.
chunks.source: Second class lever; load between fulcrum and effort.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Science-Machines at Home and in Agriculture
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: Machines at Home and in Agriculture
chunks.text: Q: What simple machine is a **spanner**? A: A lever.
chunks.source: A lever.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Science-Machines at Home and in Agriculture
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: Machines at Home and in Agriculture
chunks.text: Q: A **crowbar** is an example of which class of lever? A: First class lever; fulcrum between effort and load.
chunks.source: First class lever; fulcrum between effort and load.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Science-Machines at Home and in Agriculture
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: Machines at Home and in Agriculture
chunks.text: Q: Explain how a **jack** lifts a car. A: It uses a screw thread to turn a small effort into a large lifting force.
chunks.source: It uses a screw thread to turn a small effort into a large lifting force.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Science-Machines at Home and in Agriculture
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: Machines at Home and in Agriculture
chunks.text: Q: Name two simple machines found in a **bicycle**. A: Wheel and axle, levers (pedals), and gears.
chunks.source: Wheel and axle, levers (pedals), and gears.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Science-Machines at Home and in Agriculture
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: Machines at Home and in Agriculture
chunks.text: Q: Which component of a **sewing machine** is a **wheel and axle**? A: The handwheel.
chunks.source: The handwheel.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Science-Machines at Home and in Agriculture
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: Machines at Home and in Agriculture
chunks.text: Q: Define **effort** in the context of machines. A: The force applied to a machine to do work.
chunks.source: The force applied to a machine to do work.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Science-Machines at Home and in Agriculture
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: Machines at Home and in Agriculture
chunks.text: Q: What does **efficiency** measure? A: The ratio of useful work output to work input, expressed as a percentage.
chunks.source: The ratio of useful work output to work input, expressed as a percentage.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Science-Machines at Home and in Agriculture
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: Machines at Home and in Agriculture
chunks.text: Q: If a machine has an efficiency of 80%, what does that mean? A: 80% of the input work becomes useful output; 20% is lost mainly as heat.
chunks.source: 80% of the input work becomes useful output; 20% is lost mainly as heat.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Science-Machines at Home and in Agriculture
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: Machines at Home and in Agriculture
chunks.text: Q: Give one way to increase the efficiency of a **wheelbarrow**. A: Lubricate the wheel axle to reduce friction.
chunks.source: Lubricate the wheel axle to reduce friction.

chunks.id: L-P7-Science-Living Things Depend on Each Other
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: Living Things Depend on Each Other
chunks.text: Living Things Depend on Each Other. I can explain how energy moves through food chains and food webs and name the roles of producers, consumers, predators, prey and decomposers. Living things depend on each other through food chains and webs; producers, consumers, predators, prey and decomposers all play roles in a habitat. Keywords: food chain: a series of organisms each eating the next; food web: many food chains linked together; producer: an organism that makes its own food; consumer: an organism that eats other organisms; predator: an animal that hunts and eats other animals; prey: an animal that is hunted and eaten; decomposer: an organism that breaks down dead material; habitat: the natural home of an organism
chunks.source: Living things depend on each other through food chains and webs; producers, consumers, predators, prey and decomposers all play roles in a habitat.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Science-Living Things Depend on Each Other
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: Living Things Depend on Each Other
chunks.text: Q: What is a **producer**? Give one example from a Ugandan garden. A: A **producer** makes its own food, e.g. a maize plant. Reason: producers use sunlight to produce energy.
chunks.source: A **producer** makes its own food, e.g. a maize plant. Reason: producers use sunlight to produce energy.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Science-Living Things Depend on Each Other
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: Living Things Depend on Each Other
chunks.text: Q: Define **consumer** and name a primary consumer in a grassland. A: A **consumer** eats other organisms; a grasshopper is a primary consumer. Reason: primary consumers eat producers.
chunks.source: A **consumer** eats other organisms; a grasshopper is a primary consumer. Reason: primary consumers eat producers.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Science-Living Things Depend on Each Other
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: Living Things Depend on Each Other
chunks.text: Q: Distinguish between **predator** and **prey** using a frog and a grasshopper. A: The frog is the **predator** that hunts; the grasshopper is the **prey** that is hunted. Reason: predator eats prey.
chunks.source: The frog is the **predator** that hunts; the grasshopper is the **prey** that is hunted. Reason: predator eats prey.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Science-Living Things Depend on Each Other
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: Living Things Depend on Each Other
chunks.text: Q: What role do **decomposers** play in a **food web**? A: **Decomposers** break down dead matter and recycle nutrients. Reason: they return nutrients to the soil for producers.
chunks.source: **Decomposers** break down dead matter and recycle nutrients. Reason: they return nutrients to the soil for producers.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Science-Living Things Depend on Each Other
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: Living Things Depend on Each Other
chunks.text: Q: Draw a simple **food chain** with four levels and label each level. A: Example: maize (producer) → grasshopper (consumer) → frog (predator) → snake (top predator). Reason: shows energy flow.
chunks.source: Example: maize (producer) → grasshopper (consumer) → frog (predator) → snake (top predator). Reason: shows energy flow.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Science-Living Things Depend on Each Other
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: Living Things Depend on Each Other
chunks.text: Q: Explain how a **food web** differs from a **food chain**. A: A **food web** is many interconnected **food chains**; a **food chain** is a single line. Reason: webs show multiple feeding relationships.
chunks.source: A **food web** is many interconnected **food chains**; a **food chain** is a single line. Reason: webs show multiple feeding relationships.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Science-Living Things Depend on Each Other
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: Living Things Depend on Each Other
chunks.text: Q: If a **habitat** is destroyed, what happens to the **food web**? A: The **food web** collapses because organisms lose food and shelter. Reason: habitat loss removes the base of the web.
chunks.source: The **food web** collapses because organisms lose food and shelter. Reason: habitat loss removes the base of the web.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Science-Living Things Depend on Each Other
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: Living Things Depend on Each Other
chunks.text: Q: Name two **decomposers** found in Ugandan soils. A: Earthworms and fungi (mushrooms). Reason: both break down organic matter.
chunks.source: Earthworms and fungi (mushrooms). Reason: both break down organic matter.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Science-Living Things Depend on Each Other
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: Living Things Depend on Each Other
chunks.text: Q: Why is the **producer** the most important level in a **food chain**? A: Producers capture solar energy and start the energy flow. Reason: without producers, no energy enters the chain.
chunks.source: Producers capture solar energy and start the energy flow. Reason: without producers, no energy enters the chain.

chunks.id: L-P7-Science-Plants and Animals Depend on the Environment
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: Plants and Animals Depend on the Environment
chunks.text: Plants and Animals Depend on the Environment. I can describe how plants and animals exchange gases, help each other reproduce and live together in symbiotic or parasitic relationships. Plants and animals depend on each other for gases, pollination, seed dispersal and shelter; some relationships are mutual (symbiosis) while others are harmful (parasite on host). Keywords: oxygen: gas released by plants during photosynthesis; carbon dioxide: gas taken in by plants and released by animals; shelter: a place that protects an organism; pollination: transfer of pollen from male to female flower parts; seed dispersal: movement of seeds away from the parent plant; symbiosis: close relationship where both organisms benefit; parasite: organism that lives on or in a host and harms it; host: organism that a parasite lives on or in
chunks.source: Plants and animals depend on each other for gases, pollination, seed dispersal and shelter; some relationships are mutual (symbiosis) while others are harmful (parasite on host).

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Science-Plants and Animals Depend on the Environment
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: Plants and Animals Depend on the Environment
chunks.text: Q: State the gas that plants release during photosynthesis. A: Plants release **oxygen**. Reason: photosynthesis produces oxygen as a by‑product.
chunks.source: Plants release **oxygen**. Reason: photosynthesis produces oxygen as a by‑product.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Science-Plants and Animals Depend on the Environment
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: Plants and Animals Depend on the Environment
chunks.text: Q: State the gas that animals release during respiration. A: Animals release **carbon dioxide**. Reason: respiration uses oxygen and produces carbon dioxide.
chunks.source: Animals release **carbon dioxide**. Reason: respiration uses oxygen and produces carbon dioxide.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Science-Plants and Animals Depend on the Environment
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: Plants and Animals Depend on the Environment
chunks.text: Q: Define **pollination** and name one pollinator in Uganda. A: **Pollination** is transfer of pollen; bees are common pollinators. Reason: bees move pollen between flowers.
chunks.source: **Pollination** is transfer of pollen; bees are common pollinators. Reason: bees move pollen between flowers.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Science-Plants and Animals Depend on the Environment
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: Plants and Animals Depend on the Environment
chunks.text: Q: Define **seed dispersal** and give two methods. A: **Seed dispersal** moves seeds away; methods include wind and animals eating fruit. Reason: dispersal reduces competition.
chunks.source: **Seed dispersal** moves seeds away; methods include wind and animals eating fruit. Reason: dispersal reduces competition.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Science-Plants and Animals Depend on the Environment
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: Plants and Animals Depend on the Environment
chunks.text: Q: Explain **symbiosis** with an example from a Ugandan forest. A: **Symbiosis** benefits both; e.g. ants protect acacia trees and get shelter. Reason: both gain advantage.
chunks.source: **Symbiosis** benefits both; e.g. ants protect acacia trees and get shelter. Reason: both gain advantage.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Science-Plants and Animals Depend on the Environment
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: Plants and Animals Depend on the Environment
chunks.text: Q: Distinguish between a **parasite** and its **host**. A: A **parasite** benefits and harms the **host**; the host is harmed. Reason: parasite takes nutrients from host.
chunks.source: A **parasite** benefits and harms the **host**; the host is harmed. Reason: parasite takes nutrients from host.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Science-Plants and Animals Depend on the Environment
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: Plants and Animals Depend on the Environment
chunks.text: Q: Why is **shelter** important for animals? A: **Shelter** protects animals from weather and predators. Reason: it increases survival.
chunks.source: **Shelter** protects animals from weather and predators. Reason: it increases survival.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Science-Plants and Animals Depend on the Environment
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: Plants and Animals Depend on the Environment
chunks.text: Q: If a **parasite** kills its **host**, what happens to the parasite? A: The parasite may die or need a new host. Reason: parasites depend on living hosts.
chunks.source: The parasite may die or need a new host. Reason: parasites depend on living hosts.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Science-Plants and Animals Depend on the Environment
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: Plants and Animals Depend on the Environment
chunks.text: Q: Describe how **oxygen** and **carbon dioxide** cycle between plants and animals. A: Plants take in carbon dioxide and release oxygen; animals do the opposite. Reason: gas exchange sustains both.
chunks.source: Plants take in carbon dioxide and release oxygen; animals do the opposite. Reason: gas exchange sustains both.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Science-Plants and Animals Depend on the Environment
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: Plants and Animals Depend on the Environment
chunks.text: Q: Give one way humans can protect **pollination** in their farms. A: Plant flowering hedgerows to attract bees. Reason: more pollinators improve crop yields.
chunks.source: Plant flowering hedgerows to attract bees. Reason: more pollinators improve crop yields.

chunks.id: L-P7-Science-How Humans Depend on the Environment
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: How Humans Depend on the Environment
chunks.text: How Humans Depend on the Environment. I can list the resources humans obtain from the environment and explain why sustainable use is necessary. Humans rely on the environment for food, timber, medicine, water, raw materials, tourism, farming and fishing; wise use ensures these resources last for future generations. Keywords: food: plants and animals eaten for nutrition; timber: wood used for building and fuel; medicine: substances from plants used to treat illness; water: essential liquid for drinking, cooking and irrigation; raw materials: natural substances used to make products; tourism: travel for pleasure that brings income; farming: growing crops and raising livestock; fishing: catching fish from water bodies
chunks.source: Humans rely on the environment for food, timber, medicine, water, raw materials, tourism, farming and fishing; wise use ensures these resources last for future generations.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Science-How Humans Depend on the Environment
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: How Humans Depend on the Environment
chunks.text: Q: Name two sources of **food** that come directly from the environment. A: **Farming** crops and **fishing** provide food. Reason: both harvest natural resources.
chunks.source: **Farming** crops and **fishing** provide food. Reason: both harvest natural resources.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Science-How Humans Depend on the Environment
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: How Humans Depend on the Environment
chunks.text: Q: Give one use of **timber** in a Ugandan home. A: **Timber** is used for roofing and furniture. Reason: wood is strong and available.
chunks.source: **Timber** is used for roofing and furniture. Reason: wood is strong and available.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Science-How Humans Depend on the Environment
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: How Humans Depend on the Environment
chunks.text: Q: State one **medicine** obtained from a local plant. A: Moringa leaves are used as **medicine** for nutrition. Reason: traditional knowledge uses plant parts.
chunks.source: Moringa leaves are used as **medicine** for nutrition. Reason: traditional knowledge uses plant parts.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Science-How Humans Depend on the Environment
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: How Humans Depend on the Environment
chunks.text: Q: Why is **water** considered a vital resource? A: **Water** is needed for drinking, cooking, and irrigation. Reason: life cannot exist without water.
chunks.source: **Water** is needed for drinking, cooking, and irrigation. Reason: life cannot exist without water.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Science-How Humans Depend on the Environment
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: How Humans Depend on the Environment
chunks.text: Q: List two **raw materials** from the environment used in building. A: Clay for bricks and sand for cement. Reason: both are mined from the earth.
chunks.source: Clay for bricks and sand for cement. Reason: both are mined from the earth.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Science-How Humans Depend on the Environment
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: How Humans Depend on the Environment
chunks.text: Q: How does **tourism** benefit a local community? A: **Tourism** creates jobs and brings money. Reason: visitors pay for guides, lodging, crafts.
chunks.source: **Tourism** creates jobs and brings money. Reason: visitors pay for guides, lodging, crafts.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Science-How Humans Depend on the Environment
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: How Humans Depend on the Environment
chunks.text: Q: Explain one way **farming** can cause soil erosion. A: Clearing vegetation leaves soil exposed to rain. Reason: rain washes or blows away topsoil.
chunks.source: Clearing vegetation leaves soil exposed to rain. Reason: rain washes or blows away topsoil.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Science-How Humans Depend on the Environment
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: How Humans Depend on the Environment
chunks.text: Q: Describe a sustainable **fishing** practice. A: Using nets with larger mesh lets young fish escape. Reason: protects future fish stocks.
chunks.source: Using nets with larger mesh lets young fish escape. Reason: protects future fish stocks.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Science-How Humans Depend on the Environment
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: How Humans Depend on the Environment
chunks.text: Q: What happens if **raw materials** are over‑extracted? A: Resources become scarce and ecosystems degrade. Reason: overuse exceeds natural regeneration.
chunks.source: Resources become scarce and ecosystems degrade. Reason: overuse exceeds natural regeneration.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Science-How Humans Depend on the Environment
chunks.subject: Science
chunks.unit: How Humans Depend on the Environment
chunks.text: Q: Suggest one action to protect **water** sources in your village. A: Plant trees along riverbanks to filter runoff. Reason: vegetation reduces pollution and erosion.
chunks.source: Plant trees along riverbanks to filter runoff. Reason: vegetation reduces pollution and erosion.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Protecting the Balance of Nature. I can identify threats to biodiversity and explain conservation actions supported by law. Conservation, stopping poaching, preventing deforestation, saving wetlands and obeying the law protect biodiversity and prevent species from becoming extinct. Keywords: conservation: protecting natural resources and wildlife; poaching: illegal hunting of wild animals; deforestation: clearing forests without replanting; wetland: land area saturated with water; biodiversity: variety of life in an area; extinct: no living members of a species remain; law: rules made by government; reserve: protected area for wildlife
chunks.source: Conservation, stopping poaching, preventing deforestation, saving wetlands and obeying the law protect biodiversity and prevent species from becoming extinct.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Define **conservation** in your own words. A: **Conservation** is the careful protection of nature and wildlife. Reason: it aims to keep ecosystems healthy.
chunks.source: **Conservation** is the careful protection of nature and wildlife. Reason: it aims to keep ecosystems healthy.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is **poaching** and why is it illegal? A: **Poaching** is illegal hunting; it threatens species survival. Reason: laws protect endangered animals.
chunks.source: **Poaching** is illegal hunting; it threatens species survival. Reason: laws protect endangered animals.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Explain the effect of **deforestation** on **biodiversity**. A: **Deforestation** destroys habitats, reducing **biodiversity**. Reason: loss of trees removes homes for many species.
chunks.source: **Deforestation** destroys habitats, reducing **biodiversity**. Reason: loss of trees removes homes for many species.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why are **wetlands** important for the environment? A: **Wetlands** filter water, control floods, and support diverse life. Reason: they provide ecosystem services.
chunks.source: **Wetlands** filter water, control floods, and support diverse life. Reason: they provide ecosystem services.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What does **biodiversity** mean and why does it matter? A: **Biodiversity** is the variety of life; it makes ecosystems resilient. Reason: more species mean better stability.
chunks.source: **Biodiversity** is the variety of life; it makes ecosystems resilient. Reason: more species mean better stability.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give an example of a species that is **extinct**. A: The dodo bird is **extinct**. Reason: no living individuals remain.
chunks.source: The dodo bird is **extinct**. Reason: no living individuals remain.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How does the **law** help protect wildlife in Uganda? A: The **law** sets penalties for **poaching** and establishes **reserves**. Reason: legal protection deters illegal acts.
chunks.source: The **law** sets penalties for **poaching** and establishes **reserves**. Reason: legal protection deters illegal acts.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Describe the purpose of a **reserve**. A: A **reserve** is a protected area where wildlife can live safely. Reason: it conserves habitats and species.
chunks.source: A **reserve** is a protected area where wildlife can live safely. Reason: it conserves habitats and species.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: List two human activities that threaten **biodiversity**. A: **Deforestation** and **poaching** are major threats. Reason: both destroy habitats and kill organisms.
chunks.source: **Deforestation** and **poaching** are major threats. Reason: both destroy habitats and kill organisms.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Propose one community action to support **conservation**. A: Organise tree‑planting days to restore degraded land. Reason: replanting rebuilds habitats and fights **deforestation**.
chunks.source: Organise tree‑planting days to restore degraded land. Reason: replanting rebuilds habitats and fights **deforestation**.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Types of Resources. I can classify resources as renewable or non-renewable and give Ugandan examples. Renewable resources like sunshine, water, forests, wildlife, and soil regenerate naturally. Non-renewable resources like minerals (copper, limestone, phosphates) and petroleum take millions of years to form and deplete when used. Sustainable use keeps renewable resources available. Keywords: renewable: can be replaced naturally; non-renewable: cannot be replaced once used; mineral: natural substance from the earth; forest: large area covered with trees; water: liquid needed by all living things; soil: top layer of earth where plants grow; wildlife: animals and plants in their natural home; sunshine: light and heat from the sun
chunks.source: Renewable resources like sunshine, water, forests, wildlife, and soil regenerate naturally. Non-renewable resources like minerals (copper, limestone, phosphates) and petroleum take millions of years to form and deplete when used. Sustainable use keeps renewable resources available.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Group these into renewable and non-renewable: sunshine, copper, water, limestone. A: Renewable: sunshine, water. Non-renewable: copper, limestone. Reason: sunshine and water cycle naturally; copper and limestone are mineral deposits that deplete.
chunks.source: Renewable: sunshine, water. Non-renewable: copper, limestone. Reason: sunshine and water cycle naturally; copper and limestone are mineral deposits that deplete.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why is wildlife classified as a renewable resource? A: Wildlife breeds and populations recover if habitats are protected. Reason: renewable resources regenerate through natural processes within a human lifetime.
chunks.source: Wildlife breeds and populations recover if habitats are protected. Reason: renewable resources regenerate through natural processes within a human lifetime.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: A quarry mines limestone for cement. Is limestone renewable? Explain. A: No. Limestone is a mineral formed over millions of years. Once extracted, it cannot be replaced in human time. Reason: non-renewable resources have geological formation timescales.
chunks.source: No. Limestone is a mineral formed over millions of years. Once extracted, it cannot be replaced in human time. Reason: non-renewable resources have geological formation timescales.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give two examples of renewable resources from Uganda's environment. A: Forests (e.g. Mabira), water (e.g. Lake Victoria), sunshine, wildlife, soil. Reason: these regenerate through natural cycles like rain, plant growth, solar radiation.
chunks.source: Forests (e.g. Mabira), water (e.g. Lake Victoria), sunshine, wildlife, soil. Reason: these regenerate through natural cycles like rain, plant growth, solar radiation.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give two examples of non-renewable resources found in Uganda. A: Copper (Kilembe), limestone (Tororo), phosphates (Tororo), petroleum (Albertine Graben). Reason: these are mineral deposits formed over geological time.
chunks.source: Copper (Kilembe), limestone (Tororo), phosphates (Tororo), petroleum (Albertine Graben). Reason: these are mineral deposits formed over geological time.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: A farmer says soil is non-renewable because his field is exhausted. Is he correct? A: No. Soil is renewable but degrades if mismanaged. With conservation (mulching, crop rotation), soil fertility renews. Reason: renewability depends on rate of use vs. rate of regeneration.
chunks.source: No. Soil is renewable but degrades if mismanaged. With conservation (mulching, crop rotation), soil fertility renews. Reason: renewability depends on rate of use vs. rate of regeneration.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: PLE 2021 style: Which of these is a non-renewable resource? A) Sunshine B) Forest C) Petroleum D) Water A: C) Petroleum. Reason: petroleum is a fossil fuel formed over millions of years; the others regenerate naturally in short periods.
chunks.source: C) Petroleum. Reason: petroleum is a fossil fuel formed over millions of years; the others regenerate naturally in short periods.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Explain why hydro power is considered renewable while petroleum is not. A: Hydro power uses flowing water, which is renewed by the rain cycle. Petroleum is a finite mineral deposit. Reason: renewable resources rely on continuous natural flows; non-renewable on finite stocks.
chunks.source: Hydro power uses flowing water, which is renewed by the rain cycle. Petroleum is a finite mineral deposit. Reason: renewable resources rely on continuous natural flows; non-renewable on finite stocks.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Minerals and Energy Resources. I can identify Uganda's main minerals and energy sources and explain how they are extracted and used. Uganda's key minerals: copper (Kilembe) for wires, limestone (Tororo) for cement, phosphates (Tororo) for fertilizer, petroleum (Albertine Graben) for fuel. Energy: hydro power (Nile dams) gives most electricity; geothermal (Rift Valley) is future potential. Extraction removes minerals; refinery processes crude oil into usable fuels. Keywords: copper: reddish metal used for wires and pipes; limestone: white rock used for cement; phosphates: mineral used for fertilizers; petroleum: oil pumped from underground; hydro power: electricity from moving water; geothermal: heat energy from inside the earth; extraction: removing minerals from the ground; refinery: factory that processes raw oil
chunks.source: Uganda's key minerals: copper (Kilembe) for wires, limestone (Tororo) for cement, phosphates (Tororo) for fertilizer, petroleum (Albertine Graben) for fuel. Energy: hydro power (Nile dams) gives most electricity; geothermal (Rift Valley) is future potential. Extraction removes minerals; refinery processes crude oil into usable fuels.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name the mineral mined at Kilembe and state its main use. A: Copper — used for electrical wiring and pipes. Reason: specific location (Kilembe) and use (conductivity) are required for full marks.
chunks.source: Copper — used for electrical wiring and pipes. Reason: specific location (Kilembe) and use (conductivity) are required for full marks.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Where is limestone mined in Uganda and what is it used for? A: Limestone is mined at Tororo and Moroto. It is used to manufacture cement. Reason: PLE expects district names and industrial use.
chunks.source: Limestone is mined at Tororo and Moroto. It is used to manufacture cement. Reason: PLE expects district names and industrial use.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What are phosphates used for in agriculture? A: Phosphates are processed into fertilizers that supply phosphorus to crops, improving soil fertility and yields. Reason: link mineral to agricultural use.
chunks.source: Phosphates are processed into fertilizers that supply phosphorus to crops, improving soil fertility and yields. Reason: link mineral to agricultural use.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: In which region of Uganda has petroleum been discovered? A: Petroleum has been discovered in the Albertine Graben (Albertine Rift) near Lake Albert, in districts like Hoima, Buliisa, Nwoya. Reason: specific geological location.
chunks.source: Petroleum has been discovered in the Albertine Graben (Albertine Rift) near Lake Albert, in districts like Hoima, Buliisa, Nwoya. Reason: specific geological location.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is the function of a refinery in the petroleum industry? A: A refinery processes crude petroleum through fractional distillation into usable products like petrol, diesel, kerosene, and gas. Reason: distinguishes refinery (processing) from extraction (drilling).
chunks.source: A refinery processes crude petroleum through fractional distillation into usable products like petrol, diesel, kerosene, and gas. Reason: distinguishes refinery (processing) from extraction (drilling).

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why is hydro power considered a renewable energy source? A: Hydro power uses flowing water which is continuously renewed by the rain/water cycle. It does not deplete the water resource. Reason: renewability definition applied to energy.
chunks.source: Hydro power uses flowing water which is continuously renewed by the rain/water cycle. It does not deplete the water resource. Reason: renewability definition applied to energy.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give two advantages of hydro power over petroleum for electricity generation. A: 1) Hydro power is renewable; petroleum is non-renewable. 2) Hydro power produces no direct air pollution; petroleum burns releasing CO2. Reason: compare renewability and environmental impact.
chunks.source: 1) Hydro power is renewable; petroleum is non-renewable. 2) Hydro power produces no direct air pollution; petroleum burns releasing CO2. Reason: compare renewability and environmental impact.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name one place in Uganda where geothermal energy is being explored. A: Geothermal energy is being explored at Katwe (Kasese) and Buranga (Bundibugyo) in the Rift Valley. Reason: specific Ugandan sites show curriculum knowledge.
chunks.source: Geothermal energy is being explored at Katwe (Kasese) and Buranga (Bundibugyo) in the Rift Valley. Reason: specific Ugandan sites show curriculum knowledge.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: PLE style: Which of the following is NOT a mineral resource? A) Copper B) Limestone C) Hydro power D) Phosphates A: C) Hydro power. Reason: hydro power is an energy resource from moving water; the others are solid minerals extracted from the ground.
chunks.source: C) Hydro power. Reason: hydro power is an energy resource from moving water; the others are solid minerals extracted from the ground.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Explain the difference between extraction and refinery in petroleum production. A: Extraction is drilling and pumping crude oil from underground. Refinery is the industrial plant that separates crude oil into finished fuels. Reason: two distinct stages — upstream vs. downstream.
chunks.source: Extraction is drilling and pumping crude oil from underground. Refinery is the industrial plant that separates crude oil into finished fuels. Reason: two distinct stages — upstream vs. downstream.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Sustainable Use of Resources. I can explain conservation, recycling, afforestation, agroforestry, and by-laws as ways to use resources sustainably. Sustainable use balances today's needs with tomorrow's supply. Conservation protects resources; recycling turns waste into resources; afforestation plants new forests; agroforestry mixes trees with crops; by-laws let communities enforce protection. Depletion happens when use exceeds renewal — sustainable practices prevent it. Keywords: conservation: protecting resources from waste or loss; recycling: turning waste into new useful things; afforestation: planting trees where none grew before; agroforestry: growing trees and crops together; sustainable: meeting today's needs without harming tomorrow; depletion: using up a resource completely; waste: materials thrown away as useless; by-laws: local rules made by communities
chunks.source: Sustainable use balances today's needs with tomorrow's supply. Conservation protects resources; recycling turns waste into resources; afforestation plants new forests; agroforestry mixes trees with crops; by-laws let communities enforce protection. Depletion happens when use exceeds renewal — sustainable practices prevent it.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Define conservation and give one example from your community. A: Conservation is protecting resources from waste or loss. Example: fixing leaking taps to conserve water; planting trees to conserve soil. Reason: definition + local example shows understanding.
chunks.source: Conservation is protecting resources from waste or loss. Example: fixing leaking taps to conserve water; planting trees to conserve soil. Reason: definition + local example shows understanding.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Explain how recycling reduces depletion of non-renewable resources. A: Recycling uses waste materials (e.g. metals, paper) to make new products, reducing the need to extract new mineral ores or cut forest trees. Reason: links recycling directly to reduced extraction of non-renewables.
chunks.source: Recycling uses waste materials (e.g. metals, paper) to make new products, reducing the need to extract new mineral ores or cut forest trees. Reason: links recycling directly to reduced extraction of non-renewables.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Distinguish between afforestation and agroforestry with examples. A: Afforestation: planting trees on bare land to create a forest (e.g. bare hill). Agroforestry: growing trees and crops together on farmland (e.g. coffee under musizi trees). Reason: clear distinction + Ugandan examples.
chunks.source: Afforestation: planting trees on bare land to create a forest (e.g. bare hill). Agroforestry: growing trees and crops together on farmland (e.g. coffee under musizi trees). Reason: clear distinction + Ugandan examples.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State two ways agroforestry improves soil fertility. A: 1) Nitrogen-fixing trees add nitrogen to soil. 2) Leaf fall and pruning provide mulch and organic matter. Reason: specific mechanisms, not just 'improves soil'.
chunks.source: 1) Nitrogen-fixing trees add nitrogen to soil. 2) Leaf fall and pruning provide mulch and organic matter. Reason: specific mechanisms, not just 'improves soil'.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What does 'sustainable use' mean? Give an example from fishing. A: Sustainable use meets present needs without compromising future availability. Example: using nets with large mesh so young fish escape to breed. Reason: definition + practical application.
chunks.source: Sustainable use meets present needs without compromising future availability. Example: using nets with large mesh so young fish escape to breed. Reason: definition + practical application.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How do by-laws help in resource conservation? Give an example. A: By-laws are local rules that communities enforce themselves. Example: a by-law banning cultivation in wetlands protects water filtration and prevents flooding. Reason: shows community governance role.
chunks.source: By-laws are local rules that communities enforce themselves. Example: a by-law banning cultivation in wetlands protects water filtration and prevents flooding. Reason: shows community governance role.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: A farmer practises contour ploughing and mulching. Which resource is he conserving? A: He is conserving soil. Contour ploughing reduces water runoff speed; mulch protects soil from rain splash. Both prevent erosion. Reason: identifies the specific resource and mechanisms.
chunks.source: He is conserving soil. Contour ploughing reduces water runoff speed; mulch protects soil from rain splash. Both prevent erosion. Reason: identifies the specific resource and mechanisms.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: PLE style: Which of these is NOT a sustainable practice? A) Agroforestry B) Recycling plastic C) Burning all crop residues D) Afforestation A: C) Burning all crop residues. Reason: burning destroys organic matter, pollutes air, and wastes nutrients that could rebuild soil. The others conserve or regenerate resources.
chunks.source: C) Burning all crop residues. Reason: burning destroys organic matter, pollutes air, and wastes nutrients that could rebuild soil. The others conserve or regenerate resources.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Explain why depletion of forests leads to drought. A: Forests release water vapour through transpiration, contributing to rainfall. Deforestation reduces transpiration, disrupts local rain cycles, and exposes soil to sun, reducing moisture recycling. Reason: explains the forest-rainfall link.
chunks.source: Forests release water vapour through transpiration, contributing to rainfall. Deforestation reduces transpiration, disrupts local rain cycles, and exposes soil to sun, reducing moisture recycling. Reason: explains the forest-rainfall link.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name two by-laws a village could make to protect water sources. A: 1) No farming within 30m of streams/springs. 2) No washing clothes or vehicles directly in water sources. 3) All pit latrines must be 30m downhill from water points. Reason: specific, enforceable local rules.
chunks.source: 1) No farming within 30m of streams/springs. 2) No washing clothes or vehicles directly in water sources. 3) All pit latrines must be 30m downhill from water points. Reason: specific, enforceable local rules.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Resource Degradation. I can identify causes and effects of resource degradation in Uganda and suggest solutions. Resource degradation chains: deforestation → erosion → flooding/drought; overgrazing → compaction → erosion; mining → pollution; swamp drainage → flooding + drought. Conservation (afforestation, agroforestry, wetland protection, by-laws) breaks these chains. Sustainable use prevents degradation before it starts. Keywords: deforestation: clearing forests without replanting; overgrazing: keeping too many animals on too little land; mining: digging minerals from the earth; pollution: harmful substances in air, water, or soil; erosion: wearing away of topsoil by water or wind; swamp drainage: draining wetlands for farming or building; flooding: water covering normally dry land; drought: long period without rain
chunks.source: Resource degradation chains: deforestation → erosion → flooding/drought; overgrazing → compaction → erosion; mining → pollution; swamp drainage → flooding + drought. Conservation (afforestation, agroforestry, wetland protection, by-laws) breaks these chains. Sustainable use prevents degradation before it starts.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: State two causes of deforestation in Uganda. A: 1) Charcoal and firewood demand. 2) Clearing land for agriculture (crops, grazing). Reason: direct drivers; PLE expects specific human activities.
chunks.source: 1) Charcoal and firewood demand. 2) Clearing land for agriculture (crops, grazing). Reason: direct drivers; PLE expects specific human activities.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Explain how overgrazing leads to soil erosion. A: Overgrazing removes vegetation cover, exposing soil to rain splash and wind. Hooves compact soil, reducing infiltration, increasing runoff. Both accelerate erosion. Reason: two distinct mechanisms — cover loss + physical compaction.
chunks.source: Overgrazing removes vegetation cover, exposing soil to rain splash and wind. Hooves compact soil, reducing infiltration, increasing runoff. Both accelerate erosion. Reason: two distinct mechanisms — cover loss + physical compaction.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give three effects of swamp drainage on the environment. A: 1) Increased flooding (loss of water storage). 2) Water pollution (loss of filtration). 3) Loss of wildlife habitat. 4) Drought vulnerability (lower groundwater). 5) Soil oxidation. Any three with brief explanation. Reason: wetlands provide multiple ecosystem services.
chunks.source: 1) Increased flooding (loss of water storage). 2) Water pollution (loss of filtration). 3) Loss of wildlife habitat. 4) Drought vulnerability (lower groundwater). 5) Soil oxidation. Any three with brief explanation. Reason: wetlands provide multiple ecosystem services.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How does mining cause water pollution? A: Mining exposes sulphide minerals to air/water → acid mine drainage. Processing uses chemicals (cyanide, mercury) that leak into streams. Silt from erosion clouds water. Reason: specific pollution pathways from extraction and processing.
chunks.source: Mining exposes sulphide minerals to air/water → acid mine drainage. Processing uses chemicals (cyanide, mercury) that leak into streams. Silt from erosion clouds water. Reason: specific pollution pathways from extraction and processing.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: A steep slope is deforested for crops. After two years, yields fall. Explain why. A: Deforestation → erosion washes away topsoil (nutrients, organic matter) → soil fertility drops → yields fall. Also: less water infiltration → drought stress. Reason: links deforestation to productivity loss via erosion.
chunks.source: Deforestation → erosion washes away topsoil (nutrients, organic matter) → soil fertility drops → yields fall. Also: less water infiltration → drought stress. Reason: links deforestation to productivity loss via erosion.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: PLE style: Which human activity does NOT directly cause soil erosion? A) Deforestation B) Overgrazing C) Afforestation D) Mining A: C) Afforestation. Reason: afforestation plants trees, which prevent erosion. The other three remove vegetation or disturb soil, causing erosion.
chunks.source: C) Afforestation. Reason: afforestation plants trees, which prevent erosion. The other three remove vegetation or disturb soil, causing erosion.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Describe the link between deforestation and drought. A: Forests recycle water through transpiration, contributing to local rainfall. Deforestation reduces transpiration, lowers humidity, reduces rain, and exposes soil to sun, increasing evaporation. Result: more frequent/severe drought. Reason: explains the forest-rainfall feedback loop.
chunks.source: Forests recycle water through transpiration, contributing to local rainfall. Deforestation reduces transpiration, lowers humidity, reduces rain, and exposes soil to sun, increasing evaporation. Result: more frequent/severe drought. Reason: explains the forest-rainfall feedback loop.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name two by-laws that can reduce resource degradation in a village. A: 1) Ban charcoal burning in protected forest areas. 2) Require contour farming on slopes. 3) Prohibit cultivation in wetlands. 4) Limit herd size per acre to prevent overgrazing. Reason: specific, enforceable local regulations targeting degradation causes.
chunks.source: 1) Ban charcoal burning in protected forest areas. 2) Require contour farming on slopes. 3) Prohibit cultivation in wetlands. 4) Limit herd size per acre to prevent overgrazing. Reason: specific, enforceable local regulations targeting degradation causes.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Explain why flooding and drought can both result from the same degradation. A: Degradation (deforestation, swamp drainage, erosion) reduces soil's water-holding capacity. Rain → fast runoff → flooding. Dry season → no stored groundwater → drought. Same root cause: lost infiltration and storage. Reason: shows integrated understanding of hydrology.
chunks.source: Degradation (deforestation, swamp drainage, erosion) reduces soil's water-holding capacity. Rain → fast runoff → flooding. Dry season → no stored groundwater → drought. Same root cause: lost infiltration and storage. Reason: shows integrated understanding of hydrology.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: A factory pollutes a river. List two effects on downstream communities. A: 1) Waterborne diseases from contaminated drinking water. 2) Loss of fish/livelihoods. 3) Crop failure from irrigation with polluted water. 4) Skin diseases from contact. Reason: connects pollution to human welfare impacts.
chunks.source: 1) Waterborne diseases from contaminated drinking water. 2) Loss of fish/livelihoods. 3) Crop failure from irrigation with polluted water. 4) Skin diseases from contact. Reason: connects pollution to human welfare impacts.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Population Size and Distribution. I can explain population size, density, distribution, and how a census works. Population size is counted by a census; density and distribution show how people are spread; migration changes where people live. Keywords: population: the total number of people in an area; census: an official count of all people in a country; density: how many people live in a unit of land area; distribution: the way people are spread across an area; urban: relating to towns or cities; rural: relating to the countryside; migration: movement of people from one place to another; settlement: a place where people make their homes
chunks.source: Population size is counted by a census; density and distribution show how people are spread; migration changes where people live.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is the meaning of population density? A: Population density is the number of people per unit area. It is calculated by dividing total population by land area.
chunks.source: Population density is the number of people per unit area. It is calculated by dividing total population by land area.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: A census is carried out every ten years in Uganda. Why is a census important? A: A census provides accurate data on population size, distribution, and density for planning services.
chunks.source: A census provides accurate data on population size, distribution, and density for planning services.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Which of the following describes population distribution? A: Population distribution refers to how people are spread across a given area, such as urban vs rural.
chunks.source: Population distribution refers to how people are spread across a given area, such as urban vs rural.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give one reason for rural-urban migration in Uganda. A: People migrate to urban areas to find jobs, better education, and health services.
chunks.source: People migrate to urban areas to find jobs, better education, and health services.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: If a district has a population of 200,000 and an area of 500 km², what is its population density? A: 400 people per km² (200,000 ÷ 500 = 400).

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is the difference between urban and rural settlements? A: Urban settlements are towns with high population density and services; rural settlements are villages with lower density and more agriculture.
chunks.source: Urban settlements are towns with high population density and services; rural settlements are villages with lower density and more agriculture.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How does migration affect population density in urban areas? A: Migration increases urban population density because more people move into a limited space.
chunks.source: Migration increases urban population density because more people move into a limited space.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why does the government need census data for planning settlement? A: Census data shows where people live, helping the government allocate land, services, and infrastructure.
chunks.source: Census data shows where people live, helping the government allocate land, services, and infrastructure.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Effects of High Population. I can list and explain the problems caused by high population growth. High population leads to many problems including congestion, deforestation, unemployment, pressure on services, land fragmentation, and pollution. Keywords: overpopulation: a situation where too many people live in an area for the resources available; congestion: overcrowding of people or vehicles in a place; deforestation: clearing of forests for settlement or farming; unemployment: lack of jobs for people who are willing to work; pressure: heavy demand on something such as services or land; services: public facilities like health, water, electricity, and education; land fragmentation: division of large land into small plots; pollution: contamination of air, water, or soil by waste
chunks.source: High population leads to many problems including congestion, deforestation, unemployment, pressure on services, land fragmentation, and pollution.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Define overpopulation. A: Overpopulation is when the number of people exceeds the resources and space available in an area.
chunks.source: Overpopulation is when the number of people exceeds the resources and space available in an area.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give two examples of congestion in Uganda. A: Traffic jams on major roads and overcrowded markets are examples of congestion.
chunks.source: Traffic jams on major roads and overcrowded markets are examples of congestion.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How does overpopulation lead to deforestation? A: People clear forests to create settlement and farmland, causing deforestation.
chunks.source: People clear forests to create settlement and farmland, causing deforestation.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Explain the link between high population and unemployment. A: High population means more job seekers than available jobs, leading to unemployment.
chunks.source: High population means more job seekers than available jobs, leading to unemployment.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is land fragmentation? A: Land fragmentation is the division of large pieces of land into smaller plots, often due to inheritance or population pressure.
chunks.source: Land fragmentation is the division of large pieces of land into smaller plots, often due to inheritance or population pressure.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: List two types of pollution caused by high population. A: Air pollution from vehicles and water pollution from waste are common.
chunks.source: Air pollution from vehicles and water pollution from waste are common.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why does high population put pressure on services? A: More people need water, electricity, health care, and education, stretching limited resources.
chunks.source: More people need water, electricity, health care, and education, stretching limited resources.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Suggest one way to reduce pressure on health services. A: Family planning to slow population growth can reduce pressure on health services.
chunks.source: Family planning to slow population growth can reduce pressure on health services.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Population and Health Services. I can explain how population growth affects health services and what improves health outcomes. Population pressure strains health services; immunisation, family planning, sanitation, and literacy improve health outcomes. Keywords: immunisation: giving vaccines to protect against diseases; family planning: methods to control the number and spacing of children; sanitation: keeping the environment clean to prevent disease; health centre: a local place where people get medical care; disease: an illness that affects the body; malnutrition: poor nutrition caused by not enough or wrong food; mortality: death rate, especially of children or mothers; literacy: ability to read and write
chunks.source: Population pressure strains health services; immunisation, family planning, sanitation, and literacy improve health outcomes.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is immunisation? A: Immunisation is giving vaccines to protect people against specific diseases.
chunks.source: Immunisation is giving vaccines to protect people against specific diseases.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How does family planning reduce child mortality? A: Family planning allows child spacing, so each child gets better nutrition and care, lowering mortality.
chunks.source: Family planning allows child spacing, so each child gets better nutrition and care, lowering mortality.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why is sanitation important in a crowded community? A: Good sanitation prevents the spread of diseases like cholera and diarrhoea.
chunks.source: Good sanitation prevents the spread of diseases like cholera and diarrhoea.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name two services provided at a health centre. A: Health centres provide immunisation, antenatal care, treatment of common illnesses, and health education.
chunks.source: Health centres provide immunisation, antenatal care, treatment of common illnesses, and health education.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How does literacy of mothers improve child health? A: Literate mothers can read health guidelines, understand medicine instructions, and seek care early.
chunks.source: Literate mothers can read health guidelines, understand medicine instructions, and seek care early.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is malnutrition? A: Malnutrition is poor health caused by insufficient or unbalanced food intake.
chunks.source: Malnutrition is poor health caused by insufficient or unbalanced food intake.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Explain the link between high population and disease outbreaks. A: High population density makes it easier for infectious diseases to spread quickly.
chunks.source: High population density makes it easier for infectious diseases to spread quickly.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Give one way the government can improve health services under population pressure. A: The government can build more health centres and train more health workers.
chunks.source: The government can build more health centres and train more health workers.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Controlling Population Growth. I can describe methods and policies that help control population growth. Controlling population growth requires education, family planning, late marriage, child spacing, contraceptives, supportive policies, sensitisation, and empowering the girl child. Keywords: family planning: methods to control the number and spacing of children; education: process of learning, especially in school; late marriage: marrying at an older age; child spacing: waiting between births; contraceptive: a device or drug to prevent pregnancy; policy: a government plan or course of action; sensitisation: raising awareness about an issue; girl child: a female child, often focusing on her rights and education
chunks.source: Controlling population growth requires education, family planning, late marriage, child spacing, contraceptives, supportive policies, sensitisation, and empowering the girl child.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Define family planning. A: Family planning refers to methods that help couples decide the number and spacing of their children.
chunks.source: Family planning refers to methods that help couples decide the number and spacing of their children.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How does education of girls reduce population growth? A: Educated girls tend to marry later, have fewer children, and use family planning.
chunks.source: Educated girls tend to marry later, have fewer children, and use family planning.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is meant by late marriage? A: Late marriage means marrying at an older age, which shortens the reproductive period.
chunks.source: Late marriage means marrying at an older age, which shortens the reproductive period.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Explain child spacing and its benefits. A: Child spacing is waiting at least two years between births; it improves mother and child health.
chunks.source: Child spacing is waiting at least two years between births; it improves mother and child health.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Name two modern contraceptive methods. A: Condoms and oral contraceptive pills are common modern methods.
chunks.source: Condoms and oral contraceptive pills are common modern methods.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: What is a population policy? A: A population policy is a government plan to manage population growth, often through family planning and education.
chunks.source: A population policy is a government plan to manage population growth, often through family planning and education.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: Why is sensitisation important for family planning? A: Sensitisation raises awareness, reduces myths, and encourages uptake of family planning services.
chunks.source: Sensitisation raises awareness, reduces myths, and encourages uptake of family planning services.

chunks.subject: Science
chunks.text: Q: How does empowering the girl child affect population? A: Empowered girls stay in school, marry later, and have fewer children, slowing population growth.
chunks.source: Empowered girls stay in school, marry later, and have fewer children, slowing population growth.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Reading the Map of Africa. I can locate Africa on the world map using lines of latitude and longitude and describe its position and size. Africa is the second largest continent. The Equator (0° latitude) and Prime Meridian (0° longitude) cross it, placing Africa in all four hemispheres. Latitude lines run east-west; longitude lines run north-south. Together they give exact position on a map. Keywords: africa: the continent where Uganda is found; continent: a very large land mass on Earth; map: a drawing that shows where places are; latitude: lines that run east to west on a map; longitude: lines that run north to south on a map; equator: the line of latitude at 0 degrees that divides the Earth; hemisphere: half of the Earth; prime meridian: the line of longitude at 0 degrees; position: where something is found; world: the Earth and all its people and places
chunks.source: Africa is the second largest continent. The Equator (0° latitude) and Prime Meridian (0° longitude) cross it, placing Africa in all four hemispheres. Latitude lines run east-west; longitude lines run north-south. Together they give exact position on a map.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Name the line of latitude at 0 degrees that crosses Africa. A: Equator — it divides the Earth into northern and southern hemispheres.
chunks.source: Equator — it divides the Earth into northern and southern hemispheres.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Name the line of longitude at 0 degrees that crosses Africa. A: Prime Meridian — it divides the Earth into eastern and western hemispheres.
chunks.source: Prime Meridian — it divides the Earth into eastern and western hemispheres.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: In which two hemispheres does Africa lie because of the equator? A: Northern and Southern Hemisphere — the equator cuts Africa horizontally.
chunks.source: Northern and Southern Hemisphere — the equator cuts Africa horizontally.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: In which two hemispheres does Africa lie because of the prime meridian? A: Eastern and Western Hemisphere — the prime meridian cuts Africa vertically.
