chunks.source: Eastern and Western Hemisphere — the prime meridian cuts Africa vertically.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: What is the approximate latitude and longitude of Kampala? A: 0° latitude, 32° East longitude — Kampala sits on the equator.
chunks.source: 0° latitude, 32° East longitude — Kampala sits on the equator.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Which ocean lies to the west of Africa? A: Atlantic Ocean — it forms Africa's western boundary.
chunks.source: Atlantic Ocean — it forms Africa's western boundary.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Which ocean lies to the east of Africa? A: Indian Ocean — it forms Africa's eastern boundary.
chunks.source: Indian Ocean — it forms Africa's eastern boundary.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Which sea lies to the north of Africa? A: Mediterranean Sea — it separates Africa from Europe.
chunks.source: Mediterranean Sea — it separates Africa from Europe.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Which sea lies to the northeast of Africa? A: Red Sea — it separates Africa from the Arabian Peninsula.
chunks.source: Red Sea — it separates Africa from the Arabian Peninsula.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Why is Africa's position on the world map described as unique? A: It is the only continent crossed by both the Equator and the Prime Meridian.
chunks.source: It is the only continent crossed by both the Equator and the Prime Meridian.

chunks.id: L-P7-Social-The Continents and Oceans of the World
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: The Continents and Oceans of the World
chunks.text: The Continents and Oceans of the World. I can name the seven continents in order of size and identify the oceans and seas around Africa. Seven continents by size: Asia, Africa, North America, South America, Antarctica, Europe, Australia. Four oceans by size: Pacific, Atlantic, Indian Ocean, Arctic. Africa touches Atlantic (west), Indian Ocean (east), Mediterranean Sea (north), Red Sea (northeast). Keywords: asia: the largest continent in the world; europe: the continent north of Africa across the Mediterranean Sea; australia: the smallest continent, also called Oceania; antarctica: the icy continent at the South Pole; ocean: a very large body of salt water; atlantic: the ocean west of Africa; pacific: the largest ocean in the world; indian ocean: the ocean east of Africa; mediterranean sea: the sea north of Africa between Africa and Europe; red sea: the sea northeast of Africa between Africa and Asia
chunks.source: Seven continents by size: Asia, Africa, North America, South America, Antarctica, Europe, Australia. Four oceans by size: Pacific, Atlantic, Indian Ocean, Arctic. Africa touches Atlantic (west), Indian Ocean (east), Mediterranean Sea (north), Red Sea (northeast).

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-The Continents and Oceans of the World
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: The Continents and Oceans of the World
chunks.text: Q: List the seven continents in order of size from largest to smallest. A: Asia, Africa, North America, South America, Antarctica, Europe, Australia — memorise the sequence for PLE.
chunks.source: Asia, Africa, North America, South America, Antarctica, Europe, Australia — memorise the sequence for PLE.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-The Continents and Oceans of the World
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: The Continents and Oceans of the World
chunks.text: Q: Which continent is the largest in the world? A: Asia — it covers about 44 million square kilometres.
chunks.source: Asia — it covers about 44 million square kilometres.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-The Continents and Oceans of the World
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: The Continents and Oceans of the World
chunks.text: Q: Which continent is the second largest? A: Africa — it covers about 30 million square kilometres.
chunks.source: Africa — it covers about 30 million square kilometres.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-The Continents and Oceans of the World
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: The Continents and Oceans of the World
chunks.text: Q: Which continent is the smallest? A: Australia — also called Oceania, it is the smallest continent.
chunks.source: Australia — also called Oceania, it is the smallest continent.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-The Continents and Oceans of the World
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: The Continents and Oceans of the World
chunks.text: Q: Name the four oceans of the world from largest to smallest. A: Pacific Ocean, Atlantic Ocean, Indian Ocean, Arctic Ocean — Pacific is biggest, Arctic is smallest.
chunks.source: Pacific Ocean, Atlantic Ocean, Indian Ocean, Arctic Ocean — Pacific is biggest, Arctic is smallest.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-The Continents and Oceans of the World
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: The Continents and Oceans of the World
chunks.text: Q: Which ocean lies to the west of Africa? A: Atlantic Ocean — it forms Africa's western coastline.
chunks.source: Atlantic Ocean — it forms Africa's western coastline.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-The Continents and Oceans of the World
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: The Continents and Oceans of the World
chunks.text: Q: Which ocean lies to the east of Africa? A: Indian Ocean — it forms Africa's eastern coastline.
chunks.source: Indian Ocean — it forms Africa's eastern coastline.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-The Continents and Oceans of the World
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: The Continents and Oceans of the World
chunks.text: Q: Which sea lies to the north of Africa between Africa and Europe? A: Mediterranean Sea — it separates Africa from Europe.
chunks.source: Mediterranean Sea — it separates Africa from Europe.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-The Continents and Oceans of the World
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: The Continents and Oceans of the World
chunks.text: Q: Which sea lies to the northeast of Africa between Africa and Asia? A: Red Sea — it separates Africa from the Arabian Peninsula.
chunks.source: Red Sea — it separates Africa from the Arabian Peninsula.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-The Continents and Oceans of the World
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: The Continents and Oceans of the World
chunks.text: Q: Why is the Mediterranean Sea called a sea and not an ocean? A: It is smaller than an ocean and almost enclosed by land — seas are smaller than oceans.
chunks.source: It is smaller than an ocean and almost enclosed by land — seas are smaller than oceans.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: The Regions of Africa. I can name the six regions of Africa and list countries found in each region. Africa has six regions: North Africa (above Sahara), West Africa (the bulge), Central Africa (Congo Basin), East Africa (Great Lakes), Southern Africa (bottom), Horn of Africa (northeast peninsula). Each region has key countries and capital cities. Island countries like Madagascar are also part of Africa. Keywords: region: a large area with common features; west africa: the region of Africa west of Lake Chad; east africa: the region of Africa around the Great Lakes; north africa: the region of Africa north of the Sahara; central africa: the region in the middle of Africa around the Congo Basin; southern africa: the region at the bottom of Africa; horn of africa: the peninsula in northeast Africa shaped like a horn; country: a nation with its own government; capital city: the main city where government sits; island: land completely surrounded by water
chunks.source: Africa has six regions: North Africa (above Sahara), West Africa (the bulge), Central Africa (Congo Basin), East Africa (Great Lakes), Southern Africa (bottom), Horn of Africa (northeast peninsula). Each region has key countries and capital cities. Island countries like Madagascar are also part of Africa.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Name the six regions of Africa. A: North Africa, West Africa, Central Africa, East Africa, Southern Africa, Horn of Africa — all six must be listed.
chunks.source: North Africa, West Africa, Central Africa, East Africa, Southern Africa, Horn of Africa — all six must be listed.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Which region lies north of the Sahara Desert? A: North Africa — it includes Egypt, Libya, Tunisia, Algeria, Morocco.
chunks.source: North Africa — it includes Egypt, Libya, Tunisia, Algeria, Morocco.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Which region includes Nigeria and Ghana? A: West Africa — the bulge of Africa west of Lake Chad.
chunks.source: West Africa — the bulge of Africa west of Lake Chad.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Which region is around the Congo Basin? A: Central Africa — includes DR Congo, Cameroon, Central African Republic.
chunks.source: Central Africa — includes DR Congo, Cameroon, Central African Republic.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Which region includes Uganda, Kenya, and Tanzania? A: East Africa — the Great Lakes region.
chunks.source: East Africa — the Great Lakes region.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Which region is at the bottom of Africa? A: Southern Africa — includes South Africa, Zambia, Zimbabwe, Botswana.
chunks.source: Southern Africa — includes South Africa, Zambia, Zimbabwe, Botswana.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Which region is a peninsula in northeast Africa? A: Horn of Africa — shaped like a horn, includes Ethiopia, Somalia, Eritrea, Djibouti.
chunks.source: Horn of Africa — shaped like a horn, includes Ethiopia, Somalia, Eritrea, Djibouti.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: What is the capital city of Nigeria? A: Abuja — Nigeria is in West Africa.
chunks.source: Abuja — Nigeria is in West Africa.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: What is the capital city of Ethiopia? A: Addis Ababa — Ethiopia is in the Horn of Africa.
chunks.source: Addis Ababa — Ethiopia is in the Horn of Africa.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: What is the capital city of DR Congo? A: Kinshasa — DR Congo is in Central Africa.
chunks.source: Kinshasa — DR Congo is in Central Africa.

chunks.id: L-P7-Social-Countries of Africa and Their Capitals
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: Countries of Africa and Their Capitals
chunks.text: Countries of Africa and Their Capitals. I can name key African countries, their capital cities, and identify the island countries of Africa. Key country-capital pairs: Uganda-Kampala, Kenya-Nairobi, Tanzania-Dodoma, Ethiopia-Addis Ababa, Egypt-Cairo, Nigeria-Abuja, Madagascar-Antananarivo. Island countries: Madagascar, Seychelles, Comoros, Mauritius, Cape Verde, Sao Tome & Principe. Uganda's neighbours: Kenya, Tanzania, Rwanda, DR Congo, South Sudan. Keywords: uganda: our country in East Africa; kenya: our neighbour to the east; tanzania: our neighbour to the south; ethiopia: a country in the Horn of Africa; egypt: a country in North Africa; nigeria: the most populous country in Africa; madagascar: a large island country off the east coast; capital: the main city where government sits; island country: a country that is an island; neighbour: a country next to another country
chunks.source: Key country-capital pairs: Uganda-Kampala, Kenya-Nairobi, Tanzania-Dodoma, Ethiopia-Addis Ababa, Egypt-Cairo, Nigeria-Abuja, Madagascar-Antananarivo. Island countries: Madagascar, Seychelles, Comoros, Mauritius, Cape Verde, Sao Tome & Principe. Uganda's neighbours: Kenya, Tanzania, Rwanda, DR Congo, South Sudan.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-Countries of Africa and Their Capitals
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: Countries of Africa and Their Capitals
chunks.text: Q: What is the capital city of Uganda? A: Kampala — Uganda is in East Africa.
chunks.source: Kampala — Uganda is in East Africa.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-Countries of Africa and Their Capitals
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: Countries of Africa and Their Capitals
chunks.text: Q: What is the capital city of Kenya? A: Nairobi — Kenya is Uganda's neighbour to the east.
chunks.source: Nairobi — Kenya is Uganda's neighbour to the east.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-Countries of Africa and Their Capitals
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: Countries of Africa and Their Capitals
chunks.text: Q: What is the capital city of Tanzania? A: Dodoma — official capital since 1996; Dar es Salaam is the largest city.
chunks.source: Dodoma — official capital since 1996; Dar es Salaam is the largest city.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-Countries of Africa and Their Capitals
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: Countries of Africa and Their Capitals
chunks.text: Q: What is the capital city of Ethiopia? A: Addis Ababa — also headquarters of the African Union.
chunks.source: Addis Ababa — also headquarters of the African Union.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-Countries of Africa and Their Capitals
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: Countries of Africa and Their Capitals
chunks.text: Q: What is the capital city of Egypt? A: Cairo — largest city in Africa, in North Africa.
chunks.source: Cairo — largest city in Africa, in North Africa.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-Countries of Africa and Their Capitals
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: Countries of Africa and Their Capitals
chunks.text: Q: What is the capital city of Nigeria? A: Abuja — replaced Lagos as capital in 1991; Nigeria is in West Africa.
chunks.source: Abuja — replaced Lagos as capital in 1991; Nigeria is in West Africa.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-Countries of Africa and Their Capitals
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: Countries of Africa and Their Capitals
chunks.text: Q: What is the capital city of Madagascar? A: Antananarivo — Madagascar is the largest island country in Africa.
chunks.source: Antananarivo — Madagascar is the largest island country in Africa.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-Countries of Africa and Their Capitals
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: Countries of Africa and Their Capitals
chunks.text: Q: Name three island countries of Africa and their capitals. A: Seychelles-Victoria, Comoros-Moroni, Mauritius-Port Louis (also Cape Verde-Praia, Sao Tome-Sao Tome).
chunks.source: Seychelles-Victoria, Comoros-Moroni, Mauritius-Port Louis (also Cape Verde-Praia, Sao Tome-Sao Tome).

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-Countries of Africa and Their Capitals
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: Countries of Africa and Their Capitals
chunks.text: Q: Which neighbour of Uganda has its capital at Kigali? A: Rwanda — southwest neighbour of Uganda.
chunks.source: Rwanda — southwest neighbour of Uganda.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-Countries of Africa and Their Capitals
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: Countries of Africa and Their Capitals
chunks.text: Q: Which neighbour of Uganda has its capital at Juba? A: South Sudan — north neighbour of Uganda.
chunks.source: South Sudan — north neighbour of Uganda.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: The Climate Zones of Africa. I can name the main climatic zones of Africa and describe their key features. Africa has five main **climate** **zones** — **equatorial**, **tropical**, **desert**, **temperate**, and **montane** — each defined by its **temperature**, **rainfall**, **sunshine**, and **humidity**. Keywords: climate: the usual weather over many years; weather: day‑to‑day conditions like rain or sun; equatorial: near the equator, hot and wet; tropical: warm with a wet and a dry season; desert: very dry, little rain; temperature: how hot or cold it is; rainfall: amount of rain that falls; sunshine: bright light from the sun; humidity: water vapour in the air; zone: an area with similar climate
chunks.source: Africa has five main **climate** **zones** — **equatorial**, **tropical**, **desert**, **temperate**, and **montane** — each defined by its **temperature**, **rainfall**, **sunshine**, and **humidity**.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Which climatic zone lies on the equator and receives rain every month? A: Equatorial zone – it has constant sunshine and heavy rainfall.
chunks.source: Equatorial zone – it has constant sunshine and heavy rainfall.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Name the zone with extreme daytime heat, cold nights, and almost no rain. A: Desert zone – very low rainfall and humidity.
chunks.source: Desert zone – very low rainfall and humidity.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: What two factors make equatorial areas very humid? A: Strong sunshine and heavy rainfall increase water vapour.
chunks.source: Strong sunshine and heavy rainfall increase water vapour.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: A place with a wet season and a dry season, warm all year, belongs to which zone? A: Tropical zone – distinct wet and dry seasons.
chunks.source: Tropical zone – distinct wet and dry seasons.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: High mountains like Kilimanjaro create which climate zone? A: Montane zone – temperature falls with altitude.
chunks.source: Montane zone – temperature falls with altitude.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: If a region has mild temperatures and four seasons, it is likely which zone? A: Temperate zone – found far from the equator.
chunks.source: Temperate zone – found far from the equator.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Which zone would you expect to find dense rainforest vegetation? A: Equatorial zone – high rainfall and humidity support rainforest.
chunks.source: Equatorial zone – high rainfall and humidity support rainforest.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: What is the main reason deserts have low humidity? A: Very little rainfall means little water vapour in the air.
chunks.source: Very little rainfall means little water vapour in the air.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Match: ‘hot, wet, all year’ → ______. A: Equatorial zone.
chunks.source: Equatorial zone.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Match: ‘hot, dry, little rain’ → ______. A: Desert zone.
chunks.source: Desert zone.

chunks.id: L-P7-Social-Why Climates Differ From Place to Place
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: Why Climates Differ From Place to Place
chunks.text: Why Climates Differ From Place to Place. I can explain the factors that cause different climates across Africa. Africa’s varied **climate** is shaped by **latitude**, **altitude**, **relief**, **wind**, **ocean current**, **vegetation**, **distance** from water, and human **influence**. Keywords: factor: something that causes a change; altitude: height above sea level; wind: moving air; ocean current: flow of sea water; latitude: distance north or south of the equator; relief: shape of the land (mountains, valleys); vegetation: plants covering the land; distance: how far away something is; influence: effect on something; mountain: very high land
chunks.source: Africa’s varied **climate** is shaped by **latitude**, **altitude**, **relief**, **wind**, **ocean current**, **vegetation**, **distance** from water, and human **influence**.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-Why Climates Differ From Place to Place
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: Why Climates Differ From Place to Place
chunks.text: Q: Name the factor that measures distance north or south of the equator. A: Latitude – it controls the angle of sunshine.
chunks.source: Latitude – it controls the angle of sunshine.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-Why Climates Differ From Place to Place
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: Why Climates Differ From Place to Place
chunks.text: Q: Which factor causes temperature to fall about 6 °C per kilometre of height? A: Altitude – higher ground has thinner air.
chunks.source: Altitude – higher ground has thinner air.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-Why Climates Differ From Place to Place
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: Why Climates Differ From Place to Place
chunks.text: Q: What is the effect of a cold ocean current on a coastal climate? A: It cools the air and reduces rainfall.
chunks.source: It cools the air and reduces rainfall.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-Why Climates Differ From Place to Place
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: Why Climates Differ From Place to Place
chunks.text: Q: How does relief (mountains) affect rainfall? A: Mountains force moist wind to rise, cool, and drop rain on the windward side.
chunks.source: Mountains force moist wind to rise, cool, and drop rain on the windward side.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-Why Climates Differ From Place to Place
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: Why Climates Differ From Place to Place
chunks.text: Q: Which factor describes the shape of the land such as mountains and valleys? A: Relief.
chunks.source: Relief.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-Why Climates Differ From Place to Place
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: Why Climates Differ From Place to Place
chunks.text: Q: Dense vegetation adds moisture to the air through transpiration – what is this factor called? A: Vegetation.
chunks.source: Vegetation.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-Why Climates Differ From Place to Place
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: Why Climates Differ From Place to Place
chunks.text: Q: Places far from large water bodies receive less rain because of which factor? A: Distance from water bodies.
chunks.source: Distance from water bodies.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-Why Climates Differ From Place to Place
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: Why Climates Differ From Place to Place
chunks.text: Q: Human activities like deforestation change local climate – this is an example of which factor? A: Human influence.
chunks.source: Human influence.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-Why Climates Differ From Place to Place
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: Why Climates Differ From Place to Place
chunks.text: Q: Match: ‘low latitude → hot’ – factor? A: Latitude.
chunks.source: Latitude.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-Why Climates Differ From Place to Place
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: Why Climates Differ From Place to Place
chunks.text: Q: Match: ‘high mountain → cool, wet’ – factor? A: Altitude / relief.
chunks.source: Altitude / relief.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: How Climate Shapes People's Work. I can link each climatic zone to the main economic activities people do there. Africa’s **climate** zones dictate **livelihood**s: **desert** → **irrigation**, **mining**; **equatorial** → **tourism**, **hunting**, **lumbering**; **tropical** → **farming**, **livestock**; **semi‑arid** → **nomadism**; **montane** → **farming**, **tourism**. Keywords: farming: growing crops; irrigation: supplying water to crops artificially; nomadism: moving with livestock to find pasture; tourism: travel for pleasure to see nature or culture; mining: extracting minerals from the earth; lumbering: cutting trees for timber; livestock: animals kept for meat, milk, or work; hunting: catching wild animals for food or trade; activity: something people do for a living; livelihood: way of earning a living
chunks.source: Africa’s **climate** zones dictate **livelihood**s: **desert** → **irrigation**, **mining**; **equatorial** → **tourism**, **hunting**, **lumbering**; **tropical** → **farming**, **livestock**; **semi‑arid** → **nomadism**; **montane** → **farming**, **tourism**.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Which activity is typical in the desert because of low rainfall? A: Irrigation farming – water is supplied artificially.
chunks.source: Irrigation farming – water is supplied artificially.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: What economic activity is linked to the equatorial rainforest’s wildlife? A: Tourism (e.g., gorilla trekking).
chunks.source: Tourism (e.g., gorilla trekking).

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Nomadism is practiced mainly in which climatic zone? A: Semi‑arid zone – seasonal pasture forces movement.
chunks.source: Semi‑arid zone – seasonal pasture forces movement.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Lumbering of hardwoods like mahogany occurs in which zone? A: Tropical zone – abundant trees and moderate rainfall.
chunks.source: Tropical zone – abundant trees and moderate rainfall.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Mining of oil and phosphates is common in which zone? A: Desert zone – large mineral deposits under arid land.
chunks.source: Desert zone – large mineral deposits under arid land.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: People in the tropical savanna combine crop growing with keeping animals – name this activity. A: Mixed farming (farming and livestock rearing).
chunks.source: Mixed farming (farming and livestock rearing).

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: High mountain areas (montane) attract visitors for scenery – what activity? A: Tourism (mountain trekking).
chunks.source: Tourism (mountain trekking).

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Hunting for bushmeat is traditional in which zone? A: Equatorial forest zone.
chunks.source: Equatorial forest zone.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Match: ‘dry, hot, irrigation’ → ______. A: Desert zone.
chunks.source: Desert zone.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Match: ‘wet, hot, tourism’ → ______. A: Equatorial zone.
chunks.source: Equatorial zone.

chunks.id: L-P7-Social-Reading Climate Graphs and Maps for PLE
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: Reading Climate Graphs and Maps for PLE
chunks.text: Reading Climate Graphs and Maps for PLE. I can read and draw climate graphs, charts, tables and maps showing rainfall and temperature. A climate **graph** uses bars for **rainfall** and a line for **temperature**; read the **scale**, identify **wet** and **dry** **season**s, and calculate **average** values from the **data** in a **table** or **chart**. Keywords: graph: a diagram showing data; chart: a visual display of information; table: rows and columns of numbers; average: typical value found by adding and dividing; season: a period of the year with distinct weather; wet: rainy; dry: little or no rain; record: to write down data; data: facts and figures collected; scale: the numbers on the axes of a graph
chunks.source: A climate **graph** uses bars for **rainfall** and a line for **temperature**; read the **scale**, identify **wet** and **dry** **season**s, and calculate **average** values from the **data** in a **table** or **chart**.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-Reading Climate Graphs and Maps for PLE
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: Reading Climate Graphs and Maps for PLE
chunks.text: Q: What do the bars on a climate graph represent? A: Rainfall in millimetres.
chunks.source: Rainfall in millimetres.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-Reading Climate Graphs and Maps for PLE
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: Reading Climate Graphs and Maps for PLE
chunks.text: Q: What does the line on a climate graph represent? A: Temperature in degrees Celsius.
chunks.source: Temperature in degrees Celsius.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-Reading Climate Graphs and Maps for PLE
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: Reading Climate Graphs and Maps for PLE
chunks.text: Q: Name the two main seasons shown on a tropical climate graph. A: Wet season and dry season.
chunks.source: Wet season and dry season.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-Reading Climate Graphs and Maps for PLE
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: Reading Climate Graphs and Maps for PLE
chunks.text: Q: How do you calculate the average annual temperature from a graph? A: Add the twelve monthly temperatures and divide by 12.
chunks.source: Add the twelve monthly temperatures and divide by 12.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-Reading Climate Graphs and Maps for PLE
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: Reading Climate Graphs and Maps for PLE
chunks.text: Q: If a table shows rainfall for each month, how do you find the average monthly rainfall? A: Sum the twelve values and divide by 12.
chunks.source: Sum the twelve values and divide by 12.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-Reading Climate Graphs and Maps for PLE
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: Reading Climate Graphs and Maps for PLE
chunks.text: Q: What should you check first when reading a climate graph? A: The scale on both axes.
chunks.source: The scale on both axes.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-Reading Climate Graphs and Maps for PLE
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: Reading Climate Graphs and Maps for PLE
chunks.text: Q: A month with 10 mm rain belongs to which season? A: Dry season.
chunks.source: Dry season.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-Reading Climate Graphs and Maps for PLE
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: Reading Climate Graphs and Maps for PLE
chunks.text: Q: A month with 200 mm rain belongs to which season? A: Wet season.
chunks.source: Wet season.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-Reading Climate Graphs and Maps for PLE
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: Reading Climate Graphs and Maps for PLE
chunks.text: Q: Match: ‘bars = rainfall, line = temperature’ – true or false? A: True.
chunks.source: True.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-Reading Climate Graphs and Maps for PLE
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: Reading Climate Graphs and Maps for PLE
chunks.text: Q: Match: ‘average = highest value’ – true or false? A: False – average is the mean, not the maximum.
chunks.source: False – average is the mean, not the maximum.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: The Vegetation Zones of Africa. I can name and locate the main vegetation zones of Africa. Africa has several vegetation zones: equatorial forest, rainforest, mangrove forest, savannah, montane, grassland, veld, and desert, each shaped by climate and location. Keywords: vegetation: all plant life in an area; equatorial forest: dense forest near the equator; mangrove forest: forest growing in salty coastal water; savannah: grassland with scattered trees; montane: vegetation on high mountains; grassland: open land covered with grass; veld: temperate grassland in southern Africa; desert: very dry area with few plants; rainforest: wet forest with heavy rainfall; plant: any living green organism
chunks.source: Africa has several vegetation zones: equatorial forest, rainforest, mangrove forest, savannah, montane, grassland, veld, and desert, each shaped by climate and location.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Name the vegetation zone that grows near the equator and receives heavy rainfall throughout the year. A: Equatorial forest – it lies near the equator with high rainfall.
chunks.source: Equatorial forest – it lies near the equator with high rainfall.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Which vegetation zone is found in coastal areas where salt water floods the land? A: Mangrove forest – it tolerates salty water.
chunks.source: Mangrove forest – it tolerates salty water.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: The Serengeti plain is an example of which vegetation zone? A: Savannah – open grassland with scattered trees.
chunks.source: Savannah – open grassland with scattered trees.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: What type of vegetation is found on high mountains such as Mount Elgon? A: Montane – altitude creates cooler, wetter conditions.
chunks.source: Montane – altitude creates cooler, wetter conditions.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: The Veld in South Africa is a type of what? A: Grassland – temperate grassland with few trees.
chunks.source: Grassland – temperate grassland with few trees.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Which zone covers the Sahara and has very little plant life? A: Desert – low rainfall limits plant growth.
chunks.source: Desert – low rainfall limits plant growth.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Give one example of a plant adaptation in the desert. A: Succulent stems store water – a desert plant adaptation.
chunks.source: Succulent stems store water – a desert plant adaptation.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Why does the equatorial forest have many layers of trees? A: High rainfall and constant warmth allow dense growth – multiple canopy layers.
chunks.source: High rainfall and constant warmth allow dense growth – multiple canopy layers.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Why Vegetation Grows Differently. I can explain the factors that influence where different vegetation grows in Africa. Vegetation distribution depends on climate, soil, relief, altitude, rainfall, and human activity; each factor influences plant growth and where species can survive. Keywords: factor: something that causes a result; soil: the top layer of earth where plants grow; climate: average weather over a long time; relief: the shape and height of the land; altitude: height above sea level; rainfall: amount of rain that falls; human activity: things people do that change the land; distribution: how something is spread out; growth: the process of increasing in size; nature: the natural world and its processes
chunks.source: Vegetation distribution depends on climate, soil, relief, altitude, rainfall, and human activity; each factor influences plant growth and where species can survive.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Name the most important factor that determines vegetation type in Africa. A: Climate – especially rainfall and temperature.
chunks.source: Climate – especially rainfall and temperature.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: How does soil type affect vegetation? A: Fertile soil supports dense forests; sandy soil supports grassland.
chunks.source: Fertile soil supports dense forests; sandy soil supports grassland.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: What is relief and how does it influence vegetation? A: Relief is the shape of the land; mountains create cooler, wetter conditions for montane vegetation.
chunks.source: Relief is the shape of the land; mountains create cooler, wetter conditions for montane vegetation.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Explain the effect of altitude on plant growth. A: Higher altitude lowers temperature, slowing plant growth and changing species.
chunks.source: Higher altitude lowers temperature, slowing plant growth and changing species.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Give two examples of human activity that change vegetation distribution. A: Deforestation for farming and urban expansion.
chunks.source: Deforestation for farming and urban expansion.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Why do areas with high rainfall have forests? A: Abundant water allows trees to grow tall and form dense canopy.
chunks.source: Abundant water allows trees to grow tall and form dense canopy.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: What happens to soil when trees are cut down? A: Soil is exposed to rain and wind, causing erosion.
chunks.source: Soil is exposed to rain and wind, causing erosion.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Describe how climate and soil together shape the savannah. A: Seasonal rainfall and well‑drained soils favour grasses with scattered trees.
chunks.source: Seasonal rainfall and well‑drained soils favour grasses with scattered trees.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Animals of the Vegetation Zones. I can match animals to their vegetation zones and explain why populations differ. Animals such as elephant, giraffe, lion, and zebra live in specific vegetation zones; their populations depend on habitat quality, food availability, and protection from poaching. Keywords: animal: a living creature that moves and eats; elephant: large grey mammal with a trunk; giraffe: tall animal with a long neck; lion: big cat that hunts in groups; zebra: striped horse‑like animal; habitat: the natural home of an animal; graze: to eat grass; wild: living in nature, not tamed; species: a group of similar animals that can breed; population: number of individuals of a species in an area
chunks.source: Animals such as elephant, giraffe, lion, and zebra live in specific vegetation zones; their populations depend on habitat quality, food availability, and protection from poaching.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Which animal grazes on savannah grass? A: Zebra – it feeds on grass in open grassland.
chunks.source: Zebra – it feeds on grass in open grassland.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Why do lions live in the savannah? A: Savannah has many herbivores like zebra for lions to hunt.
chunks.source: Savannah has many herbivores like zebra for lions to hunt.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Name one animal adapted to montane habitat. A: Mountain gorilla – lives in cool, forested highlands.
chunks.source: Mountain gorilla – lives in cool, forested highlands.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: What is the main threat to elephant population in unprotected areas? A: Poaching for ivory reduces numbers.
chunks.source: Poaching for ivory reduces numbers.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: How does habitat loss affect a species? A: Reduces food and shelter, causing population decline.
chunks.source: Reduces food and shelter, causing population decline.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Give an example of a wild animal that browses on trees. A: Elephant – eats leaves, bark, and branches.
chunks.source: Elephant – eats leaves, bark, and branches.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Why are giraffes absent from dense rainforest? A: They need open space and tall trees for feeding.
chunks.source: They need open space and tall trees for feeding.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Define population in ecology. A: Number of individuals of a species in a given area.
chunks.source: Number of individuals of a species in a given area.

chunks.id: L-P7-Social-Game Parks and Caring for Wild Animals
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: Game Parks and Caring for Wild Animals
chunks.text: Game Parks and Caring for Wild Animals. I can explain the importance of game parks, the problems they face, and ways to care for wild animals. Game parks protect wildlife through rangers, wardens, anti‑poaching laws, feeding, treatment, and habitat preservation; responsible tourism provides essential funding. Keywords: game park: protected area where wild animals live; game ranger: person who patrols and protects the park; game warden: official in charge of the park; protection: keeping something safe from harm; feeding: giving food to animals; treatment: medical care for sick or injured animals; preserve: to keep something in its original state; habitat: natural home of an animal; tourism: travel for pleasure to see wildlife; poaching: illegal hunting of wild animals
chunks.source: Game parks protect wildlife through rangers, wardens, anti‑poaching laws, feeding, treatment, and habitat preservation; responsible tourism provides essential funding.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-Game Parks and Caring for Wild Animals
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: Game Parks and Caring for Wild Animals
chunks.text: Q: What is the main purpose of a game park? A: Protection of wild animals and their habitat.
chunks.source: Protection of wild animals and their habitat.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-Game Parks and Caring for Wild Animals
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: Game Parks and Caring for Wild Animals
chunks.text: Q: Name two duties of a game ranger. A: Patrol to stop poaching and monitor animal health.
chunks.source: Patrol to stop poaching and monitor animal health.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-Game Parks and Caring for Wild Animals
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: Game Parks and Caring for Wild Animals
chunks.text: Q: How does tourism support conservation? A: Revenue funds protection, feeding, and treatment programs.
chunks.source: Revenue funds protection, feeding, and treatment programs.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-Game Parks and Caring for Wild Animals
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: Game Parks and Caring for Wild Animals
chunks.text: Q: Define poaching. A: Illegal hunting of wild animals.
chunks.source: Illegal hunting of wild animals.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-Game Parks and Caring for Wild Animals
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: Game Parks and Caring for Wild Animals
chunks.text: Q: Give one method used to preserve habitat in a park. A: Controlled burning to maintain grassland.
chunks.source: Controlled burning to maintain grassland.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-Game Parks and Caring for Wild Animals
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: Game Parks and Caring for Wild Animals
chunks.text: Q: Why is feeding sometimes necessary in parks? A: During drought natural food is scarce.
chunks.source: During drought natural food is scarce.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-Game Parks and Caring for Wild Animals
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: Game Parks and Caring for Wild Animals
chunks.text: Q: What is the role of a game warden? A: Overall management, law enforcement, and staff supervision.
chunks.source: Overall management, law enforcement, and staff supervision.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-Game Parks and Caring for Wild Animals
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: Game Parks and Caring for Wild Animals
chunks.text: Q: Explain how treatment helps animal populations. A: Medical care saves injured or sick individuals, keeping populations stable.
chunks.source: Medical care saves injured or sick individuals, keeping populations stable.

chunks.id: L-P7-Social-Explorers and Slave Traders in Africa
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: Explorers and Slave Traders in Africa
chunks.text: Explorers and Slave Traders in Africa. I can explain why European explorers and traders came to Africa and describe the triangular slave trade and its effects. European **explorer**s and **trader**s came for **ivory** and other **goods**, but the **slave trade** and **triangular trade** across the **Atlantic** caused massive **capture** of **slave**s and deep harm to African societies. Keywords: explorer: a person who travels to unknown places to learn; trader: someone who buys and sells goods; slave trade: the buying and selling of people as slaves; slave: a person owned by another and forced to work; triangular trade: a three‑part trade route linking Europe, Africa and the Americas; atlantic: the ocean between Africa, Europe and the Americas; coast: the land beside the sea; ivory: hard white material from elephant tusks; goods: items that are bought and sold; capture: to catch and take by force
chunks.source: European **explorer**s and **trader**s came for **ivory** and other **goods**, but the **slave trade** and **triangular trade** across the **Atlantic** caused massive **capture** of **slave**s and deep harm to African societies.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-Explorers and Slave Traders in Africa
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: Explorers and Slave Traders in Africa
chunks.text: Q: Name two **goods** European **trader**s brought to Africa. A: **Goods** included cloth, guns, beads and alcohol. (Reason: these were exchanged for **ivory** and **slave**s.)
chunks.source: **Goods** included cloth, guns, beads and alcohol. (Reason: these were exchanged for **ivory** and **slave**s.)

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-Explorers and Slave Traders in Africa
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: Explorers and Slave Traders in Africa
chunks.text: Q: What is the **triangular trade**? Describe its three legs. A: Europe → Africa (goods for slaves), Africa → Americas (slaves), Americas → Europe (sugar, cotton). (Reason: matches the definition of **triangular trade**.)
chunks.source: Europe → Africa (goods for slaves), Africa → Americas (slaves), Americas → Europe (sugar, cotton). (Reason: matches the definition of **triangular trade**.)

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-Explorers and Slave Traders in Africa
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: Explorers and Slave Traders in Africa
chunks.text: Q: Explain the meaning of **capture** in the context of the **slave trade**. A: **Capture** means seizing people by force to sell as **slave**s. (Reason: direct definition.)
chunks.source: **Capture** means seizing people by force to sell as **slave**s. (Reason: direct definition.)

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-Explorers and Slave Traders in Africa
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: Explorers and Slave Traders in Africa
chunks.text: Q: Which ocean did the **slave** ships cross? A: The **Atlantic** Ocean. (Reason: the **triangular trade** crossed the **Atlantic**.)
chunks.source: The **Atlantic** Ocean. (Reason: the **triangular trade** crossed the **Atlantic**.)

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-Explorers and Slave Traders in Africa
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: Explorers and Slave Traders in Africa
chunks.text: Q: Give one effect of the **slave trade** on African villages. A: Loss of young people and broken families. (Reason: major social disruption.)
chunks.source: Loss of young people and broken families. (Reason: major social disruption.)

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-Explorers and Slave Traders in Africa
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: Explorers and Slave Traders in Africa
chunks.text: Q: Why did **explorer**s map the African **coast**? A: To find safe harbours for **trader** ships and locate **ivory** sources. (Reason: practical trade needs.)
chunks.source: To find safe harbours for **trader** ships and locate **ivory** sources. (Reason: practical trade needs.)

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-Explorers and Slave Traders in Africa
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: Explorers and Slave Traders in Africa
chunks.text: Q: Define **ivory** and state why it was valuable. A: **Ivory** is elephant tusk material, prized for ornaments and piano keys. (Reason: high demand in Europe.)
chunks.source: **Ivory** is elephant tusk material, prized for ornaments and piano keys. (Reason: high demand in Europe.)

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-Explorers and Slave Traders in Africa
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: Explorers and Slave Traders in Africa
chunks.text: Q: What does **slave trade** mean? A: The buying and selling of human beings as property. (Reason: core definition.)
chunks.source: The buying and selling of human beings as property. (Reason: core definition.)

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-Explorers and Slave Traders in Africa
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: Explorers and Slave Traders in Africa
chunks.text: Q: State one reason the **triangular trade** was profitable for European merchants. A: They sold **goods** in Africa, **slave**s in the Americas, and brought back valuable crops. (Reason: three‑way profit.)
chunks.source: They sold **goods** in Africa, **slave**s in the Americas, and brought back valuable crops. (Reason: three‑way profit.)

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-Explorers and Slave Traders in Africa
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: Explorers and Slave Traders in Africa
chunks.text: Q: How did the **slave trade** affect African political systems? A: It weakened some kingdoms and strengthened others who cooperated with **trader**s. (Reason: shift in power.)
chunks.source: It weakened some kingdoms and strengthened others who cooperated with **trader**s. (Reason: shift in power.)

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Missionaries and Settlers in Africa. I can describe the work of European missionaries and settlers, and explain the causes and effects of the Great Trek in South Africa. **Missionary**s spread **christianity**, built **church**es and **school**s, and wrote African **language**s, affecting **culture**. The **great trek** was a **journey** by Boer **settler**s fleeing British rule, creating new republics and causing land conflicts in **south africa**. Keywords: missionary: a person sent to spread religion; settler: someone who moves to a new land to live permanently; great trek: the mass migration of Boer families northwards in the 1830s; south africa: the country at the southern tip of Africa; church: a building for Christian worship; school: a place where children learn; christianity: the religion based on Jesus Christ; language: the system of words people use; culture: the way of life of a group; journey: a long trip from one place to another
chunks.source: **Missionary**s spread **christianity**, built **church**es and **school**s, and wrote African **language**s, affecting **culture**. The **great trek** was a **journey** by Boer **settler**s fleeing British rule, creating new republics and causing land conflicts in **south africa**.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: State two activities of **missionary**s in Africa. A: They built **church**es and **school**s, and translated the Bible into local **language**s. (Reason: core missionary work.)
chunks.source: They built **church**es and **school**s, and translated the Bible into local **language**s. (Reason: core missionary work.)

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Why did **missionary**s write African **language**s? A: To teach reading and spread **christianity**. (Reason: education and religion.)
chunks.source: To teach reading and spread **christianity**. (Reason: education and religion.)

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Define **settler**. A: A person who moves to a new area to live permanently. (Reason: definition.)
chunks.source: A person who moves to a new area to live permanently. (Reason: definition.)

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: What was the **great trek**? A: A mass migration of Boer **settler**s northwards in the 1830s. (Reason: historical event.)
chunks.source: A mass migration of Boer **settler**s northwards in the 1830s. (Reason: historical event.)

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Give two causes of the **great trek**. A: British rule at the Cape and shortage of land. (Reason: push factors.)
chunks.source: British rule at the Cape and shortage of land. (Reason: push factors.)

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Describe one hardship faced during the **great trek** journey. A: Disease, attacks, and rough terrain. (Reason: typical journey difficulties.)
chunks.source: Disease, attacks, and rough terrain. (Reason: typical journey difficulties.)

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Name two republics formed after the **great trek**. A: Transvaal and Orange Free State. (Reason: historical outcome.)
chunks.source: Transvaal and Orange Free State. (Reason: historical outcome.)

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: How did the **great trek** affect African communities? A: Loss of grazing land and wars with Boer **settler**s. (Reason: land dispossession.)
chunks.source: Loss of grazing land and wars with Boer **settler**s. (Reason: land dispossession.)

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: What is one way **missionary** schools changed African **culture**? A: Introduced Western education and new religious ideas. (Reason: cultural impact.)
chunks.source: Introduced Western education and new religious ideas. (Reason: cultural impact.)

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Why is the **great trek** important in South African history? A: It shaped the political map and led to Boer republics. (Reason: long‑term effect.)
chunks.source: It shaped the political map and led to Boer republics. (Reason: long‑term effect.)

chunks.id: L-P7-Social-The Scramble and Partition of Africa
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: The Scramble and Partition of Africa
chunks.text: The Scramble and Partition of Africa. I can explain how colonialists scrambled for Africa, the methods they used to acquire colonies, and how they established colonial rule. The **scramble** and **partition** carved Africa into **colony**s. **Colonialist**s used **method**s like treaties and force, drew **boundary** lines, appointed **governor**s to **administer** **rule**, and faced African **resistance**. Keywords: scramble: the rush by European powers to claim African territory; partition: the division of Africa among European countries; colony: a territory controlled by a foreign power; colonialist: a person who supports or practices colonialism; boundary: a line marking the edge of a territory; administer: to manage and govern a territory; governor: the official who heads a colony; method: a way of doing something; resistance: opposition to foreign rule; rule: the exercise of authority over a territory
chunks.source: The **scramble** and **partition** carved Africa into **colony**s. **Colonialist**s used **method**s like treaties and force, drew **boundary** lines, appointed **governor**s to **administer** **rule**, and faced African **resistance**.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-The Scramble and Partition of Africa
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: The Scramble and Partition of Africa
chunks.text: Q: Define **scramble** in the context of African history. A: The rapid rush by European powers to claim African territory in the 1880s. (Reason: definition.)
chunks.source: The rapid rush by European powers to claim African territory in the 1880s. (Reason: definition.)

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-The Scramble and Partition of Africa
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: The Scramble and Partition of Africa
chunks.text: Q: What was the **partition** of Africa? A: The division of the continent among European countries at the Berlin Conference. (Reason: key event.)
chunks.source: The division of the continent among European countries at the Berlin Conference. (Reason: key event.)

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-The Scramble and Partition of Africa
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: The Scramble and Partition of Africa
chunks.text: Q: Give two **method**s used to acquire colonies. A: Treaties with chiefs and military force. (Reason: common methods.)
chunks.source: Treaties with chiefs and military force. (Reason: common methods.)

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-The Scramble and Partition of Africa
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: The Scramble and Partition of Africa
chunks.text: Q: Explain the term **boundary** as used in colonial Africa. A: A line drawn by Europeans to mark the limits of a **colony**, often ignoring ethnic groups. (Reason: impact of boundaries.)
chunks.source: A line drawn by Europeans to mark the limits of a **colony**, often ignoring ethnic groups. (Reason: impact of boundaries.)

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-The Scramble and Partition of Africa
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: The Scramble and Partition of Africa
chunks.text: Q: Who was the **governor** and what did he do? A: The senior colonial official who **administer**ed the **colony** on behalf of the metropolitan power. (Reason: role description.)
chunks.source: The senior colonial official who **administer**ed the **colony** on behalf of the metropolitan power. (Reason: role description.)

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-The Scramble and Partition of Africa
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: The Scramble and Partition of Africa
chunks.text: Q: Name one form of African **resistance** to colonial **rule**. A: Armed uprisings such as the Maji Maji rebellion. (Reason: example of resistance.)
chunks.source: Armed uprisings such as the Maji Maji rebellion. (Reason: example of resistance.)

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-The Scramble and Partition of Africa
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: The Scramble and Partition of Africa
chunks.text: Q: Why were many treaties signed with chiefs considered unfair? A: Chiefs often did not understand the terms, and treaties ceded sovereignty. (Reason: nature of treaties.)
chunks.source: Chiefs often did not understand the terms, and treaties ceded sovereignty. (Reason: nature of treaties.)

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-The Scramble and Partition of Africa
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: The Scramble and Partition of Africa
chunks.text: Q: What was the effect of the Berlin Conference on African **boundary** lines? A: It formalised arbitrary borders that split communities. (Reason: long‑term consequence.)
chunks.source: It formalised arbitrary borders that split communities. (Reason: long‑term consequence.)

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-The Scramble and Partition of Africa
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: The Scramble and Partition of Africa
chunks.text: Q: Describe how a **colonialist** company (e.g., IBEA) helped establish a **colony**. A: It obtained a charter, signed treaties, and administered territory before the government took over. (Reason: company role.)
chunks.source: It obtained a charter, signed treaties, and administered territory before the government took over. (Reason: company role.)

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-The Scramble and Partition of Africa
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: The Scramble and Partition of Africa
chunks.text: Q: State one reason why colonial **rule** faced **resistance**. A: Loss of land, forced labour and taxes angered Africans. (Reason: causes of resistance.)
chunks.source: Loss of land, forced labour and taxes angered Africans. (Reason: causes of resistance.)

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: How Foreign Influence Changed Africa. I can describe the effects of foreign influence on Africa: loss of independence, exploitation of raw materials, new crops and infrastructure, and new religions and languages. Foreign **influence** caused **exploitation** of **raw material**, loss of **independence**, but also built **infrastructure** like the **railway**, introduced new **crop**s, and spread **religion** and **language** — a mixed **effect** still felt today. Keywords: influence: the power to affect change; exploitation: using resources or people unfairly for profit; raw material: natural resources like minerals and timber; infrastructure: basic facilities like roads, railways, ports; railway: a track for trains to carry goods and people; religion: a system of faith and worship; language: the system of communication used by a community; crop: a plant grown for food or sale; independence: freedom from foreign control; effect: a result or consequence of an action
chunks.source: Foreign **influence** caused **exploitation** of **raw material**, loss of **independence**, but also built **infrastructure** like the **railway**, introduced new **crop**s, and spread **religion** and **language** — a mixed **effect** still felt today.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Define **exploitation** in the colonial context. A: Unfair use of African **raw material** and labour for European profit. (Reason: definition.)
chunks.source: Unfair use of African **raw material** and labour for European profit. (Reason: definition.)

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Name two **raw material**s taken from Africa during colonial rule. A: Gold, copper, ivory, timber, rubber. (Reason: examples.)
chunks.source: Gold, copper, ivory, timber, rubber. (Reason: examples.)

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: What is **infrastructure**? Give one colonial example. A: Basic facilities like roads, **railway**, ports. Example: Uganda Railway. (Reason: definition and example.)
chunks.source: Basic facilities like roads, **railway**, ports. Example: Uganda Railway. (Reason: definition and example.)

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: How did the **railway** change trade in East Africa? A: It linked the interior to the coast, lowering transport costs for **raw material** and **crop** exports. (Reason: economic impact.)
chunks.source: It linked the interior to the coast, lowering transport costs for **raw material** and **crop** exports. (Reason: economic impact.)

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: State one new **crop** introduced by colonial powers. A: Coffee, tea, cotton, sisal. (Reason: cash crops.)
chunks.source: Coffee, tea, cotton, sisal. (Reason: cash crops.)

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Explain how **religion** spread during colonial times. A: Through **missionary** schools, hospitals and conversion campaigns. (Reason: mechanisms.)
chunks.source: Through **missionary** schools, hospitals and conversion campaigns. (Reason: mechanisms.)

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: What role did European **language**s play after colonisation? A: They became official languages for administration, education and law. (Reason: lasting legacy.)
chunks.source: They became official languages for administration, education and law. (Reason: lasting legacy.)

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Give one negative **effect** of colonial **influence** on African **independence**. A: Loss of political sovereignty and forced labour. (Reason: direct consequence.)
chunks.source: Loss of political sovereignty and forced labour. (Reason: direct consequence.)

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Give one positive **effect** of colonial **influence** still seen today. A: Transport **infrastructure** (e.g., **railway** lines) and introduction of cash **crop**s. (Reason: enduring benefits.)
chunks.source: Transport **infrastructure** (e.g., **railway** lines) and introduction of cash **crop**s. (Reason: enduring benefits.)

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Why is the **effect** of foreign **influence** described as mixed? A: Because it brought both **exploitation** and new **infrastructure**, **religion**, **language** and **crop**s. (Reason: balanced view.)
chunks.source: Because it brought both **exploitation** and new **infrastructure**, **religion**, **language** and **crop**s. (Reason: balanced view.)

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Pan-Africanism and Nationalism. I can explain the meaning of Pan-Africanism, nationalism and patriotism, and describe how Pan-Africanists and nationalists worked to unite and free Africa. **Pan-africanism** united **African** **leaders** in a **movement** for **freedom**. **Nationalism** fought for each country's **independence**. **Patriotism** builds the nation daily with **pride** and **unity**. Keywords: pan-africanism: the idea that all African people should unite and work together; nationalism: strong love for one's own country and the wish to govern it; patriotism: love for your country shown by working for its good; unity: people joining together as one; pride: a feeling of honour in who you are; movement: a group of people working together for a cause; african: belonging to Africa or its people; freedom: the power to act, speak and choose without control; independence: a country ruling itself without foreign control; leader: a person who guides or directs others
chunks.source: **Pan-africanism** united **African** **leaders** in a **movement** for **freedom**. **Nationalism** fought for each country's **independence**. **Patriotism** builds the nation daily with **pride** and **unity**.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Define **pan-africanism** in your own words. A: **Pan-africanism** is the belief that all African people should unite and work together for common **freedom** and progress.
chunks.source: **Pan-africanism** is the belief that all African people should unite and work together for common **freedom** and progress.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Explain the difference between **nationalism** and **patriotism**. A: **Nationalism** is the political desire for **self-rule** and **independence**; **patriotism** is the daily practice of loving your country through actions like keeping it clean and obeying laws.
chunks.source: **Nationalism** is the political desire for **self-rule** and **independence**; **patriotism** is the daily practice of loving your country through actions like keeping it clean and obeying laws.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Why was **unity** important for the independence **movement**? A: **Unity** allowed **African** **leaders** to share strategies, support each other at the UN, and present a strong front against colonial powers.
chunks.source: **Unity** allowed **African** **leaders** to share strategies, support each other at the UN, and present a strong front against colonial powers.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Give one example of **patriotism** in Uganda today. A: Paying taxes, protecting wetlands, voting, or volunteering in community clean-ups.
chunks.source: Paying taxes, protecting wetlands, voting, or volunteering in community clean-ups.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Name two **leaders** who promoted **pan-africanism**. A: Kwame Nkrumah, Julius Nyerere, Jomo Kenyatta, Haile Selassie, or Nelson Mandela.
chunks.source: Kwame Nkrumah, Julius Nyerere, Jomo Kenyatta, Haile Selassie, or Nelson Mandela.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: How did **nationalism** grow in Uganda before **independence**? A: Through protests like the 1949 cotton boycott, formation of political parties (UNC, DP, UPC), and demands for African representation in Legco.
chunks.source: Through protests like the 1949 cotton boycott, formation of political parties (UNC, DP, UPC), and demands for African representation in Legco.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: What does **pride** have to do with **pan-africanism**? A: **Pride** in being **African** gave people the confidence to reject colonial inferiority and demand **freedom**.
chunks.source: **Pride** in being **African** gave people the confidence to reject colonial inferiority and demand **freedom**.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: If a country achieves **independence** but ignores **pan-africanism**, what risk does it face? A: Isolation, border conflicts, weak trade, and loss of collective bargaining power in world affairs.
chunks.source: Isolation, border conflicts, weak trade, and loss of collective bargaining power in world affairs.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Complete: The **movement** for ______ succeeded because ______ and ______ walked together. A: The **movement** for **independence** succeeded because **unity** and **pride** walked together.
chunks.source: The **movement** for **independence** succeeded because **unity** and **pride** walked together.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: PLE-style: 'Pan-Africanism promoted African unity.' Support this statement with two historical facts. A: 1. The 1945 Manchester Pan-African Congress united future **leaders** like Nkrumah and Kenyatta. 2. The OAU (1963) was formed to coordinate liberation struggles across the continent.
chunks.source: 1. The 1945 Manchester Pan-African Congress united future **leaders** like Nkrumah and Kenyatta. 2. The OAU (1963) was formed to coordinate liberation struggles across the continent.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Why Africans Demanded Independence. I can explain why Africans demanded independence: to control their natural resources and land, stop exploitation and oppression, and regain their dignity and rights. Africans **demand**ed **independence** to control **resources** and **land**, stop **exploitation** and **oppression**, and regain **dignity**, **equality**, **rights**, and **self-rule**. Keywords: demand: to ask for something firmly as your right; resource: something valuable a country owns like minerals, forests, or water; land: the ground people live on and farm; exploitation: using someone unfairly for your own gain; oppression: cruel or unfair treatment by people in power; dignity: the feeling that you deserve respect; equality: being treated the same as everyone else; rights: things you are allowed to do or have by law; discrimination: treating people differently because of race or tribe; self-rule: a country governing itself
chunks.source: Africans **demand**ed **independence** to control **resources** and **land**, stop **exploitation** and **oppression**, and regain **dignity**, **equality**, **rights**, and **self-rule**.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: State two **resources** Uganda lost control of during colonial rule. A: Cotton, coffee, copper, land, or timber — any two.
chunks.source: Cotton, coffee, copper, land, or timber — any two.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Explain how the **hut tax** was a form of **oppression**. A: It forced Africans into wage labour on European farms or mines to earn cash, disrupting family farming and **dignity**.
chunks.source: It forced Africans into wage labour on European farms or mines to earn cash, disrupting family farming and **dignity**.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Give one example of **discrimination** in colonial Uganda. A: Separate hospitals, schools, residential areas (e.g. Kololo for Europeans, Kisenyi for Africans), or different pay for same work.
chunks.source: Separate hospitals, schools, residential areas (e.g. Kololo for Europeans, Kisenyi for Africans), or different pay for same work.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Why did Africans **demand** control of their **land**? A: Colonial laws (Crown Lands Ordinance 1903) declared 'vacant' land Crown property, allowing allocation to European settlers, pushing Africans to reserves.
chunks.source: Colonial laws (Crown Lands Ordinance 1903) declared 'vacant' land Crown property, allowing allocation to European settlers, pushing Africans to reserves.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: How did **exploitation** of **resources** fuel **nationalism**? A: Farmers saw their coffee/cotton sold abroad at high profits while they received low fixed prices, creating anger and political organisation.
chunks.source: Farmers saw their coffee/cotton sold abroad at high profits while they received low fixed prices, creating anger and political organisation.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Define **self-rule** in the context of the independence struggle. A: **Self-rule** means Africans making their own laws, controlling the budget, managing **resources** and **land**, without a colonial Governor's veto.
chunks.source: **Self-rule** means Africans making their own laws, controlling the budget, managing **resources** and **land**, without a colonial Governor's veto.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: What is the link between **dignity** and the **demand** for **equality**? A: **Discrimination** (separate benches, passes, schools) told Africans they were inferior. **Demand**ing **equality** was **demand**ing back their **dignity**.
chunks.source: **Discrimination** (separate benches, passes, schools) told Africans they were inferior. **Demand**ing **equality** was **demand**ing back their **dignity**.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: PLE-style: 'The colonial economy was designed to benefit the coloniser.' Support with two Ugandan examples. A: 1. Marketing boards fixed low producer prices for cotton/coffee. 2. Railway built from coast to interior to extract **resources**, not link African markets.
chunks.source: 1. Marketing boards fixed low producer prices for cotton/coffee. 2. Railway built from coast to interior to extract **resources**, not link African markets.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Complete: The **demand** for **independence** was a **demand** for ______, ______, ______, and ______. A: The **demand** for **independence** was a **demand** for **dignity**, **equality**, **rights**, and **self-rule**.
chunks.source: The **demand** for **independence** was a **demand** for **dignity**, **equality**, **rights**, and **self-rule**.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Worked example: A PLE question asks: 'Why did the Bataka movement protest in the 1940s?' Model answer: 'They protested against the colonial government's control of **land** and **resources** (cotton/ginneries) which caused **exploitation** and loss of **dignity**. They wanted **self-rule** over Buganda's affairs.' A: undefined

chunks.id: L-P7-Social-Heroes Who Fought for Africa's Freedom
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: Heroes Who Fought for Africa's Freedom
chunks.text: Heroes Who Fought for Africa's Freedom. I can identify leading Pan-Africanists and nationalists, name the countries they fought for, and explain their contributions to Africa's freedom. **Marcus Garvey** (vision), **Kwame Nkrumah** (**Ghana**, action), **Haile Selassie** (**Ethiopia**, diplomacy), **Patrice Lumumba** (Congo, **resources**), **Nelson Mandela** (**South Africa**, reconciliation) — five **heroes**, one **struggle** for **freedom**. Keywords: hero: a person admired for courage and great deeds; kwame nkrumah: first President of Ghana and leading Pan-Africanist; nelson mandela: anti-apartheid leader and first Black President of South Africa; marcus garvey: Jamaican Pan-Africanist who founded the UNIA; haile selassie: Emperor of Ethiopia who defended independence and supported African unity; patrice lumumba: first Prime Minister of independent Congo, killed for his stand; ghana: first sub-Saharan African country to gain independence; south africa: country where apartheid ruled until 1994; ethiopia: ancient African empire never colonised except brief Italian occupation; struggle: a long, hard effort to achieve something
chunks.source: **Marcus Garvey** (vision), **Kwame Nkrumah** (**Ghana**, action), **Haile Selassie** (**Ethiopia**, diplomacy), **Patrice Lumumba** (Congo, **resources**), **Nelson Mandela** (**South Africa**, reconciliation) — five **heroes**, one **struggle** for **freedom**.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-Heroes Who Fought for Africa's Freedom
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: Heroes Who Fought for Africa's Freedom
chunks.text: Q: Match each **hero** to their country: **Kwame Nkrumah**, **Nelson Mandela**, **Patrice Lumumba**, **Haile Selassie**. A: **Kwame Nkrumah** — **Ghana**; **Nelson Mandela** — **South Africa**; **Patrice Lumumba** — Congo (DRC); **Haile Selassie** — **Ethiopia**.
chunks.source: **Kwame Nkrumah** — **Ghana**; **Nelson Mandela** — **South Africa**; **Patrice Lumumba** — Congo (DRC); **Haile Selassie** — **Ethiopia**.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-Heroes Who Fought for Africa's Freedom
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: Heroes Who Fought for Africa's Freedom
chunks.text: Q: State one contribution of **Marcus Garvey** to **pan-africanism**. A: Founded UNIA (1914), promoted 'Africa for the Africans', inspired mass Black pride and future **leaders** like **Nkrumah**.
chunks.source: Founded UNIA (1914), promoted 'Africa for the Africans', inspired mass Black pride and future **leaders** like **Nkrumah**.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-Heroes Who Fought for Africa's Freedom
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: Heroes Who Fought for Africa's Freedom
chunks.text: Q: Why is **Ghana**'s 1957 **independence** a turning point for Africa? A: First sub-Saharan colony free; **Nkrumah** used it as base to fund/train liberation **movements** continent-wide.
chunks.source: First sub-Saharan colony free; **Nkrumah** used it as base to fund/train liberation **movements** continent-wide.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-Heroes Who Fought for Africa's Freedom
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: Heroes Who Fought for Africa's Freedom
chunks.text: Q: What was **Patrice Lumumba**'s famous stand at **independence**? A: He denounced Belgian colonialism in his speech, demanding Congo's **resources** benefit Congolese, not foreign companies.
chunks.source: He denounced Belgian colonialism in his speech, demanding Congo's **resources** benefit Congolese, not foreign companies.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-Heroes Who Fought for Africa's Freedom
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: Heroes Who Fought for Africa's Freedom
chunks.text: Q: How did **Haile Selassie** support African unity? A: Hosted 1963 OAU founding summit in Addis Ababa; advocated collective security and decolonisation at UN and League of Nations.
chunks.source: Hosted 1963 OAU founding summit in Addis Ababa; advocated collective security and decolonisation at UN and League of Nations.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-Heroes Who Fought for Africa's Freedom
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: Heroes Who Fought for Africa's Freedom
chunks.text: Q: Explain why **Nelson Mandela** is a global **hero**. A: Led anti-apartheid **struggle**, endured 27 years prison, negotiated peaceful transition, became first Black President, preached reconciliation.
chunks.source: Led anti-apartheid **struggle**, endured 27 years prison, negotiated peaceful transition, became first Black President, preached reconciliation.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-Heroes Who Fought for Africa's Freedom
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: Heroes Who Fought for Africa's Freedom
chunks.text: Q: PLE-style: 'The **struggle** for **freedom** in **South Africa** was different from **Ghana**.' Give two differences. A: 1. **Ghana**: constitutional negotiations, 1957 **independence**. **South Africa**: armed **struggle**, apartheid ended 1994. 2. **Ghana**: British colony. **South Africa**: settler colony with white minority rule.
chunks.source: 1. **Ghana**: constitutional negotiations, 1957 **independence**. **South Africa**: armed **struggle**, apartheid ended 1994. 2. **Ghana**: British colony. **South Africa**: settler colony with white minority rule.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-Heroes Who Fought for Africa's Freedom
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: Heroes Who Fought for Africa's Freedom
chunks.text: Q: Worked example: 'Explain how **Marcus Garvey** influenced **Kwame Nkrumah**.' Model answer: '**Garvey**'s UNIA and 'Back to Africa' ideology shaped **Nkrumah**'s **pan-africanism**. **Nkrumah** read *Negro World* in the US, adopted Garvey's mass mobilisation tactics, and named Ghana's shipping line *Black Star* after Garvey's *Black Star Line*.' A: undefined

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-Heroes Who Fought for Africa's Freedom
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: Heroes Who Fought for Africa's Freedom
chunks.text: Q: Complete: **Heroes** of the **struggle** include ______ (diaspora), ______ (**Ghana**), ______ (**Ethiopia**), ______ (Congo), ______ (**South Africa**). A: **Heroes** of the **struggle** include **Marcus Garvey** (diaspora), **Kwame Nkrumah** (**Ghana**), **Haile Selassie** (**Ethiopia**), **Patrice Lumumba** (Congo), **Nelson Mandela** (**South Africa**).
chunks.source: **Heroes** of the **struggle** include **Marcus Garvey** (diaspora), **Kwame Nkrumah** (**Ghana**), **Haile Selassie** (**Ethiopia**), **Patrice Lumumba** (Congo), **Nelson Mandela** (**South Africa**).

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-Heroes Who Fought for Africa's Freedom
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: Heroes Who Fought for Africa's Freedom
chunks.text: Q: If a PLE question asks: 'Name one **hero** who used diplomacy, not war,' who would you choose and why? A: **Haile Selassie** — he appealed to the League of Nations (1936) and hosted the OAU (1963), using diplomacy for African unity.
chunks.source: **Haile Selassie** — he appealed to the League of Nations (1936) and hosted the OAU (1963), using diplomacy for African unity.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Ethiopia and Liberia: Never Colonised. I can explain why Ethiopia and Liberia were never colonised, and compare single-party and multi-party systems in independent Africa. **Ethiopia** (Adwa, **army**, **diplomacy**) and **Liberia** (freed slaves, US link, 1847 **independence**) stayed free. Post-independence, single-**party** sought **unity**; multi-**party** seeks **accountability** for **resources** and **rights**. Keywords: ethiopia: East African empire that defeated Italy at Adwa (1896) and kept independence; liberia: West African state founded by freed American slaves, declared independence 1847; colonised: brought under foreign political control; independence: self-government without foreign rule; king: a male monarch; in Ethiopia, the Emperor; army: organised military force; diplomacy: managing relations between countries through talk; party: an organised political group; government: the system that runs a country; multi-party: a system where several parties compete in elections
chunks.source: **Ethiopia** (Adwa, **army**, **diplomacy**) and **Liberia** (freed slaves, US link, 1847 **independence**) stayed free. Post-independence, single-**party** sought **unity**; multi-**party** seeks **accountability** for **resources** and **rights**.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Give two reasons **Ethiopia** was not **colonised**. A: 1. Victory at Battle of Adwa (1896) under **King** Menelik II. 2. Modern **army** and effective **diplomacy** (League of Nations).
chunks.source: 1. Victory at Battle of Adwa (1896) under **King** Menelik II. 2. Modern **army** and effective **diplomacy** (League of Nations).

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Give two reasons **Liberia** was not **colonised**. A: 1. Founded by freed US slaves (1822), declared **independence** 1847. 2. US protection and European diplomatic recognition deterred colonisation.
chunks.source: 1. Founded by freed US slaves (1822), declared **independence** 1847. 2. US protection and European diplomatic recognition deterred colonisation.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Define single-**party** system. A: A system where only one political **party** is legally allowed to exist and contest elections.
chunks.source: A system where only one political **party** is legally allowed to exist and contest elections.
