chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Define multi-**party** system. A: A system where several political **parties** compete freely in elections for **government**.
chunks.source: A system where several political **parties** compete freely in elections for **government**.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: State one advantage and one disadvantage of single-**party** rule. A: Advantage: national **unity**, rapid decision-making. Disadvantage: no opposition, risk of **oppression**, corruption unchecked.
chunks.source: Advantage: national **unity**, rapid decision-making. Disadvantage: no opposition, risk of **oppression**, corruption unchecked.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: State one advantage and one disadvantage of multi-**party** democracy. A: Advantage: **accountability**, choice, **equality** of voice. Disadvantage: can cause division, slow **government**, coalition instability.
chunks.source: Advantage: **accountability**, choice, **equality** of voice. Disadvantage: can cause division, slow **government**, coalition instability.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: PLE-style: 'The Battle of Adwa (1896) was a turning point for African **nationalism**.' Explain. A: **Ethiopia**'s victory proved a **African** **army** could defeat a European power. It inspired **pan-africanism** and **pride** — **freedom** was possible.
chunks.source: **Ethiopia**'s victory proved a **African** **army** could defeat a European power. It inspired **pan-africanism** and **pride** — **freedom** was possible.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Worked example: 'Compare how **Ethiopia** and **Liberia** maintained **independence**.' Model answer: '**Ethiopia** used military victory (Adwa) and **diplomacy** (League of Nations). **Liberia** relied on US **diplomacy** and early **independence** declaration (1847). Both avoided **colonised** status but through different means: **army** vs great-power shield.' A: undefined

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Complete: **Ethiopia** kept **independence** by ______ and ______; **Liberia** by ______ and ______. A: **Ethiopia** kept **independence** by **army** and **diplomacy**; **Liberia** by US link and early **independence** declaration.
chunks.source: **Ethiopia** kept **independence** by **army** and **diplomacy**; **Liberia** by US link and early **independence** declaration.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Uganda moved to multi-**party** in 2005. Name the referendum that decided this. A: The 2005 national referendum on political systems.
chunks.source: The 2005 national referendum on political systems.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: The Birth of the OAU. I can explain when and why the Organisation of African Unity was formed, name its founder members, and state its objectives. The OAU was formed on 25 May 1963 in Addis Ababa by 32 founder members. Its charter aimed for unity, liberation from colonialism, and cooperation among African states. Keywords: organisation of african unity: a group of African countries working together; oau: short name for Organisation of African Unity; unity: being together as one; founder: a person who starts something; member: a country that belongs to a group; objective: a goal or aim; addis ababa: the capital city of Ethiopia; headquarters: the main office of an organisation; cooperation: working together for a common goal; charter: a written document of rules and goals
chunks.source: The OAU was formed on 25 May 1963 in Addis Ababa by 32 founder members. Its charter aimed for unity, liberation from colonialism, and cooperation among African states.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: In which year was the Organisation of African Unity formed? A: 1963 — The OAU was formed on 25 May 1963.
chunks.source: 1963 — The OAU was formed on 25 May 1963.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Where is the headquarters of the OAU located? A: Addis Ababa, Ethiopia — The headquarters was established in Addis Ababa because Ethiopia was never colonised.
chunks.source: Addis Ababa, Ethiopia — The headquarters was established in Addis Ababa because Ethiopia was never colonised.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Name any two founder members of the OAU. A: Ghana and Egypt (or any two of the 32 founder members) — The charter was signed by 32 independent African states.
chunks.source: Ghana and Egypt (or any two of the 32 founder members) — The charter was signed by 32 independent African states.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: What document established the OAU? A: The OAU Charter — The charter was signed by the heads of state at the Addis Ababa summit.
chunks.source: The OAU Charter — The charter was signed by the heads of state at the Addis Ababa summit.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: State one objective of the OAU. A: To promote unity and solidarity among African states — This is the first objective listed in the charter.
chunks.source: To promote unity and solidarity among African states — This is the first objective listed in the charter.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Why was Addis Ababa chosen as the headquarters? A: Ethiopia was never colonised, making it a symbol of African independence — This historical fact made it the natural choice.
chunks.source: Ethiopia was never colonised, making it a symbol of African independence — This historical fact made it the natural choice.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: How many founder member states signed the OAU Charter? A: 32 — Thirty-two independent African countries attended the 1963 summit.
chunks.source: 32 — Thirty-two independent African countries attended the 1963 summit.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: What does OAU stand for? A: Organisation of African Unity — The full name shows the goal of continental unity.
chunks.source: Organisation of African Unity — The full name shows the goal of continental unity.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Which committee did the OAU create to support liberation movements? A: The Liberation Committee — It coordinated support for freedom fighters in Southern Africa.
chunks.source: The Liberation Committee — It coordinated support for freedom fighters in Southern Africa.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Name the Ethiopian emperor who hosted the 1963 summit. A: Emperor Haile Selassie — He played a key role in bringing African leaders together.
chunks.source: Emperor Haile Selassie — He played a key role in bringing African leaders together.

chunks.id: L-P7-Social-What the OAU Achieved and Where It Failed
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: What the OAU Achieved and Where It Failed
chunks.text: What the OAU Achieved and Where It Failed. I can list the achievements and failures of the OAU and explain how the African Union was formed. The OAU succeeded in ending colonialism and apartheid but failed to stop civil wars due to its non-interference principle. The African Union was formed in 2002 with stronger powers to intervene for peace and security. Keywords: achievement: something done successfully; failure: something that did not succeed; apartheid: a system of racial separation in South Africa; colonialism: control of one country by another; liberation: setting free from oppression; border conflict: fighting over boundary lines; civil war: war between groups within one country; african union: the organisation that replaced the OAU in 2002; peace: absence of war and conflict; formation: the act of creating something
chunks.source: The OAU succeeded in ending colonialism and apartheid but failed to stop civil wars due to its non-interference principle. The African Union was formed in 2002 with stronger powers to intervene for peace and security.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-What the OAU Achieved and Where It Failed
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: What the OAU Achieved and Where It Failed
chunks.text: Q: State two achievements of the OAU. A: 1) Supported liberation movements that ended colonialism in Southern Africa. 2) Played a key role in ending apartheid in South Africa through diplomatic pressure.
chunks.source: 1) Supported liberation movements that ended colonialism in Southern Africa. 2) Played a key role in ending apartheid in South Africa through diplomatic pressure.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-What the OAU Achieved and Where It Failed
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: What the OAU Achieved and Where It Failed
chunks.text: Q: State two failures of the OAU. A: 1) Could not prevent or stop civil wars (e.g. Nigeria, Rwanda) due to non-interference principle. 2) Had no standing army or enforcement mechanism to implement decisions.
chunks.source: 1) Could not prevent or stop civil wars (e.g. Nigeria, Rwanda) due to non-interference principle. 2) Had no standing army or enforcement mechanism to implement decisions.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-What the OAU Achieved and Where It Failed
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: What the OAU Achieved and Where It Failed
chunks.text: Q: In which year was the African Union formed? A: 2002 — The AU was launched in Durban, South Africa, replacing the OAU.
chunks.source: 2002 — The AU was launched in Durban, South Africa, replacing the OAU.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-What the OAU Achieved and Where It Failed
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: What the OAU Achieved and Where It Failed
chunks.text: Q: What was the Sirte Declaration? A: A 1999 declaration by African leaders calling for the establishment of the African Union to replace the OAU.
chunks.source: A 1999 declaration by African leaders calling for the establishment of the African Union to replace the OAU.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-What the OAU Achieved and Where It Failed
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: What the OAU Achieved and Where It Failed
chunks.text: Q: Name one organ of the African Union that the OAU did not have. A: The Peace and Security Council — It can intervene in member states during war crimes, genocide, or crimes against humanity.
chunks.source: The Peace and Security Council — It can intervene in member states during war crimes, genocide, or crimes against humanity.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-What the OAU Achieved and Where It Failed
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: What the OAU Achieved and Where It Failed
chunks.text: Q: Why did the OAU fail to stop the Rwandan genocide? A: The OAU Charter prohibited interference in internal affairs, and the OAU had no rapid deployment force or mandate to intervene.
chunks.source: The OAU Charter prohibited interference in internal affairs, and the OAU had no rapid deployment force or mandate to intervene.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-What the OAU Achieved and Where It Failed
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: What the OAU Achieved and Where It Failed
chunks.text: Q: How did the OAU help end apartheid? A: Through diplomatic isolation, sporting bans, economic sanctions, and consistent pressure at the UN — not military action.
chunks.source: Through diplomatic isolation, sporting bans, economic sanctions, and consistent pressure at the UN — not military action.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-What the OAU Achieved and Where It Failed
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: What the OAU Achieved and Where It Failed
chunks.text: Q: What is the difference between the OAU and AU on intervention? A: The OAU respected non-interference; the AU's Constitutive Act allows intervention in grave circumstances (Article 4(h)).
chunks.source: The OAU respected non-interference; the AU's Constitutive Act allows intervention in grave circumstances (Article 4(h)).

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-What the OAU Achieved and Where It Failed
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: What the OAU Achieved and Where It Failed
chunks.text: Q: Where was the OAU Liberation Committee based? A: Dar es Salaam, Tanzania — It coordinated material and diplomatic support for liberation movements.
chunks.source: Dar es Salaam, Tanzania — It coordinated material and diplomatic support for liberation movements.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-What the OAU Achieved and Where It Failed
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: What the OAU Achieved and Where It Failed
chunks.text: Q: Give one example of a border conflict the OAU tried to resolve. A: The Uganda-Tanzania border conflict (1978) or the Ethiopia-Eritrea border dispute — The OAU mediated but with limited success.
chunks.source: The Uganda-Tanzania border conflict (1978) or the Ethiopia-Eritrea border dispute — The OAU mediated but with limited success.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Africa's Regional Economic Groupings. I can name Africa's main regional economic groupings, their member states, and their work. Africa has five main regional economic groupings: EAC (East Africa), COMESA (Eastern/Southern Africa), ECOWAS (West Africa), SADC (Southern Africa), IGAD (Horn of Africa). Uganda belongs to EAC and COMESA. Each promotes trade and development for its member states. Keywords: economic grouping: countries working together for trade and development; comesa: Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa; ecowas: Economic Community of West African States; sadc: Southern African Development Community; igad: Intergovernmental Authority on Development; eac: East African Community; market: a place or system for buying and selling; trade: buying and selling of goods and services; member state: a country that belongs to an organisation; region: a large area with common features
chunks.source: Africa has five main regional economic groupings: EAC (East Africa), COMESA (Eastern/Southern Africa), ECOWAS (West Africa), SADC (Southern Africa), IGAD (Horn of Africa). Uganda belongs to EAC and COMESA. Each promotes trade and development for its member states.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Name two regional economic groupings that Uganda is a member of. A: EAC and COMESA — Uganda is a founding member of both.
chunks.source: EAC and COMESA — Uganda is a founding member of both.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: What does ECOWAS stand for? A: Economic Community of West African States — It covers the West African region.
chunks.source: Economic Community of West African States — It covers the West African region.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Which grouping covers the Horn of Africa? A: IGAD — Intergovernmental Authority on Development, based in Djibouti.
chunks.source: IGAD — Intergovernmental Authority on Development, based in Djibouti.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: State one aim of the East African Community. A: To create a common market with free movement of goods, services, labour, and capital — Leading to monetary union and political federation.
chunks.source: To create a common market with free movement of goods, services, labour, and capital — Leading to monetary union and political federation.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Where is the headquarters of SADC? A: Gaborone, Botswana — SADC coordinates development in Southern Africa.
chunks.source: Gaborone, Botswana — SADC coordinates development in Southern Africa.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: How many member states does COMESA have? A: 21 — From Egypt to Eswatini, covering Eastern and Southern Africa.
chunks.source: 21 — From Egypt to Eswatini, covering Eastern and Southern Africa.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: What is ECOMOG? A: The ECOWAS Monitoring Group — A peacekeeping force that intervened in Liberia and Sierra Leone.
chunks.source: The ECOWAS Monitoring Group — A peacekeeping force that intervened in Liberia and Sierra Leone.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Name three member states of the EAC. A: Uganda, Kenya, Tanzania (also Rwanda, Burundi, South Sudan, DRC) — The EAC has 7 member states as of 2024.
chunks.source: Uganda, Kenya, Tanzania (also Rwanda, Burundi, South Sudan, DRC) — The EAC has 7 member states as of 2024.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: What is the main difference between a Free Trade Area and a Common Market? A: Free Trade Area: no tariffs on goods. Common Market: adds free movement of services, labour, and capital.
chunks.source: Free Trade Area: no tariffs on goods. Common Market: adds free movement of services, labour, and capital.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Which regional grouping aims for a single currency called the Eco? A: ECOWAS — The Eco is planned for West African monetary union.
chunks.source: ECOWAS — The Eco is planned for West African monetary union.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Working Together: African Cooperation. I can explain the advantages and disadvantages of African economic cooperation and suggest solutions to problems. African cooperation brings advantages (larger market, shared funds, peace) but faces disadvantages (unequal benefits, dependence, funds shortages). Solutions: enforce dues, binding courts, harmonised laws, infrastructure, and political will to stay together. Keywords: cooperation: working together for shared benefit; advantage: a benefit or good point; disadvantage: a drawback or bad point; problem: a difficulty that needs solving; solution: a way to fix a problem; funds: money for a purpose; dependence: relying on others; support: help or backing; conflict: serious disagreement or fighting; together: united, as a group
chunks.source: African cooperation brings advantages (larger market, shared funds, peace) but faces disadvantages (unequal benefits, dependence, funds shortages). Solutions: enforce dues, binding courts, harmonised laws, infrastructure, and political will to stay together.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: State two advantages of economic cooperation among African states. A: 1) Larger market for goods and services. 2) Pooling of resources and funds for large infrastructure projects.
chunks.source: 1) Larger market for goods and services. 2) Pooling of resources and funds for large infrastructure projects.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: State two disadvantages of economic cooperation. A: 1) Stronger economies may dominate weaker ones, creating dependence. 2) Loss of some national policy sovereignty.
chunks.source: 1) Stronger economies may dominate weaker ones, creating dependence. 2) Loss of some national policy sovereignty.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Give two problems facing regional economic groupings in Africa. A: 1) Member states delay or fail to pay subscriptions. 2) Political conflict leads to border closures and disrupted trade.
chunks.source: 1) Member states delay or fail to pay subscriptions. 2) Political conflict leads to border closures and disrupted trade.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Suggest two solutions to the problem of unpaid subscriptions. A: 1) Automatic deduction of dues from shared customs revenue. 2) Penalties like suspension of voting rights for persistent defaulters.
chunks.source: 1) Automatic deduction of dues from shared customs revenue. 2) Penalties like suspension of voting rights for persistent defaulters.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: How does a common market benefit a Ugandan trader? A: Goods move without tariffs across member states, and the trader can work or invest freely in any partner state.
chunks.source: Goods move without tariffs across member states, and the trader can work or invest freely in any partner state.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: What is meant by 'trade imbalance' in regional cooperation? A: When one member state imports far more than it exports to partners, leading to loss of revenue and dependence.
chunks.source: When one member state imports far more than it exports to partners, leading to loss of revenue and dependence.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Name one mechanism for resolving trade disputes in the EAC. A: The East African Court of Justice — It interprets the treaty and settles disputes between member states.
chunks.source: The East African Court of Justice — It interprets the treaty and settles disputes between member states.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Why is political commitment essential for economic cooperation? A: Without peace and stable borders, trade stops, investments flee, and protocols become meaningless.
chunks.source: Without peace and stable borders, trade stops, investments flee, and protocols become meaningless.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: How can harmonisation of standards solve a cooperation problem? A: Common standards allow goods certified in one country to be accepted in all, removing technical barriers to trade.
chunks.source: Common standards allow goods certified in one country to be accepted in all, removing technical barriers to trade.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Give one reason why some African countries depend on foreign donors to fund their regional groupings. A: Member states do not pay their assessed contributions on time, forcing secretariats to seek external funding.
chunks.source: Member states do not pay their assessed contributions on time, forcing secretariats to seek external funding.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Africa's Great Economic Resources. I can name Africa's major economic resources and explain how each one helps development. Africa's major **economic** **resources** are **land**, **soil**, **mineral**, **water**, **people**, **vegetation** and **climate**. Each **resource** contributes to **development** when managed well. **People** are the ultimate **resource** because they use all others. Keywords: economic: to do with money, jobs and production; resource: something useful that a country has; land: the solid ground where we live and farm; soil: the top layer of earth where plants grow; mineral: a valuable substance found in the ground; water: the liquid from rain, rivers and lakes; people: the human beings who work and create; vegetation: all the plants and trees in an area; climate: the usual weather over many years; development: growth and improvement in living standards
chunks.source: Africa's major **economic** **resources** are **land**, **soil**, **mineral**, **water**, **people**, **vegetation** and **climate**. Each **resource** contributes to **development** when managed well. **People** are the ultimate **resource** because they use all others.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Define the term **economic** **resource** and give three examples from Uganda. A: **Economic** **resource** = anything useful for production/wealth. Examples: fertile **soil** (coffee), **water** (Lake Victoria fish), **mineral** (gold in Karamoja). Reason: PLE wants definition + local examples.
chunks.source: **Economic** **resource** = anything useful for production/wealth. Examples: fertile **soil** (coffee), **water** (Lake Victoria fish), **mineral** (gold in Karamoja). Reason: PLE wants definition + local examples.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: State two ways **land** contributes to **development** in your district. A: 1) Farming crops for food/income. 2) Space for schools, markets, roads. Reason: Link **land** to specific **development** activities.
chunks.source: 1) Farming crops for food/income. 2) Space for schools, markets, roads. Reason: Link **land** to specific **development** activities.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Explain why **water** is called a multipurpose **resource** in Uganda. A: Used for fishing, irrigation, **hydro-electric power**, transport, domestic use. Reason: 'Multipurpose' means many uses — list at least three.
chunks.source: Used for fishing, irrigation, **hydro-electric power**, transport, domestic use. Reason: 'Multipurpose' means many uses — list at least three.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: How do **people** act as a **resource** for **economic** **development**? A: Provide labour, skills, entrepreneurship, innovation, management. Reason: **People** activate all other **resources**.
chunks.source: Provide labour, skills, entrepreneurship, innovation, management. Reason: **People** activate all other **resources**.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Name two **mineral** **resources** found in DR Congo and their uses. A: Cobalt (batteries, electronics), Copper (wiring, pipes), Diamonds (jewellery, cutting tools). Reason: Country-specific **mineral** knowledge.
chunks.source: Cobalt (batteries, electronics), Copper (wiring, pipes), Diamonds (jewellery, cutting tools). Reason: Country-specific **mineral** knowledge.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Describe how **vegetation** supports the **economy** of Uganda. A: Timber, cash crops (tea, oil palm), tourism (forests), medicinal plants, fuelwood. Reason: Group uses into categories.
chunks.source: Timber, cash crops (tea, oil palm), tourism (forests), medicinal plants, fuelwood. Reason: Group uses into categories.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Why is **climate** an **economic** **resource** for farmers in Uganda? A: Two rainy seasons = two harvests; warm temps = livestock; sunshine = solar/drying crops. Reason: Connect **climate** features to farm **development**.
chunks.source: Two rainy seasons = two harvests; warm temps = livestock; sunshine = solar/drying crops. Reason: Connect **climate** features to farm **development**.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Give one reason why **soil** conservation is necessary for **development**. A: Prevents erosion, keeps fertility for future crops, protects **water** quality. Reason: **Development** must be sustainable.
chunks.source: Prevents erosion, keeps fertility for future crops, protects **water** quality. Reason: **Development** must be sustainable.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Match: **Resource** → Main **economic** use. (a) **Land** (b) **Mineral** (c) **Water** (d) **People**. A: (a) Farming/building space (b) Mining/export (c) Power/irrigation/fishing (d) Labour/skills. Reason: PLE matching questions test resource-use links.
chunks.source: (a) Farming/building space (b) Mining/export (c) Power/irrigation/fishing (d) Labour/skills. Reason: PLE matching questions test resource-use links.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: If Uganda discovers more **oil**, what **development** benefits could come? A: Revenue for roads/schools, jobs, fuel for industry, reduced imports. Reason: Apply **resource** → **development** logic to a current issue.
chunks.source: Revenue for roads/schools, jobs, fuel for industry, reduced imports. Reason: Apply **resource** → **development** logic to a current issue.

chunks.id: L-P7-Social-Country Studies: Oil, Irrigation and Mining
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: Country Studies: Oil, Irrigation and Mining
chunks.text: Country Studies: Oil, Irrigation and Mining. I can explain how Libya, Sudan, South Africa and DR Congo use their resources for economic development. **Libya** uses **oil** for **industry** and **irrigation** (Great Man-Made River). **Sudan** uses the Nile for **Gezira** **irrigation** (cotton) and **hydro-electric power**. **South Africa**'s **mining** (gold, platinum, coal) built railways and diverse **industry**. **Congo** has vast **minerals** (cobalt, copper) and **vegetation** but faces **instability**. Keywords: libya: a North African country with large oil reserves; sudan: a country in North-East Africa with the Nile river; south africa: a southern African country rich in minerals; congo: DR Congo in Central Africa with vast minerals and forests; oil: a liquid fossil fuel used for energy and products; irrigation: supplying water to crops artificially; gezira: a large irrigation scheme between the Blue and White Nile; hydro-electric power: electricity generated from moving water; mining: extracting minerals from the ground; industry: factories that process raw materials into goods
chunks.source: **Libya** uses **oil** for **industry** and **irrigation** (Great Man-Made River). **Sudan** uses the Nile for **Gezira** **irrigation** (cotton) and **hydro-electric power**. **South Africa**'s **mining** (gold, platinum, coal) built railways and diverse **industry**. **Congo** has vast **minerals** (cobalt, copper) and **vegetation** but faces **instability**.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-Country Studies: Oil, Irrigation and Mining
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: Country Studies: Oil, Irrigation and Mining
chunks.text: Q: Name the **irrigation** scheme in **Sudan** and the two rivers it lies between. A: **Gezira** scheme, between the Blue Nile and White Nile. Reason: PLE asks for specific scheme name and location.
chunks.source: **Gezira** scheme, between the Blue Nile and White Nile. Reason: PLE asks for specific scheme name and location.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-Country Studies: Oil, Irrigation and Mining
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: Country Studies: Oil, Irrigation and Mining
chunks.text: Q: State two ways **Libya** used **oil** revenue for **development**. A: 1) Built **industry** (petrochemicals). 2) Funded Great Man-Made River **irrigation**. 3) Free education/healthcare. 4) Infrastructure. Reason: Link **resource** → revenue → **development** projects.
chunks.source: 1) Built **industry** (petrochemicals). 2) Funded Great Man-Made River **irrigation**. 3) Free education/healthcare. 4) Infrastructure. Reason: Link **resource** → revenue → **development** projects.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-Country Studies: Oil, Irrigation and Mining
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: Country Studies: Oil, Irrigation and Mining
chunks.text: Q: Explain how **hydro-electric power** supports **Sudan**'s **economy**. A: Runs **industry** in Khartoum, pumps **water** for **irrigation**, provides domestic electricity. Reason: Connect **hydro-electric power** to specific **economic** activities.
chunks.source: Runs **industry** in Khartoum, pumps **water** for **irrigation**, provides domestic electricity. Reason: Connect **hydro-electric power** to specific **economic** activities.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-Country Studies: Oil, Irrigation and Mining
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: Country Studies: Oil, Irrigation and Mining
chunks.text: Q: List three **mineral** **resources** mined in **South Africa** and one use for each. A: Gold (jewellery/electronics), Platinum (catalytic converters), Coal (electricity/synthetic fuel), Diamonds (jewellery/cutting). Reason: Country-specific **mineral** knowledge with uses.
chunks.source: Gold (jewellery/electronics), Platinum (catalytic converters), Coal (electricity/synthetic fuel), Diamonds (jewellery/cutting). Reason: Country-specific **mineral** knowledge with uses.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-Country Studies: Oil, Irrigation and Mining
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: Country Studies: Oil, Irrigation and Mining
chunks.text: Q: How did **mining** lead to **industry** in **South Africa**? A: **Mining** needed railways → transport **industry**; needed steel → Iscor; needed chemicals → Sasol; needed machinery → engineering **industry**. Reason: Show the multiplier effect of **mining**.
chunks.source: **Mining** needed railways → transport **industry**; needed steel → Iscor; needed chemicals → Sasol; needed machinery → engineering **industry**. Reason: Show the multiplier effect of **mining**.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-Country Studies: Oil, Irrigation and Mining
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: Country Studies: Oil, Irrigation and Mining
chunks.text: Q: Name two **mineral** **resources** found in **Congo** (DR Congo) and their modern uses. A: Cobalt (rechargeable batteries), Copper (electrical wiring), Coltan (mobile phones), Diamonds (jewellery/industrial). Reason: **Congo**'s **minerals** are critical for global technology.
chunks.source: Cobalt (rechargeable batteries), Copper (electrical wiring), Coltan (mobile phones), Diamonds (jewellery/industrial). Reason: **Congo**'s **minerals** are critical for global technology.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-Country Studies: Oil, Irrigation and Mining
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: Country Studies: Oil, Irrigation and Mining
chunks.text: Q: Why has **Congo**'s vast **mineral** wealth not led to high **development** for its **people**? A: **Instability**, **corruption**, poor **transport**, **illiteracy**, foreign exploitation. Reason: PLE tests understanding that **resources** alone ≠ **development**.
chunks.source: **Instability**, **corruption**, poor **transport**, **illiteracy**, foreign exploitation. Reason: PLE tests understanding that **resources** alone ≠ **development**.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-Country Studies: Oil, Irrigation and Mining
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: Country Studies: Oil, Irrigation and Mining
chunks.text: Q: Compare **Libya**'s **oil** and **South Africa**'s **mining** as bases for **industry**. A: Both funded **industry** and infrastructure. **Libya**: **oil** → petrochemicals. **South Africa**: **mining** → steel, chemicals, manufacturing. **South Africa**'s **industry** is more diversified. Reason: Compare case studies.
chunks.source: Both funded **industry** and infrastructure. **Libya**: **oil** → petrochemicals. **South Africa**: **mining** → steel, chemicals, manufacturing. **South Africa**'s **industry** is more diversified. Reason: Compare case studies.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-Country Studies: Oil, Irrigation and Mining
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: Country Studies: Oil, Irrigation and Mining
chunks.text: Q: What is the Great Man-Made River and what **resource** does it move? A: A pipeline network moving fossil **water** from southern aquifers to northern farms in **Libya**. Funded by **oil** revenue. Reason: Unique **irrigation** project linked to **oil** **resource**.
chunks.source: A pipeline network moving fossil **water** from southern aquifers to northern farms in **Libya**. Funded by **oil** revenue. Reason: Unique **irrigation** project linked to **oil** **resource**.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-Country Studies: Oil, Irrigation and Mining
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: Country Studies: Oil, Irrigation and Mining
chunks.text: Q: State one **challenge** facing **Sudan**'s **hydro-electric power** projects. A: Siltation from Ethiopian highlands reduces dam capacity. Reason: Environmental **challenge** affecting **resource** use.
chunks.source: Siltation from Ethiopian highlands reduces dam capacity. Reason: Environmental **challenge** affecting **resource** use.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Challenges Slowing Africa's Development. I can identify and explain the social, economic and political challenges that slow Africa's economic development. **Challenges** slowing Africa's **development** are social (**illiteracy**, **disease**, **poverty**), economic (**unemployment**, poor **transport**, **famine**) and political (**corruption**, **instability**, **refugee** crises). They reinforce each other in vicious cycles. Breaking cycles needs targeted **solutions**. Keywords: challenge: a difficulty that must be overcome; poverty: the state of being very poor; illiteracy: inability to read and write; disease: illness that spreads or affects many people; unemployment: when people who want to work cannot find jobs; corruption: dishonest use of power for personal gain; famine: extreme shortage of food over a wide area; instability: lack of peace and steady government; refugee: a person forced to flee their home country; transport: systems for moving people and goods
chunks.source: **Challenges** slowing Africa's **development** are social (**illiteracy**, **disease**, **poverty**), economic (**unemployment**, poor **transport**, **famine**) and political (**corruption**, **instability**, **refugee** crises). They reinforce each other in vicious cycles. Breaking cycles needs targeted **solutions**.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Define **challenge** in the context of **economic** **development**. A: A difficulty that hinders growth, e.g., poor **transport**, **corruption**, **illiteracy**. Reason: Simple definition + examples.
chunks.source: A difficulty that hinders growth, e.g., poor **transport**, **corruption**, **illiteracy**. Reason: Simple definition + examples.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Explain how **illiteracy** slows **development** in Uganda. A: Low skills → low productivity → low income → cannot adopt new technology → slow **development**. Reason: Chain from **illiteracy** to **economic** outcome.
chunks.source: Low skills → low productivity → low income → cannot adopt new technology → slow **development**. Reason: Chain from **illiteracy** to **economic** outcome.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: State two ways **disease** (e.g., malaria, HIV/AIDS) reduces **economic** output. A: 1) Absenteeism from work/school. 2) Loss of skilled **people**. 3) High treatment costs divert savings. 4) Orphans strain extended families. Reason: Direct **economic** impacts.
chunks.source: 1) Absenteeism from work/school. 2) Loss of skilled **people**. 3) High treatment costs divert savings. 4) Orphans strain extended families. Reason: Direct **economic** impacts.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: How does **unemployment** among youth lead to **poverty** and **instability**? A: No income → **poverty** → frustration → crime/unrest → **instability** → scares **investment** → fewer jobs. Reason: Link **unemployment** to social **challenges**.
chunks.source: No income → **poverty** → frustration → crime/unrest → **instability** → scares **investment** → fewer jobs. Reason: Link **unemployment** to social **challenges**.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Give two effects of **corruption** on **development** projects. A: 1) Funds stolen → projects incomplete/poor quality. 2) Investors lose trust → less **investment**. 3) Services (health, education) deteriorate. Reason: **Corruption** = misallocation of **resources**.
chunks.source: 1) Funds stolen → projects incomplete/poor quality. 2) Investors lose trust → less **investment**. 3) Services (health, education) deteriorate. Reason: **Corruption** = misallocation of **resources**.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Why does **famine** still occur in parts of Africa despite fertile **land**? A: Drought + **instability** (blocks farming/aid) + poor **transport** (food can't reach) + **poverty** (no reserves) + **corruption** (aid diversion). Reason: Multiple **challenges** combine.
chunks.source: Drought + **instability** (blocks farming/aid) + poor **transport** (food can't reach) + **poverty** (no reserves) + **corruption** (aid diversion). Reason: Multiple **challenges** combine.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Explain how **instability** in a neighbouring country becomes a **challenge** for Uganda. A: **Refugee** influx strains **land**, **water**, schools, clinics, budgets. Border **trade** disrupted. Security costs rise. Reason: Regional **instability** has cross-border **economic** effects.
chunks.source: **Refugee** influx strains **land**, **water**, schools, clinics, budgets. Border **trade** disrupted. Security costs rise. Reason: Regional **instability** has cross-border **economic** effects.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Describe the link between poor **transport** and **poverty** in rural Uganda. A: High **transport** costs → expensive inputs, low farm-gate prices → low income → **poverty** → cannot improve **transport**. Reason: **Transport** as a binding constraint.
chunks.source: High **transport** costs → expensive inputs, low farm-gate prices → low income → **poverty** → cannot improve **transport**. Reason: **Transport** as a binding constraint.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Name one **challenge** that is BOTH a cause and a result of slow **development**. A: **Poverty** (also **illiteracy**, **disease**). Reason: Cyclical relationship — key PLE concept.
chunks.source: **Poverty** (also **illiteracy**, **disease**). Reason: Cyclical relationship — key PLE concept.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: How does hosting **refugees** create both **challenges** and **opportunities** for Uganda? A: Challenges: pressure on **resources**, services. Opportunities: **refugees** bring **skills**, labour, **trade**, aid **investment** (roads, schools in settlements). Reason: Balanced view — PLE values nuance.
chunks.source: Challenges: pressure on **resources**, services. Opportunities: **refugees** bring **skills**, labour, **trade**, aid **investment** (roads, schools in settlements). Reason: Balanced view — PLE values nuance.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Building a Better African Economy. I can propose solutions to Africa's development challenges and explain how technology, skills and planning improve economies. **Solutions** to Africa's **challenges** require **plan**, **investment**, **technology**, **skill**, **trade** and good governance. **Technology** (mobile, digital, green) leapfrogs old **development** stages. **Skill** training turns **people** into the ultimate **resource**. Regional **trade** (EAC) expands **economy**. The **future** depends on implementing **solutions** now. Keywords: solution: a way to solve a problem; technology: tools and methods that make work easier; skill: an ability learned through practice; plan: a detailed proposal for achieving something; project: a planned piece of work with a goal; investment: putting money into something for future profit; trade: buying and selling goods and services; improvement: making something better than before; economy: the system of production, trade and money in a country; future: the time that is yet to come
chunks.source: **Solutions** to Africa's **challenges** require **plan**, **investment**, **technology**, **skill**, **trade** and good governance. **Technology** (mobile, digital, green) leapfrogs old **development** stages. **Skill** training turns **people** into the ultimate **resource**. Regional **trade** (EAC) expands **economy**. The **future** depends on implementing **solutions** now.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Define **solution** in the context of **economic** **development**. A: A practical action that addresses a **challenge** and leads to measurable **improvement** (e.g., **irrigation** solves drought). Reason: Clear definition + example.
chunks.source: A practical action that addresses a **challenge** and leads to measurable **improvement** (e.g., **irrigation** solves drought). Reason: Clear definition + example.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: State two ways **technology** improves farming **development** in Uganda. A: 1) Mobile market prices → better income. 2) Weather alerts → planting decisions. 3) Mobile money → access to credit. 4) Drip **irrigation** → water efficiency. Reason: Specific **technology** → **economic** benefit.
chunks.source: 1) Mobile market prices → better income. 2) Weather alerts → planting decisions. 3) Mobile money → access to credit. 4) Drip **irrigation** → water efficiency. Reason: Specific **technology** → **economic** benefit.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Explain how **skill** training reduces **unemployment** among youth. A: Matches youth **skills** to **economy** needs (construction, ICT, agro-processing) → employability or self-employment. Reason: Link **skill** supply to **economic** demand.
chunks.source: Matches youth **skills** to **economy** needs (construction, ICT, agro-processing) → employability or self-employment. Reason: Link **skill** supply to **economic** demand.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Give one example of a **plan** and one **project** in Uganda's current **development** strategy. A: **Plan**: NDP III / Vision 2040 / Parish Development Model. **Project**: Karuma Dam / SGR / Industrial parks / **Irrigation** schemes. Reason: Distinguish **plan** (strategy) from **project** (implementation).
chunks.source: **Plan**: NDP III / Vision 2040 / Parish Development Model. **Project**: Karuma Dam / SGR / Industrial parks / **Irrigation** schemes. Reason: Distinguish **plan** (strategy) from **project** (implementation).

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: How does **investment** in **transport** **improvement** boost **trade**? A: Lower **transport** costs → cheaper goods, wider markets, more **investment**, job creation. Reason: **Transport** as enabler of **trade** and **development**.
chunks.source: Lower **transport** costs → cheaper goods, wider markets, more **investment**, job creation. Reason: **Transport** as enabler of **trade** and **development**.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Why is regional **trade** (EAC) a **solution** to small national markets? A: Combines 300M+ **people** → economies of scale, attracts **investment**, diversifies **economy**. Reason: **Trade** expands **economic** space beyond borders.
chunks.source: Combines 300M+ **people** → economies of scale, attracts **investment**, diversifies **economy**. Reason: **Trade** expands **economic** space beyond borders.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Describe how **technology** can reduce **corruption** in **development** **projects**. A: E-procurement (open bidding), digital payment trails, project tracking portals, whistleblower apps. Reason: **Technology** increases transparency and accountability.
chunks.source: E-procurement (open bidding), digital payment trails, project tracking portals, whistleblower apps. Reason: **Technology** increases transparency and accountability.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: State two **solutions** to **famine** in drought-prone areas like Karamoja. A: 1) **Irrigation** **projects** (valley tanks, boreholes). 2) Drought-resistant crops (sorghum, millet). 3) Early warning **technology**. 4) Strategic grain reserves. 5) **Trade** corridors for food movement. Reason: Multiple **solutions** for complex **challenge**.
chunks.source: 1) **Irrigation** **projects** (valley tanks, boreholes). 2) Drought-resistant crops (sorghum, millet). 3) Early warning **technology**. 4) Strategic grain reserves. 5) **Trade** corridors for food movement. Reason: Multiple **solutions** for complex **challenge**.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: How does **investment** in **skill** and **technology** secure Africa's **future** **economy**? A: Creates adaptable workforce for 4th Industrial Revolution, enables value addition, attracts high-value **investment**, reduces **unemployment**. Reason: Human capital + **technology** = long-term **development**.
chunks.source: Creates adaptable workforce for 4th Industrial Revolution, enables value addition, attracts high-value **investment**, reduces **unemployment**. Reason: Human capital + **technology** = long-term **development**.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Propose a **solution** for high **unemployment** in your district using **plan**, **project**, **investment**, **skill**. A: District **plan** identifies local **resources** (e.g., cassava) → **project** (cassava processing factory) → **investment** (government + private) → **skill** training (machine operation, quality control) → jobs + **trade**. Reason: Integrated **solution** framework.
chunks.source: District **plan** identifies local **resources** (e.g., cassava) → **project** (cassava processing factory) → **investment** (government + private) → **skill** training (machine operation, quality control) → jobs + **trade**. Reason: Integrated **solution** framework.

chunks.id: L-P7-Social-Why the United Nations Was Formed
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: Why the United Nations Was Formed
chunks.text: Why the United Nations Was Formed. I can explain how the two world wars led to the formation of the United Nations, its objectives, organs and importance. The United Nations was formed in 1945 after two world wars to promote peace, security and cooperation. It has 193 member states and six main organs. Uganda joined in 1962. Keywords: united nations: an organisation of countries working together for peace; world war: a large war involving many countries across the world; peace: a state without war or fighting; member: a country that belongs to an organisation; objective: a goal or aim; organ: a main part of an organisation that does specific work; cooperation: working together for a common purpose; unity: being united as one; formation: the act of creating or starting something; security: safety from danger or threat
chunks.source: The United Nations was formed in 1945 after two world wars to promote peace, security and cooperation. It has 193 member states and six main organs. Uganda joined in 1962.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-Why the United Nations Was Formed
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: Why the United Nations Was Formed
chunks.text: Q: In which year was the United Nations officially formed? A: 1945 — The UN Charter came into force on 24 October 1945.
chunks.source: 1945 — The UN Charter came into force on 24 October 1945.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-Why the United Nations Was Formed
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: Why the United Nations Was Formed
chunks.text: Q: Name the organ of the UN that has the power to authorise military action. A: The Security Council — It is the only organ with enforcement power under Chapter VII of the Charter.
chunks.source: The Security Council — It is the only organ with enforcement power under Chapter VII of the Charter.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-Why the United Nations Was Formed
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: Why the United Nations Was Formed
chunks.text: Q: How many founding members did the UN have? A: Fifty-one — They signed the Charter in San Francisco in 1945.
chunks.source: Fifty-one — They signed the Charter in San Francisco in 1945.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-Why the United Nations Was Formed
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: Why the United Nations Was Formed
chunks.text: Q: Give two objectives of the United Nations. A: 1) Maintain international peace and security. 2) Develop friendly relations among nations. (Also: achieve international cooperation; be a centre for harmonising actions.)
chunks.source: 1) Maintain international peace and security. 2) Develop friendly relations among nations. (Also: achieve international cooperation; be a centre for harmonising actions.)

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-Why the United Nations Was Formed
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: Why the United Nations Was Formed
chunks.text: Q: When did Uganda become a member of the UN? A: 25 October 1962 — Soon after independence on 9 October 1962.
chunks.source: 25 October 1962 — Soon after independence on 9 October 1962.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-Why the United Nations Was Formed
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: Why the United Nations Was Formed
chunks.text: Q: Which organ of the UN is composed of all member states? A: The General Assembly — Every member state has one vote here.
chunks.source: The General Assembly — Every member state has one vote here.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-Why the United Nations Was Formed
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: Why the United Nations Was Formed
chunks.text: Q: What was the name of the organisation that existed before the UN? A: The League of Nations — Formed in 1919 after the First World War.
chunks.source: The League of Nations — Formed in 1919 after the First World War.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-Why the United Nations Was Formed
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: Why the United Nations Was Formed
chunks.text: Q: Why did the League of Nations fail? A: It had no army and powerful countries ignored its decisions — This led to the Second World War.
chunks.source: It had no army and powerful countries ignored its decisions — This led to the Second World War.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-Why the United Nations Was Formed
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: Why the United Nations Was Formed
chunks.text: Q: Name the current Secretary-General of the UN (as of 2024). A: António Guterres — He has served since 2017. (Check current name if exam year differs.)
chunks.source: António Guterres — He has served since 2017. (Check current name if exam year differs.)

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-Why the United Nations Was Formed
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: Why the United Nations Was Formed
chunks.text: Q: What does the veto power in the Security Council mean? A: A permanent member can block a resolution — The 5 permanent members (USA, Russia, China, UK, France) each have this power.
chunks.source: A permanent member can block a resolution — The 5 permanent members (USA, Russia, China, UK, France) each have this power.

chunks.id: L-P7-Social-The Agencies of the United Nations
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: The Agencies of the United Nations
chunks.text: The Agencies of the United Nations. I can name the major UN agencies and explain their functions in Uganda and the world. The UN works through specialised agencies: UNICEF (children), WHO (health), UNESCO (education/culture), FAO (food/agriculture), UNHCR (refugees), UNDP (development). Each has a clear mandate and works in Uganda. Keywords: agency: a specialised organisation that does specific work for the UN; unicef: United Nations Children's Fund — helps children worldwide; unesco: United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organisation; who: World Health Organisation — deals with global health issues; fao: Food and Agriculture Organisation — works on food security; unhcr: United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees — protects refugees; undp: United Nations Development Programme — fights poverty; children: young human beings below the age of 18; health: the state of being well in body and mind; education: the process of teaching and learning
chunks.source: The UN works through specialised agencies: UNICEF (children), WHO (health), UNESCO (education/culture), FAO (food/agriculture), UNHCR (refugees), UNDP (development). Each has a clear mandate and works in Uganda.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-The Agencies of the United Nations
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: The Agencies of the United Nations
chunks.text: Q: Write the full name of UNICEF. A: United Nations Children's Fund — Originally United Nations International Children's Emergency Fund.
chunks.source: United Nations Children's Fund — Originally United Nations International Children's Emergency Fund.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-The Agencies of the United Nations
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: The Agencies of the United Nations
chunks.text: Q: Which UN agency is responsible for coordinating international health work? A: WHO (World Health Organisation) — Established in 1948, headquarters in Geneva.
chunks.source: WHO (World Health Organisation) — Established in 1948, headquarters in Geneva.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-The Agencies of the United Nations
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: The Agencies of the United Nations
chunks.text: Q: What does FAO stand for? A: Food and Agriculture Organisation — Works on food security, agriculture, fisheries, forestry.
chunks.source: Food and Agriculture Organisation — Works on food security, agriculture, fisheries, forestry.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-The Agencies of the United Nations
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: The Agencies of the United Nations
chunks.text: Q: Name the UN agency that protects refugees. A: UNHCR (United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees) — Mandate from 1951 Refugee Convention.
chunks.source: UNHCR (United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees) — Mandate from 1951 Refugee Convention.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-The Agencies of the United Nations
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: The Agencies of the United Nations
chunks.text: Q: Which agency promotes education, science and culture? A: UNESCO (United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organisation) — Also designates World Heritage Sites.
chunks.source: UNESCO (United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organisation) — Also designates World Heritage Sites.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-The Agencies of the United Nations
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: The Agencies of the United Nations
chunks.text: Q: What is the main work of UNDP? A: Eradicate poverty and reduce inequality through sustainable development — Works in ~170 countries.
chunks.source: Eradicate poverty and reduce inequality through sustainable development — Works in ~170 countries.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-The Agencies of the United Nations
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: The Agencies of the United Nations
chunks.text: Q: Uganda hosts the largest refugee population in Africa. Which agency leads the refugee response? A: UNHCR — Works with Uganda's Office of the Prime Minister (OPM).
chunks.source: UNHCR — Works with Uganda's Office of the Prime Minister (OPM).

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-The Agencies of the United Nations
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: The Agencies of the United Nations
chunks.text: Q: A child in a Ugandan village receives a polio vaccine. Which two UN agencies are most involved? A: UNICEF (procures/delivers vaccines) and WHO (sets policy/guidelines) — They partner on immunisation.
chunks.source: UNICEF (procures/delivers vaccines) and WHO (sets policy/guidelines) — They partner on immunisation.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-The Agencies of the United Nations
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: The Agencies of the United Nations
chunks.text: Q: The Kasubi Tombs and Bwindi Forest are World Heritage Sites. Which agency designates them? A: UNESCO — It maintains the World Heritage List under the 1972 Convention.
chunks.source: UNESCO — It maintains the World Heritage List under the 1972 Convention.

chunks.id: LQ-P7-Social-The Agencies of the United Nations
chunks.subject: Social
chunks.unit: The Agencies of the United Nations
chunks.text: Q: Which agency helps Ugandan farmers with improved seeds and animal vaccines? A: FAO — Food and Agriculture Organisation, works with Ministry of Agriculture.
chunks.source: FAO — Food and Agriculture Organisation, works with Ministry of Agriculture.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Human Rights for Every Person. I can explain human rights in the UN Charter and Universal Declaration, how rights are violated, and how they should be respected. Human rights are universal, inalienable, and indivisible. The UDHR (10 Dec 1948) and Uganda Constitution Chapter 4 guarantee them. Violations include child labour, torture, discrimination. Respect rights — know them, defend them, live them. Keywords: human rights: basic rights and freedoms that belong to every person; charter: a written document that sets out the rules and purposes of an organisation; declaration: a formal public statement; freedom: the right to act, speak, or think without unfair control; equality: the state of being equal in status, rights, and opportunities; dignity: the quality of being worthy of respect; life: the right to live and not be killed; liberty: freedom from arbitrary arrest or detention; torture: causing severe pain or suffering on purpose; respect: treating someone with consideration and honour
chunks.source: Human rights are universal, inalienable, and indivisible. The UDHR (10 Dec 1948) and Uganda Constitution Chapter 4 guarantee them. Violations include child labour, torture, discrimination. Respect rights — know them, defend them, live them.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: When was the Universal Declaration of Human Rights adopted? A: 10 December 1948 — Exact date required by PLE.
chunks.source: 10 December 1948 — Exact date required by PLE.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Name the UN document that first mentioned human rights. A: The UN Charter (1945) — Preamble and Articles 1, 55, 56.
chunks.source: The UN Charter (1945) — Preamble and Articles 1, 55, 56.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: List three civil and political rights from the Declaration. A: Right to life, liberty, freedom of speech, freedom of religion, fair trial, freedom from torture, freedom from slavery.
chunks.source: Right to life, liberty, freedom of speech, freedom of religion, fair trial, freedom from torture, freedom from slavery.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: List three economic, social and cultural rights. A: Right to work, education, health, housing, food, social security, cultural participation.
chunks.source: Right to work, education, health, housing, food, social security, cultural participation.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Which article of the Uganda Constitution guarantees equality before the law? A: Article 21 — 'All persons are equal before and under the law.'
chunks.source: Article 21 — 'All persons are equal before and under the law.'

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: What does Article 24 of the Uganda Constitution prohibit? A: Torture and cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment.
chunks.source: Torture and cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Name the body in Uganda that monitors human rights. A: Uganda Human Rights Commission (UHRC) — Established under Article 51 of the Constitution.
chunks.source: Uganda Human Rights Commission (UHRC) — Established under Article 51 of the Constitution.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Give two examples of human rights violations in Uganda. A: Child labour, early marriage, domestic violence, police brutality, unlawful detention, discrimination against PWDs.
chunks.source: Child labour, early marriage, domestic violence, police brutality, unlawful detention, discrimination against PWDs.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: What is the difference between the UDHR and the Uganda Constitution Chapter 4? A: UDHR is a UN declaration (1948), not legally binding. Chapter 4 is part of Uganda's supreme law, legally enforceable in Ugandan courts.
chunks.source: UDHR is a UN declaration (1948), not legally binding. Chapter 4 is part of Uganda's supreme law, legally enforceable in Ugandan courts.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: How can a P.7 pupil promote human rights at school? A: Respect classmates, report bullying, share knowledge of rights, participate in child rights clubs, treat everyone equally.
chunks.source: Respect classmates, report bullying, share knowledge of rights, participate in child rights clubs, treat everyone equally.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: The Commonwealth of Nations. I can explain the Commonwealth of Nations, its membership and functions, and compare it with the United Nations. The Commonwealth is a voluntary association of 56 independent countries, mostly former British territories. It promotes democracy, trade, development, and the Commonwealth Games. Unlike the UN, it has no enforcement power but works by consensus and shared values. Uganda has been a member since 1962. Keywords: commonwealth: a voluntary association of 56 independent countries; membership: the state of being a member of an organisation; function: the purpose or role of something; assistance: help or support given to someone; games: a multi-sport event held every four years; trade: buying and selling of goods and services; compare: to examine similarities and differences; support: to help or encourage; country: a nation with its own government; meeting: a gathering of people for discussion
chunks.source: The Commonwealth is a voluntary association of 56 independent countries, mostly former British territories. It promotes democracy, trade, development, and the Commonwealth Games. Unlike the UN, it has no enforcement power but works by consensus and shared values. Uganda has been a member since 1962.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: How many member countries are in the Commonwealth of Nations? A: 56 — As of 2024 (Gabon and Togo joined 2022).
chunks.source: 56 — As of 2024 (Gabon and Togo joined 2022).

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Who is the Head of the Commonwealth? A: King Charles III — Since September 2022. Symbolic role, not political.
chunks.source: King Charles III — Since September 2022. Symbolic role, not political.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: When did Uganda host the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM)? A: November 2007 in Kampala — Major diplomatic event for Uganda.
chunks.source: November 2007 in Kampala — Major diplomatic event for Uganda.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Name two countries that joined the Commonwealth without a British colonial past. A: Mozambique (1995) and Rwanda (2009) — Also Gabon and Togo (2022).
chunks.source: Mozambique (1995) and Rwanda (2009) — Also Gabon and Togo (2022).

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: What is the main function of the Commonwealth Fund for Technical Cooperation (CFTC)? A: Provide technical experts, training, and advisory services to member countries — Not direct cash grants.
chunks.source: Provide technical experts, training, and advisory services to member countries — Not direct cash grants.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Give two differences between the UN and the Commonwealth. A: 1) UN: 193 members, universal. Commonwealth: 56, mostly former British. 2) UN has Security Council with enforcement power. Commonwealth has no enforcement. 3) UN focuses on security; Commonwealth on trade, democracy, culture.
chunks.source: 1) UN: 193 members, universal. Commonwealth: 56, mostly former British. 2) UN has Security Council with enforcement power. Commonwealth has no enforcement. 3) UN focuses on security; Commonwealth on trade, democracy, culture.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Which Ugandan won a gold medal at the 2022 Commonwealth Games in Birmingham? A: Jacob Kiplimo (10,000m) or Victor Kiplangat (Marathon) — Check current medallists. Any correct Ugandan gold medallist accepted.
chunks.source: Jacob Kiplimo (10,000m) or Victor Kiplangat (Marathon) — Check current medallists. Any correct Ugandan gold medallist accepted.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: What are the core values required for Commonwealth membership? A: Democracy, human rights, rule of law, good governance — Set in the 2009 Trinidad Declaration.
chunks.source: Democracy, human rights, rule of law, good governance — Set in the 2009 Trinidad Declaration.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: How does the Commonwealth support Uganda's education sector? A: Commonwealth Scholarships for postgraduate study in UK, teacher training programmes, education policy sharing.
chunks.source: Commonwealth Scholarships for postgraduate study in UK, teacher training programmes, education policy sharing.

chunks.subject: Social
chunks.text: Q: Why is the Commonwealth described as a 'voluntary association'? A: Countries choose to join and can leave anytime — No legal obligation to stay. Membership is by consensus of existing members.
chunks.source: Countries choose to join and can leave anytime — No legal obligation to stay. Membership is by consensus of existing members.
